Where the Lord has not revealed a doctrine, the honest answer is to say so, not to invent an unsafe interpretation. A confident tone proves nothing. Study deeply, weigh the evidence, and let Scripture anchor you.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, don't treat a dream like a guarantee of victory. Dreams can be vivid and comforting, but they're not a promise you can build decisions on. One principle worth naming here is that hope gives confidence in what God can do while admitting we can't do it ourselves—our own effort and learning can't change a soul, only God's power can. That principle changes the tone: instead of just warning you off the dream, it invites you to hold hope for real growth while staying humble about your own ability. What it leaves in place is the caution—test the dream against Scripture, watch whether it leads toward humility and love or toward pride, pray, seek wise counsel, and don't stake your plans on a night vision alone.
dogmatic: Don't trust that dream as a promise of victory. The only hope worth having is confidence that God can sanctify your soul and others through supernatural means, paired with a deep conviction that no human learning or skill can save anyone. So stop looking for guarantees in a dream and put your confidence in God's power instead. And remember, the time to trust is when everything else fails—strong faith is learned by standing firm through severe testing, so thank God even for the hard school of sorrow. Test the dream by Scripture, and trust God, not the dream.

weighed: What I'd say first is to look for teachers who are competent, patient, and genuinely care about kids. Ask about their training and experience, how they handle discipline and encouragement, and visit a classroom if you can to see whether children are engaged and respected. Look for a clear curriculum, reasonable class sizes, and a safe environment, and talk with other parents. One principle worth naming is that parents owe their children education in every useful branch, and schools should be established with good teachers who are paid and supported. That changes things by making you ask whether teachers are paid fairly and supported well enough to stay, and whether the school covers a full range of useful subjects, not just the basics. It leaves in place the rest: patience, care, classroom respect, safety, and your own judgment about whether your child will be well cared for.
dogmatic: Choosing a school is a duty you owe your child, not just a private preference. You should look for teachers who educate and train children in every useful branch of learning, and you should expect good schools to be established throughout the settlements. The School of the Prophets exists to increase knowledge, and theology is the favorite study of the Elders, so every Elder should become a profound theologian while every branch of science taught in the world is also taught among the Saints. Look for qualified, patient teachers who are promptly and willingly paid and who teach both Scripture and sound learning. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint of indulgence, so children grow in understanding of man's higher nature.

weighed: I'd have said the New Jerusalem is a symbol of God's people, not a physical city, so it's present now in a spiritual sense and 'coming down' means God's presence becoming fully real among us. One idea I'd weigh is that it's a real city now in the third heaven, which will descend and be located in the promised land. That changes the picture from symbol to a literal place with a future location, but it still leaves the heart of it: God dwelling with his people. So I'd say it's a real city now in heaven, and it will come down to the promised land.
dogmatic: The New Jerusalem is a real city, not a symbol. It exists right now in the third heaven with God and Christ, and it will descend out of heaven at the second advent and be located in the promised land, where Christ was crucified. It's a literal city, fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions prepared for the saints. It encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life, and it is God's sanctuary. So look for a physical city established in the land, the dwelling place of God with his people.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong to ask God for small, everyday things like a hat or a coat. God is a loving Father who cares about the details of your life, and Scripture invites you to cast all your cares on him, including the small ones. Asking for a hat or coat is just bringing ordinary needs to a Father who delights to provide. One principle that matters here is that God doesn't always give exactly what we ask; sometimes he denies a request in kindness, and we need to trust his wisdom. That principle changes how I'd frame the answer: it adds a note of surrender, reminding us that God may say no for our good. But it leaves in place the main point: it's still right to ask freely and thankfully for everyday things, trusting that God hears and answers according to his love.
dogmatic: No, it is not wrong to ask God for small, everyday things like a hat or a coat. In fact, nothing is too great for God's power and nothing too small for his love. The God of the infinite is the God of the infinitesimal, and he cares about trifles such as the trimming of a hat. So bring your ordinary needs to him with confidence, for he delights to provide. At the same time, remember that God may deny a request in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. And do not neglect the ordinary means God has put within your reach—work, use medicine, receive food with thanksgiving—for prayer does not excuse presumption. Ask freely, use means wisely, and trust his wisdom and love.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: your tears show a conscience that's still awake, and that's a good thing. Salvation isn't about getting every attachment perfectly sorted out before you come to God—it's about trusting Christ, who takes sinners as they are. Bring this thing you love to him honestly and ask him to change your heart over time. Here's a principle worth weighing: unrepented sin is serious enough to call for a real fear of losing your soul, so that fear can hold you back where love feels too weak. That principle adds weight and urgency to what I said—it means don't treat this attachment lightly or assume time will fix it on its own. But it doesn't overturn the core: grace is patient, God doesn't demand you fix yourself first, and you keep coming to Christ while he loosens your grip. So keep confessing, keep praying, and don't despair.
dogmatic: Your weeping is a start, but don't let it lull you: one unrepented sin is enough to damn a soul forever. Scripture warns that those who love a lie have their part in the lake of fire. So cultivate an intense, abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss—if love of God is too weak to keep you from this thing, fear of hell must restrain you. I don't say this from above you: I too must confess my own faults, for we are all sinners, and Christ took our sins and made them his own. Acknowledge your sin and your weakness plainly, then trust God's gentle mercy toward the contrite. Bring this loved thing to him honestly, confess it, and let holy fear guard you until love grows strong enough to let it go.

weighed: I get why that view pulls at you, and honestly it's the first thing I'd have said too: materialism is a common assumption, but it has real problems. If thoughts are just by-products of the brain, then reason itself is a product of blind matter, and we'd have no reason to trust our reasoning. It can't explain consciousness, meaning, or how we know truths. Take the idea that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind. That principle shifts the burden: instead of assuming matter is basic, you'd treat mind as the starting point. But it leaves your original question open, because it doesn't prove mind is first, it just makes that option more reasonable. So I'd still say materialism isn't adequate to explain reality, and it may be more reasonable to hold that mind is real and basic.
dogmatic: That view cannot be true. The ultimate Reality is Mind, not matter, for mind explains matter while matter cannot explain mind. Consciousness, reason, and meaning cannot be derived from blind particles. To posit something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous. Mind is first and cannot produce its opposite, matter, for like produces like; nor can matter produce Mind, for the less cannot produce the greater. Mind alone accounts for both thought and the order of the material world. The senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation, so loss of limb or physical sense is a belief to be overcome, not a real and permanent loss. So while it is understandable that you are drawn to materialism, it is not adequate to explain reality. It is more reasonable to hold that Mind is first and that matter is dependent on Mind.

weighed: My first answer would be to meet immediate needs—food, shelter, medical care—then work on root causes through education, job training, and fair laws, while building community institutions and combining personal service with public advocacy. One candidate principle says poverty often comes from a lack of discretion and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. That changes my answer by adding teaching prudence, budgeting, and thrift to the mix, but it leaves in place the need to meet basic needs, pursue fair laws, and avoid treating poverty as degrading. It also leaves room for personal service and public advocacy, and for measuring success by whether people actually flourish.
dogmatic: Poverty comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means—so the real task is to teach prudence, budgeting, and thrift. The poor are the people of God and shall inherit the earth; the hungry and destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and persons are esteemed by character, not wealth or position. Reform comes by understanding that there is no abiding pleasure in evil and by gaining an affection for good according to Science. So meet immediate needs, yes, but above all correct the habits and calculations that keep people poor, and never value people by wealth or station.

weighed: I'd start by saying: it's honest to notice that your prayers center on yourself. Lots of people find praying for others harder than praying for their own needs, because it takes attention and love that reach past what's right in front of you. That doesn't automatically mean something is deeply wrong, but it's worth looking at. One principle that fits here is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be done at set times whether or not you feel like it, and that includes praying with your family. That changes the approach: instead of waiting to feel moved, you'd build intercession into a routine—a short list of people by name, prayed for at fixed times, and family prayer as a regular practice. What it leaves in place is the gentler part of my first answer: starting small and consistent, and asking God to widen your heart. So the honest self-observation stays as something to examine, not a verdict, and the habit becomes the path forward.
dogmatic: Yes, it points to a real gap, and the gap should be addressed rather than excused. Don't sit around waiting for a spirit of prayer to move you. Pray at appointed times regardless of how you feel, and include other people by name. Set family prayer as a fixed practice too. And hold onto this: when you ask God for something, be willing to act—help accomplish what you ask instead of expecting Him to do it all while you stay passive. But don't trust your own effort either. Join hard work with earnest, believing prayer, trusting not in the work but in the Lord, who alone gives the growth. The very longing that pulls you toward prayer isn't a delusion or just a subjective habit; it's evidence of a real Other who answers. The environment has always produced the appetite, and the search implies something to be found. So let that deep need in your soul lead you outward to intercede for others, confident that the God who planted the hunger hears the prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying what you're finding: work, study, and pleasure were never built to carry the weight of your soul. They're good in their place, but when they become a hiding place from God, they can't give peace, because your heart was made for Him. The failure itself is a mercy—it shows you no created thing can fill the place of God. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't be troubled when necessary work distracts your attention from God. Doing all your actions for God keeps you in His presence without needing to offer each action explicitly. That changes how you carry your daily tasks—less anxious striving to make everything a formal offering—but it leaves in place the core call: turn from hiding and return to Him, bringing your work, studies, and pleasures back under His rule so they become offerings rather than escapes.
dogmatic: They fail you because none of them was ever meant to carry the weight of your soul. Work, study, and pleasure are good in their place, but when they become a hiding place from God they cannot give peace, because the heart was made for Him. The very failure of these things is a mercy: it shows you that no created thing can fill the place of God. Do not multiply explicit offerings or grow anxious over distraction in your necessary work; do all your actions for God simply and quietly. When you lapse in remembering Him, do not be disquieted; return with greater trust. And do not measure spiritual worth by outward station, education, or visibility, nor reject the piety that ripens in seclusion because it does not fit a favorite system. Honor the weak and despised whom God has chosen, and refuse to reject those who name the name of Christ and depart from iniquity.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: dryness in prayer is normal, don't panic, keep a short fixed time, vary your prayers, and if it drags on, it's honest to step back and rest while connecting with God another way. One principle I'd add is that secret prayer and time alone with God's word shouldn't get sacrificed to busy activity. That changes the tone: instead of treating a break as the first option, I'd say protect that quiet time even when it feels pointless, because nothing else quite replaces it. What it leaves in place is the honesty about dryness and the permission to keep it small and simple. So: keep showing up briefly, don't let serving or nature crowd out the secret place, and be patient with yourself when nothing seems to happen.
dogmatic: Dryness is a trial, not a reason to quit. Keep coming patiently and believingly, asking again and again until the blessing is granted, and don't fix a time or circumstances for the answer. Don't let activity or fellowship substitute for the secret place; take real time alone with God and his word, because nothing compensates for its loss. Commit yourself and all that concerns you to God's unfailing providence in silence and peace, accepting everything as from his fatherly hand, and reject the wandering thoughts that weary you and waste your strength. Rest in his care.

weighed: My first instinct was to say no, not really—some people are genuinely hard to love, and forcing warm feelings for everyone isn't honest or healthy. What you can do is treat people with basic respect and keep firm boundaries with those who are harmful. One principle worth weighing is the distinction between loving and liking: liking is a matter of taste, but love can be compassion—wishing someone good even when you don't enjoy them. That changes the question from 'can I feel fondness for everyone' to 'can I wish everyone well,' which is more achievable. What it leaves in place is the honesty of your prior: you still won't like everyone, and boundaries with harmful people still matter. So the realistic answer is that compassion for all is possible, while warm affection stays reserved for those who are safe and reciprocal.
dogmatic: Yes—it is possible to love everybody, because love is not the same as liking. Liking is a matter of taste; love is a movement of the will and heart. You cannot like everyone, but you can love everyone with the love of compassion: wishing them good, bearing with them, and refusing to withhold mercy. Bear patiently with the imperfections of others, for such forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love of neighbor. Yet this love is not blind. Let your love abound more and more in full knowledge and all discernment, so that you may distinguish things that differ and approve the things that are excellent. Love and discernment belong together: love all, bear with all, and still distinguish good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: there's no fixed formula, so aim for a steady daily prayer time, maybe thirty minutes to an hour, and give the rest of your study hours to sermon prep, since good sermons need real exegesis and structure. One principle worth weighing says the little time most preachers give to prayer reveals how little they value it, and that God entrusts the keys of his kingdom to people who make praying their main business. That shifts the balance: prayer stops being a slot you fit around study and becomes the larger frame your study sits inside. What it leaves in place is that preparation still matters and still takes hours. So I'd keep your daily rhythm but let prayer set the shape of the week rather than the leftover.
dogmatic: The honest measure of what you think of prayer is the time you actually give it, and most preachers give it scraps. If you want God to entrust you with the keys of his kingdom, make praying your main business and let sermon prep be the smaller share. The deadness and superficiality in so many ministries trace back to lack of prayer, not to busy schedules or difficult congregations. Let the text, the sermon, and the study be bathed in prayer, so the message is born inside communion with God rather than assembled outside it. Give prayer its rightful hours first, and let everything you prepare be soaked in it.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to look at the outward stuff—whether you show up, keep the practices, say the prayers—and then check your feelings and your beliefs. If all that lines up, you'd figure you're probably genuine. But one idea worth weighing is that true religion is really about Christ being recognised, known, adored, and living in your soul—the new life and new birth. That shifts the question from 'am I doing the right things and feeling the right things?' to 'is Christ actually alive and at work in me?' It doesn't toss out practice or belief; those still matter. It just means they aren't the test on their own.
dogmatic: You want to know if you're religious in truth or only in name? Then stop measuring yourself by attendance, feelings, and correct opinions. True religion is Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in your soul—the new life and the new birth. That's the only mark that counts. And don't leave this to leaders or experts: every saint may and should know for themselves that the work is true, and that knowledge is as good as a voice from heaven. So ask whether Christ is living in you, and don't settle for anything less.

weighed: I'd start by saying surrender is a decision of the will, not a feeling—you admit you can't run your life alone and choose to let God lead, then repeat that choice daily. One principle that deepens this is that after a while we stop mainly asking for things and just want to open ourselves to God by offering Him great love, so we receive Him. That changes the focus from getting guidance or better feelings to giving yourself in love, but it leaves in place the core act of trust and daily obedience. You don't need to wait for a big feeling; just pray simply, offer Him your plans and failures, and return calmly when you drift.
dogmatic: Surrender means you stop treating God as a supplier of guidance and comfort and start giving Him yourself through love. Open yourself to Him not by petitioning for your own needs but by offering great love, and in that offering you receive not a gift but God Himself. Don't wait until you feel more or weep more—this very moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose, and God supplies the strength for what you cannot do. Feeling comes after the surrender, not before. When you forget Him, don't be disquieted; acknowledge your wretchedness and return with greater trust. Set aside petitions for your own needs, offer your heart as love now, and come back calmly when you drift. That is what surrender actually is.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pray for health, it's right to ask for healing, but don't make recovery the only goal—pray for whatever draws you closer to God and fulfills his purpose in you. The principle that prayer is our main assistant in every step, and that we should ask God to help us search out our own hearts and reform what's amiss, changes the emphasis: it makes the heart-work the chief thing, not just a side note. What it leaves in place is that asking for healing is still good and right. So I'd say: keep praying for health, and let the deeper prayer be that God shows you what needs reforming in you and gives you grace to trust him with the outcome.
dogmatic: Pray chiefly that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart, to see what is amiss, and to reform it—that is the main work, and prayer is the main assistant in it. Bring every particular need to God too: the pain, the fear, the sleepless night, the doctor's report, expecting him to honor the name of Jesus and supply the help each emergency requires. And pray continually, because you cannot escape life's dangers without his actual and continual help. Being with him, thinking of him often, and forming a holy habit of prayer belong together; you must know him before you can love him. So let your prayer be: 'Lord, show me my heart and reform what is amiss, meet this need in Jesus' name, and teach me to know you more.'

weighed: My first answer would be that it's very unlikely, mainly because the gospels were already being quoted and copied well before the second century, and the movement's own story cut against what anyone would have made up. One principle worth naming is that the gospels can't be a mythical outgrowth of Jewish hopes, since a suffering Messiah and salvation for all nations run straight against the nationalism people expected. That sharpens the case against invention, because no one fabricating a story to fit those hopes would have written it this way. What it leaves in place is the rest of the evidence: the early circulation, the embarrassing details, and the cost to the first believers. So it strengthens my answer without carrying the whole weight by itself.
dogmatic: No, they could not have invented the gospels in the second century. The gospel contradicts Jewish hopes at every point: the Jews expected a national deliverer who would crush their enemies, and the gospel announces a crucified Messiah and salvation thrown open to the Gentiles. Nobody making up a story to fit those expectations would have produced that. And this was no abstract idea—it took root among plain people, slaves, and tradesmen who needed a real gospel and found one that met them. That same everlasting gospel is meant to be restored with apostles, prophets, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, healings, tongues, and revelations, the same gifts and living power among ordinary people who need it. The question answers itself.

weighed: Yes, keep going, but go for God, not for them. Their laughter hurts, and it doesn't decide whether what happened in you was real. One thing worth weighing here is the warning against imitating hypocrites and chasing human praise, since woe comes when people bless you and those who call you blessed can lead you astray. That principle sharpens things: it tells you to keep your faith inward and honest rather than performing for the crowd or trying to prove them wrong. What it doesn't change is the core answer. Their mockery still doesn't settle whether the awakening was genuine, and their accusation still deserves honest self-examination and repentance where there's truth to it. So go back to the sermon, to prayer, and to Scripture quietly, find a few sincere believers who encourage you, and let a changed life answer their laughter over time.
dogmatic: Keep going, but watch yourself closely. Don't imitate the hypocrites who look outwardly holier than they know themselves to be, and don't go looking for human praise. Woe comes when people bless you, and those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. When they laugh and call you a hypocrite, don't retaliate or seek vengeance. Resist not evil. Bless those who curse you and leave judgment to God. And remember that moral ignorance or sin hinders the demonstration of God's healing power and must be overcome, so examine yourself honestly, repent where their accusation has truth, and press on toward purity of heart. Keep your religion between you and God, and let a changed life answer their laughter.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, don't build your faith around any human theory, no matter how brilliant the author. Faith belongs on God and his Word, not on the shifting opinions of scholars. One principle worth weighing here is that if God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship in the Old Testament, he can also use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how you can read theories about authorship: they don't have to threaten faith, because God can inspire truth through ancient ways of writing. What it leaves in place is the main point: your foundation stays God and Scripture, not the theory itself. So treat the theory as a tool, not a foundation.
dogmatic: Don't build your faith on a scholar's theory, full stop. But don't shrink from the idea that God can use literary methods belonging to a rude and undeveloped age as vehicles of inspiration without any fraud. That's not a threat to faith; it's how God condescends. Let historical study serve reverent obedience and prayer, so knowledge leads to a more stalwart and intelligent faith. And consider the gospel's rapid progress against scepticism, hatred, and persecution as evidence of its divine origin. Let that strengthen your faith, and let study lead you to worship.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, you can't be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. God isn't fooled by a legal fiction, and true righteousness is a change of heart and life. One principle I'd weigh is that salvation is an individual work, no one is saved by another's righteousness, and each must receive or reject it for himself. That principle changes how I'd frame the answer: it makes clear this is your own response to Christ, not something inherited or borrowed. But it leaves in place the core point that the righteousness God counts is real, not just a label. So I'd still say: don't settle for a mere status. Seek the reality of a changed life.
dogmatic: No, you cannot be counted righteous without actually becoming righteous. Any idea that you can be declared righteous while remaining unchanged is a false hope. Salvation is not a legal fiction where righteousness is merely credited to you. It is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life He lived. When you surrender to Christ, His Spirit transforms you from within, often through trials. Count it all joy by faith, reckoning the trial a blessing even when feelings fail. Fix your heart and choose to rejoice until praise becomes a habit. Do not wait for joyful feelings. And remember, salvation is an individual work: each must receive or reject it for himself. No one is saved by another's righteousness. So do not seek a righteousness that is only imputed; seek the actual transformation that comes from abiding in Him.

weighed: What I'd say first is that feeling nothing in prayer is common, and it doesn't mean God has abandoned you. Feelings come and go; his presence doesn't depend on your emotions. Keep praying even when it's dry, and offer that dryness as trust rather than failure. Tell God honestly how you feel, let a Psalm pray for you, and gently check whether exhaustion or distraction is dulling things. One principle worth naming is the picture of waiting before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—just keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, bringing it back calmly instead of getting upset with yourself. That changes the tone: the wandering mind becomes something to gather back in tranquility, not another failure to mourn. What it leaves in place is everything else—honest words, Scripture, checking your heart, and talking with a pastor if the dryness lingers. The desire to pray is itself a sign of his work in you.
dogmatic: Don't expect prayer to be easy or naturally pleasant. It is humbling work that cuts against your pride and shows you your own bankruptcy before God. So come and wait before him like a beggar at a rich man's gate: make it your business to keep your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, don't fuss over it—quietly bring it back, because fretting only scatters you more. At the same time, pray with confidence, leaning on the merits of Jesus Christ, since God offers grace at every step unless we forget to ask. Ask boldly in his name, and don't be discouraged by dryness or sin. And beware of excusing a little prayer as good enough: little praying is worse than no praying, because it's make-believe. Give yourself to prayer as the humbling work it is, and keep at it.

weighed: I'd start by saying that looking to heaven for help means your ultimate trust is in God, not in your own strength or the people and plans you lean on. Your host is probably your own resources, and God alone is the real source of help, so pray for wisdom, work hard, and rest your confidence in Him. One principle I'd weigh in is that a pastor owes his own soul's care first: regular self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are indispensably necessary, because you can't kindle charity in others if it's gone out in you. That changes the picture by making care for your own soul part of what trusting God looks like, not a distraction from it, and it leaves in place the core point that your confidence belongs in the Lord rather than your own host.
dogmatic: Looking to heaven for help means your trust is in God, not in human resources or your own strength, and your host means your own plans and abilities. But hear this plainly: if you're a pastor or teacher, you must not neglect your own soul while you're busy with external works. Regular retirement, self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are your first duty to your own soul. Without them you cannot kindle charity in others. Looking to heaven also means attending to the sick and dying. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty for every Christian, not just the minister. Seize the time Providence gives in a lingering illness and warn the dying to flee from the wrath to come, for while there is life there is hope. Yet do not be too solicitous for sensible devotion, sweetness, and tears. Chiefly care to remain inwardly united to God by good will in the intellectual part of the soul, denying yourself to follow Christ, who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. So look to heaven by keeping up prayer and devotion, by caring for the sick, and by seeking union with God above all feelings.

weighed: I'd have started by wondering whether you're longing for something real or just projecting your own needs onto an idea. Many people spend years seeking a God who's basically a mirror of what they want, and the honest answer might be that the search is one-sided. That doesn't make your longing worthless—it could point to real human needs for meaning and connection that can be met elsewhere. One principle I'd weigh is that the search is double: the God you're seeking is also seeking you. That changes the picture from a one-way effort to a relationship, which might ease the pressure you feel. But it leaves in place the hard truth that you might still be doing all the seeking, and that your expectations could be unrealistic. So be gentle with yourself—you're not necessarily doing anything wrong.
dogmatic: You're not doing anything wrong—the search is double. Your longing for God is real, and it's matched by God's own longing for you. He is seeking you and will spare no cost to bring you into fellowship. Don't try to manufacture comfort by denying evil, sickness, and pain; that's a narcotic, not a redemption. Face those truths and walk the way of redemption through heroism, not cowardice. And know that finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering—but joy increases so greatly that for the first time joy is greater than pain, and good becomes so much greater than evil that evil becomes negligible. Keep seeking with courage and hope, trusting that the One you seek is seeking you and will be found.

weighed: I'd first say no, human love isn't worthless. The emptiness you feel doesn't cancel out the real love you have for your family. One principle I'd bring in is that we shouldn't be troubled by the fear that our love is useless or false when we feel no pleasure, but instead show steady faithfulness, serving for love of God's will. That principle changes the focus from what you feel to what you choose to do—it says your love can be real even when it feels empty. But it leaves in place the honesty that the emptiness is real and painful, and it doesn't dismiss your family love as nothing. So I'd still say your love matters, and the dryness might be a call to keep loving faithfully rather than to conclude it's worthless.
dogmatic: No, human love is not worthless, but you must not be troubled by the fear that your love is useless or false when you feel no pleasure. Manifest invincible fidelity to your Savior, serving Him purely for love of His will. The soul is a strange, piteous, futile thing, and its futility is precisely what God's love addresses: seeing none but I makes much of naught. Love is life's only sign: the spring of the regenerate heart is true love of Christ, and whoever loves the Lord aright finds no soul worthless, chiefly Christian souls glistening with baptismal dew. So do not conclude that your family love is worthless because you feel empty. Instead, persevere in love, serving God and family not for feelings but for His sake. The emptiness may be a refining fire, drawing you closer to God and purifying your love. Hold fast to love, and let it be rooted in God's unchanging love for you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: pew-rents have a long history and can be a practical way to fund ministry, but if they make some people feel unwelcome or divide the congregation by wealth, it's worth reconsidering, and you should talk it through with your pastor and church leaders. One principle worth naming is that the pew-rent system and fixed salaries for ministry are unscriptural, promote caste distinctions, and should be replaced by free-will offerings. If you take that seriously, it changes the default from 'handle it prayerfully and fairly' to 'work toward replacing it with voluntary giving.' What it leaves in place is your role and your constraints: you're still the one raising this with your church, still weighing how to honor God and love your neighbor, and still free to move at a pace that fits your congregation rather than declaring the matter settled for everyone.
dogmatic: Pew-rents should not continue. They set rich and poor apart in the house of prayer, and that contradicts the gospel. The Lord's work is to be supported by free-will offerings alone, not by fixed salaries or pew-rents that prop up caste. New Testament giving was voluntary and cheerful, never coerced or tied to privilege. So advocate for their abolition and call your church back to biblical stewardship, even if that means trusting God's provision. And while you're at it, don't stop there: parents and pastors must remove irreligious, immoral, or untrue books from the reach of the young and supply works that train the mind to truth and virtue. And don't skip congregational worship because you feel you get nothing out of it; go chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger, under the governance of love.

weighed: My first instinct is that this is a question sincere believers read differently, and it's wise to hold it loosely. Some see the Holy City as a symbol of the faithful, others as a literal city prepared for them, and Revelation's imagery is rich enough to support either. One principle I'd weigh says the saints aren't the city at all; they're being prepared to enter a real city now in the third heaven that will descend at Christ's return. That shifts the emphasis toward a future, literal dwelling, but it leaves in place the heart of the hope: God dwelling with his people and the faithful sharing his presence.
dogmatic: The Holy City is not the saints themselves. It's a real city, the New Jerusalem, now in the third heaven with God and Christ, and it will descend out of heaven at the second advent and be located in the midst of the promised land where Christ was crucified. The saints are being built together as a temple, but they are being prepared to enter the city, not to be it, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up to enter it. And while they wait, the saints must be self-sustaining, producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and storing up provisions against a day of scarcity.

weighed: I'd start by saying that colours and sounds may depend on the mind, but the objects you touch and handle aren't dissolved by that. When you touch something solid and shaped, you're in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. One candidate principle here is that matter can't exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter—sensations and relations, including space—implies mind. That principle changes how I'd frame the object's reality: it's not independent of mind, and spatial relations themselves imply a mind that knows them. But it leaves in place the solid, shaped thing you handle as real and regular, not an illusion.
dogmatic: Colours and sounds only exist for minds, and the same goes for the solid, shaped objects you touch. Matter has no existence of its own apart from a mind that knows it. All we know of matter is sensations and relations, including space, and those imply mind. So the object you handle is real, but its reality is not independent of mind—there must be a universal Mind in which and for which all things exist. Don't treat touch as giving you a mind-independent world; it gives you a world that is already mental through and through.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, keep praying if that's what your heart is doing — bring your love and your fear to God honestly, and don't feel guilty for asking for healing. What I'd add is that prayer can hold you and give you strength even if the healing you're begging for doesn't come, so it's also wise to prepare for what may be ahead and to lean on the people around you. One principle worth naming is that God can heal in answer to prayer, and that Jesus is the same yesterday, today, and forever. That changes something real: it means your asking isn't pointless, and you don't have to treat hope as naive. What it leaves in place is the honesty that prayer isn't a guarantee of recovery — so keep asking boldly, and still hold comfort, time with your child, and the support of your community close.
dogmatic: Keep praying for your child's healing, and don't stop asking God for mercy — God can and does heal in answer to prayer today, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Don't let a lack of feeling excuse you from prayer; keep your set times of prayer no matter how you feel, and gather your family to pray together. Bring your request boldly and persistently, and do as much as you're able to help bring about what you're asking for. Hold to God as ever-present and almighty, and trust that his power and presence are near your child's bedside. Trust his goodness and leave the outcome in his hands.

weighed: I'd start by saying that worrying your sorrow isn't strong enough doesn't mean your repentance is fake. Repentance isn't mainly about how intense your feelings are; it's about turning from sin and turning toward God. Feelings vary a lot from person to person and day to day, so measure your repentance by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God, not by the intensity of your emotions. One principle worth naming is that repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as you know it, and that genuine repentance shows itself in obedience. That adds a concrete test: are you still doing what you know is wrong? If so, stop now. What it leaves in place is the core point that your feelings aren't the measure, so a quiet heart doesn't automatically mean a false repentance.
dogmatic: Stop measuring your repentance by how much sorrow you feel and start measuring it by what you do. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong the moment you know it is wrong; ignorance may be excused, but once you learn a thing is wrong you must refrain from it immediately and for good. Don't put repentance off. It isn't desperate to have been wounded; it's desperate to neglect the cure. A merchant who loses his ship doesn't sit and mourn, he works to repair his losses, and a wrestler or soldier who falls gets up and fights again. Beware of unregretted sin: it piles up and destroys your ability to do right, and a guilty conscience only grows harder. So examine yourself honestly. Are you still doing what you know to be wrong? If so, stop at once and reform your life.

weighed: I'd first say that hoping for better conditions for your family is completely natural, and a change of government might bring practical improvements. There's nothing wrong with wanting good government and better circumstances. At the same time, it's wise not to put all your hope in political change, since governments come and go and can't guarantee happiness. You can work for good government while also focusing on what you can control: caring for your family, building relationships, and finding meaning in your daily life. Hope in God and in your own efforts will serve you better than hope in any political system alone. One principle worth considering is that a change in the form of government doesn't materially better people's condition—happiness and peace are gifts of God, not products of republics or monarchies. That principle shifts the emphasis away from expecting political change to deliver happiness, but it leaves intact the value of hoping for practical improvements and working for good government. So it doesn't cancel your hope; it just reframes where ultimate trust should lie.
dogmatic: No, it's not wrong to hope for better conditions, but you should not expect a change of government to regenerate society or produce happiness. Forms of government do not materially alter the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, and revolutions only change men and parchments. Be peaceable and submissive to existing authorities, pray for rulers, and patiently wait for the Lord to establish his own government in his own time. Do not turn to revolt or violent resistance. Instead, care for your own relatives and the poor, for it is a disgrace not to do so, and plan for them work they are able to perform. Place your hope in God and in faithful labor.

weighed: Yes, it's natural to feel discouraged when the same faults keep tripping you up, but don't let discouragement drive. Progress is rarely a straight line, and everyone has recurring weaknesses. Treat each failure as information: find the trigger, pray about it, make a small practical plan, and ask a trusted friend to keep you accountable. One principle worth holding onto is that fidelity is yours while failure comes from infirmity—so stay faithful in your exercises and don't be astonished when you stumble. That changes the tone: you stop treating each fall as a crisis and keep your routine steady. What it leaves in place is the honest grief you feel and the real work of watching, praying, and beginning again. Your conscience being grieved is itself a sign you haven't given up. God's grace is bigger than your repeated mistakes, and He isn't surprised by them. Take heart and start again.
dogmatic: Don't be troubled or astonished by recurring faults—fidelity is yours, and failure comes from infirmity, so keep your exercises steady and calm. Understand error rightly: it's the supposition that life, intelligence, pleasure, and pain reside in matter, and it's unreal because it's untrue. Failure isn't a real power set against you; it's a false claim to be seen through, not feared. Refuse to impute sin or mortality to God, for infinite Mind creates neither, and infinite Mind sets at naught such a mistaken belief. Meet each fault quietly, correct what you can, and continue the same faithful routine, knowing what is untrue has no real hold. Begin again without agitation.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: holiness is being set apart for God, and purification is part of it, but it's not just scrubbing flaws off a list. At its heart it's a relationship—belonging wholly to God and letting His character show up in your everyday life. One of the principles you raised fits here: sanctification as a gift of the Holy Ghost received by faith, not self-improvement or grim self-punishment. That changes the tone—it means you're not white-knuckling your way to purity, you're receiving something God gives. What it leaves in place is the relational core: it's still about belonging to God and reflecting Him, and it still grows through prayer, Scripture, community, and obedience, with your cooperation alongside God's work. So purification is involved, but it serves something bigger—a life shaped more and more by God's presence and love, walked out day by day.
dogmatic: Holiness isn't a vague process—it's a life wholly yielded to God, and being filled with the Holy Ghost is not an optional extra but a command to claim. Bring an empty, honest, trusting heart and ask to be filled, not half-filled, but filled for purity, victory, and power. Receive sanctification as God's gift through the Holy Ghost, not as human self-improvement or painful mortification; it comes by faith, and He walks you in His statutes by His own impulse. And this gift gets formed in you through real praying—prayer is what makes saints, and where praying increases, true saints increase. So claim the filling as commanded, expect it by faith, and give yourself to prayer. Holiness is the Spirit-occupied life, received as a gift and lived out in trusting, praying obedience.

weighed: Going to church and keeping the commandments are good and important, but they aren't by themselves the whole of being a Christian. Christianity is fundamentally a relationship with God through Jesus Christ, and church attendance and moral effort can be part of that life or can become external habits without inward reality. One principle worth weighing here is that Christianity is a life, not an act done by hands—that keeping commandments and believing the right facts isn't enough. That changes how you see your practices: they're not the finish line but the soil where a living faith grows. It leaves your churchgoing and commandment-keeping in place as good things, just not as replacements for a genuine relationship with God. So keep attending and keep the commandments, but also ask whether your faith is living and personal.
dogmatic: Going to church and keeping the commandments are good, but they are not enough to make you a Christian. Christianity is a life, not an act done by hands. Mere commandment-keeping, baptism, or believing that Christ lived and was crucified does not make one a Christian—Jews and Mahommedans believe those things too. Nor must you always be at church to be with God: you can make an oratory of your heart, conversing with Him in meekness, humility, and love, and everyone is capable of that familiar conversation. Do not stop at trivial devotions that change daily. Quicken and enliven your faith and take it as the rule of conduct, for the way of faith is the spirit of the Church and suffices to bring you to a high degree of perfection. The real question is whether Christ lives in you and whether your life is shaped by His Spirit.

weighed: My first answer would be: yes, your preaching can still carry truth, because God's Word doesn't come back empty, but sermons that give life usually flow from a preacher who's connected to God. If you rarely pray, your preaching may drift toward information instead of transformation. So start small: pray daily, ask God to shape your heart before your sermon, and let others pray with you. One principle worth naming is that a preacher can't keep his spirit in tune with his calling without much prayer, and sermon-making by itself, with prayer neglected, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That changes my answer by making prayer not just an improvement but a necessity, and by warning that sermon prep can quietly pull you away from God. It leaves in place what I said first: your preaching can still communicate truth, and this is fixable, so begin where you are.
dogmatic: No, preaching without prayer cannot give life in any deep sense. Life-giving preaching costs the preacher everything: death to self, crucifixion to the world, the travail of his own soul. Only a crucified man can preach crucified preaching. And preaching is not harmless. Rightly done, its benefits are untold; wrongly done, no evil exceeds its damage, because the preacher holds keys that lock as well as unlock. You cannot keep your spirit in harmony with your calling without much prayer. Sermon-making itself, when prayer is neglected, will engross and harden and estrange your heart from God. So stop treating prayer as optional and let it, not routine, shape your preaching, so that you unlock rather than lock and give life rather than damage.

weighed: What you're carrying sounds heavy, and it makes sense that the memory keeps coming back. First, be gentle with yourself: everyone carries something from their past. Guilt can show you have a conscience, but it isn't a life sentence. Talking to a trusted counselor or therapist can help you process the memory without being overwhelmed by it. Practical steps help too—naming honestly what happened, making amends where you can, and building new patterns that reflect who you want to be now. Over time, the memory may lose its grip. You are not defined by the worst thing you've done, and safety is possible as you work through it patiently. One idea worth weighing is that small faults, if we keep choosing them, can quietly grow into bigger ones—so it's worth taking even the small stuff seriously. That adds a nudge toward honesty and early course-correction, but it doesn't change the core: you're not doomed, and healing still comes through patient, supported work rather than fear.
dogmatic: The memory that keeps returning is not a verdict you have to rehearse—it's a call to take every fault seriously. Small faults, wilfully committed, are dangerous beginnings from which dreadful falls arise, so nothing should be slighted. Yet don't impress the wrong upon your thought or name it over and over as though it had power. Deny it mentally; refuse to accept relapse as a real reaction, and meet its cause mentally and courageously—trace the fear to its source in thought and answer it with what is true. There is no real relapse in Truth, only a false belief to be corrected. Make amends quietly where you can, without self-punishment. A trusted counselor may help you hold thought steady. Safety comes not from dwelling on the fault but from meeting its cause in mind, conquering fear, and holding thought to what is true and good.

weighed: I'd start by saying that temptation itself isn't sin—it only becomes sin when you consent to it. So when a tempting thought shows up, don't panic. Notice it, turn your attention to God, and choose to do the right thing. Anxiety and scrupulosity usually come from over-focusing on yourself and fearing failure. Instead, rest in God's grace and remember he's patient with you. Practical steps help: avoid triggers, build good habits, pray briefly and often, and talk with a trusted mentor. When you fall, confess quickly and move on rather than spiraling. The goal is steady, peaceful obedience, not constant self-monitoring. One principle that fits here is this: hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—keep your mind in his presence, and if it wanders, don't disquiet yourself; bring it back calmly. That principle changes the tone of prayer and attention: it replaces anxious self-checking with quiet, patient waiting. But it leaves in place the core advice—temptation isn't sin, don't panic, turn to God, act rightly, confess and move on, and aim for peaceful obedience rather than constant self-monitoring.
dogmatic: Resisting temptation without anxiety starts with seeing that temptation itself is not sin, and that temptations which displease you are nothing to fear. The trouble they cause is actually God's mercy refining the gold of your soul—so despise the temptation and embrace the tribulation it brings rather than dreading it. The deeper practice is prayer: wait before God like a dumb or paralytic beggar at a rich man's gate. Your business is simply to keep your mind in the presence of the Lord. When it wanders, do not disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. The will must bring it back in tranquility. Avoid hurry and anxiety above all, since these are the greatest obstacles to progress in perfection. Acknowledge tempting thoughts calmly, turn to God, and choose to act rightly. When you fall, confess quietly and move on. The goal is humble, peaceful waiting before God, trusting that the suffering of temptation is a mercy showing your will does not consent.

weighed: My first instinct is that love should hold both together—respect what they want, but also care about what they truly need—with a lot of listening and humility. One principle that sharpens this is that love is discerning, not blind: it's about knowing the difference between good, better, and best. That changes how I'd frame the answer—it makes 'need' less about my assumptions and more about careful, informed judgment. But it leaves in place the core idea that their wants still matter and that you shouldn't override them just because you think you know better.
dogmatic: Love isn't mainly a warm feeling—it's the steady will to please and benefit the person you love, even when it costs you. And that kind of love isn't blind; it's full of knowledge and discernment, able to tell good from bad, better from best. So don't just ask what they want—ask what is truly good here. Watch out for a love that's really about your own delight, or that quietly rejoices when they give up their comfort for you. Real love doesn't seek its own pleasure; it gives its ease for the other and builds heaven even in hell's despair. Wants matter because love honors dignity, but love doesn't just gratify wants—it seeks their real good at cost to itself. This grows through frequent acts of service and by remembering what's been done for you. Serve quietly, offer what's needed as an invitation, and let discernment guide the sacrifice.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: your fear is natural, and quality of life matters more than length, so live each day fully, love God and others, and trust that whether your life is long or short, He is with you. One idea worth naming is that we're meant to prepare to live, not just to die, and to build health and strength early so longevity can begin to return. That changes the tone: instead of only preparing your soul for eternity, you'd also treat your body and habits as something worth investing in for a long road ahead. What it leaves in place is the core: don't obsess over death, cultivate gratitude, serve others, and leave the number of your days in God's hands.
dogmatic: The real answer is that you shouldn't be preparing to die at all. Prepare to live. Teach children in the morning of their days to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. Life is a school of experience and probation, where we learn, improve, and increase continually, not stand still. And ultimately mortality isn't real, because being is immortal and inseparable from Deity. So don't wish life away. Embrace each day as a chance to progress, and stop treating death as the thing to plan around.

weighed: I'm really sorry for your loss, and I can hear how much this weighs on you. My first answer would be that yes, you can be forgiven—God is merciful, and the fact that you care shows your love for your friend. One principle I'd hold onto here is that you shouldn't let your soul live in sadness or scrupulous fear, because the One who loved your friend is good and kind. That principle changes the tone: instead of just telling you to confess and move on, it says don't let guilt become your home. But it doesn't erase the real missed opportunity—if your silence was deliberate, that still calls for honest repentance. So you can be forgiven, and you can also learn from this without being crushed by it.
dogmatic: You're asking about forgiveness for neglect, and here's the truth you need to hear: the Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong. If you deliberately put off speaking to your friend about his soul, that is not a small oversight—it is serious, and there is no forgiveness for such a thing without humble and most contrite repentance. Don't soften this with talk of God's mercy while you're still holding back. You must repent deeply, not just feel bad. And don't let yourself wallow in self-condemnation either—that's weakness, not healing. Face what you did, turn from it completely, and then trust in truth, not in your own guilt.

weighed: I'd start by pointing out that Genesis actually holds two creation accounts with different aims. The garden-and-rib story reads as figurative, about human origins and relationships, not a science report, while chapter one is more cosmic and liturgical. Many people treat both as ancient near-eastern literature, so the clash with modern cosmology fades. Read them for what they say about God as creator and our place and responsibility, and let science handle the mechanisms. One idea worth weighing is that revealed religion presents the Science of Mind and its formations as matching Genesis one, where God, Mind, spoke and it was done. That shifts how you read chapter one, toward divine order and spiritual formation rather than material mechanism, but it leaves the figurative reading of chapter two and the basic split between meaning and mechanism intact.
dogmatic: Read Genesis one as the spiritual account: the Science of Mind and its formations, where God creates by His word and everything is pronounced good. Chapter one sets out divine order and spiritual formation, not material mechanism, so it doesn't compete with modern science at all; the second account is the material, figurative picture. As 1 Peter 1:20 says, Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake, the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot. When our Lord appeals to the Old Testament, He isn't resting on questions of authorship or date but on its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself. His authority stands whole and unfallen; read Scripture as He did, for the truth that speaks of Him.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: name the pattern honestly, sort out what's actually yours from what isn't, and take one small concrete step today rather than waiting to overhaul everything at once. One principle here says that being faithful in your exercises matters while occasional failure comes from infirmity, so you shouldn't be rattled by it. That changes the tone—it turns a relapse into something you return from quickly instead of a verdict on you—but it leaves the practical work in place: you still have to look at the pattern, act, and get outside perspective. It also doesn't promise the cycle just dissolves, so keep the counseling or trusted person in the picture if it keeps repeating.
dogmatic: That pile of failures is not your fate, so stop treating it like one. Resist the error at the root of it firmly, because error is opposed to Life and flees before Truth. Be utterly faithful in your exercises: examine yourself daily, watch your thought, word, and deed, pray without ceasing, and take one right step today. Find leaders who will tell you plainly where you've gone wrong and correct you—if they won't rebuke you, they've fallen from their station, and a people that can't be corrected has betrayed the faith. And when infirmity makes you stumble now and then, don't be troubled or astonished; return at once to your exercises and keep going.

weighed: I get why you're snapping—being at your limit makes kindness feel impossible. My first instinct is to say pause, breathe, and name your triggers so you can respond calmly instead of reacting. One principle that fits here is self-control: check your words, step back from anger, and mind your own business rather than faultfinding. That principle sharpens the pause into a deliberate habit—catch yourself before you speak and ask what's really yours to manage. It leaves in place the practical stuff: deep breaths, stepping away, and calm communication when you need to set a boundary. So you're still doing all that, just with a clearer focus on managing your own reaction first.
dogmatic: You need to bridle your tongue and subdue your anger before anything else. Stop trying to fix your coworker and examine why their habits provoke you. Attend to your own duties and mind your own business. Learn contentment from the willow: live thankfully on the least you're given, stay patient under rude assault, and wear a willing smile again after the storm. Withdraw as much as you can from acquaintance and from people; abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose; seek out quiet and contemplation; embrace silence and solitude; fly the agitation of a world never at rest. You cannot control others, only your reaction—so practice self-control and choose kindness, not because it's easy, but because it's right.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: treat prayer as a real habit you build—set times, honest confession, praying in line with what God has promised, patience when answers are slow, and pure motives. One thing worth adding is that prayer can be as simple as a child asking a parent. That doesn't erase the disciplines; it just keeps them from turning into a checklist you perform to get God to respond. So keep the structure, but let it stay plain and childlike.
dogmatic: Prayer isn't a technique you master. It's a child talking to a Father—plain, natural, all day long. Drop the idea that you need special rules or a complicated procedure; just bring God your everyday needs, because He actually delights to be asked. And don't put Muller on a pedestal. He was an ordinary man with the same weaknesses you have, and his power was simply leaning on God. What he knew, you can know. Let prayer become like breathing—constant, quiet, feeding the life of God in you—and just ask plainly and keep drawing near.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is a matter of personal conscience. A visible cross can be a real reminder of your faith and of Christ's victory, and plenty of people find it meaningful going into a hard thing. But it shouldn't become a substitute for actual preparation—prayer, wise planning, honest effort—and if it turns into superstition or a mindless habit, you're free to set it aside without guilt. One principle worth naming is that the sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, used in every sacrament and devotion, made with faith and devotion rather than mere custom. That changes the tone: it pushes the sign from optional reminder toward a real spiritual weapon against the devil. What it leaves in place is the caution—it still has to be done with faith, not as a charm, and it still doesn't replace preparation or trust in God rather than the object.
dogmatic: Yes—bear the sign of the cross before you into the struggle. It is the Christian's rampart, used in every sacrament and devotion, and it drives away devils when it's made with faith and devotion rather than by mere custom. Let it confess that you stand under Christ's victory. And don't stop at the sign: the Cross turns the bitterest herbs to sweetness, especially when your hopes fade or a friend scorns you. Christ still suffers in His lowly members while we ride triumphant, and His wounds are the refuge of broken hearts. So be willing to be fashioned by God with brush, hammer, or chisel according to His good pleasure, and desire that the cross before you be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ—His sign, His victory, His patience.

weighed: I'm so sorry for your loss. Guilt after losing a child is very common, but it doesn't mean you did something wrong. Praying for your child's healing was an act of love, not a sin, and her death isn't a punishment for weak faith or a faulty prayer. God isn't a vending machine that only responds to perfect requests; He's a loving Father who grieves with you. One thing worth weighing, though, is the idea that we sometimes pray out of our own comfort rather than for God's glory. That can add a layer of honest self-examination, but it doesn't turn your prayer into a sin or make you responsible for her death. Let yourself mourn, accept support, and be gentle with yourself. If the guilt keeps weighing on you, talking with a pastor or counselor can help you carry it.
dogmatic: Your prayer wasn't the problem, but your motives might need sifting. Many pray and don't receive because they ask amiss, out of selfish and earthly motives, praying for children merely for their own comfort rather than for God's glory. So examine whether your request was tangled with self-concern, worry about your reputation or your own ease. That said, her death is not a punishment for a faulty prayer. Take comfort in her baptism: a few calm words of faith and prayer and a few bright drops of holy dew work a wonder earth's charmers never knew, and she is marked to be nursed for Jesus' sake. Now pray chiefly for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, and accustom yourself to familiar, humble, affectionate conversation with God, watching that you neither do, say, nor think anything displeasing to Him. That watchfulness brings the peace of paradise even in this life.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: that feeling of having ruined everything is real pain, but it isn't the final truth about you. Plenty of people made a mess of their youth and still built good lives after. Own what happened without drowning in shame, make amends where you can, forgive yourself, and move forward in small steps—one goal, one habit, people who support you rather than shame you. One principle here says a relapse can't really happen because there's only one Mind, so meet the cause mentally and courageously instead of planning for a fall. That changes the advice about relapse: instead of bracing for setbacks, you'd face the fear behind them head-on. What it leaves in place is everything else—owning your part, making amends, self-forgiveness, and small forward steps. Your past shapes you, but it doesn't have to define your future.
dogmatic: There is only one Mind, so a relapse cannot in reality occur. Stop planning for failure and meet its cause mentally and courageously—conquer your fear rather than managing it. Do not lean on your own powers to save you. The soul is stripped piece by piece, its harness hewn away, its dreams failing, until it stands naked and defenceless before God—and that stripping ends self-reliance, not hope. The world is old and its mirth has gone, and it is Youth that must come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance and keeping alive the hope of Spring. So rise, own your part, make amends, refuse to plan for falling back, and let your renewed youth carry freshness and strength into a weary world.

weighed: I'd start where you're starting: the New Testament describes the return in plain, physical terms—coming in the clouds, every eye seeing him, appearing the same way he ascended. That's the natural reading, and it's the answer I'd give first. One principle worth naming is that the second coming is literal and personal, as real as the events of the first advent, and that spiritualizing it away leaves no tangible ground to stand on. What that changes is the weight you give to the inward-presence reading: Christ dwelling in believers is real, but it isn't the same event as his promised return, so it can't replace it. What it leaves in place is your own honest uncertainty about timing and details—it settles the manner of the coming, not the schedule. So take the promises at face value, and hold the inward experience as something true but not a substitute.
dogmatic: The second coming is literal, personal, and visible—as real as the first advent—and any reading that turns it into a mere inward experience or something already fulfilled in the saints drains the promise of its substance. The angels said this same Jesus would come in the same manner, and every eye will see him. That's not a metaphor to be softened; it's the ground God's people stand on. You don't need to hedge about proof. The convergence of prophecy, the long preparation of Israel, and the beauty of God's redemptive process give the highest corroborative evidence history can offer. So be convinced, make your commitment once for all, and stay put through the season of establishing and testing until hope becomes a habit. Spiritualizing this away leaves you with nothing tangible, and that is not where you want to stand.

weighed: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is already a kind of conviction, and it may be enough to start with. Not everyone feels dramatic agony over sin; some are led to repentance through a quieter recognition that things have gone wrong. What matters is whether that recognition turns you toward God and a changed life. Agony isn't the measure of sincerity—honesty is. One principle worth weighing here is that sin is a kind of insanity, and sickness is error, a loss of harmony, so the senses' testimony can't be true of man or his Maker. That reframes your question: conviction isn't about how much you suffer but about whether you stop believing the error. What it changes is the pressure to manufacture agony; what it leaves in place is the real need for honesty and a turned life. Bring your sense of error to God, ask for clearer light on what needs to change, and let that awareness grow into repentance and trust in his mercy.
dogmatic: Stop measuring your conviction by agony. Sin is insanity in different degrees, and every sickness is error, a loss of harmony—the corporeal senses are mortal beliefs whose testimony cannot be true of man or his Maker. So deny that testimony. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries; don't be incensed against those who inflict them, and don't entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honored by men. The sinful misconception of Life as something less than God falls back upon itself and, after reaching the climax of suffering, yields to Truth and returns to dust. You need not fight a permanent enemy—stop believing the error, and it dissolves. That is sufficient conviction.

weighed: I'd start by saying that Christian nations fight because nations, even Christian ones, are full of fallible people chasing security, power, and national interest, and when those clash, governments turn to force while churches get caught between blessing the troops and calling for peace. Praying to the same God for victory is a tragic irony, since each side thinks its cause is just. One idea that sharpens this is that war is the natural penalty by which evil passions punish themselves under God's ordinary laws of human nature, so wars grow out of lusts and injustice rather than God's design. That changes how I see the causes, making them moral and self-inflicted rather than just political, but it leaves in place the point that God doesn't take sides in the slaughter and that Christians still answer for letting patriotism crowd out the gospel's call to peacemaking.
dogmatic: War doesn't come from God's design; it comes from wickedness, from lusts and covetousness and injustice, and God's righteousness works through the ordinary laws of human nature so that evil passions punish themselves. Praying to the same God for victory on both sides is a tragic irony, because God takes no side in the slaughter, and peace will never come until people receive God's truth. But victory, not defeat, is God's purpose for believers, and the secret is Christ himself living in you, entered by resting in him. When your heart rests in Christ, the passions that breed war are overcome from within.

weighed: Yes, you can be holy while flaws remain, because holiness isn't something you reach all at once; it grows gradually. Honest flaws don't disqualify you, as long as you're not excusing them or getting comfortable with them. One thing worth adding: we help each other by advice and even more by good example, so let people see your honest walk and receive their counsel humbly. That changes the picture from a private project to a shared one, but it leaves in place the core answer: keep turning from what's wrong, keep growing, and don't despair over what's still unfinished.
dogmatic: You can be holy with flaws still showing, but don't let that turn into a soft excuse. Holiness is not attained all at once, yet you must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since a love that settles for less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. And don't imagine sin can be pardoned while it is tolerated. God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. So acknowledge your blemishes honestly, forsake them, and let grace reform you together with the community of faith.

weighed: I'd start by saying that believing Jesus lived and was crucified is a real starting point, but it's not the whole of the Christian life. The Gospels call us not just to affirm facts but to follow Jesus and take up our cross. One principle that shapes this is that we should frequently think of Jesus crucified, covered with wounds and despoiled of everything, and acknowledge that our sufferings can't compare with His. That changes how we measure our own hardships—it puts them in perspective. But it leaves in place the core call to trust Christ, repent, and bear fruit in obedience and love. So thank God for the historical foundation, but don't stop there.
dogmatic: Believing Jesus lived and was crucified is only a beginning. You must frequently think of Jesus crucified, considering Him covered with wounds and despoiled of everything, and acknowledge that your sufferings cannot compare with His. The living Christ is not the person that was but the person that still is, present with you always in an unbroken and continuous presence. Christ must be formed in you; you are to live not your own life but the Christ-life, showing forth His excellencies as incarnations of the living Christ. So do not treat Him as only a figure of the past or a hope of the future. Rest in His continuous presence now, and let Christ be formed in you, living the Christ-life through you.

weighed: I'd start by naming the worry honestly to God, then deliberately placing it in his hands each day: pray plainly, release it, and don't rehearse it afterward. Keep a simple budget, do your work faithfully, and treat provision as God's concern and diligence as yours. When anxious thoughts come back, recall past provision and turn to the present duty; trust grows by practice, so hand over the same worry as often as it returns, and let gratitude replace fear. One principle worth taking seriously is that you should never pray for riches, only for daily bread, since chasing more than that strays from the path that leads to life. That changes the content of your asking: instead of vague requests for security or comfort, you'd pray specifically for enough to keep yourself and your family from want. What it leaves in place is the rest of the practice: honest naming, daily release, faithful work, and gratitude. It sharpens the prayer without replacing the habit of handing things over.
dogmatic: Come to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and stay there. Name your worry, then hold yourself in his presence with empty hands, and make it your business simply to keep your mind there. If it wanders, don't be troubled; disquiet only scatters you further. Bring your will back in tranquility and wait again. And never pray for riches. Those who ask for more than daily bread wander off the track that leads to eternal life, so ask only for enough to keep yourself and your family from want. Remember those who gave themselves and their goods to God's work without salary, trusting him to supply, and let their cheerful self-denial be your pattern. Do your work faithfully, hold your money loosely, ready to give where he calls. Provision is his concern; your part is humble, trusting waiting.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling attached to creatures isn't automatically a sin. God made them good, and loving people and good things can actually draw you toward Him—the key is keeping God first. So examine your attachments: do any of them pull you away from prayer, virtue, or trust in God? If so, gently detach. Practice gratitude for good things as gifts from God rather than replacements for Him. Grow in prayer, receive the sacraments, and ask God to enlarge your heart. Over time, love for God can become the center that orders all other loves. Don't be discouraged by feelings; love is shown in choices, and every small choice for God strengthens your wholehearted love. One principle that speaks to this is that love is rational and voluntary, not mere emotion, and it's subject to holiness. That changes how you see the struggle: it's not about waiting to feel differently but about choosing God as your true good and letting every affection be regulated by holiness. It leaves in place the goodness of creaturely loves—they're still gifts to receive with gratitude—but it reframes the goal as ordering them under God's will rather than eliminating them.
