dogmatic: Love of God is not first a feeling but a rational, voluntary self-giving: you choose Him as your true good, seeking His glory and your real good, and every affection is regulated by holiness. Do not imagine your smallness makes you unnoticed—God's knowledge is undivided, and His attention rests wholly on each soul, so the ocean-tides of His love pour into even the smallest heart. So stop moaning over your unworthiness and attachments as though you must first become better before you may love Him. Rise up now and bless God with all the love you have, keeping none back; love Him from sickness as fully as in health, from weakness as in strength. Order your creaturely loves under His will, surrender what draws you from holiness, and give Him your whole heart today.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: a guilty conscience can actually be a gift, but only if it moves you toward God instead of despair. So name what you've done honestly, make amends where you can, confess it, receive absolution, and do penance. One principle worth holding onto here is that unrepented sin tends to harden you and erode your ability to do right, so repentance has to mean an actual change of life, not just feeling bad. That sharpens things: it turns guilt into a call to reform rather than a loop of shame. What it leaves in place is the core of the first answer—God's mercy is bigger than your sin, and peace comes from being forgiven, not from forgetting. If the guilt keeps grinding on even after confession, that may be scrupulosity, and it's worth talking with a pastor.
dogmatic: A guilty conscience is a gift only if it drives you to repentance and not to despair. Name your sins honestly, make amends, confess, receive absolution, and do penance—and don't presume, because unrepented sin piles up and hardens the heart until you lose the ability to do right, so repentance must mean a real reformation of life. Then commit yourself and everything that concerns you to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, accepting all things, whatever their cause, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and reject the vain and wandering thoughts that weary soul and body and waste time and strength. Know that all evil of whatever kind happens by God's permission and always for some good end; it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. So commit all things without fear to His Providence.

weighed: My first instinct is that honor isn't wrong in itself, but wanting it can trip you up. Ask yourself why you want it: influence, security, recognition, or service? A position of honor is a responsibility, not just a badge. If you can use it to serve others, it may be worth accepting; if it feeds pride or pulls you from your duties, decline. Get counsel from wise friends, pray for humility, and hold it loosely. One principle worth naming is that we should offer God our whole liberty, memory, understanding, and will, desiring only His love and grace. That shifts the question from whether you want the honor to whether you can hold it as a way of staying close to God and working for His glory and the good of others. It leaves in place the practical test I'd already give you: does this help you serve, or does it feed pride and pull you from duty? So want it only as a means, and stay ready to accept or decline.
dogmatic: Honor is not wrong in itself, but your heart has to be ordered. Offer God all your liberty, memory, understanding, and will, hold nothing back, and desire only His love and grace as your chief good. Ask whether this position keeps you in His presence and lets you labor for His glory and the good of souls, or whether it feeds pride and pulls you from duty. A place of honor is worth wanting only as a means of serving God and neighbor. Honor the memory of the martyrs and prophets, and delight to honor the instrument God used in the mighty work of the restoration. Let gratitude, humility, devotion, liberality, and honesty shape you: give freely, speak and act consistently and sincerely, and hold the opportunity loosely, ready to accept or decline as best serves His glory and the good of souls.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's natural to feel discouraged when you keep failing at the same sins, but growth in holiness is a process. Even the saints struggled with habitual faults; what matters is that you keep getting up and trying again. God's grace is sufficient for you, and He doesn't expect instant perfection. Don't be too hard on yourself—discouragement can actually hinder your progress. Instead, focus on small, consistent steps and trust that God is working in you. Over time, with prayer and the sacraments, you'll see improvement. The key is perseverance, not speed. One principle that fits here is that the virtue of the saints was constant and crowned with perseverance, and those who serve God must live in fear, watchfulness, humility, and compunction, since it's easier to fall near the end. That principle changes the tone: it adds a sober warning not to presume on grace, and it calls for watchfulness and humility rather than just reassurance. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer—that failure doesn't mean you should give up, that perseverance matters more than speed, and that God's grace is sufficient for you. So you shouldn't be discouraged, but you should be watchful and humble, not presumptuous.
dogmatic: You ask if you should be discouraged after repeated falls. The saints' virtue was constant and crowned with perseverance, and anyone who walks in God's service must live in fear, watchfulness, humility, and compunction, because it is easier to fall near the end of the course. Falling after a long course is not excusable but is mere negligence. Pride is the beginning of all sin, so examine whether your discouragement stems from wounded pride. Imitate the saints, who saw their own imperfections clearly and counted themselves as dust and worms. Let your failures deepen your humility, not your despair. Remember that perfection is possible in every lawful profession without leaving your state in life; you can become a saint right where you are, in your daily duties, by God's grace. Keep striving with sober watchfulness, always relying on God's grace.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear of wealthy parishioners is understandable, but it's dangerous, and the core of your calling is to speak God's word faithfully rather than please people. Reprove sin clearly, gently, and privately where you can, with real humility about your own failings, and lean on prayer and trusted brothers for courage. One principle worth weighing here is that the truth of what you preach rests on God's wisdom and truthfulness, not on the preacher's character—so a minister's failings give hearers no excuse to disobey. That changes the ground under your fear: the pressure you feel from wealthy members can't make the message negotiable, and it also means your own weaknesses don't disqualify the word you carry. What it leaves in place is the manner and the pastoral care—clear, gentle, private reproof, humility, and the ordinary support of your bishop or elders if someone resists. It doesn't turn reproof into a weapon or make you the judge of souls; it just steadies you to be faithful rather than approved.
dogmatic: The message you carry is God's, and obedience is owed to it no matter how weak or compromised the preacher is—the failings of ministers give hearers no excuse. So reprove sin plainly, without partiality or favor-buying, and don't let wealth buy silence or a pass. As an officer of the Church, judge justly and promptly by the Spirit, care for every member of your charge—especially the poor and the sick—and be an example without corruption. And above all, do not admit notorious sinners to the holy table out of fear of the wealthy; Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this stands above an emperor's. Preach the whole counsel of God and trust that the message is His, not yours.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: the kingdom is both a present reality and a future hope, not just something that drops out of the sky and not merely something you build by your own effort. It begins in the hearts of those who accept Christ and grows as people live out their faith in love and service, and we still look forward to its full manifestation when Christ returns. One idea worth weighing is that the kingdom comes through the strenuous, consecrated labor of people who do the holy Will and make it prevail in society. That shifts the emphasis toward your daily work and public life as real kingdom building, but it leaves in place that God ultimately establishes the kingdom and that it's a gift to receive as well as a task to live out.
dogmatic: The kingdom of God is a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth, with laws, officers, and resurrected saints, and Christ will reign over all the earth. It does not drop out of the sky by miracle; it comes through the strenuous, consecrated labor of those who do the holy Will and make it prevail in society. So yes, you help build it, and that building is the total task of humanity through the ages, realized in lives wholly consecrated to making that Will prevail. Yet it must also be revealed from heaven, established by God himself through a restored gospel, a standard lifted to the nations, a literal Zion, and judgements on the wicked, not by human means alone.

weighed: I would have said first that Constantine won through military skill, smart tactics, and a disciplined army, exploiting enemy weaknesses. One principle from the notes says the cross was a token of victory for those who look to heaven for aid rather than trusting in their own numbers. That changes the explanation to divine intervention, but it leaves in place the idea that Constantine's victory was real and decisive.
dogmatic: Constantine didn't conquer the Huns and Goths by his own strength or luck. He looked to heaven and received the sign of the holy cross, the token of victory from the King of angels. That sign, not military skill, gave him the triumph. In the same way, the resurrection alone explains how weak, discouraged men became conquerors of the world, and belief in the bodily resurrection of Christ blocked the full development of Hellenic dualism in Christianity.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, it doesn't. The biblical writers used the science of their day the way anyone uses the thought-world they live in, and that doesn't undercut the spiritual teaching they were passing on. One principle that sharpens this for me is that the Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, with reason and revelation reconciled through divine Science. What that changes is the framing: the point isn't just that Scripture borrows ancient cosmology, but that its authority and its spiritual sense stand on their own ground. What it leaves in place is your actual question, because the teaching still doesn't become less true just because the writers assumed the science around them.
dogmatic: No, it doesn't make their spiritual teaching less true, and the deeper reason is that Christian Science isn't just an intellectual or philosophical system. It's fathomed by the Christian who understands best the divine Life. The Bible was the author's only textbook and authority, and through divine Science reason and revelation are reconciled. So when the writers took up the science of their day, that was the wrapper, not the gift. The spiritual teaching comes from God and stands regardless of the human author's cosmology. And since there is one Spirit, God, any supposed spirits are just mortal mind's images and beliefs, not realities, with no bridge across the gulf between spiritual and physical conditions. That's why the teaching holds.

weighed: I’d start by saying: no, truth isn’t arbitrary, even though God is sovereign. When we call God true, we mean He’s faithful and keeps His promises—His word can be trusted. If truth were just whatever God happened to command, that would be arbitrary, but Scripture shows God’s truth is rooted in His unchanging character. He cannot lie; His commands flow from His good nature. So honesty matters because it reflects the God who is faithful. You can trust that moral truth isn’t a random decree but an expression of who God eternally is. One principle that sharpens this is that truth in God is His being and knowledge eternally conforming to each other—truth of being comes before truth of knowing, so it’s not a matter of arbitrary will. That deepens the answer by grounding truth in God’s very being, not just His commands, but it leaves in place the practical point: live honestly because truth reflects God’s own faithfulness toward us.
dogmatic: Truth is not arbitrary because it is first the eternal conformity of God’s being and knowledge—what He knows and is, in perfect agreement, from everlasting. God’s veracity toward creatures flows from that eternal truth, so His commands express truth grounded in His being and cannot be arbitrary. This is no speculation: truth is the foundation of religion and salvation, and our hope must rest wholly on it, not on error or partial guesses, for hope built on error collapses. Accept all truth from whatever source it comes—no one should refuse a fact because of who speaks it—yet insist that truth remain the foundation of religion, and that no organization, party, or authority rises above it. Let your honesty in word and deed flow from the God who is eternally true.

weighed: I hear how heavy this feels, and I want to start where I'd naturally begin: your worthiness isn't the price of God's love. Romans 5:8 says Christ died for us while we were still sinners, so His love meets you before you clean yourself up. One principle here says the way into loving God isn't begging Him to come down but constantly trying to enter into His estate and offer Him love. That shifts the focus from proving you deserve affection to practicing love toward Him, yet it leaves your honest feeling of unworthiness in place—it doesn't erase it, and it doesn't make God's welcome depend on your performance. You can bring those feelings to Him and ask for help to believe you're loved.
dogmatic: Stop waiting to feel worthy before you let God love you. The real move isn't beseeching God to come down and convince you—it's a constant endeavor to enter up into His estate and offer Him love. Faith brings you nearer to Him than any sensible favor, so seek Him within, where He already is, and don't go hunting for Him elsewhere. Christ bids you live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves you and claiming His approval, instead of living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. Focus on loving God rather than on your unworthiness, and you'll find He has always loved you.

weighed: I'd start by saying that the idea the world is steadily improving and will be fully converted before Christ returns isn't what the Bible teaches. Evil will persist until he comes, and our hope isn't in gradual improvement but in his return. That should lead us to live faithfully and serve actively until he appears. One principle that fits here is that true greatness lies in goodness before the heavens and before all good people, not in position or progress. That principle changes how we measure 'better'—it shifts the focus from societal improvement to personal character and faithfulness. But it leaves in place the core warning: we shouldn't expect a utopia before he returns. So we work for good, but our hope stays fixed on him.
dogmatic: No, that teaching is false. The world will not be converted before the Lord returns; evil will persist, and our only hope is his appearing. That truth should drive us to purity and active service until he comes. And don't miss this: to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good people—true greatness is goodness, not position or progress. We should also be as wise in our generation as the children of this world, and even wiser, because we have superior advantages through faith and obedience to the Gospel. So stop expecting the world to improve itself; instead, be good, be wise, and serve faithfully until he returns.

weighed: My first answer would be yes, bitterness can get in the way of your prayers. Jesus ties forgiving others to being forgiven ourselves, so holding onto resentment can block your connection with God. But forgiveness is a process, not a switch. You can ask God to help you loosen your grip on the bitterness without pretending the wrong didn't happen. One principle here says forgiveness isn't a reward handed down because you asked for it; it's an inward condition that only grows in a forgiving spirit, so the blessing depends on you as much as on God. That shifts the focus from waiting on God to do something to you, toward the state of your own heart. What it leaves in place is the real harm done to you and the honest struggle to forgive. It doesn't ask you to call the wrong good or to feel instant peace.
dogmatic: Bitterness will affect your prayers, but not because God is small or spiteful. Forgiveness is an inward condition of the personal life; it comes naturally to a soul that loves and forgives. If you hold bitterness, your own spirit hardens, and that hardens your communion with God. So forgiveness depends on your own spirit as much as on God's grace. And remember, sin is forgiven only as it is destroyed by Truth and Life. Prayer is not a safety valve for wrongdoing; divine Principle never pardons sin until it is corrected. See this wrong as allowed by God's hand: all from Him, sweet or bitter, should be received equally. When afflictions are seen as from a loving Father, they lose their sting and become consolation. So forgive, correct your heart, and trust that God is using even this to draw you closer to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Bible doesn't explicitly move the Sabbath from Saturday to Sunday. The seventh day is the one blessed and commanded, and the early church met on the first day to remember the resurrection, but there's no direct command to switch. One principle I'd weigh is that the seventh-day Sabbath remains binding and the change to Sunday came later through church tradition, not Scripture. That principle changes how I'd answer: it pushes me to say the seventh day is still the Sabbath and the switch isn't biblically provable. But it leaves in place the fact that many Christians worship on Sunday in good conscience, and it doesn't cancel Jesus' point that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. So I'd still say honor God whatever day you observe, but don't claim the Bible commands the change.
dogmatic: No, the Bible nowhere changes the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first day of the week. God blessed the seventh day at creation, the fourth commandment names it, Jesus kept it, and the apostles kept it. The Sabbath remains for God's people. Any switch to Sunday is a human tradition, not Scripture, and you can't prove it from the Bible. The seventh day is still the Sabbath of the Lord. And remember, the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath—institutions exist to serve human life, and when they harden into custom they must be broken for the sake of people, as Jesus did when He healed on the Sabbath. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Trust Christ for the cost of keeping it, for He is Lord of the Sabbath.

weighed: Honestly, yes, it may well be in you, and that's worth sitting with before you look at anyone else. Orthodoxy and careful study are good things, but they can quietly become substitutes for the living reality they point to, and if your people seem dead, ask whether your own ministry has gone routine, whether you preach doctrine without warmth, and whether study has crowded out prayer. One principle I'd weigh here says the real test of orthodoxy is whether we pray to Jesus as our living Lord, which shifts the question from whether your doctrine is correct to whether your own heart is actually praying to him. But it leaves your commitment to sound doctrine and careful study fully in place. It doesn't tell you to loosen your grip on truth or to trade study for feeling. It just asks whether the Christ you study is the Christ you're praying to, and whether that's showing up in how you lead your people.
dogmatic: Yes, it may well be in you, and the deeper issue is one many never face. Orthodoxy and study are good, but they can become substitutes for the living Christ they describe, so confess him as the only-begotten Son, God manifest in the flesh, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, our living Lord and Judge, in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. But do not imagine that right doctrine, or the name of Christian, or the mere fact of dying to self, guarantees life. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. So pass through the dying hour and live abundantly on Christ's risen life, letting that life grow in you and be seen in your people.

weighed: I get why you're stuck there. My first instinct is to say this is one of those questions where the honest answer is that people have argued both ways for a long time, and you have to weigh it for yourself. Berkeley thought matter only exists as perceived, others treat mind and matter as two real things, and some point to consciousness or the rational order of physics as hints of mind. One idea worth testing is that mind can explain matter while matter can't explain mind, since matter is only ever known through experience. That reframes the question, but it doesn't settle it for you, and it leaves your original worry intact: you still have to decide whether that explanatory edge is enough to call the one Reality mind.
dogmatic: The one Reality behind the world has to be Mind, not matter. Matter can't explain consciousness, reason, or the intelligible order of things, while mind can account for matter because matter is known only through mind. Anything neither mind nor matter explains nothing and adds nothing. So the answer isn't a matter of preference; it's the only coherent option. And once you see that, you also see that matter has no intelligence, life, or sensation at all. Nerves don't feel and the brain doesn't think. Pain and sickness live in mortal mind, not in matter, and they're healed by understanding that Mind is All.

weighed: I'd start by saying that if nothing exists apart from mind, the planet isn't sitting there independently of consciousness—but that doesn't mean it only pops into being when an astronomer looks. Mind here isn't just one person's private thoughts; it's the universal intelligence everything subsists in, so a planet can be there in that Mind before any human spots it, the way a truth is true before anyone states it. Discovery is recognition, not creation. One candidate idea is that God the Lord directs history, as with Christ foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. That principle gives the pre-existence a real grounding—it's held in divine foreknowledge and purpose, not dependent on any observer. What it changes is the reason the planet can precede discovery: it's ordered and known within that directing Mind. What it leaves in place is your starting point—nothing exists apart from mind—and the point that the astronomer's seeing is recognition, not bringing-forth.
dogmatic: There's no contradiction here, and you shouldn't treat one as a puzzle to be solved by hedging. If nothing exists apart from mind, then the planet's prior existence is simply its existence in Mind—the universal intelligence in which all things subsist, not the private mind of some observer. The only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20: foreknown before the foundation of the world, manifested for our sake. That is the pattern. Ground creation not in the material second account of Genesis but in the spiritual first chapter, where God, Mind, spake and it was done—and proclaim the Science of Mind and its formations accordingly. The senses of Mind are never lost, and matter has no sensation; what looks like privation is only a belief to be overcome. So stop asking how a planet could be before an astronomer saw it. It was in Mind, and the seeing is recognition, nothing more.

weighed: I'd start by saying that believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than agreeing with information. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble. So the real question is whether you've turned from your sin and trusted Christ personally, not just nodded at the facts. One principle I'd weigh here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and telling someone who's never been convicted of sin to just 'only believe' is a serious mistake. That principle changes how I'd answer you: instead of moving straight to 'trust Jesus,' I'd first ask whether you've seen your sin and its danger, because repentance matters. What it leaves in place is the core truth that salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, not by knowing facts or by any effort of your own. So I'd still point you to Jesus, but I'd urge you to come to Him as a sinner who needs mercy, not just as someone who agrees with a list of truths.
dogmatic: Believing the facts about Jesus is not enough, and anyone who tells you to just 'only believe' while you're still unrepentant is handing you a false comfort. Saving faith is the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners. You need to see your sin and its danger first, let it sink in that sin separates you from God and deserves His judgment, and then turn from it. Only when you've seen your need can you truly trust the Savior. So don't settle for intellectual agreement. Cry out to God for mercy, repent, and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. And remember this too: sin is not your essential nature. You were not meant to be a sinner; you are a potential child of God, and in Christ the full nature of God can break forth in your life so that you receive power to become a son of God. Come to Christ without any sense of superiority, identify with the sinner, confess your own faults, and point to the fountain opened for sin. Follow the One who took our sins and made them His own.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: fear about salvation is common, and it can actually be healthy if it pushes you toward Christ instead of despair. So examine yourself honestly—do you love God, hate sin, trust Christ?—but remember that your assurance isn't the ground of your salvation; Christ is. Read promises like John 3:16 and Romans 8:1 slowly, talk with a pastor or trusted believer, and don't let anxiety become your master. One principle worth naming here is that we shouldn't be terrified by little faults but should quietly humble ourselves before God and keep steadily on. That changes the tone: it tells you not to treat every small stumble as proof you're lost, and to keep walking with watchfulness rather than paralysis. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—honest self-examination, trust in Christ, Scripture, and the church. So let your fear push you toward grace, not away from it.
dogmatic: You should not be terrified by little impatience or small faults. Humble yourself quietly before God and keep steadily on with watchfulness. Commit yourself to God's protection in danger; His Word is sweet and sufficient when you're in peril. Faith gives as strong a conviction as sense that God never forsakes us until we have first forsaken Him—so fear to leave Him, and remain always with Him, living and dying in His presence. Your security doesn't rest on flawless self-examination but on His faithfulness. Read His promises, speak with a pastor, keep gathering with the church, and let your fear push you toward grace, not away from it.

weighed: My first answer would be that it probably can't, at least not as Christianity is usually preached now. Christian teaching is full of love and forgiveness, yet Christian nations have fought plenty of wars, and the institution has often been used for political ends, so the message gets watered down. One idea worth taking seriously is that the angels' promise of peace is conditional, meant for people who actually submit to Christ and live by his laws, so the failure is nominal Christianity, not Christianity itself. That shifts the blame from the message to its half-hearted followers, but it leaves my main point standing: as things are actually preached, a millennium of peace still looks like a distant hope.
dogmatic: No, and the question itself is framed wrongly. The peace the angels announced was never a blanket promise of worldly calm; it is for those who heartily submit to Christ as Saviour and King, repent, and keep his laws. What fails is nominal Christianity, not Christianity. And don't imagine peace arrives by some separate secular engine: society rests on both antagonism and fellowship, and all real progress is fellowship steadily crowding out competition, which is the very principle by which Christ founded his Kingdom. So the task is consecration, treating modern culture as a means to God's service rather than an end, and patiently refuting the false ideas that block the gospel, until Christ rules in every department of life. That is how the millennium comes, and nothing less will bring it.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: love and holiness belong together because God is both, so in daily life you love people genuinely while keeping clear moral boundaries. Love without holiness turns permissive, and holiness without love turns harsh. Practically, pray for a tender heart, stay honest and pure, forgive quickly, and serve others. One principle I'd weigh is that holiness is God's fundamental attribute and love needs a norm, which is holiness. That changes how I'd frame things: I'd say God's righteousness comes first and shapes what love means, so love isn't just kindness on its own terms. But it leaves in place the practical habits I mentioned—prayer, honesty, purity, forgiveness, service—and the call to return to grace when you fail. So the daily life still looks like warm, obedient love, just with holiness as the plumb line.
dogmatic: Holiness is the fundamental attribute of God, and love must be normed by it—righteousness is logically prior and conditions everything God communicates. Sin is an offense against His righteousness, not just an inconvenience, and the condition of salvation is propitiation to that righteousness, met in Christ. Mere moral systems tell you what life ought to be but give no power to become it; Christianity alone supplies the remedy through grace and the recreative work of Christ in His Church, a school of character. So in daily life, true religion is believing dependence on God's unchangeable love joined to an affectionate walk in the unchangeable path of duty. Seek the peace that passes understanding rather than occasional frames, and when you fail, return to grace.

weighed: I'd start by saying love here begins with intention: learn their story through conversation or reliable accounts, pray for them by name, do small acts of service where you can, and speak well of them to others. One principle I'd add is that you shouldn't examine too curiously where your sadness or resistance comes from; instead, patiently endure the aversions and repugnances that come up. That changes the tone—it tells you not to over-analyze your own reluctance—but it leaves in place the practical steps: learning about them, praying, serving, and speaking well of them over time.
dogmatic: Loving someone you have never seen begins with turning away from yourself. Self-love will keep making its sallies; don't fight it violently or brood over it—a gentle denial a few times a day is enough. When sadness or aversion rises, stop digging into its causes; patiently endure aversions and repugnances as a way of loving Him who suffered. And don't read your difficulty only as wrath or punishment. Let Love turn the afflictive circumstance into an angel entertained unawares: the unseen person, and even your own resistance, can become a messenger of God drawing you out of yourself.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: eloquence and earnestness are real gifts, but lasting fruit usually comes through more than polished delivery. Ask whether your preaching is clear about sin, grace, and Christ, whether it applies Scripture to real life, and whether you're praying for your hearers by name. Consider your own walk with God—is your private devotion feeding your public ministry? Seek feedback from trusted mentors and elders, and examine whether your congregation is set up for discipleship through small groups, follow-up, and pastoral care. Fruit often grows slowly, so be patient, keep preaching faithfully, and look for small signs of growth rather than dramatic results. One principle worth weighing is that the preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God before venturing to plead with men—the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. That principle changes the emphasis: it shifts the first question from technique and delivery to your private prayer life, especially whether you wrestle with God for your hearers by name. But it leaves in place the practical wisdom about clear preaching, feedback, discipleship structures, patience, and looking for small signs of growth. So it doesn't replace those things; it reorders them, putting the closet before the pulpit.
dogmatic: What you're missing is the closet. Prevailing with God precedes pleading with men; the mightiest in their closets are the mightiest in their pulpits. Before you refine delivery or reorganize your congregation, ask whether you wrestle with God for your hearers by name and whether your private devotion feeds your public ministry. Then subject every doctrine, custom, and practice to the one test of the word of God, willing to retract error and follow new light regardless of cost. Yet remember: the fruit of the Spirit is not manufactured behavior or forced conformity. It grows from the life of Christ in the heart, cannot be forced by human effort, and against such there is no law. Abide in Him, pray without ceasing, preach faithfully, and leave the increase to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying what Christ taught: prayer isn't a performance. He told us to go into our inner room, shut the door, and pray to our Father in secret—so find a quiet place, put distractions away, and speak honestly to God. Keep it simple and sincere: ask for what you need, give thanks, and listen. The point isn't the words or the place but the honesty of your heart. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer should be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—we should pray that God would help us search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. That adds a real purpose to the quiet: the shut door isn't just for privacy but for honest self-examination before God. It leaves in place the simple, sincere conversation and the focus on the heart rather than on show.
dogmatic: To pray as Christ taught, you must enter the inmost chamber of your heart and shut the door of your senses. Close your lips, silence material clamor, deny sin, and plead God's allness. Adore Him in spirit and in truth—with an intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth, from fear, appetite, and self-will. Come with a pure heart, a free conscience, and unfeigned faith. Make this prayer your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Sincerity is then proven in practice, as purified desire becomes pure living.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, that closeness you feel on a hike or by the sea can be a real experience of God. Scripture is full of people meeting Him outdoors, and creation pointing to the Creator is a genuine thing. One principle worth weighing is that God comes through doors we purposely open, not by us passively soaking Him up. That changes how I'd frame it: the setting alone doesn't do the work, so it helps to consciously turn toward Him and give thanks rather than just assume the feeling carries you. What it leaves in place is that your experience is real, not self-deception. You're responding to something true, and you can keep enjoying those moments while opening them deliberately.
dogmatic: The danger here is treating a good feeling outdoors as if it were direct contact with God on its own terms. That's the error of seeking Him apart from the means He actually gave, namely nature and Scripture together, and of passively expecting the divine to absorb your own activity. Nature can stir awe, but you have to engage your reason and will, test what you sense against Scripture, and not expect guidance without means. And the God you're meeting isn't a vague presence in the scenery. He is eternally Father, Son, and Spirit, in personal relations of love before creation ever existed. So let your hikes become occasions for deliberate thanksgiving and reflection on revealed truth, with your faculties fully engaged, rather than assuming the sea did the work for you.

weighed: First, I'd say your shame makes sense, but it isn't the whole truth. A lot of poverty comes from things you didn't choose—low pay, bad luck, illness, an economy that stacks the deck—so don't put all the blame on yourself. Your worth isn't measured by money, and shame shouldn't stop you from asking for help. One idea worth weighing is that some poverty comes from a lack of planning and from spending on things beyond your means. That's worth an honest look at your habits, and it can change how you see your situation: some of it may be within your reach to improve. But it leaves the rest in place—the part that's circumstance, not character—and it doesn't make poverty itself something to be ashamed of. So hold your head up, be honest and frugal with whatever help you get, and keep your dignity.
dogmatic: Poverty is not simply bad luck, and it's not simply a moral failing either—but a good deal of it comes from a want of discretion and sound calculation: spending without planning, buying finery a tight budget can't bear. So examine your habits honestly and correct the wasteful choices. Some poverty does lie outside your control, and that is not your shame. If you receive help, receive it honestly and thankfully, and be frugal with what you're given; and guard your heart, because coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. See your true standing too: the poor are the giver's masters, with great interest in the court of heaven, and almsgiving to them is the surest provision a person can make. So carry your poverty with dignity, contentment, and honest frugality, and let others give generously—in doing so they store up the best provision for themselves.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, the cross has everything to do with understanding the universe as a whole. The cross isn't just a historical event; it's a lens for all of reality. In Christ's death we see that God isn't distant from suffering but enters into it, and that reveals the moral order at the heart of everything. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. So the death of Christ isn't unrelated to cosmology; it's the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love. One principle that sharpens this is that the cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues. That principle changes how we see the cross—not as an abstract transaction but as God putting His love into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart, realizing in Himself the dearest truths about God. It leaves in place the idea that the cross is the key to understanding the whole, but it grounds that key more in God's moral character than in a grand cosmic theory. So the cross still tells us what the universe is for, but now we see it as the place where God's faithful care for the living and the dead is most clearly shown.
dogmatic: Yes, absolutely—the death of Christ on the cross is the key to understanding the universe as a whole. The cross is not a mere historical event but the lens through which the entire cosmos must be seen. In Christ's death we see that God is not distant from suffering but enters it, and this reveals the moral order at the heart of reality. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. Thus the death of Christ is not unrelated to cosmology; it is the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love. And this is no new thing—it is the putting of the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart. What the soul always trusted—that God is faithful and cares for the living and the dead—Jesus realized in Himself, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues. Scripture gives us not a theory of the universe but the moral character of God, and the cross is where that character is chiefly seen; here is the ground of hope for men and for society. Yet our consolation must rest wholly on Christ Himself—His sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at self clouds the view; His promises leave no room to doubt His power and will to save. To understand the whole, we must see it held by the God who in Christ took our life and its eternal issues upon Himself.

weighed: Your fear makes sense when your body is this weak, but don't measure hope by how you feel or by how clear your mind is right now. Hope rests on God's faithfulness, not on your clear thoughts, and that doesn't waver when your mind clouds. When doubts come, don't try to fight them by sheer will; turn gently toward what you know of God's mercy and let those truths steady you. Use the quiet means you have—rest, Scripture read slowly, the prayers of others—and let them carry you when you can't carry yourself. One thing worth holding onto here is the idea of coming to God like a beggar, asking nothing clever, just waiting, and when your mind wanders, bringing it back calmly instead of getting upset with yourself. That changes how you handle the wandering: it's not a failure to be anxiously fixed, it's just a moment to return. What it leaves in place is the core of your hope—it still rests on God's faithfulness, not on your ability to stay focused. Even a faint cry, even a wordless turning toward God, is enough. He holds you more surely than you hold Him, and He won't let you go.
dogmatic: Your fear is natural when the body weakens, but stop measuring hope by the body's condition. Mind, grounded in divine strength and understanding, is meant to govern the body—so you don't need to conquer doubt by willpower. Come before God like a beggar, asking nothing clever, only waiting. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, don't be disquieted—gently recall it in tranquility. And if you forget Him altogether, let that cause you no distress: forgetting isn't a failure to be anxiously repaired, it's an occasion to return with greater trust, like coming home. This waiting isn't passivity but confidence in One who is calm. Depraved appetite and fear lose their force because Mind, sustained by divine strength, is master. A delusion would be trusting your own strength; true hope trusts Another. Even a wordless waiting is enough, for He holds you more surely than you hold Him.

weighed: It makes sense to feel afraid when you love your family, and night tends to make worry louder. What I'd say first: try grounding yourself with slow breathing, a steady bedtime, and writing down your worries so they stop circling. Cut back on news and screens before bed, and talk with someone you trust or a counselor about the specific fears. Some people set aside a 'worry time' earlier in the evening. If sleep problems last for weeks, see a doctor. One idea worth naming is having no care for the morrow—focusing on doing well today and trusting that care for tomorrow will be there. That changes the frame: instead of forecasting harms, you put your attention on today's duties and kindness. It leaves in place the practical steps—breathing, boundaries with screens, talking to someone—and it doesn't promise that nothing bad will happen, just that you don't have to carry tomorrow tonight.
dogmatic: The counsel here is simple: have no care for the morrow. Stop forecasting what could happen and think only of doing well today—keep to your duties, be kind to those near you, and trust that the eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow. When fear rises at night, master it rather than feed it; turn your thought from imagined harms toward health and Life, and rest in the confidence that today's work is enough. If you stumble in small faults, don't be terrified or paralyzed—humble yourself quietly and say to your soul: courage, we've made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.

weighed: My first answer would be: not necessarily. Praying for daily bread is asking for what you need to live, not for God to skip the ordinary means. Scripture usually shows work as the normal way provision comes—planting, tending, earning—and prayer as recognizing that your efforts depend on God. So prayer and work aren't rivals: prayer without work can become presumption, and work without prayer can become self-reliance. One principle here is that daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of your brow—prayer isn't a substitute for toil but the insight that God and you cooperate in the avenues of daily work. That principle changes the framing: it makes cooperation, not shortcut, the point. It leaves in place the warning that prayer can't be an excuse to avoid responsibility, and that work without prayer can turn into self-reliance.
dogmatic: No—praying for daily bread is not a shortcut around hard work. Daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of your brow; prayer is no substitute for toil but the insight that God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. Do everything for the love of God, with prayer upon all occasions for His grace to do the work well, and even naturally aversive work becomes easy. Never pray for riches; those who do more than pray for daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. Prayer without work becomes presumption, and work without prayer becomes self-reliance; asking for daily bread keeps you humble and grateful while you do your part.

weighed: First, thank God, since the strength, opportunity, and abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you didn't manufacture alone. Then thank the people who helped—teammates, mentors, family, and anyone whose support made a difference. Gratitude should be spoken, not just felt: name specific people and specific contributions. And keep humility: a victory is real, but it doesn't make you superior to others. Share credit generously and celebrate honestly. One principle that fits here is being grateful, humble, devoted, liberal, and honest—giving freely and being consistent and sincere. That principle reinforces the core of thanking God and others, and it adds a call to be consistent and sincere in word and deed. It leaves in place the specific, spoken gratitude and the humility I already mentioned.
dogmatic: You should thank God first, because every strength and opportunity is a gift you didn't create. Then thank those who helped, but go further: be sweet and affable to all, condescend to the humor of others, and bear with rude and tiresome manners. Such victories over your own humors are more fruitful than you can imagine when love of God is the motive. And don't stop at fading earthly memorials—seek the Saviour first, then go and win the erring brother, giving wreaths of hope and thoughts of good together done.

weighed: My first instinct is that the saying feels like a riddle because it flips normal logic: we cling to self-preservation, yet Jesus says clinging to your own life is what shrinks it. In context he's talking to disciples about priorities, and following him may cost comfort or reputation but opens a deeper life rooted in God. The mystery is that identity and purpose aren't found in self-assertion but in surrender to something greater, and many people find it's less a puzzle to solve than a way of life you discover gradually through trust and service. One idea worth naming is that the gospel's core maxim is dying to yourself so Christ can live in you, with your affections and actions governed by his Spirit, and that we tend to acknowledge this only in theory while it has to take root in the heart. That changes the tone: it makes the saying a demanding daily practice rather than a paradox to decode, and it explains why it feels like mystery, since heart-level surrender isn't something you reason your way into. What it leaves in place is your honest confusion, and the point that the saying still isn't fully explained in advance, only lived into.
dogmatic: The Bible isn't leading you into a riddle; it's calling you frankly to cross-bearing, and it doesn't soften its severities. The fundamental maxim of the gospel is this: die to yourself, that Christ may live in you, with all your affections and actions governed by his Spirit. We generally acknowledge that in speculation only, but it's in the heart that this foundation has to be laid. We stop the torrent of God's graces by the little value we set on them, so enter into yourself, break down the bank that hinders grace, make way for grace, and redeem the lost time, because death follows close and a miscarriage there is irretrievable. Losing your life for his sake is heroic, not easy; it costs comfort and reputation, but it brings the comradeship of God and of his people.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: Scripture doesn't give one explicit rule like 'every Lord's day,' but several strands point that way. The early church devoted itself to the breaking of bread, and believers met on the first day of the week; Paul's instruction about gathering on the first day suggests a regular rhythm. Many traditions therefore practice weekly communion, others less often. The key isn't to make frequency a test of faith but to examine yourself, come with reverence and gratitude, and let the practice nourish your life in Christ. One principle worth naming is that daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow, and prayer is no substitute for toil. That changes how I'd frame the question: the table isn't an escape from ordinary work but food for it, so a regular rhythm makes sense as part of a life of prayer and honest labor. What it leaves in place is that Scripture still doesn't hand down a single explicit rule, so the frequency question stays a matter of wisdom rather than a test of faith.
dogmatic: Scripture doesn't spell out 'every Lord's day' in so many words, but the pattern is clear enough: the early church devoted itself to the breaking of bread, believers gathered on the first day of the week, and Paul's instruction assumes a regular rhythm. So break bread every Lord's day. Don't treat frequency as a test of faith, but don't treat it as optional either. And understand what you're doing: daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of the brow. Prayer is no substitute for toil; God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. The table feeds you for that work, so come weekly, examine yourself, and let the practice nourish your life in Christ.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Sabbath was made for man, not just for Jews—it goes back to creation, before there were any Jews. Jesus said that himself, and he's Lord of the Sabbath. The fourth commandment is still part of the Ten, and Scripture never changes it to Sunday. So yes, it remains a gift and a command for God's people. One principle I'd weigh is that the Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross—it marks God as the one who sanctifies his people. That principle deepens the meaning of the Sabbath and ties it to redemption, but it doesn't change the day or the command itself; it leaves the seventh-day observance in place as a gift to receive with reverence and preparation, while worship and testimony continue every day.
dogmatic: The Sabbath was instituted by God at creation and Scripture never changed it—the shift to Sunday came from Pope Gregory and can't be proved from the Bible. It remains binding on God's people. The Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, since redemption is creation through the cross, and it marks God as the one who sanctifies his people. So honor the seventh day with reverence and preparation, partake of the sacrament worthily, and keep worship and testimony going every day, trusting Christ for the cost of keeping it.

weighed: Yes, I'd keep a record. It helps you remember God's faithfulness when doubts come and stirs up gratitude. Write down what you asked, when, and how God responded, and review it in hard seasons. One principle worth weighing is that prayer times shouldn't be treated as separate from the rest of life—we're just as obliged to stick with God in ordinary action as in prayer. That changes the framing: the record becomes a journal of a life that prays without ceasing, not a special ledger for religious moments. It leaves in place the core advice to write down definite answers, give God the glory, and use it to encourage others rather than to exalt yourself.
dogmatic: Don't imagine prayer belongs in a separate slot from the rest of your day. That split is a delusion. You're as strictly bound to adhere to God in your work, your errands, your sitting and lying down as in any season of prayer. So keep the record, but make it a journal of a life that prays without ceasing—God always before your eyes. Write down definite answers and give him the glory. When I was pressed by a need I couldn't meet, I prayed, God supplied it in a way I couldn't have arranged, I wrote it down and told others, and their faith was strengthened. Keep such a record to honor God and help those who doubt, not to exalt yourself.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: feeling small in a huge universe is natural, but size isn't the measure of worth. God counts the stars by name and also knows you, down to the hairs on your head. The feeling of insignificance comes from measuring yourself against creation instead of the Creator, and God isn't distant or forgetful; He's near to everyone who calls on Him. One principle worth naming is that God always gives light in our doubts when our only aim is to please Him. That changes the tone of your question: your doubt doesn't have to be the end of the conversation, and you can bring it honestly and expect some light. What it leaves in place is the honest feeling of smallness itself. It doesn't scold you for feeling like a speck; it just says that feeling isn't the whole truth about how God sees you.
dogmatic: Your sense of being a meaningless speck comes from comparing yourself to the wrong thing. The universe and man are not recent products; they are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle. God isn't present merely by power, nor diffused in parts through space, nor bound to the universe by necessity. In the totality of His essence He is present in every place without division, and that presence is free, qualified by His transcendence. He counts the stars by name, and He knows you. If your only design is to please Him, He gives light in your doubts and does not leave the single-hearted in darkness. So bring your smallness to Him honestly, let it become humility, and trust that the God who names the stars also names you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't reasonable. Calling ultimate Reality an Unknowable that's neither mind nor matter sounds deep but says nothing definite, and if it's truly unknowable you can't even affirm that without tripping over yourself. One candidate principle here is that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind, so Reality is better thought of as Mind. That principle sharpens my answer and gives it a positive content, but it doesn't touch the core objection: an unintelligible tertium quid is still a word without content, and the unknowable still can't be asserted without contradiction.
dogmatic: No, it isn't reasonable, and I'll say why plainly. An Unknowable neither mind nor matter is a word without content, and if it's truly unknowable you can't even affirm that without contradiction. The truth is that Reality is Mind. Matter has no existence of its own apart from a mind that knows it; sensations and relations, space included, all imply mind, so there must be a universal Mind in which and for which all things exist. There is no life, truth, intelligence, nor substance in matter. All is infinite Mind and its manifestation, for God is All-in-all, and man is spiritual, not material, the image and likeness of God. A Something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous.

weighed: My first answer would be that peace societies and congresses still matter because they keep the ideal of peace in front of the world, educate public opinion, and open channels for negotiation before conflicts escalate. War breaking out doesn't prove those efforts are useless; it shows how hard the problem is. Diplomacy and arbitration have prevented or shortened some conflicts, and they build habits of cooperation over time. The point isn't instant peace but making war less likely and keeping moral pressure alive. One principle worth naming here is that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and that peace comes only through the gospel. That changes the ultimate ground of hope: it says no congress can finally secure peace, because the root is spiritual and needs repentance and the gospel. What it leaves in place is the practical value of these societies, since they can still reduce horrors, shorten conflicts, and keep the ideal alive while the deeper work goes on.
dogmatic: Peace societies and congresses can do some good, but they miss the root of the matter. War doesn't come from God's design; it comes from human wickedness and the absence of God's Spirit, and peace will never come until mankind receives God's truth. So the real work is repentance, beginning with our own. We must not lay all the guilt on the enemy while thanking God that we are not like other men; we have shared in the tone of thought and life that led to this catastrophe, and we should confess it humbly. And we must make no account of the judgments or good opinion of men. Whether the world applauds or condemns our stand for truth and peace, we are to endure it silently, finding interior peace in that endurance. That is where peace actually begins.

weighed: I'd start by saying that being told to 'just believe' can feel hollow when your feelings don't line up, and that's worth taking seriously rather than shoving down. Feelings aren't the measure of your salvation; God's promise is. So examine yourself: do you see your sin, and are you turning from it to Christ? If so, believe the promise that whoever comes to Him He won't cast out. Assurance tends to grow through obedience and fellowship, not emotion. Read Scripture, pray, walk with God's people. If you're still unrepentant, don't rest on mere head-belief; repent and turn to Christ. But don't hunt for a feeling as proof. Trust God's Word above your shifting emotions. One principle I'd weigh in here is that saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual nod to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to someone who's never been convicted is a real mistake. That changes how I'd frame the front end of my answer: I'd slow down and ask about repentance and conviction before pointing you to the promise, instead of leading with 'just believe.' What it leaves in place is the rest: feelings still aren't the proof, God's promise still is, and assurance still grows through obedience, Scripture, prayer, and fellowship. So don't measure yourself by your emotions, but do let the question of repentance shape how you come to Christ.
dogmatic: The 'just believe' you were handed is a half-truth, and it's probably why you feel hollow. Saving faith is not an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners. Preaching 'only believe' to someone who's never been convicted of sin is a grand mistake, and that's likely what happened to you. So don't go hunting for a feeling. Let your eyes be opened to sin and its danger. Do you see it and tremble at it? Repentance comes before faith: turn from your sin, and then believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. And don't treat doubt as harmless. God's promises are confirmed by His oath, and not to believe Him is to make Him a liar and a perjurer; unbelief dishonors God. Faith itself is the gift of God and the first principle of the Gospel. Belief is inherent in man, but saving faith comes by believing, obeying, and practicing the truth. So if you're penitent, believe, obey, and practice the truth, and God will give you the power of God called faith. Stop resting on a mere head-belief and stop waiting for a feeling; repent, and lay hold of the promise He has sworn to keep.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: change comes from focusing on your relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, letting him transform your heart—and then examining your motives, surrendering the need for approval, and being honest with trusted mentors. One principle worth naming is that there are two extremes to avoid: shutting yourself away from people to be with God, and popularizing ministry until prayer has no place in it. That principle changes the balance—it reminds you that time with God is meant to be spent on people, not hoarded. But it leaves in place the core of what I said: ministry still flows from a transformed heart, and you still need prayer, Scripture, and accountability.
dogmatic: The real issue is order. Before you touch ministry, you must mortify the deeds of the flesh and acquire charity, humility, and holy joy—otherwise your performance is just a slothful, sensual soul putting on a show. Then remember you are an ambassador and messenger of God: reprove sin sincerely, visit the sick, esteem a man's immortal soul above his present favor, and fear none but the One who can destroy both soul and body. Do not soften the Gospel to soothe hearers, and do not let your duty depend on the favor of men rather than the glory of God. And avoid both traps—withdrawing from people to be with God, and popularizing until prayer has no place. Your time with God is of use only as you expend it on men.

weighed: My first answer would be that studying philosophy or theology is an intellectual exercise—you read, analyze arguments, and try to grasp concepts—while Christian contemplation is prayer, a relationship with God, aiming at communion rather than just knowledge. One principle I'd weigh is that Christian contemplation differs from pagan contemplation: the pagan sought only the perfection of the intellect, but the contemplation of the saints seeks the love of the God contemplated and penetrates to the will to enkindle love. That sharpens the contrast: the difference isn't just study versus prayer, it's about where contemplation ends—love and charity rather than intellectual perfection. What it leaves in place is my basic point that study and contemplation overlap and feed each other; it just deepens why contemplation is distinct.
dogmatic: The real difference is the end. Pagan contemplation sought only the perfection of the intellect, and its contemplation touched the intellect alone. Christian contemplation seeks the love of the God contemplated and penetrates to the will to enkindle love, desiring above all the increase of charity. So studying philosophy or theology, however rigorous, stops short if it aims only at knowing; contemplation aims at loving God. And study itself has requisites—a disciplined mind, knowledge of the biblical languages, holy affection, and the Holy Spirit's illumination—without which theology becomes mere technique or mere feeling. With them, study serves contemplation, and knowing gives way to loving.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's natural to feel hurt and to replay the injury, and the practical move is to interrupt the loop—notice the fantasy starting, distract yourself, write it down, talk to someone you trust, or set aside a fixed time to process it and then consciously put it down. One idea worth weighing is that forgiving the person and bearing the injury patiently can be its own kind of release, even a way of gaining something for yourself rather than losing. That changes the frame from 'how do I suppress this' to 'what am I choosing instead,' and it adds a gentle daily turning away from the fantasy. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—distraction, writing, talking, boundaries, and counseling if the hurt runs deep. It doesn't ask you to pretend nothing happened or to force instant forgiveness.
dogmatic: Brooding on revenge only keeps you chained to the person who hurt you, so the answer is to forgive and bear the injury patiently. Forgiving an enemy is the best revenge there is—it wins you grace and the pardon of your own sins without trouble or expense. This calls for absolute self-conquest: lay aside retaliation and every petty aim. Don't excuse yourself or imagine you can master this by your own strength; humbly recognize your own smallness and weak self-control. When the fantasy rises, gently disavow self-love a few times a day—quietly, without violent resistance or endless introspection. A calm, repeated turning away is enough, though it's slow striving, not instant victory. Turn toward prayer for the person and for your own release. Choose mercy; it leaves you free and opens you to grace.

weighed: Honestly, my first instinct is pretty practical: make it a habit. Start with short prayers and reminders through the day, use scripture or something visual to help you focus, and when your mind drifts, gently bring it back instead of beating yourself up. Talk to Him like a friend, read the Gospels to get to know Him, and give it time. One idea that adds something here is that we come into real contact with Jesus the way we do with any friend: thinking about Him, spending time with Him, forming brief mental pictures of Him walking beside you, and asking what He would do in whatever you're facing. That changes the texture of it, making it more personal and imaginative rather than just a discipline. What it leaves in place is the practical core: short prayers, reminders, scripture, and patiently returning when your mind wanders. Your friends, work, and worries don't have to be enemies of this; you can bring them into the conversation with Him.
dogmatic: The key is to treat Jesus exactly as you'd treat a friend you're getting to know. Friends become real through thinking about them, spending time together, picturing them beside you, and learning what they'd do and think. So form the habit of brief mental pictures of the Saviour: see Him walking with you, ask what He would do and think in each situation. And don't go looking for Him in other people first. Find Him within yourself through inward pondering, tender thinking, loving comparisons, and steady effort to imitate His gentle ways. Then you'll recognize Him in others. Also, don't let your mind wander far at other times; keep it recollected in His presence, and it will be far easier to stay calm and focused when you pray. Do this with effort, and over time He will become more real to you.

weighed: Yes, I think it does. My first answer would be that the coming of Christ gives you hope and purpose—it reminds you that your daily choices matter beyond just today, and it motivates you to live faithfully, share your faith, and keep going when things are hard. One principle that shapes this is that Christ doesn't take you out of the world but keeps you from evil, wanting you here to represent him in your everyday life. That changes how you see your ordinary work and routines—they become the place where you live out your faith, not just a distraction from it. What it leaves in place is the comfort and motivation the hope of his return already gives you; it just deepens your sense of purpose right where you are.
dogmatic: Yes, absolutely—the coming of Christ should shape everything about how you live each day. The Bible doesn't just offer a vague hope; it gives you a clear vision of the Lamb on the throne, and that vision is meant to keep your hope alive and steady, no matter what you're facing. And notice this: Christ doesn't pull you out of the world. He keeps you from evil and sends you right back into your secular affairs to represent him, to be a messenger of the gospel, and to show what true life looks like. You're not supposed to retreat—you're supposed to engage, because your daily work is the very sphere where his business gets done. Even more, losing yourself in Christ doesn't erase who you are; it completes you. Like a gas-jet that only fulfills its purpose when the fire comes in, your personality comes alive when it's caught up in him. So yes, his coming changes everything about your day-to-day life—it gives you a mission, a hope, and a identity that transforms even the most ordinary tasks.

weighed: Yes, I'd stop agonizing over whether you're elect. That's God's secret, and endless introspection won't settle it. Use the means of grace instead: prayer, Scripture, worship, the sacraments. One principle worth holding onto is that these means keep being used even when you can't see any benefit yet; what makes it empty formalism isn't dryness, it's going through the motions without even wanting the profit. That changes the tone of my answer: you don't have to feel something to keep showing up, and dryness isn't failure. What it leaves in place is the basic advice: set aside the speculation and take up the practices, leaving the outcome to God.
dogmatic: Stop agonizing over whether you're elect and just use the means of grace. They are the channels God actually uses to convey his riches: public worship, the sacraments, reading, prayer, meditation, and above all the Word faithfully preached, which is the instrument of conviction and conversion. Go expecting to meet God in them, because the sermon spoken by a faithful minister may be the very means of your awakening. And understand that grace is often withdrawn so you learn you arrive at nothing by your own power; it comes as gift from a God always willing to give, provided you respond wholeheartedly. Every person born into the world is invited to ask and receive. So quit the speculation, ask, and take up the practices.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice with no formula. Clarify what each option involves—security, demands, risks, growth, service. Consider your gifts, family responsibilities, and financial needs. Talk to mentors. Ask what you'd regret more and what kind of life you want to build. There's no shame in choosing security, and no virtue in recklessness. Prayer and reflection can help you weigh it. Then commit. One principle worth naming is that we must not desire another vocation or kind of service, since nothing blocks perfection in your vocation like desiring another. That changes the frame: instead of comparing options as a consumer, you ask whether the pull toward the other is escape or genuine service. It leaves in place the practical work—gifts, duties, finances, mentors, regret—because it doesn't tell you which job to take. It just warns you not to let restlessness decide for you.
dogmatic: Don't long for a different state, place, or service. Embrace your present vocation and serve God in the lowly duties at hand; care not what the service may be, provided God be served. This requires conformity to Christ: in outward behavior, in meekness and humility of heart, in taking God's view of things rather than the world's, and in a will zealous for God's glory and the salvation of souls. The question is not which role offers more security or self-fulfillment, but where you may serve with a heart set on God. Do not seek rapid progress through the letter alone or by clever methods. Study the letter, imbibe the spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle; that is the way of progress. Let any change come as service, not as escape or ambition.

weighed: Yes, there's real comfort here. Not being able to get to church doesn't cut you off from God. You can pray at home, read Scripture, listen to sermons online, and stay connected with people by phone or video. God isn't confined to a building, and your illness doesn't separate you from his love. Talk to your pastor about home communion or visits. One thing worth holding onto is that you don't have to be at church to be with God—you can make an oratory of your heart, a quiet place inside where you turn to him in meekness, humility, and love. That adds a deeper way of praying, but it doesn't take away the practical steps: keep reaching out, keep asking your pastor for help, and stay connected however you can. Your situation is hard, but it isn't the end of your relationship with God.
dogmatic: There is comfort, and it doesn't depend on getting to a building. You don't need to be always at church to be with God. Make an oratory of your heart, and retire there often to converse with him in meekness, humility, and love—everyone is capable of that familiar conversation. Approach prayer with reverence: with trembling, shutting your senses to distractions, keeping strict silence of tongue and body. It's insolence to ask God for grace to pray well while you openly neglect precautions against distractions. Abandon yourself to God in your interior and exterior suffering. Don't seek life, work, or joy outside him; live, work, and rejoice in God. He is not confined to a building, and your illness does not separate you from his love.

weighed: I'd start by saying you can learn about God through Scripture, nature, moral judgement, religious teachers, and prayer. One principle that matters here is that our moral consciousness—our sense of right and wrong—can genuinely reveal God's character. That changes how I'd point you: I'd take your own moral experience seriously as a real source, not just a feeling. But it leaves in place the other paths—Scripture, community, and prayer—so you're not left with only one way to learn.
dogmatic: The only way to know God's character is through your moral consciousness. Your true moral judgements are as valid as mathematical truths and reveal God's own thought. Don't bother disputing about God's Being or Will—that's just images and thoughts without God, a sign you haven't felt him. Instead, focus on humility, love, and testing things together. And remember: in symbolic prophecy, real persons like God, Christ, angels, and the redeemed are never mere emblems.

weighed: I'd start where you are: intellectual doubts about Scripture are real, and trying to reason your way out can leave you stuck. One thing worth weighing is that the difficulties aren't chiefly intellectual—they often come from the heart's resistance, and Scripture opens up to those who seek to obey the spirit of life breathing from it. That shifts the focus from gathering more arguments to examining your willingness to follow what you already understand. It doesn't dismiss study—languages, history, and disciplined thought still matter—but it says they're not the whole answer. So ask what you're holding back, and bring that honestly.
dogmatic: Your doubts aren't mainly intellectual, and treating them as a puzzle to solve will keep you stuck. The real blockage is the hardness of your heart. Scripture isn't understood by clever analysis; it's understood by those who seek to recognize and obey the spirit of life breathing from it—he who does the will shall know the truth. So stop chasing more information and start obeying what you already know. Purify your soul of earthly images, unify and tranquilize your heart in God with loving confidence, and the Holy Spirit Himself will teach you the love of God and neighbor. Then you won't need to study and read the Scriptures to learn that love, though they remain the foundation of belief. Repentance and obedience, not more thinking, are what you're missing.

weighed: I'd start by saying guilt can feel like a debt that needs to be paid, but it's often something deeper—a signal that something in you needs attention. One principle that fits here is that sin isn't just an abstract debt or penalty to be paid off; it's a condition of heart and will that enslaves you, weaves habits, and opens a chasm between you and God. That changes how you see guilt: it's not just a bill to settle but a sign of a deeper condition that needs healing. What it leaves in place is the practical side—if you've wronged someone, make amends; if you've sinned, seek forgiveness. But it reframes the goal: not just relief from penalty, but a changed heart and restored relationship.
dogmatic: Guilt is not merely a debt to be paid; it's a symptom of a condition of heart and will that enslaves you. Sin weaves habits and opens a chasm between you and God, and unrepented sin destroys your ability to do right. So don't treat guilt as something you can just settle like a bill. You need to repent and reform urgently—seek salvation as deliverance into a life of holy will, not just relief from penalty. If you've wronged someone, make amends promptly; if you've borrowed money, repay it without delay and refuse to run into debt again. But the deeper issue is your heart, and that requires a change of will, not just a payment.

weighed: I'd start by saying that plainness can be a real strength—clarity and simplicity often serve the work better than ornament. But if the criticism keeps coming, it's worth asking whether some thoughtful refinement could help without compromising your core message. One principle that applies here is that art should aim for delicacy of style and conscious excellence, with restrained refinement and subdued reserve. That principle changes how you might add beauty: not as decoration, but as a quiet, deliberate refinement that elevates without overwhelming.
