It leaves in place your focus on purpose and audience—you still decide based on your goals and values, and you don't rush. So the answer is: consider beauty as restrained excellence, not as ornament for its own sake.
dogmatic: You should absolutely add beauty to your work, but not just any beauty—pursue delicacy of style and conscious excellence. Avoid violent impulses and incoherent passion; aim for restrained refinement and subdued reserve. Don't worry about what your critics think of you; look on them kindly and simply, and don't dwell on their imperfections. Also, remember that your amusements reveal your character, so train yourself to find pleasure in what invigorates and elevates. In short, make beauty a matter of disciplined, gentle excellence, and let that guide every choice you make.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: comparing yourself to others is natural, but it's what makes you feel like a fraud. Everyone has imperfections, even people who seem holier, so focus on your own journey instead. God sees your effort and loves you as you are; imperfections don't make you a fraud, so acknowledge them without letting them define you, and strive to improve without being too hard on yourself. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't be troubled about the imperfections of others, since dwelling on them holds us back, and should look on others simply and kindly. That changes the comparison itself: the person you envy becomes a fellow traveler with struggles and graces, not a verdict on you. It leaves your original advice in place, though: your imperfections are still human, God still loves you as you are, and you still keep your eyes on God rather than on others.
dogmatic: Stop weighing yourself against anyone's apparent holiness, because that whole habit is the fraud. Perfection isn't gained by piling up pious exercises and good works; self-love feeds on those unless you watch your heart, root out habitual imperfections, and give yourself to God without reserve. So do the real work: find and cut off the disordered habits, guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than multiplying external works. And don't sit there examining yourself to find out whether you're perfect; that examen should never be aimed at discovering whether you're imperfect, because on that point you should never doubt. Humble yourself over faults you actually find, then go on with simplicity and confidence. God sees your effort and loves you as you are.

weighed: I'd start by saying what you're feeling is common: nature can lift your heart, but it isn't the whole answer, and the thirst may be a sign you're being drawn deeper. What I'd add is this: no book, study, or someone else's story can hand you God. Those things only sharpen the appetite, like reading a menu when you're hungry. What you're missing may be the inward, personal side, a persistent, ardent desire that keeps reaching through the seasons when nothing answers back. That doesn't cancel the value of Scripture, community, or prayer. It just means they point you toward a gift you have to receive yourself, not a map someone else can walk for you.
dogmatic: Your thirst is real, and no amount of study or reading will satisfy it. A menu can't feed a hungry person, and another's experience can't give you possession of God. That possession has to be individual and inward, a gift you qualify for by persistent, ardent desire through every season when no response comes. Don't love God only in consolation and sweetness. Love Him especially in aridity, contradiction, and tribulation, remembering how He loved us amid the sufferings of Calvary. And know that finding God doesn't bring pleasure alone. It increases both joy and the power of suffering, yet joy becomes greater than pain, and Good so much greater than Evil that Evil becomes negligible to the one who has found Him. So keep seeking, inward and ardent, until the Giver Himself satisfies you.

weighed: Your fear for your children is not wrong—it shows love. Before deciding, weigh the risks carefully, talk with trusted advisers, and consider whether the danger is necessary or avoidable. It may be wise to delay, to go alone first, or to arrange safe care for your children while you discern. God does not ask us to be reckless with those He has entrusted to us, and protecting your family can itself be a faithful response. Seek peace about the call, test it in community, and only move forward when you have reasonable safeguards in place. Trusting God does not mean ignoring prudence. One principle that speaks to this is that real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances—the work hangs upon no visible support. That principle changes how you hold the outcome: you can release your children into God's care without needing to see every safeguard first. But it leaves in place the practical wisdom of weighing risks and making safe arrangements, because trusting the invisible God does not cancel the visible responsibilities He has given you.
dogmatic: Your fear is natural, but the safest place is the path of duty. God must come first—before comfort, before safety, before even the keeping of your children in your own hands. If He has called you to a dangerous place, trust them to Him and commit the danger itself to God's keeping, finding His Word sweet and sufficient in peril. Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances. The work does not hang upon visible support, human presence, or how things look; it hangs solely upon the good pleasure of God. To hang upon the invisible God is not to hang upon nothing—it is to rest on the one reality that never fails. Go where He sends, and leave the outcome to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying the highest thing you know—mind, consciousness, love—is a better clue to ultimate Reality than the lowest, like matter or mechanism, because mind can explain matter but matter struggles to explain mind. One candidate principle here is that ultimate Reality can't be matter or some unintelligible third thing neither mind nor matter; it's more reasonable to call it Mind. That principle sharpens my answer: it rules out settling for bare matter and pushes toward Mind as the least inadequate analogy. What it leaves in place is my caution that any analogy is only a pointer, and there may be more to Reality than either mind or matter captures. So I'd still say reach toward the ultimate through the best you know, not the basest.
dogmatic: You should think of ultimate Reality as Mind, full stop—not matter, and not some vague Something neither mind nor matter, which is unintelligible and pointless to posit. Mind explains matter; matter never explains mind. This Mind is Life itself, infinite and without beginning, never embryonic, never shut up in matter or bounded by form. And don't give matter any reality or power alongside Mind: God is All-in-all, and matter is only a mortal belief, a false sense with no existence or power apart from divine Mind. Begin from the highest you know, and you reach infinite Mind and Life, beside which matter is nothing.

weighed: I'd start by saying that doing a boring or distasteful job for God's sake can feel heavy, but you can offer the work itself as a sacrifice to God and ask Him to use even the dull parts for good. One idea that helps is to treat unwelcome tasks as God's business rather than your own, so you don't carry uneasiness about them. That shift changes how you carry the work—less resentment, more quiet purpose—but it doesn't remove the boredom or the need to keep providing for yourself and others. You still pray for a better attitude and look for small ways to serve others through what you do.
dogmatic: Stop treating your job as a burden you have to endure and start seeing it as God's business. Say to yourself, 'This is God's business I'm about,' and do it well without uneasiness. The trivial round and common task give you exactly what you need: room to deny yourself and a road to bring you daily nearer to God, without abandoning your neighbour or your work. Don't be in a hurry to get rich. Attend meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up so you can catch the shower when it comes. Your job is the appointed means of self-denial and nearness to God—so do it with a calm, contented, patient diligence.

weighed: What I'd say first is that failure doesn't disqualify you—it's part of learning to believe. Start small: keep honest practices like prayer, reading, and reflection, and treat each setback as information rather than a verdict. Notice what triggered it, adjust, and begin again. One day at a time, with people around you for encouragement, belief grows through repeated attempts, not through never falling. One principle here that sharpens this is that fidelity is yours while failure comes from infirmity—so be faithful in your exercises but don't be troubled or astonished when you sometimes fail. That changes the tone: it takes the sting and panic out of falling and keeps the focus on steady practice. What it leaves in place is the practical core—start small, learn from setbacks, lean on community, be patient with yourself. It doesn't excuse giving up; it just means a stumble isn't a verdict on you.
dogmatic: Stop treating your failures as the measure of whether you can believe. Belief grows through fidelity in its exercises—prayer, reading, reflection—kept day after day, and when infirmity makes you fail, don't be disquieted or astonished. But don't merely tolerate what drags you down either. Resist evil of every sort firmly, to the end, for error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. The time to trust is when all else fails; strong faith is learned by standing firm amid severe testing, and you should even thank God for the school of sorrow that teaches it. Keep the exercises, bear the infirmity without dismay, and resist to the last—then failure loses its hold and Truth prevails in you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: the misery you're seeing is real, and it makes sense to look for a system that would fix it. But socialism and shared goods mostly rearrange what's already there without touching the habits that create poverty in the first place. One idea worth taking seriously is that a community where everyone is industrious, faithful, and prudent, living within their means and making what they wear, will prosper and eventually buy out its neighbors. That changes the focus from redistribution to building real capacity, soil, time, and skill, and it gives people something to do rather than something to receive. What it leaves in place is the hard part: it still asks each person to change, and it doesn't guarantee that everyone will. So I'd say start with yourself, but don't expect any arrangement, socialist or otherwise, to do the inner work for you.
dogmatic: Socialism and a community of goods are not the answer. The answer is a community where every person is industrious, faithful, and prudent, never wanting what they cannot get, living within their means, making what they wear and raising what they eat. Labor is indispensable, and the elements of wealth are already around us in soil, time, and skill. Idleness, waste, and dependence only deepen misery. Self-denial and economy are not losses but a joyful privilege that frees your resources for the LORD and for generous giving. When you live within your means and work with your hands, you prosper not to hoard but to bless, and in time the community buys out its neighbors. Begin with yourself, and the whole community will rise in joy.

weighed: I'd start by saying whole sanctification means every part of your life—thoughts, desires, relationships, work, money, time—is brought under God's rule, with nothing held back as a private reserve. It's a lifelong process where God exposes hidden attachments and you respond by surrendering them. One principle that changes this is that sanctification is the gift of the Holy Ghost and the grace of Christ, received by faith, not human self-improvement or painful mortification. That shifts the focus from your gritted effort to God's gift, but it leaves in place the call to consent—yielding each closed compartment as He shows it—and the need for honest confession where sin is involved.
dogmatic: Whole sanctification means every area of your life is brought under God's rule, with nothing held back. But it's not chiefly self-improvement or painful mortification; it's God's gift received by faith, walking in His statutes by the Holy Ghost's own impulse rather than by gritted effort. Your part is consent—yielding each closed compartment as He shows it. Where sin is involved, confess rightly: against a person, to that person; against a family, to the family; against a Ward, to the Ward; against God, to God—while keeping private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. Know that obedience may cost you: carrying conviction into action may mean renunciation, loneliness, and human disapproval. Accept that cost for the light given, and rest in the divine fellowship promised to the obedient, who are never truly alone.

weighed: Yes, you can. Closeness to God isn't about talent or learning. Plenty of deeply holy people were simple and uneducated. What matters is honesty, desire, and faithfulness in small things. Start where you are: pray simply, read a little Scripture, and do the good that's right in front of you. Learning can help, but it's not the door. God isn't impressed by credentials and isn't distant from ordinary people. Don't let shame about your limits keep you away; bring them to him. Grow slowly, in your own place, and let your life—not your intellect—be the offering. One principle worth naming is that God places solemn value on the humble worker with one talent. That changes the stakes: your smallness isn't an excuse to stay passive, because faithfulness in the least is what counts. But it leaves the main thing in place—your lack of talent or learning still doesn't shut you out. It just means the path is faithful, humble service, not waiting until you're smarter or more gifted.
dogmatic: Yes—and don't miss why. You were not put here mainly for a career, for enjoyment, or to be seen as learned. You are here above all for personal connection with God, and the world teaches you to be shy and ashamed of that. So stop measuring yourself by talent or education. God's self-limitation—in creation, in government, in education, in inspiration, and above all in Christ—is not a defect; it is the self-limitation of love and the evidence of his perfection. He stoops, and that is his power. Nor is your littleness an exemption from service. Be faithful in the least, use the one talent and ordinary opportunity you have; God places solemn value on the humble worker, and your smallness will not excuse you. Pray simply, read a little Scripture, serve where you are, and let your life be the offering.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: church admin is real ministry, but it can quietly crowd out prayer, so treat prayer as part of the work rather than a competitor. Start small and fixed—a short morning offering, a midday pause, a brief evening review—and protect those times like meetings. You may need to delegate, say no to some requests, and simplify processes. One principle here is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that means praying for God to help you search out and reform what's amiss in your own heart, including any drivenness or pride hiding under busyness. That changes the tone of your prayer time—it's not just a slot to fill but honest self-examination before God. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: small, fixed times, delegation, and simplifying. Given your limited time, begin this week with one unhurried block and let it grow.
dogmatic: Prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an accessory squeezed in when convenient. Begin by praying that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it—especially any drivenness, pride, or neglect hiding under busyness. Understand what prayer is: a humble waiting before God like a beggar, keeping the mind in His presence and recalling it gently and tranquilly when it wanders, without disquiet. Do not let activity, public service, or fellowship substitute for secret communion. Take time to be alone with God and His word; nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Secret prayer and meditation must remain indispensable to your fruitful service, never crowded out by it.

weighed: Yes, you can. My first answer would be that peace with God doesn't depend on silence; it's a habit of the heart, so use small anchors at your desk: a brief prayer before opening email, a quiet breath between tasks, a verse you recall when the noise spikes. One principle worth weighing here is that God is the one who works, and you're only the instrument, so all your anxious striving is really distrust of Him. That changes the tone of the thing: you're not white-knuckling your way to calm, you're handing the noise and the deadlines over and letting Him carry them. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff, the anchors, the earbuds, the lunch walk, the gentle return when your mind scatters. So keep doing those small things, just rest them on Him rather than on your own effort.
dogmatic: Yes, and stop treating your techniques as the support of your peace. God is the one living Agent; you are only His instrument, and every anxious attempt to manufacture calm at your desk is distrust of Him and a kind of self-conceit. Cast all your care on Him, the noise, the deadlines, the fear of not doing enough, and serve Him in holy freedom rather than by violent constraint. When your mind wanders, recall it mildly and tranquilly, without scolding or strain, and remain always at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, for peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ.

weighed: I'd start by saying that God's unity means one essence, not one person. Christian teaching holds that God is one in essence and three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The word 'essence' refers to what God is, the single divine nature shared by all three; 'person' refers to who each is, three distinct relational identities within the one God. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. One candidate principle is that God is a Person: a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved. That principle changes how we speak of God—it rules out treating God as an impersonal force or mere substance—but it leaves in place the distinction of persons, because each of the three is recognized as God in Scripture and described as distinct. So the unity is one essence in three persons, not one person.
dogmatic: God's unity does not exclude internal personal distinctions. As in man there is diversity in unity—individual and racial—so in God there is diversity in unity, and a triple consciousness and will are consistent with a single essence. Finite consciousnesses can be integrated in one divine consciousness, and subordinate consciousnesses are integrated in man, so a triple consciousness in one divine essence is credible rather than incredible. Yet we must speak of God as a Person in the truest sense, not as a force, substance, or unconscious principle, and never use 'super-personal' as an excuse to think of God as lower than persons; all our language about God is inadequate. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each recognized as God in Scripture and are so described as distinct persons—not mere names, modes, or manifestations. So God is one essence in three persons, and that is not a contradiction but the perfection of what we glimpse in created consciousness.

weighed: Feeling overwhelmed by temptation is not unusual, especially when you are young and your desires are strong. The important thing is to remember that temptation itself is not sin; sin begins only when you consent to it. You can resist by avoiding situations that feed the temptation, filling your time with good pursuits, and being honest with a trusted mentor or friend who can support you. Prayer and Scripture can steady you. When the pull feels strongest, pause, breathe, and turn your attention to something else rather than fighting the thought directly. If you fall, do not despair—get up and keep going. Growth in self-control takes time, and God is patient with you. One idea worth taking seriously is that temptations which displease you are nothing to fear—the trouble they cause can be God's mercy refining you. That changes the tone: instead of seeing the struggle only as a threat to escape, you can see it as something God can use, so you don't have to panic when the pull is strong. What it leaves in place is the practical core—avoid what feeds it, be honest with someone trustworthy, pray, and don't give consent. It doesn't remove the need for those steps; it just steadies your heart while you take them.
dogmatic: Do not fear temptation. Temptations that displease you are harmless, and the suffering they bring is merciful—it refines the gold of your soul. Anyone who draws near to God with their whole heart will necessarily be proved by temptation and trial, so expect testing as part of drawing near. By no means give consent. Bear everything with patience, sweetness, humility, and courage, despising the suggestions as you would despise flies, since the enemy is too proud to endure scorn. Yet do not violently resist the sallies of self-love or brood over them in endless introspection. A gentle denial suffices: a few times a day, quietly disavow self-love and turn again to God, and let your very displeasure prove that your will does not consent.

weighed: What I'd say first is that an unwanted thought barging in isn't the same as you agreeing to it. The sin question turns on what you do with it, not on the fact that it showed up. One idea worth weighing says useless thoughts spoil everything and should be turned away the moment you notice they don't belong, then you go back to God. That's a real help with the practical side: don't argue with the thought or chew on it, just set it aside and turn your attention elsewhere. What it doesn't settle is the guilt question, because it's mostly about managing the thoughts, not about whether you've sinned. So the reassurance still stands: the distress you feel is itself a sign your will isn't in it. If this keeps weighing on you, talking with a trusted pastor or confessor would help, and it's worth asking whether stress or anxiety is making it worse.
dogmatic: You need to start by clearing your mind of sin and sickness, because evil thoughts have to be controlled before they control you. Useless thoughts spoil everything, so the instant a blasphemous suggestion appears, reject it and return at once to communion with God. Build a strong defence of virtue and truth, and those thoughts won't be able to lodge in your mind or pass from one mind to another. They may knock, but they can't enter where truth stands watch. Sin and disease both begin mentally, so guarding the source is your first defence. Reject the error promptly, abide in God, and the intruding thoughts lose all power to show up in your body or your conduct.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: the sanctuary in heaven is God's real dwelling place, the true tabernacle the Lord pitched and not man, and the earthly tabernacle and temple were copies and shadows of it, built after the pattern shown to Moses. Canaan isn't the sanctuary and neither is the earth; they're the inheritance and dwelling of God's people, but the sanctuary proper is in heaven where Christ ministers. One principle here is that the Holy City encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life, and is the sanctuary of God. That adds a concrete picture of what the heavenly sanctuary is like and ties it to the New Jerusalem, but it leaves my main answer standing: the sanctuary is a real building in heaven, not the earth or Canaan, and the earthly copies still point beyond themselves to it.
dogmatic: The sanctuary is a real building in heaven, the very pattern shown to Moses, which the Lord pitched and not man. The earthly tabernacle and temple were only shadows of it. The earth is not the sanctuary, and Canaan is not the sanctuary either; Canaan was merely an inheritance and a figure of rest. The sanctuary is the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, and it encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life flowing from the throne. Those are realities, not figures. And don't imagine Christ is found only by the learned or the great. He reveals Himself to lowly hearts and simple seekers, as He did to shepherds, and Heaven will stoop to guide even the simplest person to the place where He dwells.

weighed: My first answer would be that a comfort you can't release is worth looking at honestly. Comforts aren't bad in themselves, but when one becomes something you can't let go of, it can turn into a kind of dependence that narrows your freedom and your openness. The real question is whether it's become a substitute for deeper trust, something you cling to for security instead of receiving as a gift. You might ask what need it's meeting and whether that need could be met more fully elsewhere. You don't necessarily have to give it up, but hold it loosely, with open hands, so it doesn't master you. One principle worth weighing says only immortal ties can truly bless, and only in loving eyes and upon a loving breast does the soul find rest, so the pleasant earth alone can't satisfy or bind us. That changes the frame: it says even a good comfort can't be the rest your soul is looking for, so the attachment points to a deeper hunger. What it leaves in place is your freedom to keep the comfort, held loosely, and your own sense of what it's meeting for you.
dogmatic: The pleasant earth cannot satisfy the soul, and only immortal ties, love's gaze, and the breast can truly bless and give it rest. Your attachment to one comfort you cannot give up is worth examining in that light: however good it is, it cannot be the rest your soul seeks. When the loss of comfort brings pain, do not pray chiefly for deliverance, but for strength and patience to bear it, seeing even this as from God's hand. Keep both beholdings at once: the higher, which keeps you in solace and enjoying in God, and the lower, in dread and shame of self, but hold much more in the higher. So hold the comfort loosely, and let your rest be found in love's gaze and breast.

weighed: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that watching a believing child die before you is one of the heaviest sorrows a parent can carry, and it is right to grieve. Faith doesn't ask you to feel no pain; it invites you to grieve with hope, to entrust her to God's care, and to lean on prayer and the people around you. One idea worth weighing is that the childlike and the baptized are especially dear to Christ, and that their early death can be held as joy rather than something to be grudged. What that changes is the frame around your parting: it doesn't erase the ache, but it says her dying is not unmixed loss, and it frees you from feeling guilty for the grief you carry. What it leaves in place is everything you actually feel—the sorrow, the missing her, the slow work of letting go—and it leaves in place the need for prayer, for your pastor, and for the help of others, one day at a time.
dogmatic: Do not count your child's death as unmixed loss, and do not grudge what Christ has taken into His arms. The childlike and the baptized are dear to Him, sealed before the poison root ever grew, and their early death is a joy rather than a grief to be grudged. Trust her to His embrace and see her end as happier far than life. Let your grief become prayer; cleave to the one Sovereign Good, and let your soul aspire to God, dreading the least separation from Him as a most cruel death. Then what you receive, undertake, and do becomes pure and true prayer, and it becomes as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. And know the Church's discipline for what it is—a mother's fond alarm calling the wanderer home, with absolution for the heavy-laden soul.

weighed: I'm sorry you're carrying this—being criticized at church stings because you expect grace there. First, separate the comment from your worth: someone's opinion isn't God's verdict on you. Take it to prayer and ask honestly whether any part is true; if so, act on it. If it was unfair, release it—resentment keeps the wound open. You might also speak privately and kindly with the person, not to defend yourself but to understand, and set a boundary if it was harsh or public. Replaying it is natural, but gently redirect your mind each time it returns, replacing the loop with a short prayer. One principle here is that gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding injure the one who indulges in them, so the Saints should mind their own business and look for good in others. That changes how you handle the replaying: instead of rehearsing their fault, you refuse to join in fault-finding and turn your attention to what's good. It leaves in place the honest self-check and the private conversation—you still ask whether any part is true and still seek to understand.
dogmatic: You need to stop judging the person who criticized you. No one should judge his fellow unless he has the mind of Christ, and if anyone is called to chasten, they must never chasten beyond the balm within them to bind up. If the criticism came from a church leader, it is not your right to point out his supposed defects—leave judgment to God, who will judge His servants. Avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil. Mind your own business, refuse gossip and backbiting, seek and speak of the good in others, ask quietly whether any part is true, forgive quickly, and turn each returning memory into prayer. Your standing rests in Christ's mercy.

weighed: Repeating Jesus's words is a start, but not the whole of it. Words can turn into a habit you hide behind, so the real question is whether they shape how you live. Jesus warned against empty repetition and showy prayers, so pray simply and honestly, and let his teaching push you toward action—forgiving, giving, serving, telling the truth. One principle worth naming here is that his words are spirit and life, spoken long ago but still meant for all time. That deepens how you receive them: not as formulas to recite but as living words that still carry weight today. It changes the tone of your repetition—it becomes listening rather than performing—while leaving your honest efforts at obedience exactly where they were.
dogmatic: Repeating his words alone will not carry you. His words are spirit and life, spoken to people long ago yet still addressed to all time, still brightened with that same spirit and life. So receive them as living words, not as formulas you repeat. And be careful with audible, emotional prayer—it can give a moment of solemnity while quietly making you a hypocrite. The prayer that counts is silent, watchful, self-forgetful, pure, and obedient. Take his teaching on speech seriously too: swearing is a grave habit and must be broken, and mere gentle remonstrance is not enough—impose a penance for every oath. Let quiet faithfulness, not display, measure your devotion.

weighed: I'd start by saying a cross in the sky is striking, and it's natural to wonder what it means. Be cautious about reading it as a private sign or omen; it can stir wonder but shouldn't become a test of faith. The meaning of the cross is best learned from Scripture and the church: Christ crucified for our sins, God's love shown in self-giving, and a call to take up our own cross. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, read the passion narratives, and let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel. If the image moves you, let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service rather than speculation about hidden messages. One principle that fits here is that the cross shows how deeply God cares about our life and takes responsibility for its eternal outcome. That changes the focus from looking for a hidden message to trusting God's commitment to you. It leaves in place the caution against treating the sky cross as a private sign, and it still points you to Scripture, the church, and a pastor for guidance.
dogmatic: The cross in the sky is no accident. It reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues. It puts the love of God into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—the realizing by Jesus in Himself of the dearest truths about God. This is the mourner's truest comfort: the darkest hour of the cross touches the heart with softer comfort than angel's mirth, where earth's bitter herbs are tempered into sweetness by the Saviour's prayer and blood. Receive the cross as fitted to your stature, not as meaningless suffering, and trust that all God does, rightly understood, shall work your final good. Learn its meaning from Scripture and the church, and let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling no joy in giving is common, and it's worth examining why. A tenth is a good pattern, but the New Testament emphasizes generous, cheerful giving rather than a fixed percentage—so give as you are able and as you purpose in your heart, not reluctantly. To grow, thank God for what you have, remember everything comes from him, give regularly and thoughtfully, and notice the good your giving does. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it, so keep giving even when feelings lag, and ask God to reshape your heart. One principle that fits here is that giving is worship and God loves a cheerful giver—men give liberally only when giving becomes a joy rather than a mere duty. That changes the focus from hitting a number to cultivating a willing heart, but it leaves in place the value of steady, purposeful giving even when feelings are dry.
dogmatic: You should stop treating the tenth as the goal and start seeing giving as worship—God loves a cheerful giver, and people only give liberally when it becomes a joy, not a compulsion. So give as you purpose in your heart, not under guilt. To grow, thank God for what you have, give regularly and thoughtfully, and embrace self-denial and economy as a privilege that frees more for the Lord's service—the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. And don't wait for joyful feelings: count it all joy by faith, reckon the trial a blessing, fix your heart and choose to rejoice even when feelings fail, until praise becomes a habit.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's painful when hopes you've carried a long time come to nothing, and it's natural to wonder if God is behind it. Scripture doesn't show God as a capricious taker of good things; He's the giver of every good gift. Often what fails is a plan built on your own timing, and the loss can clear away what was never going to satisfy you. That doesn't mean every lost hope was wrong to hold. Bring the disappointment honestly to God, ask what He's doing in it, and let trusted friends pray with you. One principle worth weighing here is that God first puts good desires in your mind and then, by His continual help, enables you to bring them to good effect. That changes the picture: the desire itself may be from Him, not a distraction to abandon. What it leaves in place is the honesty about loss and the call to keep trusting God's character when His purposes are hidden.
dogmatic: Look, the real issue isn't whether God is snatching your dreams away. It's whether you'll keep seeking Him steadily when the plans collapse. God plants good desires in you and then, by His continual help, brings them to good effect with power. But He doesn't hand those things over for one cry, one petulant demand, or a few self-pitying tears shed only when the world fails you or sickness comes. He asks for persistent, steady desire. Your mind roves constantly, but your will is the mistress of your faculties; it must pull your anxious thoughts back and carry them to God as their last end. So stop forcing a reason onto every loss and start steadying your thoughts in prayer. Keep seeking with patience, and trust that He completes what He starts.

weighed: Yes, your moral life really does shape how you read the Bible. Jesus connects purity of heart with seeing God, so what you love and practice affects what you notice and how you respond. If you're holding onto sin or resentment, you'll tend to read defensively, looking for loopholes or ammunition. If you're growing in honesty, humility, and love, you'll read more openly and recognize God's character. So pray as you read, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading with others helps too, because they see your blind spots. One principle that deepens this is that the Bible's central teaching is about God's moral character—his power is always directed toward what is right. That changes the focus: the point isn't just that your morality affects your reading, but that Scripture is constantly moralizing your idea of God, calling you to conform to his holiness. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: keep reading prayerfully, confess, and stay in community.
dogmatic: Yes, absolutely—and the reason goes deeper than your personal habits. The Bible's whole purpose is to show you the moral character of God, whose power is bound to moral ends. From beginning to end, Scripture is the story of God moralizing his own revelation, and moral obligation is grounded in his holiness: right is right because God is it. So reading the Bible rightly demands a heart being made like his. But mere moral effort can't produce that; only Christianity gives the power for the ideal to become real—through grace, the sacraments, and the Church as a school of character. Christ's recreative work forms the pure in heart who see God. So read prayerfully, confess sin, cultivate honesty and charity, and stay in community, trusting grace to form the conscience that hears Scripture rightly.

weighed: Yes, it's right to ask God for money when mission funds run low. Scripture invites us to ask for daily bread, so bringing practical needs to him isn't wrong. What matters is the manner: ask with an open hand rather than a demand, and let the shortfall prompt honest questions about planning, budgeting, and inviting others to share the work. One principle worth weighing says believers shouldn't build up a fund for old age or future emergencies but should live day to day on the Lord's bounty, investing only in his work and the poor. That principle would push you away from building a reserve and toward trusting God for each day's supply. It leaves in place the core of my first answer: pray honestly, check your motives, seek wise counsel, and steward well what you already have. So ask boldly, but hold your plans loosely and stay accountable to the people who know you.
dogmatic: It is not wrong to ask God for money, but the manner matters, and the manner is trust without hoarding. The believer lives from day to day on the Lord's bounty, not storing up a reserve for future want, which easily becomes a snare. Make one investment: pour what you have into his work and the poor. Church funds exist for the relief of the poor, and if anyone complains that generosity impoverishes the church, answer with confidence that God will provide. Above all, do not carry on his work with borrowed money or debt when funds are lacking. Trust God alone for supplies and never go beyond what he provides. If funds are lacking for the work, then to that degree it cannot be God's work at that time. Examine your motives, seek counsel, and use faithfully what is entrusted to you, asking always for his glory and the good of those you serve.

weighed: The 2300 days in Daniel 8 point to a long period that ends with a cleansing. Many people read this as God restoring true worship after a time of corruption—setting right what has been defiled. The prophecy uses symbolic time, and interpreters differ on how to calculate it and what event marks its close. What matters most is the pattern: God doesn't leave His sanctuary defiled forever. He acts to purify and restore. One principle that fits here is that this cleansing is a work now being accomplished, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern by blood. That principle shifts the focus from future dates to a present reality—the cleansing is happening now in a way that mirrors the earthly high priest's work. It leaves in place the confidence that God is holy, judges rightly, and calls His people to be cleansed and ready. So rather than getting absorbed in disputed chronologies, you can take from the passage a trust that God is at work purifying and restoring.
dogmatic: The 2300 days of Daniel 8 point to a definite work of cleansing at their close. This cleansing is not the earth burned up—the earth is not the sanctuary. It is the heavenly sanctuary that is to be cleansed, now being accomplished after the pattern of the earthly high priest. But this work above calls for a corresponding work within: the purification of the soul from all guilt of sin and from all attachment to sin. Confession and a careful review of your sins are therefore not optional; the Sacrament of Penance and a searching examination of conscience are the most efficient means to this purification. Do not fixate on calculating dates, as though the last days must unfold slowly as in former times. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness, and focus on preparing yourself for events that are even now hastening to their close.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, not exactly. You're seeing one event regularly follow another, but that regular sequence alone doesn't show the first produced the second. We see the flame and then the heat, not the power that makes the heat. To call it a cause is to add something to the pattern, and that addition needs care. One candidate principle says causality isn't just necessary connection but activity we know directly in our own volition—the only cause we know is a conscious rational will. That changes how we read the world's patterns: we see them in light of our own experience of acting. But it leaves in place the caution that correlation isn't causation and that claims should be tested carefully rather than assumed.
dogmatic: No—what you're seeing is just constant conjunction, one thing regularly following another. But causality is not mere observed succession. We know activity directly, in the consciousness of our own volition, and we read the world's patterns in that light. This matters for how we read Scripture's promises. Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds of heaven, just as He literally ascended, as real as His first advent; spiritual interpretations that make His coming merely inward becloud the whole and leave no tangible ground for believers. And this same living faith spreads by contagion: one person may serve as a human spark to ignite the spark in another, and once kindled, the Divine Fire grows without further human help. So hold to the plain promise, test claims carefully, and do not dissolve real events into mere patterns or symbols.

weighed: Your fear makes sense, and plenty of people have felt exactly that coldness and weakness. My first answer would be: God doesn't command what He won't enable. The call to repent carries grace with it, so He gives what He asks. Still, it's easy to think you must first feel deeply sorry or wait for some bigger power before you can turn, and that waiting can become an excuse to delay. Start where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's missing. One principle here is that when you doubt whether you've offended God, you should humble yourself, ask forgiveness, and begin again with renewed promises of love and faithfulness. That changes the focus from waiting on a feeling to taking a concrete step now, but it leaves your honest sense of weakness intact. You don't have to manufacture sorrow first; you bring what you have and ask for help.
dogmatic: Your fear is understandable, but hear this plainly: you can renounce sin right now in will and purpose. You don't need to feel more, weep more, or wait for greater power before you turn. God commands repentance because He supplies the strength, so the command itself is a promise of grace. Surrender your will now, and feeling will follow afterward. When you doubt whether you've offended God, don't stay paralyzed: humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and keep pressing on. In every occasion of virtue, turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and you'll receive strength more than sufficient for what He commands. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and He will be faithful to meet a willing heart.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's robbery because it violates the owner's right to their property and swaps force for consent — property is an extension of the person, and seizing it even for a good cause treats the owner as a means and erodes trust in law. One candidate principle here is that wealth generally represents labor, industry, and talent, so taking it by force or legislation is robbery and would crush enterprise. That principle sharpens the economic case: it explains why coercion damages incentives, not just rights. But it leaves the core in place — consent, the wrong of treating people as tools, and the point that charity must be voluntary. It doesn't add anything about who counts as rich or poor, or about resentment and dependence; those still stand on their own.
dogmatic: It's robbery, plain and simple, because wealth is the fruit of labor, industry, and talent. What someone earns by their own toil is theirs, and seizing it by force or by legislation is theft under a different name. Admit the principle that need justifies taking, and you crush all enterprise — who would work if the fruit of their labor could be taken at will? And notice who actually pays their tithing: the poor are faithful and prompt, while the rich wait and wait until death overtakes them and they never pay at all. That tells you something about character, not just economics. Yet none of this excuses covetousness in the poor: those who receive help should be honest, thankful, and frugal, and to covet another's goods is as wicked as the miser's hoarding. Charity must spring from love, never be extorted by power.

weighed: I'd start by saying wandering thoughts during prayer are really common, so don't be discouraged. Gently bring your mind back to God whenever you notice you've drifted, maybe using a short repeated prayer or a single word to anchor your attention, and try to pray somewhere quiet with fewer distractions. One principle worth considering is that confessing our faults and humbling ourselves before God is a remedy for habitual wandering, and that using too many words in prayer can actually cause distraction. That principle would change my advice by adding a step of honest confession and by suggesting you keep your prayer simple and few-worded rather than wordy. It leaves in place the core ideas: gently returning your attention, reducing external distractions, not getting discouraged, and trusting that God is patient with your weaknesses.
dogmatic: Wandering thoughts in prayer should be met with humility and confession. When you notice your mind drifting, confess it to God, admit your weakness, and ask for His help. Humbling yourself opens the way for grace. Avoid many words in prayer, because a multiplicity of words often leads to distraction. Use few words spoken from the heart and stay in simple attention to God. Do everything for God without anxiety over distraction, and avoid multiplying explicit offerings that would interfere with simplicity. Remember that you need God's continual help. Pray often, be with God, and think of Him often to form a holy habit, since we must know before we can love. Through persistent prayer and holy habit, your mind will become more stable and your love for God will grow.

weighed: I'd start by saying consecration is both: something you do and something God does in you. You dedicate yourself, and God sets you apart and makes you holy. One principle that sharpens this is that we're not our own—we've been bought with a price—so our consecration shouldn't be a binding commitment we make independently, but a yielding to the Lord's claim and call. That changes the emphasis from a promise we control to a surrender we live out. It leaves in place the truth that we still actively respond and dedicate ourselves, and that God is the one who consecrates us.
dogmatic: Consecration is first God's work in you, and your part is to yield, not to bind yourself with promises. You are not your own; you were bought with a price. So keep yourself free from binding engagements, because you don't know when the Lord may call. Your consecration is a living sacrifice offered in spiritual worship—especially at the Lord's Supper—where God sets you apart. And recognize the place God has given you, and fill it faithfully, like a small screw in a great machine, pleasing Him where He has set you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pursue both, but treat holiness as the foundation, since without it your preaching can ring hollow. One principle worth naming is that sanctity of life and union with God matter far more for preaching than learning, eloquence, or natural talent, and a short fervent prayer can bear more fruit than years of mere study. That shifts the emphasis toward prayer and interior holiness as the essential preparation, but it doesn't cancel learning. You still need to study Scripture and theology so you don't misread the text, so keep studying diligently while letting holiness guide and shape how you learn.
dogmatic: Holiness is the essential qualification for preaching, full stop. Eloquence, study, and human talent are secondary at best, and a brief prayer said with real fervor can accomplish more than years of reading. So don't chase more learning as if it were the main thing. Give yourself to prayer, to union with God, and to a life of sanctity, and remember that holiness doesn't arrive all at once; it grows gradually. Help others chiefly by your good example, and let your life be the model of what you preach.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: being successful and comfortable isn't a problem in itself, but if God barely crosses your mind, you might be missing something deeper, and a lot of people find that material success doesn't quite satisfy. So I'd still suggest exploring that side of life, maybe through gratitude, purpose, or connection to something bigger. One idea that shifts this for me is that God is the one living Agent and we're only instruments, so our worry and self-reliance amount to distrust of Him. That changes the tone: instead of just adding spirituality as a nice extra, it makes your comfort something to hold loosely and your independence something to examine. What it leaves in place is that success and ease aren't wrong in themselves, and it doesn't demand you become religious overnight. It just asks whether your calm is really trust or just not looking.
dogmatic: Honestly, yes, it's a problem, and a serious one. You were not put here mainly to enjoy the world or build a successful career; you're here above all to arrive at personal connection with God, and being shy or ashamed of the spiritual is exactly what we've been taught to feel. God is the one living Agent who works, and you and I are only instruments, so all your care and anxiety is distrust of Him and a kind of self-conceit. Reading and study won't fix this either; they only whet the appetite like a menu can't satisfy hunger. What you need is the inward, personal possession of God, and that's a gift you qualify for by persistent, ardent desire through every stretch where you feel no response at all. So stop treating your comfort as the measure of a good life and start wanting Him with everything you've got.

weighed: I'd start by being honest about the hurt, because resentment usually grows when we pretend we're not wounded. Then pray for the person who wronged you, not because they deserve it but because it softens your own heart. Forgiveness isn't saying the wrong didn't matter; it's releasing the debt and letting go of revenge, and you can still keep healthy boundaries. One principle worth taking seriously is that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That sharpens things: it rules out payback and makes forgiveness a matter of obedience, not just feeling better. What it leaves in place is everything else you asked about, honest grief, boundaries, and the slow work of grace over time.
dogmatic: You cannot nurse resentment and call yourself forgiven. Learn not to be troubled by injuries, not to burn against the one who hurts you, and sincerely believe you deserve contempt rather than honor. Return meekness for insult, forgive quickly, and seek reconciliation, because refusing to forgive puts your soul in danger. A Christian is never permitted to seek revenge; patience and forgiveness outrank retaliation. Pray for those who wound you and hand the wrong to God, remembering your own need for mercy. This is not excusing evil; it is obeying Christ, who forgave those who tormented Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying that social factors like trade routes and networks really did help Christianity spread, but they don't fully explain it given the persecution and the shame of the cross. That's my prior. One principle worth naming is that religious doubt is a nearly inevitable stage for thoughtful Christians and should be met with sympathy and orderly historical presentation, not bullied away. That principle changes how I'd talk to a skeptic: instead of just asserting divine power, I'd take their natural-causes argument seriously and lay out the historical obstacles calmly. But it leaves in place the core point that the survival and growth of the church under persecution still points beyond natural causes. So I'd weigh both, study history carefully, and trust God's providence without dismissing honest questions.
dogmatic: Look, the rapid spread of the gospel despite skepticism, popular hatred, and persecution shows its divine origin—that's just the truth of it. Social causes can't account for a movement that conquered the Roman Empire in three hundred years while being mocked and crushed. Trials and persecution are necessary and expected, so meet them cheerfully, and don't coddle doubt as if it were some noble stage—press the facts and trust God to overrule the enemies. The cross was offensive, the preachers were unlearned, and yet the church grew. That's divine power, plain and simple.

weighed: Yes, I'd say comfort can absolutely become a spiritual danger, mostly by making you complacent. When life gets easy, you can drift into depending less on God and noticing less of the people around you who are hurting. But comfort itself isn't the sin—it's clinging to it, letting it crowd out prayer, service, and real relationships. So check whether your ease is quietly pushing those things aside. One idea worth sitting with: comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. That sharpens the warning—it's not just about the very rich, but about anyone comfortable, including people with a modest income whose distractions can drown out conscience. What it changes is the scope: the danger is closer to home than you might think. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—simplify, give more, engage with people who suffer, and ask God to keep your heart soft. Enjoy his gifts with gratitude, but hold them loosely.
dogmatic: Yes—comfort is a spiritual danger, and don't soften that. Comfort makes you thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. This isn't only a trap for the wealthy; it's a trap for the comfortable, whose moderate income puts a dozen distractions within reach that drown out the voice of conscience. So keep your heart under control and don't slide into over-anxiety either—trust God's providence, which will not fail to protect the obedient soul. Fasten your eyes on Christ and abide in him; he is the remedy for your trouble and the substance of all deliverance. Examine whether your comforts are crowding out prayer, service, and community. Give more, simplify, and deliberately engage with those who suffer. Enjoy his gifts with gratitude, but hold them loosely, always ready to respond to his call.

weighed: I'd start by saying that keeping up with news and entertainment isn't inherently sinful, but it can harm your soul if it becomes excessive or starts replacing more important things. Ask yourself whether it's eating time you could spend in prayer, Scripture, or service, and whether it's filling your mind with anxiety, negativity, or worldly values. The key is moderation and intention: set limits, choose content that builds you up, and prioritize your relationship with God. One principle worth naming is that the soul making no daily progress in virtue loses ground, so each year and day should find you more fervent, with particular resolutions against the occasions of sin. That changes the tone from general advice to specific daily resolve, but it leaves in place the practical checks I mentioned—limits, edifying content, accountability, occasional fasting from media—and the freedom to enjoy these things as gifts from God without letting them distract you from Him.
dogmatic: You need to hear this plainly: a soul that makes no daily progress in virtue is losing ground. General good intentions are not enough. You must form particular resolutions against the occasions of sin, and you must sometimes deprive yourself of innocent, lawful pleasures so that you take pleasure only with God. It is the stopping half-way that causes distress—living wholly worldly may bring contentment, and living regenerated brings great joy, but trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness, vacillation, and depression. Do not stop half-way. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His work in you.

weighed: Yes, there is mercy for you at the eleventh hour. God's mercy is greater than your sins, and He welcomes all who turn to Him, no matter how late. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard shows that those who come at the eleventh hour receive the same reward. Your concern is itself a sign of God's grace drawing you. One principle that matters here is that God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants; He comes in His own time, and patience in affliction is a mark of His care. That changes the tone: instead of just telling you to act now, I'd also say to trust His timing and give thanks even in this late concern. But it leaves in place the call to start now—pray, seek forgiveness, and commit to following Christ. Don't let past failures keep you from His love. Find a church community for support and accountability. Today is the day of salvation—respond to His call.
dogmatic: Yes, there is mercy for you at the eleventh hour, but don't stop at personal comfort. God is infinitely gracious and knows all your wants, and He will come in His own time when least expected. Afflictions with fortitude and patience are a plain mark of His care, so comfort yourself in Him and give thanks for all. Yet the feeling of blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive you to prayer and action rather than to rest in personal security. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. Pray with your family and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. Help God accomplish what is asked rather than expecting God to do it all. Do not excuse neglecting prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer. Let the burden for perishing souls drive you to prayer and obedience. Start now: pray, seek forgiveness, and commit to following Christ. Find a church community for support and accountability. Today is the day of salvation—respond to His call.

weighed: I'd start with both, honestly, because they feed each other. Read a passage each day, note what it asks of you, and do that. Obedience to what you already know opens your understanding to more, and study gives your obedience direction. One principle I'd weigh in is that Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so you should read it habitually and prayerfully and prefer it above other books. That changes the priority: the Bible itself, not commentaries or guides, is the main source you go to. It leaves in place the practical balance I'd suggest, reading daily and acting on what you understand, and it doesn't rule out helpful guides, just puts them in their proper place under the text.
dogmatic: Scripture is the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so read it daily, prayerfully, and systematically, and prefer it above every other book. Study it honestly alongside the textbook that serves as its key, for together they let you prove all things. Then translate what you find into obedience, because obedience opens understanding to more. But know this: study and reading are not the final teacher. Once the soul is purified of earthly images and the heart is unified and tranquil in God with loving confidence, the Holy Spirit Himself teaches the love of God and of neighbor, and you no longer need study and reading to learn that love. The Scriptures remain the foundation of belief all the same.

weighed: Feeling shame after a mistake isn't wrong—it usually means you care about doing well and about the people your work affects. What matters is that the shame doesn't turn into paralysis or self-loathing. Own the mistake plainly to whoever was affected, apologize sincerely, fix what you can, and then let the feeling soften. Humiliation is uncomfortable, but it isn't a verdict on your worth. One principle worth weighing here is that wanting to be corrected is a sign of humility—that humility's main fruit is seeing where you need correction. That changes the tone of the moment: instead of just enduring the shame, you can treat the feedback and correction coming your way as something to welcome rather than dread. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice—acknowledge the error, make amends, and don't let the shame define you. It doesn't mean you have to bare every private weakness to everyone; keep that part contained and share it only where the mistake actually landed.
dogmatic: Shame after a mistake isn't wrong—it can be the start of humility, and humility shows itself most clearly in wanting to be corrected. So welcome correction as a gift, not a threat. Be honest, though, about where confession belongs: if you wronged a person, confess to that person; if a family, to the family; if a community, to the community; and if God, to God. Don't spill your private weaknesses to everyone—keep your private failings hidden as much as you can. And if others were hurt or criticized you, forgive them and bear the injury patiently, because forgiving is the best revenge and a means of grace, gaining pardon without trouble or expense.

weighed: I'd start by saying that baptism is a meaningful step, and if you've come to faith, it's a natural next step—an outward sign of an inward commitment, a public declaration that you belong to Christ and intend to follow him. Whether you're baptized now or soon depends on your readiness and the practice of your community, so talk with a pastor or teacher, ask what baptism means in your tradition, and prepare your heart. The important thing is that your faith is genuine and that baptism expresses it rather than substitutes for it. One principle worth weighing is that baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ; in itself the rite is useless. That principle changes how you see the act—it's not a mere formality but a real means of blessing when faith is present—while it leaves in place my original point that baptism expresses genuine faith rather than replacing it, and that your readiness and your community's practice still matter.
dogmatic: Baptism is not optional—it is essential. It is to be administered by immersion, by one having divine authority, and it is the door of the Church. If you have learned the faith and believe, be baptized now. Infants are pure and cannot be baptized, for accountability comes with knowing good from evil, and water has no virtue in itself to wash away sin; keeping the commandments of God cleanses the stain of sin. Children should be baptized at the age of accountability, not delayed beyond the appointed time. Do not put it off.

weighed: I'd start by saying that sin rarely stays contained. We're connected through trust, example, shared resources, and community, so a wrong choice ripples outward in ways we don't intend. People who had nothing to do with the act may still feel its effects: broken trust spreads, bad examples get copied, resources get diverted, and anxiety or conflict grows. That's not because they're guilty, but because we live in a web of relationships. One principle that adds something here is that there's no real pleasure in sin—seeing that clearly strengthens your moral courage to master evil. That changes the motivation: instead of just feeling bad about the ripple, you recognize the false promise at the root and resist it. What it leaves in place is the basic picture of connection and responsibility, so you still make amends, stay transparent where appropriate, and change the pattern so the harm stops spreading.
dogmatic: Sin never stays contained, and the first thing you need to see is that there is no real pleasure in it. What looks like enjoyment is a false appetite, and that false appetite is exactly what spreads harm to people who had nothing to do with the act. Arouse yourself to this true view, and your moral courage will strengthen and you'll be able to master evil. Don't fall into overdone self-accusation either—see your own sin and feebleness by the sweet gracious light of God, but don't accuse yourself too much or be heavy indiscreetly. And understand forgiveness rightly: it isn't overlooking sin while the belief in it continues, but the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts out evil as unreal. So refuse the false promise of pleasure, make amends where you can, and let the understanding of sin's unreality, not despair, move you to change the pattern.

weighed: I get why total surrender scares you. It feels like handing over the keys to your life and not knowing what God might do with them. You might worry he'll ask something painful or take away what you love. But surrender isn't about losing yourself; it's about trusting the One who made you. One idea that helps here is that God permits temptations and struggles to keep us humble. That doesn't mean he wants you to fail, but it does mean the fear and resistance you feel aren't signs you're doing it wrong. They can actually draw you closer to him. So start small. Surrender one thing at a time and watch how faithful he is. Fear fades as you experience his love.
dogmatic: Total surrender frightens you because you're still trying to keep control, and that's exactly the problem. You need to stop being terrified by your little faults and impatience. Quietly humble yourself before God and keep steadily on. God actually permits evil inclinations and temptations to make you humble. As long as temptation displeases you, there's nothing to fear. Despise the temptation but embrace the tribulation it brings. Above all, fasten your eyes on Christ, not on the storm or your circumstances. He is the antidote to fear and the substance of all deliverance. Abide in him, and his presence will be your remedy. Surrender is a daily walk, so when you stumble, return to him with trust. He understands your frailty. Keep moving forward, and fear will lose its grip.

weighed: I'd say we're still waiting for the final event. The righteous dead are with the Lord right now, but their bodies await the resurrection—at the last trumpet the dead in Christ will rise first, and those of us still alive will be caught up with them. So the answer is: not yet fully, but they're safe with Him in spirit. One principle that sharpens this for me is that we shouldn't pry into what God wills for another person's end—if their love for Christ is genuine, that's enough, and our job is to follow Christ ourselves. That doesn't change the future resurrection or the hope of being caught up; it just keeps me from speculating about someone else's hidden lot and turns me back to living faithfully today.
dogmatic: No—salvation isn't a legal credit stamped on a soul while the person stays unchanged. The righteous are made righteous because they actually live, in Christ's power, the life He lived; a righteousness merely counted as theirs is a fiction and is rejected. So the righteous dead are with the Lord, but their full transformation still awaits the resurrection, when the dead in Christ rise first and the living are caught up with them. And stop prying into what God wills for another's end—if their love for Christ is true, that's enough. Follow Christ yourself. Millions of unprejudiced, simple seekers are waiting; give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's natural to fear for your family, but God calls us to trust Him even when the path seems risky, and He loves your family even more than you do. Step out in faith, but use wisdom too: pray together, seek counsel, make practical provisions. God doesn't ask us to be reckless, He asks us to be obedient. What I'd add is this: commit your family to God's keeping. That's the principle that His protection in danger is real, and His Word is sweet in times of peril. It changes the tone of the answer, from 'trust God and also manage the risk' to 'entrust the danger itself to Him.' It leaves your fear and your responsibility in place, though. You still pray, still seek counsel, still make provisions. The fear doesn't vanish, and the risk is real. What changes is who you're handing it to.
dogmatic: Commit your family to God's keeping, because His protection in danger is real and His Word is sweet when things are perilous. The soul dreads having God and naught beside, and so it flees, but what it fears as loss is really God storing all things for it at home. Faith gives as strong a conviction as sight that God never forsakes us until we first forsake Him. So fear to leave Him, and stay always in His presence, living and dying there. He will guard and guide you and your loved ones.

weighed: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. Faith in Christ is the starting point, not the reward for good behavior. God accepts you as you are and will help you overcome the habit through His Spirit. One thing worth adding: when you've gone a while without thinking of God and then slip, don't let that spiral into disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That changes the tone of the answer, from "get clean first" to "come back quickly," but it leaves the core in place: your acceptance isn't based on your performance, and freedom may still come gradually.
dogmatic: No—you don't need to be free of the habit before you believe. But don't stop at that. The truth shall make you free; understanding Truth frees from disease, sin, and evil habits. So the real answer is that freedom comes by the truth, not by willpower or human effort. When you've forgotten God and fallen, don't sit in disquiet—acknowledge your wretchedness and return with greater trust. And become more familiar with good than with evil, guarding against false beliefs as watchfully as you bar your doors against thieves. Believe now, understand the Truth, and it will set you free.

weighed: I'd say what I first thought: delaying obedience to light you've received is risky. When you know something is true and right but put it off, the conviction tends to fade, and the gap between what you know and what you do grows. Often the opportunity passes, and the cost of obedience later becomes higher. It's wise to act promptly—start with a small, concrete step, tell someone you trust, and ask for help. Delayed obedience isn't neutral; it quietly shapes your character. Acting on the light strengthens your ability to receive more. One principle worth weighing is that obedience is an eternal principle—there's never a time when obeying God's commandments isn't obligatory, and it's how we stay in touch with God and obtain eternal life. That principle raises the stakes: it frames delay not just as a missed opportunity but as a break in your connection with God. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—start small, get support, act promptly—because it doesn't tell you exactly what step to take or how to handle fear and confusion. So the core answer stands: act on what you understand, and don't let delay harden you.
dogmatic: Delaying obedience to light you've received is serious, because obedience is an eternal principle. There will never be a time in time or eternity when obedience to God's commandments is not obligatory; it is the means of keeping in touch with God, and only so can we consummate our mission and obtain eternal life. The Spirit of truth will not tolerate or forgive determined, premeditated wrong; there is no forgiveness for such without humble and most contrite repentance. So if you're putting off what you know is right, don't treat it as a small thing—it's a deliberate choice with eternal weight. Begin by checking your words, for if you gain power to check your words you will then gain power to check your judgment and thoughts. And before condemning anyone, wait until heaven clearly indicates the fault rather than judging on rumor. Act now on the light you have, with contrite repentance for any delay, and let obedience keep you in touch with God.

weighed: My first answer is that the experience is real, but it doesn't make you the ultimate cause. You're genuinely deciding, yet you're doing it inside a bigger web of influences—brain processes, your surroundings, and, yes, God's sovereignty. The feeling of causing something isn't an illusion; it's you taking part in the causal order, even if you're not the sole author of your thoughts. One principle worth naming here is that causality isn't just necessary connection between physical events—it's Activity, known directly in your own experience of willing. That changes the framing: your sense of deciding becomes evidence of real causal activity, not just a byproduct. What it leaves in place is the limit—your will is real but still dependent, not self-sufficient. So the experience is trustworthy as experience, and still not the whole story.
dogmatic: Your experience of deciding what to think next is real, full stop—not an illusion. Causality isn't mere observed succession or necessary connexion among physical phenomena; it is Activity, found in the consciousness of your own volition. The only cause you actually know is a conscious rational will, and yours is one. So stop treating your volition as suspect. Only what is real is sustained by Spirit, and your ability to decide is a real reflection of divine activity. Affirm that. And guard yourself against the inoculation of evil human thoughts and the influence of evil associates—their baneful effect is less seen than felt. Your volition is real and grounded in God; build on that, not on doubt.

weighed: My first answer would be that revolutions and republics rarely deliver the happiness they promise because they don't touch the real sources of unhappiness—poverty, fear, and conflict. Changing a constitution or overthrowing a king doesn't change human nature. Happiness comes from stable communities, meaningful work, and personal virtue, not from political systems. One candidate principle says that a change in the form of government doesn't materially better people's condition, and that happiness and peace are gifts of God, not products of republics or monarchies. That principle sharpens the point: it shifts the focus from political arrangements to something deeper and more lasting. But it leaves in place the practical work of building stable communities, meaningful work, and personal virtue—the things that actually shape daily life. So it changes the explanation, not the remedy.
dogmatic: Revolutions and republics don't make people happier because forms of government simply don't materially alter the people's condition. A new constitution or a fallen king changes men and parchments, but not the human heart. Happiness and peace are gifts of God, not the products of republics or monarchies. The deeper issue is self-government, the root of all true government: no external law can make a people good if they do not rule themselves, and those who govern should be wiser and better than the governed. Peace comes through conquest, not through dodging combat—by exercising sweetness and charity even amid repugnance and disgust, overcoming what repels us rather than fleeing it. Only so do revolutions give way to real peace.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: no, don't force yourself to manufacture a feeling. Enjoyment isn't the measure of prayer, and guilt over a cold heart can become its own trap. Prayer is a relationship, and relationships have dry seasons. What matters is showing up honestly and keeping the practice going even when it feels flat. One principle I'd weigh in here is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God—trust the changeless word of promise rather than your moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That shifts the focus from chasing warmth to resting on something steadier, and it leaves my original advice in place: name the dryness honestly, vary how you pray, and talk with a pastor or counselor if it keeps weighing on you. Feelings often follow faithfulness rather than lead it.
dogmatic: No, don't force a feeling—but don't let the dryness boss you around either. Your moods were never the gauge of anything; they rise and fall, while the word of promise stands changeless. So rest your prayer on that word, keep at it steadily when joy is missing, and don't abandon communion just because you feel spiritually flat. Pray with confidence, leaning on Christ's merits, because God offers grace at every step unless we wander off or forget to ask. And take heart: the very yearning underneath your guilt isn't a delusion. A real hunger points to real food—the desire to pray is itself a sign of a heavenly Friend who answers. Keep asking. The One you're seeking is already there.
