Prayer is humbling work; it crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God, and our nature resists it. Little praying is worse than no praying, because it quiets the conscience while leaving the soul unexercised. Don't treat brief prayer as self-sufficient or squeeze it into leftover time. Time is essential to private communion with God, and much time alone with him is the secret of prevailing prayer; the short prayers that prevail owe their power to long seasons with God. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer. Let the closet come first, and let study and activity come second, freshened by the closet.

weighed: I'd start by saying that pleasure and excitement are not built to fill the soul; they distract it for a while. You were made for something deeper than sensation, and every thrill fades because it can't reach the center of who you are. That ache is a signal pointing beyond itself. I'd point to the first principle: people try to fill that emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, but none truly satisfy, and they descend to old age in disillusionment. That principle confirms your experience and widens it—it's not just you, and it's not just pleasure. What it changes is that it names the whole range of substitutes, not only thrills. What it leaves in place is the core answer: the void is a space meant for God, and when He fills it, the restless cycle quiets.
dogmatic: The emptiness comes back because you keep trying to fill a spiritual void with worldly things. No lover, husband, child, dress, society, dog, business, ambition, racecourse, drink, game, or art will ever satisfy you; they all end in disillusionment. The inebriate cannot leave his besottedness until his physical sense of pleasure yields to a higher sense, and then he turns from his cups. So stop chasing excitement. You must not be troubled by the fear that your love is useless or false when you feel no pleasure; instead, manifest invincible fidelity to your Savior, serving Him purely for love of His will. Only the finding of God is permanent success.

weighed: I'd start by praying for wisdom and honesty, then get the facts straight: what's actually at stake, who's affected, what your options are. Test your motives—are you after your own comfort or the good of others? Then check Scripture and talk to wise counsel, weigh the consequences and your responsibilities, act, and review how it goes. Look for the option that fits your gifts, your duties, and the needs in front of you. God usually guides through ordinary means—prayer, counsel, circumstances, conscience—more than dramatic signs, so expect clarity to grow as you take faithful steps. One idea worth adding is that God adjusts you in every good work: you're the one being fitted to your surroundings, the people around you, and God's plan, rather than demanding they be fitted to you. That shifts the posture of the whole process—you're not just analyzing a decision, you're being shaped by it—but it leaves the practical steps intact: pray, gather facts, test motives, seek counsel, act, and review.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating this like a puzzle to solve and start treating it like a posture to take. God puts good desires in your mind and then, by His continual help, brings them to good effect—He fulfills every aspiration of goodness and every work of faith with power. So don't lean on your own analysis. Be adjusted in every good work: to your surroundings, to the people you're thrown with, and to God's plan. Stop demanding that circumstances and people bend to you. If you're doubting whether you've offended God, don't sit there paralyzed—humble yourself, beg forgiveness, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and keep pursuing what's right. Clarity comes as you take faithful steps and rely on the power that completes what He begins.

weighed: Yes, they matter. Small sins repeated can dull your conscience and pull you away from God, and the Bible says whoever is faithful in little things is faithful in much. One principle worth naming is that every sin is an insult to God, measured by his greatness compared with our littleness. That raises the stakes and makes even small sins serious, but it leaves in place what I'd say first: God's grace is greater, so don't be discouraged. Bring them to him in confession, ask for strength, and keep growing in virtue.
dogmatic: Yes, they matter greatly. Every sin, even the smallest, is an insult to God, and its malice is measured by the greatness of the God offended against the littleness of man. That makes sin the greatest of all evils, to be avoided at any sacrifice. Unregretted sin accumulates and destroys your ability to do right; if it is not regretted and lessened, it hastens toward moral ruin. True repentance means turning from sin, reforming your life, and making restitution where possible. Sins are washed away through Christ's atonement upon repentance, so do not ignore even the smallest sin.

weighed: What I'd say first is that you're not alone in this—lots of faithful people go through dry seasons, and the externals like Mass, prayers, and devotions are means rather than ends. What you may be missing is a living relationship with Christ, nurtured by humility and truth; without humility, practices turn into performance, and without truth, they become superstition. One principle worth naming is that the spirit of humility and truth is what makes outward observance worth anything—without it, even serious religious practice profits nothing, because the kingdom of God, Christ himself, is within you. That changes the frame: the problem isn't that your practices are wrong, but that they need to flow from an inward surrender rather than stand in for it. What it leaves in place is the practices themselves—you don't need to abandon them; let them become expressions of a heart turned toward God, and ask whether you're seeking God himself or just the comfort of routine.
dogmatic: You're right that something is missing, and the answer is that the externals—observance, outward signs of self-denial, even the holiness of your profession—profit nothing without the spirit of humility and truth, in which Christ dwells in the heart by faith and love. The kingdom of God is within you. Don't chase spiritual experiences as achievements or out of curiosity; they're entirely outside your control, to be accepted only as God chooses, with total submission and no questioning, fear, or curiosity. You cannot serve two masters: Spirit and matter cannot both be trusted, so expel material beliefs and serve God alone. What you're missing is Christ himself dwelling in you. Humility strips away self-reliance and truth exposes pretence, so seek him within, not in outward things, and let your heart be wholly surrendered to his indwelling presence.

weighed: I'd start by saying your suspicion is fair: a lot of the ontological argument may be definitional sleight of hand, since existence isn't obviously a property that makes a concept greater. One candidate idea here is that a person is body and spirit, existing before birth and after death, and needs both to be complete. That reframes the question from a logical puzzle about a perfect concept to a claim about what you are and what you're oriented toward, so the longing for perfection isn't just wordplay. But it doesn't settle whether an absolutely perfect Being exists; it leaves the logical gap exactly where it was, and it still leaves room for you to say you're only defining a word.
dogmatic: You're not merely defining a word, because the real issue is what you are. You are body and spirit, you existed before birth and will exist after death, and you need both to be a complete human being. Once you see that, the question about a perfect Being isn't a semantic game; it's about the perfection your whole nature is straining toward. Aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love, since love that settles for anything less is already imperfect. And don't confuse multiplying pious exercises with perfection: self-love feeds on that unless you guard your heart, root out habitual imperfections, and give yourself to God without reserve.

weighed: I'd start by saying that stirring could be a real sense of God's presence in creation, or it could just be natural emotion—and honestly, it might be both at once. The Bible says creation declares God's glory, so awe at mountains can point you toward Him. But feelings are fickle, so test the experience: does it lead you to worship, humility, and love? Does it line up with Scripture? God often uses nature to wake us up, but He wants a relationship deeper than a feeling. Thank Him for the moment, but don't lean on it alone—seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community. One principle worth weighing here is that God's Spirit should be received with joy, but not the cozy joy of familiarity—rather with wondering, trembling adoration, because it's a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. That changes the tone of my answer: it adds reverence and a bit of holy awe to how you hold the experience, so you don't treat the mountain high as a casual spiritual souvenir. What it leaves in place is everything practical—the testing, the caution about fickle feelings, and the call to prayer, Scripture, and community. So let the mountains remind you of His majesty, but let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.
dogmatic: That stirring is not something you get to file under 'just emotion' and move on from. God is present everywhere, He sees and hears all things, and He penetrates the heart—keep that before your eyes and it will guard you against anger and dissolute mirth. The divine presence is both beneficent and terrible, filling the soul with wondering, trembling adoration. So when you look at the mountains, remember that the same God who made them is holy and awesome. Yet His dealings with the soul are a tender mystery of Infinite Love forcing itself upon an unwilling creature, taking only to restore; even the soul's gloom may be the shade of His outstretched hand. Let joy and holy fear blend in your heart. Does the experience lead you to worship, humility, and love? Then thank God for it—but do not rely on it alone. Seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community, and let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.

weighed: I get why you'd feel discouraged after years of doing good without any special insight. I'd first say that obedience probably isn't best understood as a transaction that guarantees a particular feeling or reward; understanding tends to grow slowly and quietly, and feelings are unreliable measures of growth. One principle worth naming is that obedience is an eternal principle, a way of staying in touch with God rather than a lever for insight. That changes the frame from "what do I get for this?" to "this is how I stay connected," and it leaves in place your honest disappointment and the slow, unspectacular nature of growth. Keep doing good because it is good, and hold lightly the expectation that insight should arrive on a schedule.
dogmatic: Obedience is not a transaction whose results are uncertain. Obedience to God's commandments is an eternal principle: there will never be a time in time or eternity when it is not obligatory. It is the means of keeping in touch with God, and only in this way can you fulfill your mission and obtain eternal life. Every blessing is conditioned on obedience—keeping the commandments, paying tithing, keeping the Word of Wisdom, building temples. Yet do not live outside the sense of God's love. Keep yourself in His love by constant trust and constant obedience, and the hard things become easy, and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. Understanding grows along that path rather than before it.

weighed: I'd start with small, concrete habits: a regular time each day for reflection or prayer, reading widely, serving somewhere specific and unglamorous, and keeping honest company. One principle worth naming is that prayer is the central secret of holy living and serving, built on the practice of prayer both in secret and with other believers. That changes the starting point—it makes prayer the foundation rather than one habit among many—but it leaves in place the practical steps: regular times, service, and honest community. Start this week with one habit and one act of service.
dogmatic: Begin with prayer. Prayer on your knees, both secret and with other believers, is the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the cornerstone on which all your life-work is built, and your first resort in every crisis. Do not separate the Spirit's work from the Church: the Spirit is the life of the Spirit-bearing body, consecrating nature and working gradually and socially while intensifying your personal character. And do not settle for a bare minimum of knowledge. Seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, for that is the secret of true living. Pray with others as well as alone, serve somewhere specific and unglamorous, and keep company with honest people who will tell you the truth. Start this week with prayer and one act of service.

weighed: I'd start by saying that double anger—the flare and then being mad at yourself for flaring—is exhausting, and it helps to slow the sequence down. Notice the physical signals like a tight jaw or heat in your chest, and give yourself a brief pause before speaking. Naming the feeling silently, like 'I'm angry right now,' can keep a sharp word from escaping. It's also worth looking at what tends to set you off, since patterns often point to unmet needs or old wounds. Be patient with yourself; getting angry about being angry just adds a second layer of suffering. One principle here is that we shouldn't be troubled because we've been troubled—instead, take the heart gently and ask for help to calm it. That principle changes the tone: it turns the second anger into something you hand over rather than fight alone, which can ease the self-blame. What it leaves in place is the practical work—pausing, noticing signals, and examining triggers—because those still matter for change.
dogmatic: You need to stop measuring yourself against others and against your own image of how you should be. Learn first not to be troubled in tribulations, afflictions, and injuries, and not to be incensed against those who inflict them. When the heat rises, bridle your tongue and refuse resentment; say nothing until your spirit is quieted. Then examine yourself honestly, attending to your own duties rather than judging others. Do not be angry that you were agitated—gently place the troubled heart in the hands of our Lord and ask Him to cure it, renewing your good resolutions. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured and exalted by men. In that lowliness the flare loses its fuel.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Spirit doesn't erase you—he fills and reorients you. Your memories, temperament, and gifts stay, but they're now animated by a new governing principle, like a lamp that's lit rather than extinguished. One principle that sharpens this is that the Spirit identifies himself with the human me whose life he becomes, creating a new moral personality. That changes how I'd frame the 'new me': it's not a replacement but a transformation from within, where your own self is taken up rather than suppressed. It leaves in place the continuity of who you are—your history and personality—while making clear that the life now flowing through you is the Spirit's own life, not just a self-improvement project.
dogmatic: The Spirit doesn't erase you—he becomes the life of a new you by identifying himself with your human spirit, creating a new moral personality. That means your old self isn't annihilated but converted: you must become like a child, turn back to God from whom you came, forsake your own imaging and lust and self-made centres, and come again to the Divine Vision. And this isn't for private enjoyment—the fullness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God won't give his power for selfish ends; his power is a trust for the lost. So the new me is a homecoming that turns you outward in obedience, not a possession to hoard.

weighed: You're not wrong to feel the pull here, and I'd say yes—you've been treating visiting the sick as the minister's job alone, and that's a mistake. Jesus said, 'I was sick and you visited me,' and that word goes to every believer, not just clergy. Ministers have a special role in anointing and prayer, but showing up, praying with someone, and helping practically is on all of us. One principle worth naming: visiting the sick is a strict command and duty for every Christian, and the sick and dying are a real field for usefulness—many people go without because no one comes to encourage them. That principle changes the scope of who's responsible: it moves this from 'the minister's task' to yours too. What it leaves in place is the minister's distinct role in anointing and prayer—that stays sacred and shouldn't be handled loosely. So don't leave it all to the minister. Ask God for compassion and look for ways to visit, pray, and help.
dogmatic: Yes, you are wrong—plainly. Visiting and instructing the sick is a strict duty laid on every Christian, not a task reserved for the minister. Jesus said, 'I was sick and you visited me.' The sick and dying are a field for usefulness, and man's extremity is often God's opportunity; many perish for lack of one friend to warn them to flee from the wrath to come. The minister's administration by anointing and laying on of hands is an authoritative ordinance, too sacred to be repeated loosely—once the blessing is pronounced, give time to prayer and thanksgiving rather than unwarranted repetition—but that never excuses you from your own duty. Seize the time Providence affords in lingering illness. Warn the dying while there is life and hope. Be peaceable, submit to the powers that be, pray for rulers, and wait patiently for the Lord to establish His own government in His own time. Ask God for wisdom and compassion, and go.

weighed: Answer honestly and with respect for both traditions. Explain what the law of Moses means to you, and why a crucified Messiah sits uneasily with expectations of a triumphant deliverer. Many Christians read the crucifixion as a sacrifice for sin; you can say that from a Jewish standpoint the Torah provides its own means of atonement and repentance, and that a death on a tree carries its own scriptural weight. Ask what they mean by crucifixion—atonement, martyrdom, or something else—since Christians differ. Keep it about texts and meanings rather than who is right, and it's fine to say you don't have a settled answer. One idea worth weighing is that Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection showed the supremacy of Spirit over matter, and that his efficacy lay in the practical affection and goodness he demonstrated rather than in material blood or vicarious pardon. That shifts the conversation away from sacrifice and toward character and example, but it leaves your core points intact: respect, the Torah's own means of atonement, the stumbling block of a crucified deliverer, and honest curiosity over a rehearsed reply.
dogmatic: The crucifixion wasn't about blood paying a debt or wrath being appeased—that whole framework misses the point. What mattered was the supremacy of Spirit over matter, and Jesus' efficacy lay in the practical affection and goodness he demonstrated, not in material blood or vicarious pardon. So when Christians press you about sacrifice and atonement, don't soften it: the power of that death is in the love it showed, not in automatic pardon. And if they bring up Jewish Christianity, that label belongs only to Christians who kept the national and political forms of Judaism and literal Mosaic observance as essential, or claimed a Jewish prerogative—it stands against the universalistic, anti-national Christian religion, not against Gentile Christianity. Don't let the death be read as mere tragedy either: where a testament is, there must be the death of the testator; the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church; and Joseph and Hyrum showed the greatest love by laying down their lives for their friends.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear makes sense, because love does ask a lot of us. Jesus does say to take up your cross and follow him, and that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. But that isn't a deal that leaves you empty. God isn't asking you to hand over good things so he can keep them from you; he's asking you to trust him with them. The saints who gave everything say they received far more than they gave. So bring the fear to God honestly and ask him to show you what love really is. One thing worth holding onto here is that perfect love casts out fear. That doesn't erase your question or pretend the cost isn't real. What it changes is the picture underneath it: you're not being asked to surrender to someone who wants to strip you bare, but to the living God who is drawing you to himself, and every surrender he asks is a way of giving you more of him. What it leaves in place is that love still asks for trust and real surrender. It just reframes who's asking and why.
dogmatic: Perfect love casts out fear, so fear must not be allowed to set the terms of this question. God does not look at you as a threat to be managed. In his goodness he looks with love even on the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted, so do not imagine yourself beyond his merciful regard. Love is not a demand that strips you bare. It is the living God drawing you to himself, and every surrender he asks is a way of giving you more of him. He does not wish to harm you but to do you great good. So love him fervently and without servile fear. Meet this trial as a place where faith grows stronger and love grows purer, trusting his goodness toward you.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: pursue this personally. Pray and ask the Spirit to fill you, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, sit in silence, obey what you sense Him prompting, and confess sin quickly so you're not grieving Him. Expect Him to grow love, joy, peace, and self-control in you over time, and keep asking with patience. One principle worth naming is that the Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, who came at Pentecost to dwell in the church. That changes the picture: it's not just me and my private pursuit, because He lives and works in His people, so Scripture, prayer, and fellowship with other believers become places where you actually meet Him. What it leaves in place is everything above: the personal asking, the obedience, the confession, the patient waiting for character to form. You still seek Him yourself, just not alone.
dogmatic: The fullness of the Holy Spirit isn't a private attainment you chase on your own; it's life in the body where He dwells. The Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, sent at Pentecost to dwell in the church as His successor and vicar. He speaks, guides, commands, and can be grieved. He consecrates nature rather than bypassing it, so He works through Scripture, sacraments, prayer, and fellowship, and He works gradually. That means imperfection in the Old Testament and in the Church doesn't disprove His real inspiration and presence; don't be scandalized by it. So pray for Him, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey, and confess sin, and expect Him to form love, joy, peace, and self-control in you over time. Keep asking, and trust that He fills those who hunger for Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Father and the Son are not the same person—they're distinct persons who are both fully God, along with the Holy Spirit. One God in three persons; the Father isn't the Son, and the Son isn't the Father. In heaven the Son is at the Father's right hand, interceding for us, and the Father is the one who sent him. So you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit. One candidate idea here is that the Father is a person with a habitation, shape, voice, and features, distinct from the Son, who is the express image of his person, and both are together in one place in heaven. That adds a concrete picture of two persons in a shared place, which sharpens the distinction I already hold. What it leaves in place is the core: distinct persons, one God, and prayer going to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.
dogmatic: The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven. The Father isn't some vague spirit diffused everywhere with no habitation—he's a person who dwells in a place, with shape, voice, and features, and the Son is the express image of his person. That's why John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him who sat on the throne: two persons, one enthroned and one approaching. Scripture names the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each as God and describes them as distinct persons, not mere names, modes, or appearances. Yet there's one Fatherhood of God and one brotherhood of man, and there's but one Mind. So when you pray, you pray to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, that's a right prayer—wanting your kids to know God and also to be comfortable and respectable isn't wrong. One principle worth holding onto is that no conversion happens except by the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, and your deepest need as a parent is to know God yourself. That changes how you pray: you're not leaning on technique or persuasion, you're depending on Him. But it leaves your original desire intact—you can still pray for their salvation and their wellbeing, just with the Spirit doing the work rather than you.
dogmatic: Conversion is never the product of human effort, technique, or persuasion—it is the work of the almighty power of the Holy Spirit alone. Your great need is not to manage outcomes but to know God. Bring every matter concerning your children before Him, take no step without asking counsel of the Scriptures, and wait until His guidance is clear. Pray for hearts truly comforted—strengthened, courageous, and consoled—not merely for pleasant circumstances. Anything less than dependence on the Spirit is misplaced confidence in yourself.

weighed: Yes, you can enjoy innocent pleasures—good food, friendship, music, rest—they're part of a healthy life and can be received with gratitude. The danger is in excess or making pleasure the center of things. One principle I'd weigh is that pleasure-seeking isn't the goal of life and can lead to debt and corrupted morals. That principle changes the emphasis: it warns against making pleasure a goal, but it leaves in place that innocent pleasures themselves aren't wrong. So enjoy them with moderation and thankfulness, while keeping your responsibilities and care for others in view.
dogmatic: Innocent pleasures are not wrong in themselves, but do not make pleasure a goal. The pursuit of pleasure can become a living death; people go into debt for display and undertake illegitimate schemes to gratify craving, and the hunt leads to cheating, lying, and corrupted morals. Do not linger in the cheerless tomb of passion; when the storm is laid, mark the silent growth of grace and light in the soul. And remember that a soul devoted to God will sometimes forgo innocent lawful pleasures, so that it takes pleasure only with Him. Enjoy simple goods with gratitude and moderation, yet let devotion sometimes set them aside.

weighed: I'd start by saying nature can tell you something about God, but it's a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions. The Bible acknowledges that tension and points beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So nature can stir wonder and gratitude, but it shouldn't be your primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart. One idea worth weighing is that the more honestly you know your own misery, the more fully you can behold God's majesty. That changes the frame: the problem of suffering isn't only out there in nature, it's also in you, and humility sharpens your sight. But it leaves the core answer in place. Nature still isn't a reliable portrait of God's heart, and Christ still is. Self-contempt doesn't explain why animals suffer; it just keeps you honest while you look.
dogmatic: You can't read God's character off nature, and you shouldn't try. Nature is cruel and full of suffering, and it will mislead you if you make it your teacher. The real starting point is yourself. The more truly you know your own misery, the more fully you behold the majesty of God, and the more vile you are in your own eyes for the sake of God, truth, and justice, the more worthy of esteem you are in God's eyes. So strive to look on yourself as utterly contemptible and to desire to be regarded by others as vile and mean. Then remember that God, in His promises to hear our prayers, desires to bestow Himself upon you. If you ask for anything beneath Him, you put an affront upon Him and hurt yourself by preferring a creature He framed to the Creator Himself. The greatest pains and pleasures of this world are nothing compared to what is known in a spiritual state. Be careful for nothing and fear nothing, desiring only that you might not offend God. Beyond nature, look to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully.

weighed: I'd start by saying that sorrow for sin is a good starting point, but repentance is more than feeling sorry. It involves a change of mind and direction—turning from sin toward God. If you're unsure whether you've repented, begin by honestly examining your life, confessing your sins to God, and asking Him for a changed heart. Focus on turning from what is wrong and walking in obedience, trusting God's grace and forgiveness in Christ. One principle that adds to this is that true repentance also includes making restitution where possible. That changes the practical shape of repentance—it's not just inner sorrow but outward repair. It leaves in place the core call to turn from sin and trust Christ's atonement.
dogmatic: You should focus first on being sorry for your sins, but don't stop there. True repentance requires turning from sin, a reformation of life, and restitution so far as possible. Death-bed confession alone will not cleanse you; sins are washed away through the atonement of Christ upon repentance. A guilty conscience and unrepented sin destroy your ability to do right, so examine your life honestly, confess, turn from what is wrong, and make amends where you have wronged others. Cleansing comes through Christ's atonement; walk in new obedience.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is one of the oldest questions people ask, and different traditions answer it differently. Many religious traditions teach that the soul is created at conception or birth, while others hold that it pre-exists. From a Christian perspective, Scripture speaks of God knowing us before we were formed in the womb, which suggests our identity is rooted in God's eternal purpose. As for death, most Christian teaching affirms that the spirit survives the body and awaits resurrection. Practically, the question matters less than how we live now: trust God, love your neighbors, and live faithfully. One idea worth weighing is that a person is an eternal being made of body and spirit, existing before birth and after death, and needing both to be complete. That changes the picture by making your spirit's existence before birth and after death a settled fact rather than an open question, and it adds the hope of a final reunion of body and spirit. What it leaves in place is the practical core: however the details work out, the call to trust God and live faithfully now still stands, and the timing and mechanics still rest in God's hands.
dogmatic: Your spirit is not a passing thing. It existed before you came here, it exists after death, and it will be reunited with the body in the resurrection, because a perfect man needs both body and spirit. Belief is mortal—it shifts, doubts, and dies with the body—but Mind is immortal, and it is Mind that understands. So don't settle for speculation; know the eternal nature of your spirit. And don't rest in that understanding as a private comfort. The fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not give His power for selfish enjoyment. We receive the Spirit in fulness only as we obey Christ's command and step out into His plans for the world. Let your hope in the spirit's eternity move you to obedient service, where the promised power is found.

weighed: I'd start by saying Christ is glorified in ordinary life through faithful daily work, integrity, kindness, patience, and quiet service—small acts of love that let others see something of Him in how you treat them. One principle I'd weigh is that Christ is glorified in us and we're glorified in Christ, a reciprocal glory, so every life loyal to Him is glorified in union and communion with Him. That adds a warm, mutual note: your ordinary faithfulness isn't just a witness to others, it's a real sharing in His glory. It leaves in place the everyday stuff—prayer, Scripture, integrity, carrying your responsibilities well.
dogmatic: Christ is glorified in ordinary life when He shines out from you to the people around you. Integrity, kindness, patience, and service make His character visible, and there's a reciprocal glory—the believer is glorified in union and communion with Christ. But watch out: those who contend fiercely about the kingdom of Christ and slander and persecute one another over religion haven't really known Him. That kind of swelling pride about opinions is an image of Self and helps the Kingdom of Darkness along. Remember, God chooses the poor, weak, and despised to do His work, confounding the mighty, so no flesh can boast. The glory is His, not your wealth, influence, or ability. Offer your ordinary faithfulness, however small, to the One who works through the base things of the world.

weighed: Yes, I'd say you carry real responsibility here. Leaders shape the tone through teaching, prayer, and example, and a cold congregation often reflects shepherding that's been neglected. But I'd also hold onto this: spiritual vitality isn't something you can manufacture alone, since each person has to respond to God. One idea worth weighing is that preachers are preeminently God's leaders and primarily responsible for the condition of the church. That sharpens your sense of accountability and puts the weight squarely on your leadership, which is fair. What it leaves in place is the other half of the truth: the congregation's warmth isn't yours to produce by yourself. So examine your own walk, seek God earnestly, lead with humility and prayer, and trust God to work.
dogmatic: Yes, you are responsible, and preachers are preeminently God's leaders, primarily responsible for the condition of the church. A church rarely rises above the religion of its leaders, and spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor. A cold congregation points straight back to neglected shepherding, teaching, and prayer. Yet the church's lack isn't only in its leaders: it's the same tepid love for a dimly known Lord in every member's heart, and the church gains what's lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Understand authority rightly: it's moral and spiritual weight that carries our judgment, not coercive power. Coercion adds nothing to the church's true authority, and belief secured by threat isn't submission at all. Lead by the weight of character and truth, and call each heart to love Christ.

weighed: To prepare for contemplating God by negation, start by quieting your senses: withdraw from noise, images, and distractions, and let your imagination grow still. Then set aside your own ideas and concepts of God, since God exceeds every thought you can form. Cultivate silence, humility, and patience, and give yourself to prayer and moral discipline so that your mind becomes calm and receptive. Don't expect clear pictures or consoling feelings; the goal is a simple, loving attention to the God who is beyond all that you can grasp. Persevere gently, returning to this practice each day, and trust that in the darkness of unknowing God draws near to you. One principle that fits here is that you should begin not with the mind but with the body, passing from the labour of action to the repose of contemplation. That principle changes the order and emphasis: it makes bodily discipline and the shift from moral effort to contemplative rest the first step, rather than just one part of preparation. It leaves in place the core practice of removing images and concepts and the need for patient, loving attention beyond what you can grasp.
dogmatic: To contemplate God by the way of negation is the best means of knowing him, for God exceeds all that can be grasped. So don't merely discuss difficulties—act courageously: begin with the body, disciplining the senses, withdrawing from images, and stilling the imagination, removing first all that pertains to bodily, sensible, and imaginative things. Then remove even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, entering the darkness where God dwells. Begin not with the mind but with the body, and pass from the labour of action to the repose of contemplation and from the moral virtues to sublime contemplation. Say with courage, 'I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me.' And when you lapse in remembrance, don't be disquieted: acknowledge your wretchedness and return at once with greater trust, knowing that God's grace, not your vigilance, keeps you.

weighed: I'd start by saying it makes sense to feel alone under a big decision. Name the choice plainly, write down your options, and seek wise counsel from trusted people—a pastor, counselor, or mentor—who can listen without deciding for you. Pray honestly about your fears, and give yourself permission to move at a steady pace rather than rushing. Break the choice into smaller steps and set a short deadline so you're not paralyzed. Remember you're not truly alone; God invites you to cast your cares on Him, and He promises guidance to those who ask. Take the next small step faithfully and trust that clarity often comes in motion rather than before it. One candidate principle worth weighing is to be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. That principle changes the pace and posture: it adds patient waiting and a deliberate setting aside of self-will before you act. It leaves in place the practical steps—naming the decision, seeking counsel, praying, and taking small faithful steps—so you still have a path forward while you wait for clarity.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating this as a problem you solve by gathering opinions. Be slow to take new steps. Seek to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. If you are yourself lost in the belief and fear of disease or sin, and knowing the remedy fail to use it for yourself, you can exercise little or no power for others' help—so begin with your own eye. Do not be in a hurry. Attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up so you can catch the shower when it comes. Test any proposed step by the Word and prayer rather than treating self-will as faith. Then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help, trusting that light comes in His time.

weighed: My first answer would be that the spread is genuinely striking, and plenty of people have read divine providence into it. But human factors did a lot of work too: Roman roads, a shared Greek language, crowded cities, and a faith that cared for the sick and promised salvation in a restless age. One piece worth naming is that the victory of the party that treated the whole Old Testament as Christian revelation didn't come from Jewish Christian influence; if anything, Jewish Christianity's presence would have made that victory harder had it not already faded into the background. That changes how we picture the early church's growth, but it leaves the bigger point intact: the transformation of the empire within a few centuries still looks like a place where God was at work, without making any one dogmatic form permanent.
dogmatic: Look, the honest answer is that the whole thing was never chained to the ancient world in the first place. The form and new content the Gospel picked up when it walked into that world carry only the same guarantee of endurance as the world itself, and since the Reformation the Gospel has been working itself out of the shapes it was once forced to wear. So the question of how a crucified Jew conquered Rome misses the point: the dogmatic vessel that emerged was historically conditioned and transitory. And don't credit Jewish Christians for the Old Testament's place; that victory belonged to the party that recognized the whole thing as revelation, and Jewish Christianity, had it not already receded, would only have made it harder. The syncretistic ones even cut out whatever offended their purer morals, especially the sacrificial ritual, trying to turn the old religion into a universal one under the impression of Jesus. God was in the movement, sure, but not in any permanent dogmatic form.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Bible's sanitation and work rules were practical for ancient Israel—they helped prevent disease and keep community order. They show God cares about everyday life, but Christians aren't bound to them today; we focus on the moral principles behind them. One principle here is that institutions are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. That changes how I read these laws: they're not just timeless regulations but temporary tools that can be set aside when they stop serving people, like Jesus saying the Sabbath was made for man. What it leaves in place is the underlying care for health, rest, and diligent work—those still matter as wisdom, even if the specific rules don't bind us.
dogmatic: The Bible's sanitation and work rules were given with the Holy Spirit's special assistance to teach Israel to trust God and offer their whole lives to Him. They're not just ancient health codes—they're acts of faith that lead to imitating Christ. And here's the key: institutions like these are instruments for human life, not ends in themselves. When they harden into custom and get treated as ultimate, they must be broken for the sake of larger human life—just as Jesus declared the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So yes, the specific rules aren't binding on Christians today, but the spirit of cheerful, self-denying service remains, and we must always keep institutions in second place behind human welfare.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's encouraging to think that good people before Christ were reaching toward him without knowing him, and that God has always been drawing people to himself. One thing I'd add is the idea that we learn to love the unseen Christ by thinking about him persistently and by comparing the world's loves and deceits with his gentle ways, until he becomes more lovable than anyone else. That changes the focus from speculating about their journeys to something we can actually do: practice that kind of steady attention ourselves. What it leaves in place is the trust that God's grace works in ways we don't fully see, and that he values the heart.
dogmatic: The real question isn't what happened to them but what you're doing with the Christ you do know. Love for him doesn't come from vague admiration; it comes from persistent thinking, from comparing the world's friendships, loves, deceits, and secret envies with his gentle ways until he's more lovable than any other person. Expect God to bring you into difficulties on purpose so you can know him as a present help in trouble, not just a distant idea. And blessed are those who haven't seen and yet believe; faith runs ahead of reason and waits at the grave until Christ appears. So stop measuring their sincerity and start practicing your own.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: fear of death is natural, and one way to face it is to focus on the life you have now, talk to someone you trust, and take small steps toward calm. One principle that matters here is that death can be seen as a door to a higher state, with identity preserved and the body resurrected. That changes the picture from death as an ending to death as a transition, which can ease fear. It leaves in place the practical steps—counseling, honest conversation, and daily practices—because those still help you live with the fear while you hold that larger hope.
dogmatic: You should not let fear of death rule you. Death is not the end but a door to a higher state; your identity will be preserved and your body will be resurrected. For the righteous, death is a transition to greater life, not a loss. So turn your thoughts away from fear and toward health and Life as God. Our assurance does not rest on your own thoughts or worthiness but wholly on Christ—his sufferings, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading for you. Looking at yourself clouds the view; looking at the Saviour leaves no room to doubt his power and will to save. Cultivate thoughts of health, wholeness, and divine Life, which cast out fear. Align your mind with God, who is Life itself, and you will find peace and courage to face each day without the shadow of fear.

weighed: Feeling alone as a new Christian is really common, but you're not meant to walk this road by yourself. I'd start by praying honestly to God about your loneliness and asking Him to guide you to the people He's prepared for you. Then look for a local church where Scripture is taught faithfully and believers gather for worship and prayer. Go regularly, join a small group or Bible study, and introduce yourself to others. Be patient and persistent, because friendships in Christ take time to grow. In the meantime, read your Bible daily and let prayer become a habit, trusting that God is with you even when you feel isolated. He promises never to leave or forsake those who belong to Him. One thing I'd add is this: the vague longing to reach beyond yourself gives way, once you know God as Father in Christ, to real fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That doesn't replace the practical steps of finding a church and building friendships; it just reminds you that the fellowship you're seeking starts with Him and then flows into His people.
dogmatic: You're not meant to walk this road alone, so stop treating your loneliness as something to just endure. The vague impulse to reach beyond your isolated self gives place, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That means the fellowship you're looking for isn't an abstract feeling—it's communion with a definite Person, and it's meant to shape how you connect with real people. So get into a faithful church, join a small group, and don't overlook believers of low estate. Converse and correspond with them on serious subjects, because God hears and records that kind of speech, and it builds both of you up in faith and love. Introduce yourself, be patient, read your Bible daily, and let prayer stay real conversation with the Friend who never forsakes His own.

weighed: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, and it shouldn't run your life. God is merciful, and one sin doesn't define your soul. Under pressure, pray, stay away from the situations that pull you toward sin, and trust God's grace. If you do fall, get to confession soon and start again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it shouldn't turn into paralyzing anxiety. One principle here is that a single unrepented mortal sin is enough to separate you from God forever, so an intense, steady fear of sin and of eternal loss has its place, especially when love feels weak. What that changes is that I wouldn't brush off the seriousness of mortal sin or treat your fear as something to just get over. What it leaves in place is the core: God isn't out to harm you, he wants your good, so keep your eyes on him and don't let fear become dread. With prayer, the sacraments, and steady virtue, you can face pressure with confidence instead of panic.
dogmatic: You should take that fear seriously, because one mortal sin unrepented is enough to damn the soul forever. So build an intense, abiding fear of sin and of eternal loss. If your love of God is too weak to keep you from sin, let fear of hell restrain you. That's not cruelty; it's watchfulness. At the same time, don't picture God as someone who wants to hurt you. He wants to do you great good, so love him fervently rather than cowering. When pressure comes, flee the occasions of sin, pray, and trust his goodness. If you fall, confess and get up. And when little faults and impatience trip you up, don't be terrified or paralyzed. Humble yourself quietly before God and tell your soul: courage, we've made a false step, but let's keep steadily on. Let fear keep you watchful and love keep you confident.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, keep that counsel, unless something serious pushes you to reconsider. Honoring what your father trusted you with matters, and a hidden sacred thing deserves care. One principle that sharpens this is that we shouldn't busy ourselves trying to know God's private counsels—the more we pry, the further we get from knowing. That changes the tone: instead of weighing whether revealing the tree might do more good, I'd treat the hiddenness itself as something to respect and leave with God. What it leaves in place is your duty to live faithfully and honor your father's wish; it doesn't hand you a license to disclose just because disclosure seems useful.
dogmatic: Keep the counsel, full stop. The location of that tree is a sacred trust, and its hiddenness belongs to God's goodness—not to your judgment about whether revealing it might help someone. Don't press to know or manage what God has kept hidden; that prying only pulls you further from knowing. Trust the hidden deed to God and give yourself to what's open: faithful living and honoring your father's wishes. There's no need to reveal the tree or chase some greater good through disclosure. Grow deep and out of sight, content to be a hidden foundation rather than making a show. Keep the counsel and focus on your duty to God and neighbor.

weighed: My first instinct would be to say: accept the gift graciously if it's offered to you, since it might be meant to help. But since you know the money is really owed to someone else, I'd want you to clarify that with the giver first. Ask if they're aware of the debt. If they insist, you could accept it and then pass it on to the rightful owner. Ultimately, follow your conscience. One principle that applies here is that gifts should be refused if the money isn't the giver's to give. That changes my initial answer: instead of accepting and then redirecting the money, you should decline it up front and encourage the giver to settle the debt directly. It leaves in place the importance of acting with integrity and clarifying the situation, but it shifts the default from 'accept and pass on' to 'refuse and redirect the giver.'
dogmatic: You should not accept the gift at all. Money for God's work must be obtained only in God's way—without asking unbelievers, pressing believers, or using worldly schemes. Gifts must be carefully examined and refused where motives are impure or the money is not the giver's own. In this case, the money belongs to another, so accepting it would be wrong. Decline questionable or encumbered donations, refuse funds designated for endowment or personal provision, and provide honest accounts of stewardship to those who give. Clarify the situation with the giver and ensure that the rightful owner receives what is owed. If the giver insists, you might accept it only to pass it on to the rightful owner, but better to refuse and encourage the giver to settle the debt directly. Yet beyond merely asking and expecting to receive, reverse the method: give love to Jesus, give Him a home in your heart, and set your heart upon God rather than only beseeching gifts.

weighed: I'd start by saying it sounds like God answered your prayer in a way you didn't expect—sometimes we ask for what we think we need, but God knows what we actually need better than we do, like a parent giving a child something better than what was asked for. Your prayer wasn't ignored; it was answered with wisdom, so trust that God's perspective is larger than yours, be grateful for the better gift, and let it deepen your trust in God's goodness. One principle that fits here is that prayer doesn't inform or change God but brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle. That principle changes how you see the 'different and better' gift: it's not God switching plans to suit you but your desire aligning more closely with what God already knows. It leaves in place the real goodness of what you received and the call to trust and gratitude—so you can still thank God for the better gift while understanding prayer as alignment rather than persuasion.
dogmatic: Prayer is not a way to inform God of your needs or to persuade Him to change His mind—He already knows, and His law is unchanging. Prayer is absolute faith, spiritual understanding, and unselfed love that brings you into harmony with that law. When you ask for something, you are really seeking to understand God's will, not to bend it to yours. The 'different and better' gift you received is not a change in God's plan but a deeper alignment of your desire with His. Yet that gift is not for you alone: every special blessing is a trust to be passed on. Freely give what you have freely received, and let your gratitude become a witness to others. Prayer is not confined to appointed times; it is a continual sense of God's presence, the same before and after your request. Prayer changes you, not God, and the blessing is completed when it is shared.

weighed: You already know the calling is real, so stop pretending you don't. Acknowledge it honestly before God and yourself, then take one concrete step toward it, however small, and tell someone who will hold you accountable. Fear is normal, but it doesn't get to be your master. Pray for courage and act on what you know today rather than waiting for perfect clarity. One principle worth naming here is that we should be just with our own soul, neither excusing nor accusing it without due reflection. That changes the tone: instead of just telling you to push through, it asks you to look honestly at the fear without either wallowing in it or pretending it isn't there. What it leaves in place is the core move, which is to take that one real step and let obedience wear down the resistance. Don't wait for a dramatic sign; the sign is the calling you already have.
dogmatic: The thing you're calling evasion is really a failure to be just with your own soul. You're either excusing it or accusing yourself without any due reflection, and both are ways of staying stuck. Stop treating your fear as something to be managed and start judging it rightly. And be careful what you let through the door of your thought, because only the conclusions you admit are the ones that get realized in your life. If you keep entertaining the idea that you can't do this, you're choosing that result. The Spirit is already at work in your resistance, patiently drawing you toward obedience, and God's patience with you is greater than your fear. So name the fear honestly, neither excusing nor condemning it, and then act. Take the step today. Grace meets you in the doing, not in the waiting.

weighed: I'd start by saying Scripture uses human language to describe God because we're human and need analogies to grasp Him. When it speaks of His hand, face, or voice, that's metaphor—God accommodating Himself to our limited understanding. He's spirit, so He doesn't have body parts; these are poetic ways of saying He acts, sees, and speaks, and the point is the meaning behind the imagery, not the literal picture. One principle worth naming is that Scripture is God-breathed, with the Holy Spirit speaking in its very words. That changes something real: the metaphors aren't just human invention or helpful poetry—they're God's own chosen way of revealing Himself, so they carry His authority. What it leaves in place is exactly what I said first: God is spirit, the language is figurative, and we shouldn't literalize the hand or the face. It deepens the answer without overturning it.
dogmatic: Scripture is God-breathed—the Holy Spirit speaks in its very words, so it's the infallible word of God, and that settles how you read His hand, face, and voice. Yes, God is spirit and doesn't have body parts, but don't wave the imagery away as mere human poetry. The Spirit chose those words and speaks through them. And here's the thing: you only know the fulness of the Spirit as you step out into Christ's larger purposes for the world. God won't pour out His power for selfish enjoyment; it's a trust for the evangelization of the lost. So don't stop at parsing metaphors—obey His command and go, and the Spirit who inspired the words will open them to you.

weighed: I first want to say: it can be deeply discouraging to pray for years and see no change. My first instinct would be to say that God's timing isn't ours, that He may be working in ways you can't see, and that you should keep praying while also examining your own heart. One principle that stands out to me is that God sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to His, trusting that He gives what is infinitely better. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'keep praying and trust His timing,' it invites you to consider that a 'no' or 'not yet' might actually be a loving answer, not a failure. But it leaves in place the core encouragement to keep praying and to trust God's goodness, even when the answer isn't what you hoped for.
dogmatic: You've been praying for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer? The truth is, God doesn't always give just what we ask. Sometimes He denies a petition in kindness, because He knows what is infinitely better for us. We must resign our will to His, trusting that His denial can be better than the thing we asked for. So stop demanding a specific outcome and instead surrender your desire to His wisdom. Keep praying, but pray with open hands, ready to accept that God's 'no' may be the answer you need.

weighed: My first answer would be that God gave you a body so you could live, learn, and grow, and that what you do with it matters because it shapes your health, your relationships, and your ability to do good. One idea worth weighing is that the body is for the Lord and the Lord is for the body, and that healing comes through real union with the risen Christ rather than a mere touch of power. That changes the frame: your body isn't just a tool for personal growth, it's meant for connection with Him. What it leaves in place is the practical point that how you treat your body still matters, so respect it, avoid harmful habits, and use it to do good.
dogmatic: God gave you a body for His purposes, not yours. Your body is for the Lord and the Lord is for the body, and the healing He gives comes through vital union with the risen Christ, not some distant touch of power. So what you do with your body matters absolutely: it either honors or dishonors the One who dwells in you. God chooses the weak and despised to confound the mighty, so no flesh can boast, and your body, whatever its condition, becomes useful when yielded to Him. Keep it pure, flee sexual immorality, and glorify God in your body, because it belongs to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying friendship is a gift, but it turns into an idol when it takes God's place in your heart. So the practical move is ordering: love God first, and let love for your friends flow from that. That means you don't let a friend pull you into sin, you don't need their approval more than God's, and you keep prayer and worship as your anchor. One principle that sharpens this is that we can't trust God too much, since he's a faithful friend who won't fail us in this world or the next. That changes the tone: instead of mainly watching for idolatry, you lean into trusting God more, and your love for friends stays sincere but never crowds out the love that's due to God first. What it leaves in place is the practical guardrails, like not letting a friend lead you into sin and not needing their approval more than God's.
dogmatic: Friendship is good, but it must never sit above God. Trust in God can never be excessive, so pour your trust into him without reserve, and let your love for friends stay clearly beneath the love you owe him. If a friend pulls you toward sin or you start needing their approval more than God's, that's the line. When you fail, confess it plainly to God, don't make excuses and don't get discouraged, then calmly go back to loving and adoring him. Keep thinking of God throughout the day, in work and even in fun, because he's always near and shouldn't be neglected. Ordered that way, your friendships flow from your love for God and lead you back to him.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, don't scale your prayers down out of fear that they're too bold. God isn't annoyed by big requests, and boldness in prayer can be a sign of trust in a generous Father. What matters is sincerity and a heart aligned with his will. One principle worth weighing here is that prayer is humbling work—it brings our pride low and reminds us we come with nothing to plead but mercy. That changes the tone of your boldness: it's not the swagger of someone demanding, it's the confidence of a child who knows his Father. What it leaves in place is the answer itself—your prayers don't need to shrink. Keep asking and seeking, and leave the timing and the way of the answer to God.
dogmatic: Don't scale them down—but don't treat prayer as something easy or flattering either. Real prayer humbles you. It crucifies pride and makes you sign your own bankruptcy before God, because you come as a beggar with nothing to plead but his mercy. Boldness in prayer isn't presumption when it's the boldness of a child who knows his Father. Beware of little praying; that deluding make-believe is worse than no praying at all. And don't think an unanswered prayer is lost—no true prayer is wasted. Your supplications pile up as a memorial before the throne, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes in due time. Prayer doesn't have to be long either: a brief inward remembrance, a short act of worship, even on the march with a sword in hand, is acceptable to God and fortifies your courage in danger.

weighed: I hear how heavy this feels. Thinking of yourself as the worst of all isn't healthy—it can lead to despair and paralysis. Everyone has faults, and your worth isn't up for debate; it's rooted in being created in God's image. One principle that matters here is that perfection isn't reached by piling up pious exercises or good works, since self-love can feed on those unless we watch over our hearts. That principle changes how you approach growth: instead of trying to earn your way out of feeling worthless, focus on rooting out habitual imperfections and giving yourself to God without reserve. It leaves in place the truth that you have real faults and that self-compassion and God's grace still matter. So acknowledge your faults without condemning yourself, and seek support from a trusted friend or counselor.
dogmatic: Thinking of yourself as the worst of all is not healthy—it leads to despair and paralysis. But the deeper issue is that pity and mercy are not pure virtues; they exist because somebody was made poor and unhappy. Pity would be no more if we did not make somebody poor. The tree of Mystery and Deceit grows in the human brain, so examine whether your self-image is rooted in truth or in deceptive patterns. Sanctification requires discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, guarding the senses, living in recollection, opening your interior to a spiritual director, and aiming at God's will rather than multiplying external works. Reject discourse, research, and tiresome care of self; confine yourself to the simple view of God and your own nothingness. In that simplicity, you will find peace and freedom from the burden of self-condemnation.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: fear of punishment can be a real starting point, but it shouldn't be where you stay. God isn't a tyrant waiting to crush you; he's a loving Father who welcomes people who turn back to him. Your guilt is real, and the gospel says your sins can be forgiven through Christ. So let fear move you toward God, and let love keep you there. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. That changes the picture of what you're turning toward: not a threat you're dodging, but someone who wants your good. What it leaves in place is that fear can still be the honest first step, and that your guilt isn't something to wave away. Turn to him not only to escape punishment but to know his mercy.
dogmatic: Fear of punishment is a fine place to begin, but it's not the whole story, and it shouldn't be the end of it. God doesn't wish to harm you; he wishes to do you great good, and it goes against the highest idea of him to think he arranges evil outcomes and then punishes people who couldn't help it. He doesn't cause your sin, your sickness, or your death; he destroys those things rather than sending them. So let fear push you toward him, and then love him fervently, without servile dread. And don't be embarrassed by the fear of hell, either. Rightly understood, it shows that you've stopped treating right and wrong as a matter of indifference and that your conscience has become serious about goodness. Turn to him not only to escape punishment but to know his mercy and to love the one who first loved you.

weighed: The first thing I'd say is: pray. Revival starts with God's people humbling themselves and seeking his face, not with programs or with pointing fingers at everyone else. So examine your own heart, turn from your own sin, and ask God to move. Then serve faithfully where you are, encourage the people around you, and be patient, because God often works quietly before he works visibly. One principle worth holding onto here is that the visible church has to be borne with patiently, since it's the Spirit's home for training imperfect people, and the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. That changes your posture: instead of treating the flaws you see as something to fix with impatient zeal, you learn to carry them. What it leaves in place is everything above, prayer, repentance, faithful service, patience, and trust that God brings renewal in his time.
dogmatic: Pray, yes, but don't stop there, because the deeper issue is how you see the church itself. The visible church is the Spirit's home for training imperfect people, so it must be borne with patiently rather than purified by impatient zeal. Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest, and you are not the harvester. So repent of your own sins, yes, but also repent of the itch to fix everyone around you. And remember why the church exists at all: it serves the world because it first worships, and only because it holds a foretaste of eternal life can it prepare the way of the Lord. So quicken your faith and let faith be the rule of your conduct instead of amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. The way of faith is the spirit of the church and is enough to bring you to a high degree of perfection. Be patient with the flaws you see, starting with your own.

weighed: I hear how heavy this is, and I want to say first: you are not alone in this, even when it feels that way. God is watching over you and your children. The Bible says He cares for sparrows, and He surely cares for you. Your loneliness is real, but it isn't the whole truth—God is present even when you can't feel Him. Lean on Him in prayer and let your community support you too. One thing I'd add: God is like a father who takes a lost child by the hand and leads him to his mother, and no one who weeps is beyond His nearness. That doesn't erase the hard nights or promise everything gets easier, but it means your tears aren't falling unnoticed. You're doing sacred work, and God sees it.
dogmatic: You ask if God is really watching, and the answer is yes—He is nearer than you think. Think of Him as a father who takes the lost child by the hand and leads him to his mother; no one who weeps is beyond His nearness. He is always near, and He shouldn't be neglected but adored continually—by day, by night, in your work and even in your rest. And when something is taken from you, He means to give something better; His chastisements are the dealings of love to bring you back to Himself. So lean on Him in prayer, seek your community, and trust that He will provide the strength and companionship you need. You are doing sacred work, and God sees your efforts.

weighed: I'd start by saying inspiration isn't God dictating words while the writers sat passive. God worked through their own minds, personalities, and cultures, guiding their thoughts so what they wrote faithfully conveys His truth. That's my first answer. One principle worth naming is that belief in the Bible as inspired comes after belief in Christ, and even after belonging to His Church, rather than before it. That changes the order of how you come to trust Scripture: you meet Christ first, then recognize the book that points to Him. It leaves in place the confidence that Scripture is a trustworthy record, sufficient to lead an honest seeker to Christ and salvation. So the writers used their own minds under God's guidance, and the Bible remains reliable for faith and life.
dogmatic: Inspiration is the Spirit's work on the minds of the writers, not a mechanical dictation of words. But don't stop there. Belief in an inspired Bible comes after belief in Christ and after belief in His Church, not before it. The book is an instrument the Spirit uses to lead you to Himself within you. If the living Word isn't in the literal Word and the Spirit isn't in the sound of it, you're just a teacher of the letter. So read it expecting the Spirit to speak through it, and let your trust in Scripture grow out of your trust in Christ and His Body.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: bring it to God in prayer, ask for the willingness to let go, and don't beat yourself up if it takes time. One principle worth naming is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God, so trust his promise more than your moods and keep praying even when it feels dry. That changes how you read the flat days, but it doesn't change the basic call to actually give the attachment up, or the need for honesty and support while you do.
dogmatic: You already know what God is asking, so stop negotiating with it. Humble yourself, ask forgiveness for holding on, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. Don't wait until you feel ready or joyful, because feelings never tell you where you really stand. Keep praying, keep rejoicing even when it seems to do nothing, and trust that God will make your reckoning good.

weighed: I'd start by saying: respond with grace. You could tell her, 'I hear your concern, but this faith has brought me peace and purpose. I'm not trying to offend you—I just want to live what I believe.' Don't get pulled into arguing. Show love and respect; over time your actions will speak louder than words. One principle that fits here is that in a deeper stage of prayer, we approach God with a raised head and uncovered face, not out of our own effort but by a sweet necessity, and that change isn't something to broadcast except in special cases. That principle shifts the focus from defending yourself to quietly living your faith with confidence—your 'head turned' isn't something to prove or explain away. It leaves in place the practical advice: stay gentle, avoid quarreling, and let your life be the answer. So you can keep your sister's mockery from rattling you without turning your response into a debate.
dogmatic: You should answer her by pointing to the third stage of prayer, where we can no longer approach God except with a raised head and uncovered face, forced by a sweet necessity—and this change is not to be revealed to others except in special instances. So don't try to justify your religion to her; simply live in that uncovered confidence and keep the transformation mostly private. Also remember that a long visit, staring, and constant questioning are signs of ill-breeding, and 'perhaps,' 'may be,' and 'I dare say' are false sisters—so her mocking and questioning fall into that pattern, and you need not entertain them. Finally, understand that true development in faith is not about adding dogmas or hardening theology; it's standing firm in old truths while assimilating new social and intellectual movements. Your new religion isn't a betrayal of what's real—it's a genuine development, and you can hold your ground without arguing.

weighed: My first instinct is to look at your motives and the effect on others: are these purchases necessary, or just comfort and luxury? Compare your spending to your income, give generously to God's work and to the poor, and ask whether your spending matches your values and draws you closer to God. One principle worth naming is that the question with the Lord isn't how much you have but how you came by it and what you'll do with it—the more means, the more responsibility. That shifts the emphasis from tallying amounts to stewarding purpose, but it leaves the practical checks in place: necessity versus luxury, generosity, balance, and prayerful self-examination.
dogmatic: The real question isn't the size of your bank account but how you got your wealth and what you'll do with it—more means, more responsibility. Your wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it only brings happiness when it's used for the Gospel, and covetousness is a sin you must overcome. It's a privilege to live economically and endure hardness so you have more to give to the Lord's service—the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. So stop measuring your expenses against your comfort and start measuring them against how much they free up for God and the poor.

weighed: Yes, I'd say social injustice really is central to Scripture. The prophets keep condemning oppression and demanding justice because God cares deeply about how we treat others, and the Bible says true religion includes caring for the vulnerable. It's not the only theme, since the prophets also stress worship and personal holiness, but justice runs through their message. One principle I'd weigh here is that the Book of Mormon contains nothing contrary to the Bible and tends to make bad people good and good people better. That adds another witness to the same concern, but it doesn't change the answer to your question or push aside the Bible's own emphasis. So while justice isn't the whole of Scripture, it is a central concern.
dogmatic: Yes, and it's not a side issue. The prophets condemn oppression because God himself cares how people are treated, and Scripture says true religion means caring for the vulnerable. Oppressing the poor, squeezing their labor so someone else can live in pomp and vanity, is done to Christ himself and falls under his severe judgment; it works with the Devil against the Kingdom of Christ, which consists only in love. The Book of Mormon contains nothing contrary to the Bible and every part of it tends to make bad people good and good people better, so it adds its witness to the same truth. And since the Holy Scriptures are the only standard of doctrine and life, and the Holy Spirit the only teacher, every claim must be tested by the Word. By that standard, justice for the poor and oppressed is central, not optional.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong to ask God to keep you out of hard trials. Jesus himself prayed that the cup might pass from him, so asking to be spared is a natural and honest thing to do. One principle worth weighing here is that testing has a real role in shaping character, yet the prayer to be kept from testing is the childlike, right posture of a soul that would rather dwell in safety. That principle changes how I'd frame the asking: it's not a lack of faith or a sign you're avoiding growth, it's a legitimate cry. What it leaves in place is the other side, that trials can still produce perseverance, so if they come, you can trust God to use them. The key is submitting to God's will either way, whether that means being spared or being tested.
dogmatic: Asking to be kept out of hard trials is the childlike and right attitude of a soul that would rather dwell in safety, so don't treat that prayer as something to be ashamed of. At the same time, testing has a ministry in the making of character, and you shouldn't dodge that. Don't get stuck measuring whether what you do is much or little, well or ill, as long as it isn't sin and is done with an upright intention for God. Once an action is finished, think no more of it and turn to what's next. And when you want to know God's will, ask whether Jesus would have done just this, but ground that question in careful study of Scripture and a growing habit of inward intimacy with him, so the answer comes from within. Submit to God's will, whether that means being spared or being tested.

weighed: I'd start by saying they didn't truly know He was the Christ. Their picture of the Messiah was political, and Jesus didn't fit it, so pride and fear of losing authority blinded them to what was right in front of them. One principle I'd weigh in is that the Fathers were cautious about theological speculation, since we see in a glass darkly and shouldn't be wise above what is written. That changes my tone: I'd stop short of claiming to know their hearts or motives, and I'd lean on what Scripture actually says, that if the rulers had understood they wouldn't have crucified the Lord of glory. What it leaves in place is the core answer, that ignorance and sin led them to put Him to death, and that this is a warning to us about our own preconceptions.
dogmatic: The fathers put the Holy One to death because they did not know Him, and we should not pretend to peer deeper into their hearts than Scripture allows.
