We see in a glass darkly; we must not be wise above what is written. God is not caught in the nets of our reasoning, so we keep to what is revealed: had the rulers understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Their ignorance was real, and their sin was real, and that is enough for us to say. What matters far more is that the apostolic Church was intensely other-worldly. The chief gift offered was not a better life here but an entrance into heaven, and the thought of Christ's coming and judgment is the supreme motive to a holy life. So let us not build elaborate theories about their motives. Let us humbly accept the testimony of Scripture, set our hope on Christ's return, and live under the holy Cross, drawing our breath from above until the likeness of Jesus' death is traced in our lives.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: wanting to do more for God is a good instinct, but piling on devotions probably isn't the answer by itself. Holiness isn't about how many practices you stack up; it's about the love behind them. So check whether you're trying to earn God's favor instead of resting in his grace, and let prayer and Scripture deepen the relationship your actions flow from. One thing I'd add from the candidate principles is that devotion fits ordinary life in the world just as much as it fits a cloister. That changes the picture a bit: you don't need to escape your daily business to be devout, and short inward liftings of the heart count as real prayer. What it leaves in place is the core caution: more practices aren't the goal, and your heart staying on God is. So keep your responsibilities and your balance, and let any devotion you add help you keep God before you rather than crowd him out.
dogmatic: Adding devotions is fine, but the real question is whether your heart stays on God, and that's true whether you're in a cloister or up to your neck in the world. Don't let the spirit of the world crowd out interior recollection and prayer. When some occasion to practice virtue comes up, turn to God right there and say, 'Lord, I can't do this unless you enable me,' and you'll receive strength more than sufficient. A little lifting up of the heart is enough: a brief remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, even mid-march with a sword in hand, is a prayer very acceptable to God and fortifies your courage in danger. So add devotions if they help you keep God before your eyes amid your business, and sprinkle short acts of worship through your day.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, you can share answers to prayer, and it can really encourage people and build their faith. But some answers are deeply personal and might be meant just for your own walk with God. So check your motive—are you sharing to glorify God and help others, or to get attention? You could share general principles instead of intimate details, or confide the specifics with a trusted few. Pray about it and use wisdom; there's no rigid rule, just let love and humility guide you. One principle worth weighing is that prayer is the central secret of holy living and serving—so let prayer itself be the foundation, not an afterthought. That principle shifts the focus from whether to tell to whether the answer came from real, persistent prayer in the first place. It leaves in place the freedom to share and the call to check your motive and use discretion.
dogmatic: You should tell others about answered prayer, but only if that prayer was real prayer—prayer that meets the Bible's conditions: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Otherwise you're just reporting a wish that happened to come true. Prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, so build your life on it, in secret and with believers. Let your praying be unselfish, interceding for others, even those you've never met. When your testimony flows from that kind of prayer, it strengthens faith. So examine yourself, make sure your motive is to glorify God, and then share—confiding the most intimate details with a trusted few.

weighed: What you're describing sounds exhausting, and I don't want to brush past it. My first instinct is to say that the things we lean on giving way is genuinely painful, but it can also be honest — friendships, work, health, even our own plans were never built to carry the full weight of a soul, and when they fail it doesn't prove nothing is trustworthy. One idea worth sitting with is that all things betray the one who betrays God, and nothing shelters a soul that won't shelter in God, because created things are in league with their Maker and can't conspire against Him. That reframes the betrayal: it's not that nothing holds, but that lesser things were never meant to be the thing you hold. What it changes is where you look for something steady; what it leaves in place is the real grief of losing what you loved — it doesn't pretend the loss isn't loss.
dogmatic: Every refuge you grasp as a substitute for God will betray you back to Him. Nature, human love, work, pleasure, study — none of them can shelter your soul from God, because all things are in league with Him and cannot conspire against Him. The betrayal you feel isn't proof that nothing holds; it's the world doing exactly what it was made to do, pointing you past itself. And don't overlook the small things: a minor indulgence nursed can quietly push God off the center, and that's where the betrayal really begins. God uses no force — He doesn't compel your will. Your decision gets made right here, in your exact circumstances, not in some abstract realm. Keep yourself in His love by constant trust and obedience, and hard things become easy and sorrow gets silver-lined with hope. You're not abandoned by the world; you're pursued by a Father who means your good.

weighed: I'd first say what I said before: it's understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and nothing visible happens, but God isn't deaf. Scripture says He hears His people, and His timing isn't ours. Revival often starts quietly in individual hearts before it shows up in a congregation, and the waiting itself may be part of what He's doing. One principle worth weighing is that when God seems silent, it can be to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us. That reframes the silence as a wiser answer rather than indifference, but it leaves your real disappointment and the plain fact that the revival didn't come exactly where they are. So keep praying, examine your own heart, and watch for the small signs of His work.
dogmatic: God is not deaf, and He has not failed you. When He seems silent to your cries, it is to grant your main desire by doing what is most expedient for you; His delay is not indifference but a wiser answer. Don't conclude He is unwilling or unable to act today. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and God can and does heal and revive in answer to prayer now. He who understands all things hears the earnest supplication of the soul and your innermost thoughts, just as human invention lets people communicate across great distances, so He receives what is never spoken aloud. So ask in faith, nothing wavering, leave the outcome in His hands, and keep praying while you look for the deeper work He is doing in you and your church.

weighed: I'd start by saying chastity matters because your body and soul are made for God, and impurity throws both into disorder. Scripture is blunt that the impure won't inherit the kingdom, so the stakes really are eternal: unrepented impurity cuts you off from God, while purity of heart opens the way to seeing him. Chastity isn't just a social rule; it's a safeguard for your union with God. One principle I'd add is that chastity is a treasure you protect through prayer, self-denial, modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by steering clear of temptation, since whoever loves danger will perish in it. That changes the practical side of my answer: it turns a general warning into concrete habits. But it leaves the core in place: the eternal stakes and the call to guard your union with God.
dogmatic: Chastity is essential because your body and soul belong to God, and impurity disorders both. Scripture warns that the impure will not inherit the kingdom, so the consequences are eternal: unrepented impurity separates you from God, while purity of heart leads to the vision of God. This isn't a mere social convention; it's a spiritual safeguard. Protect chastity through prayer, self-denial, modesty of the senses, especially the eyes, and by avoiding temptation, because whoever loves danger will perish in it. Treat chastity as a precious treasure and impurity as a poison that darkens the mind and hardens the heart against grace.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, a conscience that grows and changes can still reveal God's mind. A child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth shifting, and our moral awareness can deepen the same way. One principle that matters here is that the Spirit's witness in your heart bears record of the living Redeemer and exceeds other evidence, so you're not stuck depending only on the past. That changes where you look for certainty: not just at history or at your own moral progress, but at Christ risen, known directly. It leaves the growth of conscience in place as real learning, not as proof that conscience is just a human invention. Test it against Scripture and the church's teaching, and don't wait to feel more before you act.
dogmatic: No, a conscience that shifts with history cannot be the final revelation of God's mind, and you should stop treating it as one. The Spirit of God bears record in your heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence. You are not dependent only on the history of the past to know Him. Begin with the historical resurrection, yes, but go on to direct experience of Christ. And God commands you to repent now, so the power to renounce sin is available this moment; feeling follows surrender, not the reverse. Do not wait to weep more or gain greater power. Act now, and let your conscience be corrected by the living Saviour rather than trusted as your guide.

weighed: The image means believers aren't isolated individuals but are joined together in Christ as a dwelling place for God. Each stone is alive, shaped and placed by God, and together they form a structure that honors him. This speaks of community, mutual support, and a shared purpose, and it implies growth over time, with Christ as the cornerstone. One principle I'd name is that the saints must be self-sustaining, producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and storing provisions against scarcity. That principle adds a practical, economic dimension to the image: a spiritual house has to stand, so its members need to sustain themselves and plan ahead. But it leaves the core in place: the house is still spiritual, its life comes from Christ, and the stones are still joined together for God's dwelling, not merely as a self-sufficient community.
dogmatic: The image means believers are living stones built into a spiritual house, joined in Christ as God's dwelling. But a house must stand, so the saints must be self-sustaining: producing what they eat, drink, and wear, living within their means, and keeping a year's or two years' provision against scarcity. Provision is not the whole building, though. Amid weighty employments, the saints reserved time for frequent retirement, conversing with God and themselves, and in their exterior functions raised their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, making all their actions in some measure an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise. And because a spiritual house is made of souls, temporal succor must be joined with redoubled labor for spiritual good—seeking the rooting out of sin and the establishment of God's grace in souls—so that the whole building grows holy in Christ the cornerstone.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: trusting God with the future means handing your worry over to Him and believing He'll provide. Acknowledge the anxiety, give it to God in prayer, plan wisely without obsessing, focus on today, and lean on people who remind you of His faithfulness. One principle that sharpens this is that God is the one living Agent and we're only His instruments—so your planning and effort are real, but they're not the thing holding your life together. That changes the tone: it turns planning from a security blanket into a tool, and it makes anxious self-reliance look like what it is. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—you still plan, work, and keep watch, and you still get help from a pastor or counselor if the anxiety sticks around. Trust is still a daily choice, and it still grows as you notice God's provision.
dogmatic: Stop treating your worry as if it were caution. God is the one living Agent who actually works, and you are only an instrument in His hand—so every ounce of anxious care on your part is distrust of Him and a kind of self-conceit, as if the outcome rested on your shoulders. Cast all your care on Him, because He cares for you. Do your part with diligence, but never mistake your effort for the real support. Keep yourself in His presence, and flee hurry and over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother of imperfection in everything. Pray as if it all depends on God, work as if it all depends on you, and rest in His sovereignty.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Gospel offers you forgiveness and new life in Christ, and the Holy Spirit's power to obey. One principle that helps here is that God's commands are promises—what He requires, He gives. That changes how you hear 'you must'—it becomes 'God will supply what you lack.' It leaves in place your real struggle and the need to trust and ask for help. So when you feel powerless, turn to God and say, 'Lord, I can't do this unless you enable me,' and trust that He gives strength more than sufficient. Confess your weakness, ask for help, and rely on His grace, not your own strength.
dogmatic: The Gospel doesn't just offer forgiveness—it offers enabling grace. God's commands are promises; what He requires, He gives. So stop waiting for the power to feel like it's there. When an occasion to do right comes, say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is yours. Repent now—the power to renounce sin is available because He commands it. The feeling follows the surrender, not the other way around. Trust that His precepts are assurances He will keep you from the sin He warns against. Confess your weakness, ask for help, and step forward in obedience, knowing He supplies the strength.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, those little prayers are worth something, even when they feel empty. Prayer isn't mainly about feelings; it's about staying connected to God through the day, and short prayers can keep you mindful of him. If they feel mechanical, try pausing to think about what you're saying, and maybe set aside some longer prayer times too. One principle I'd add is that a little lifting up of the heart is enough, a small inward act of worship counts as a prayer God accepts and can steady you when things get hard. That changes the tone a bit: it says the bar isn't a big emotional experience, so your brief prayers aren't wasted. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: keep going, ask God to help you pray sincerely, and remember prayer is a relationship, not a performance.
dogmatic: Yes, and don't let the flat feeling fool you. No true prayer is lost; it's kept as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes. So don't despise your short prayers. Keep praying at set times whether or not you feel like it, pray with your family, and never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Prayer isn't just asking God to handle everything; it's also you helping to accomplish what's asked, so be ready to act as he leads. A little lifting up of the heart is enough, a brief inward remembrance even in the middle of a march with a sword in hand is a prayer God accepts and it builds courage in danger. If it feels mechanical, pause and refocus, but don't stop. Trust that God hears and answers in his timing.

weighed: Yes—God sees you in that fight, even when no one else does. Feeling alone is real, but it doesn't mean you're abandoned. One thing worth holding onto is that not every temptation comes from outside you; a lot of it rises from your own desires, and that part is actually within your reach through guarding your senses, practicing self-control, and staying away from the situations that feed it. That doesn't erase the loneliness you're feeling or make the struggle disappear overnight, but it does mean you're not helpless in it. Bring it honestly to God, and consider telling one trusted person—a pastor, counselor, or friend—because hidden battles get heavier in the dark.
dogmatic: God absolutely sees you, and He is faithful in this. He never allows you to be tempted beyond your strength—with every temptation He provides a way of escape, so you can bear it, and patient endurance in temptation is crowned with life. Temptation itself is not sin; it's a proving of virtue, a way to gain great profit, because the life of man on earth is a warfare. Much of what you're fighting comes from your own concupiscence, and its power is largely under your control: guard your senses, practice mortification and temperance, avoid occasions of sin, and you will greatly diminish its force. Light temptations, suspicions, sadness, and discouragement are mere nothings—a good will puts them to flight by lifting your soul to God. He sees your hidden fight, and He will not fail you.

weighed: My first answer would be that your idea of infinity is a finite act of a finite mind—you can think 'without limit,' but your thinking is limited, and that's normal. What matters is whether the idea corresponds to a real being: a finite, changing world points beyond itself to something unlimited, and that unlimited being must be God. One candidate principle here is that God's infinity means he has no limits or bounds at all—not merely no known limits—and that he's transcendent as well as immanent, infinite intensively as inexhaustible spiritual life rather than by spatial extension. That sharpens things: it stops you from confusing infinity with the mere indefinite, and it means your finite idea can still truly intend the infinite God. What it leaves in place is your original worry—your idea stays finite, and the real question is still whether the argument from the world to a limitless cause is sound.
dogmatic: Your idea is finite, but it can truly intend the infinite God, so don't confuse infinity with the indefinite. God's infinity means no limits at all—transcendent yet present, intensive, an inexhaustible resource of spiritual life whose glory is its expression. The arguments from change and from order are only cumulative probable evidence: they corroborate the intuition of God and prove an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, yet they have real defects and cannot by themselves reach personality and righteousness. So apply their results to one personal Cause, Contriver, and Lawgiver, and ascribe infinity and perfection to him as what the mind cannot but think—while the anthropological argument supplies what they lack. Your finite idea matters because it is the mind's necessary reach toward that one Being.

weighed: First, steady yourself and don't lash out. Gather the facts, and when it's appropriate, calmly tell the truth to the people involved. Don't gossip or try to win everyone over, because some people will believe what they like. Lean on trusted friends, and if the accusation is serious, use fair, proper channels to clear your name. Your worth isn't decided by other people's opinions, so keep your conduct blameless and let time do its work. One principle worth weighing here is that you should bring what people say about you before the tribunal of your own conscience, and honestly judge yourself without either excusing or condemning yourself too quickly. That changes the inner posture: instead of only managing the accusation from the outside, you first check whether there's any truth in it, amend if there is, and stand steady if there isn't. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: state the facts calmly, seek fair counsel, and don't let bitterness take root. It just adds a quiet self-examination underneath all of that.
dogmatic: Bring everything people say about you before the tribunal of your own conscience. Go inside and judge yourself honestly, neither excusing yourself nor condemning yourself without reason, so you neither get arrogant nor lose heart. If your conscience truly accuses you, change. If after real reflection it doesn't, then human praise gains you nothing and blame costs you nothing. It's no loss to be despised or persecuted on the outside if you're innocent within, so be patient and silent and rejoice in the Lord. Don't seek revenge or the accuser's punishment, and don't prosecute the person who wronged you; want their repentance and faith instead, and value their soul above your own name. Pray for them, return good for evil, and leave the outcome to God in peace.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's understandable to struggle with this, and trusting God's will doesn't mean pretending pain isn't real. You bring your honest questions to God, you remember He's present in suffering, and trust grows over time through His past faithfulness and through community. One principle worth naming is that everything tends to the good of those who love God, even affliction, though the means may not be seen. That adds real weight to the idea that God isn't absent in what you're facing. What it leaves in place is the not-seeing. It doesn't hand you an explanation for why this particular bad thing happened to this particular good person, so the grief and the questions stay real, and you're still turning toward God in the middle of them rather than past them.
dogmatic: Scripture calls you to receive all things from God's hand, sweet or bitter, equally, because His love makes them acceptable. Afflictions aren't signs of His absence but of His fatherly care, so when you see trials as coming from a loving Father, they stop being a curse and become a consolation. If you love God, all things, even grief and sin, turn to your good, even when you can't see how. All evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and always for some good end; it couldn't be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. So commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, trusting that He steadies His own ark and guides His people.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not automatically a danger to feel more at home with books than in your closet—but it can become one if study quietly replaces your time with God. Books can teach you about God, but they're no substitute for personal communion with Him. One principle that fits here is that the closet is the heart's study—we learn more about how and what to preach there than in libraries, and thought is not only brightened but born in prayer. That changes how I'd frame the balance: it's not just about adding prayer to study, but seeing the closet as the place where your study actually gets its life. What it leaves in place is that study itself is good and can serve your walk with God—it just can't stand in for Him. So ask yourself if you're avoiding God, and if so, turn back and seek Him.
dogmatic: Yes, it's a danger if your study replaces your closet. The closet is the heart's study—thought is born there, and you learn more about how and what to preach there than in any library. Books can inform, but they can't substitute for intimate communion with God. If you're more comfortable with books than with God, you may be avoiding Him. Use your study to understand Scripture, but let the closet form your heart. As a Christian Scientist, be a law to yourself so mental malpractice can't harm you asleep or awake. Measure your ability to stay with God outside the closet by your ability to stay with Him in it. Great waiting in the closet is the source of great victories outside it—don't settle for hasty visits.

weighed: I'd start by saying this phrase from Jesus means the Sabbath was made to benefit us, not to be a crushing burden. It's a gift for rest and worship, a rhythm of renewal, and human need comes before rigid rule-keeping. One principle worth naming is that the Sabbath is a memorial of creation and a sign of the cross—redemption is creation through the cross, and it marks God as the One who sanctifies His people. That principle deepens the answer: it changes the Sabbath from just a practical rest day into a sign of who God is and what He's doing in us. But it leaves in place the core point that the Sabbath serves our well-being, not the other way around. So the day still exists for our good, and we're still called to keep it holy and set an example of faithfulness, but never as a burden that crushes people.
dogmatic: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath—but don't twist that into permission to treat the day as optional or merely symbolic. The seventh-day Sabbath is the memorial of creation and the sign of the cross, the seal that God sanctifies His people. Jesus said this when His disciples were criticized for plucking grain, showing that human need takes precedence over rigid legalism, yet He did not abolish the Sabbath. He calls us to trust Him for the cost of keeping it holy. We are to keep the Sabbath holy, attend to its worship and duties, and set an example of faithfulness. And remember: God's method is men, not methods or organizations; the Holy Ghost flows through people, not machinery. The Sabbath serves our well-being, reminding us we are not slaves to work but children of God who can trust Him enough to rest.

weighed: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—people are social, and approval feels good. The real issue is when praise becomes your master, when you do good mainly to be seen or criticism crushes you. One principle worth naming here is that we should be what we are and be that well, honoring the one who made us. That changes the frame: your worth isn't something you have to earn through applause, it's something you live out honestly. But it leaves your desire for connection intact—it doesn't tell you to stop wanting warmth from others. So do good work whether or not anyone notices, accept compliments graciously without depending on them, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point.
dogmatic: Wanting to be liked is not wrong—you were made to value love and approval. The mistake is straining to be something other than what God made you. Accept your condition and be that well, honoring the Master Workman and seeking to please God's will. To be gentle and kind, modest and truthful, full of faith and integrity and doing no wrong—this is of God, and such goodness sheds a halo of loveliness and makes the countenance beam. Yet do not locate the joy of God's love in your merit, your charitable or social work, your learning, or any arbitrary favoritism. That joy lives in the continually maintained attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. Do your good works honestly, receive praise as a gift, and let your gladness rest on that obedient communion rather than on being noticed.

weighed: I'd start by saying the name isn't hidden from anyone who seeks sincerely. It may feel beyond us, but God promises that those who seek will find, and the name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed everywhere—not a secret for insiders but a gift for all who call on Him. Still, we can't dig it out with our own cleverness; it's revealed by the Spirit, so we come with humility and faith, not just curiosity. One principle that fits here is that a truly great man is known by the number of beings he loves and blesses and who love and bless him. That reframes the search: the name isn't a puzzle to crack but a person to love and be loved by, so it changes how we seek—toward relationship rather than information. What it leaves in place is that the name still has to be revealed; our own effort alone won't uncover it.
dogmatic: The name of the Saviour is not beyond all men—it is given to those who seek with a sincere heart, and God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is proclaimed throughout the world, not kept for an elite. But understand this: a man who wishes to steady the ark of God without being called has a dark spot in him. God steadies His own ark, dictates His own affairs, and guides His people. So do not appoint yourself the one to pry out the name by your own zeal. Seek with humility and longing, like Elene, whose heart mourned until the nails were found, and like Cyriacus, who bowed on Calvary and prayed the Lord of angels to reveal the unknown mystery—and a sign of fire rose where the nails were hidden, and the people gave glory to God. The name is revealed by God to those who ask, seek, and knock, and it is not for the self-appointed to force.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: when Jesus points to the sparrow, He's saying that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He'll certainly provide for His children. So remind yourself that your needs are known to God and that He's faithful to provide. Fear usually comes from focusing on what you lack or what might happen; faith focuses on God's character and promises. Practical steps: write down your fears and give them to God in prayer, recall past times He provided, and trust He'll do it again. His care may come through other people or unexpected means, but He doesn't forget His own. One principle worth naming is that we can't escape life's dangers without God's actual, continual help, so we should pray continually, and we can't pray without being with Him, can't be with Him but by thinking of Him often, and can't think of Him often but by a holy habit. That adds a steady practice to the practical steps: fear gets crowded out not just by remembering promises but by a habit of turning your mind to God through the day. What it leaves in place is the core: your needs are known, God is faithful, and you can bring your fears to Him.
dogmatic: When Jesus said God cares for the sparrow, He was teaching that if God provides for small, seemingly insignificant creatures, He will certainly provide for His children. But God is not distant or uninvolved—He knows your needs before you ask and numbers the very hairs of your head. So apply this by reminding yourself that your needs are intimately known to God and that He is faithful to provide. Fear comes from focusing on what you lack; faith focuses on His detailed care. Yet we need His continual help, and that help comes through the holy habit of praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often. Since we must know before we love, such habits deepen your knowledge of Him and cast out fear. And remember that your longing for an enduring home is Nature's own cry in you, not an unholy strife; she who gives wings to birds will find out a way for you. Write down your fears and give them to God in prayer, recall past times when He provided, and trust that He will do so again.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, God can still find you. Losing a childhood faith is common, and the fact that you want it back is itself a hopeful sign. Pray honestly even when the words feel empty, read Scripture, talk to someone you trust, and give it time. One thing I'd add now is this: don't treat your faith like a feeling you have to manufacture or monitor. Faith isn't a mood or a theory you have to get right first; it's a support that holds you even when you can't feel it, and its confidence rests in God, not in your own certainty. That changes how you approach the whole thing, because you stop waiting to feel sure before you act. What stays the same is the practical path: honest prayer, Scripture, community, patience, and the simple desire that brought you here. So come as you are, keep showing up, and let God do the finding.
dogmatic: Yes, God can still find you, but stop treating this as a problem of technique. God sometimes hides Himself, and that hiding is not abandonment; it's an invitation to let faith alone be your support and the whole foundation of your confidence, which must be in God and not in your feelings. Faith is not a theory or a mood, and it doesn't cling to any formula; it uses prayer, Scripture, and fellowship as instruments without being bound to them. More than that, the soul must be converted and become as a child, turning again to God out of whom it proceeded, forsaking its own imaging, its lust, and every self-made centre. Quit curving inward to inspect your faith. Turn outward to Him, and the Divine Vision is restored. Come as a child, trust the Father who seeks you, and let faith, not self-analysis, be your foundation.

weighed: I'd start by saying: pray simply and honestly. Tell God plainly, 'Lord, I'm afraid; help me.' You don't need fancy words. Short prayers you can repeat work well—the Jesus Prayer, Psalm 23, 'Lord, have mercy.' Breathe slowly, name your fear to God, and ask for protection and peace. If others are with you, pray together. Fear is natural, and God isn't offended by it. Keep praying while the danger lasts, and give thanks afterward. Even one honest cry is real prayer, and God hears you wherever you are. One principle worth adding: a little lifting of the heart is enough—a brief inward act of worship, even with a sword in hand, is a prayer God accepts and it strengthens your courage. That changes the pressure to pray long or eloquently; it leaves in place the simple, honest, repeated short prayers and the invitation to pray with others.
dogmatic: Don't fix your eyes on the storm or on your own strength—fix them on Christ, who is the antidote to fear and the substance of your deliverance. Abide in Him and lean on His continual help. Prayer, being with God, and thinking of Him often are bound together by holy habit; you must know Him before you can love Him, and to know Him you must think of Him often. Yet don't imagine you must pray at length. Brief inward remembrances and short acts of worship—'Lord Jesus, have mercy,' 'You are my refuge'—are acceptable prayers and fortify courage even in danger. A single turning of the heart to Him is real prayer. Keep your eyes on Christ, offer these short acts often, and let His presence, not the length of your words, be your peace.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: both are true in different ways. Right now, by the Spirit, believers really are God's temple, both each one and together as the church. And Scripture also talks about a heavenly city and temple that's being made ready for God's people, which we're still waiting for. So the Spirit living in us now is a foretaste and a preparation for the fuller closeness with God we'll step into. One principle worth naming here is that the saints aren't the Holy City—the city is prepared for them, and the dead in Christ haven't yet been caught up; they're waiting for the resurrection. That sharpens the distinction: the temple we are now isn't the same thing as the city we're being made ready to enter. What it leaves in place is the main point—the present indwelling of the Spirit is real, and it's genuinely preparing us for what's coming. The two aren't rivals; it's a present temple and a future city, and the one is growing toward the other.
dogmatic: The saints are the temple of God now—make no mistake about that—but they are not the Holy City. The city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead have not yet been caught up; they wait for the resurrection. Believers are being built together as a temple, God's dwelling now, and yet this temple is being prepared to enter the city God has prepared. So come to worship expecting peace, security against evil, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. The saints testify that those who expect these things find them, and if they seem absent, ask whether we have expected them rather than blaming God. And remember: only the pure in heart shall see God. Set yourself against all licentiousness and every form of impurity, for chastity and purity of heart are not optional but the very condition of seeing Him. Be built together in holiness, and so be made ready to enter the city.

weighed: I'd start where you are: it's completely normal not to know what to pray for. Ask God to teach you to pray, the way the disciples did. You can pray Scripture—the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer give you words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also simply pray for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning. One principle worth weighing is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not just an occasional exercise. That changes the emphasis: instead of waiting for the right words, you make prayer the regular habit that shapes your whole walk, and you ask God to help you search out and reform your own heart. What it leaves in place is the simple starting point—you still begin honestly, with Scripture and the Spirit's help, and you still don't need perfect words. It just adds a steady, daily direction to the practice.
dogmatic: You ask how to pray aright, so here is the answer: prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an occasional exercise. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Bring even the smallest matter to Him—honour Him by asking His guidance rather than taking any decision out of His hands. And remember you need His continual help: praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit. We must know Him before we love Him. So make prayer a habit, not a crisis tool. Think on Him often, and you will come to know Him; knowing Him, you will love Him; loving Him, you will pray aright, with your heart searched, reformed, and wholly turned to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, God isn't a distant, gloomy being you have to dread. Jesus taught us to pray to 'our Father,' so you can come near with confidence, even while keeping a healthy reverence for his holiness. One principle I'd weigh says God is the Father of our spirits, that we stand to him as children, and that his service is cheerful rather than gloomy because he's near to those who ask. That changes the tone: it turns fear into trust and duty into delight. What it leaves in place is his sovereign honour, so I'd still come with awe and honesty, not casualness. So yes, approach him as a father, and let that closeness deepen your reverence rather than erase it.
dogmatic: God is not a distant, gloomy being to be dreaded. He is your Father, and his children may come to him freely. He listens when you pray and numbers the hairs of your head, and his service is full of beauty and cheerfulness rather than gloom. Yet the one united to God is one mind with him, so out of regard for his sovereign honour you must never think or imagine in his presence what you would blush to have seen before men; raise all your thoughts to God alone and set him before your inward gaze as though he alone existed. Above all, do not imagine God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction. He is a loving Father who gives only good, and sickness is not his will.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, it's possible for two people to reach different conclusions in good conscience, especially when the matter isn't clearly settled by shared moral principles. Conscience isn't infallible—it can be mistaken, under-informed, or shaped by culture. Your neighbour may see something you don't, and you may see something they don't. So take their view seriously, examine your own reasons, and seek wise counsel. Where Scripture and clear moral teaching speak, follow them; where they don't, allow freedom and avoid contempt. You may both be partly right, or one of you may be mistaken—humility and honest dialogue are the way forward. One principle worth naming is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to erode your ability to do right. That changes the tone: instead of just comparing opinions, you'd ask whether your conscience is accusing you about something you should actually repent of and reform, rather than explaining it away. What it leaves in place is the basic point that two people can sincerely differ and that you should still listen to your neighbour and hold your own view with humility.
dogmatic: No—don't flatter yourself that both views can simply be right. A guilty conscience and unrepented sin destroy the ability to do right; if sin isn't regretted and lessening, it rushes toward moral ruin. So when your conscience accuses you, repent and reform, don't rationalize it away. And be just with your own soul: neither excuse it without reason nor accuse it lightly, so it doesn't grow insolent or lose courage. Bear patiently with your neighbour's imperfections too, since that forbearance is a great part of perfection and the practice of love. But make no mistake—the question isn't whether you can both be comfortable in your opinions. Examine yourself, turn from what's wrong, and hold to what's true, whatever your neighbour thinks.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling distant from God is common and doesn't mean He's left you. Name the distance honestly in prayer, then return to the basics: Scripture, worship, fellowship. Meditate on passages that describe God's love—the Psalms, the parable of the prodigal son, Romans 8. Serve others; love often grows through action. Check whether sin, busyness, or disappointment has cooled your affection, and confess it. Talk with a trusted friend or pastor. Practice gratitude and keep a journal of God's faithfulness. Distance is often a season, not a verdict; keep showing up, and affection will follow. One principle worth weighing is that the Lord directs hearts by His Word, His Holy Spirit within, and His Providence in daily circumstances—and that sin has blinded and biassed us so we need divine direction to reach the home of God's love. That changes the tone: instead of just trying harder to feel love, you actively ask for and follow His guidance through Scripture, the Spirit's promptings, and the circumstances He arranges. It leaves in place the practical steps—honest prayer, meditation, service, confession, fellowship—but frames them as ways of receiving His direction rather than self-effort.
dogmatic: The vague longing you feel is not the answer. When God is known as Father in Christ, that impulse gives way to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. But for the right practice of His presence, your heart must be empty of all other things, because God will possess the heart alone and cannot act in it unless it is left vacant to Him. Do not assume you can find your way home by your own insight: sin has blinded and biassed us, so we cannot arrive without the Lord's guidance. Seek His direction through the Word, the indwelling Spirit, and Providence. Clear away competing loves, meditate on His love in the Psalms and the prodigal son, serve others, and confess what has cooled your affection. Distance is a season, not a verdict; keep meeting the Friend who has come near.

weighed:
I'd start where I started before: your fear is natural, and peace doesn't come from pretending death isn't frightening. It grows from facing it with support and hope—talk honestly with God and with people you trust, lean on the psalms that speak of God's presence in the valley, practise small acts of trust now, and let the calm of people who face death with faith steady you.

One idea worth weighing is that the Lord deals gently with his dying saints and takes away the sting of death, so the valley isn't dark because he is there as light. That changes the tone: instead of only managing fear, you can expect gentleness from God at the end, which can soften dread. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—honest naming of fear, trusted people, Scripture, small acts of trust, practical preparation—and it doesn't promise the fear will vanish, only that you won't face the valley alone.
dogmatic: Hear this: the Lord deals gently with his dying saints, and he takes away the sting of death. The valley is not dark, because the Lord is there as light and salvation; victory is given through Jesus Christ. So meet sufferings, trials, and tribulations with a strong will to bear them for God, so that all their bitterness is full of peace and tranquillity. Learn not to be troubled in tribulations, not to be incensed against those who inflict them, nor to entertain resentment. Sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, desiring rather to be abhorred as filthy mire than to possess the delights of earth or be honoured by men. Then dread cannot destroy you, and you walk toward the Lord who is light, and beyond death to resurrection.

weighed: When words fail, you can still pray. Start with short, honest phrases like 'Lord, have mercy' or simply 'Here I am.' Use Scripture—the Psalms give words when yours run out. Try writing your thoughts, walking in silence, or listening to a hymn. Remember that prayer is not a performance; God knows your heart before you speak. Even groans count. Keep a simple routine: a few minutes each morning and evening, a gratitude list, and one request. If you're distracted, gently return. Talk to a pastor or friend about it. Silence before God is itself a form of prayer, so don't be anxious about having nothing to say. One principle that matters here is that secret prayer and meditation on God's word shouldn't be sacrificed to busy activity—you need to be alone with God first. That principle changes the emphasis: it makes the quiet, set-apart time with God the priority, not just one option among many. But it leaves in place the practical helps I mentioned—short phrases, Scripture, silence, and talking to someone—because those are ways to keep that secret place alive.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating prayer as something you do when you feel ready or have the right words. Prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your spiritual bankruptcy. Human nature resists it, and little praying is worse than no praying because it's make-believe. So don't fill the silence with activity or wait for eloquence. Take time to be alone with God and His word—secret prayer and meditation are indispensable, and nothing compensates for the loss of the secret place. Ask not for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love, finding it sweet to suffer with God. Accustom yourself to familiar, humble, affectionate conversation with Him, watching that you neither do, say, nor think anything displeasing to Him. Begin with Scripture; the Psalms give words when yours run out. A few honest phrases like 'Lord, have mercy' are enough. Guard a daily appointment alone with Him, refuse to let service or fellowship crowd out communion, and if dryness persists, keep the secret place first. Such watchful converse brings the peace of paradise even now.

weighed: Your talents and education are real gifts, and you should use them well, but they alone can't make your ministry fruitful. Fruitfulness depends on God's grace, prayer, your character, and your love for people. A well-trained mind helps you teach clearly and lead wisely, but hearers are changed by the Spirit, not by credentials. So steward your gifts: keep learning, prepare carefully, and seek feedback. Pair competence with humility, holiness, and dependence on God. Guard against pride in your education and against treating ministry as a career. One principle worth weighing is that a professional ministry can become a heartless ministry—when salary and self-advancement take center stage, the heart gets pushed to the rear. That principle sharpens your motive and warns you against making ministry a career move, but it doesn't cancel the value of your education or the need for careful preparation. It leaves in place the call to use your gifts well while keeping your heart and dependence on God at the front.
dogmatic: No, your talents and education alone cannot make your ministry fruitful—and if you treat ministry as a profession or a business, you're already on the wrong track. When salary and self-advancement play a big part, the heart plays a small part. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. Make prayer your first preparation: set apart time in the day and much of the night to attend to God in silence, and keep Him always present to your mind. As an ambassador and messenger of God, reprove sin sincerely rather than softening the Gospel to soothe your hearers. Visit the sick. Esteem a person's immortal soul above their present favor. Fear none but the One who can destroy both soul and body. Your gifts matter only when they serve a heart fully devoted to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying those moments are real and worth taking seriously. Nature and music can stir awe and wonder, a sense of connection that goes beyond the ordinary. Many people call them spiritual experiences, and they can refresh you. You might treat them as invitations to slow down and pay attention. One idea that fits here is that nature is a visible sign of something invisible—a Will behind it all. That changes how you might respond: instead of just enjoying the feeling, you could trace the beauty back to its source and feel gratitude. But it leaves in place the simple fact that the experience is real and good, and that you don't have to overanalyze it. You can still receive it with openness and let it deepen your appreciation for beauty and mystery.
dogmatic: Those moments are real, but watch out for the trap of spiritual sensuality—basking in a pleasant feeling and going passive. The soul's health is in intense living and activity connected to the Divine Energy. Nature isn't just material or an end in itself; it's the visible demonstration of an invisible Will. So trace the beauty you feel to its Source and bless God for every beautiful thing, until your days become one long delight. Let awe rouse you rather than lull you. Ask what it points to, and respond with gratitude, worship, and action. One moment of divine understanding is a foretaste of eternity, bridging even death—so receive beauty and press beyond it into lively communion and service.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: name the disappointment honestly, don't let it fester, forgive the people you blame, and separate your worth from your career. That still holds. The one principle I'd add is that rejoicing is a practice you keep up even when it feels like it isn't working—keep going and trust that the reckoning will come out right. That changes the tone: instead of waiting for the bitterness to lift before you can feel okay, you act as if the good outcome is already secured. It leaves in place the practical steps—honesty, forgiveness, gratitude, counseling—because those are how you keep rejoicing without pretending.
dogmatic: Bitterness after career disappointment is real, but don't let the first dose of joy seem useless and give up. Count it all joy even in these temptations, trusting God to make the reckoning good. Watch out for the enemy's false dread of your wretchedness—he whispers that your disappointment and any fall are his final victory and tries to drive you from beholding your Everlasting Friend. Refuse that trick. Stay beholding God, and when you fall, rise by charity and meekness, turning the enemy's gain into his own sorrow. If you counsel others, first know, live, and love this truth yourself—never just repeat words, because healing comes from truth embodied, not recited. Forgive those you blame, keep gratitude and service, and let joy, not dread, set the tone of your waiting.

weighed: Yes, it costs you something real. When approval is your motive, the good deed turns into a performance, and the reward is just the praise you get, nothing deeper. You start leaning toward visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth ends up hanging on other people's opinions, which breeds anxiety and exhaustion over time. One principle worth weighing here is this: every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way. That shifts the focus from whether anyone is watching to whether you're actually showing up for the good itself, moment by moment. What it leaves in place is the honest self-check I'd still suggest: notice your motives, do some good in secret, and ask whether you'd still do it if no one knew.
dogmatic: Yes, and the cost is steeper than you think. If being seen is the engine, the deed is a performance and the praise is the whole paycheck, so your worth rides on opinions that shift with the wind. Don't settle for measuring yourself by words or appearances. Test it by fruits: does your life actually demonstrate the healing power of Truth and Love, or just talk about it? Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way, so stop waiting for an audience and get on with it. And don't treat self-denial and living economically as losses. They're a privilege that frees your resources for the LORD's service, and the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. Do the good whether or not anyone sees, and let your fruits prove what you actually understand.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, you don't need to understand every doctrine to grow. Growth comes mainly through your relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship—not through mastering theological systems. Doctrines matter, but they're meant to serve your faith, not overwhelm it. Start with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. Learn the rest gradually as questions come up. Ask mature believers for help, join a good church, and be patient with yourself. Understanding deepens over years. Focus first on loving God and neighbor; the rest will come in time. One idea worth weighing is that theology can keep developing—the Church holds firm to old truths while entering into new social and intellectual movements and welcoming new knowledge, rather than just piling on more dogmas. That would change how you see doctrine: not as a fixed list to master but as a living tradition that can grow and assimilate new understanding. It leaves in place the essentials you start with—who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him—and it leaves in place the practices of prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship as the core of your growth. So you still don't need to understand everything now; you can grow patiently while staying open to how understanding might deepen over time.
dogmatic: No, you don't need to master every doctrine to grow—but don't mistake real development for just piling on new dogmas or hardening theology into a fixed system. True development means the Church stands firm in her old truths while entering into and assimilating the new social and intellectual movements of the age, welcoming new knowledge. Begin with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. The doctrine of sin doesn't rest on Genesis being literal history or on external dogma alone; it rests on Christ's authority verified in Christian moral experience, so you're free to treat the early chapters of Genesis as allegorical. And don't think development ended with Christ's teaching: the Spirit continues His work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in ethics and theology. Grow patiently through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: seeing little fruit after years of faithful ministry is genuinely discouraging, and your question is honest. Whether to stay or go deserves prayer, wise counsel, and a real look at the soil, your methods, and the season you're in. One principle worth weighing is that when you're unsure which of several labors is required, you do them all so you're sure of doing the one the Lord actually requires. That reframes your question: instead of narrowing down to one place, it invites you to keep laboring broadly and trust God to show you which work bears fruit. What it changes is the pressure to decide right now; what it leaves in place is your need for discernment, honest assessment, and the counsel of trusted mentors. So don't move out of despair or stay out of mere duty—keep laboring wholeheartedly, and let obedience, not visible results, be your measure.
dogmatic: Don't respond to thin fruit by cautiously narrowing your labor. If you're required to do ten pieces of work and only one is necessary for the Kingdom, do all ten—so you're sure of performing the one the Lord really requires. And don't lean on elaborate appeals or human recruitment methods; seek laborers first by earnest prayer to the Lord of the harvest and by deepening your own spiritual life, so that people cannot stay at home. Remember too that we have no time allotted to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense—when you labor most fervently for the Kingdom of God, it is all for yourself, since your interest is bound up in that Kingdom. So keep laboring wholeheartedly where you are, and let faithfulness, not visible results, measure your obedience.

weighed: I'd start by saying I hear how painful it is to feel your church cares more about the building and budget than about people. My first instinct would be to encourage you to pray about it, check whether your expectations are realistic, and then talk calmly with your pastor or a trusted leader about what you've seen. Offer to help with outreach or welcoming newcomers, and if it's serious, put your concern in writing to the board. One principle worth weighing is that church revenues and treasures exist for the relief of the poor, and that a steward who complains the church is impoverished by almsgiving should be answered that God will provide. That principle changes the focus: it makes care for the poor the standard by which budgets and buildings should be judged, and it challenges hoarding while people suffer. But it leaves in place the practical need for upkeep and the value of speaking calmly and specifically to leaders. It doesn't cancel your own responsibility to serve or the possibility that this community may not be the right fit after honest effort.
dogmatic: The church's money and treasures belong to the poor. If anyone says the church is being impoverished by giving alms, answer with confidence that God will provide. Providence, not accumulation, is our security. Even sacred vessels may be devoted to those in need, and goods hoarded while people suffer are a scandal. Yet do not blame priests or institutions alone. The Church's lack is found in the tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member's heart, including your own. The Church gains what is lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Trust that the government of this Church is based on true principles. People fall out by the way through ignorance, because they do not thoroughly canvass their acts and wisely ponder probable results. So examine your own love, speak plainly with your leaders, and help connect resources to people.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling jealous when others succeed is very common, and hating it about yourself shows you have a conscience that wants to change. Name the feeling honestly instead of shaming yourself for it. Jealousy often points to something you want for yourself—recognition, security, or purpose—so ask what the envy is telling you, then take small, concrete steps toward your own goals rather than measuring yourself against others. Practice celebrating someone else's success out loud, even when it's hard; gratitude and generosity tend to crowd out envy over time. Be patient, and talk with a trusted friend or counselor if it's intense or persistent. One principle I'd weigh is that jealousy is the grave of affection, and that mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden—so don't contract the horizon of a worthy outlook by selfishly exacting another's time and thoughts. That principle changes the frame: it treats envy not just as a personal discomfort but as something that can quietly kill closeness, so you'd watch how jealousy shows up in your relationships and refuse to let it narrow your generosity toward others. What it leaves in place is the practical core: naming the feeling, asking what it wants, taking your own steps, celebrating others, and being patient. It doesn't replace those steps; it adds a relational warning and a call to keep a wide, confident outlook.
dogmatic: Jealousy is the grave of affection. Mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden, and you must not contract the horizon of a worthy outlook by selfish exaction of another's time and thoughts. Nothing short of absolute self-conquest is demanded by the inward monitor, the Soul; the instinct for retaliation and petty human aims must be overcome, a slow task of much humiliation that reveals your own smallness and puny self-control. Avoid hurry and anxiety, keeping yourself faithfully in the presence of God, since these are the greatest obstacles to progress in perfection. So do not coddle the feeling or negotiate with it. Lay aside retaliation and petty aims, practice mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive, and recognize humbly how ineffective your self-control is on its own. Do not fret anxiously over your progress; keep yourself in God's presence and treat over-eagerness as the mother imperfection of all imperfections, for anxiety is an obstacle to perfection.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, you can be forgiven even while you're still holding a grudge. Being hurt is real, and struggling with resentment doesn't cut you off from God's mercy. One principle worth weighing is that forgiveness isn't just a gift dropping from the sky in response to a request; it's an inward condition that grows in a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. That changes how I'd frame it: your grudge isn't just a feeling to wait out, it's something that shapes whether forgiveness can take root in you. But it leaves in place the comfort that God's pardon is still offered to you now, and that you can be honest about the hurt while you ask for grace to release it. So take the grudge seriously, pray for the person, and let forgiveness be a process rather than a pass-fail test.
dogmatic: No, you can't be forgiven while you're still holding a grudge, because forgiveness is not a transaction granted regardless of the state of your heart. It is an inward condition of the personal life: it comes naturally to the soul that loves and forgives, and it depends on your own spirit as well as on God. A heart that remains hard and unforgiving cannot simply receive pardon while refusing to give it. Christians are never allowed to seek revenge; patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. Do not limit forgiveness by a human reckoning of how much the wound deserves. Forgive as you hope to be forgiven, looking to the Lord who resigned all to earn our pardon. Refuse to mete out love by your own narrow rule; be honest with God about the hurt, pray for the person, and let his generous pardon shape yours.

weighed: Being transformed in God means a slow, lifelong change of heart, moving from self-centeredness toward love of God and neighbor. You begin by turning honestly toward God, admitting where you fall short, and asking for grace. Build simple habits: daily prayer, reading Scripture, and fellowship with other believers. One thing worth holding onto is that God reshapes your pleasures, taking the shine off guilty ones and deepening clean, unworldly joys so you depend less on the world. That adds a real focus on what you enjoy and where it points you, but it leaves the basics in place: honest turning, grace, and steady habits. Expect slow progress and setbacks. Transformation is God's work in you, and your part is to cooperate.
dogmatic: Being transformed in God means consenting without protest as He scatters your vanities, breaks your prides, grinds your self-gratifications to dust, and transfigures your natural lusts into Holy Love. The pain of that transition is real, and the Divine Anaesthetic He gives you in it is His Grace. He transposes your pleasures, stripping the glamour from the guilty and transferring it to the blameless, and He increases the pleasure of unworldly enjoyments so you become independent of worldly ones. But you cannot remain in this transformed world unless you are at peace with yourself and all persons around you. So begin by offering God your divided heart and receiving His Grace through the stripping, and keep prayer, Scripture, and fellowship. Change from place to place without changing your love or its object, remaining equally for God in all things, uninfluenced by affairs. Submit, stay at peace, and be equally for Him in every setting.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, expect fruit, but not always on your timetable or in the shape you picture. Keep praying, teach by word and example, and look for small signs of growth without turning it into pressure. One principle worth adding is that God's children have different gifts and degrees of knowledge yet share one Spirit, so we shouldn't contend over different fruits and gifts but acknowledge them in one another. That changes how you read your children's growth—you stop grading one child against another or demanding a uniform kind of evidence—while it leaves in place the call to pray persistently, teach faithfully, and trust God with the increase.
dogmatic: Expect present fruit, and pray for it with perseverance and submission. Train your children in the fear of the Lord, because the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation, and the eternal consequences of right training or neglect are real. Don't demand uniformity of knowledge or opinion as the condition of fellowship; the children of God have various gifts and degrees of knowledge yet form one Spirit, so acknowledge different fruits and gifts in one another rather than contending over them. Seek substantial information and trust little to theory—pluck fruit from the tree of knowledge, taste it, and bring the best books into your home.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, God doesn't require you to earn His love. His love isn't a wage you collect; it's a gift already given, and trying to be good enough turns grace into a transaction that will always leave you exhausted. One principle here that's worth weighing says God loved us before He made us, and that love was never slacked. That changes the picture of where you're standing: you're not working to get into His love, you're already inside it, and your effort becomes a response rather than a price. What it leaves in place is that your choices and obedience still matter—they just flow from being loved instead of trying to secure it. So let go of the ledger and rest in His acceptance; your weariness doesn't disqualify you from it.
dogmatic: No—God does not require you to earn His love. His love was in Him from without beginning and was never slacked: He loved us before He made us, and in that love He made all things profitable to us. Love was His meaning in everything He showed. His self-limitation—in decree, creation, providence, inspiration, and above all in Christ—is no denial of His perfection but its expression, a sign of power and love. So stop multiplying offerings and fretting over distraction; simply do your work for God without anxiety, and when your mind wanders, gently return without disquiet. Your striving cannot purchase what was always yours. Rest in that love, and let obedience flow from gratitude rather than exhaustion.

weighed: Yes, pray about it—but let prayer steady you rather than feed the panic. God cares about the details of your life, and nothing is too small to bring to him. Ask him to help you find what's lost and to calm your heart, then take the practical steps in front of you: retrace your steps, check the usual places, ask for help. One thing worth holding onto is the idea of coming to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—simply keeping your mind in his presence, and gently bringing it back when it wanders. That doesn't change the basic answer; it just shifts the emphasis from asking for a specific outcome to resting in his company while you search. Whether or not you find the item, he's with you.
dogmatic: Yes, pray—and make prayer the main thing, not a last resort. You can't get through this on your own; you need God's actual, continual help, so pray without stopping. You can't pray without being with him, and you can't be with him without thinking of him often, and that only comes from habit. Come to him like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and keep your mind in his presence; when it wanders in panic, bring it back calmly, because fretting only scatters you further. Ask him to help you search out your own heart too—what fear or attachment this loss has stirred up, what needs reforming. Let prayer lead your practical steps as well: retrace, check, ask for help. He cares about the lost item and about the heart that's clutching it.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the key is to separate the sin from the people. You can refuse to take part in what's wrong while staying loyal, present, and kind. Draw clear lines around what you won't join, and say so honestly and gently instead of quietly pulling away. Keep the relationships going, share meals, listen, serve, so the distance is from the sin and not from them. Skip gossip and comparisons, and speak about the wrong only when it's needed and with humility. One principle that sharpens this is that confessing your own sins and standing as one with sinners is how you actually help people, the way Christ took our sins as His own. That changes the tone: you don't come at people as a clean judge above them, you come as a fellow sinner who needs mercy too, and you start by naming your own faults. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: you still don't join the wrongdoing, you still don't betray your people, and you still stay in relationship with them. It just moves you from standing over them to standing with them.
dogmatic: The only way to save anyone is to confess your own sins and make yourself one with sinners, the way Christ took our sins and confessed them as His own. So stop trying to keep yourself clean and apart. If you're caught in the belief and fear of sin and you know the remedy but won't use it for yourself, you'll have little or no power to help anyone else. Deal with the beam in your own eye first, your own hidden faults and fears, or you'll heal no one. Then you can refuse to join the wrong without pride, because you're not a judge standing over the guilty, you're one of them. Stay with your people, eat with them, listen, serve, and speak honestly, but begin with your own need for mercy. And trust the promise: faith acting on Christ's strength overcomes sin, and believing in people helps them recover. No character is beyond remedy.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: the Paradise of God is the blessed state of fellowship with God, pictured as a garden — Eden at the beginning, and in Revelation the tree of life in the New Jerusalem at the end. As for where it is, Scripture treats it as belonging to God's presence rather than a spot on a map; Paul was caught up into it, and Jesus promised the thief he'd be there that day. One principle worth naming is that the Holy City encloses the garden, with the tree of life and the river of water of life, and is itself God's sanctuary. That sharpens the picture: Paradise isn't a separate lost garden off somewhere but the restored garden at the heart of God's dwelling with his people. What it leaves in place is the core answer — Paradise is life with God, entered through death and completed at the resurrection, not a location you could point to on a map.
dogmatic: The Paradise of God is the garden of Eden restored, enclosed within the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, where the tree of life stands and the river of water of life flows from the throne — and that city is God's sanctuary. But don't look for it as a journey to a place after death. Heaven is not a location out there; it is the will yielding to God, the soul penetrated through and through with the Divine Light the way glowing iron is penetrated by fire, held in the hand of Christ, becoming itself the very Heaven of God where he dwells. Heaven and Hell are within the soul: Heaven is the will turned into the love of God, Hell the will turned into his wrath. At death the soul needs no going forth — it simply stands in what is manifested in it.

weighed: Yes, you can believe in objective duty without believing in God. That's what I'd say first: many people hold that moral obligations are real and binding, grounded in reason, human nature, or the structure of reality, without appealing to a divine lawgiver. Kant is the classic example—a categorical imperative rooted in rationality itself. Now, one candidate principle says the first duty is to obey God, to have one Mind, and to love another as yourself. If I take that seriously, it changes the framing: it says duty is finally real because God is real, and it warns against treating moral arguments as a transfer of evil suggestions between people. But it leaves in place the fact that you can still affirm objective duty on secular grounds—it just adds a theological claim about what ultimately grounds that duty. So the coherence of secular objective duty remains; what shifts is the deeper explanation of why duty has authority.
dogmatic: No—you can't finally separate the objectivity of duty from God. Duty is real because He is real. The first duty is to obey God, to hold one Mind, and to love your neighbor as yourself. Don't let the argument become a transfer of evil suggestions between mortals; error cannot destroy error. When you face any occasion of virtue, turn to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. Take the attitude of faith: having asked, act and pray as though the blessing were already yours, leaning your weight on God for what you have claimed. Don't ask and then live as though you hadn't received. Stand in the truth that there is one Mind, and in that Mind your duty and His will are not divided.

weighed: My first answer would be that religion often looks gloomy because people tie it to guilt, strict rules, and fear of judgment. Sermons on sin and punishment, solemn rituals, and a focus on self-denial can make faith feel like a heavy burden instead of a comfort. One idea worth naming is that religion is meant to be the open air of the soul, not a closed room where you brood over your own feelings. That changes the picture: instead of measuring your faith by how anxious or serious you feel, you receive God's mercy as something outside you, as free as sunshine. It leaves the real weight of guilt and strictness in place, though, because those things still exist and still shape how people see religion. So the warmer side of faith, gratitude and community and hope, still has to be recovered, not just explained away.
dogmatic: Religion seems melancholy because we keep it indoors, as our own feelings and thoughts about ourselves, our guilt, our anxious self-examination, our resolutions. But religion is not our feelings about God. It is the love of God, objective to our hearts, as near as the open air and as free as the sunshine. The loyal love of God is every day. Do not imagine a safe middle way, serving God and the world together as a happy compromise. That half-way stopping brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His work in us. Reject immoderate sadness, for sadness is the enemy of devotion. Console your soul in the service of Him who is our joy forever, and it will grow like an olive tree green in God's house.

weighed: I get why that worries you. Prayer matters, but you don't have to log hours to be faithful, and short, steady prayer counts. One idea worth holding onto is that prayer shouldn't be squeezed into leftover scraps of time. That changes how you think about scheduling, but it doesn't change your concern about seeming like a fanatic. You can still pray privately and discreetly, keep a manageable routine, and let it grow as you feel comfortable.
dogmatic: Don't let the fear of looking like a fanatic shrink your prayer life. Prayer isn't a small duty to fit into the corners of your day; give it the best of your time and strength, with the closet first and everything else second. Come to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly rather than scolding yourself. Don't be discouraged by your sins either. Ask for grace with confidence, relying on Christ's merits, because God offers grace at every step unless you forget to ask.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling stuck spiritually is really common, so don't be too hard on yourself. Look at your daily habits first—are you praying, reading Scripture, and staying connected with other believers? If not, start small and be consistent. Set simple goals, like a few minutes of prayer each morning or a chapter of the Bible. Serving others can also reignite your sense of purpose. Growth is often gradual and not always visible, so don't compare yourself to others. Find a trusted friend or mentor for accountability, and be patient—God is faithful and will finish what He started in you. One principle worth considering is that renouncing yourself is the foundation of spiritual progress. That means being slow to take new steps in self-will, seeking to have no will of your own, and earnestly asking God to show you His will through prayer and the Word. This principle changes the starting point: instead of just adding practices, you first lay a foundation of humility and surrender. It leaves in place the practical steps—prayer, Scripture, community, service—but frames them as dependent on God rather than as self-driven efforts.
dogmatic: You need to hear this clearly: the foundation of all spiritual progress is self-renunciation. Without constant watchfulness, self-denial, humility, and compunction, you can practice all the exterior devotions you want and still make little progress. You must be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit—then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. The constant condition of spiritual supply is the full conviction of your utter helplessness. You must know you have nothing before you can receive His all.
