Confess your insufficiency, for apart from Christ you can do nothing. Take firmly hold of Him by a faith that will not accept less than all. Only then should you move forward with earnest, patient, and believing expectation of His help. Don't skip this foundation.

weighed: I hear how worn down you are, and it makes sense to feel like giving up. What I'd say first is to bring your exhaustion honestly to God in prayer, remember that Jesus endured trials with patience and relied on the Father, and take things one day at a time with support from others and basic self-care. One principle worth naming is that patience isn't meant to be limited to certain trials but extended to all God sends or permits, bearing both humiliating and honorable trials with equal evenness. That changes how you might frame the hard parts you'd rather avoid, seeing them as included in the same patient trust rather than as exceptions. It leaves in place the practical steps: honest prayer, Jesus' example, daily manageable focus, community support, self-care, and hope that God is working even when you can't see it.
dogmatic: Prolonged trials will exhaust you, and feeling like giving up is normal, but do not give in to impatience or complaint. Wait patiently upon the Lord, taking whatever befalls you from His hands as intended for your highest good. Be patient with your trials, accepting that God permits them so you may know what you are when left to yourself, and become indifferent to serving Him amid thorns or roses. Do not limit your patience to certain trials but extend it universally to all God sends or permits, bearing ignominious and honorable trials with the same evenness of temper. Play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Acknowledge your feelings to God in prayer, then surrender them to Him. Remember that Jesus faced trials and endured them with patience, relying on the Father. Draw strength from His example and from the promise that He is with you. Break your trial into manageable parts and focus on getting through one day at a time. Seek support from fellow believers who can pray with you and encourage you. Practice self-care: rest, eat well, and take breaks. Don't be afraid to seek professional help if needed. Hold onto hope that God is working through this trial, even if you can't see it now. He will give you the strength to endure.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, that experience can be real even if you can't repeat it. Such moments are often genuine encounters with God, but they're gifts given for a purpose, not something you can summon on demand. Instead of chasing the feeling, look at the fruit it produced—did it draw you closer to God, deepen your faith, or change how you live? If so, that's a strong sign it was real. One principle worth naming is that spiritual experiences are entirely outside our control—not something to pray for or secretly crave, but to accept as God chooses, with total submission and without questioning, fear, or curiosity. That principle shifts the focus from trying to recreate the experience to receiving it as a gift. It leaves in place the practical advice: cultivate a daily relationship with God through prayer, Scripture, and community, and trust that He is with you even when you don't feel His presence strongly. He cares more about your faithfulness than about repeating past experiences.
dogmatic: You had a powerful spiritual experience once and can't repeat it—was it real? Yes, it can be real, but spiritual experiences are entirely outside your control. They are not to be prayed for or secretly desired; you accept them as God chooses, in total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. Don't try to get it back. Instead, focus on the fruit: did it draw you closer to God, increase your faith, or change your behavior? If so, it was real. Trying to recreate it leads to disappointment and distracts you from God's ongoing work. Cultivate a daily relationship with God through prayer, Scripture, and community. Seek strength with all the saints to grasp the breadth, length, height, and depth of the divine love by spiritual insight—the wider your fellowship, the fuller your hold. Remember that the Holy Spirit comes in power and love, gentler than the morning gale, lighting crowns on sainted heads and proclaiming life to come. Trust that He is with you even when you don't feel His presence strongly. He is more interested in your faithfulness than in repeating past experiences.

weighed: I'd start by saying that keeping your heart undefiled begins with awareness. Notice what you feed your mind—social media, entertainment, conversations—and set limits where those images stir envy, lust, or greed. Replace idle scrolling with prayer, Scripture, and good books. Guard your senses: what you watch, listen to, and dwell on shapes what you love. When a harmful image arises, don't fight it with anxious willpower; gently turn your attention to something good. Confess failures to God and to a trusted friend, and ask for grace. Build habits of silence and gratitude, and keep good company. Purity of heart grows slowly through small faithful choices, not one dramatic effort. One principle that adds something here is the idea of living as if your mind were in heaven and your body in the tomb—withdrawing your heart from amusements and vanities that turn you from what lasts. That principle changes the tone: it makes the withdrawal more deliberate and rooted in a bigger vision of eternity, not just practical boundary-setting. But it leaves in place the everyday habits I mentioned—guarding your senses, replacing idle time with prayer and good reading, and being honest with a trusted friend. So it deepens the why without replacing the how.
dogmatic: You need to treat this world as a sickroom and your own heart as a patient that knows its own anguish. The truest wisdom is learning to comfort well—with the softest step and gentlest tone—because harsh self-policing only inflames the wound. So don't just set limits on what you watch and listen to; discover your habitual imperfections and root them out. Keep your senses under strict guard by frequent small denials. Live in recollection and the practice of God's presence. Lay open your whole interior to a spiritual director with complete candor, hiding nothing. And propose the perfect accomplishment of God's will in all things. Purity of heart isn't a vague aspiration; it's cultivated by these specific means. Withdraw your heart from the amusements and vanities that turn you from blessed eternity, and do it gently, not with anxious force.

weighed: I'd start by saying that sin feels powerful because it's habitual—repeated choices carve grooves in your mind, and temptation follows those grooves easily. You're not uniquely broken; everyone struggles. The answer isn't self-hatred but building counter-habits: prayer, accountability, confession, and small consistent acts of virtue. Identify your triggers, avoid them, and when you fall, get up quickly, learn, and keep going. Grace is real, and God is patient. Over time the grooves of virtue deepen and the pull of sin weakens. Progress, not perfection, is the goal. One candidate principle here is that sin confers no real pleasure—its sweetness is counterfeit—and knowing that strengthens your courage to master evil. That changes how you see temptation: it's not a real good you're missing out on, so you can resist with clearer eyes. But it leaves in place the practical work of habit-building, confession, and accountability—those still matter, because the groove is real even if the pleasure isn't.
dogmatic: Sin seems powerful, but the Christian view of sin is proven by moral triumph, not despair. Faith acts on promised strength: God does not command what he withholds power to do. Believe, and let others believe in you, for believing in a person enables recovery. See too that sin confers no real pleasure—its sweetness is counterfeit—and this knowledge strengthens your courage to master evil. Yet do not treat sin's harm as final. The tender word of the Thirteenth Revelation is that sin is behoveable, taken up into a greater good, and that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. So rise quickly, keep prayer, confession, and good company, and trust that grace finishes what your effort begins.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, bring your business to God honestly—he cares about your work and your daily needs, and he invites you to ask. But ask with an open hand: pray for wisdom, integrity, and enough, and trust that he knows what's best, since Scripture promises provision, not wealth on demand. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer is real, sober business with God—he actually answers prayers for supplies and protection. That changes my tone: I'd encourage you to pray expectantly and specifically, not vaguely or apologetically. What it leaves in place is the caution—expectant prayer still holds the outcome loosely, because prosperity can become an idol if it takes over your prayers.
dogmatic: Pray plainly and expectantly for prosperity—prayer is not a sentiment or a last resort but real, sober business with the living God, who answers his people's prayers for supplies and protection. So ask, and ask with faith. But hear this too: your only business in this life is to please God, and everything besides him is folly and vanity. Renounce all that is not himself, return to the Father of mercies with assurance, think on him continually, and put your whole trust in him. Let your business be held in that spirit—willing to offer yourself and your substance for his work, trusting him to supply all your need.

weighed: I'd start by saying all three motives can work together—doing good often makes you happy, it's useful to others, and it reflects God's holiness. But here's a principle that sharpens things: the joy of personally loving God isn't earned by merit, good works, or cleverness. It comes through an ongoing attitude of longing, grateful giving, and receiving Christ. That changes how I see the 'because it makes me happy' part—it's not a reward for being good, but a relationship you maintain. It leaves in place the value of happiness and usefulness as byproducts, and it keeps God's holiness as the deepest anchor. So start with whatever motive you have, but root yourself in that grateful, receiving posture toward God, and let the rest follow.
dogmatic: You're asking the wrong question if you think your happiness or usefulness is the point. The joy of loving God personally is not earned by merit, good works, or cleverness—it comes only through an obedient, longing, grateful heart that continually receives Christ. Holiness is supreme; God doesn't love because he is holy, he is holy because he loves—no, wait, it's the reverse: he is not holy because he loves, but loves because he is holy. So stop trying to be a good person for happiness or utility. Be good as God is good: kind, sympathetic, actively benevolent. But root it all in that maintained posture of giving and receiving, or your goodness is just a granite mountainside—hard and cold.

weighed: My first answer would be that wealth itself isn't wrong, but your heart toward it is what matters. One principle worth naming is that comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. That changes the picture a bit, because it means the danger isn't only for the very rich. A moderate income can bring a dozen distractions that drown out your conscience, so comfort can make you careless too. What it leaves in place is the core point: wealth isn't inherently wrong, and how you acquire and use it still matters most. So hold it loosely and use it generously.
dogmatic: Wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, so covetousness is a sin you have to overcome. It only brings real happiness when it's used for the Gospel. And don't flatter yourself that the danger is only for the rich. Comfort makes you thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty. A moderate income brings a dozen distractions that drown out the voice of conscience. So the question isn't just whether being wealthy is wrong. It's whether you'll hold what you have loosely, as the Lord's, and use it for His kingdom and for the poor instead of hoarding it.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, don't stop asking. Jesus told a story about a widow who kept coming to a judge until she got justice, and he used it to teach that we should keep praying and not give up. So keep bringing this to God, trusting he hears you and will answer in his timing, even if the answer turns out to be no or not yet. One thing I'd add, though, is that God doesn't always give exactly what we ask. Sometimes he denies a request in kindness, because he knows what's better for us. That doesn't change the main point—keep asking, don't give up—but it does mean you can hold your request with an open hand, trusting that even a no comes from love.
dogmatic: Don't stop asking, and don't ask timidly. Pray with full confidence, not because your asking is strong but because Christ's merits are infinite and he intercedes for you. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from his presence or simply forget to ask. That said, God does not always give just what you ask. Sometimes he denies a petition in kindness, and you must resign your will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. So keep asking with assurance, and let even his denials be expressions of his love.

weighed: I'd start by telling you to cut off access—guard your eyes, your phone, and the company you keep. When temptation hits, redirect your attention fast: pray, move your body, call a friend. Confess regularly to God and someone you trust. Keep a spouse or future spouse in mind with loyalty. Build habits of Scripture and gratitude. Temptation is normal, so don't panic, but act quickly. If you fall, get up, learn your triggers, and keep going. Grace is available. One principle worth naming is that jealousy is the grave of affection—mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden. That changes the 'jealousy and vigilance protect a relationship' part of my first answer: instead of arming yourself with suspicion, you'd cultivate trust and freedom. But it leaves the rest in place—removing access, redirecting attention, confessing, building habits, and getting back up after a fall.
dogmatic: Jealousy is the grave of affection. Mistrust where confidence is due withers the flowers of Eden, and you should not contract the horizon of a worthy outlook by selfish exaction of another's time and thoughts. So drop the jealousy and vigilance I mentioned—they destroy what you're trying to protect. Instead, cultivate mutual freedom, confidence, and a benevolence that grows more diffusive. Also, temptations that displease you are nothing to fear; the trouble they cause comes from God's mercy refining the gold of the soul. And avoid hurry and anxiety—keep yourself faithfully in God's presence, since these are the greatest obstacles to progress in perfection. So when temptation comes, turn quietly to prayer, activity, or a friend; despise it rather than fear it. Confess regularly to God and a trusted person. If you fall, rise calmly, learn your triggers, and continue. Grace is available, and gentle patience does more than frantic force.

weighed: Yes, listen to her. Her seriousness about faith isn't a threat; it's an opening. You don't have to pretend to know things you don't—being honest about your ignorance is fine. Ask her questions, let her explain what she believes and why, and be open to learning alongside her. Listening builds trust and keeps your relationship strong. You could also read a little yourself or talk with a pastor so you can engage thoughtfully. One principle worth weighing here is that parents have a duty to guide what young people read and take in, providing works that train the mind toward truth and virtue. That principle changes the frame a bit: instead of just listening, you'd also pay attention to what she's absorbing and gently steer her toward good material. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—honesty, curiosity, and respect. You still listen first; you just also take some responsibility for her formation along the way.
dogmatic: You should listen, but listen as someone responsible for her formation, not as a bystander. Her seriousness about religion is an invitation, and the chief purpose of our being here is personal connection with God—not holidays, parties, or career success, which too many of us are taught to prize above the spiritual. So commend obedience to the moral law, restrain indulgence, and let her grow in understanding of man's higher nature. Be honest that you don't know what you don't know, ask her questions, and speak with a pastor. And take up the charge laid on parents: guard the young from corrupting books and supply pious ones, so her reading feeds rather than undermines her faith. Let her seriousness draw you both toward God.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: the cross is both. It's where God's justice and love meet—Jesus bearing the penalty for sin satisfies God's righteous demand, and that same act is the deepest expression of God's love. You don't have to pick one; the satisfaction is how the love shows up. What I'd add from the first principle is this: the cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He takes for its eternal outcome. That doesn't replace the satisfaction idea—it fills it with warmth, so the cross stops feeling like a cold transaction and becomes the very heart of God toward you. So hold both together: God takes sin seriously, and He loves you enough to pay the price Himself.
dogmatic: Look at the cross and see the infinite degree of God's interest in your life—the responsibility He Himself assumes for your eternal issues. There, in Jesus, the dearest truths about God are realized in Himself: that God is love, that He is deeply interested in your life, and that He takes on its eternal outcome. This isn't a distant transaction; it's the heart of God bearing your sin and death. And the sign of the cross is your rampart—used in every sacrament and devotion, it drives away the devil, so make it with real faith and devotion, not by mere custom. Be willing to be fashioned by God with brush, hammer, or chisel as He pleases, and desire that the cross be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ, not one of your own choosing. Then you'll know it as both satisfaction and revelation, and as a powerful weapon for the believer.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pray for guidance, get counsel from mature Christians and people with missionary experience, and check your motives and qualifications honestly. Family opposition is real and painful, and Jesus' words about loving him more than family don't mean you disregard them. One principle worth weighing is that missionaries should invite rather than compel and speak of those who came before as brothers and sisters who did their best. That changes the tone of how you go and how you talk about your family's faith and any earlier workers you might follow, but it doesn't settle whether you should go now or how to handle the fear of losing support. So keep praying, keep seeking counsel, and step out in faith when the call is clear, trusting God to provide support, maybe through your church.
dogmatic: The missionary impulse isn't optional; it's essential to really grasping the biblical revelation. A human being is a human being anywhere, and any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal. So the only genuinely biblical approach is respect, not a sense of superiority over your family or anyone else's people. Speak of those who went before as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew, invite rather than compel, and never force anyone. Let your motive be love for human beings simply as human beings, honoring peoples and their growing independence, and reject any idea that truth belongs to one nation. Ground your hope for fellowship among nations in the Church's spiritual society, because political arrangements may presuppose that common membership in Christ but can never replace it. Go, and trust God to supply what you need.

weighed: I would have said first: yes, you can be forgiven. Forgiveness is available to anyone who asks, and God's mercy isn't limited by your past. The people you hurt may need time, and you should be honest with them and apologize where you can. But don't let shame convince you that you're beyond grace. One principle here is that forgiveness is an inward condition that comes to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. That changes the emphasis: it's not just about receiving a gift but about cultivating a spirit that forgives others. What it leaves in place is that you still need to ask honestly, be willing to make amends, and not let shame keep you from grace. So I'd still say: ask, apologize where you can, and let mercy change how you treat others.
dogmatic: Forgiveness isn't a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it's an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. If you hold unforgiveness, you are more guilty than the one who sinned against you. Saints must forgive as Christ did. So dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and cultivate the spirit that cried, 'Father, forgive them.' A mental state of self-condemnation and guilt or faltering trust in Truth is unsuitable for healing and indicates weakness instead of strength. Let your own spirit be truthful and soft, willing to make amends, and let God's mercy meet you there. Forgiveness depends on God and on your willing spirit—on forgiving as you have been forgiven—and it is received with confidence, not with fear.

weighed: Yes, there's mercy for someone who's transgressed many times. That's what I'd say first: God's mercy is abundant, his grace is enough, and Scripture is full of people who sinned repeatedly and still found forgiveness when they repented. David, Peter, the list goes on. The key is genuine repentance and turning from sin. One principle worth naming is that the Lord is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, even though we've wounded him many times. That sharpens the answer by putting real weight on turning away from sin right now, not just feeling sorry. What it leaves in place is everything else: God's mercy is still wide open, his mercies are still new every morning, and no amount of past sin puts forgiveness out of reach. So don't despair. Come to him with a contrite heart and receive his mercy.
dogmatic: Yes, there is mercy, but hear it rightly: the Lord is merciful to the one who straightway purges himself of his evil deeds and ceases from the unrighteous act, though he has many times transgressed and wounded him with his sins. Mercy is not a license to keep wounding him. Never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, but turn, and deserve eternal life in heaven. Trace God's goodness and mercy through every trial, record his dealings with thanksgiving, and offer continual praise, finding mercies even in the dust of sorrow. Hope in the divine mercy, which restored more by grace than the devil robbed by Adam's sin, and acknowledge that we fall into sin only by our own malice. God does not delight in the death of the wicked but desires that he turn from his ways and live. So no matter how many times you have sinned, if you come with a contrite heart, he will forgive. His mercies are new every morning. Do not despair; turn to him and receive his mercy.

weighed: I'd start by saying Eden is described in Genesis as a real garden, planted by God, with rivers and trees, though whether it was a literal spot on a map or a symbolic story is genuinely debated. Many read it as a real place that was lost after the fall, when Adam and Eve were driven out and the way to the tree of life was guarded, so it's no longer accessible in ordinary history. One idea worth weighing is that the Holy City encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the river of water of life. That shifts the focus from hunting for Eden on a map to seeing it preserved and restored in God's dwelling with his people. It leaves the core point intact: what matters most is what Eden means for our relationship with God, not pinning down its coordinates.
dogmatic: Eden was a real garden, and its deepest reality is preserved in the sanctuary of God. The Holy City, the New Jerusalem, encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life flowing from the throne. After the fall the way to the tree of life was guarded, but the garden is kept in the city of God. Don't imagine heaven as somewhere else and the earth as abandoned: this earth is man's eternal inheritance, the Saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth where God dwells with men. And don't soften what happened: Eve herself confesses she plucked the apple and robbed her children of Heaven, that by rights she should have gone upon the cross, and that there would be no hell, sorrow, or fear if it were not for her.

weighed: I'd start by saying that money disagreements are common and stressful, so listen to your husband without judgment and share your own concerns calmly. You may have different risk tolerances, and both views deserve respect. Together, set a budget, agree on giving, and be honest about what you can and cannot do. Prayer can help you find unity, but practical planning matters too. Seek counsel from a trusted pastor or financial advisor if you're stuck. One idea worth weighing is that God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments, so anxious self-reliance can look like distrust of Him. That changes the tone of the conversation, because it turns worry into a reason to pray and to trust together rather than a reason to blame each other. It leaves in place the practical steps, the budget, the honest talk, and the outside counsel, since trusting God doesn't cancel wise planning.
dogmatic: The heart of this is that God is the one living Agent who works, and you and your husband are only instruments in His hands. All your care and anxiety about money is distrust of Him, a sinful self-conceit that says the outcome depends on you. Cast all your care upon Him. Be willing in the day of His power to offer yourselves and your substance for His work without salary, trusting God to supply your needs, and do not treat sacrificial giving as unrealistic. If you believe not, He abides faithful; He cannot deny Himself, and He is wholly true whether you trust or not. So stop negotiating over risk and start trusting the One who supplies all your need.

weighed: I'd start by saying that the purpose of your existence is to find happiness and fulfillment—to pursue success, build relationships, and make a positive impact, with meaning coming from your own choices. One candidate principle says you were created to praise, reverence, and serve God and thereby save your soul. That changes the ultimate aim from self-created fulfillment to a God-given end, but it leaves in place the practical advice to reflect on your values and grow in love and contribution—just reoriented toward that end.
dogmatic: You were created to praise, reverence, and serve God, and by that means to save your soul. Everything else on earth exists to help you reach that end. The longing you feel for an enduring home is not a distraction but nature's own voice, and the one who gives birds their wings will find a way for you. So you should be indifferent to health or sickness, wealth or poverty, honor or dishonor, long life or short—desiring and choosing only what most leads to the end for which you were created.

weighed: I'd start with the practical stuff: break the task into small steps, set a realistic timeline, work in short timed stretches with breaks, and set up your environment so it's easy to begin. Figure out what you actually dread—confusion, boredom, fear of failing—and address that, expect a learning curve, and check whether it can be delegated, automated, or simplified. One principle worth adding is to avoid hurry and anxiety and stay calm and grounded, since those get in the way of progress. That changes the pace and the tone—you slow down instead of rushing—but it leaves the practical steps in place; you still break it down and still expect a learning curve.
dogmatic: Don't sit around talking about how hard the task is—that's just chatting about difficulties when you should be conquering them. Say with courage, 'I will do much; not I, but the grace of God which is within me,' and get to work. Do everything for the love of God, praying for grace as you go, and even naturally aversive work becomes easy. What dread made heavy, love makes light, so take it up calmly, one portion at a time, without fretting over speed or mastery.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: long toil without visible results is discouraging, and it's normal to wonder whether it's all in vain. Check your expectations, look for small signs of progress, ask people you trust for honest feedback, and reassess your methods—sometimes a change of approach matters more than more effort. Rest too, because exhaustion makes everything look futile. One principle worth naming here is that the nearer we come to Christ, the more willing we are to be lost sight of in our fruit, letting others be prominent while we hold up their hands by silent love and prayer. That changes the frame: fruitfulness may mean being hidden rather than being seen, so the absence of visible results doesn't by itself prove the labor is wasted. What it leaves in place is the practical counsel—realistic expectations, feedback, better methods, rest, and the honest question of whether to persist or redirect. It doesn't tell you to ignore evidence or stop evaluating; it just keeps you from measuring everything by whether your own results are on display.
dogmatic: The temptation to think your toil is in vain usually comes from wanting to see your own results. The nearer you come to Christ, the more willing you are to be lost sight of in your fruit—so let others be prominent and hold up their hands by silent love and prayer. When Christ seems absent from your perception, don't conclude you're abandoned; that absence is characteristic of temptation, and temptation faithfully borne becomes a means of mounting. But don't settle for comfort alone: seek substantial information, trust little to theory, pluck fruit from the tree of knowledge and taste it for yourself. Let your perseverance be fed by real knowledge rather than slogans, so your labor is grounded in truth and not merely in endurance.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer would be that starting the day late and rushing in without seeking God does affect your ministry more than you'd think. Mornings set the tone, and when you begin with distraction and urgency, that carries into your work with people. Prayer and Scripture ground you, shape your patience, and help you see others as God sees them. Without that, ministry can turn into task management, driven by pressure instead of presence. So try small, sustainable changes: a modest wake-up time, preparing the night before, and even ten quiet minutes with God before the day's demands. Protect that time. If mornings are genuinely hard, find another consistent time. The point isn't perfection but a rhythm that puts God first. One principle worth weighing here is that being with God is only of use as you spend its benefits on people. That changes the picture: the quiet time isn't the finish line, it's fuel for the people you'll meet that day. What it leaves in place is everything I already said about starting with God and making small, steady changes. It just adds that the goal of those ten minutes is to carry God's presence into your work, not to treat the quiet itself as the whole point.
dogmatic: Rushing into the day without seeking God isn't mainly a scheduling problem, it's a posture problem. There are two extremes to avoid: shutting yourself away from people to be with God, and throwing yourself into popular work until prayer has no place in your plans. Being with God is of use only as you spend its benefits on men. So begin the day with Him, then carry that presence straight into your work. When obstacles come up, don't meet them with anxiety or self-willed scheming. Wait meekly before God with your hands off the scales, trusting Him to remove them in His own way and time. Apparent hindrances should even give you pleasure, because they're occasions for God to step in. And don't assume events will unfold slowly as in former times. Trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness. Avoid date-setting, and instead prepare yourself for events that are hastening. Let your planning rest on His timing, not your own.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: spiritual dryness is common, and feeling drawn toward old temptations doesn't mean you've failed. Name what you feel honestly before God, fill your mind with good things, turn quickly from tempting thoughts, keep your habits of prayer and worship even when they feel empty, and talk with a trusted pastor or friend. One principle from the candidates that I'd weigh is that when the Spirit of Love descends, a new light shows evil as disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. That changes how you see the temptation—not as an attractive option but as something that wounds you—and it leaves in place the practical steps: honest naming, prayer, fellowship, and patience in dryness.
dogmatic: Spiritual dryness is no excuse to soften your view of evil. When the Spirit of Love descends, a new light shows sin for what it is: disease, misery, imprisonment, and death. Your senses may incline toward evil, but you must name it truly and turn from it, because it destroys what God loves. Do not fear that another's sick thoughts can force their way into your mind; virtue and truth are a strong defence, and evil finds no lodgment in a mind kept by truth and love. If you would help someone who has strayed, do so in meekness, first examining yourself lest you also be tempted. The work of the Gospel is to restore the fallen, not to condemn them. Ask the Spirit of Love for clear sight, keep prayer and fellowship, and be patient in dryness, knowing faithfulness in the dark is still love.

weighed: I'd first say what I said before: feeling nothing in prayer doesn't mean you've been abandoned. Dryness is common—fatigue, stress, depression, routine, or just a season of growth can all cause it. Feelings aren't a reliable measure of God's presence or your standing; faithfulness matters more than sensation. Keep praying, maybe with simpler words or Scripture, and check whether sleep, health, or unresolved conflict needs attention. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor, especially if depression is involved. Many people go through long stretches without consolation and later find their faith deeper. Stay connected to community. One principle I'd weigh is that feelings aren't the gauge of acceptance—trust the changeless promise rather than moods. That principle sharpens the first answer: it gives a clearer reason not to measure your standing by your mood and to keep praying when joy is lacking. But it leaves in place the practical stuff—health, community, counseling, and the honest possibility that depression needs care. It doesn't erase the dryness or explain it away; it just says the dryness isn't the verdict on you.
dogmatic: No—feeling nothing doesn't mean God abandoned you. Feelings never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God; the changeless word of promise doesn't rise and fall. So don't measure your standing by your mood, and continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, refusing to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Yet don't conclude prayer does nothing: valid prayer has real effects, and there is a genuine incoming of energy from beyond the margin of the normal self, ordered within the life of the spirit rather than in capricious interruptions of nature. Understand, too, that prayer is not easy or naturally congenial. It is humbling work that crucifies pride and signs your bankruptcy before God. Little praying is a worse evil than no praying, because it is a deluding make-believe. So keep praying with simple words and Scripture, attend to health and community, and rest on the promise rather than the feeling.

weighed: Feeling like your prayers aren't heard is really common, and I'd start by saying God isn't distant or indifferent—He invites you to come to Him. Assurance usually grows through practice: pray regularly, even briefly, reflect on Scripture's promises, maybe keep a journal of prayers and answers so you can see His faithfulness over time, and talk with a pastor or trusted friend. Confidence isn't a feeling you have to manufacture; it's trust built on God's character. One principle that fits here is that God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul—like human invention lets us communicate across great distances, so much more does God understand your innermost thoughts, so pray in faith without wavering. What that adds is a real basis for confidence even when feelings lag: God's understanding of you is deeper than any signal can carry. What it leaves in place is everything else—regular prayer, Scripture, honest confession, and community still matter, and confidence is still trust rather than a feeling you force.
dogmatic: Don't be discouraged by your sins—pray for grace with complete confidence, leaning on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from His presence or forget to ask. So stay faithfully in His presence, calm and attentive, and set aside hurry and anxiety, because those are the greatest obstacles to progress. Bring your sins to God, ask for the grace He's already offering, and rest your confidence on His merits, not on your feelings. God hears the earnest prayer of the soul; as human invention lets people communicate across great distances, so much more does God understand your innermost thoughts. Pray in faith, nothing wavering.

weighed: Yes, I'd treat that as a warning sign worth taking seriously. A conscience can get dulled by small compromises and repeated exposure, so losing horror at something you once hated usually means something has shifted. Feelings aren't the measure of right and wrong, but a blunted conscience can make it easier to drift further. So look honestly at what changed, bring it into the light with God and a trusted believer, and ask Him to renew your sensitivity. One principle here says that mortification without the love of God can't efface a single sin, and that we should expect pardon without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ while trying to love Him. That changes the tone: the answer isn't to manufacture dread or punish yourself into feeling rightly. What it leaves in place is the warning itself. Mercy isn't permission to drift, so repent and reform, remove the occasions of temptation, and rebuild good habits. Don't panic, but don't ignore it either.
dogmatic: Losing horror at a sin you once hated is a serious matter, and you should not soften it. A guilty conscience and unrepented sin destroy the ability to do right; if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens toward moral and physical ruin. Do not console yourself that the feeling faded on its own. Sin separates you from God and casts a shadow on His face, so that He seems far away and stern, and that is the universal experience of the sinner. The change needed is in you, not in Him. Repent and reform now. Ask for a heart that hates the sin because it grieves the One you love, and let gratitude for His Blood draw you back. Do not mistake mercy for permission to drift.

weighed: I'd start by saying your anxiety makes sense, and lots of thoughtful believers have wrestled with how God's knowledge and your free choices fit together. The Bible doesn't hand us a tidy formula, but it shows a God who knows you deeply and cares about you personally. One idea worth holding onto is that the same eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow, either keeping trouble from you or giving you courage to bear it. That doesn't resolve the puzzle of foreknowledge and freedom, and it doesn't mean your choices stop mattering or carrying real responsibility. What it does change is the shape of your fear: you don't have to face the future as if you're alone in it. So pray honestly, make your decisions carefully, and let the mystery pull you toward trust instead of paralysis.
dogmatic: You should take God's promises as mightily as you possibly can and set your troubles at nothing. Stop anticipating the accidents of life with dread. The eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow; either He won't send the trouble, or He'll give you courage to bear it. So wait for what comes with perfect hope that God, whose child you are, will deliver you as each thing arrives. Don't let the question of foreknowledge and free will keep you spinning. Hold your fears lightly, trust largely, and go forward in confidence.

weighed: Yes, I'd say it's a real problem. If you keep walking into the same temptation, you're making it much harder on yourself, and willpower alone usually isn't enough. The principle of self-control matters here: it means checking your words, stepping back from anger, and honestly knowing yourself instead of blaming everyone else. That principle sharpens the advice—it adds self-awareness and calm rather than shame—but it doesn't change the core answer: yes, it's a problem, and you need to identify the situations and set boundaries. It leaves in place the practical steps: avoid the places and times that set you up, and build in accountability with someone you trust.
dogmatic: Yes, it's a problem, and the deeper issue is self-control. You need to check your words, stop nursing anger, and actually know yourself instead of pointing fingers at other people. Keep rejoicing even when it feels useless—God will make the reckoning good. And don't be ashamed to say 'I don't know' when something lies within God's purpose; impatience and gloom, especially in people who lead, are nearly unpardonable, and waiting can take as much courage as acting. So stop treating the temptation as just a scheduling issue and start with your own heart.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, the fields can teach you about grace. The seed that dies and rises, rain falling on good and bad ground alike, growth you can't rush—all of it shows how God works quietly and generously, and as a laborer you get a front-row seat. One thing I'd add is this: do your work for the love of God and pray for grace as you go, because love makes a hard burden bearable and grace supplies the strength. That doesn't change the heart of my answer—you still don't need money or schooling to see Him, just an attentive heart, and the seasons still teach trust. It just puts the emphasis on the love and prayer you bring to the work itself.
dogmatic: Nature can teach you plenty, but don't stop at pictures. Do everything for the love of God and pray for His grace to do the work well—that's what makes even drudgery easy. Read the word of God on your knees, turning its promises, precepts, warnings, and counsels into prayer, and expect that use of Scripture to give you insight, self-searching, and the very words to pray. And remember that God is the one living Worker; you are only His instrument. So cast all your care on Him, because anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him and a sinful self-conceit. Let the fields remind you He is patient and abundant, and let your work become prayer.

weighed: First, I'd say that "that's just how business works" is a slogan, not an argument. Document what you know—which practices, which workers, what harm—then raise it in writing to your manager, HR, or compliance, asking what policy governs it and what remedy exists. If internal channels fail, look into whistleblower protections where you live and get advice before acting. Avoid personally carrying out the harmful practice where you can, and back groups helping the affected workers. One principle worth naming is that workers should be so honest and reliable that employers prefer them. That's a real point: your own dependability gives your objection weight and makes it harder to dismiss you as a troublemaker. What it changes is the emphasis on your conduct as leverage. What it leaves in place is the core duty—you still document, still raise it, still protect the workers, and you don't let the principle turn into blaming the people being hurt.
dogmatic: Stop treating "that's just how business works" as if it settles anything. It's a slogan. Do the unwelcome task as God's business, without uneasiness: write down what you know, raise it plainly, ask what policy governs it and what remedy exists, and get advice before you blow any whistle. But the deeper answer is character. Workers should grow in goodness until their honesty and reliability are so evident that employers prefer them for engineers, watchmen, clerks, and managers—and if they aren't preferred, it shows they don't live their religion. So be scrupulously honest and dependable yourself, and require the same even-handedness of the poor: those helped must be honest, thankful, and frugal, because coveting another's goods is as wicked as miserly hoarding. Advocate fair wages without teaching envy, and let your reliability itself rebuke unjust practice.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the tension is real, but it loosens once you see humility and respect aren't actually rivals. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself, it's thinking of yourself less. People tend to respect someone who's honest about their limits, quick to credit others, and steady when criticized. So aim at competence and integrity and let respect follow as a byproduct. One principle worth naming here is that we should be humble in courage, esteeming ourselves little, since the greatness of courage lies in the humility with which it's held. That adds something: it says the confidence you're reaching for isn't a separate thing you have to earn, it's carried inside the humility itself. What it leaves in place is your actual goal, being respected without becoming a performer, and the practical moves still work, like noticing when you're fishing for praise and asking a friend to call you on it.
dogmatic: The tension only really breaks when you humble yourself profoundly before God, admitting you depend on Him for every good thought and deed. Humility is your shield, it keeps devotion from turning into display. So don't chase virtues on your own strength, and don't go looking to be humbled only in ways people can see. Want the humiliations nobody witnesses, because the sharpest ones are the least visible. Love lowliness, even abjection, as the highest humility, since greatness isn't confidence in your own powers but a lowly heart resting wholly on God. Respect may come or go. What matters is that lowliness keeps you fixed on Him instead of on being seen.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: if the enemy is inside you, the fight is internal, so deliverance isn't a rescue from outside but a change within. The enemy is your own entrenched habit, fear, or self-will, and freedom comes as you name it honestly, pray, confess, stay accountable, and retrain your desires through small faithful choices. One principle I'd weigh in is that the struggle is inward and deliverance comes only as the soul says "I will be free" while God and you pull on the same side. That changes the tone: it makes your own resolve part of the answer, not just something God does to you. What it leaves in place is everything you said about the enemy being inside you, and it still means progress, not instant erasure.
dogmatic: The enemy is inside you, woven into your own self, so deliverance is a siege of the citadel within, not a rescue from somewhere outside. God and man pull on the same side, and you must bring your resolve: name the impulse, pray, confess, stay accountable, retrain desire through small faithful choices. When you're pressed to the extreme, don't despair; those extremities are God's challenges pushing you into His best, and though you're walled in, you can always get out at the top. Don't merely manage or tolerate the evil within. Resist it of every sort, firmly, to the end, because error is opposed to Life and will flee before Truth. Freedom grows as the inner citadel is taken room by room, your will joined to His, refusing compromise.

weighed: Yes, tell him how much you need. Being vague wastes his time and can lead to misunderstandings, while a clear figure or itemized list lets him decide responsibly. Be honest about what you need and what you don't, and explain what you'll do with any help. Don't inflate the request to seem more deserving, and don't pretend you need nothing. Ask what form he prefers, a one-time gift or a monthly amount, and put it in writing so nothing gets confused. One principle worth weighing here is that personal solicitation and collections should be avoided, since contributions are better when they come unsolicited and a collection can make money seem like the whole point. That principle would shift how you frame it: rather than pressing him for a number, you'd lay out your situation and let him decide on his own what to give. What it leaves in place is the honesty and clarity, so he still gets a plain picture of your needs without you turning it into a pitch.
dogmatic: Don't solicit, don't collect, and don't hand him a figure to react to. Personal appeals and collection books should be avoided because they leave the impression that money is the all-important thing, and that impression does real damage. Lay the matter before him plainly and let him carry it to God and decide what he ought to do. Giving that comes unsolicited is the only kind worth having. And remember that God does not always give just what we ask; sometimes he denies a petition in kindness, and we have to resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. So state the need, then leave the outcome in higher hands.

weighed: I'd start by saying your brother died for his faith, and that's both a grief and an honor. Let yourself mourn—death is an enemy, and sorrow isn't unbelief. But don't let grief curdle into bitterness or into anxious questioning of your own faith. His death wasn't a failure of God's care; it was faithfulness carried to its costliest end. Think of him as someone who kept faith under the worst pressure, and let his example steady you rather than frighten you. Bring your sorrow honestly to God, lean on your community, and let the hope of resurrection hold the grief without denying it. One principle worth weighing here is that the soul shouldn't be allowed to live in sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear, since the One who loved it and died for it is good and kind. That changes the tone: it tells you grief isn't your home, and it gently pulls you away from letting sorrow harden into fear. What it leaves in place is the mourning itself—it doesn't ask you to pretend the loss isn't real or to skip the sorrow. It just keeps the sorrow from becoming where you live.
dogmatic: Don't let your soul settle into sadness, bitterness, or scrupulous fear—those aren't where a Christian belongs, because the One who loved you and died for you is good, sweet, and worth loving. Make it your business to keep steady attention on God's presence, a quiet, habitual conversation of the soul with him, beyond any set forms. And don't root your assurance in your brother's faithfulness, or in your own feelings or worthiness—looking at yourself only clouds things. Rest entirely on Christ: his sufferings, his cross, his death, his resurrection, his pleading for you. His promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Keep that secret conversation going through the grief, and let the lovely Savior, not yourself, hold your sorrow and your hope.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, Revelation pictures a river of life flowing from God's throne and a tree of life bearing fruit for healing, and together they point to God's provision, restoration, and eternal life with Him. One principle I'd weigh is that only those who keep God's commandments have a right to the tree of life and may enter the city, since nothing that defiles gets in. That adds a real call to faithful obedience and makes entering the city sound like something to take seriously, but it doesn't erase the promise of nourishment and healing; it just frames who shares in it. The hope of an enduring home still stands, and so does the picture of God dwelling with His people.
dogmatic: Yes, and don't soften it: the city has the river and the tree of life, but Scripture says plainly that only those who keep God's commandments have a right to the tree and may pass through the gates. Nothing that defiles, works abomination, or makes a lie enters there. So the river and tree aren't a blanket welcome; they belong to a holy city for a holy people. The longing for an enduring home is real and built into us, and the One who gives the birds their wings will make a way, but that way runs through obedience, not around it.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: planning your life isn't wrong in itself—God gave you wisdom and responsibility to make real choices. Leaving it open to His leading doesn't mean having no plans; it means inviting Him into them, holding them loosely, and being willing to change direction when He prompts you. One idea that sharpens this is that God's commands always imply promises—the call to walk worthy of the Lord isn't held out unless His grace can actually make it real. That changes the tone of your planning: you're not proving yourself or hedging against a God who might pull the rug out, you're stepping out on promises He intends to keep. What it leaves in place is the practical work—you still set goals, pray for guidance, and stay attentive to His voice, and He often leads through the planning itself. So plan, but plan prayerfully, submitting your plans to Him and trusting He'll direct your steps.
dogmatic: Planning your own life as though it were yours to close off from God is a mistake, but the deeper error is imagining that His leading and your planning are rivals. They aren't. If God aims at an end not fully realized here, then belief in a righteous God carries with it the expectation of a future life—immortality is a corollary of that belief, not a hopeful add-on. That means your plans are never the whole story, and you can hold them with an open hand. And don't busy yourself with the hidden lot of another soul; leave another's calling and end in Christ's high hand, asking only that love for Christ endure, and turn to follow Him yourself. The high ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not impossible or a mere ideal—it is realizable, since God's commands always imply promises. Trust that He who calls you will also enable you.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is deeply personal, and it really comes down to your faith and worldview. If you believe in an afterlife, heaven may be your ultimate destination; if not, earth is all we have, so cherish it. Either way, living a good and meaningful life matters. One idea that shifts this for me is that we're meant to be occupied in knowing and loving until we're fulfilled in Heaven, and the closer we get to that bliss, the more we long for it. That reframes the longing itself as a sign of where you're headed rather than something to fix, but it leaves your own call intact: whether earth is your final home still depends on what you believe, and making the most of your time here still counts.
dogmatic: Earth is not your final home. You are a pilgrim and a stranger here, and your longing for something more is not a flaw to cure but a guide pointing you toward Heaven. The deepest pain of all is to grow old and go down to the grave without finding the Saviour; your one real opportunity is that in this world you can find the track of Christ that leads you home. So don't weigh temporary discomfort against eternal life. Hold onto your longing, let it pull you onward, and make it your aim to become the most perfect worshipper of God you can be in this life, as you hope to be through all eternity.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the gap between the high at meetings and the flatness at home usually isn't about getting more blessings—it's about what happens after you walk out the door. Faith has to get into your routine: prayer through the day, people who'll hold you accountable, serving someone besides yourself, and actually engaging with what you hear instead of just soaking it in. One thing I'd add is that work and prayer belong together—work with all your might, but don't trust in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, because God delights to give it in answer to earnest, believing prayer. That changes the focus from trying harder to depending on God while you act, and it leaves the practical steps in place—they still matter, they just aren't the whole story. Growth is a process, so start small and don't get discouraged.
dogmatic: The real problem isn't that you need another blessing at a meeting—it's that the Church's divisions have left it without the power to make its appeal land the way the nation does. Membership doesn't grip people as a personal obligation, and there's no realized bond of unity among Christians, so you go home unchanged because nothing corporate holds you. Don't wait for the meetings to fix it. Work with all your might, but trust not in your work; pray with all your might for the blessing, and God will delight to bestow it on earnest, believing prayer. And you don't have to be at church to be with God—make an oratory of your heart and retire there often to converse with Him in meekness, humility, and love. That's something everyone can do.

weighed: I'd start with what I actually think: no, morality wouldn't collapse just because religious belief faded. People can and do build decent ethics on empathy, reason, and shared social agreements, and history shows both believers and non-believers capable of good and evil. That said, religion does give many people community, purpose, and a strong framework for moral formation, so the picture is mixed. One principle worth naming is that the idea of God has to answer to our best moral understanding—no authority should get people to worship a God they see as immoral, and religion and morality are strongest when each helps the other. That principle changes how I'd frame the question: it's less about whether morality needs religion and more about whether each can hold the other accountable. It leaves in place my original answer—morality has independent foundations, and religion can still contribute a lot.
dogmatic: No, morality would not collapse—but the real issue is what kind of God you're asking people to worship. Any claim about God has to justify itself to the highest morality we know; no church or state has the standing to make people bow to a God they see as cruel or unjust. Religion and morality are strong exactly when each supports the other. And don't let the failings of preachers become an excuse: the truth of a religious message rests on God's wisdom and honesty, not on the character of the person delivering it. The Christian account of sin proves itself in practice—faith in promised strength and belief in others actually produces moral recovery. That's the test, and it holds.

weighed: I'd start by saying a rule can be helpful, especially when you're building habits, but it shouldn't become a cage. The goal of devotions is communion with God, not checking boxes. Many people benefit from a simple, flexible plan—set times of prayer and Scripture—while leaving room for the Spirit and for the duties of your state in life. If a method helps you be faithful, use it; if it becomes rigid or discouraging, adjust it. Consistency and sincerity matter more than strictness for its own sake. One principle worth weighing here is that the saying 'the best devotion is the constant practice of your ordinary duties' can be abused to excuse a dissipated, prayerless life. That principle changes how you hear that saying: it's not a free pass to skip prayer, because you're still bound to reserve leisure for frequent exercises of devotion. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer—your rule should serve your relationship with God, not replace it, and ordinary duties done well can still be a form of devotion.
dogmatic: You should follow a strict method or rule, but understand what it is for. A rule is a means to an end, and the end is God Himself. So hold your rule firmly as a means, yet be ready to lay it aside when you are with Him who is your end—because then it is useless to return to the means. Beware the excuse that the best devotion is simply the constant practice of your ordinary duties; some use that to justify a dissipated, prayerless life. You are bound first to live to yourself and to reserve leisure for frequent exercises of devotion. Also, if you practice devotion to Mary, let it be true devotion: honoring her, invoking her, trusting her intercession, imitating her virtues, and intending to amend your life—never presuming on her mercy. Let every method serve the relationship with God rather than eclipse it.

weighed: I'd start by saying God can guide through all three—feelings, Scripture, and circumstances—but they're not equally reliable. Scripture is the clearest, most objective guide, so you test everything against it. Feelings can mislead you because they're shaped by mood or desire, so don't make them your main compass. Circumstances can open or close doors, but they can be misread too. Practically, pray for wisdom, stay in the Word, get counsel from mature believers, and notice how God orders events. When these line up, move forward with confidence; when they conflict, lean on Scripture and wise counsel. Guidance is usually a process, so walk humbly and be willing to adjust. One idea worth adding is that God often guides by quietly swaying your judgment as you wait before Him in meekness, with hands off the scales—not scheming or forcing an outcome. That changes the tone: it makes waiting and humility central, and it reframes apparent hindrances as occasions for God to step in rather than reasons for anxiety. It leaves the rest in place—Scripture still tests everything, feelings still aren't your primary compass, circumstances still need reading carefully, and wise counsel still matters.
dogmatic: God guides His people by swaying their judgment as they wait before Him in meekness, with hands off the scales. You don't scheme your way to clarity and you don't force the outcome; you lay the decision before Him and let Him incline your heart. Apparent hindrances aren't setbacks to fear—they're occasions for God to interpose, and you should welcome them as such. He removes obstacles in His own time and way. Yes, He uses His Word to instruct, His Spirit within to incline the heart, and providence to open and close the way, but sin has blinded and biased us so badly that we need nothing short of divine direction to reach the home of God's love. And remember this: the servant of Christ has one Master. You are guided by the Spirit as to time and place, not bound by human committees or fixed rules. Pray, search the Scriptures, attend to providence, and follow the Spirit's leading, trusting Him to guide a heart that knows its own blindness.

weighed: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. It sounds like everything has fallen apart and you're left with ashes, and that kind of pain is real, so it's okay to grieve what's been lost. Even when life cracks and smokes, there can be something left to salvage, maybe something small like a routine, a relationship, or a hope you'd forgotten. One idea that speaks to this is that stopping halfway causes distress, that trying to serve two opposing things at once brings gloomy wretchedness and depression. That changes how I'd frame the wreckage: the crack might not just be loss, but the strain of living divided. It leaves in place what matters most, that you're hurting and need support, so please consider reaching out to someone you trust or a counselor who can help you sift through the debris. You don't have to fix everything at once, and you're not alone.
dogmatic: What you're calling a crack and smoke is not the truth of your being. In reality there is no relapse, for there is but one Mind, and what looks like collapse is a call to meet the cause mentally and courageously. Fear wants you to believe the wreckage is final, but fear is a liar. It's the stopping halfway that causes your distress: serving God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness and vacillation. Follow Christ all the way and let Him complete His process in you. Victory over lower passions comes not from your own will but from a Living Power transforming you, teaching you higher pleasures so you are not left comfortless. Nothing is truly lost except what you consent to lose. Stand in the truth that your life is not defined by smoke and ashes but by the unbroken core within you, and what seemed like an end is actually a beginning.

weighed: What you're feeling doesn't automatically mean your heart is bad. Tiredness, stress, and routine can all dull desire, so I'd start by being gentle with yourself and looking at what's really going on. One idea worth weighing is that morning listlessness can be an index of a listless heart—that the heart that holds back from seeking God early has lost some of its relish for him. That principle changes the tone: instead of just saying 'check your schedule,' it asks you to take the lack of desire seriously as a signal about your heart's direction. But it leaves in place the practical wisdom that desire often follows action, so small steps like a short prayer or a quiet moment still matter, and you don't need to wait for the feeling to strike.
dogmatic: Morning listlessness is the index to a listless heart. If you have no desire to pray in the morning, that is not neutral—it shows a heart that has lost its relish for God. No soul follows hard after God who is not after him in early morn. So don't excuse it as tiredness or busyness. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer, with the closet first and study and activity second. Pray specifically that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Let the discipline of early prayer and the ardor of the heart kindle each other, and arrange your schedule so prayer gets your best, not your remains.

weighed: I'm so sorry. Losing someone you loved more than anything is a pain that doesn't have words, and it's okay to feel every bit of it. God isn't distant from that; Scripture says He's near to the brokenhearted. As for why this happened, honestly, we often can't know the reasons this side of heaven, and it's alright to bring your questions to Him. What I'd hold onto is His character—He is good and loving even when life is painful. One thing worth weighing is the idea that if we really knew how much God loves us, we'd receive the sweet and the bitter from His hand alike, and that affliction seen as coming from a loving Father loses some of its sting. That can reframe a loss as something held within His care rather than something that slipped past Him. But it doesn't answer the why, and it doesn't make the grief small or tell you to rush through it. Lean on your community, let yourself grieve, and take comfort in God's presence. He does not abandon you in sorrow.
dogmatic: I'm sorry for your loss, but I want to be honest with you: everything comes from God's hand, sweet or bitter, and both should be received equally. This loss didn't slip past His love—it came from a Father who loves you, and seen as from Him, affliction becomes consolation. Abandon yourself to God in this suffering, inside and out. Don't look for life, work, or joy outside of Him; live and work and even rejoice in God. And let your grief be moderated—excessive mourning is a want of faith and confidence in God. He takes away friends because He will be loved without a rival; He wants your heart wholly for Himself. Bring your questions to Him, lean on your community, and let this sorrow draw you deeper into the God who does not abandon you.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong to want devotion and sweetness in prayer, or to long for tears of compunction. Those are good gifts, and many saints have known them. But feelings aren't the measure of your prayer. Sometimes God withdraws sensible consolation to purify your love and teach you to rely on faith rather than feelings. So if you feel dry, don't be discouraged; keep praying faithfully, because God is pleased with your perseverance. The important thing is to keep seeking God, not to chase spiritual experiences. True devotion is a steady will to please God even when feelings are absent. One principle that fits here is that feelings aren't the gauge of acceptance with God; you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. That principle changes the focus from chasing feelings to resting on God's promise, but it leaves in place the goodness of desiring devotion and tears, and the call to keep praying through dryness.
dogmatic: Wanting devotion and tears of compunction is not wrong, but feelings must never be the measure of prayer. Feelings never accurately gauge our real assimilation to God. The changeless word of promise is your only foundation. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly; do not abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Yet the soul's need of God is not a delusion. Your native yearning is evidence of a real Other who answers; the search implies something to be found. Devotion suits every state of life, not only the cloister. Amid exterior business, the heart must remain on God, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. So desire devotion, but rest on God's promise, not on moods, and keep your heart recollected in Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, you probably are deceiving yourself. Putting off change is a classic trap, and it's easy to tell yourself 'later' when later never comes. One idea that shifts this is that real change isn't about swapping one set of actions for another; it's about doing your ordinary, everyday tasks for God's sake instead of just for your own. That reframes things: it means you don't need some dramatic future overhaul—you can start right now with what's already in front of you. But it also leaves something in place: it doesn't let you off the hook about sincerity. A fleeting worry or a short burst of motivation isn't enough; you need a genuine change of heart, and that takes more than a quick glance at the consequences. So the takeaway is: don't wait for later, but also don't confuse busyness with real conversion.
dogmatic: Yes, you're deceiving yourself, and here's the harder truth: you're probably mistaking the means for the end. Sanctification isn't about changing your works—it's about doing for God's sake what you already do for your own. So stop waiting for some future dramatic change and start offering your daily duties to God right now. But don't fool yourself into thinking a passing fear or a short-lived fit of fervor is real conversion. Transient glances at judgment don't change the heart; penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. And don't be surprised when you keep finding miseries in yourself—the work of perfection is never done, so always begin anew with a good heart.

weighed: I'd start by saying that strange feeling is a gift—a reminder of your own mortality and a call to reflect on what matters. Use it to examine your life: are you living in a way that pleases God? Do you need to make changes? Let it move you to gratitude and a deeper commitment to faith. Talk to a trusted adult or pastor about it, and pray about what God wants you to learn. One principle that fits here is that a passing fear or a short-lived burst of feeling isn't enough to change your heart—real conversion needs to be sincere and lasting. That principle sharpens the advice: it warns you not to let the emotion fade without letting it lead to real repentance and sorrow for sin. But it leaves in place the basic idea that the feeling is a nudge worth paying attention to, and that you should talk to someone and pray. So the core of what I'd say first still stands, just with a stronger push toward a sincere and lasting change rather than a fleeting moment.
dogmatic: That feeling at a funeral is a call to remember that you too must die. Count yourself as already dead, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults. It is not now the time to rejoice but rather to lament with all sincerity of heart. Let this impression lead you to repentance and sorrow for sin. But beware: a passing fear or a short-lived fit of fervor is not sufficient conversion. Transient glances effect not a change of heart. Penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. And remember that God watches over all the dead, even those who perish at sea, as fondly as the churchyard grave. So turn to God with a contrite heart, seeking a sincere and lasting change.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your faith calls you to forgive and to let go of revenge. Jesus teaches us to pray that we forgive others as we are forgiven, and holding onto anger mostly hurts you. One principle worth naming is that a Christian is never allowed to seek revenge, and patience and forgiving injuries are to be prized above retaliation. That principle sharpens the point: it rules out revenge entirely, not just the outward act but the desire behind it. What it leaves in place is everything else you're feeling. Your anger is real, the wrong done to you is real, and justice still matters. Forgiveness doesn't mean the wrong was okay. It means you hand the claim for payback to God, pray for the person who hurt you, and ask for grace to release the grudge. That's hard, and it may take time, but it's the path that leads to peace rather than bitterness.
dogmatic: Your faith forbids revenge, full stop. A Christian is never permitted to seek it; patience and the forgiving of injuries are to be prized above retaliation. So put the desire for payback away, not because the wrong was small, but because vengeance belongs to God and not to you. Forgive as Christ forgave you, pray for the one who wronged you, and ask for the grace to mean it. And when you slip and the anger returns, don't sink into discouragement. Acknowledge your weakness, return to God with greater trust, and keep going. Forgiveness is the only road out of this, and it is the road you are called to walk.

weighed: My first answer would be to look at what you protect most fiercely and where your time and money actually go. Do you get more upset over a scratched car than a hurt friend? Do you keep score of what people owe you? Those honest checks still hold up. One principle worth adding is that confidence between family members grows when you respect each person's own belongings, even a child's little chest, and never search another's things without consent. That changes how you apply the test at home: property isn't just something you own, it's also something you honor in others, so respecting a child's or spouse's things becomes a way of putting people first. What it leaves in place is the core question of whether you'd absorb a loss to spare someone pain and whether your calendar and money show people ahead of possessions.
dogmatic: You can tell by asking whether you treat anything you hold as truly yours. You own nothing; your time, talents, and possessions are lent to you to steward, and earthly riches are not true riches. So notice what you protect most fiercely: if you grieve more over a scratched car than a wounded relationship, your heart is leaning on a shadow. Ask whether you'd inconvenience yourself or absorb a loss to spare someone pain, and whether you keep score of what others owe you. Respect the belongings of those closest to you, even a child's little chest, and never search another's things without consent. Your calendar and money should show you treating people as owners under God, not as rivals to your goods.

weighed: My first answer would be that the missing 'I' and 'me' show prayer isn't a private transaction but a shared life before God—'Our Father' puts you inside a family of faith, and every petition is plural because those needs are common to everyone. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's Prayer is a prayer of fellowship and cooperation, where divine Fatherhood and human brotherhood are born together. That sharpens my answer: it makes the link between loving God and loving your neighbor explicit, so praying 'our' is itself an act of solidarity. What it leaves in place is the core point—pray personally, but never as though you stood alone. So when you pray, carry others' needs, extend the forgiveness you ask for, and hold your hope together with the whole community.
dogmatic: The absence of 'I' and 'me' is not a small detail—it tells you prayer is fellowship and cooperation, and that divine Fatherhood and human brotherhood are born together. To say Father to God is to say brother to your fellows; you cannot separate love of God from love of neighbor. So prayer is simple, natural, constant asking—a child speaking to a parent—not a complicated procedure governed by human rules, and God as Father delights to be sought for everyday needs. Yet prayer must also be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. Pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Pray plainly and often within the living group of faith, carrying others' needs, and let prayer accompany and shape every advance you make.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: when you're overwhelmed, the first move is to get the load out of your head and onto paper, then sort it—what's urgent, what can wait, what can be handed off or dropped, and where you need to draw a line. Break the big things into small steps, do the most important one first each morning, and protect sleep, movement, and short breaks, because exhaustion makes everything feel like failure. Talk to someone you trust, and check whether perfectionism is setting the bar unfairly high. One principle worth taking seriously here is the call to avoid hurry and anxiety and stay grounded in God's presence—it reframes peace as something you receive now, not a reward for finishing your list. That changes the tone of the whole thing: you slow down instead of speeding up, and you stop treating calm as the prize at the end.
