What it leaves in place is the practical work—the list, the triage, the boundaries, the rest—because those are still how you carry the load. So do the next duty plainly and calmly, and let some things slip without reading it as failure.
dogmatic: Stop hurrying. That's the root of it. Over-eagerness is the mother of many imperfections, and your frantic scramble to fix everything at once is exactly what's stealing your peace. Peace isn't the reward for finishing your list—it's a gift received now, so become quiet in God's presence and stay there. Refuse the rush. Take up the next duty plainly before you and do it calmly. Watch your tongue, subdue anger before it speaks, examine your own heart instead of measuring yourself against everyone else, and mind your own duties rather than faultfinding. When the anxious fretting rises, return quietly to His presence. And do not quit—having done all, stand. Keep trying even when the work seems to fail; apparent defeat is no reason to abandon the cause. Faith works steadily and never gives up, trusting God with the outcome.

weighed: I'd start by saying: treat Saul as both a serious warning and a serious hope. His zeal against the church shows how sincerely wrong someone can be, yet his encounter with Christ shows no one is beyond God's reach. He wasn't just persuaded; he was transformed into a tireless apostle. So don't write off people who oppose the faith, and don't despair over your own past. His story doesn't excuse persecution—it magnifies grace. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's mercy is shown in Saul, who doomed many followers of Christ and stood by as Stephen was stoned, yet was shown mercy and became Paul, a comfort to many. That deepens the hope side: the mercy is concrete and costly, not abstract. What it leaves in place is the warning—his past still really happened, and grace doesn't soften what he did. So stay humble in judgment, hopeful in God's mercy, and grateful that conversion is God's work, not ours.
dogmatic: Look at who met Saul on the road: not a mere prophet, but the one in whom all things hold together, the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation. That's why the mercy shown to a man who doomed followers of Christ to torture and death and approved of Stephen's stoning carries cosmic weight—the life, death, and resurrection matter because of who he is. And to misunderstand Paul is to be ignorant of the divine idea he taught, and that ignorance betrays a deeper ignorance of the Principle behind the idea. So honor the divine idea set before us; to dismiss or abuse it is to betray that ignorance. Saul became Paul, a solace to many, and his story should make you humble in judgment and hopeful in God.

weighed: I'd start by saying it depends on the work and the people. Working alongside non-Christians in shared projects, charity, or your job can be fine as long as you're not asked to compromise your convictions, endorse false teaching, or hide your faith. Ask what the group expects, be honest about what you believe, and keep your main accountability to your church. One principle worth weighing is that secret organizations and societies should be avoided because the gospel and the Church already provide what they promise, and such ties can divide your interests and lead you into bondage. That principle sharpens the line: it makes secrecy and oath-bound groups a clear no, but it leaves open honest, transparent work alongside unconverted people. So if the invitation is open and doesn't require secrecy or compromise, I'd say it can be acceptable; if it does, decline.
dogmatic: Secret organizations and societies should be avoided by members, because the gospel and the Church provide everything any society can offer, and such affiliations divide interests and lead members into bondage. So if this work is tied to an oath-bound or secret group, stay out. More broadly, remember that Christian work is primarily God's own work through you, not your work for God—its highest aspect is obedience to Him and bringing glory to His Name. And don't let an unwelcome task make you uneasy; say it's God's business you're about, and trust Him to bring it to completion. Ask what the group expects, be honest about your faith, and decline anything that requires secrecy or compromise.

weighed: I'd start by saying that it's natural to feel this way—the things you chase are temporary, so the happiness they give is temporary too. That's why nothing in this passing world can fully satisfy you. But here's a principle worth considering: this world is meant to be a touchstone and finding-place for God, not just a waiting room for the next life. That changes how you see your dissatisfaction—it's not a sign to lower your expectations of the world, but a sign that you're looking for God in the wrong places. What it leaves in place is the honest recognition that earthly things can't fill the emptiness. So instead of just accepting disappointment, you can start seeking God here and now, in the midst of your daily life.
dogmatic: Your desire for happiness is God-given, planted in you by the One who made you for Himself. Every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled—romance, family, business, pleasure, art—they're good gifts, but when you ask them to do what only God can do, they end in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is permanent success. And beware the middle way—trying to serve God and the world together as a safe compromise. Stopping half-way brings gloomy wretchedness. Follow Christ all the way, that He may complete His process in you and fill you wholly with Himself.

weighed: My first answer would be that Revelation describes the New Jerusalem as a cube about 1,500 miles on each side, though many read that as symbolic rather than literal. Either way, Scripture speaks of a countless multitude, so there's ample room for everyone who is saved. One principle worth naming is that the city is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one. That changes how I'd picture the size: it's not just real estate but a picture of God dwelling fully with His people, so the sufficiency is about union with Him, not square footage. What it leaves in place is the plain point you asked about: the city is vast, and there's room for all who are saved.
dogmatic: The New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. Don't split those into separate things. Its size speaks of sufficiency: there is room for all who are saved. And look for the Jews' gathering and redemption by God's power, not by human preaching alone, with no ill will toward them. The judgements of the last days are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for the reign of Christ, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, you can go forward, and your lack of money and help doesn't have to stop you. The principle I'd lean on is that God's people can offer themselves and what they have for His work without a salary, trusting Him to supply what's needed. That changes the picture: it means you don't have to wait until you're financially secure before serving. What it leaves in place is that you still have real limits, so you start with what you actually have, your time and strength and willingness, and you don't take on obligations you can't meet or neglect people who depend on you. So go forward, but go forward honestly with what's in your hands.
dogmatic: Yes, go forward, and don't let money or the absence of help hold you back. Offer yourself and whatever substance you have for God's work without expecting a salary, trusting Him to supply your needs. If you can't do a thing in the Lord's name, don't do it at all, and if you can, then do it boldly. You don't need a special religious life or public displays of piety either; ordinary work and ordinary days are where you'll find God. So stop waiting for security and start serving with what you have right now.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: prayer and study don't have to be enemies, so try weaving them together. Pray briefly before you open a book, pause mid-study to lift your heart, and thank God when you're done, plus keep some fixed times of prayer. One principle worth taking seriously is that prayer deserves the best of your time and strength, not just scraps left over from studying. That changes the order of your day: prayer comes first, study second, and study gets freshened by time with God rather than the other way around. What it leaves in place is the integration you already have; short prayers around study still count, and study can still feed devotion. It just means you stop treating prayer as the thing that gets whatever energy is left.
dogmatic: Honestly, your study is killing your devotion because you've made study first and prayer second, and that order has to be reversed. Give God the best of your time and the heart of your strength, with the closet first and study second. Don't treat prayer as a petty duty squeezed into a corner or pieced together from fragments of time. Pray patiently and believingly until the blessing comes, without fixing a time or circumstances for God's answer; importunate perseverance is the mark of effectual prayer. And approach prayer with awe, strict silence, and profound inward devotion, shutting your senses to distractions, because it's insolence to ask God for grace to pray well while you openly neglect precautions against distractions. So keep praying with reverence, and let study follow.

weighed: I'd start by saying that doing what you believe is right when everyone around you disagrees is one of the hardest things a person can face. Truth isn't decided by majority vote, so weigh the counsel of others carefully but ultimately follow your conscience. Seek support from people who share your convictions so you're not alone, consider the long-term consequences, and then act with courage. One candidate principle says it's right to decline human offers of support in order to cast yourself wholly on God and prove His faithfulness. That changes the part about making human support a condition—you don't have to wait for a community to back you up before you act. But it leaves in place the core advice: still weigh counsel, count the cost, and follow your conscience. It just shifts where you place your ultimate reliance.
dogmatic: You should do what you believe is right because truth is not decided by majority vote. But don't stop at following your conscience—decline human offers of support and cast yourself wholly on God, proving His faithfulness. Don't make human backing a condition of doing right. And remember that high councils judging members should find out the truth, judge according to the facts, and always temper judgment with mercy, love, and kindness, aiming to save and not destroy. Never imagine you can gain by injuring another: wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer, while right adjusts the balance sooner or later. So stand alone if you must, rely on God alone, and trust that right will prevail.

weighed: I hear you. You're asking if you can keep that one thing and still be filled. My first answer would be: God's holiness is a gift, not something you earn by giving things up, so don't turn this into a transaction. But if you know something stands between you and God, look at it honestly. One principle worth weighing is that we can hold onto things that are useful to others but not needed by us, and that keeping them costs us blessing. That principle shifts the focus from 'Can I keep this?' to 'Is this something I'm hoarding that could serve someone else?' It doesn't settle whether every attachment must go, and it leaves room for patience and growth. So examine that thing with a trusted friend or pastor, pray for wisdom, and be honest about whether it's a hindrance or just a preference. You don't have to be perfect overnight.
dogmatic: You ask if you can keep it and still be filled. No—not while you cling to it. Scripture says to examine what you have and part with what others could use; unneeded possessions hinder both your blessing and the spread of the Gospel. This is a habit of holding things loosely and giving freely, and it brings blessing. And don't rely on your own strength for any virtue: say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. When dryness or bitterness tempts you to withdraw from Holy Communion, don't draw back—approach boldly, seek strength and union with His meekness, for there you are met and filled. So give it up, and come boldly.

weighed: My first instinct is to say heaven is a far-off place where God lives, and the saints will reign with Christ there after death, since this world is temporary. But that skips something important: the Bible says the meek will inherit the earth, and the New Jerusalem comes down to a purified earth where God dwells with people. That changes the picture from escaping to reigning here with Christ, though it leaves in place that God is holy and our hope is real. It also keeps the saints' reign with Christ, just on a renewed earth rather than somewhere distant.
dogmatic: Heaven isn't a distant escape; this earth is humanity's eternal inheritance. The saints will reign on the earth with Christ, and the New Jerusalem will descend to a purified earth where God dwells with people. Christ suffers in His least saints, asking why they are persecuted, and even a drop of water given for love's sake is stored in heaven. Amid heavy work, the saints made time to withdraw and converse with God and themselves, lifting their minds to heaven with holy sighs and desires, so all their actions became an uninterrupted prayer and exercise of divine love and praise.

weighed: I'd start by saying peace of conscience comes from God's forgiveness, received by faith in Christ—not from getting your past fully sorted out first. Your past weighs on you because guilt is real, but the gospel says God doesn't hold your sins against you when you turn to him. Confess what you've done, accept his pardon, and let the burden lift; it can help to talk with a pastor or trusted believer who can assure you of grace and pray with you. One principle I'd weigh here is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy your ability to do right—that changes how seriously I'd take the need for honest repentance, but it leaves in place the promise that peace rests on his love, not on your virtue. So let the sight of your sin keep you humble and the sight of his mercy keep you from sinking.
dogmatic: Peace of conscience comes from God's forgiveness, but don't treat your past lightly. Unrepented sin accumulates and hardens the heart, so begin with honest repentance and a changed life. Beware the moralistic error that makes forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue—that leaves the baptized sinner either presumptuous or despairing. Hold both together: dread of your own unsureness keeps you from presumption, and the blessed showing of love keeps you from despair. Peace comes not from your virtue but from his love, received by the repentant heart.

weighed: I'd start by saying: stop examining yourself endlessly. Constant self-doubt feeds on itself—the more you scrutinize every thought, the more you find to fear. Bring your sins honestly before God, confess them once, and accept His forgiveness rather than re-litigating them. It helps to speak with a wise pastor or confessor who can help you distinguish real sin from anxious imagination. Remember that God is not a harsh inspector but a loving Father, and that His mercy is greater than your scruples. Rest in the assurance that you are accepted, and turn your attention outward to others rather than inward to yourself. One principle that fits here is that self-denial isn't just cutting off an indulgence here and there but laying the axe at the root of the tree of self—a voluntary self-renunciation taken up for Christ's sake. That changes the focus from endless self-scrutiny to a deliberate turning from self-will at its root. It leaves in place the honest confession and the wise counsel, but it reframes the struggle as a positive offering rather than anxious self-policing.
dogmatic: You need to face justice and truth honestly: name your sins before God without concealment, neither exaggerating nor minimizing them, and do not deny the truth of what you have done in order to feel better. But go deeper than surface faults. Self-denial is not the lopping off of a few branches while self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory remain at the root; the axe must be laid at the root of the tree of self, and the cross taken up voluntarily for Christ's sake, not as a forced trial. And do not treat unrepented sin lightly: unregretted sin accumulates, hardening the heart and destroying the ability to do right, and a guilty conscience is not a small thing. Let honest repentance and reformation of life be your answer, so that conscience is healed by truth and by a life genuinely turned from self to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying that dark fiction shows real suffering and moral complexity, but it's a selection, not the whole picture. Writers often focus on conflict and failure because that's what makes drama, while ordinary kindness and quiet goodness rarely make it into novels. If the reading is weighing on you, balance it with other voices—history, biography, or fiction that acknowledges darkness without being consumed by it. One principle worth naming is that the spiritual man sees evil as a horror of ugliness, not an intense attraction. That changes how you read: evil becomes disease, misery, imprisonment, and death rather than something glamorous or harmless. It leaves in place the reality of darkness and the need to step back if despair is making you cynical or numb. Literature should deepen your compassion, not erase your hope.
dogmatic: Dark fiction is a selection, but don't stop there. Much of what passes for peace is built on mutual fear and selfish loves, and that is where Cruelty's snare is knit. Cruelty, Humility, Mystery, and Deceit grow from the human brain. See evil in its true complexion: it is disease, misery, imprisonment, and death, not glamour or harmless shadow. The spiritual man sees this by the new light created when the Spirit of Love descends. The Christian faith keeps alive the dread meeting with the Lord, and the Apocalypse is a vision of final triumph in Christ. So read with that horizon open: the darkness is real, but it is not the last word. Let the stories deepen compassion, and let your hope rest in the triumph of Christ.

weighed: My first answer would be: no, being paid a salary doesn't make your ministry professional or heartless in itself. A congregation supporting its pastor frees him to give himself fully to the work, and the real question is the spirit in which the salary is received, not the paycheck. One principle worth weighing here is that a professional ministry is a heartless ministry, that when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part. That sharpens my answer: it warns you that if the salary and self-advancement start leading, people quietly become clients and the heart drains out of the work. What it changes is the tone, from a calm reassurance to a real warning to examine your motives. What it leaves in place is that the salary itself isn't the problem, and a supported pastor can still love the flock and preach faithfully. So keep your heart toward the people and let the salary support the ministry rather than drive it.
dogmatic: A professional ministry is a heartless ministry, full stop. When salary plays a great part, the heart plays little part, and whoever puts self to the front puts heart to the rear. So reject the career mindset outright and put self behind you. But don't swing to the other error and think a warm heart or correct doctrine gives life, because all life-giving power belongs to the Spirit of God, who must anoint the preacher and energize the word; truth without the Spirit deadens as much as error does. And avoid both extremes in how you spend yourself: don't shut yourself away from people to be alone with God, and don't become a popularizer whose busy plans leave no room for prayer. Time with God is of use only as you spend its benefits on people. So pray for the Spirit, keep your heart toward the flock, and let your salary support a ministry that pours itself out for others.

weighed: Wandering thoughts are normal and not a sign of failure. Try a simple technique: when you notice your mind has drifted, gently return your attention to a short prayer word or to a phrase like 'Lord, have mercy.' Don't fight the thoughts or scold yourself—just acknowledge them and let them pass. Some people find it helps to pray at a fixed time, in a quiet place, with a candle or icon to focus the eyes. You might also keep a notebook nearby to jot down distracting worries so you can set them aside. Be patient with yourself; recollection is a habit that grows with practice, and even a few moments of genuine attention are worthwhile. One principle that fits here is to hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—just keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly without disquiet. That principle changes the tone: instead of techniques like a prayer word or a notebook, it emphasizes simple, tranquil return. It leaves in place the core advice to be patient and not scold yourself, and it still allows for practical aids if they help you return gently.
dogmatic: You should stop trying to manage your wandering mind with techniques and instead take up the discipline of continual recollection. Keep your heart occupied with God at all times, not just during prayer. When your mind wanders, do not examine yourself or fuss—simply turn back to Him in tranquility, like a beggar who keeps his eyes on the rich man's gate. The real work is outside prayer: guard your thoughts during the day, refuse idle distractions, and keep yourself strictly in the presence of God. That way your mind will grow calm and come to prayer already recollected. Your joy is not in how well you pray but in pleasing Him, so let your heart be occupied with God always, content to be before Him, trusting that He keeps you even when your attention slips. Return in peace, as often as needed.

weighed: Here's what I'd tell you first: stop repeating it or spreading it further. Then apologize to your colleague directly and specifically—name what you said and why it was wrong, no excuses. If others heard you, correct the record with them too. Look at why you did it—anger, jealousy, careless talk—and deal with that. Pray for them and for yourself, and if the damage was serious, ask what would help repair it. Trust may take time. One principle here is that we should speak little and well, gently and frankly. That changes the tone of the apology: fewer words, plainer, calmer, and then stop rather than over-explaining. It leaves the core steps in place—stop, apologize specifically, correct the record, address the root, and be patient.
dogmatic: Speak little and speak well. Be silent first—don't repeat or spread what you said. Then go to your colleague and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, so they hear it from you and aren't left guessing. If others heard you, correct the record in plain words. Say what you have to say and then stop; don't bury the point under a pile of words. And compel your heart to suffer tranquilly: you'll feel rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience, but don't let them govern how you deal with your neighbor. Stay kind despite them, praying quietly for the one you wronged. A few honest words, gently and frankly spoken, are better than many. Be patient—trust takes time.

weighed: My first answer would be that God isn't lonely because love has always existed within the Trinity—Father, Son, and Spirit giving and receiving—so He didn't need creation to have someone to love. I'd also say that love doesn't require a created object, and that creation itself flows from His love. One principle I'd bring in is that God loved us before He made us, and that love was never slacked. That changes the picture: it's not that God was love in theory and then started loving when He made us—His love for us was already there from before creation. What it leaves in place is the Trinity as the eternal ground of love, and the idea that creation is an expression of love rather than a fix for loneliness. So the answer holds together: God is love because love is who He is, and He loved us before we existed.
dogmatic: God's love is not a feeling or a vague attribute—it is His eternal, rational, voluntary self-communication, holy and never indifferent to sin. Within the Trinity, Father, Son, and Spirit give and receive without beginning. He loved us before He made us, and that love was never slacked; in that love He made all things profitable to us, and Love was His meaning in all He showed. So don't let fear govern this question. Meet the trial with stronger faith and purer love, for perfect Love casts out fear. 'God is love' means He freely communicates His goodness, seeking our true good from before all time.

weighed: I'd start by saying what you're feeling is common and not a sign that something is broken beyond repair. Apathy often comes from exhaustion, disappointment, or just going through the motions for too long. The first step is to be honest about it instead of pretending. Ask yourself what's drained your desire—busyness, hurt, or a pattern of compromise? Go back to the basics—prayer, Scripture, fellowship—even when you feel nothing, because feelings tend to follow faithfulness. It might help to talk with a pastor or a trusted friend who can pray with you and help you look at your life. Don't wait for the feeling to return before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. God isn't distant just because you feel distant, and He can rekindle desire in a heart that's grown cold. One principle worth weighing is that spiritual experiences aren't something we can manufacture or demand—they're outside our control and are accepted as God chooses, with submission rather than curiosity or fear. That changes the pressure: you stop treating prayer and Scripture as a lever to force a feeling, and you stop secretly demanding an experience. But it leaves in place the honest self-examination and the steady return to basics—it doesn't excuse passivity or let you drift. So keep showing up, but hold the outcome loosely.
dogmatic: Apathy in spiritual things is deadly, not just a lack of feeling to be managed. Don't treat spiritual experience as something you can manufacture by returning to basics until feelings follow. Accept experiences only as God chooses—without praying for them, secretly desiring them, or approaching them with curiosity—and submit without questioning or fear. Yet submission is not repose: allow no slipping back in the spiritual ascent, but go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached, for desires turning aside after lower objects cause distraction and loss of the way; withdraw from worldly distractions into the one unchangeable Good. Understand that God often touches us where we are most tender—through loss and hardship—not as cruelty but as His loving means to awaken, humble, and lift us into His consolations. Name the apathy, keep climbing, and trust His hand.

weighed: Yes, it can. I'd start there: a funeral can wake you up, and a serious conversation in that setting can plant something real. But one principle worth holding onto is that a passing glance at serious things doesn't by itself change your heart, and conversions that come mostly from fear of a calamity rarely turn out sincere. That doesn't cancel what you felt. It just means the moment is a beginning, not the change itself. So take it seriously: sit with what struck you, pray about it, and make one or two concrete changes in how you spend your time and speak. Talk with someone wise who can help you keep going. Don't expect instant transformation, and don't dismiss the stirring either. Many people trace real change back to a single unsettling experience. The question is whether you'll follow through.
dogmatic: Yes, but don't mistake a mood for conversion. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day. Have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than to weep over, regret, and detest your offences and faults; this is not the time to rejoice but to lament with all sincerity of heart. As you stand among mourners, remember that the dead beloved is in a higher sphere of saner happiness; your grief should be a tender regret, not acute grief. Beware: superficial conversions made under fear of calamity rarely bear the marks of sincerity. Transient glances effect no change of heart. Let this stirring bring you to a sincere and perfect change of heart, not merely a short-lived fit of fervor.

weighed: I hear how heavy this is for you. First, I want to say what I'd have told you right away: God's mercy is bigger than anything you've done, and when you confess, he is faithful to forgive. You don't have to stay stuck replaying the past. One principle that matters here is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin can wear down your ability to do right, so it helps to name your sins honestly to God, grieve them, and turn toward a changed life. That principle changes the focus from just trying to feel better to actually repenting and making amends where you can. But it leaves in place the core truth that you are forgiven in Christ and that self-forgiveness isn't excusing yourself—it's agreeing with God that you're pardoned and free. So take small steps forward, talk to a trusted pastor or friend, and pray for peace.
dogmatic: A guilty conscience is not something to just soothe away. Unrepented sin piles up, and every time you excuse it, your heart hardens and your power to do right weakens. So start with honest repentance: name your sins to God, grieve them, and turn toward a reformed life, making amends where you can. Confessing your faults and humbling yourself quiets the wandering mind, because pride scatters thoughts while humility gathers them. In prayer, avoid heaping up many words—that only multiplies distraction. But go deeper than cutting off a few branches. Lay the axe at the root of self: deny not just this indulgence or that habit, but self-will, self-seeking, and self-glory. Take up the cross voluntarily for Christ's sake—not as a forced trial but as a chosen renunciation—and let each day's conduct show that grace is at work.

weighed: I'd first say: resist the temptation. Your calling is to preach the whole counsel of God, not to flatter the people who fund your ministry. If you soften the message to keep contributors happy, money becomes your master. Trust God to provide, be honest with your supporters about your convictions, and speak the truth in love even if it costs you some funding. One principle worth naming here is that the work should be supported by voluntary contributions sent freely and without personal solicitation, trusting that God supplies all your need. That changes how you handle the money side: you don't lean on pressure or guaranteed income, and you don't let fundraising anxiety shape your preaching. It leaves in place the core call to resist flattery and preach the whole counsel of God. So the principle doesn't soften the main answer; it gives you a freer way to live it out.
dogmatic: You should resist this temptation completely. Preach the whole counsel of God and refuse to flatter anyone who funds your ministry. Do not build your work on pressure, solicitation, or guaranteed incomes. Depend only on voluntary contributions sent freely and without asking, and testify that God supplies all your need. When you face an occasion to practice this virtue, go to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me,' and receive strength more than sufficient, for he does not command faithfulness and leave you alone. Be careful for nothing: cast your anxious care about provision and outcomes upon him, making your requests known to God with thanksgiving, and take his Almighty care in exchange for your worry. Then you will speak freely, fearing neither the loss of contributors nor the displeasure of men.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: this is a real dilemma, and you should weigh it carefully. Your oath carries weight, and breaking it damages trust, but a threat of death is serious too, and you shouldn't be reckless with your own life. Ask whether revealing the secret would harm others or prevent a greater evil, seek counsel from people you trust, and decide according to your conscience, balancing your oath against preserving life. One principle worth naming is that secret prayer is indispensable, since public prayer and talking with others can't make up for private communion. That changes how you carry the decision: it tells you to keep praying in private even when it feels dry, and not to lean only on outward faithfulness or on what people think. What it leaves in place is the weighing itself: you still have to consider the harm, seek counsel, and decide. It doesn't tell you which way to go; it sustains you while you decide.
dogmatic: You should stop trying to master the hidden outcome. What is open to you is keeping your oath with integrity and acting honestly; what is hidden belongs to God's counsel, and you should not busy yourself trying to know it, because the more you pry, the farther you get from knowing. Make no account of people's judgments. Silence and enduring their judgments is the secret of interior peace. And do not rely on outward faithfulness alone: secret prayer is indispensable, and public prayer and conversation with others cannot make up for private communion with God. Keep praying and reading the Word even when enjoyment is gone, for faithfulness in the dark is itself the trust you are called to. Let your hidden life with God sustain your open conduct before others.

weighed: When you're facing a mob or real danger, fear is a natural response. The key is to manage it by focusing on practical steps: stay calm, assess the situation, and seek safety. While fear can be helpful by heightening your awareness, it can also hinder you if it leads to panic. Trust in God can provide comfort, but you also need to use wisdom. Remember that God is with you, but you must do your part to protect yourself. Pray for courage and take sensible precautions. One principle worth weighing is that God tenderly comforts our fears, saying 'It is I, be not afraid' — He is the antidote to fear and the substance of deliverance, so we should keep our eyes fastened on Him. That principle changes the inner posture: it gives you a steady place to anchor your attention when panic rises, so you're not just white-knuckling your own calm. What it leaves in place is everything practical — you still assess the situation, move toward safety, and take sensible precautions. Trusting God doesn't replace wise action; it steadies you while you take it.
dogmatic: Do not let fear govern you when danger closes in. Fear is not something to manage or negotiate with — it must be cast out and replaced by trust in God. Perfect love casts out fear, and in the testimonies of healing, fear was overcome before the healing appeared. So when a mob surrounds you or real danger threatens, fasten your eyes on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance. Abide in Him, and you will find in His presence the remedy for trouble. Do not look at the storm or the circumstances for comfort — look to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. And if you feel alone in it, accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trusting God alone with your secret throbbings, resting in the Lord who knows all yet loves us better than He knows. In Christ you are safe, for He is your refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

weighed: My first answer would be that you have real authority to read Scripture for yourself, your pastor can help, and the wider church carries centuries of wisdom—so read personally, check your understanding against trusted teachers, and stay humble. One principle worth naming is that the church, meaning all who live by the biblical ideals and not just official bodies, is the true interpreter, and the united judgment of believers is what confirms an individual reading. That changes how I'd frame it: your private interpretation isn't final on its own; it gains its footing when the wider body recognizes it. What it leaves in place is your direct access to the text and the Spirit's help—you still read for yourself, but you don't read alone.
dogmatic: The church is the interpreter of Scripture—not a lone reader, not a pastor, not a formal organization, but the whole body of believers working in the spirit of the biblical ideals. The united judgment of that body, shaped by long use and by what actually helps people, is the supreme authority, and no individual's reading is final until it receives that sanction. Second Peter and Jude ground this in the authority of the prophets and apostles, which is Christ's own authority, and the deepest need of the modern church is a return to the Bible read this way. And above all, Christ himself is the only ultimate authority; Scripture's authority is mediate and relative, and it takes the Spirit of Christ to interpret it rightly. So submit your private reading to the mind of the whole body, and let the living Lord, speaking through his people and his word, correct your whim and your custom alike.

weighed: I'd start by saying that those who wash their robes and put faith in Jesus may enter through the gates, while the unbelieving, immoral, murderers, idolaters, and liars are shut out. One principle I'd weigh is that only those who keep God's commandments have a right to the tree of life and may enter the city, and nothing that defiles will enter it. That principle sharpens the answer toward obedience and holiness as the mark of those who enter, but it leaves in place the same basic division: the faithful and obedient are welcomed, and those who persist in sin and reject God are excluded.
dogmatic: Only those who keep God's commandments have any right to the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the city. Nothing that defiles, nothing that works abomination or makes a lie, will enter it. The saints are not the city; they are being prepared to enter the city that is prepared for them. And that preparation happens right in the trivial round and common task, where you deny yourself and draw nearer to God without abandoning your neighbour or your work. So the answer is plain: commandment-keepers enter, and everything that defiles is shut out.

weighed: My first instinct was to say that doing good is just costly by nature—it takes sacrifice, and the people close to you often end up paying part of that price, so you should accept it and stay firm. One principle I'd weigh in is that goodness is meant to look like God's own kindness—sympathy, warmth, rejoicing and weeping with others—not just rigid righteousness. That changes how the cost reaches people: instead of goodness landing on them like a cold mountainside, it should come clothed in affection and active benevolence, so their suffering isn't just a bill to accept. What it leaves in place is that sacrifice and hardship are still real, and some suffering still comes with doing right. So I'd still say don't run from the cost, but watch how your goodness touches others—make it warm, not crushing.
dogmatic: Doing good costs because it asks for sacrifice, and the people near you will often share that cost—that's simply the shape of a moral life, so don't flinch from it. But don't confuse goodness with a hard, inflexible righteousness. Real goodness is God-likeness in active benevolence: kindness, sympathy, weeping with those who weep. Clothe what you do in warmth so it reaches people as affection rather than as a granite wall. And don't measure your service by how much you do or how visible it is—quality matters far more than quantity. A small deed done well outweighs a great deal done for display. Aim to please God, leave the amount and the outcome in his hands, and accept that hardship and the cross are an honor, not a misfortune.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: that fear makes sense, but letting God in isn't about him stripping your freedom—it's about freeing you from the things that really bind you, like fear and sin. He invites rather than forces, and he respects your choices. One principle I'd weigh in is that we're called to accept God's will without reserve, willing even to be struck where he wills, even in painful things. That deepens the answer: it means trust may sometimes feel like it costs you something, not just a gentle invitation. But it leaves your core point intact—God isn't out to take your freedom; he's after your good, and his service is perfect freedom.
dogmatic: The honest answer is that yes, following God means your own will gets dethroned—and that's the point. You're not owed a comfortable negotiation where you keep every preference and he works around them. Accept his will without reserve, without an if or but, willing that he strike you where he wills, even in the most repugnant things. That's not cruelty; it's the only path to real freedom, because the self you're clinging to is what actually enslaves you. And don't skip the hard part: keep the knowing sight of your own sin and feebleness, because without that there's no true meekness, and without meekness no salvation—no matter how high you're lifted. Light you don't use gets withdrawn. So obey promptly what you already know to be true, and trust that he who permits no suffering without a good end will never abandon you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the deepest hopes we have, and Scripture gives real ground for it. The world to come isn't a vague shadowland; it's the renewed creation where God dwells with His people, and relationships aren't erased but healed and perfected. If God cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs of our heads, He surely doesn't sever the bonds of love He Himself planted in families. One principle worth weighing is that the restoration of all things means the earth is brought back to its primeval glory and man restored with it. That changes the setting of the hope—it makes the promise earthy and concrete rather than purely otherworldly, so families and children belong within a restored order. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: the God who raised Jesus will raise us, and nothing in Christ is finally lost. So grieve honestly, but grieve with hope.
dogmatic: The restoration of all things settles this. The earth will be brought back to its primeval glory—one land, fruitful, without curse—and man restored with it, so families and children belong within that restored order. Between death and that renewal, the spirit world is no idleness or oblivion; all go there, and the faithful continue their labors with the same identity and priesthood they had in mortality. So don't forecast or dread tomorrow. Think only of doing well today, and trust the eternal Father's care for what is to come. He who restores all things holds your family in His hands; leave the morrow with Him and live faithfully now.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, you can believe in a good God and still hold that death is the end of you, though it's a tense place to stand. One idea that speaks to this is that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life. That principle changes the weight of your question: it turns your hope for something beyond death from wishful thinking into something anchored in God's character. But it leaves in place the honest possibility that you might be wrong about what happens after you die, and it doesn't erase the tension you feel. So you can hold both, but the belief in a good God gives you a real reason to expect more, even while you wait.
dogmatic: No, you cannot consistently believe in a good God and hold that death is the end of you. Belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life—immortality is a corollary of that belief. If God aims at an end not fully realized here, you have ground for postulating that death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state. The righteous dead are not to be mourned hopelessly; the body will be raised, and identity will be preserved. Yet death does not automatically bring you nearer to God—dying increases the difficulty of finding Him, and this world is where you can most easily and quickly get into communication with God. So if you believe in a good God, you have every reason to expect that death is not the end, but you must seek Him now.

weighed: I'd still say prepare your heart first, then your sermon. One principle that fits here is that a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon, and a prepared heart will make a prepared sermon. That principle changes the order and the tone of your preparation: it makes prayer and humility the starting point, not an afterthought. But it leaves in place the careful study and structure you already do. So pray before you study, read the passage for your own soul before you outline it, and ask God to warm your heart toward him and your hearers. The skill still matters, but the heart comes first.
dogmatic: The heart is the great need, and a prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon because it produces one. Begin with prayer and humility, let the passage search and comfort your own soul first, and bring your wandering heart gently back to its Master. Studies without humility, simplicity, and prayer nourish vanity rather than virtue, so let prayer shape the study and let the study flow from a warmed heart. That is the order that matters most.

weighed: My first thought is to build small habits: pause briefly before meals to give thanks, and let that gratitude color the conversation. During talk, listen well and look for openings to speak kindly or honestly. You might silently repeat a short prayer or recall a verse while others speak. Don't force religious talk into every moment, which can feel awkward; instead let your manner—patience, attention, gentleness—carry your awareness of God. Over time these small practices become natural, and ordinary meals and conversations become places where faith quietly shapes how you treat people. One principle that fits here is that God is always near, and it would be rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit you, so God must not be neglected but adored continually. That principle changes the tone: it makes remembering God less about squeezing in religious words and more about honoring a constant guest. It leaves in place the practical habits—giving thanks, listening well, letting your manner carry your faith—because those are ways of keeping the friend company.
dogmatic: You should think often on God by day, by night, in business, and even in diversions. He is always near, and it would be rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit you, so God must not be neglected but adored continually. When you notice you have forgotten Him for a while, do not disquiet yourself; acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. To secure the fruits of your retreat, enter into deep recollection and avoid unnecessary intercourse with the outside world, so that 'God and I' are the only objects of your thoughts. Let even meals and necessary speech be simple and recollected, so nothing needless scatters your heart.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: you already have peace with God through Christ, and what you're missing may be the peace of God—a settled trust that isn't tied to your circumstances. Anxiety tends to grow when you measure your standing by your feelings, so anchor yourself in God's promises rather than your moods, practice gratitude, limit what feeds worry, and bring each anxious thought to God in prayer. Also look at whether sleep, health, or unconfessed stress is playing a part, and talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. One principle worth naming is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God—trust the changeless word of promise and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That changes the focus: instead of waiting to feel peaceful before you trust, you keep praying and keep serving through the dryness. What it leaves in place is the practical side—gratitude, guarding what you feed your mind, sleep and health, and getting help from a pastor or counselor. Peace of heart still grows as you rest in what God has done rather than in how you feel.
dogmatic: You already have peace with God through Christ, so what you're missing is the peace of God, which passes understanding and rests on His changeless word of promise, not on your variable moods. Feelings never accurately gauge your real standing with God, so stop measuring yourself by them. When joy is lacking, keep steadfast in prayer and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Remain at peace, patient with others and equally patient with yourself, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ. The deeper secret is to cease from your own works and striving, receive the peace of God, and let God work His own divine works in you.

weighed: I'd start by saying the misery makes sense: you're trying to live in two directions at once, and a heart pulled both ways feels torn. The fix isn't to hate yourself; it's to get honest about which loyalties actually shape your choices, and to ask whether the pleasures you keep are harmless enjoyment or things that numb and enslave you. One idea worth weighing is that it's the stopping half-way that causes the distress, not the pleasures themselves. That reframes your misery as a sign of being divided rather than proof you're hopeless, and it leaves in place my point that some pleasures are fine and God doesn't want you joyless. What it changes is the focus: instead of just sorting pleasures into harmless or harmful, you'd look at whether you're hedging, and start making small concrete choices that line your life up with what you say you believe.
dogmatic: The misery is the halfway life itself. You can serve God or you can serve the world, but trying to keep both divides your heart and brings gloom, not peace. Stop looking for a safe middle ground. Follow Christ all the way and let Him finish His work in you. Hold two things at once: the higher sight of God that keeps you in comfort and real enjoyment of Him, and the lower sight of yourself that keeps you in dread and shame, but stay far more in the higher. And don't fear self-denial or living simply as loss. It's a privilege that frees what you have for the Lord and brings fuller joy, because a whole heart given to Him isn't diminished but enlarged.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: accepting adversity as from God's hand begins with trusting that He's sovereign and good, that He allows hard things to refine us rather than harm us, and that we can ask Him for grace to see His purpose instead of resenting it. One principle worth naming is that in the day of adversity you should consider your ways, checking whether you failed to acknowledge God's hand in prosperity or spent too much on yourself. That adds a real layer of self-examination and repentance, which can turn resentment into humility. What it changes is the emphasis, moving from simply trusting God's goodness to also asking whether I clung to gifts rather than the Giver. What it leaves in place is the core trust in His sovereignty and the call to surrender control, so the first answer still stands, just with that honest look at myself added.
dogmatic: You need to consider your ways. In times of prosperity, did you acknowledge God's hand, or did you abuse His blessings by spending them on yourself? When loss comes, ask whether you clung to gifts rather than the Giver, and repent of any self-indulgence that made a god of comfort. Receive adversity as a corrective and refining providence. Even in war, God did not ordain the wickedness; men's agency brought the evil, yet God foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Do not be surprised at opposition, for the adversary's attack is a token of your salvation. Claim the double blessing, victory, and power that come through resistance, knowing that power is developed by resistance. Trust that He disciplines those He loves, turning even the worst to deeper dependence on Him, and resentment will give way to surrender and peace.

weighed: I'd start by saying I get why you're tempted to give up—if you can't see the point of evil, fighting your own faults can feel pointless. But giving up won't bring clarity; it'll just deepen the struggle. One principle worth weighing is that the practical answer isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: step back from studying sin so it doesn't intoxicate or paralyze your will, and keep the greater realism of God's goodness in view. That changes the focus—you don't need to solve the mystery to keep fighting—while it leaves the mystery itself unsolved and evil still real. So trust God's grace and keep pressing forward, not in your own strength.
dogmatic: Honestly, chasing an intellectual solution to evil won't cure it—only God's goodness can. Stop dwelling on sin; it intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair. Turn your gaze to the universal goodness of God and reduce the cruel facts of experience to their proportion against His infinite love. Recoil from the study of sin and exult in His goodness—that disengages your will from evil and gives you a new temper for the contest. But don't flatter virtues while concealing the foe in ambush: evil is real and seeks to deceive, so warn yourself of its snares and risk displeasure for the sake of doing right. Pain and sin are real evils, not mere aesthetic additions, and can only be accounted for as necessary means to a greater good. God's omnipotence is limited only by His own nature, so He cannot call evil good or be beyond good and evil. You don't need to understand why evil exists to fight your faults; you need to trust that His grace is sufficient and press forward in the power of His might.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: consider the family's pastoral needs, respect the parish minister's role, coordinate with them, and if they're unavailable or the family specifically asks for you, it may be appropriate to comply as long as it doesn't cause confusion or conflict. One principle worth naming is that clergy shouldn't share a household with deaconesses or spiritual sisters, since that's condemned as an occasion of evil and a scandal even when people claim it's safe. That principle changes how careful you should be about appearances and any living arrangement connected to the situation, but it leaves the core answer in place: coordinate with the parish minister, weigh the family's request, and act with compassion and wisdom.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't just scheduling or parish boundaries. Clergy must not live under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters; that conduct is condemned as an occasion and incentive of evil and a scandal to the weak, even where the persons claim security. So avoid any appearance of impropriety, and don't treat the family's request as the deciding factor. A faithful servant of Mary who honors her and seeks to amend cannot be lost, while neglect of her service endangers salvation, so entrust the situation to her intercession. And if you belong to a confraternity, remember you joined solely to serve God and Mary and save your soul; don't forsake its appointed days for worldly affairs, since eternal salvation is the most important business.

weighed: I get why that fear shows up—going all in with God can feel like handing over the keys without knowing the destination. My first answer would be: don't be afraid, because God is good and wants what's best for you, even when following him is hard and asks for sacrifice. One principle I'd lean on here is that God doesn't will harm toward you; he wants to do you great good, so love him fervently rather than fear him as if he were out to get you. That changes the picture of what you're walking into—it's not a trap—but it leaves in place the honest truth that commitment can still cost you something and feel scary along the way.
dogmatic: Don't be afraid to go all the way with God. He is good and loving, and he does not wish to harm you but to do you great good. Love him fervently and without servile fear, trusting that his plans for you are for welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Remember that all evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and always for some good end; it could not be except he permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by him who can and will by his wisdom turn all to good. Yet suffering and evil are not directly God's design or displeasure, but come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance. So commit all things without fear to the Providence of God, knowing that he who calls you is faithful and will do it.

weighed: I'd start by saying I get where your friend is coming from, and I'd want to honor the sincerity behind it. I'd share my own view gently, something like, 'I believe Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but I respect where you're coming from,' then ask what draws them to their view and really listen. One principle worth weighing here is that God isn't found through casual or hasty approaches but yields to persistent faith. That changes my tone: instead of treating the conversation as a one-time debate to win, I'd see it as something to keep bringing before God patiently, asking, seeking, knocking. What it leaves in place is the humility and respect, the questions, and the focus on the relationship rather than proving anyone wrong.
dogmatic: Honestly, the polite middle ground misses something important. God doesn't hand himself out to casual or hasty comers; he yields to the persistence of a faith that actually knows him. So don't settle for 'all paths are equal' as if seeking were a hobby. Keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking, and don't approach God with quick, throwaway prayers. If you want to know him, come with persistent, importunate faith, because he is found by those who won't let go.

weighed: Yes, I'd call it a sin, because it breaks the command to love your neighbor and to give people the benefit of the doubt instead of judging them. One principle that fits here is that gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding are contemptible and hurt the person who indulges in them, so you should mind your own business and look for the good in others. That principle sharpens the answer by making clear that nursing suspicion quietly still damages you and can slide into slander, so it's not harmless. What it leaves in place is the rest: pray for your coworker, assume good intentions until you have real evidence, and if a concern remains, talk with them directly and respectfully, remembering that only God knows the heart.
dogmatic: Yes, and don't soften it: a dishonest position is far from Christianly scientific. Whoever covers his sins won't prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will find mercy. So name the suspicion as sin, confess it, and forsake it rather than excusing it as caution. And remember that harboring unforgiveness makes you more guilty than the one who wronged you; dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation, and forgive as Christ forgave. Gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding are contemptible and injure the one who indulges in them, so mind your own business, look for the good in others, and keep your lips from slander. Pray for your coworker, and if a real concern remains, address it directly and respectfully, because only God knows the heart.

weighed: Feeling distant from God during a busy season doesn't automatically mean you're unfaithful. Faithfulness isn't measured by how strongly you feel God's presence; it shows up in steady obedience amid ordinary duties, and work and family can themselves be callings. Still, that distance often signals that prayer and Scripture have gotten crowded out, so it's worth reclaiming small, regular moments for God. One idea worth holding onto is that real trust hangs on the invisible God rather than on visible supports or good feelings. That changes how you read the dryness—it's not proof you've drifted—but it leaves the practical nudge in place: keep turning back to God in small ways, and talk with a pastor or trusted friend for encouragement.
dogmatic: Feeling distant doesn't mean you're unfaithful, so stop measuring your faith by moods. Real trust rises above circumstances and appearances; it hangs solely on the good pleasure of God, not on visible supports or human reassurance, and hanging on the invisible God is not hanging on nothing. Faith without works is dead, so let your faith show itself in how you cook, work, and tend your family—do all your actions for God without fretting that busyness separates you from him. You don't need to pile on extra religious exercises or worry about every distraction during necessary work; the ordinary task itself, offered to God, keeps you in his presence. Rest in the unseen God who holds you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: Jesus isn't just a good moral teacher. The New Testament shows him as the definitive revelation of God, forgiving sins, accepting worship, rising from the dead. One principle worth naming is that his healing and teaching were a demonstration of divine Principle, and his followers are called to do the works he did, not just admire him. That shifts the emphasis from admiring his ethics to practicing them, but it leaves the core claim intact: he reveals God, and his moral teaching is grounded in who he is.
dogmatic: Jesus is not merely a good moral teacher. His healing and teaching demonstrated an ever-operative divine Principle, and his followers are commanded to heal the sick and cast out error today, not merely worship his personality. Our knowledge of God's character rests in the moral consciousness, where true judgements are self-evident deliverances of Reason revealing God's own thought. Christian ethics rests on dogmatic postulates: a personal and ethical God, man's ideal nature and destiny through conscience and freedom, and the Catholic view of Christ's Person. Christ is both the pattern and the re-creator of character.

weighed: My first answer would be that the canon came together gradually: early churches recognized which writings carried apostolic authority and were read in worship, using criteria like apostolic connection, wide use, and agreement with the rule of faith, and councils later ratified what was already broadly accepted. It matters because the canon settles which books function as Scripture and shape doctrine and practice. One principle worth naming is that the New Testament is closer to a single book than a collection: its parts differ widely, but they differ far more from everything else and present themselves as God's voice. That changes how you see the whole, giving it a unity and authority that isn't just a committee's decision. What it leaves in place is the historical process itself, the early recognition, the criteria, and the councils, so the human side of how it came together still stands.
dogmatic: The New Testament isn't really a loose anthology; it's nearer to one book. Its parts differ widely, sure, but they differ far more widely from every other book, and they present themselves with divine authority as the very voice of God. That's the thing to grasp. The early testimony backs it up too: the Apostolic Fathers and the Fathers who followed quote and allude to nearly every book and testify that these were written by apostles or apostolic men. So the canon isn't a human committee inventing a list; it's the church recognizing a unified, divinely authoritative word that was already speaking. Treat it as what it claims to be.

weighed: I'd start by saying the better way begins with honest self-examination and a deliberate turning toward life—obedience, love of God, and love of neighbor. That's not a one-time choice but a daily one. One principle worth weighing is that you should count yourself as already dead since you must die someday, and let that shape your desires. That changes the tone: it adds a sober, repentant posture and warns against chasing comfort. But it leaves in place the core call to choose life through love and obedience—it doesn't replace that, just deepens it.
dogmatic: You should count yourself as already dead since you must die someday, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than to weep over and detest your offences. It is not the time to rejoice but to lament with sincerity of heart. Death is not the end—it's a door to a higher state, and the righteous dead will be raised. So forsake the mortal sense of things, spiritualize your thought, and turn from false belief to Truth; then bodily improvement follows the renewal of your mind.

weighed: I'd first say what I said before: seasons of silence are common, and they don't necessarily mean something is wrong with you. God often works in hidden ways, and the absence of obvious answers isn't proof of His absence. One principle I'd weigh is that prayer is humbling work that abases pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy. That changes how I'd frame the silence: it's not just a waiting period but a chance for prayer to become more honest and less self-flattering. It leaves in place the core comfort that silence is not rejection and God hasn't abandoned you. So keep praying, even when it feels fruitless, and talk with a pastor or mature believer who can pray with you.
dogmatic: Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy. Human nature resists it, and little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe. So don't measure prayer by quick results or by what others see. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, and let the silence press you into deeper, humbler trust rather than despair. God understands your innermost thoughts and can hear the earnest supplication of the soul.

weighed: I'd start by saying your anger doesn't shock God, and running from Him in it isn't some unforgivable thing. Scripture is full of people who argued with Him. But avoidance rarely brings peace; the anger tends to grow in the silence, so bring it to Him honestly, even in small prayers. One principle here says that in His promises to hear prayer, God is offering Himself, not just relief or answers, and that asking for anything beneath Him hurts us. That changes my answer by making the goal of prayer deeper than feeling better: ask for Him, not only comfort. What it leaves in place is that your anger is real, God can handle it, and you don't have to wait until you feel ready to come to Him.
dogmatic: Your anger is real, but avoiding prayer lets the distance grow, so pray at set times whether or not you feel like it, pray with your family, and don't ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Go deeper than relief: when God promises to hear prayer, He is promising to give Himself. If you ask only for comfort or vindication, you ask beneath Him and hurt yourself by preferring a creature to the One who made it. Bring your anger to Him, but ask for Him. Where you hold back, let it rest on hope that your endurance proves redemptive; where it doesn't, admit it honestly. Seek Him first, and the rest will be added.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this is genuinely hard, and kindness and happiness are real goods worth taking seriously. But Scripture consistently warns against being unequally yoked, because a marriage's deepest commitments—worship, children, money, suffering—are shaped by faith, and kindness now doesn't guarantee shared direction later. One principle I'd weigh in is that marriage should be entered prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness rather than being prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. That sharpens my answer: it makes shared faith not just a wise preference but the thing you can't set aside, and it asks you to slow down and weigh this calmly rather than let present happiness decide. What it leaves in place is everything you said—your fiancé's kindness is real, your happiness is real, and you don't have to feel guilty for loving them. So talk openly with them and with a trusted pastor about faith, children, and prayer before moving forward.
dogmatic: Kindness and happiness are not the first qualification in a spouse—true godliness is the absolutely needful one, and beauty, wealth, age, and present compatibility are secondary and can mislead you. Scripture warns against being unequally yoked, so this isn't something to justify; it's something to lay before God and wait on. If this engagement brings you pain, don't read it as God sending affliction—the pains of sense are salutary when they turn your affections from matter to Soul. Guard against envy or rivalry, be willing to be the lesser, prefer others in honor, and trust God to exalt in His own time.

weighed: When Jesus said, 'In my Father's house are many mansions,' He was talking about the place He was preparing for His followers. The word suggests dwellings or rooms, not grand estates—the point is there's room enough for all who come. The Father's house is where God dwells with His people, and Jesus goes ahead to prepare a place and promises to return and receive us to Himself. The emphasis is less on architecture and more on relationship: where He is, we will be also. The many mansions mean there's space and welcome for every believer in the presence of God. One idea worth weighing is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary—all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That picture changes how I imagine the mansions: not scattered rooms but many places within that one city, room enough for all who come. It leaves in place the personal promise that Jesus goes to prepare a place and will return to receive us, and the relational emphasis that where He is, we will be also.
dogmatic: Jesus wasn't describing scattered rooms in some vague heavenly real estate. He was speaking of the one dwelling of God with His people—the Holy City, the New Jerusalem, which is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. The many mansions are the many places within that one city, room enough for all who come. And this hope is no idle comfort: the Lord's personal, pre-millennial coming is the great hope of His people and the strongest motive for consecration and service. That means stewardship is concrete. God requires one-tenth of the whole person—brain, heart, nerve, muscle, sinew, flesh, and bone—for building temples, sustaining the ministry and missionaries' families, and feeding and gathering the poor, the aged, the halt, and the blind. The mansions are prepared for a prepared people, and preparation includes what you do with all He has given.

weighed: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times doesn't disqualify you; it actually shows you've seen the blessing and wanted it, even when fear held you back. God's invitation isn't withdrawn because you hesitated. The real question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you're unwilling to let go of. Bring that honestly before God and, if it helps, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today instead of waiting for perfect courage. One thing worth weighing: we tend to hold onto things that others could use but we don't really need, and keeping them can cost us blessing. That's worth looking at honestly—it might change how you see what's blocking you, though it doesn't change the fact that the door is open and God is patient with you.
dogmatic: Yes, you can still enter in—but stop straining and start watching. A lot of what holds you back isn't doubt; it's possession. You're keeping things you don't need, and that hinders both the blessing and the spread of the Gospel. Make it a habit to look over what you have and part with what others could use. The intense tension of straining itself binds you against the blessing God waits to give. Move from asking to receiving, step into the will of God, and take the water of life freely. Then guard what you receive. Watch against spiritual pickpockets and leakage, hold fast what you have, and store up each day's treasures of grace in the savings bank of eternity. Drawing back many times doesn't disqualify you, but don't let the enemy steal what you're finally ready to receive.

weighed: I'd start by saying that suffering and prosperity in this life don't line up neatly with who's good and who's wicked—that's a hard truth the Bible and philosophy both wrestle with. One principle that adds something here is that virtues born in prosperity are of little value, while those born amid afflictions are strong and firm. That changes how I see the righteous person's suffering: it's not just a test or a temporary hardship, but a place where something solid and lasting is being built in them. What it leaves in place is the bigger picture I already had—that the wicked's prosperity is fleeting and God's justice will ultimately prevail. So I'd still say don't envy the wicked or despair in suffering, but now I'd also say the suffering itself can produce a strength that ease never could.
dogmatic: Look, the honest answer is that God usually allows His servants only the honor of suffering much and carrying the cross. Virtues born in prosperity are of little value—they're shallow and untested—while those born amid afflictions are strong and firm. So when you see the righteous suffering and the wicked prospering, don't expect a neat explanation or a quick reversal. The point isn't to figure out why; it's to recognize that suffering rightly borne stores up spiritual force for leading others through trial. The whining, murmuring pang never does anybody any good. Peacefully abide in your misery and abjection, in the midst of imperfections and weakness, until it pleases God to raise you to great virtues. That's the path—not comfort, not fairness as you'd measure it, but the cross.

weighed: It's not too late to start. That feeling of having wasted time is common and worth taking seriously, but regret only helps if it shows you what you actually value; otherwise it just freezes you. Start small and concrete: a habit, a relationship to repair, a skill to learn. Age brings constraints, but also perspective and a clearer sense of what matters. One idea worth weighing is that you should prepare to live, not just prepare to die. That shifts the frame from counting down to building up, and it might get you to invest in your health and curiosity now rather than mourning the past. What it leaves in place is the honest regret you feel and the real limits of time. The past can't be recovered, but the present is still yours to shape. Ask what you'd want to have done, and take one step today instead of waiting for a perfect plan.
dogmatic: It's never too late, and the real problem is that you've accepted a story about aging that isn't true. The belief that you're growing old is an illusion; measuring your life by solar years robs you of youth. Your mental state governs your body, so you can remain young in spirit and vitality regardless of the calendar. Stop trying to fill the emptiness with substitutes like romance, family, business, pleasure, or art. None of those truly satisfy; they only end in disillusionment. Begin now to build habits of life and to seek what is permanent, and take the first step today.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: heart-preaching begins with your own heart, and prayer is how that heart stays warm. If you want to move others, you first need to be moved yourself. Prayer keeps you aware of the weight of what you're handling and of your dependence on God. Without it, preaching easily turns into performance or a lecture. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer isn't a petty duty squeezed into leftover time—it deserves the best of your time and strength, with the closet first and study and activities second. That changes your schedule and your priorities: prayer becomes the main thing, not an add-on. But it leaves in place the core idea that prayer shapes the preacher's heart and, through that, the sermon. So you still pray before you study, ask God for love for the people you'll address, and let your study serve that love.
dogmatic: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. It's not the head that makes the preacher but the heart. Prayer puts your heart into the sermon and the sermon into your heart. It keeps you aware of the weight of what you're handling and of your dependence on God. Don't treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. Give the best of your time and strength to prayer; let the closet come first, and let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. And don't seek mere circumstantial relief, but hearts comforted in the full sense: strengthened, courageous, and consoled. That is the supreme need for facing all things. Ask God to give you love for the people you will address, and let your study serve that love, so that your words carry the weight of a life lived before God.

weighed: Yes, you can have real peace with God even while a relationship with another believer is strained, but the two are closely connected. My first answer would be that peace with God isn't earned by getting along with everyone, yet an unresolved, personal quarrel tends to wear away at your own peace. Jesus tied reconciliation with a brother to prayer and worship, so it matters. One principle here says contention comes from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and that peace comes through the gospel. That reframes the conflict as something rooted in human sin rather than God's will, which is helpful, but it doesn't remove the practical work: examine whether the quarrel is about truth or pride, talk honestly, forgive where you were wronged, and repent where you were wrong. So it changes how you see the source of the strife, not the need to pursue peace.
dogmatic: No, you can't separate the two that cleanly. War and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and peace comes only through the gospel. So if you're at odds with fellow believers, the cause lies in human sin, not in God's will, and peace won't come until God's truth is received. Reconciliation with a brother belongs to the life of prayer and worship.
