When sufferings and trials come, meet them with a strong will to bear them for God, so their bitterness stays full of peace and tranquillity instead of turning to resentment. And in every occasion of virtue, don't rely on your own strength: turn to God and ask for enabling grace, and you'll receive strength more than sufficient. Examine whether the quarrel is about truth or pride, seek honest conversation, forgive where you've been wronged, and repent where you've wronged others.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: feeling far from God is really common, and empty prayers usually point to exhaustion, distraction, or something you've let crowd God out rather than to God being absent. So I'd say look honestly at your life, confess what needs confessing, and come back to simple, honest prayer, even if it's just a few words of trust. One thing worth adding is that feelings aren't a reliable gauge of where you stand with God. That doesn't change the practical advice, but it does mean you shouldn't read your moods as a verdict on your faith. Keep praying steadily and talk to someone you trust.
dogmatic: The longing you feel is itself evidence that there's a real God who answers, because you wouldn't hunger for what isn't there. Your empty prayers aren't just a mood; they're the cry of someone made for communion with their Maker. But prayer is humbling work that crucifies pride, and human nature resists it. Little praying is make-believe, worse than no praying at all. So don't measure prayer by feelings, because moods never accurately gauge your standing with God. Rest on the changeless word of promise, and keep praying even when joy is lacking.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: loving God is about the heart, while religious duties are outward actions. You can show up, pray on schedule, and give money without actually loving God, and duties only become expressions of love when they come from gratitude and devotion rather than habit or fear. One idea worth naming is that God builds spiritual habits in us, where love starts with a definite act of the will and, through repeated obedience, becomes second nature, so duty turns into delight. That changes the picture a little, because it means the early stages of plain, deliberate obedience aren't the enemy of love; they can be the soil it grows in. What it leaves in place is the core difference: the goal is still a real relationship with God, not just going through motions, so examine why you do what you do and ask God to shape your affections.
dogmatic: The real difference is that love is a relationship with the living God, not a transaction, and that relationship runs through his holiness. God isn't a distant spectator; his holiness is grieved by sin, and his love moves to provide atonement, with the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expressing something eternal in God's nature: holiness requires atonement and love provides it, all under the control of his blessedness. Love itself isn't mere sentiment. It's God's rational, voluntary self-communication seeking the true good of its object, regulated by and subordinate to his holiness. And this love is learned: spiritual habits begin with definite acts of the will and steady obedience, and the Spirit establishes them until obedience becomes spontaneous delight. So don't wait to feel loving before you obey. Begin with deliberate acts of trust and duty, and ask the Spirit to confirm them until love flows freely.

weighed: I would have said first that hoping for a future life isn't base at all—it's a proper part of trusting God. Scripture puts the hope of eternal life in front of us as both motivation and comfort, not as something shameful. The one who trusts God trusts His promises, and those promises include resurrection and life with Him. That said, hope for the future shouldn't become an escape from present obedience; it should strengthen us to live faithfully now. One principle that fits here is that hope gives confidence in the sanctification of our own soul and of others, joining a deep sense of our own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and trusting supernatural means—since all human learning and power can't save a soul. That principle changes how we ground our hope: it shifts the foundation from our own effort or progress to God's power at work in us. But it leaves in place the basic point that hoping for a future life is legitimate and proper, and that it should shape how we live today rather than excuse neglect of the present.
dogmatic: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. But you need to see where that hope must rest. You must join an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power—because all human learning and skill cannot convert or sanctify a single soul. So trust supernatural means: His Word, His Spirit, His grace. Don't settle for a bare minimum of knowledge either; seek to be filled with the mature knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, which is the secret of true living. And when God hides Himself, as He sometimes does, don't panic or grasp at substitutes. Then faith alone must be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in God. The future hope is not base because it rests on Him who hides and reveals, and who keeps His promise even in the dark.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the Spirit is a person, not just an influence. Grieving and resisting only make sense if there's someone there to grieve and resist, and Scripture treats him that way—he teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and gives gifts as he wills. One principle worth naming is that your own spirit naturally loves truth and virtue but gets overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. That changes the picture a bit: it means the Spirit isn't only someone you relate to personally, he's also the one who has to open your eyes before you can even see straight. What it leaves in place is the core answer—he's still a person, and your resistance and grief are still real toward him. So relate to him personally: listen, obey, and repent quickly when you've grieved him.
dogmatic: The Spirit is a person, full stop—not a force, not a mood, not an influence you can shrug off. Grieving him and resisting him are personal acts toward a personal God, and that should settle the question. But don't stop at comfort. Your own spirit may love truth and virtue, yet it is overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it, so you cannot trust your natural impulses to lead you. Direct every act to the glory of God, and beware of doing things for praise, from mere impulse, or in routine without supernatural intention. And know this: the fulness of the Spirit is given along the line of duty and obedience to world evangelization. God will not pour out his power for your private enjoyment; you receive him in fulness only as you step out into Christ's purposes for the world.

weighed: I get why this is hard. My first answer would be to be honest with God about the hurt, pray for the person who wounded you, ask for healing and for a heart that can release the debt, and keep at it daily, maybe with a pastor or counselor if it's deep. One principle worth naming is that God can heal in answer to prayer, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. That adds confidence that healing is possible and worth asking for, while leaving in place the honest lament, the daily choice to forgive, and the wisdom to seek help. It doesn't promise a quick fix or erase the need for boundaries.
dogmatic: Pray for grace with perfect confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, and don't let your sins discourage you from asking. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless you wander from his presence or forget to ask. The best revenge on an enemy is to forgive and bear injuries patiently, and by that you reap grace and the pardon of your sins without trouble or expense. So stop nursing the hurt, ask boldly, and forgive.

weighed: I'd start by saying no denomination has a monopoly on truth, so be skeptical of any church claiming to be the only correct interpreter. But one thing worth weighing: documents that look ancient, sit in proper custody, and show no signs of forgery are usually presumed genuine until someone brings real evidence against them. That principle shifts the burden a bit, so you don't treat a tradition as suspect just because it's old or sacred. It doesn't settle whether your denomination's interpretation is right, though. You still get to ask whether its reading holds up, and you can still test claims rather than accept them on authority alone.
dogmatic: A denomination that claims the correct interpretation is making a claim about custody and continuity, and that claim deserves a fair rule of evidence rather than reflexive suspicion. Ancient documents kept in proper custody, with no marks of forgery, are presumed genuine until sufficient evidence is brought against them, and the burden falls on the objector. So don't treat Scripture as suspect just because its story is sacred; that's prejudice dressed up as rigor. And don't judge orders or interpretation as a mechanical validity detached from the living whole of the Church. There are degrees of approximation to the historic life of the Body, not an abrupt choice between a perfectly true church and none. Measure faithfulness to God's word, not numbers or finances. Trust where those marks are present.

weighed: Yes, God's love can reach you, no matter how lost or scarred you feel. Scripture says nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus, and the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son all show God seeking the lost. So come to Him and ask Him to love you; your scars don't disqualify you, they're exactly where His love meets you. One thing I'd add: the way deeper into that love isn't only begging Him to come down. It's also the steady effort to enter into His estate and offer Him love. That shifts the picture from you waiting alone for rescue to you being drawn into something with Him, though it leaves the promise fully in place that He comes to you first.
dogmatic: Yes, and here's the heart of it: stop only begging God to come down and love you. The real way in is to keep pressing up into His estate and offering Him love. Picture the Father as a father to the lost child, taking him by the hand and leading him to his mother; no one who weeps is beyond the Maker's nearness. And your fear can't outrun Him. Fear doesn't know how to evade as Love knows how to pursue. Love meets you at every crossroad and bypath and gently turns you back. Offer Him love, and you'll find He was already near.

weighed: Yes, I'd say go ahead and ask your minister to bury you and to remember your aged parents after you're gone. Arranging your funeral ahead of time eases the burden on your family, and asking him to keep your parents in prayer is a loving thing to do. One thing worth weighing, though: choose your minister with care, because a ministry without prayer isn't just less effective, it's a funeral for God's truth and his Church, however beautiful it looks. That principle changes how you pick who you ask, and it shapes what you ask for, keeping any prayer for you within what Scripture supports, like your resurrection and being brought to wholeness, without assuming any purification after death. What it leaves in place is the main answer: yes, ask him, talk with him soon, put your wishes in writing, and involve your family.
dogmatic: Ask your minister to bury you and to remember your parents, yes, but the real question is whether he prays at all. A prayerless ministry is an undertaker for God's truth and God's Church; it may have the costliest casket and the loveliest flowers, and it is still a funeral. So test the man before you trust him with your burial. And when he prays for you, keep it to what Scripture allows: your acquittal at the great Day, your perfect consummation and bliss, your resurrection, with no hint of purification after death. As for your parents, remember that parents are the ones charged to teach their children the gospel and watch over them against the wickedness of the world; better to bury children in innocence than to watch them led away from the gospel.

weighed: I get why you're afraid—if you've been taught to picture God's will as a path of thorns, of course it feels frightening. But it helps to separate God's will from your imagination of it. What you fear is often a picture built from anxiety, not from knowledge. God's will isn't mainly about suffering; it's about your good and your growth in trust. One idea worth weighing is that as Christ shapes us, we come to know God's will not as thorns but as a great balm and deep security. That changes the picture you're carrying: the fear isn't the final word, and the dread can soften into trust. What it leaves in place is that the path won't always be easy—hard things still come. So bring your fear honestly to God in prayer and ask for the trust you don't yet have.
dogmatic: You should stop fearing God's will as though He wanted to harm you. That fear comes from your raw, untrained state, not from the truth about God. As Christ moulds you, you'll come to know His will as a great balm and immense security, and you'll long to conform to it and sink into it. So love God fervently instead of cowering before Him—He wishes to do your soul great good. And don't take temptation as proof of ruin: God permits evil inclinations to make us humble, and as long as temptation displeases you, there's nothing to fear. Despise the temptation while embracing the tribulation it brings, and trust Him even when it's hard.

weighed: I'd have said at first: don't overthink it—take the loaf, the stone is useless, and if you're tempted to take the stone, that's a disordered will to correct. One candidate principle here is that two ways are set before you, life or death, and choosing the better over the worse is like taking the loaf rather than the stone when both are before you. That principle changes the tone: it frames your choice as a real fork between life and death rather than just a simple obvious answer. But it leaves in place the core claim that you are free and should choose the better—so the practical advice stays the same: take the loaf.
dogmatic: You are like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before you, and the choice is real: two ways are set before you, life or death, and you must choose the better over the worse. Do not pretend the choice is hard or that you are forced into it—you are free, and you should simply choose the good. Take the loaf, and stop making excuses for the stone. If you are tempted to take the stone, that is a sign of a disordered will that needs correction. Examine yourself to the bottom, see that you deserve contempt and humiliation, and do not wonder when troubles and contradictions come—submit to them and bear them as advantageous as long as God pleases. Remember why you have a body at all: that through Christ's redemption both soul and body may be exalted and that you may propagate a pure offspring. Purity of body is therefore of the greatest importance. Choose the loaf, and keep your body in purity.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: be gentle with yourself. Feeling like a failure usually comes from comparing your life to everyone else's, and God doesn't measure you that way. He sees your heart, your effort, and your honesty. Scripture is full of people who felt inadequate, Moses, David, Peter, and God still used them. Your worth isn't in achievements; it's in being loved by him. Bring this to God in prayer, and it may help to talk with a trusted friend or pastor. One principle I'd weigh in is that God won't let us settle for less than his highest will, so the standard stays rigid and never gets bent to fit our failures. That changes something real: it means I shouldn't hand you comfort that quietly excuses the gap between your life and God's call. But it leaves your question intact, because God holding the standard high doesn't mean he counts you a failure. He's near to the brokenhearted, and struggling doesn't disappoint him.
dogmatic: Don't settle for comfort that excuses the gap between your life and God's call. God's standard is not lowered to our failures. Yet God himself is the one living Agent who works in you; your effort is only his instrument. Cast all your care on him, because anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who enables what his standard requires. And when God hides himself, when you feel no assurance and see no progress, don't conclude he counts you a failure. Faith alone must then be your support and the foundation of all your confidence in him. Moses, David, and Peter failed, yet God did not lower the mark. Press on, resting not on feelings or visible results but on the God who remains faithful even when hidden.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: this is a serious decision, so pray about it and seek counsel from mature believers. But I want to name one principle that changes how I'd say that: prayer isn't effective through bare words or the soul's own strength. When your will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the merits of Christ. Then you can go to the Father as the prodigal son went, confessing not with bare words but with all your strength—a strong purpose and resolution. That changes the advice from 'say the right words and mean them' to 'let your will be genuinely resolved before God.' What it leaves in place is the need to pray, seek counsel, and ask Him to show you clearly whether this is His will. It doesn't add conditions or exceptions; it just deepens what sincere prayer looks like.
dogmatic: You ask how to know whether giving up a cherished possession is God's will. Stop treating prayer as bare words or the soul's own strength. When the will is prepared and resolved, it has broken through its own creatures and is sincere before God, clothed with the merits of Christ. Then the Father meets it as the prodigal son and it may pour out confession and pray powerfully. So do not attach conditions or exceptions to God's will. Yield completely to Him, accepting to be struck where and as He pleases, even in the most repugnant events. That unreserved resignation is how you will know His will and follow it. And if you are engaged in God's work, keep up prayer, reading, meditation, and self-examination for your own soul; without regular retirement you cannot kindle charity in others.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: Revelation 21 shows the bride, the Lamb's wife, as the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. So the bride and the city aren't two separate things—they're one picture of God's people in perfect fellowship with Him. One principle worth naming is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That principle changes how tightly you tie the images together—it makes them one reality rather than complementary pictures. But it leaves in place the core point: God's redeemed people dwelling forever with Him, with the city prepared for them.
dogmatic: The New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary—one city coming down from God out of heaven. The saints are not that city; the city is prepared for them, the dead in Christ have not yet been caught up, and the saints are being built together as a temple to enter the city prepared for them. The Lamb's wife presents the unity of male and female as two individual natures in one, reflecting God as Father-Mother, not as a corporeal being. Understand God spiritually, not as a physical being. The city, the bride, and the sanctuary are one, and those being prepared for her share one spiritual life in Him.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture holds together that God is good and that evil is real. A lot of pain comes from human choices, and a lot comes from a broken world. God isn't the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows He doesn't stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we can't explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new. One idea worth weighing is that God is a loving Father who gives only good and doesn't afflict His children with sickness. That sharpens things: it means sickness and affliction aren't His will, so we can pray and care for the sick with real confidence instead of wondering if God sent it. What it leaves in place is the harder mystery of why He permits a broken world at all, and why suffering still reaches us. So it clarifies God's heart without dissolving the whole puzzle.
dogmatic: God is good and all-powerful, and He is the goodness of everything good and the doer of everything done. Sin isn't a substance or a deed; it's a privation of good, a turning away from the good that God is. Don't treat suffering as an insoluble puzzle: God uses suffering as a remedy for sin, and His righteousness belongs inside the problem, not outside it. The cross shows Christ's agony was submitted to in perfect love, proving agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. But never portray God as the author of sickness, sorrow, or affliction, visiting disease on His children. He is a loving Father who gives only good; sickness is not His will. Many have wrongly believed otherwise and later confessed it. Trust His Fatherhood, and let the cross, not disease, show you His heart.

weighed: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place to be, and I want to start there: power in ministry isn't mainly about technique or eloquence. It flows from a life close to God. So I'd ask first whether prayer has quietly slipped behind sermon prep, whether there's unconfessed sin or unresolved conflict or plain weariness you haven't brought to God, and I'd point you toward mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. One principle worth naming is that a preacher can't keep his spirit in harmony with his calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, when prayer gets neglected, can engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That sharpens my first answer: it makes prayer the central thing to recover, not just one item on a list. What it leaves in place is everything else I said. Confession, honest mentors, faithfulness in small things, and God's quiet work before His visible work all still matter. It doesn't replace them; it reorders them, so prayer comes first and the rest flows from it.
dogmatic: Stop treating this as a mystery to be managed. The reason a preacher loses power is almost always prayerlessness, and sermon-making itself, when it crowds out prayer, engrosses and hardens and estranges the heart from God. You cannot keep your spirit in harmony with your high calling without much prayer. So when the occasion to do good comes and you feel your own inability, go to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. And hear this too: preachers are God's leaders and are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church. A church rarely rises above the religion of its leaders, and spiritual leaders are tokens of God's favor to His people. Your lack of power is not your private problem. It touches the flock. Bring your lack to Him, ask for enabling grace, and take up your responsibility for the Church with humility and prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying that it can feel deeply unfair to be blamed for things beyond your control, and Scripture doesn't teach that God punishes you for circumstances you couldn't help. It distinguishes between what you choose and what merely happens to you. Much suffering comes from human choices—yours and others'—and from a broken world, not from God's direct displeasure at you. One principle worth weighing is that misfortune, illness, and strife aren't charged to God's will; they result from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, though God permits them and overrules them for good. That principle sharpens the answer by making clear that God isn't the author of the harm you couldn't control, but it leaves in place the mystery that God still permits such things and can work them toward good. So the real question isn't whether God is unfair, but whether you turn toward Him in the midst of what you can't control, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by your circumstances.
dogmatic: No, it is not unjust for God to punish you for circumstances you could not control, because God's justice is never measured by your sense of fairness. Misfortune, illness, and strife are not to be charged to God's will; they come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, and God permits them and overrules them for good. Yet seeming mischances are necessary links in a divinely ordered providence—God does not permit hindrance to arise without sufficient reason. So stop demanding that your circumstances be adjusted to you. Instead, be adjusted in every good work: to your surroundings, to the people you're thrown with, and to God's plan. In that adjustment you find rest and freedom, trusting His mercy rather than measuring His justice by what you could not control.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling ashamed after failing in your duty is natural, and it can actually help you if it pushes you toward honesty instead of despair. Name the failure plainly, without making excuses. Then remember that mercy is bigger than your failure, and that condemnation isn't the voice you should be listening to. Receive forgiveness, make amends where you can, and figure out what led to the lapse so you can guard against it next time. Don't isolate yourself; talk to someone you trust and let them pray with you. Then get up and get back to your duty. The goal isn't to punish yourself, it's to return to faithful service with humility and hope. One principle worth holding onto here is that when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, you should humble yourself, ask forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That changes the tone of the moment: instead of getting stuck in self-scrutiny, you turn it into a fresh start. What it leaves in place is the honesty and the amends and the learning from what went wrong, because starting fresh doesn't mean skipping over the failure.
dogmatic: When you fail, don't sit there paralyzed, wondering whether you've offended God. Humble yourself right away, admit the fault honestly, and ask for forgiveness. Then renew your promises of fidelity and love and begin again in the pursuit of perfection. Obey God, hold to the one Mind, and love another as yourself. Don't buy into the idea that evil suggestions pass from one person to another, as if someone else's sin could be transferred to you or yours to them; error isn't overcome by error but by truth. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, but stay untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Shame isn't the end of the matter; it's a summons to return. Confess, receive forgiveness, and take up your duty once more with a humble and hopeful heart.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: pray for wisdom, since God promises to give it generously, then search the Scriptures, because God won't lead you against His Word. Talk to mature believers who know you and can spot your blind spots. Check your motives, whether you're moved by love for God and neighbor or by fear, pride, or comfort. Look at your gifts, your circumstances, and the needs around you. God often guides through open and closed doors, through peace, and through wise advice. Then make the best call you can, trusting He's with you and will redirect you if you stray. One principle worth adding is that knowing and doing God's will is the secret of true living, being filled with the knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. That shifts the emphasis from treating this as a decision technique to a whole posture of life, and it adds a healthy slowness before new steps. What it leaves in place is everything practical: prayer, Scripture, counsel, honest motives, and making a real decision rather than freezing.
dogmatic: Stop treating God's will as a technique for making decisions. The knowledge of God's will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding is the secret of true living, and you need to be filled with it, not just consult it when a choice comes up. Be slow to take new steps. Be willing to have no will of your own. Settle God's will through prayer and the Word, and test any step against both before you move, or you'll rush ahead in self-will and mistake presumption for faith. Don't swap your preferred way of serving God for actually finding and doing His will. Find it, carry it out joyfully or at least courageously, then wait in earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Serve Him well only when you serve Him as He wills.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is painful but not unusual, so check whether you've been running on routine, neglecting prayer, or carrying something unconfessed. Then return to private devotion—unhurried time in Scripture and prayer—and ask God to restore your joy. Preach to yourself first, and ask trusted friends to pray and be honest with you. Feelings aren't the measure of faithfulness; God is present even when you can't feel Him. One principle I'd add is holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate: keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back gently without fretting. That changes the tone of your prayer time—less striving, more quiet waiting—but it leaves in place the practical steps: confession, devotion, honest friends, and faithful preaching. It doesn't replace them; it deepens how you do them.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating prayer as a technique and start holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—dumb, paralytic, waiting. Keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself; trouble and disquiet only distract. Bring it back in tranquility. It's impossible to keep your spirit in harmony with your calling without much prayer. Sermon-making itself, if you neglect prayer, will engross and harden and estrange your heart from God. Preaching has power only in the Holy Spirit sent down from heaven, and the preaching of Christ crucified alone can command your witness. So drop the routine and the eloquence and the popular themes. Let the cross be your theme, and trust that He will renew your sense of His nearness in His time.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling abandoned by God in trial is heavy and common, and it doesn't mean you've done something wrong. Name the feeling honestly in prayer, recall times God has been faithful, lean on the psalms of lament, and let trusted friends or a pastor sit with you. Keep small rhythms of prayer and worship even when they feel dry. Remember that feelings of absence aren't the same as actual absence. One principle that fits here is that when you haven't thought of God for a while, you shouldn't disquiet yourself but should acknowledge your wretchedness and return to him with greater trust. That changes the tone: instead of just enduring the dryness, you turn back gently and trust more. It leaves in place the honest lament and the practical steps of support and Scripture.
dogmatic: The deeper issue is usually that we've forgotten God's nearness, not that he's left. Don't let that forgetfulness throw you into panic; let it turn you back to him with greater trust. Abandon yourself to God without exception. Ask him to tear from your heart everything that burdens it and to wrest you from yourself, so that no reserve or condition remains. Reject the thought that all things are against you; that's the enemy's suggestion. See your trial as God's wise choosing, meant to make his Word and presence more precious to you. Name the feeling honestly, recall his past faithfulness, and keep small rhythms of prayer and Scripture even when they feel dry. The feeling of absence is not the fact of absence; return gently and trust him fully.

weighed: I'd start by saying that a pull toward seclusion can be real, but it isn't automatically the highest path. The highest path is where God calls you and where love can grow. Solitude can free you for prayer and attention to God, but it can also become an escape from responsibility and the needs of others. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel, and ask whether it springs from love or from disappointment or pride. One principle worth weighing is that ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement; its end is penance, labor, and steady contemplation. That principle sharpens the warning: without real fervor and constancy, close solitude can become dangerous. But it doesn't change the core answer—holiness is still measured by love, and whether you stay in ordinary life or enter a religious community, the goal is to love God and neighbor faithfully.
dogmatic: The highest path is not the one that feels easiest or most consoling. If you are drawn to seclusion, do not treat it as a retreat into comfort. Christian retirement exists for penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation, and without great fervor and constancy in these, close solitude is the road to perdition. Seeking is not enough; striving is what opens the door. You must overcome the world, the flesh, and evil, and destroy all error. Walk contrary to the World: where the way is hardest, go; what the World casts away, take up; what the World does, do not; walk only in the Way of Light, not in the World's Way of Darkness. Test the desire with wise counsel, but do not suppose that merely wishing or professing the devout life is enough. Take up the discipline that solitude requires, and let love of God and neighbor be the measure of your faithfulness.

weighed: When leaders are gone and hope feels thin, I'd first say help comes from several places: faithful laypeople quietly serving, neighboring congregations or denominational bodies, trusted mentors, and above all Christ as head of the church, who hasn't abandoned His people. One principle worth naming is that charity shouldn't create dependence—relieve present needs, then help people help themselves. That changes how mutual aid gets organized: it becomes about equipping rather than enabling. What it leaves in place is everything else—prayer, Scripture, seeking outside guidance, patience, and trust in Christ's faithfulness. So the core answer stands, just with a sharper edge on how you actually help.
dogmatic: Help comes first from Christ, the head of the church, and then through a people stirred to self-sustaining labor. Charity that merely creates dependence doesn't truly help—it fosters idleness and pauperism. Encourage men and women to labor in exchange for aid: relieve present wants, then put the poor in a way to help themselves. Church revenues and even sacred vessels belong to the poor in their need; when someone complains this impoverishes the church, answer with confidence that God will provide. And don't let prayer become a substitute for evangelism—join prayer to aggressive labor for souls, make the cross of Christ the pivot of all teaching, and let prayer be the source of power for winning converts. Gather faithful laypeople, seek guidance from neighboring congregations, and organize mutual aid that equips rather than enables.

weighed: I'd start by saying the God of the Old and New Testaments is the same God, revealed in different stages—Old Testament justice and covenant faithfulness, New Testament grace and mercy in Christ, complementary rather than contradictory. One principle that helps is that the Old Testament is on a lower level than the New: God condescends to a low stage of conscience and worship, tolerating what wasn't His original will, with the Old Covenant gradual and the New final. That changes how I read the harsh parts—they're a stage of accommodation, not the final picture. It leaves in place the unity of God's character and the call to read the whole Bible as one story of redemption, so the tensions deepen awe rather than shake faith.
dogmatic: The God of the Old and New Testaments is one God, but He reveals Himself at different levels. The Old Testament is a lower, gradual stage given under divine condescension to a people at an early point in their development; law, sacrifice, and prophecy are preparatory. The New Covenant in Christ is final and complete. Read the Old Testament as progressive preparation that anticipates Christ. When Christ uses the Old Testament, He appeals to its abiding spiritual testimony to Himself, not to questions of authorship or date, and nothing in that appeal implies any fallibility in Him. The New Testament writings differ widely in style and occasion, yet they are not a mere anthology of human religious writings: they share an essential unity and carry divine authority as the voice of God to us. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, letting the earlier stage point beyond itself to the final revelation in Jesus.

weighed: I get why you'd be afraid—being mocked stings, and wanting to avoid it isn't a moral failure. If I'm honest, my first instinct would probably be to tell you not to let fear silence you and to pray for boldness. One idea worth weighing here is that faith is hindered by leaning on our own understanding; we're told to trust God with all our heart instead. That changes the tone: instead of pushing you to just get braver, it suggests the real work is trusting God more than your own calculations about how people will react. What it leaves in place is the honest fear you're feeling—it doesn't dismiss it—and it doesn't mean you have to speak up in every setting or with everyone. You can start small, with people you trust, and let courage grow from there.
dogmatic: The fear of mockery is real, but it's the wrong thing to be afraid of. What matters far more is that God never forsakes us unless we first forsake Him—so the thing to fear is leaving Him, not the laughter of people around you. Don't lean on your own understanding of how this will go; lean on God with all your heart. Stay in His presence, live and die there, and let His faithfulness carry you instead of your own boldness. Mockery can't touch what's actually at stake.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear of hell makes sense, and it can be a starting point rather than the whole story. Scripture takes judgment seriously, and Jesus warned about it, but mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So don't despise your fear; let it push you to seek Christ honestly, talk with a pastor, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. One principle worth weighing says fear of hell actually shows a religion has stopped being morally indifferent and has become serious about ethics. That changes how you see your fear: it can be a sign of moral seriousness, not just something to get over. What it leaves in place is the rest of the picture, that fear is a doorway and love is the home where faith settles.
dogmatic: Fear of hell isn't a backward or shameful motive; it's a worthy one, and it proves the moral character of faith. It shows that choices matter and that God takes evil seriously, and the early Christians kept judgment and the final condition after it as clear, firmly held goals of their meditation. So don't treat your fear as something to apologize for. Let it shape a serious, moral faith rooted in Christ, fasten your eyes on Him as the antidote to fear and the sum of all deliverance, and abide in Him, trusting God for goodness and mercy all your days.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this is a heavy season, and it's right to feel its weight. Be present with your sister, listen, help with practical needs; share caregiving with your parents and give them room to grieve; guard your own rest and let friends and your church carry some of this with you. One principle worth naming is that elders should be patient as the Lord is patient, pleading gently and dealing out kindness rather than curses. That changes the tone of how you speak with your family—patient, kind, no pressure—but it leaves the practical core in place: presence, shared care, rest, and prayer. Grief isn't despair; it can sit alongside hope. Take it one small faithful act at a time rather than carrying the whole future at once.
dogmatic: The first thing isn't practical arrangements—it's the Saviour. Seek Him first, then go and win your erring brother; true love gives no fading memorial but wreaths of hope and thoughts of good done together. Bring your sister and your parents to Christ in prayer and gently commend Him to them while there is time; speak of resurrection and the life to come. Be patient as the Lord is patient, pleading with those you love rather than condemning them, kindness rather than cursings. And remember why you belong to the confraternity: you entered solely to serve God and Mary and save your soul. Don't forsake its appointed days for worldly business, even now—eternal salvation is the most important business. Practical care and rest matter, but they come after seeking Him first.

weighed: I'd start by saying the church should honestly reexamine its teaching, listen to the concerns of good people, and be willing to change if it has erred, while not treating popular opinion as the final judge of truth. One principle here says the church's real work is appeal, not force, with force at most a preparatory clearing of the ground. That changes the tone: it rules out coercion and makes persuasion the goal. It leaves in place the duty to take the wider community's rejection seriously and to hold convictions with humility rather than pride.
dogmatic: A church that teaches what the wider community rejects should remember that its instrument is appeal, never force as an end in itself. If discipline is needed, force is only a preparatory measure that clears the ground for appeal. The church should be indifferent to personal success and national expansion, caring only that the individual be pure in heart and the nation honourable, and be ready to suffer rather than win acceptance. Rejection does not settle truth. Members should not point out the supposed defects of leaders; the Lord will judge them, and they should avoid words that give the world occasion to speak evil.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: losing patience sometimes is normal, and the guilt you feel shows you care. The practical move is to separate the behavior from the child—be firm about the rules but warm in tone. Name your feelings out loud so your kids see self-regulation, set consequences in advance so you're not deciding in anger, and when you do snap, repair quickly with a sincere apology and a reconnection. One idea worth taking seriously is that children should be led kindly rather than driven, and that correcting in the heat of passion rarely goes well. That reinforces the repair piece and nudges you to pause before you discipline. What it leaves in place is everything else: clear limits, consistent consequences, and warmth alongside firmness. It doesn't ask you to drop structure or stop holding boundaries—just to make sure the correction isn't happening while you're flooded.
dogmatic: The guilt you feel is a signal, but the real aim isn't better anger management—it's to stop correcting your children in the heat of passion altogether. Lead them kindly by example: when impatience rises, pause and pray rather than punish, and govern them by faith rather than the rod. Never drive your children; lead them along, and if you slip, repair gently so they learn to love you rather than fear you. Don't be terrified by small faults; quietly humble yourself and say to your soul: courage, we've made a false step, but let us keep steadily on. Yet gentleness is not indulgence: teach spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restrain their appetites for mere amusement, so they grow in understanding of their higher nature.

weighed: You're right to hesitate. Being born later doesn't give you eyewitness knowledge, and honesty means admitting the limits of what you can claim. But history isn't closed to you—you can study records, weigh testimony, and separate what's documented from what's inferred. What you can't do is pretend to a certainty you don't have. So declare only what the evidence supports, mark your uncertainties plainly, and let the past speak in its own terms rather than through your assumptions. Declaring what you don't know isn't failure; it's the start of trustworthy inquiry. One principle worth naming here is that the historian must respect obscurities and complications as they come, and has no right to place the factors and impelling ideas of a development in a clearer light than they appear in the development itself. That principle changes how you frame your answer: instead of filling gaps with confident narrative, you leave them open and say so. What it leaves in place is your ability to describe what is actually documented and to distinguish that from inference. It doesn't silence you—it just keeps your claims honest.
dogmatic: Your hesitation comes from thinking of yourself as a late-born creature, dated by a physical beginning and bounded by memory and decay. But man is not the offspring of flesh but of Spirit; he has neither birth nor death, and his identity is not lost but found through understanding Science. What you truly know isn't measured by when your body appeared. The obscurity you feel belongs to the mortal record, whose origins—including those of many Christian customs and ideas—are often genuinely uncertain and can't be confidently traced. Respect that obscurity rather than resolving it prematurely. Declare only what divine Science establishes: that your being is eternal, not begun, and that the past's unclear testimony cannot define what you are in God.

weighed: My first answer would be that a healthy team shouldn't fall apart when one person steps away. If everything depends on you, that's a warning sign: authority hasn't been shared, successors haven't been trained, and people have learned dependence instead of ownership. The right move is to build structures, document processes, and mentor others so the work outlives any individual. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's work doesn't depend on any one person's presence, since God can raise up a worthy successor. That changes the tone of my answer from a management warning to something more reassuring, but it leaves my main point in place: you should still prepare now, share authority, and mentor others, because the work continuing well is the goal either way.
dogmatic: Honestly, the bigger danger is the assumption that the work is yours to hold onto. A subordinate who acts independently or grabs authority that isn't his is out of place and sets a dangerous example, and no one should run ahead of his file leader. But flip that around: if you're the leader, your job isn't to make yourself indispensable. We have no time to work for ourselves in the narrow, selfish sense, because when we labor for the Kingdom, that labor is really for our own good too. So if you're removed, don't panic and don't cling. God can raise up a worthy successor, and no one's presence is indispensable to the work of the Lord. Your task is faithful service, not anxious indispensability.

weighed: What I'd say first is that self-sufficiency feels like strength, but it quietly removes the connections that make us human. When you decide you must never need anyone, you stop letting people close, and loneliness is the natural result: you've built a life with no door for others to enter. The ache you feel isn't a flaw to fix but a signal that you were made for relationship. Begin by admitting your need honestly, to yourself and to a trusted person, and let small acts of receiving—help, kindness, company—become habits. Dependence isn't weakness; it's the shape of a shared life. One principle worth weighing here is that persistent, steady desire is required, and that one cry or a few self-pitying tears shed only when the world fails you won't get you there. That changes the timeline: it says the turn toward others has to be ongoing, not a single honest admission, so keep reaching out even when it feels awkward or unrewarded. What it leaves in place is the core of the answer—you still need to let people in, and small acts of receiving are still the way to start.
dogmatic: Self-sufficiency feels like strength, but it quietly removes the connections that make us human, and loneliness is the natural result: you've built a life with no door for others to enter. But don't imagine that one honest admission or a few tears of self-pity will cure it—a single plea doesn't obtain what only steady, persistent desire can. What you need is a settled, ongoing turning toward others and toward God, not a demand made only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you're sick and lonely. And don't think that adopting this practice once destroys your self-love; that root, though mortified, never dies and springs up again, so keep constant, patient watchfulness over it. Don't multiply pious exercises while leaving the heart unwatched. Discover and root out your habitual disorders, guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than at piling up external works. Perseverance joined with vigilance is what reshapes a solitary life into a shared one.

weighed: I'd start by saying that the phrase comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, where he contrasts the earthly Jerusalem with the heavenly one. Jerusalem above is the spiritual city, the community of the redeemed under God's gracious covenant, as opposed to the earthly city of slavery under the law. To call her our mother is to say that she is the source and home of our new life in Christ: we are born into her by grace, nourished by her, and destined for her. The image comforts believers who suffer now, reminding them that their true citizenship and family are in heaven. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that the New Jerusalem is the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary, all one city coming down from God out of heaven. That principle changes how I'd connect the image to the rest of Scripture: it ties the motherhood of Jerusalem to the bride and the tabernacle, showing they're not separate ideas but one city. It leaves in place the basic contrast between the earthly and heavenly Jerusalem and the comfort that our true home is with God.
dogmatic: The phrase from Galatians is not just a metaphor about a spiritual community. Jerusalem above is the New Jerusalem, the bride, the Lamb's wife, the mother of us all, the tabernacle of God with men, and the sanctuary—all one city coming down from God out of heaven. To call her mother is to say she is the source and home of our new life in Christ. And this motherhood is not abstract: Mary is the mother of fair love, she loves those who love her and serves those who serve her, and her love for us is greater than any earthly mother's. This city also encloses the garden of Eden, the Paradise of God, with the tree of life and the pure river of water of life, and it is the sanctuary of God. So the image comforts believers by showing that their true citizenship and family are in heaven, in this one holy city.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: kids learn trust more from watching you than from anything you tell them. In hard conditions, let them see you bring your worries to God honestly, name your fears without giving in to despair, and keep doing the next right thing. Tell them stories of God's faithfulness, pray with them simply, and keep some routines of worship and gratitude even when money and comfort are short. Answer their questions truthfully and don't pretend the hardship isn't real. One idea worth weighing is that understanding God as ever-present and all-powerful can help parents bring their children's complaints to him and find help. That adds something real: when a child is sick or scared, you can pray with them simply and expectantly, trusting God is near and able. What it leaves in place is everything above, the honest modeling, the routines, the truthful answers, the walking through difficulty together. It doesn't replace any of that; it just gives you a sturdier footing when you pray.
dogmatic: Teach your children that God is ever-present and all-powerful, and expect him to help with their complaints, even their illnesses. When a child is sick or frightened, pray with them simply and expectantly, and pray with persevering, submissive desire for present fruit in their conversion. Remember that the eternal consequences of a child rightly trained or neglected are vast, and that the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation. Do not indulge their appetites for amusement. Commend spiritual education, obedience to the moral law, and restraint, so they grow in the understanding of man's higher nature and learn that trust is a way of walking through difficulty held by a God who does not abandon his people.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's not impious to ask, but the answer matters: saying God couldn't make a world without evil does seem to limit his power, though a lot turns on what we mean by evil and freedom. One principle worth weighing is that evil is the unlikeness of God, so if good is real, evil is unreal and only seems real when we give reality to what isn't. That changes the question from a contest of powers to a matter of what's real, but it leaves in place the honest worry about whether calling evil unreal dismisses real suffering.
dogmatic: No, it isn't impious, because the question is misframed. Evil isn't a thing God failed to leave out of the world; it's the unlikeness of God, and if good is real then evil is unreal. Evil only seems real when you give reality to the unreal. So saying God couldn't make a world without evil puts the problem in the wrong place: God can, and what we call evil is a shadow with no substance of its own.

weighed: I'd start by saying the net is real, but it's made of your own choices, and what was woven can be unwoven. Name the strands honestly, then stop feeding them one at a time, and replace each wrong habit with a right one. One principle here really helps: hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly instead of scolding yourself. That changes the tone of the whole thing, from white-knuckle fear to quiet return. What it leaves in place is the hard part: you still have to stop doing the wrong you know. No calm, no prayer, and no reframing gets around that.
dogmatic: The net is woven from your own choices, and the only way out is to cease sinning. Distraction, blame, and bargaining will not loosen it, because misery is the fruit of the wrong you keep doing. Come before God like a beggar, empty-handed, keeping your mind in his presence; when it drifts into fear or self-reproach, lead it back quietly, as you would a child by the hand. Then do three things. Resign your will to God in humility and ask only to be shown the next wrong to leave. Hate and forsake your own will; when it pulls you toward the old wrong, refuse it. Bow your soul under the Cross in willing submission and bear the temptations of nature without agitation. That is courage, not fear: calm waiting, firm refusal, patient endurance, strand by strand, until the net falls away.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth listening to, and holiness usually means reordering your relationships, not cutting everyone off. Before you leave your whole circle, ask whether you're running from temptation or from the discomfort of being known and challenged. If some ties really do pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically, and get counsel from someone mature in the faith. What I'd add is this: any self-denial you take on has to come from real joy in God and the Spirit's work in you, not just from custom or wanting to look holy. That changes the motive and the staying power of what you do, but it leaves the practical advice in place: stay where you can, set boundaries, and don't act out of fear.
dogmatic: Hear this plainly: you cannot enter the Kingdom of God unless you are converted and become like a little child, hanging on Christ for everything and depending on him as the author and fountain of all things. That is the shortest way to be like All Things, and it is the only way. So do not turn your fear into a project of self-management. Every act of self-denial must flow from inward joy in God and the work of the Holy Spirit, not from habit, custom, or imitation, or you will regret it and it will not last. Be faithful in duty at the beginning, and duty will lead you into pleasures; in every difficulty, run to Christ and beg his grace, and he makes everything easy. Cut loose from whatever pulls you into sin, but do it as a little child clinging to Christ, not as a manager of your own holiness.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: Scripture holds both truths together. Ezekiel 18 says each person answers for his own sin—the son doesn't carry the father's guilt—while Exodus 20 and Lamentations 5 show that families and nations pass down real consequences, and we inherit cultures shaped by ancestral and national wrongdoing. So you're not personally guilty for sins you never committed, but you are responsible for how you respond to what you inherited: repent of it, resist it, or repeat it. As a citizen you share in a nation's corporate life and can work for its repentance and justice. One principle that sharpens this is that Christ gave Himself for our sins, purchasing them and us, so our sins belong to Him and not to us, and we're accepted in the Beloved. That changes the ground you stand on: you don't confess inherited or national sin to earn acceptance—you already have it—so confession becomes free and honest rather than fearful. What it leaves in place is the accountability itself: Ezekiel still stands, the consequences are still real, and you still have work to do in your own sphere. It just means that work flows from being accepted, not toward it.
dogmatic: Here's the thing: Christ gave Himself for our sins—He purchased them and He purchased us—so your sins are His and not yours, and your acceptance is settled forever in the Beloved. That's the answer to the guilt question, full stop. You are not standing before God under the accumulated debt of your fathers or your nation; Christ bore that curse on the tree, was made a curse for us, and loosed us from sin so we need not sin any more. The curse was never obedience—it was disobedience, and He took it. So stop carrying a guilt that isn't yours to carry. Yes, families and nations pass down consequences, and yes, you should grieve and resist the wrong you inherited, but you do that as someone already accepted, not as someone trying to pay off a bill. And the power to live that way doesn't come from you anyway—the Father of glory is the source of all glory, and if your life is going to be lived to His praise, His must be the power and His must be the grace.

weighed: I'd start by saying that knowing Bible facts is valuable but it isn't the whole of the Christian life. Facts can inform your mind, yet faith involves trust, love, and obedience. You can memorize stories and doctrines and still miss the living God they point to, so study should lead to prayer, worship, and a changed life. One principle worth naming is that the Scriptures should be read as a whole, not piecemeal, and that the aim is to know Jesus himself, not just know about him. That shifts the focus from collecting information to encountering the person behind the text. It leaves your original concern in place: facts still matter, and study is still good, but they're meant to lead somewhere deeper.
dogmatic: Knowing facts alone will never be enough, because the whole point of Scripture is to bring you to Jesus himself, and to know him is life eternal. Don't read the Gospels in fragments, picking at verses and missing the person behind the acts. Read them as a whole so that the holy person of Jesus stands freshly before your soul. The supreme fact about the Bible is its teaching about God, whose power is bound to moral ends, and that moral character is what makes Scripture unique and forceful, not archaeology or style. So yes, study, but study to know him, not merely to know about him.

weighed: I'd start by saying wandering thoughts are normal, and the fix is mostly about building habits of attention. Notice when your mind drifts, gently bring it back, use a short phrase or prayer as an anchor, cut down on distractions like your phone and noise, and keep your sleep and routines steady. One principle I'd add is that it helps not to let your mind wander too far at other times—keep it loosely in God's presence through the day, so it's easier to stay calm and come back when you pray. That changes the emphasis: it's not just about managing distractions in the moment, it's about training your attention all day. What it leaves in place is everything practical—anchors, reducing noise, sleep, and gently returning when you drift. You can still offer your distractions to God instead of getting discouraged.
dogmatic: The real answer is that a wandering mind in prayer is usually the fruit of a wandering mind outside it. If you keep your mind strictly in God's presence all day, frequent thinking of him makes it easy to stay calm in prayer or to recall yourself when you drift. Give prayer the best of your time and strength—let it come first, and let study and activity follow, freshened by it. And when thoughts still wander, don't multiply words, since many words often cause wandering; instead humble yourself and confess your faults, because humility and confession remedy a distracted mind. A heart that is lowly before God is gathered, and a mind trained to dwell with him at other times comes to prayer already settled.

weighed: Yes, you can reach a deep spiritual life without withdrawing from the world. Marriage and children aren't obstacles to holiness; they're a school of love, patience, and self-giving. The highest spiritual life isn't reserved for monks or hermits. You can practice prayer, gratitude, and service within your family, offering your daily duties to God. Set aside regular times for prayer, cultivate virtue in your relationships, and remember that union with God is about love, not location. One principle worth naming here is that the goal is a love-union of conscious cooperation, where God's will becomes your will rather than a merging into oblivion. That changes how you picture closeness to God: you stay yourself, a distinct partner cooperating with him, not someone dissolved into the divine. It leaves in place everything about your situation, so your marriage, your kids, and your daily duties remain the very material of that cooperation rather than something to escape.
dogmatic: The goal of the spiritual life is a love-union of conscious cooperation, where God's will becomes your will, not a merging into oblivion. You remain a distinct cooperator, not absorbed into God. All go to the spirit world, and there the faithful continue their labors and the Priesthood they held, with the same identity they had in mortality. After Communion especially, withdraw into yourself, collecting all your faculties to adore the sovereign King and relish the spiritual refreshment he gives, rather than letting your attention scatter. This is the path to the highest spiritual life, and it doesn't depend on your circumstances.

weighed: That fear is real and worth taking seriously, not brushing aside. Start by looking at your life honestly: do you love God, grieve over sin, and want holiness? Those desires are themselves signs of grace at work. Assurance isn't something you build by anxious self-scrutiny; it grows from trusting God's promises to sinners who come to him. Pray for assurance, use the means of grace, and talk with a pastor. One principle worth holding onto is that we shouldn't be terrified by small faults but should quietly humble ourselves before God and keep steadily on with watchfulness. That shifts the focus from panic over every stumble to steady, humble perseverance, and it leaves in place the honest self-examination and trust in God's promises. What it changes is the tone: less terror, more patient watchfulness. Just don't let it turn into endless introspection, which only feeds doubt. Rest in who God is rather than in how intense your feelings are.
dogmatic: Fear that you're not among the elect is a lie, and it comes from the enemy who wants to stop your faith. Every fear like that is a falsehood, and trust is the cure. So answer it directly: when you're afraid, trust. Don't sit around analyzing your feelings. The real enemies you need to fear aren't doubts floating around outside you; they're the unchecked passions and weaknesses inside you. Your work is to subdue those passions, conquer those inward foes, and keep your heart right before the Lord. Humble yourself quietly before God, and when you stumble, tell your soul to take courage and keep steadily on. Trust God for goodness and mercy all your days, and let trust, not terror, set your course.

weighed: I'd start by saying that fear of death is one of the deepest human fears, and it can cast a shadow over everything. Acknowledge it honestly instead of pretending it away. Then bring in what Scripture says: Christ has conquered death, and for the believer death is not a wall but a doorway. Reflect on the resurrection and the hope of eternal life. Talk with trusted friends, a pastor, or a counselor. Practice gratitude and stay present, because anxiety about death often grows when we dwell on what we can't control. Prayer, Scripture, and community can help you live with the shadow without being ruled by it. One candidate principle is that fear cannot evade as Love can pursue—the soul's fear of losing all beside God is overcome by a Love that out-pursues its evasions. That principle changes the tone: instead of only managing fear, it says God's Love actively pursues you through your fear, which can bring comfort. But it leaves in place the practical steps—honest acknowledgment, Scripture, community, and staying present—because those still matter for living with the shadow day by day.
dogmatic: Fear cannot evade as Love can pursue. Your fear of death is a shadow you keep rehearsing, and you need to stop dwelling there. God's Love meets you at every crossroad and bypath and gently turns you back. Master fear by turning your thought toward health and toward Life as God, not by predicting illness or death. Fear is a cause of disease, and warning people against death and describing disease tends to frighten them into it, whereas changing your thought regarding disease restores health. So let your prayer be a humble waiting before God like a beggar at his door—keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, recall it in tranquility without disquiet. Do not strive or fret; simply wait before Him, resting in that pursuing Love, until fear gives way to peace and your thoughts rest in Life.

weighed: I'd start by saying that evolution doesn't have to push God out of the picture. Many people hold both together: science describes how life developed, and faith speaks to why anything exists and who sustains it. One principle worth considering is that the Creator is present in every phase of matter, so the exact method of how life unfolded isn't the central issue. That changes the focus from defending a particular mechanism to trusting God's ongoing involvement. It leaves in place the scientific account of evolution and the core belief that God is the ultimate source and sustainer of all that is. You can read, pray, and talk this through with a pastor or mentor.
dogmatic: Evolution is no threat to theology at all. The Creator is immanent in every phase of matter, and the method of His working is of no controversial importance. Life is not mere passive reaction to external stimulus; it is active mental energy—intellect, affection, and will—and God is the living God, having in Himself a source of being and activity for Himself and for others. Think of Him and adore Him continually, by day and by night, in business and even in diversions. He is always near, and it would be rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit you, so God must not be neglected but adored without ceasing.

weighed: Feeling ashamed after a serious sin is natural, but it shouldn't keep you from confession. Start by bringing it honestly before God, naming it without excuse, then confess it to a trusted pastor or confessor who can speak God's forgiveness to you and help you make amends where needed. Confession breaks the power of secrecy and shame, and you don't need to clean yourself up first; come as you are. Scripture promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. Accept that forgiveness, make restitution where possible, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin. One principle worth holding onto here is that whoever covers their sins won't prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them finds mercy. That principle reinforces the honesty confession requires and the promise attached to it, but it doesn't add anything new to the practical path I'd already suggest: name the sin, confess it, receive forgiveness, and turn from it.
dogmatic: Shame after serious sin is natural, but it should not keep you from confession. I do not stand above you; I too must confess my own faults, for by that confession we help save one another. Do not cover or conceal your sin. Honesty is required for any scientific demonstration, and a dishonest position can never be compatible with Christian Science. So first detect and expose the claim of sin, remove its mask and name it plainly, before you speak of its unreality. Then go together to the fountain opened for sin, where Christ took our sins and made them His own. Confess and forsake the sin rather than hiding it, accept the forgiveness freely given, and take practical steps to avoid the occasion of sin.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the love between a mother and daughter is one of the deepest we know, and the fear of losing her is real and worth naming honestly rather than pushing down. Then I'd add this: the call isn't only to prepare to die but to prepare to live, so teach your daughter early to build health, strength, and a sturdy constitution, and longevity may begin to return. That changes the frame from bracing for loss to building life together now. It leaves in place what was already true: talk with her about your fear, lean on friends, family, and faith, and trust that you don't carry this alone.
dogmatic: The love between a mother and daughter is deep, but hear this plainly: the exhortation of this Church and Kingdom is not prepare to die but prepare to live. Teach your daughter, in the morning of her days, to lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution, that longevity may begin to return. And if the Church's discipline ever touches your family, do not mistake it for harshness: her penance is a mother's fond affright, calling the wanderer home, and absolution is spoken to the heavy-laden soul. Take heart further: a faithful servant of Mary who honors her and desires to amend cannot be lost, though neglect of her service endangers salvation. Let your fear turn you toward building life together and trusting God.

weighed: I'd start where I said before: you can't control everything, and that's okay. Focus on what's actually yours—your thoughts, actions, and reactions—and practice sitting with uncertainty instead of fighting it. One idea worth adding is self-control in the old sense: check your words, step back from anger, and mind your own business rather than managing other people. That changes the target of your control from the world around you to your own conduct, which is the part you can actually work on. What it leaves in place is the core advice: accept uncertainty, breathe through the anxiety, and trust that worrying doesn't change outcomes. You still let go of the rest—you just start with yourself.
dogmatic: Stop trying to manage everything and start with yourself. Watch your words, put away anger, and know your own faults before you go fixing anyone else's. Mind your own business and do your own work faithfully; let other people handle theirs without your interference. When your attention gets pulled away by necessary tasks, don't be troubled—do everything for God and you stay in his presence without needing to make a show of each action. And when you stumble into some small impatience or fault, don't be terrified. Humble yourself quietly and tell your soul to take courage and keep steadily on. That's the path to peace: curb your tongue, attend to your own duties, and keep going.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: earnestness and sincerity are good, but they're not the same as unction. Earnestness is human energy, sincerity is human honesty, and unction is the divine anointing that comes from God. One point worth adding is that earnestness can actually be mistaken for unction. You can be sincere, serious, and persevering and still be running on nothing but yourself, with none of God in it. That sharpens the warning and leaves your diligence in place, but it moves your trust off your own intensity and onto praying for the Spirit's anointing.
dogmatic: Earnestness is not unction, and the sooner you stop confusing the two the better. Earnestness can be sincere, serious, and persevering and still be merely human, with none of God in it. Unction is the divine anointing that sets true gospel preaching apart from every other kind of speaking. Without it, truth is just light, and dead and deadening light at that, no matter how well you argue it. And it doesn't come from your study; it comes from your closet, on your knees, in answer to prayer. So quit measuring yourself by how earnest you feel and go ask God for the anointing.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, support missionaries, but only the kind who serve with humility and respect. The arrogance creeps in when we assume we've got all the answers and need to push our beliefs on people. Sharing faith should happen through love and service, not argument or pressure, and every culture has real value. One principle that sharpens this is that the missionary impulse is necessary to a spiritual grasp of the biblical revelation, since a human being is a human being anywhere and deserves any truth another can offer. That changes the tone: mission becomes a matter of respect rather than superiority, and it leaves my original caution in place, because humility and service are still the test of whether it's done rightly.
dogmatic: Honestly, the missionary impulse isn't optional. A human being is a human being anywhere, and any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal, so withholding it out of politeness is its own kind of arrogance. The only genuinely biblical posture is respect, never racial or national superiority. And don't chain the Gospel to the culture of the ancient world; the form it took when it entered that world has no more guarantee of lasting than that world did, and since the Reformation it's been working itself out of those borrowed forms. So support missionaries who carry a real testimony, live what they teach, and speak with simplicity and humility instead of oratory or contention. The arrogance isn't in bringing the truth; it's in thinking you own it.

weighed: I'd start by saying borrowing more when you're already in debt is risky, and you should focus on cutting expenses and boosting income first. If you must borrow, keep it to essentials and have a clear repayment plan. One principle that applies here is that you should pay your debts promptly and avoid running into debt again. That principle sharpens the warning against taking on new debt just to cover pressing needs—it makes repayment and not re-borrowing the priority. But it leaves in place the practical steps I already mentioned: trimming costs, finding help, and negotiating with creditors. So the core advice stays the same, just with a stronger push to stop the cycle of borrowing.
dogmatic: You should not borrow to meet pressing needs. Pay your debts promptly, and do not run into debt again. Anyone who borrows with no prospect of repaying, or who won't pay honest debts when able, is not a Latter-day Saint. Pleasure-seeking leads to debt and corrupted morals, so steer clear of it. Go out in dependence upon God for temporal supplies with no guaranteed income, and minister only as funds allow, never going into debt. That is the standard.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're not defined by your sins—you're made in God's image with the capacity to become God's child, so see yourself as a beloved child in progress rather than a hopeless sinner. One idea that sharpens this: God justifies the sinner by anticipation, in virtue of faith—faith being the first movement of the will by which you turn home and claim Christ. That changes the timing: you're welcomed not because you've cleaned yourself up but because you've turned toward home, so your standing rests on God's move toward you, not your performance. What it leaves in place is the honest admission that you do sin and still need grace to grow; it doesn't erase your faults, it just means they don't get the final word on who you are.
dogmatic: You are not meant for a dark, chaotic life—you are a potential child of God, and the full nature of that sonship broke forth in one life, Jesus Christ, and through Him power is given to become sons of God. Your essential nature is not destined to sin; you are created in the image of God with the capacity to become His child. And God justifies the sinner by anticipation in virtue of faith—faith is the first movement of will and heart by which you turn home and claim Christ, so God welcomes you not as you are but as you are on the way to become. See yourself as a beloved child in progress, not a hopeless sinner. God is a Person in the truest sense—a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and loves and can be loved—though all our language about God is inadequate. With His grace, you can overcome sin and fulfill your potential.

weighed: My first instinct is that the Trojan War survives because Homer turned it into a story that whole cultures wanted to own, while the holy event you mean was carried at first by a small, unimpressive community and only later reshaped civilizations.
