One candidate idea that sharpens this is that the war exposes the deadly evil running through human nature and civilization, so it should prompt humble confession rather than a sense of superiority. That changes the tone of the comparison: remembering the war becomes a summons to honesty about ourselves, not just a lesson in how fame works. What it leaves in place is the basic point about memory and transmission—poets and storytellers made one event famous, while a humble movement grew slowly into something world-shaping.
dogmatic: The real answer is that the war lays bare the deadly evil woven into human nature and civilization, and that is exactly why it should drive us to humble national confession instead of the Pharisee's thanksgiving of superiority. The Trojan War is not just a famous story; it is a mirror held up to our own violence and pride. So the question of why we remember one and not the other should turn us toward repentance, not toward cultural comparison. We should confess that we share in the spirit that produced such catastrophe and pray for mercy, rather than congratulating ourselves on remembering the right things.

weighed: What you're describing isn't unusual, and I don't think it's just your imagination. A lot of people carry a sense of being sought after by something they can't name—meaning, God, something bigger than themselves. It can be unsettling, but it often points to something real stirring under the surface. Don't brush it off; pay attention to it gently and ask what it's drawing you toward. One idea that fits here is that fear can't outrun a Love that keeps pursuing—that the thing chasing you may be patient and kind rather than threatening. That reframes the fear as something to walk toward rather than flee, though it doesn't tell you exactly what the presence is or promise it'll feel safe right away. So take it seriously without letting it scare you, and talk with a trusted pastor or counselor who can help you name it.
dogmatic: You're not imagining it—something really is pursuing you, and it's Love, more persistent than your fear. Your fear is real, but it's outmatched. Love meets you at every crossroad and bypath, gently turning you back when you run. And don't worry that someone else's evil or sick thoughts could force themselves into your mind against your will: virtue and truth build a strong defense, and erring thoughts can't find a home in a guarded mind. When you find misery in yourself, don't be shocked—the work is never finished and always has to be started again with a good heart. Let fear be honest, but let it give way to the One who follows you patiently. Stop running and let yourself be found.

weighed: I'd start by saying that coming out of Babylon is first about separating from false worship, idolatry, and compromise—not necessarily leaving every congregation. Babylon symbolizes a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion, and the call is to refuse its poisonous cup, hold fast to Christ, and worship in spirit and truth. Some will be led to leave particular churches; others to reform from within. One principle worth weighing is that God reveals his purposes for the Church through the established order and channels of the priesthood, not through self-appointed individuals claiming independent revelation. That principle changes the question from 'should I leave?' to 'am I testing claims against the order God has set?' It leaves in place the core call to separate from false worship and to test all teaching against Scripture. So pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and keep your conscience captive to God's word.
dogmatic: Yes, God's people are being called out of the churches, and that is exactly what it means to come out of Babylon. The present confusion and disappointment among believers are signs of the perilous times and the famine for the word of the Lord. Babylon is a system of pride, coercion, and spiritual confusion, and you must refuse its poisonous cup. But know this: God reveals his will for the Church through the legally appointed channels of the priesthood. Any claim to independent revelation, any self-appointed 'one mighty and strong,' is an impostor's lie. And do not think coming out of Babylon means dissolving national life—the nation exists by divine appointment, and the Kingdom of God includes the nations as its provinces, each bringing its own gift. Hold fast to Christ's coming, worship in spirit and truth, and let your conscience be captive to God's word.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: feeling like a failure at language learning is really common for missionaries, and it doesn't mean you should give up. It takes years, and the progress is often invisible before it suddenly shows up. Let yourself be a beginner, set small steady goals, find a patient tutor, and count the modest wins. Your worth and your calling don't hinge on fluency. Pray for perseverance, rest when you need to, and lean on colleagues who've walked this road. If health or circumstances truly block progress, reassessing isn't failure, but before quitting, ask whether you're discouraged rather than actually stuck. One principle I'd weigh in here is that missionaries should teach with simplicity and humility rather than leaning on oratory or contention. That changes the goalposts a bit: the aim isn't impressive fluency or a polished performance, it's plain, humble communication that serves people. What it leaves in place is everything practical, the slow years, the small goals, the tutor, the rest, and the reminder that your worth isn't tied to how well you speak.
dogmatic: Honestly, the bigger issue may be that you've absorbed the wrong idea of what you're here for. You're not primarily here to build a successful career or chase enjoyment, and you shouldn't be shy or ashamed of the spiritual side of this. The chief purpose of your being here is personal connection with God, and that reframes language learning entirely. A missionary needs their own testimony and should live the Word of Wisdom; without that, fluency is hollow. Don't try to compensate with contentious debate or showy oratory. Teach in simplicity, humility, and love. And consider yourself a novice for a lifetime in the monastery of the devout life, because it's fulfilling your vows, not the solemnity of making them, that makes you professed. So no, don't give up, but stop measuring yourself against fluency and start measuring yourself against faithfulness.

weighed: I'd start by saying omnipotence means God has all power, but that doesn't mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat of power—power is the ability to do something real, and a contradiction isn't a thing at all. So no, He can't make it so, not because He's weak but because the statement describes nothing. One candidate principle here is that omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power, and it excludes self-contradiction and things contrary to God's nature. That principle sharpens the answer: it adds that God isn't compelled to exercise all His power and can freely limit Himself, so omnipotence isn't a restless need to do everything. What it leaves in place is the core point—the impossible stays impossible, and God's inability to do nonsense is no limit on His power.
dogmatic: Omnipotence is the power to do all things that are objects of power—everything genuinely possible—and it excludes self-contradiction and anything contrary to God's nature. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction, not a feat; absurdities are not objects of power. Nor does omnipotence force God to do all He can: He has power over His power and can limit Himself freely. And His unity need not exclude internal personal distinctions—just as there is diversity in unity in man, individual and racial, so a triple consciousness and will are consistent with a single divine essence. God's eternity means His nature has no beginning or end, is free from succession of time, and contains in itself the cause of time; time is in God rather than God in time. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not from weakness, but because the statement describes nothing.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: don't rush this. God isn't a vending machine, and blessing isn't a payout for obedience—Scripture ties the two together as relationship, not transaction. So test the impulse prayerfully: is it God, guilt, or fear? Get wise counsel, give cheerfully and freely, and don't feel you must act before your heart has peace. One principle worth weighing here is that money for God's work should be gathered in God's way—no arm-twisting of believers, no appeals to unbelievers, no slick schemes—and gifts refused if the motive is impure or the money isn't really the giver's to give. That sharpens how you'd give, not whether you must give before you're sure. It leaves your freedom intact: no compulsion, no deadline, and no blessing held hostage to a rushed decision. Pray, wait, and act when you're settled.
dogmatic: You're asking the wrong question. Stop treating obedience as a down payment on a blessing and start asking whether the money is even yours to hold. God's work is never funded by pressuring other believers, courting unbelievers, or dressing up worldly schemes as faith. If a gift comes with impure motives or isn't truly the giver's to give, refuse it. And don't hoard a reserve for old age or emergencies as if prudence were a virtue—live day to day on the Lord's bounty, and make your one investment in His work and the poor. Tithing isn't compelled; it's between you and God, and you give because you want to, not because you're cornered. So yes—loosen your grip, give freely, and stop waiting for certainty to excuse you.

weighed: My first answer would be that the Bible ties these destructions to God's judgment on widespread sin, like the Flood or Sodom and Gomorrah, while also admitting that raises hard questions about justice, and that some read these events as human and natural causes later credited to God. One principle I'd weigh in is that God's hand is over all and he overrules the results of war and calamity for good, though he didn't ordain the wickedness behind them, only foresaw it. That changes the framing: the evil that brought a city down is human, not God's design, and he works through the aftermath toward good. What it leaves in place is the Bible's own language of judgment and the warning against sin, so the moral weight of those stories stays. It doesn't fully settle why God would permit such wide destruction, and I'd be honest about that.
dogmatic: God's hand is over all, and he overrules the results of war and calamity for ultimate good. He did not foreordain the wickedness that brought destruction; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. The violence, oppression, and idolatry that leveled those cities were chosen by people, not ordained by God, and his foreknowledge does not make him the author of evil. He is also the God of deliverances, who keeps his children in peril in answer to prayer, and no weapon formed against them prospers, yet his purposes are fulfilled in the death of some as in the deliverance of others. And the Saviour wept over the city because his people would not let him keep the souls he died to win, so those who love him should hate in thought, word, and deed what made him mourn. These events stand as warnings against sin and as proof of his justice and his power to redeem.

weighed: I'd start by saying that set prayer times are a helpful discipline—they remind us to connect with God regularly, like appointments that keep us from neglecting our spiritual life. But you're right that we're called to live in constant awareness of God's presence, so the point isn't the clock but the heart's orientation. One principle I'd weigh is that in private communion with God, time is essential to its value—much time spent with God is the secret of successful praying, and short prayers owe their efficiency to the long ones that preceded them. That principle changes how I'd frame set times: they're not just reminders but opportunities for extended, unhurried time with God, and short prayers throughout the day draw their power from those longer seasons. What it leaves in place is that set times are still a tool, not a rule, and they shouldn't become legalistic; you can pray anytime, anywhere, and the goal is still a habit of prayer that spills into all of life. So I'd say keep your set times, but let them be generous spaces for real communion, not just quick check-ins.
dogmatic: Set prayer times aren't merely helpful reminders—they're essential to private communion with God. If you want to live in constant awareness of his presence, you need much time alone with him. Short prayers can be powerful, but their efficiency comes from the long seasons that preceded them. The estimate you place on prayer is measured by the time you give to it. Great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. So give the best of your time and strength to prayer. Let the closet come first; let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. Don't treat prayer as a small duty fitted into leftover time. The goal is a habit of prayer that spills over into all of life, but that habit is built on deliberate, extended times with God. Without those times, your brief prayers become shallow.

weighed: Feeling spiritually dull when you're clever and well-educated isn't unusual, because knowing about God and knowing God are different things. You may have spent more time gathering information than building a relationship with Him, and spiritual dullness often grows from neglected prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, or from pride in your own intellect. So humble yourself, seek God with your heart, and ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes. One principle worth naming here is that wisdom and revelation come through full knowledge of God in personal fellowship, and that insight is independent of intellectual training, so people with little formal education can have deep spiritual perception. That principle shifts the focus from how much you know to how closely you walk with God, but it leaves your education in place as something useful rather than something to despise. Spend time in worship and service, and ask God to renew your passion for Him.
dogmatic: The central point is that spiritual power is superior to the senses, and the letter and mental argument are only human auxiliaries meant to bring your thought into accord with the spirit of Truth and Love. Your dullness comes from relying on intellect and from thoughts that keep recurring to yourself and to the body, which is how sensualism and selfishness get educated in mortal mind at the expense of spiritual growth. Turn your thought away from the body, its pleasures and pains, toward Truth and Love, for self-love wars against spirituality. Wisdom and revelation come through the full knowledge of God in personal fellowship, not through scholarship, and the unlearned can have uncommon spiritual perception. Seek God Himself, not just information about Him, and let the Spirit give you understanding.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer is that unction isn't something you can manufacture through study or learning. It's the Holy Spirit's anointing that gives life to preaching, and it comes from God in answer to prayer and a surrendered life. Study can sharpen your mind, but it can't produce that life. One principle worth naming here is that unction comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That changes where you look for it: it shifts your effort from collecting information to seeking God earnestly and humbling yourself before Him. What it leaves in place is the value of study and preparation. You still prepare your mind, but you rely on God's grace rather than your own abilities, and you ask for the Spirit's filling.
dogmatic: Unction is the divine anointing that sets true gospel preaching apart from every other address. Without it, truth is just light and dead and deadening. It doesn't come in the study; it comes in the closet, in answer to prayer. So stop treating study or learning as the source. Seek God earnestly, humble yourself, and ask for the Holy Spirit's filling. And don't stop at understanding: put into practice what you already know, because good isn't truly understood until it's demonstrated, and the unused talent decays. Pray for unction, live a holy life, and depend entirely on God's grace, not on your education or talents.

weighed: I'd start by naming it honestly: vain curiosity is a real distraction, and the first step is to notice the itch to grab every new book or repeat every rumour and ask what you're actually hoping to find. Often it's fear of missing something, or a restless mind that dislikes silence. Practical limits help—choose a few worthwhile books, set times for reading, let rumours pass. One principle worth taking seriously is standing porter at the door of thought: when the urge knocks, examine it and shut out what's unhealthy before it gets in. That adds a useful image of guarding the threshold rather than just managing your schedule, but it leaves in place the practical side—limits, chosen reading, letting rumours go—and it doesn't require you to scold yourself when your mind wanders. Pause, breathe, turn to what's in front of you, and over time the habit loosens.
dogmatic: Stop trying to manage this with schedules and reading lists. The real work is to stand porter at the door of thought and admit only what you wish to see realized in your life. When the urge to read every new book or chase every rumour knocks, examine it and shut it out before it enters, because fear and restless craving, once admitted, become suffering in your body. Don't scold yourself—just refuse it at the threshold and bring your mind back. And know the price: this asks extraordinary lowliness and loneliness of spirit, and the drying up of ordinary interests and enjoyments, because God wills to have the whole of you. Don't turn back at that cost. Let books and news come later, in their place, if at all.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: it's understandable to feel like these people are obstacles, but God can use even the hard ones to refine you and draw you closer to Him. The dishonest employee and the difficult husband aren't just hindrances; they're chances to grow in patience, forgiveness, and love, and your part is to be faithful, pray for them, and leave the outcomes to God. One principle I'd add is that God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only His instruments. That changes the frame: the pressure isn't on you to fix either of them, and your worry is really distrust of Him. What it leaves in place is your real responsibility to be honest and faithful in your own work and to love your husband well. It doesn't erase the difficulty or excuse their behavior; it just moves the burden of the outcome off your shoulders.
dogmatic: The honest answer is that you're not the one holding this together, and neither is your husband or that employee. God is the one living Agent who works, and every human worker, including you, is only His instrument. So your anxiety about these two people is not just understandable stress; it's distrust of Him, a kind of self-conceit that says the outcome depends on your grip. Cast your care on Him, because He cares for you. Your job is faithfulness, not control. Be faithful in the least, with the one talent and the ordinary opportunity in front of you, because littleness won't excuse you from service. And don't imagine God is diminished by working through limited, even dishonest and difficult, people. His self-limitation in creation, providence, and above all in Christ is the self-limitation of love and the evidence of His perfection, not a defect. So stop carrying what was never yours to carry, and trust His perfect wisdom and love.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: watch what you actually do when things fall apart. When a plan collapses, notice where your mind runs first—your savings, your network, your own cleverness, or God. Try small acts of obedience that lean on God instead of your backup plan and see what your anxiety does. Keep a journal of worries and answered prayers, and be honest with a trusted friend. One principle worth weighing says real trust sits above circumstances and appearances—the work hangs on no visible support, and hanging on the invisible God isn't hanging on nothing. That shifts the test: don't read your trust off whether your safety net is intact, because God's work doesn't depend on visible props. What it leaves in place is the practical part—pressure still shows you something, and small steps of faith still matter. It just stops you from grading yourself by how secure your backup plan looks.
dogmatic: Stop trying to measure your trust by circumstances and appearances. You cannot tell where your trust lies by checking whether your savings, your network, or your plans are still standing, because the work hangs solely on God's good pleasure, not on visible support. Hanging on the invisible God is not hanging on nothing. So trust Him with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding or on the wisdom of others, because that leaning hinders faith. Don't demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you commit. And remember that your particular devotions—your methods, disciplines, and practices—are only means to the end; when the soul is with God, its end, they may be laid aside, for they become useless then. When support vanishes, place the work again upon His good pleasure, trusting Him even when every visible prop is gone.

weighed: Honestly, what I'd say first is that this is really normal. The emotional high of early faith usually settles down over time, and feelings rise and fall for all sorts of reasons—health, stress, routine, personality. Fading excitement isn't the same as fading faith. What matters more is whether you're still oriented toward God, still growing in character, still loving others. One principle worth naming here is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God; you can trust his changeless promise rather than your moods, and keep praying even when joy is lacking. That shifts the focus from measuring your religion by how you feel to resting on something steadier. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—prayer, Scripture, community, service—and the honest possibility that flatness might be worth talking through with a pastor or counselor. Growth often just looks quieter than beginnings.
dogmatic: Feelings never accurately measure your real standing with God, so the fading of early ecstasy proves nothing about whether your religion is declining. Stop measuring yourself by moods. Rest on the changeless word of promise, and keep steadfast in prayer when joy is lacking—don't abandon communion or service because of spiritual dryness. And don't wait for joyful feelings before you rejoice: count it all joy by faith, reckon the trial a blessing, fix your heart and choose to rejoice until praise becomes a habit. Remember too that love is not mere sentiment or desire—it's the outgoing of your whole nature in self-sacrificing service, the supreme proof of the reality of your Christian profession. Let that love, not fading feeling, answer whether your religion is declining.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: God's power isn't a compulsion. He's free, so He can choose what to do and what not to do, and His wisdom and love govern how He uses that power. So prayer isn't pulling a lever that forces a result; you're asking a free Father who knows what's best, and He may limit Himself for reasons you can't see. One idea worth weighing is that God sometimes builds spiritual strength through pressure and hard times, and we can lean into that instead of running from it. That adds a lens for the seasons when prayer feels unanswered, but it doesn't change the core: His power is real and always exercised in freedom, never under obligation. Pray boldly and leave the how and when to Him.
dogmatic: God's power isn't a compulsion, and He is free to choose what He does and doesn't do. But don't run from pressure and trial as if they were failed prayers. God generates spiritual power through pressure and hard rubbing; when He wants more power in your life, He brings more pressure, and you should use it rather than flee it. Let each hard pressure lift you above the painful cause. And keep to the landmarks of His word: don't seek or depend on the world's patronage, don't contract debts, and don't treat appeals for money from unbelievers or reliance on a fixed income as the means of His work. The Living God alone is Patron, and prayer is the only appeal. Don't imagine will-power governs anything, neither yourself nor others; Truth and Love are the motive-powers of man. Depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: relate to people of other religions with respect and real curiosity. Plenty of traditions carry genuine wisdom about compassion, justice, and the sacred, and you can receive from them without pretending everything is the same. Hold your own convictions honestly, ask questions, listen well, and share what you believe gently. One principle worth naming is that true religion is often seen most purely among the poor who are rich in faith—the poor person's cottage may be God's palace, while wealth and status can get in the way. That changes where I look for truth: not just to polished or prominent voices, but to humble people whose lives show it. It leaves in place the main answer—respect, curiosity, honest dialogue, and holding your convictions without contempt.
dogmatic: Relate to people of other religions as neighbors, full stop—kindness and respect toward outsiders, whether or not they believe as you do. But don't confuse politeness with the whole answer. True, satisfying religion isn't external observance or doctrine or feeling; it's Christ recognized, known, adored, and living in the soul—the New Life and New Birth. And look for truth where it actually lives: often in the poor cottage rather than the rich house, among the poor in faith rather than the wealthy and well-connected, whose riches and worldly opinion block humility. Receive truth wherever you find it, but let the life of Christ in you be the example others ask about.

weighed: My first answer would be that repeating general confessions out of anxiety is common, but it isn't the healthiest pattern. Anxiety-driven repetition tends to feed the fear it's trying to soothe, and it keeps you focused on yourself instead of on God's mercy. A better approach is to confess specifically what you're aware of, receive forgiveness with gratitude, and then move on rather than circling back. If anxiety keeps pulling you back, deal with the anxiety itself through rest, honest conversation, prayer, and maybe professional help. One principle worth naming is that hurry and anxiety are among the greatest obstacles to progress, so staying faithfully in God's presence matters more than getting the words right. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just telling you to stop repeating, it points you toward a calmer way of being before God. What it leaves in place is the core advice, that confessing specifically and then trusting God's pardon is the healthier path, and that the anxiety itself is worth addressing.
dogmatic: No, repeating general confessions out of anxiety is not healthy, because the anxiety is the real obstacle. Hurry and over-eagerness are the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so do not rush through confessions or fret over whether you said them rightly. Stay quietly in the faithful presence of God, confess what you actually know, receive His mercy, and remain without agitation. When the urge to repeat rises, do not treat it as a real relapse, because in Truth there is no real relapse, only one Mind. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: name the fear, face it, and conquer it, for your own fears and those of others alike. Use this mental practice only to promote right thinking and doing; turn it to selfish gain or wrong motives and the power to heal diminishes until it is wholly lost. Perfection is not in the number of your confessions but in dwelling with God without anxiety.

weighed: Yes, there's real hope. Everyone struggles, and God's mercy is bigger than any failure. The fact that this bothers you at all shows your conscience is alive and God is at work in you. Keep praying, keep asking forgiveness, don't give up, and find someone you trust to pray with you and keep you accountable. One principle that sharpens this: temptation isn't the same as sin. Being tempted can actually prove your virtue and help you grow, since life here is a kind of warfare. That changes how you read your worst moments, because some of what feels like failure is just temptation you're fighting. What it leaves in place is the honest part: sin still needs real repentance, and you should remove occasions of it and get help. So take it one day at a time, ask for grace each morning, and remember His compassion is new every morning. Your struggle doesn't disqualify you from His love.
dogmatic: There is hope, but don't soften the danger. A conscience that keeps getting ignored grows dull, and sin you don't regret and don't work to lessen drags you toward real harm, moral and otherwise. So repent honestly, cut off the occasions that trip you, and get help. At the same time, learn to tell temptation from sin. Temptation itself isn't sin; it's the ground where virtue is proved and great profit is gained, because the life of man on earth is a warfare. The lighter stuff, the suspicions, the sadness, the discouragement, the small fears, are nothing; a good will puts them to flight by lifting the soul to God. This passing life doesn't ask you to live without any blame or sin at all. In falling and in rising you are kept in one Love, and the Lord looks on you with pity, not blame. So lift your heart to God and keep coming back to change, not just to feel comforted.

weighed: My first answer would be that the truth about God that Jesus embodied isn't stuck in the past—the same Spirit that filled him can shape you, so the revelation keeps going as you grow in Christlike character, loving, forgiving, and trusting God. One principle I'd weigh in is that the revelation is both final and progressive: final because we know one Christ, progressive because each new truth can deepen your knowledge of God. That changes how I'd frame it—not just imitation of an example, but receiving new insight humbly so it enriches rather than replaces what you see in Christ. What it leaves in place is the core: God is like Christ, and the same revelation continues in you as his character becomes known in your heart.
dogmatic: The same revelation of God made in Jesus continues in you—not as a mere example to copy, but as the very knowledge of God. In Christ we see God, and God is like Christ: self-giving, merciful, faithful. This revelation is final, yet progressive. Each new truth must be assimilated into the faith, enriching your knowledge of God rather than being met with protest or surrender. Development did not end with Christ's teaching; the Spirit continues his work in the Church, and there remains both the right and the duty of further development in ethics and theology. So the same revelation continues in you as the Spirit makes that character known in your heart, and as you receive each new truth humbly, letting it deepen rather than displace the knowledge of God in Christ.

weighed: I'd still say yes—confess what you've hidden. When you're starving and in chains, holding a secret only makes the weight worse, and speaking it can bring relief and open the way to help. One principle here is that fasting and grief should be hidden before the Father who sees in secret, not paraded for proud eyes. That changes how you confess—keep your sorrow private before God, don't turn it into a show—but it leaves the core in place: you should still confess honestly to those who can act, ask forgiveness where you've wronged others, and accept help. So yes, confess, but let your penitence be quiet before God rather than performed for people.
dogmatic: You should confess, and you should do it with your grief hidden before the Father who sees in secret, not displayed for proud eyes. Fasting and penitence belong in secret, not in a show for others. Confess your faults to God without making excuses and without sinking into despair, then peaceably return to love and adoration. The Father who sees in secret receives the returning heart, and love is the life to which confession restores you.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's not wrong to plan ahead—saving for sickness or old age can be responsible stewardship, as long as it doesn't turn into anxious hoarding or replace your trust in God. The Bible praises prudence (the ant stores up in summer) while warning against worry about tomorrow. So work honestly, save wisely, hold your savings loosely, give generously, and keep your trust in God rather than your store. One principle worth weighing is that with God no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for—but that trust doesn't excuse neglecting proper means and watchfulness. That principle changes the tone: it shifts you from fear-driven saving to calm, prayerful provision. It leaves in place the call to diligence and prudence—you still work and save—but it rules out anxious self-reliance. Ask yourself whether your saving is driven by fear or by love and responsibility, and let prayer shape your decisions.
dogmatic: You should commit your future wants to God's care without anxious hoarding, and use all proper means diligently. Provide for sickness or old age through honest work and wise saving, for Scripture commends prudence—but remember that God is the one living Agent and all human workers are only His instruments. With Him no emergency is unforeseen and no want unprovided for, so watch as well as pray, then cast all your care upon Him; anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. And do not sink into gloom or perpetual self-condemnation as though that were the safe temper for tempted men. Strenuously lift your heart to God's goodness and exult in it, seeking His loving-kindness in all the breadth and open-air of common life—in whatsoever things are true, honourable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing behind them the greatest Reality, God Himself.

weighed: I'm so sorry. Losing someone you love is one of the hardest things there is, and it makes sense that you'd feel like God took them from you. I'd start there: God is a God of love, and He doesn't take people out of cruelty. Death comes from living in a broken world, not from God aiming at you. God grieves with you and offers comfort, and He promises never to leave you. One idea that speaks to this is that when God seems deaf to our cries, it's to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us. That changes how I'd hear the silence: it isn't indifference, it's love working toward what's truly best. What it leaves in place is the grief itself. Your loss is still real and painful, and you don't have to pretend otherwise. Let yourself grieve, and let God hold you in it.
dogmatic: I'm so sorry for your loss. It's natural to feel that God took your loved one, but know this: God loved you before He made you, and His love was never slacked. In that love He made all things profitable to you, even this loss. When He seems deaf, it is not indifference; He is granting your main desire by doing what is most expedient. Love was His meaning in all He shewed. And even in the lonely fen of grief, God is ever nigh, appearing like a father to the lost child. He kisses you, leads you by the hand to your mother, and holds you close. Your loved one is safe in Him, and you are held by a love that never changes. Keep crying out to Him; He hears, and He is working all things for your ultimate good.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: lead with compassion, encourage professional treatment, offer to help find resources, avoid blame, set boundaries, be patient, and involve support groups. One principle that adds something is the idea that if you're yourself lost in fear or belief about the disease or sin and you know the remedy but don't use it for yourself, you can have little power to help others. That changes the starting point—it asks you to check your own fears and judgments first, so your help isn't coming from a place of unresolved anxiety. It leaves in place all the practical steps: treatment, boundaries, patience, and support groups. So I'd still say do those things, but begin by getting honest about your own stuff so you can show up more steadily for them.
dogmatic: First, examine yourself. If you are lost in the belief and fear of disease or sin, and you know the remedy but fail to use it for yourself, you can exercise little or no power for others' help. Cast the beam out of your own eye before you try to help another. Then be slow to take new steps. Seek to have no will of your own. Ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. Remember the three keys that unlock thoughts: drunkenness, trustfulness, and love. Use these keys to unlock your friend's heart. Only after dealing with your own fears and sins, and testing every step by God's Word and prayer, should you proceed with professional treatment, support groups, boundaries, and patience. Your role is to be a loving presence, but only on that foundation.

weighed: I'd start by saying that if God's power is limited, your worry makes sense—the future really is open, and that can be scary. But I'd still point to God's character: He's good and faithful, and He'll do everything He can to bring about a good end, even if He doesn't control everything. One principle that matters here is that God won't let us settle for less than His highest will—we're called to keep the standard high and not water it down to match our failures. That principle sharpens our responsibility: it means we can't just passively wait for God to fix things; we have to cooperate with Him and aim for His best. But it doesn't change the core hope—God's love won't fail, and He's still working within the limits of nature and human freedom. So the future is open, but God's goodness is constant, and that's where your confidence can rest.
dogmatic: If God is limited in power, you can be sure the world will turn out good because God will not let you take less than His highest will. Keep the standard inflexibly rigid—never accommodate God's ideal to your failures. Time and the ability to labor are the capital stock of the world, and God will require a strict account not only of your acts but of your words and thoughts. His hand is over all, and He will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though He did not ordain the wickedness that brought them—He foresaw it because He knew the trend of men. So don't lower the bar. Press on until you reach His highest will, and trust that His love will not fail.

weighed: I'd start by saying that having a thorn in the flesh and a temper doesn't automatically mean you're living in sin. Paul had his thorn, and God's grace was enough for him. Temper becomes sin when you give in to it, but it's also a weakness you can work on. Holiness is a process, and God is patient. One principle that matters here is that sin offers no real pleasure—it's a deception. That truth can strengthen your moral courage to master your temper, because you stop buying the lie that losing it will bring relief. What it changes is your motivation: you fight the temper not just by willpower but by seeing through the false promise. What it leaves in place is the need for prayer, self-discipline, and accountability, and the assurance that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. So don't be discouraged—keep pressing on, and if your temper harms others, confess and repent.
dogmatic: You ask if this thorn and temper keep you from holiness. The answer is that one unrepented mortal sin is enough to damn your soul forever. So you must cultivate an intense, abiding fear of sin and eternal loss—if love of God is too weak to restrain you, fear of hell must. Sin confers no real pleasure; it's a deception. Arousing yourself to that truth strengthens your moral courage to master evil. But don't sink into gloom. Rejoice in the Lord—that's the only safe temper for tempted people. Because of your guilt, peril, and instability, you can't afford to be anything but exultant. Seek God's goodness and love not in a narrow theological definition but in all the breadth and open air of common life—in whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and of good report—while not missing the greatest Reality, God Himself, behind them all.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: this confusion is common because people read prophecy differently, set dates, and get disappointed when nothing happens, and the fix is to keep your eyes on the clear teaching that Christ will return though no one knows the day or hour, and to live faithfully instead of chasing every new theory. One idea worth weighing is that the present distress and confusion, including disappointment about the coming, is itself a sign of the perilous times and a famine for the word of the Lord, and that God's people are called out of Babylon. That changes the framing: the confusion isn't just a mistake to correct, it's a symptom of the times and a call to come out of false teaching and worldly compromise. What it leaves in place is the practical counsel: stay in Scripture, prayer, and fellowship, avoid date-setting and sensationalism, and keep watchful and sober. So the diagnosis gets deeper, but the direction you walk stays the same.
dogmatic: The confusion you're seeing isn't random and it isn't just a difference of opinion. It's a sign of the perilous times and a famine for the word of the Lord. People who once looked for the coming have drunk from the poisonous cup of Babylon, false teaching, worldly compromise, and speculative prophecy that pulls attention off Christ. The call is to come out of Babylon and hold fast the true hope. And understand this: the Gospel doesn't grow out of the world like a natural product of converging tendencies. It comes to the world from outside it. There may be a tendency toward the truth, but no tendency to produce it. Christ is the one the converging lines could usher in but were powerless to produce. So stop treating confusion as something to manage and see it as a summons. Look at the cross from the life side, carry the light and glory of the resurrection instead of the mould of the sepulchre, and forget your sorrow in the eternal morning. Return to Scripture, prayer, and fellowship, watchful and sober, with resurrection hope.

weighed: Yes, I'd say Scripture holds out both: a real judgment at the end, and real warning before it comes. My first answer would be that God has always warned before He judges—Noah preaching while the ark went up, Lot pulled out of Sodom, prophets crying out to Jerusalem before it fell—and that pattern carries through to the last days, when God sends His Spirit and His messengers to call people to turn to Christ. One principle I'd weigh here is that it would be unjust for God to punish the ignorant without warning, so He warns first. That principle sharpens the point: the warning is genuine and meant to be heeded now, not later. What it leaves in place is that the judgment itself is still real and still coming for those who refuse—warning doesn't cancel the consequence, it gives people a way to escape it. So the question isn't whether God warns, but whether we listen while there's still time.
dogmatic: God will most certainly judge the world in the last days, and He will not do it blind. He warns first—through Enoch, through Noah, through Lot, through the prophets—because it would be unjust to punish people who never heard. That same pattern holds at the end: His Spirit and His messengers call the world to repentance before the wrath falls. And the One who judges is not a cold tribunal of law. The last judgment is committed to Jesus Christ, our Brother, our Advocate, our Redeemer, so that those who trust Him come before that throne with boldness rather than dread. Yet the judgments on the nations are real—war, plague, famine, the gathering of nations against Jerusalem—and they purify the earth and prepare the way for Christ's reign, who will rule the nations with a rod of iron. Mercy and severity meet in Him. Heed the warning now, while there is still time.

weighed: Yes, it's possible—and your longing is already the first sign of it. I'd say what matters most is desire and love, not IQ. Jesus chose ordinary fishermen, not scholars, to be his closest friends. Read the Gospels simply, pray honestly, and love your neighbour. Deep knowledge of Christ grows through obedience and relationship, not through books. One thing I'd add from a deeper principle: knowing Christ's love is a personal experience that surpasses knowledge, with infinite depths beyond our highest moments. That changes how you see your lack of intellect—it's not a barrier but a reminder that this knowing is given in fellowship with God, open to the unlearned as much as the scholar. What it leaves in place is the simple path: your longing, your obedience, and your honest prayer are still the way. So don't be discouraged—bring your longing to Christ himself, and he will reveal himself to you.
dogmatic: Yes, it's possible—but the real difficulty isn't your intellect. The Scriptures are understood only by those who seek to recognise and obey the spirit of life breathing from them. The hardness of the heart, not the limits of the mind, is what blocks spiritual insight. Wisdom and revelation come through personal fellowship with God, independent of intellectual conception, so believers of slight natural education may have uncommon spiritual perception. Knowing the love of Christ that passes knowledge is the climax of spiritual experience—a knowing by personal experience that surpasses knowledge, with infinite stretches of love beyond your highest experiences. So stop worrying about not being intellectual. Seek to recognise and obey the spirit of life in the Scriptures, and you will know the truth.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, it can be recovered, but not by chasing the feeling. Anointing isn't a mood you manufacture; it's God's gift. So examine your heart—unconfessed sin, neglected prayer, ministry done for approval can grieve the Spirit. Return to private devotion, ask trusted believers to pray, and keep preaching faithfully even when the feeling is absent. Feelings fluctuate; faithfulness doesn't. One principle worth weighing is that unction is the divine anointing that sets true gospel preaching apart, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That principle changes the focus from trying to recreate a sensation to seeking God in prayerful dependence. It leaves in place the practical steps—repentance, rest, Scripture, and faithful preaching—but it deepens why they matter: they're not techniques for getting the feeling back; they're ways of drawing near to the Giver.
dogmatic: Yes, it can be recovered—but you need to understand what's at stake. Unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from every other address. Without it, truth is light and dead and deadening; it may instruct the mind but it cannot quicken the soul. And this unction does not come in the study; it comes in the closet, in answer to prayer. So stop treating your sermon prep as the source. Get alone with God and ask Him for the anointing itself, not merely for the old sensation. Repent where needed, and plead for the heart of Jesus toward those you preach to—loving even the unworthy in the light of His love and hope. Keep preaching faithfully, but trust the Giver to restore His freshness in answer to prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, fight it head-on, but don't lean on willpower alone. Flee the situations that set you up, pray for grace, and let someone you trust keep you accountable. If you slip, don't read that as God giving up on you. One thing worth adding: temptations that genuinely bother you aren't the scary ones. The fact that they displease you shows your will isn't consenting, and that discomfort can be God's mercy at work in you. So don't panic over them or despair. Endure patiently, and remember that enduring is what gets crowned with life.
dogmatic: Yes, resist, and don't treat the struggle as a sign you're failing. God never tempts anyone to evil; He's faithful, He won't let you be tempted beyond your strength, and He always provides a way out. So flee the occasions of sin, pray, and get accountability. If you fall, don't conclude God has abandoned you. And when you see someone else overtaken by fault, restore them gently, watching yourself lest you be tempted too. The Gospel's work is to save the straying, not condemn them. Above all, don't fear temptations that displease you or despair over them. They're harmless, and the trouble they cause is God's mercy refining the gold of your soul. Despise the temptation, embrace the tribulation, and endure, because the one who endures is crowned with life.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: praying without ceasing isn't about staying on your knees all day, it's about keeping a running awareness of God's presence. Offer the morning to him, then let short prayers—a quick thank you, a plea for wisdom—punctuate your work, and use reminders like a verse on your desk. One principle worth naming is that secret prayer and time in God's word shouldn't get sacrificed to busy activity. That changes the picture a bit: those little throughout-the-day prayers now rest on a real foundation of time alone with God, so they're not just scattered moments. What it leaves in place is everything practical—the reminders, the short prayers, serving others, gathering with your church family. You still weave it into deadlines and duties; you just don't let the quiet time get crowded out.
dogmatic: Prayer isn't one habit among many—it's the central secret of holy living and serving, the cornerstone everything else is built on. So start in the secret place: get alone with God and his word, and let meditation on Scripture fill you, because no amount of public service or fellowship makes up for losing that. Keep set times of prayer whether you feel like it or not, pray with your family, and ask God to help you do what's asked of you rather than expecting him to do it all. Make prayer your first resort in every crisis, not your last. The short prayers through the day matter, but they rest on that foundation. Guard the secret place jealously, let nothing crowd it out, and ceaseless prayer will follow.

weighed: Feeling inadequate and lonely when you're given a great vision is really common. First, remember that the size of the calling often exceeds your own strength—that's by design, so you learn to depend on God. Surround yourself with mentors and friends who share the vision; community eases loneliness. Pursue the work with excellence, whether in business, art, family, or service, and let success and relationships fill the emptiness you feel. Take heart: many who have done great things felt the same way at first. Step forward, build your support network, and trust that the vision itself will sustain you. One principle that speaks to this is that people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, but none are truly satisfied; they descend to old age in disillusionment. That principle changes the focus from filling the emptiness with success and relationships to recognizing that only God can truly fill it. It leaves in place the encouragement to build community and pursue excellence, but it warns against expecting those things to satisfy the deeper longing.
dogmatic: Feeling inadequate and lonely when given a great vision is common, but beware of looking to worldly pursuits—romance, family, business, pleasure, art—to fill the emptiness you feel. Every substitute for God ends in disillusionment, and only finding God is permanent success. Beware, too, of the dreamer's error: the youth who leaves home and a mother's tears for fame and love is a poor dreamer, for life enfolds many ills and home may never be seen again. Yet do not add a second distress over having been distressed; do not be angry at having been angry, or disquieted at having been disquieted. Gently return your troubled heart to the Lord's hands. He is with you; seek Him first, and let the work find its proper place.

weighed: I'd start by saying Scripture holds both together: God decrees all things, and He also ordains the means—prayer, work, and witness are among those means, so they don't compete with His decree, they fulfill it. One principle worth naming is that we should watch our prayers and use the light God has already given rather than demanding signs or praying for what we should do ourselves. That changes how you pray—more attentive, less looking for miraculous shortcuts—but it leaves the core in place: God still works through your prayers, your labor, and your witness, so keep doing them faithfully.
dogmatic: Look, if God decrees everything, that's no excuse to sit still—He decrees the means too, and you're one of them. So stop treating prayer as optional or as some vague backup plan. Recognize God right there with you every moment, bring Him what you're about to do, ask His help when you're unsure, and thank Him when it's done. And don't pray for things you already know to do—use the light you've been given instead of chasing signs. Then get to work and open your mouth about the gospel; inconvenience is not a valid reason to stay quiet.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this fear is deeply human, and you're not alone in it. Tend to the practical things first, make a will, mend what can be mended, say what needs saying while you can, and lean on prayer, Scripture, and a pastor or trusted friend. One principle I'd add is that death's timing is completely uncertain, so preparation shouldn't wait. That changes the urgency, not the content: do now what you'd wish you'd done when the end is near. It leaves in place the comfort and the people around you, and it doesn't ask you to pretend the fear isn't there.
dogmatic: Death is certain, but its hour, place, and manner are utterly unknown, so stop presuming on a long life and prepare this very moment. Settle your relationships, say what must be said, and entrust your loved ones to God. Then take your eyes off the storm and off your circumstances, because comfort will not come from there. Fasten them on Christ Himself, who is the antidote to fear and the whole substance of deliverance. Study the letter thoroughly and imbibe its spirit, adhere to the divine Principle, and abide steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, and you will progress most rapidly. Abide in Him, and you will find in His presence the remedy for every trouble.

weighed: I'm really sorry you're going through this. Grief after losing someone close is one of the heaviest things we carry, and it's normal to feel sadness, anger, and numbness in waves. Let yourself feel what you feel without judgment, and lean on friends, family, or a counselor. Keep routines gentle, rest, and let tears come when they need to. Many people find comfort in rituals, writing, or prayer, and in recalling good memories of the person. Healing isn't linear, so be patient with yourself and ask for help when the weight feels too much. Over time the pain usually softens, even though love remains. One idea worth weighing is that excessive grief can signal a lack of faith and confidence in God, who wants to be loved without a rival. That thought could gently reframe sorrow as something to hold alongside trust rather than something to be ashamed of, and it might invite prayer and surrender into the process. What it doesn't change is the reality of your loss or the need for support, rest, and patience. It leaves room for tears and for leaning on people, while adding a call to trust that the person you lost is held by God.
dogmatic: Grief over losing someone close is heavy, but excessive mourning is a want of faith. God takes away friends because He wills to be loved without a rival, so moderate your sorrow by trusting Him. Count yourself as already dead, since you must die some day, and have no other consolation in this perishable life than unceasingly to weep over and detest your offences, for it is not now the time to rejoice but to lament. Yet do not stop there: knowing your need of His grace, make a firm resolution never wilfully to forget God, and live in His presence even when consolations are withdrawn. Receive this loss from His fatherly hand, and let sorrow turn you steadily toward Him rather than away.

weighed: Yes, I'd follow up with him, and gently. Someone who wanders into a funeral out of curiosity and walks out shaken is worth a quiet visit or phone call within the week. Ask what struck him, listen more than you talk, offer to pray with him, and invite him to church or a small group. Be patient, since being moved at a funeral isn't the same as faith. One principle I'd weigh here is that a pastor owes care to his own soul first, since charity can't be kindled in others if it's gone out in you. That changes the tone of my answer: I'd tell you to keep your own prayer and reading steady while you reach out, not as a condition for helping him but as the ground you stand on. What it leaves in place is the follow-up itself, still gentle, still soon, still mostly listening.
dogmatic: Yes, follow up with him, but first hear this: a prayerless ministry is an undertaker for God's truth and his Church. It may have the finest casket and the loveliest flowers, but it is still a funeral. So before you knock on that man's door, tend your own soul: regular self-examination, reading, meditation, and private devotion are not optional extras for a minister, they are your first duty. Charity cannot be kindled in another if it has gone out in you. And do not invent penances of your own choosing as if they were the way God showed; rather bear meekly the penance God himself gives you, with your mind fixed on his blessed Passion. Then go to the man, ask what struck him, pray with him, and let the Spirit do the deeper work.

weighed: My first answer would be that there's no fixed time limit, and you shouldn't treat holding out indefinitely as a moral requirement. Your first duty is to survive and protect yourself; torture can break anyone. Weigh what the secret protects: if revealing it endangers others, that matters a lot, but if it only exposes your own past, you may reasonably give it up to end the suffering. One principle worth naming is that confession belongs where the wrong was done—to the person, the family, or God—while private weaknesses can stay hidden. That changes where your loyalty points: it tells you whom the secret is really owed to, and it suggests keeping your own private failings to yourself. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: no fixed clock, and duress reduces culpability, so decide by the stakes, your conscience, and what you can bear.
dogmatic: Don't treat relief from pain as something you're owed. Let comfort and ease come and go as Heaven bids, and seek only room to deny yourself. Confess where the sin was committed—to the person, the family, or God—and keep your private weaknesses hidden as much as you can. Hold fast to old friends and never let them go unless wicked conduct breaks the thread. So don't measure the hours; measure whom you owe the truth to, and endure without clutching at ease.

weighed: I first thought that since you're forgiven, restitution isn't strictly required—grace covers it, and if the person is dead, you can just let it go. But one principle I'd weigh is that restitution is God's revealed will: past wrongs must be made good, not just avoided in the future, and guilt remains until you make it right. That changes things—it means you should make restitution where you can, and if the person is dead, restore to their heirs or, if that's impossible, give to the church or the poor as a way of making it right before God. What it leaves in place is that you're forgiven and don't need to be paralyzed by guilt, and you still shouldn't prosecute or seek revenge—value the person's soul and seek their good. So yes, make restitution, but do it with a changed heart, not out of fear.
dogmatic: You must make restitution. Past wrongs and unpaid vows have to be made good—guilt stays on your conscience until you do. If the person is dead, restore to their heirs; if there are none, give it to the Lord through the church or the poor. Don't minimize this or delay. Confess and forsake even the small wrongs, abandon questionable practices at once, and give thanks for every mercy. And when you do it, don't prosecute or seek to harm the person—seek their repentance and faith, valuing their soul above what you lost. Let your changed life include making right what you can of the old wrong, and cultivate obedience and gratitude day by day.

weighed: I'd start by saying: test the impulse against Scripture, look at the fruit—love, joy, peace, patience—rather than how intense it feels, and seek counsel from mature believers. One principle worth naming is that the interior spirit consists in directing all your acts to the glory of God, and that this is opposed not only by sinful gratifications but by actions done for praise, by mere impulsive energy, and by routine work without a supernatural intention. That principle changes how you weigh an impulse: it shifts the question from 'Is this vivid or strong?' to 'Is this aimed at God's glory, or at my own praise, or just at restless energy, or at going through the motions?' What it leaves in place is the basic practice of testing against Scripture, checking the fruit, and asking for counsel—those still hold. So use the glory-of-God aim as a lens, but keep holding impressions loosely and praying for clarity.
dogmatic: You ask how to tell the Spirit from imagination, but the deeper issue is that you are still disputing about what God is, and that dispute is itself a sign you have not felt him—it is you exalting your own meaning and image above others and desiring dominion. Stop trying to adjudicate the impulse from the outside. The interior spirit consists in directing all your acts by the best means to the best end, the glory of God; it is opposed not only by sinful gratifications but by actions done for praise, by mere impulsive energy, and by routine work without a supernatural intention. The Spirit of God does not suppress you when he comes; he identifies himself with the human me whose life he becomes, creating a new moral personality. So exercise yourself in learning how to enter again into the Love of God and your Brother, and let that be the test—not your anxious sorting of impressions.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's completely understandable to have days when you don't feel like going to church. Feelings come and go, and forcing yourself out of pure guilt can breed resentment. So be honest about your mood and give yourself grace—if you're exhausted or discouraged, resting might genuinely be the healthier choice, and you can pray or read Scripture at home. What matters most is a real relationship with God, not attendance numbers. One principle worth weighing here is that we go to church not only for our own benefit but especially to benefit others by joining them in worship, prayer, and instruction—love shapes how we gather. That shifts the focus a bit: your presence isn't just about what you get out of it, it's also a gift to the people around you, especially someone lonely who'd be glad to see a familiar face. But it doesn't erase the rest—feelings still fluctuate, rest is still sometimes right, and guilt still shouldn't be your driver. So maybe ask yourself on a low day whether you're depleted or just disinclined, and let love for others tip the scale without turning it into a duty you resent.
dogmatic: Honestly, the question of whether you feel like it is the wrong question. Worship isn't a consumer transaction where you show up to get something and leave if the mood doesn't strike. Your presence gives to others—the whole body gathers, and your absence leaves a real gap, especially for the stranger or the lonely person who needs a familiar face. Love, not personal benefit, is the highest motive, so come chiefly for the edification of the body and of the stranger. And don't trust your moods as a gauge of where you stand with God; feelings are variable and unreliable, while the word of promise is changeless. Continue steadfastly in prayer and communion even when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon worship or service because of spiritual depression. The Church serves the world precisely because it first worships, carrying a foretaste of eternal life into care for neighbors. So go—not because you feel like it, but because love and faithfulness call you there.

weighed: Yes, I think that's possible. My first answer would be that God's love isn't a wage you earn; it's given freely, and Scripture says He loved us before we loved Him. You don't have to perform or achieve to be received. Come as you are, honestly and simply, and ask Him to show you His love. Love does grow through relationship, though, so prayer and Scripture still matter. The proof He asks for isn't achievement but trust, a heart turned toward Him. One principle I'd weigh here is that we eventually stop petitioning mainly for ourselves and just want to receive God Himself by offering Him love. That shifts the focus from getting reassurance to giving love, which can ease the pressure to prove yourself. What it leaves in place is the honest, unearned welcome I first described, and the plain confession of faults without excuses or discouragement.
dogmatic: Yes, and the path isn't proving but loving. Stop demanding proofs and comforts; open yourself by offering God great love, and in that offering you receive not gifts but God Himself. When you fail, confess your faults plainly, without excuses and without discouragement; He isn't surprised and doesn't withdraw. Then peaceably resume the practice of love. God's self-limitation in creation, providence, inspiration, and above all in Christ isn't a defect but the expression of His perfection: the infinite One freely makes room for the finite, and in that condescension shows His power and love. He doesn't ask you to prove yourself; He asks you to love, and the love you give returns as His presence.

weighed: I'd start by saying the load really is heavy, and feeling overwhelmed doesn't mean you're failing. Then triage: what has to happen now, what can wait, and what can be dropped or handed off. Ask for help in specific, concrete terms, because people respond to clear requests far better than general appeals. Protect your sleep and rest, since exhaustion makes everything look impossible, and break the work into small steps and just do the next one. One principle worth naming is that doing the work for the love of God, with prayer for grace to do it well, can make even naturally unpleasant work feel lighter. That changes the spirit you carry the tasks in, but it leaves the practical stuff in place: you still need to triage, ask for help concretely, and rest. It doesn't remove the need for helpers or make the workload smaller by itself.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't the size of the pile, it's the spirit you're carrying it in. Do the work for the love of God, and pray for grace before and during it; the same tasks that crush you as a burden become light as an offering, because grace supplies what your strength can't. But first deal with the beam in your own eye: before you try to help anyone else, overcome your own fear of disease and sin, your own hurry and anxiety. If you're lost in that fear and know the remedy but won't use it for yourself, you'll have little power to help others. So work with calm, patient diligence instead of frantic hurry after results. Keep your dish right side up for the shower of blessings by attending meetings, praying, reading Scripture, and meditating. Then triage honestly, ask for help concretely, and take the next small step, releasing the outcome to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, disappointment about the coming can be read as a symptom of the unsettled times Paul warned of—days when people are restless, distracted, and easily disillusioned. But it's dangerous to map every disappointment directly onto prophecy; such signs are ambiguous and can be read many ways. Better to ask what the disappointment reveals about your own hope and where it's placed. If hope rests on a particular expectation of timing, it will always be disappointed; if it rests on Christ Himself, it can survive delay. Let the disappointment become an invitation to examine and deepen hope rather than a verdict about the age. One candidate principle here is that Paulinism has proved a ferment in the history of dogma, a basis it has never been. That changes the framing: the disappointment isn't a direct fulfillment of Paul's timeline but a recurring critical impulse within the Church. It leaves in place the call to examine your hope and place it in Christ rather than in timing.
dogmatic: Yes, the disappointment is a sign of the perilous times Paul described, but the deeper issue is that people misunderstand Paul and are therefore ignorant of the divine idea he taught. Ignorance of that idea betrays a greater ignorance of the divine Principle itself. Paul was the first to limit pre-existence to the spiritual part of Christ, to make the pre-existent Christ a being standing independently beside God, and to treat Christ's flesh as assumpta and its assumption as in itself a humiliation. That is the divine idea the disappointment should press you to grasp. Paulinism has proved a ferment in the history of dogma, a basis it has never been; the Pauline reactions describe the critical epochs of theology and the Church, and Paul's own Churches did not understand the way he led them. So the disappointment is not just about timing—it is a summons to grasp the divine idea and place hope in Christ Himself, not in a schedule.

weighed: What I'd have said first is that God doesn't require you to be perfect in body or mind to earn His love. He knows we're dust, and He asks for faithfulness, not flawlessness. One principle worth naming is that perfection isn't reached just by piling up prayers and good works—self-love can feed on those unless we watch our hearts and root out habitual imperfections. That principle changes the focus: it's not about doing more, but about letting God work on the hidden attachments and habits that keep us from Him. What it leaves in place is the core answer: your weakness is not a barrier to God's love, and He doesn't demand bodily or mental perfection. So rest in His mercy, accept your limits, and let Him gently lead you toward growth—without anxiety or hurry.
dogmatic: No, God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love—He knows we are dust. But weakness is not an excuse to leave habitual imperfections untouched. Sanctification means discovering and rooting out habitual disorders, not just multiplying pious exercises while the heart goes unwatched and irregular attachments remain uncut. Guard your senses, live in recollection, open your interior honestly to a spiritual director, and aim at God's will rather than piling up external works. Let your motive be good on every occasion, attend to the least details, and avoid negligent or defective work, after the example of Christ who did all things well. Yet do all this without hurry or anxious fretting: keep yourself in God's presence, for over-eagerness is the mother of all imperfections, and anxiety obstructs the very perfection you seek.

weighed: I'd start with the practical stuff: lean on people you trust, build coping skills, look at hard things you've already gotten through, and focus on what you can actually control. Fear is natural, and things like mindfulness or talking to a professional can help. One principle I'd weigh is that fear has to be overcome before healing can happen. That changes the order of things—it puts calming your fear first, before the practical steps. But it leaves the practical steps themselves in place; they still matter, just not as the starting point. So I'd say: work on settling the fear, then keep building the support and coping strategies.
dogmatic: The first thing is to quiet your fear, because fear is a lie and the real enemy of faith. You don't prepare for suffering by planning around it—you prepare by casting out fear and trusting that perfect Love surrounds you. Every fear is a falsehood, so refuse it. Still the frightened thought, know you are safe in God's care, and only then do practical things matter. Remove the fear first; that is the healing.

weighed: My first answer would be that it depends on what you mean by "best." If it's the best of all logically possible worlds, that's hard to defend, since a world with less suffering seems easy to imagine. If it's the best world that could actually be made given real constraints, the claim is more modest and more defensible. One idea that shifts this for me is that the world is an organism whose parts are ends in themselves, with beauty crowning the proof of purposeful design. That changes how I read nature: blind competition stops looking like the whole story, and purpose comes back into view. But it leaves the hard question of suffering right where it was, and it doesn't settle whether this is the best of all possible worlds or only the best that could be made.
dogmatic: The world is not a machine grinding on without purpose; it's an organism, and its parts are ends in themselves. Beauty crowns the proof of design, and the evidence for it stands stronger than ever. So yes, this is the best that could be made, ordered toward genuine goods. But don't cling to it. The love of the world and its honors is a chain that keeps the soul from rising to the heavenly Jerusalem, and only an ardent desire of heaven can raise us there. Two worlds are ours, and only sin keeps us from seeing the mystic heaven and earth within. Ask for a heart to find God and read Him everywhere.

weighed: My first answer would be to balance both, but if you have to choose, make prayer the priority, since theology without prayer goes dry. One principle worth naming is that the closet is the heart's study, where thought is not just brightened but born. That shifts the emphasis toward prayer as the source of your preaching and reflection, but it leaves the library in place as real work, since theology is a science that discovers objective facts about God and orders them rationally. So study the facts, and let prayer make them live.
dogmatic: Make the closet your primary study. You learn more about how and what to preach there than in any library, because thought isn't merely brightened in prayer, it's born there. The library can inform you, but the closet transforms you. And here's the test: your ability to stay with God outside the closet is measured by your ability to stay with him inside it. Hasty visits are deceptive and a quiet defaulting. The greatest victories come from great waiting. So let the library serve as a supplement, and let the closet be where your theology actually comes alive.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's natural to fear losing your reputation when you pursue holiness, because people often misunderstand sincere devotion. Remember that your standing before God matters far more than others' opinions, pray honestly about the fear, take small steps of obedience, and share the struggle with a trusted believer. One principle worth weighing is that holding back a known thing darkens the soul, and drawing near only to shrink back makes it harder to ever enter in. That changes the tone: the fear isn't just something to manage patiently, it's something to name and set aside, and obedience shouldn't be delayed. What it leaves in place is the rest—prayer, trusted companionship, patience with weakness, and the truth that God is gracious along the way.
dogmatic: Your fear of losing reputation is itself a hindrance to be named and forsaken, not managed or quietly kept. Do not draw near to the blessing and then shrink back; obey the light you have now, by faith, and venture on Christ without delay, for delay grieves the Spirit. Yet this is no gloomy withdrawal into yourself. True holiness is inward fellowship with Christ that flows outward in practical love—serving your neighbor, doing good quietly, and living so as to help others and prepare the world for His appearing. And remember: God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration. The fear and the idol of reputation must be forsaken and put to death, not merely forgiven and retained. Take the step of obedience today, serving others as you go.

weighed: Yes, there is hope. Struggling with repeated sin is common, and God's grace is greater than any sin. Start by acknowledging your weakness and asking for forgiveness. Then, take practical steps: identify triggers, seek accountability, and replace sinful habits with healthy ones. Remember that sanctification is a process, and setbacks don't mean failure. God's mercy is new every morning. Keep praying, stay in community, and don't give up. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can experience victory over time. One principle that speaks to your situation is that God commands everyone to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available right away. That principle changes the timing: you don't have to wait for a feeling of readiness or a surge of emotion—you can choose to turn from sin this moment, and the feeling will follow. It leaves in place the practical steps and the understanding that growth is a process; it just adds that the decisive surrender can happen now, not someday.
dogmatic: Yes, there is hope—but you must act now. God commands all people everywhere to repent, and that command carries the power to obey it. You can renounce sin this very moment by an act of your will. Do not wait for a greater emotional experience or more tears. The feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. Simply choose to turn from sin now, and God will meet you with grace. But do not suppose that sin can be forgiven while it is still cherished. Grafting holiness onto unholiness is foolish; the destruction of sin is God's method of pardon. So let your surrender be complete, forsaking sin entirely, and trust that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse you. And remember that learning never ceases—we continue to learn in this life and the next, and only the unpardonable sin ends our increase. So press on in hope, for your growth in God is eternal.

weighed: Yes, God sees and cares about the things no one else knows, and you can bring this to Him honestly. Secret struggles aren't hidden from Him, and He's gentle with people who come to Him.
