One thing worth holding onto is that secret prayer is indispensable. Public prayer and talking with other believers can't make up for that private communion with God, and the way to grow a spirit of prayer is simply to keep praying. That changes how you might start: don't wait until you've told someone else before you talk to God about it. What it leaves in place is that a trusted pastor or mature believer can still help when you're ready. You're not alone, and His grace is enough for you.
dogmatic: Yes, God sees what no one else knows, and He invites you to bring it into His light. But hear this clearly: whoever would help you must first deal with the beam in his own eye, so look for help from those walking honestly before God. And don't let public prayer or Christian conversation stand in for secret communion. Closet prayer is indispensable; no public devotion makes up for it. Keep praying and reading the Word even when the enjoyment is gone. Confess your faults to God without excuse and without discouragement. Don't brood, don't despair. Then peaceably resume the practice of love and adoration, returning to Him gently as a child to a father. His grace is sufficient, and He is gentle with those who come to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying evil and sin aren't things God made—they're a corruption or misuse of what is good, so God can be present in everything that exists while evil is a parasite on good, not a rival substance. One candidate principle says sickness, sin, and death are errors or illusions with no real being. That changes how I'd frame the problem: evil isn't a created thing competing with God's presence, it's an absence or mistake. But it leaves in place the hard pastoral reality that suffering feels real and devastating, and it doesn't fully explain why God permits it. So the compatibility holds, but the mystery and the need for humility remain.
dogmatic: Evil and sin are not real things at all—they're errors, illusions, absences of truth, life, and love. God, who is good, cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature, so He doesn't arrange evil results and then punish the helpless. Since evil has no genuine being, it can't conflict with God being present in all things. What looks like a contradiction is just a misunderstanding: evil is a false claim, not a substance, and God sustains only what truly exists. So the existence of evil is fully compatible with God's universal presence—there's no real rival to God at all.

weighed: I'm so sorry. Losing someone suddenly shakes everything, and it makes sense that your own death is on your mind now. What I'd say first is this: let it be real. Death comes to all of us, and it's wise to let that wake you up to what matters, without living in fear. Grief is honest, and you don't have to rush it. One idea worth sitting with is that you could count yourself as already dead, since you must die someday, and let that strip away the small stuff. What that changes is your sense of urgency and what you give your attention to. What it leaves in place is the comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future, so you can grieve with hope rather than dread.
dogmatic: You need to hear this plainly. Since you must die someday, count yourself as already dead now, and have no other desire or consolation in this perishable life than to weep over, regret, and detest your own offences. This is not the time to rejoice; it is the time to lament with all sincerity of heart. Death is not a stepping-stone to life or bliss. Sin kills the sinner as long as he sins, and the so-called sinner is a suicide. So do not imagine that dying itself frees you from sin or gives you life. Look at Mary: she died a sweet and happy death, free from attachment to earth, free from remorse of conscience, and certain of eternal glory. Let her example lift your eyes and press you to repentance, humility, and hope in God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the kingdom isn't something people build by planning, passing laws, or improving their behavior. It comes by revelation from heaven, with God himself breaking in to make his will known and set up his rule. Human effort can build organizations and tidy up behavior, but it can't produce the kingdom. One principle worth naming is that the kingdom develops gradually and requires individual labor. That doesn't replace the revelation side; it fills in how the revealed kingdom actually takes root. God establishes it, and our faithful, patient labor is caught up in it, not the engine of it.
dogmatic: The kingdom of God is not the product of human planning, legislation, or moral reform. It is established by revelation from heaven, God himself breaking into history to make his will known and set up his rule. Human effort can build organizations and improve behavior, but it cannot bring the kingdom. God sends his messenger, restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to every nation, gathers a people into a Zion, and pours out judgments that prepare the way for Christ's reign. So the kingdom comes by divine initiative and disclosure, not by committees or campaigns. Our part is to receive the revelation, repent, and align ourselves with what God is doing rather than imagining we can construct the kingdom ourselves.

weighed: My first instinct is that they're not really rivals. Science maps how nature behaves—its regularities and causes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates and sustains and relates to people. Those are different kinds of claims, so they don't have to compete. The principle that the relation between God and man is indestructible and knows no lapse from or return to harmony changes the tone here: it means the tension isn't really about God being absent or withdrawn, so the question becomes how science and faith each describe what's always been held together. What it leaves in place is the value of science for describing nature and the Bible for revealing God, and it doesn't settle every apparent conflict—those still need patient work on both sides.
dogmatic: The God of the Bible and the God science points to are not two different Gods at all. The relation between God and man is indestructible; there is no lapse from harmony and no return to it, because divine Principle and idea were never separated. Science, rightly understood, traces the order of that same divine law, and the Christian who lives that law rather than merely arguing it is the one who fathoms it best. So stop treating this as a contest between rival deities or a gap to be patched. Reflect the divine law, do violence to no man, make no false accusation, and you will see that the supposed difference is a misunderstanding, not a real division.

weighed: My first answer would be that philosophy can give you real arguments for God's existence, but proof isn't the same as knowing God. Those arguments at their best point to some ultimate cause or intelligence; they don't tell you who God is or how He relates to you, so you'd still need Scripture for that personal knowledge. One principle I'd weigh here is that the arguments from change and order are probable, not demonstrative, and can't by themselves get you to a personal, infinite, righteous God. That changes how much I'd promise: philosophy clears away objections and shows faith isn't unreasonable, but it leaves the deeper question of who God is still open, and that's where the Bible's picture still does work philosophy can't.
dogmatic: Philosophy cannot hand you the God you're asking about, and you shouldn't expect it to. The arguments from change and order are only probable; they get you an indefinitely great cause and an intelligent will, not a personal, infinite, righteous Creator. The argument from a perfect Being gives you only an ideal conclusion, what God must be if He exists, not that He does. So reason clears the ground, but it is theology as a science, grounded in revelation, that gives you the God who actually is. You still need the Bible's picture, not as a nice supplement but as the only place where the God reason gestures toward is actually made known.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's genuinely hard when your mistress doesn't share your faith and you can't get to worship, so do what you can. Set aside time for prayer and reading Scripture, maybe early morning or late at night, ask God to help you honor Him where you are, stay respectful and diligent in your duties, and let your quiet faithfulness be a witness. You could also kindly ask permission when there's an opening. One principle worth weighing is that the Sabbath is to be kept holy and not robbed, with worship and the duties of the day setting an example to those around you. That sharpens things: the day isn't optional or just for ordinary work and pleasure, so you should treat it as holy even if your circumstances limit you. What it leaves in place is exactly your situation, since you still can't attend worship and still answer to a mistress who doesn't care for religion, so the practical shape stays the same: early or late prayer and Scripture, faithfulness in your duties, and a respectful request if a door opens. It doesn't demand what you can't do; it just means you don't treat the day as ordinary.
dogmatic: The day belongs to God and must not be robbed. Don't treat it as optional or as time for ordinary labor and pleasure; keep it holy, with worship and the duties of the day, and let your example speak to everyone you're around. When you face some occasion of virtue and feel you can't manage it, turn to God and say, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless You enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. So don't lean on your own effort alone. Set aside time for prayer and Scripture, early or late, and attend to the worship and duties of the day as far as your circumstances allow. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, let your faithfulness set an example, and trust that God sees your desire to honor Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying God isn't sitting there angry, needing you to calm Him down before you can come back. Scripture shows Him as gracious and slow to anger, and Christ has already made the way for you to return. What He asks isn't that you first appease Him with enough remorse—it's that you come honestly, confess your sin, and turn from it. Your feelings might lag behind your decision, and that's normal; He doesn't require a certain emotional intensity before He'll receive you. One principle that fits here is that God commands everyone to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available—the feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. That changes the timing: you don't have to wait to feel ready or worthy; you can turn from sin in will and purpose right now, and God supplies the strength for that surrender. What it leaves in place is the call to come honestly and turn from sin—it doesn't remove repentance, it just relocates the power and the timing. So come back now, not because you've made yourself acceptable, but because He is good and ready to forgive.
dogmatic: No—God is not angry with you in a way that needs appeasing before you can return. He commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and because He commands it, the power to renounce sin is already available to you. You don't need to feel more, weep more, or wait for some greater emotional readiness. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose, and God Himself supplies the strength for that surrender; feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. So stop treating your feelings as the gate. Come back now, trusting His goodness, and let the surrender come first.

weighed: I'd start by saying: it's never too late to confess the truth to God. His mercy isn't limited by your timing—think of the thief on the cross or the workers hired at the eleventh hour. What matters is that you've come honestly now, and God doesn't turn away a contrite heart. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's work in the last days will be cut short and done more quickly than in former times. That changes the urgency—it means don't presume on endless delay or expect everything to unfold slowly. But it leaves in place the core promise: the Lord still receives you whenever you come, and your late confession can be the start of faithfulness from here.
dogmatic: It's never too late to confess the truth to God, but don't assume the days will unfold slowly as in former times. God will cut His work short in righteousness, and the events foretold are hastening. Don't set dates or calculate seasons, but do recognize that truth unveils error and sin betrays itself—concealment is impossible. Nor should you expect the world to grow better and be converted before He comes; Scripture doesn't promise that. Your hope isn't death but the return of the Lord Jesus. So let your late confession become the beginning of purity and service, living ready till He appears.

weighed: I'd start where I said before: pray, get honest counsel, and don't join anything that would make you affirm or support what you believe is unbiblical. One principle worth weighing is that work and prayer belong together—labor with all your might, but trust the outcome to God rather than to the work itself. That changes the tone of the decision: you don't have to carry the whole result on your shoulders, and you can move forward without dread. What it leaves in place is the core question—whether joining would compromise your conscience. So pray hard, work hard, and still let integrity decide between joining and starting something new.
dogmatic: Honestly, the real issue may be that you're treating a disputed point as a closed test. The Church has never been bound by one dogmatic definition of inspiration, and the field is legitimately open for free and reverent discussion—so don't let an unsettled theological question masquerade as a clear command. If the work can be done as God's business, do it without uneasiness and do it well; that's the frame you should adopt. Pair earnest, believing prayer with diligent labor and leave the increase to the Lord. Starting a new work out of anxiety rather than conviction isn't integrity—it's just fear wearing a religious coat.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling trapped by repeated mistakes is a heavy burden, and it's worth naming honestly. Many people find the cycle weakens when they examine the pattern rather than the shame: what comes before the mistake, what it promises, what it actually delivers. Freedom rarely arrives in one dramatic moment; it grows through small, deliberate choices and honest accountability with trusted people. If fear of punishment is what drives you, that fear may keep you stuck in hiding rather than change. Real change begins when you decide the mistake isn't worth its cost and act on that conviction with courage. You can be free, but the path runs through the mistake itself, not around it. One candidate principle here is that the way to escape the misery of sin is to cease sinning, and that fear of punishment never made anyone truly honest. That principle sharpens the point about fear—it confirms that punishment-driven fear keeps you hiding rather than changing. But it also changes the tone: it says there's no other way but to stop, which can leave in place the idea that you must simply will yourself out, without the gradual, pattern-examining, accountable process that actually helps people break cycles. So I'd keep the honesty about fear, but not let it erase the slow work of understanding the pattern.
dogmatic: You keep making the same mistakes because you keep choosing them. The way out isn't a technique or a workaround—it's ceasing to do the thing that binds you. No escape from the misery of sin exists except to stop sinning. Fear of punishment won't free you; it only drives you to hide. What frees you is moral courage: the decision to refuse the wrong because it is wrong. Don't accept relapse as a real reaction or an inevitable stage; in Truth there is no necessity to fall again. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: identify the thought or desire that precedes the act, face it squarely without excuse, and refuse it before it takes hold. Conquer the fear that says you cannot change. Alongside this, bridle your tongue, subdue anger, and examine yourself rather than judging or meddling in others' affairs; attend to your own duties faithfully. The misery ends where the sin ends. Take courage: you can be free, and the road is the straight one of leaving the wrong behind.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this is a real tension, and the answer depends on the need, the timing, and the worker's own sense of calling. If another field is truly desperate and you can spare the person, releasing them is the generous choice; if your own work would collapse, it's fair to decline or offer someone else. One principle that sharpens this is that missionaries should invite rather than compel and speak of predecessors as brothers who did their best. That changes the tone: you'd frame the ask as an invitation, honor the worker's freedom, and speak well of whoever served before. It leaves the core judgment intact, since need, timing, and calling still decide the case.
dogmatic: You should release your best workers whenever another field asks, and do it without hesitation. Generosity is the only posture that fits the work, and holding people back out of possessiveness is simply wrong. Invite, never compel, and treat each worker as a soul with a calling rather than a resource you own. Speak of those who came before as brothers who did their best, and trust God to supply what you lack rather than clinging to what you have.

weighed: I'd start with what Amos 8:11–12 actually says: a famine not of bread or water but of hearing the words of the Lord—people wandering from sea to sea, seeking the word and not finding it. Interpreters differ on fulfillment: some see a future judgment on a people who neglected God's word and were left without prophetic guidance; others hear a warning for any age when Scripture is ignored or religious voices grow confused. One principle here is that God warns before he punishes, as he did through Noah and the prophets. That principle changes the tone—it frames the famine as a summons to heed the warning while it's still given, not just a grim prediction. But it leaves in place the core point: the word of God is a gift that can be withdrawn, and hearing it is not guaranteed. So I'd still say the passage invites us to value and attend to God's word now.
dogmatic: Amos 8:11–12 is a famine of hearing the words of the Lord—not bread or water, but the word itself. And this famine is on us now: voices multiply, certainty fades, and disappointment spreads among believers. God's people are called out of Babylon, to hold fast the true hope of Christ's coming. Don't demand visible signs or flee the world in despair—God speaks in the still small voice, and we choose to believe rather than see, casting bread upon the waters in sure hope. Remember, God does not punish without warning; he sends messengers before judgment, as before the flood, Sodom, and Jerusalem. So heed the warning while it is still given.

weighed: My first answer was that Zion is a place of gathering and spiritual community, and whether you should gather depends on your circumstances—weigh family, work, finances, and avoid unhealthy groups. One candidate principle says church duties should be paramount above every other interest, with the cause of Zion uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love. That principle changes the framing: gathering isn't just a personal choice to weigh against practical concerns; it becomes a priority that other interests should be ordered around. But it leaves in place the practical reality that you still have to work, care for family, and use judgment about any group—it doesn't erase those concerns, just reorders them.
dogmatic: Zion is the cause of God—a people and place of holiness where the Church's duties are paramount over every worldly interest. While you must be industrious in your worldly labors, those labors serve the cause of Zion, which should be uppermost in your thoughts and highest in your love. Gathering to Zion is not a mere lifestyle preference; you order family, work, and finances around it rather than the reverse. The Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, and what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. Yet this is not escape from a worthless world: the earth abides its creation and is destined for renewal, so you do not despise or flee it but sanctify it, building up Zion here. Yes—seek Zion, let every other interest take its proper place, and labor to make the desert bloom.

weighed: I'd start by saying the struggle is real if it actually costs you something—if it changes your choices, your habits, and your relationships, not just your feelings. One idea worth weighing is that the practical answer to evil isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: stepping back from fixating on sin to the greater reality of God's goodness, so that studying evil doesn't intoxicate or paralyze your will. That changes how you fight—you fight from confidence in God's goodness rather than from obsession with the darkness—but it leaves your original test in place: the struggle still has to show up in real change, real resistance, real repair. So keep testing your life against what you profess, and let the evidence of genuine change encourage you.
dogmatic: Stop looking for an explanation of why evil is permitted—that's not the remedy. The practical solution is proportion: pull back from the study of sin, because dwelling on it intoxicates the will and paralyzes it with despair, and exult instead in the universal goodness of God. That disengages your will from evil and gives it a new temper for the contest. And don't turn the supply of workers and means into a human problem: if God orders a work, He fits the individuals to it and furnishes the means, as He did for the Tabernacle. Ideas about God and aspirations after Him strain as much as they lift and can't carry you all the way; reverence alone never saved a soul in the storm of life. It's One by your side—in trust, sympathy, and comradeship, fighting together in the ranks—who thrills your strength and keeps your right hand fresh. That's why the struggle is no sham.

weighed: Yes, God can cleanse your thoughts—his cleansing isn't limited to outward actions; it reaches the mind where sin starts. Impure thoughts are often habitual, and habits of thought can be retrained. Start by noticing when the thoughts come up without beating yourself up, then deliberately turn your attention to something worthwhile. Prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability help. Practical steps—limiting what feeds your imagination, avoiding triggering situations, filling idle time—can make a real difference. Progress is usually gradual, and setbacks don't mean failure. God is patient, and the fact that you want to be cleansed is itself a sign of grace at work. One idea worth weighing is that the soul resting in God desires only him, and if some of this turmoil is delusion, it belongs to God to remedy it. That changes the pressure you put on yourself: the struggle stops being a self-managed project, and you can leave the outcome to God. What it leaves in place is the practical work—noticing the thought, refusing it, and turning toward what's pure. So keep bringing the thoughts into the light and asking for help; over time your mind can be renewed.
dogmatic: Yes, God's cleansing reaches the mind, because that's where sin begins. The root of the disorder is in mortal mind, not just in outward acts, and cleansing has to start there—sin and sickness alike. Guard your thoughts before error shows up, because evil thoughts left unchecked come to control the body and the life. Catch the impure thought the moment it arises, refuse it, and turn your mind toward what is pure. But don't turn this into a self-managed project. A soul that truly rests in God desires only him; if some of this turmoil is delusion, leave the remedy to God. Do everything as perfectly as you can for God, then stop measuring the size or quality of what you've finished and think instead about what's next to be done. Anxiety about your progress is itself a distraction. Attend to the next right thought and the next duty, and leave the increase to God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your resentment makes sense, and God doesn't brush off the pain you're carrying. Bring it to Him honestly instead of letting it sit and fester. Forgiveness isn't pretending nothing happened; it's handing the debt to God, who judges fairly. He asks you to forgive as you've been forgiven, not because the hurt was small, but because bitterness does more damage to you than to the person who hurt you. Start by praying for them, even badly, and ask God to soften your heart over time. One idea worth weighing is that God wants to give Himself to us in prayer, and asking only for relief or for the other person to be set right can fall short of that. That idea changes what you're asking for; it doesn't change the fact that the wound is real or that forgiveness takes time. Healing is usually slow, so be patient with yourself, and get wise counsel if the resentment feels stuck.
dogmatic: Your resentment is real to you, but the truth bids you reverse the belief of injury: a person made in God's image is not truly hurt, and the harm you seem to suffer is a false claim about God's child. When the sense of injury returns, treat it as a lapse in remembering God. Meet it without disquiet and return with greater trust, knowing God is All. Go further: God, in His promises to hear our prayers, desires to bestow Himself upon us. If you ask only for relief from resentment or for the offender to be set right, you ask for something beneath Him and put an affront upon Him, hurting yourself by preferring a creature He framed to Him. Ask instead for God Himself, and in receiving Him you will find the resentment dissolved, for nothing beneath Him can hold your heart once He fills it.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: pray for wisdom, since God promises to give it generously, then look honestly at the decision—what Scripture says, what wise and mature Christians advise, what the likely consequences are, your motives and gifts, and whether an option moves you toward or away from Christ. Where Scripture is clear, obey it; where it's silent, use good judgment. You don't need perfect certainty before acting—God often guides as you step forward in faith. One principle worth taking seriously is that faith isn't working up certainty by willpower but seeing as fact that God has said it, turning his promise into a prophecy and resting in it. That changes the tone of the whole process: your confidence rests in God's character rather than in how sure you feel. What it leaves in place is the honest work—prayer, Scripture, counsel, examining motives—because resting in a promise doesn't excuse you from thinking it through. So do the work, then step forward trusting that he guides a willing heart, and don't let fear of getting it wrong paralyze you.
dogmatic: Stop treating this as a puzzle you have to solve before God will move. God has said he will guide you—take that as fact, not a faint hope. Turn his promise into a prophecy spoken over your life and rest in it, because God cannot lie. Be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, not by straining to manufacture certainty but by rejoicing that what he has said is true. Take his promises and comforts as largely and mightily as you can, and your troubles as lightly as you can—set them at nothing. The uncertainty looming so large is small beside the God who has spoken. Look at Scripture, wise counsel, your gifts, the circumstances, yes—but let your confidence rest in the God who cannot lie, not in your effort to be sure. Then step forward not as someone managing an anxious riddle but as someone carried by a promise that is already true.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: get to know the truth deeply, test every teaching against the gospel—does it honor Christ, uphold his death and resurrection, and produce real love and holiness?—and watch for flattery, quick promises, and money demands. Then look at the teacher's character and fruits, ask whether the teaching makes you more dependent on Christ or on the teacher, pray for wisdom, and stay rooted in a faithful community that can help you evaluate claims. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that teaching in the name of Truth while contradicting its spirit or rules is dangerous quackery, and that strict adherence to the divine Principle secures success. That principle sharpens my prior by making the test of consistency with the Principle itself central, and it adds a warning against attractive error that borrows truth's language while violating its spirit. But it leaves in place the core gospel tests, the concern about character and fruits, the caution about money and flattery, and the need for prayer and community—so it changes the emphasis, not the foundation.
dogmatic: Discernment has to be practised strictly according to the divine Principle, not by material means or human suspicion. Truth is one and self-consistent; error is discordant and self-contradictory. Test every teaching by the Principle itself: does it proceed from and return to God as All, or does it introduce a power, cause, or fear apart from Him? Apply the rules of the scientific method to thought: observe the claim, examine its premises, and see whether it accords with the divine Principle or merely pleases the senses. Attractive error borrows the language of truth while violating its spirit. Judge not by personalities, crowds, or outward results. And do not abandon the learner at the end of the lesson: continue in loving care and counsel until students tread firmly in the way. Yet never teach mental healing indiscriminately for fees. Refuse to impart it to the morally unfit for money; require honesty, purity, and genuine fitness in the student. The Principle is not a commodity, and its teaching must be guarded by moral fitness, not sold to whoever pays.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: superficiality usually grows out of a ministry powered by activity instead of depth. Sermons get rushed, prayer gets squeezed out, your own walk with God thins out, and the ministry ends up reflecting that thinness. Fear plays a part too, since wanting to please people or stay safe keeps the preaching shallow. What I'd add is this: the deepest root may be a lack of praying. That doesn't cancel the practical stuff like unhurried time in Scripture or honest self-examination, but it reframes it. Prayer stops being one more task on the list and becomes the source the whole ministry runs on. So I'd still tell you to slow down and preach what costs, but I'd tell you to start by tracing your shallowness back to your praying.
dogmatic: The root of superficial ministry is prayerlessness, plain and simple. We blame circumstances, methods, or the audience, but the real cause is that prayer has been left out. There are two traps. One is hiding away to study and pray and never spending any of it on people. The other is chasing relevance and activity until prayer has no place in the plans at all. Both are dead ends. Time with God only counts as it gets poured out on the people you serve. And remember this: the condition of a church rarely rises above the religion of its leaders. Where the pulpit is shallow, the people starve. So let your text, your sermon, and your study be soaked in prayer. A polished sermon made without prayer is dead; a plain ministry soaked in prayer is alive. Find your superficiality in your praying, and begin there.

weighed: What I'd say first is that your fear makes sense, and God is merciful. Scripture says he wants everyone saved and his mercy is great. If you're afraid you haven't found him, he's already seeking you. Turn to Christ now while there's time: confess, trust, receive his forgiveness. Don't despair, because his grace isn't limited by your timing. One idea worth weighing is that God never forsakes us until we've first forsaken him, so the real question is whether you'll leave him, not whether you've hit some deadline. That shifts the focus from your timing to your staying, and it leaves your fear in place as a real thing, but it doesn't leave you alone in it. Talk with a pastor, pray honestly, and let the fear push you toward God rather than away.
dogmatic: Your fear is real, but it isn't the strongest thing in the room. God never forsakes us until we've first forsaken him; he doesn't abandon a soul that hasn't abandoned him. So stop measuring yourself against a deadline and ask instead whether you'll leave him. Fear to forsake him, and stay with him, living and dying in his presence. If you've forgotten him for a while, don't let that disquiet you. Acknowledge your wretchedness and return with greater trust. Your fear can't outrun a Love that pursues you. At every crossroad and bypath, Love meets you and gently turns you back. Your anxiety isn't a successful defense; it's a door Love is already knocking through. Turn to Christ now: confess, trust, receive his forgiveness. Let forgetfulness lead you back with deeper confidence, and let the Love that pursues you be your peace.

weighed: I'd start by telling you to separate the insult from your worth—your value isn't decided by someone else's contempt. When you're mocked, pause, breathe, and don't react out of fear. Ask whether there's any truth in the criticism; if there is, learn from it quietly, and if there isn't, let it go. Set calm boundaries with people who keep being cruel, and lean on friends who see you accurately. One idea worth holding onto is that some kinds of mockery say more about the mocker than about you—mocking someone old, sick, or less sharp is just base and cruel. That idea changes how you hear the insult: it gives you a way to see contempt as the other person's ugliness rather than your shame. What it leaves in place is the rest—checking for truth, keeping boundaries, and not letting fear of scorn run your choices.
dogmatic: The real answer is to stop weighing yourself by other people's contempt at all. Some mockery is simply base: mocking an old man, a sick person, or someone simple-minded reveals the mocker's own ugliness, and you should see it that way rather than absorb it. Good manners, skill, and wisdom are fair things that hide ugliness and deserve honour, so judge yourself by those. Be sweet and affable to everyone, bend to others' humour, and bear rude manners—these victories are more fruitful than you can imagine. Don't boast when an enemy falls; when you see things as they are, flattery and reproach become alike, and you grow in humility.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Name the loss honestly, let the anger be felt without letting it rule you, and take practical steps—gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, set boundaries so the wrong isn't repeated. Guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time, and let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. One principle that sharpens this is that we must do the one thing God has set before us and refuse the side-tracks of irritation and petty grievances. That changes the focus: instead of replaying the injury, you press steadily on the main thing God has given you today, letting grievances come and go without being derailed by them. What it leaves in place is everything practical—naming the loss, seeking fair resolution, setting boundaries, and the slow work of forgiveness. It doesn't tell you to drop the dispute; it tells you not to let the dispute become your whole business.
dogmatic: Your only business in this life is to please God, and all besides is folly and vanity. So renounce all that is not Him—including the grip this dispute has on you—and put all your trust in Him. Repair the lost time, return with assurance to the Father of mercies, and think of Him perpetually. Do not let irritation, petty grievances, or other people's business pull you off the one thing God has set before you. Handle what must be handled in the name of the Lord, but hold the outcome loosely and refuse to let revenge or replaying the injury rule you. Let His goodness in by attending to what He sets before you today, in perpetual remembrance of Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying the question sets up a false dilemma. If Jesus claimed oneness with God, that doesn't force a choice between deceiver and deluded, because there's a third option: he was telling the truth. Christians point to his teaching, his miracles, and the resurrection as evidence. I'd also note the Gospel writers shaped their accounts for theological reasons, so the claim might reflect the early church's confession more than a raw historical quote. One principle worth naming is that Christ's testimony to himself can't be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God. That principle shifts the burden: it says his moral sanity and consistency rule out fraud and delusion. But it leaves the historical question in place, since you still have to weigh the sources and decide whether that testimony goes back to Jesus himself. So the dilemma isn't exhaustive, and honest inquiry should weigh the evidence and the fruit of his life.
dogmatic: The question sets up a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God doesn't force a choice between deceiver and deluded, because there's a third option: he was telling the truth. Look at his consistent holiness, his calm self-mastery under trial, his sinless conscience. A deceiver wouldn't live that way, and a deluded man couldn't sustain that kind of moral sanity. Since Jesus can't be charged with mental or moral unsoundness, his testimony must be true, and he himself must be one with God. God stays faithful even when our faith fails; unbelief costs us, not him. And it's no fraud for God to use literary methods suited to an undeveloped age, like dramatic composition or idealizing history, as vehicles of inspiration. That's different from deliberate deceit.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: repentance isn't mainly a feeling, it's a turning. So ask yourself whether you've honestly named the sin, grieved it, and actually changed direction. The signs worth looking for are sorrow over the wrong itself rather than over getting caught, a willingness to make amends where you can, and a settled change in how you live over time. If it still troubles you, bring it honestly to God, confess it, and receive forgiveness, and it can help to talk with a trusted pastor or counselor. One idea worth weighing is that there's no exaltation except through obedience, and that late repentance can't restore what sin cost you. That's a sobering point, and it's true that some consequences don't come back. But it doesn't cancel the promise of forgiveness, and it doesn't mean God is holding out on you now. It just means your repentance is real if it shows up as obedience going forward, not as recovering the past. Assurance tends to grow through that obedience and over time, not through endlessly searching your feelings.
dogmatic: Stop hunting for a feeling and look at the law. There is no exaltation except through obedience, and repenting late does not give back what sin took. You can be forgiven and still carry the loss, so don't expect your remorse to restore it. And don't settle for being told there's no sin. Forgiveness isn't God winking at sin while you keep believing in it; it's the destruction of sin through spiritual understanding that casts evil out as unreal. But you can't skip to that by declaring sin unreal while its claim sits undetected in you. First detect the claim, strip off its mask, point out the illusion, and only then prove its unreality. Do that work, and the question of whether you've repented stops being about your feelings and becomes about what you actually obey.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your suffering is real, and it hurts, and when pain drags on it's natural to feel it has no purpose. Meaning rarely shows up in the middle of it; it often appears later, in what it teaches—patience, compassion, clarity about what matters—and in small ways you can make it count now, like reaching out to someone else who hurts or letting others care for you. If the pointlessness feels crushing, please talk to a counselor or someone you trust. One principle I'd weigh in is that abandonment to God in interior and exterior suffering is excellent, and it's good to live, work, and rejoice—but in God. That changes the frame: the pain isn't just something to endure until insight arrives; it can be handed over, and your life and work and even joy can be held in God right now. What it leaves in place is everything you said—the pain still hurts, meaning still may not show up on schedule, and reaching out for help still matters. It doesn't erase the pointlessness you feel; it gives you somewhere to put it.
dogmatic: Your suffering is not pointless, and you won't find its meaning by denying it or by chasing relief on your own terms. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior pain alike; let Him be your life, your work, and your joy. Suffering serves: it can correct what needs turning, purify the heart, prevent harm, and above all unite you with God and with others who suffer. As in the Cross, the value is set before the painfulness—love, obedience, and union with God come first, and the pain serves them. So don't look for meaning outside of God or wait for the pain to vanish before you live. Give yourself wholly to Him, and let even this suffering be drawn into His purpose, making you more like Christ and closer to the God who holds you.

weighed: I'd start with the traditional answer: the true cross is known by a miracle, not by human reasoning. In the legend, Helena finds three crosses, and when the third is laid on a dead man, he comes back to life, so that's the sign. One principle here is that the cross is part of the whole process of the making of men, not a backup plan after something went wrong. That shifts the framing a bit, but it leaves the core answer in place: the miracle is still what identifies the cross.
dogmatic: You know the true cross by divine testimony, not by any human reasoning or mark on the wood. The dead man rises only when the third cross is laid on him, and that miracle is the sign. And this cross isn't some afterthought patched in after a disaster; it belongs to the whole process of the making of men and the travail for a redeemed humanity. So look to heaven for aid, not to the size of your own host, and the sign will be made plain.

weighed: I'd start by saying that other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons—its emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden understanding and foster respect. But Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. One principle that shifts this is that all Christian religion consists in learning to know ourselves: where we came from, what we are, how we fell into division and wickedness, and how we may be delivered and recover our original blessedness. That principle changes the focus from comparing religions to self-examination under Scripture—so Hinduism's meditations might sharpen our sense of the inward journey, but they don't supply the way of deliverance. What it leaves in place is the value of learning from others and the call to hold firmly to Christ, while making the Bible the one fountain of wisdom we read daily and prayerfully.
dogmatic: You should not treat Hinduism as a source of spiritual lessons on par with your own faith. All Christian religion consists in learning to know yourself: where you came from, what you are, how you went forth from unity into dissension and wickedness, and how you may be delivered and recover your original blessedness. The Holy Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength; read and study the Bible habitually and prayerfully, translating what you find into obedience, and prefer it above all other books. True religion, the religion that wholly satisfies, is to have Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in your soul—the New Life and the New Birth. Read in that light, Hinduism's meditations may sharpen your sense of the inward journey, but Scripture alone supplies the way of deliverance. So learn from other religions only insofar as they point you back to self-knowledge and Scripture, never as a substitute for Christ living in you.

weighed: I'd start by saying you can bring any request to God, but don't expect Him to break the laws of nature on demand. Asking for a weather change or a healing that defies nature is essentially asking for a sign on your terms, and Scripture doesn't present that as the way of faith. God usually works through ordinary providence—medicine, weather patterns, wise choices. So pray for healing and good weather, yes, but submit to His will and don't treat an unanswered supernatural request as failure. One principle worth weighing is that God can heal in answer to prayer, especially when doctors have done all they can or medical help is out of reach—Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. That principle shifts the focus from demanding nature-breaking signs to trusting God's power in real need, but it leaves in place the caution against making visible signs the measure of faith. You still pray boldly and leave the outcome in His hands.
dogmatic: You should absolutely pray for God to change the weather or heal someone beyond what nature allows, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever—He hasn't lost the power to act beyond the natural order. Don't settle for a faith that only trusts medicine and weather patterns; that's a diminished view of God. Bring every request boldly, expecting Him to move, and don't let anyone tell you that asking for a nature-breaking miracle is off-limits. The still small voice doesn't cancel the possibility of the extraordinary—it calls you to believe rather than demand a sign, but belief includes trusting Him for the impossible. Cast your bread upon the waters and expect to find it after many days. Lift your gaze above the world's uncertain haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, and then return to your daily world to love and serve, preparing the Lord's way of mercy with a heart fixed on the hope beyond what you can see.

weighed: I'd start where you already are: keep a simple prayer journal. Write down each request with the date, then note when and how it was answered, and review it regularly—weekly or monthly—so you can see God's faithfulness over time. Set phone reminders or carry a small notebook so you can jot down answers as they come, and sharing it with a trusted friend can help too. One principle worth adding is that testimony of what God has actually done strengthens faith, so recording definite answers to His glory and for the help of those who doubt fits naturally here. That changes the purpose of your record a bit—it becomes not just a memory aid for you but something that can encourage others. What it leaves in place is the simple habit itself: dates, requests, answers, and regular review, just as you're already doing.
dogmatic: Don't just keep a private list—treat your record as testimony. Write down each request with the date, note the definite answer, and thank God specifically, naming His faithfulness aloud. Then tell others: family, church, anyone who doubts, so God is honored and faith is strengthened beyond you. And remember that answers to prayer aren't a technique for experts—they rest on the conditions God has given: contrite humility, forsaking sin, seeking Him wholeheartedly, faith, obedience, dependence on the Holy Spirit, persistence, asking according to His will, asking in Christ's name, and willingness to make amends. So examine your heart, confess sin, and submit your requests to Him. Yet every believer, however ordinary, is freely invited into the full knowledge of Christ Himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid. Let your record lead you past the gift to the Giver, into deeper fellowship with the sufficient Savior.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear is real, and Scripture takes it seriously, but God's love doesn't stop at the grave. The psalmist asks where he can flee from God's presence and finds that even in Sheol, God is there. Death is an enemy, but not a boundary God can't cross. So yes, God's pursuit isn't limited by death. One idea worth weighing is that if God aims at something not fully realized here, that gives us ground to hope for a life beyond this one. That adds a reason for confidence, but it doesn't change the core answer, and it doesn't mean death itself brings you closer to God or lets you put off seeking him now. The fear you feel is real, but it isn't the final word.
dogmatic: Your fear of death is real, but it can't outrun the Love that's chasing you. Fear can't evade what Love means to pursue; at every crossroads, Love meets your fear and turns it back. But don't imagine dying will bring you nearer to God or finish what you left undone. This world is where you find him, and the remedy has to be found now, because here it's easiest and quickest to reach him. Immortality follows from believing in a righteous God whose purpose for us isn't exhausted by this life, but that hope doesn't excuse you from seeking him here. Trust the Love pursuing you now, and seek him while he may be found.

weighed: I'd start by saying test the burden by its fruit and its persistence. If the concern keeps returning and moves you toward love rather than anxiety or pride, it's likely from God. Ask whether it aligns with Scripture and draws you closer to Christ. A burden from God usually comes with a quiet sense of responsibility rather than pressure. You can also seek counsel from a mature believer. If the burden fades when you pray about it, it may have just been a passing emotion. Ultimately, pray about it and trust that God will confirm or remove the burden in His timing. One principle that fits here is that nothing is too small to bring to God—we honor Him by asking His guidance even in small things. That changes the tone: instead of only analyzing the burden, you deliberately hand it to God and ask Him directly. It leaves in place the practical tests of fruit, Scripture, and counsel, but it adds a clear invitation to pray about the burden itself, not just the person.
dogmatic: You should bring every burden, no matter how small or uncertain, straight to God and ask Him plainly whether it's from Him. Don't settle it by your own analysis—place it in His hands and wait for His guidance. Test it by Scripture and by the counsel of mature believers, asking God to confirm or remove it. Measure the burden not by how it makes you feel but by whether it moves you to seek His glory and the good of the one far away. Ask in faith, nothing wavering, trusting that God, who understands all things, hears the earnest prayer of the soul and your innermost thoughts. Keep bringing each impression to Him rather than deciding it alone.

weighed: I'd start by saying looking up for Christ's coming isn't a mistake, but it has to be understood rightly. He promised to return in glory, and we're to watch and wait, yet not stand idle staring at the sky. Watching means active faithfulness: repentance, prayer, love, so He finds you ready. One principle here is that Christ is found by the lowly in heart, and Heaven stoops to guide even the simplest person to where He dwells. That changes the tone: it's less about straining your eyes upward and more about trusting God's mercy to lead you, even if you're simple. It leaves in place the hope and the watching, and it still calls you to prepare the Lord's way through mercy and love each day.
dogmatic: Looking up for Christ's coming is no mistake, since He promised to return in glory. But don't turn it into idle sky-gazing. Christ is revealed to the lowly in heart, and Heaven will stoop to guide even the simplest seeker to where He dwells, so trust that mercy rather than your own straining. Don't pry into what God wills for someone else's end; if their love for Christ is true, that's enough, and your job is to follow Him yourself. Lift your gaze above the world's haze to the bright fields beyond the sky, and prepare His way of mercy, turning now to follow wherever He leads.

weighed: My first answer would be that the gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion reflect two distinct purposes in God's plan. Jerusalem is tied to the return and restoration of the Jews, while Zion is the place prepared for the saints. These gatherings aren't in competition; each serves its own role. One principle that fits here is that unity doesn't mean uniformity—the Saints are to be of one heart and one mind while each fills their own calling. That principle changes how I'd frame the two gatherings: they're not rivals, and unity doesn't require everyone to be alike. But it leaves in place the basic distinction between the two gatherings and their purposes.
dogmatic: The gathering of the Jews to Jerusalem and the gathering of the saints to Zion are two separate works with two separate purposes, and we shouldn't blur them. Jerusalem belongs to the return and restoration of the Jews. Zion is the place prepared for the saints, and the Lord guided the Saints to the mountains, where what seemed a barren desert has proved a blessing, fulfilling the prediction that Zion should flourish and the desert blossom as the rose. The earth isn't worthless or doomed to destruction; it abides its creation and is destined for renewal. So the Saints shouldn't despise or flee the earth but build up Zion here, sanctifying the land and their lives to the Lord. Unity is strength, but it's a unity of heart and purpose that honors different gifts and callings, not everyone being alike.

weighed: My first instinct is that this is still genuinely open: cosmology points to a starting point for our observable universe, but that doesn't settle whether time itself began or something came before. One idea worth weighing is that the only pre-existence no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20 as foreknown before the foundation of the world. That shifts the question from measuring a cosmic clock to asking whether history has a purpose behind it, but it leaves the scientific and philosophical debate about an infinite past exactly where it was. So I'd still say we can't observe our way to a verdict; the honest answer rests on inference and what you trust.
dogmatic: The world's beginning is not finally a puzzle for cosmology to solve. The one pre-existence no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20: foreknown before the foundation of the world, manifested for our sake. Matter and intelligence are eternal and cannot be annihilated; nothing becomes nothing, and organized existence must increase or decrease, never stand still. The world's beginning is simply the field where a foreknown purpose unfolds. This Greek Christology, Christ as first spirit and beginning of all creation who became flesh, is the root of the orthodox dogmatic system, and Christ as beginning of creation led straight to the Logos conception. So stop treating the question as an open debate and live within that purpose, growing rather than standing still.

weighed: I'd start where I said before: be honest with God that you can't fully see your own motives, ask him to search you, and set aside time to reflect on why you do what you do. Then bring what you find to a trusted friend or pastor who can help you see yourself more clearly. One principle worth adding is that purity of heart grows through specific practices, not just general honesty—keeping your senses under guard, living with a sense of God's presence, and laying your whole interior open to a wise guide with real candor. That changes the how: it turns self-examination into something concrete and shared, and it adds the idea of actively rooting out habitual imperfections. What it leaves in place is the core you already have—sincerity isn't perfect self-knowledge, it's a steady willingness to be corrected by God.
dogmatic: Stop treating sincerity as a feeling you have to verify before you act. Purity of heart is cultivated by specific means: find your habitual imperfections and root them out, keep your senses under strict guard through frequent denials, live in recollection and the practice of God's presence, and lay open your whole interior to a spiritual director with complete candor, proposing the perfect accomplishment of God's will in all things. A passing glance at judgment does not change a heart, and conversions produced by fear of calamity rarely bear the marks of sincerity—penitents must be brought to a sincere and perfect change of heart. And do not make your moods the measure of whether you are right with God; feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to him. Rest on the changeless word of promise, continue steadfastly in prayer when joy is lacking, and refuse to abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.

weighed: The first thing I'd say is that bigger crowds and more attention don't tell you much on their own. Look at the fruit instead: are people actually being changed, growing in holiness, humility, and love, or just enjoying the energy of a crowd? Check your own life too, in prayer, obedience, and love for God and neighbor, and ask whether the teaching is faithful to Scripture and making mature disciples rather than consumers. One idea worth weighing is that real growth comes through growth itself, not by piling on more stuff. That shifts how you measure things, away from additions and toward depth, but it leaves your core test intact: changed lives, faithful teaching, and your own walk with God.
dogmatic: Numbers and popularity are not spiritual growth, full stop. The real question is fruit: changed people growing in holiness, humility, and love, not crowds enjoying themselves. And you should understand growth as growth, not accretion. You don't get there by adding programs, crowds, or excitement; you get there by doing the scientific work of proving God for yourself. That is the standard, and it doesn't bend. Examine your own prayer, obedience, and love for God and neighbor, and ask whether the teaching is faithful to Scripture and producing mature disciples rather than consumers. If the growth is only accretion, it isn't growth at all.

weighed: Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee of heaven apart from a living faith. Scripture warns that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, and that we must be born again and continue in faith. Your baptism marks you as belonging to Christ and calls you to live out that faith. So examine yourself: are you trusting Christ, growing in love, and walking with God? Death itself does not change the heart. Take your faith seriously now, and let your hope rest in Christ rather than in the mere fact of being baptized or dying. One principle that speaks to this is that present salvation is what we need—religion must be with us from one Monday to the next, and we should prepare to live rather than merely prepare to die. That principle changes the focus from a future guarantee to a present walk with God, but it leaves in place the call to trust Christ and live faithfully today.
dogmatic: Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee of heaven. Scripture warns that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom. Many look to death to work a miracle, thinking that the cessation of physical life gives entry to paradise so long as we are baptized and call ourselves Christians. That is a delusion, for in character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. Present salvation is what we need: religion must be with us from one Monday to the next, and we should prepare to live rather than merely prepare to die. Do not frame religion mainly as preparation for death or the afterlife; the demand is for present, everyday salvation and the continual enjoyment of the Spirit. Live faithfully today and let the Millennium take care of itself. And ground the comfort of the bereaved not in vague hope or human speculation but in the cardinal fact of the resurrection—Christ's own victory over death and His promises—so that we speak with the Apostle's confidence of present realities rather than uncertain hopes.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's understandable to feel torn, and many people do. You can pursue your career while making real room for God—set priorities, keep prayer and community in your week, and let your work be a way of serving God done ethically. One principle worth weighing here is that we shouldn't multiply undertakings through curiosity, ambition, or restlessness, because those burden us and pull us away from God more than legitimate work does. That changes the picture: it's not just about balancing hours, it's about not letting ambition spawn endless extra commitments that scatter your heart. What it leaves in place is your desire to give yourself fully to both—your work can still be a genuine vocation, and your faith can still shape it. So the honest answer is yes, but with a guard against restlessness: keep your work legitimate and bounded, and let your devotion to God be the thing that orders everything else.
dogmatic: The Gospel stands above the tug-of-war between career and faith. Its one aim is that you find God and have Him as your own—not that you split yourself between two masters. So begin by refusing the restless curiosity and ambition that multiply your occupations and divide your heart; limit yourself to legitimate work and let go of the endless striving for more. Then abandon yourself to God in both interior and exterior suffering, including the frustration of unmet ambitions and the daily cross of your work. Live, work, and rejoice—but in God, not in career success. When you surrender your ambitions to Him, even disappointments become occasions of trust. Give yourself fully to God, and your work becomes part of that single-hearted devotion rather than a rival to it.

weighed: I'd start by saying that resistance in kids is normal—they get distracted, they question things, they test boundaries, and sometimes it's just their stage of development or friends rubbing off on them. So I'd make God more relatable, use stories, model faith in daily life, stay patient, keep the door open for questions, and not force it. One idea worth naming is that we're here above all for personal connection with God, not just a successful career or a good time. That reframes the resistance a bit: instead of only managing behavior, I'd ask whether the bigger messages around them are teaching them to be shy about spiritual things. It changes the focus from fixing a phase to shaping what they love. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—patience, consistency, open conversation, and not pushing too hard.
dogmatic: The resistance you're seeing isn't something to fight head-on. Contending with it just fixes it more firmly in their minds. Instead, put another picture in front of them—Jesus and his pure, beautiful invitations—and help them move their allegiance from the glamour of evil to the glamour of God. Teach them that God is ever-present and all-powerful, and that our chief purpose here is personal connection with God, not career success, holidays, or parties. When they catch a vision of Jesus' beauty and love, the resistance fades. Fill their minds with pictures of his goodness and pray that the Holy Spirit makes him irresistible, so they gladly follow.

weighed: Yes, you may grieve. Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, so sorrow isn't a failure of faith. One thing I'd add: your comfort rests on Christ himself—his cross, resurrection, and pleading for you—not on how steady your feelings are right now. That shifts where you look when the grief feels overwhelming, but it leaves your tears fully allowed. You can mourn the separation and still rejoice that your friend is with the Lord.
dogmatic: You ask whether you may grieve, but the deeper question is where your consolation rests. It rests wholly on Christ—his incarnation, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and intercession—not on your own frames or feelings, which are clouded by sin and unbelief. So meet this death with calm, hopeful fortitude, planting the ensign of salvation upon the grave, not giving way to despondency. Do not wish the pain away; ask for a wise and thankful heart, yield your will to God's rod, and let your grief become a sacrifice of thanksgiving that your friend is with Christ.

weighed: Start by examining your conscience — go through the Ten Commandments and the Church's teaching, ask the Holy Spirit for light, and write down your sins honestly and thoroughly. Then confess with sincerity, receive absolution, and do your penance; pray beforehand for real contrition and a firm purpose to amend. One principle worth naming is that the retreat's early days are meant to purify the soul from all guilt of sin and all attachment to sin, with confession as the most efficient means. That sharpens your preparation toward thoroughness and even small sins, but it leaves your practical steps — examination, contrition, confession, penance — exactly where they were.
dogmatic: The first days of this retreat are the most important days of your year, because your own salvation and spiritual progress come first — what does it profit you to gain the whole world and lose your own soul? So treat confession as the chief work of these days: review your sins carefully, confess promptly and thoroughly, and forsake even small sins at once. Cultivate obedience and gratitude, and let no mercy of God go unrecognized. Do not presume your salvation is already secure; purify your soul from all guilt and all attachment to sin, and let your heart overflow with thanksgiving for His forgiveness.

weighed: I'd start by saying that ordinary, unseen work is where most of us actually serve God. Faithfulness in a daily task, honesty in small dealings, patience with family, and quiet diligence are the substance of a godly life. One principle worth naming is that we must discover God's will and then do it joyfully or at least courageously, serving Him as He wills rather than in a way of our own choosing. That principle changes the focus from simply offering each task to God to actively seeking His direction first. It leaves in place the value of hidden labor and the truth that God sees what is done in secret and honors it.
dogmatic: You should not assume that any ordinary work is automatically God's will for you. You must actively seek out His will and then carry it out joyfully or at least courageously, serving Him only as He wills. Do not substitute your own preferred way of serving for the actual discovery of His will. Carry on His work within the landmarks of His word: do not seek the patronage of the world, do not depend on it, contract no debts, and let your dependence be on God's blessing in answer to prayer. Trust God to provide both the individuals and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle.

weighed: I'd start with the plain answer: yes, Christianity has done real good, and it's not just something believers say to flatter themselves. You can point to hospitals, schools, orphanages, the abolition of slavery, the civil rights movement, and a lot of humanitarian work led by people motivated by their faith. That said, Christians have also done harm, so the honest picture is mixed. One principle I'd weigh here is that the real evidence is the power of a changed life, sins forgiven and people genuinely regenerated. That principle shifts the focus from tallying historical achievements to the present experience of transformed people, which is harder to fake. What it leaves in place is your original question about actual good in the world, because a changed life still has to show up as real charity and real reform, not just inner feeling.
dogmatic: Christianity's good isn't a claim believers make to boost their own religion. The evidence is the power of a new life from above, the daily reality of sins forgiven and lives regenerated. That's not a human product or a natural byproduct of environment; it's a divine beginning that operates on ordinary people and produces moral recovery. When someone acts on faith in Christ's promised strength and believes in others, you see real transformation, and that transformed life is the abiding proof. So yes, Christianity has done good, because it brings a new life that human effort alone can't manufacture.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, holiness is possible on earth, but not as a badge you wear. My first instinct would be to say it's about love—loving God and neighbor—and that the warning against claiming holiness is just a guard against pride. So stay humble, love generously, and you're on the right track. But one idea that sharpens this is that holiness is fundamentally about being set apart for God, not just about being morally good or loving. That changes things: it means holiness starts with belonging to God, not with your performance or your feelings. What it leaves in place is the importance of love and humility—those still matter—but it reframes them as fruit of being God's own, not the root. So you can pursue holiness by yielding your heart—your mind, emotions, and will—to God, and letting that belonging shape your life, without ever needing to claim the word for yourself.
dogmatic: Holiness is not only possible—it's demanded, and it begins with God's own character. God is holy before He is loving in any way we can measure; His love is governed by His holiness, and His law flows from His righteous nature. So sin isn't merely a failure to love; it's guilt before a holy God, and that guilt is dealt with only through Christ's sacrifice. Holiness means being set apart—consecrated, belonging entirely to God. It's not about becoming nice or purified by your own effort; it's about being possessed by God. And that separation must start in the heart—the core of your intellect, emotions, and will—so that every thought, affection, and choice is yielded to Him. Anyone who claims to have achieved holiness is deceived, because belonging is God's act, not your boast. But real holiness on earth is a life lived as God's own possession, resting on Christ's work, transformed at the center, and expressed in dedicated obedience—not a claim to have arrived.

weighed: I'd start where you are: give a small, steady amount you can afford without panic, keep an emergency fund, set a giving budget, and let trust grow as you see you're still provided for. One idea worth adding is that God sometimes denies what we ask in kindness, so we can hand him our plans without assuming every request must be granted. That changes the tone of your giving—less like a transaction you must get right, more like trusting a Father who knows better—while leaving your practical safeguards and small steps exactly where they are.
dogmatic: Stop treating your resources as something to protect and start trusting God to supply what you need. Give yourself and your goods to his work without hedging, and don't set your ceiling at what feels safe. If you've drifted from him, don't sit in your guilt—acknowledge it and come back with greater trust. Ask boldly, then let go of your will, because he may deny a request in kindness and give something far better. Hold everything with an open hand, and let trust, not fear, shape your generosity.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: ask God for clarity and wisdom more than for a dramatic sign, and test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce, since good trees bear good fruit. A sign can be sought humbly, like Gideon did, but it shouldn't be demanded; God often guides through ordinary means like prayer, community, conscience, and circumstances. One principle worth naming is that the sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, made with real faith and devotion rather than out of habit. That adds a concrete, embodied way to steady yourself and mark your allegiance to Christ while you wait, and it doesn't replace the rest: you'd still pray for discernment, still weigh the fruit, still be willing to wait, and still not demand a spectacular confirmation.
dogmatic: Make the sign of the cross with real faith and devotion, not as a mere habit or superstition, because it is a rampart against the devil and a mark of your allegiance to Christ. Then ask God for clarity and wisdom, and test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce, for good trees bear good fruit. Receive every spiritual privilege with fear and love, remembering that the same gift can become a poison tree if it is beheld and not loved. Make a definite act of faith in Christ, then abide habitually in him, drawing life from him as a tree draws from the soil without effort. You may humbly seek a sign, but do not demand one; trust his quiet guidance, sealed by the cross.

weighed: I'd start by saying that praying for a miracle asks God to step in and override the usual cause-and-effect of the world—like an instant healing or a sudden reversal—while praying in a way that fits how things work accepts the regular patterns: we ask for wisdom, patience, good decisions, and we use medicine and community. Both can be faithful, but mature prayer usually works through means and processes. Now, one idea that shifts this is that what we call a miracle is just a result whose cause we don't yet understand—there's a cause for every result. That changes the sharp line between miracle and ordinary, because it says the difference is our understanding, not God's action. But it leaves in place the value of praying for wisdom and working through natural means, and it doesn't deny that God is the source of all grace.
dogmatic: Praying for a miracle and praying in a way that fits how the world works are not really two different things. Every result has a cause, and what we call a miracle is simply a result whose cause we don't understand yet. So don't set up a false divide. The guarantee of answered prayer is the grace of God—God is the source, Christ is the channel—so even high and far-reaching prayers can and will be answered. Prayer doesn't inform or change God; it's an absolute faith that all things are possible to God, a spiritual understanding, and unselfed love that brings us into harmony with the unchangeable divine Principle. That's the truth to stand on.

weighed: Yes, it's acceptable to bring your desire for a sign to God honestly. What I'd say first is that asking for guidance is good, but asking for a specific sign can slide into testing God or demanding he prove himself on your terms. One principle worth weighing is that we should watch our prayers as well as their answers, using the light God has already given rather than demanding signs. That principle sharpens the warning against demanding proof, and it leaves in place the honest, humble request you've already made. So lay it before God, but hold it loosely and be ready to act on the wisdom you already have.
dogmatic: Watch your prayers, not just their answers. It is right to ask God for guidance, but not to demand a supernatural sign as proof, because that tests God and sets terms he never promised. God has already given you light: Scripture, wise counsel, circumstances, and ordinary prudence. Don't ask God to decide what you should decide yourself in ordinary wisdom. And remember that prevailing prayer depends on the conditions Scripture records: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Don't measure whether you're heard by feelings or moods, for those never accurately gauge your standing with God. Rest on the changeless word of promise, and keep praying even when joy is lacking.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: the Old Testament often pictures God in very human terms—repenting, wrestling, changing his mind—because the writers were ancient people describing what they understood, and later revelation fills the picture out. One idea that sharpens this for me is that if God can meet people at a low stage of conscience and worship, he can also use the literary methods of an undeveloped age—dramatic storytelling, old traditions, idealizing history—as real vehicles of inspiration without any intent to deceive. That changes how I read the strange, limited-sounding passages: they're not God shrinking, they're God speaking in a form the audience could carry. What it leaves in place is the harder edge—God's standard stays inflexibly high, and we don't get to lower his ideal to excuse our own failures. So the limits look literary and historical, not a measure of his power, and his call on us stays just as demanding.
dogmatic: Look, the answer isn't to apologize for God or trim him down to fit modern sensibilities. If God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship in the Old Testament, he can just as surely use the literary methods of a rude, undeveloped age—dramatic composition, primitive tradition, idealizing history—as genuine vehicles of inspiration, with no intention to deceive or commit fraud. That's not a weakness; that's power choosing to stoop. And don't use that condescension as an excuse to settle. God will not let us take less than his highest will. Keep the standard inflexibly rigid; never accommodate his ideal to our failures. Nothing is too great for his power and nothing too small for his love—he cares about trifles, down to the trimming of a hat—so trust him in the everyday matters and press on until you reach his highest will.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pray honestly for relief, lay your desire for healing before God without shame, and then add, as Jesus did, 'not my will but yours be done.' Submission isn't passivity; it's active trust that God's purposes are good even when painful, and it leaves room to seek wisdom from Scripture, prayer, and trusted counselors about treatment or acceptance. One principle worth weighing is that God may afflict the just out of an excess of his love, to draw them closer to himself. That changes the frame: your affliction could be loving purpose rather than something to escape, so submission becomes trust in a Father's intent, not just resignation. But it leaves your question intact.
