But most thinkers answer that God's will isn't arbitrary—his nature is good, and his commands express that unchanging goodness, so cruelty could never be made good because it contradicts who he is. The fear really rests on picturing a God whose will is detached from his goodness. One principle here is that we shouldn't fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently since he wishes us great good. That changes the emotional frame—it turns speculation into trust—but it leaves the core philosophical answer in place: goodness is grounded in God's character, not bare will.
dogmatic: Look, the whole hypothetical collapses once you see who God actually is. He isn't a detached will floating above goodness—his commands flow from his unchanging character, so cruelty could never be made good. Stop treating him like a threat and love him fervently instead, because he genuinely wishes your soul good and not harm. And don't charge God with ordaining the wickedness in the world—human agency brought that evil, even though he foresaw it and will overrule its results for good. Trust that, and let it steady you instead of spinning on speculation.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's normal to feel discouraged when you don't see progress, growth is often slow and invisible, don't give up, be patient with yourself, and lean on prayer, Scripture, and community. One principle I'd add is that not advancing in the spiritual life is actually going backward. That changes the frame a little: instead of just waiting patiently, you'd take it as a nudge to keep moving, even in small ways, and to wake the Lord who dwells within you when storms hit. What it leaves in place is everything else—patience with yourself, small consistent steps, and trust that God is at work even when you can't see it.
dogmatic: Feeling discouraged about lack of progress is a common temptation, but in the spiritual life, not advancing is actually going backward. You must keep trying, but not in your own strength. Instead, awaken the Lord who dwells within you; His presence calms the soul's storms. Be careful not to rush forward in self-will. Take new steps slowly, being willing to have no will of your own. Ascertain God's will through prayer and the Word, and then wait with earnest, patient, believing expectation of His help. Remember that union with God is a love-union on a higher spiritual level, in which your will consciously cooperates with His divine will while your personal individuality is preserved. He will guide you and strengthen you as you trust in Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying: start small and start today. Pick a fixed time each day—even ten minutes—and keep it whether or not you feel like it. Keep it simple: a moment of quiet, a short passage of Scripture, a few honest words to God, and some silence. Jot down what you notice. Add short prayers through the day, and find a few others who pray so you're not alone. Expect dryness and don't quit when it comes; consistency matters more than intensity. One principle worth naming is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—praying that God would help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. That changes the focus of your prayer time: it's not just about showing up, but about asking God to do that deeper work of self-discovery and change. It leaves in place the practical stuff—the fixed time, the simple structure, the journal, the community, and the expectation of dryness—so you still start small and keep going.
dogmatic: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the cornerstone your whole life is built on, and your first resort in every matter, great or small. Get on your knees, both alone and with other believers, and begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Don't settle for blind habit or vague hope; seek the full assurance of understanding and an abundance of conviction that comes from a heart made strong and full of love. Bring your mind fully into it, because love isn't blind—it's the source of knowledge and conviction. Keep the time whether or not you feel like it; expect dryness and don't quit.

weighed: My first instinct is that Jesus is often held up as the best human being who ever lived because of his teachings and example, but Christians believe he's more than that—the Son of God, fully human and fully divine, who lived a perfect life, died for our sins, and rose again. So he's the best human being and also God incarnate. One idea that sharpens this for me is that Christ dwelling within conquers what we never could—so the question shifts from what's the best I can do to what's the best Christ can do. That changes the emphasis from admiring Jesus to trusting him to work in us, while it leaves the core claim intact: he really is both truly human and truly God.
dogmatic: He isn't merely the best human being who ever lived—he is the Son of God who dwells within believers. Stop asking what you can do in your own strength and trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could; he empowers you to do all things through him. The Gospels give us the comprehensive Jesus—Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, Saviour, both man and God—a self-evidencing, life-giving fact, while the partial Jesus of modern criticism is far too small to account for the origin of Christianity. And the Church's growth isn't due to human leaders or natural development but to God's guidance, as disciples of differing gifts share in one mighty work under his leadership. So yes, he is the best human being, but infinitely more: God incarnate, our living Lord, working in and through us.

weighed: First, name what's happening: this is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact. Answer it with what you know rather than what you feel. Recall that Christ receives all who come to Him, and His love isn't measured by your present weakness or fear. Speak Scripture aloud if you can, and ask a pastor or believing friend to pray with you. Don't argue with the enemy at length; turn instead to simple trust and to the promises of God. Rest in the finished work of Christ, and let others carry you in prayer when you're too weak to pray yourself. One thing worth adding: the only reason we fail to love Christ more ardently than anyone else is that we don't think about Him enough, and even now the quiet stretches, the waiting, the restless rests are open to you for that. That doesn't change the core answer, which is trust and the promises, but it gives your weak hours something to do, and it leaves the promise standing exactly where it was.
dogmatic: The real problem here is that you don't think about Christ enough. The only reason anyone fails to love Him more ardently than any human being is a failure of attention, and the hours on trains, waiting for appointments, and restless rests are sitting there unused. Fill them with Him, because every quality you admire is found in Him and no one is so restful to think of. When you fall into fear or sin, don't leave Christ out of the account: love is never without pity, and Christ alone keeps the charge when we fall, so turn back hastily and don't leave Him alone. And don't accept preventable evil passively and call it Christian. If you refuse force when you could stop evil, you must be able to show that your suffering offers hope of redeeming the evil-doer; otherwise you're idle and cowardly, not Christian.

weighed: I'd start by saying that holiness isn't a solo project. You can't be holy all by yourself, because we're meant to help each other grow, mainly through good example. That doesn't mean you're responsible for everyone's choices, but it does mean you can't cut yourself off from others. One principle that fits here is that we help one another by advice and even more by good example. That changes the idea that you can just focus on your own devotion and ignore others. It leaves in place the importance of personal prayer and grace. So you can pursue holiness individually, but you still need the mutual help that comes from others.
dogmatic: No, you cannot be holy all by yourself. Holiness is not a private achievement. We are meant to help one another grow, chiefly by good example. Isolating yourself from others hinders your progress. You need the mutual help that comes by advice and especially by good example. Personal devotion matters, but it is not enough. The Christian life is meant to be lived in relationship, both with God and with others. So you do have a responsibility for others, and you cannot ignore it.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: becoming a bishop is a serious commitment that calls for deep faith and spiritual maturity, so if you've lived a life of unbelief, examine your heart first, seek counsel from spiritual leaders, and pray about it. Ordination isn't just a human appointment. One principle that matters here is that a pastor must first acquire solid interior virtue and mortify his passions before safely undertaking the salvation of others. That changes the order of things: it puts the inner work of humility, charity, and self-denial ahead of any public role, rather than treating the role as the starting point. What it leaves in place is everything else I said: the need for genuine repentance and belief, the church's affirmation of your calling, and prayerful discernment. So the honest answer is that this isn't something to rush into, and the interior groundwork comes first.
dogmatic: No, you should not be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief, and the reason is not mainly administrative. A pastor must first acquire solid interior virtue and mortify his passions before he can safely undertake the salvation of others. Someone whose soul is slothful, sensual, and earthly does not deserve the name of Christian, much less minister of the gospel. Ordination is not a career move or a reward for time served; it is a calling that presumes a transformed heart. So the order is fixed: repentance, interior virtue, self-denial, and only then the care of souls. If that foundation is missing, the office will crush you rather than be served by you.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't let the criticism rattle you. If you believe God called you to serve elsewhere, trust that He's in control of the work at home too, and reassure people that He'll raise up others. Listen to their concerns rather than brushing them off, and maybe look for ways to support the work from a distance or help train someone to carry it. One principle that fits here is that unwelcome tasks shouldn't be met with uneasiness; you can treat this as God's business and answer calmly. That changes the tone of your reply, from defensive to steady. What it leaves in place is the practical part: hearing people out, reassuring them, and helping fill the gap. It doesn't remove their worry or your responsibility to respond kindly.
dogmatic: Honestly, the answer is simpler than you're making it. When people say the work will fail without you, don't get uneasy about it. Treat this as God's business you're about, and expect it to be well performed. When you feel you can't do it, tell God plainly that you can't unless He enables you, and you'll receive strength more than sufficient. Be faithful in what's yours to do, and don't be astonished when infirmity causes some failure, because fidelity is yours and failure comes from weakness. So answer them with confidence in God, not anxiety about their claims.

weighed: I'd start by saying the sign of the Son of man and the Holy City are related but not the same thing. Scripture describes the sign appearing in heaven, and separately describes the new Jerusalem coming down from God, so the city may accompany or follow the sign without being the sign itself. One idea worth weighing is that God roars from Zion and shakes the heavens and earth, and then Jerusalem is holy and the sign appears. That adds a sequence and a setting to the picture, but it doesn't collapse the sign into the city. The main point stays: Christ is plainly revealed, and God dwells with His people.
dogmatic: No, the city is not the sign, though the two are bound together in one great shaking. God roars from Zion and utters His voice from Jerusalem; the heavens and earth shake; then Jerusalem is holy and the sign of the Son of man appears. The city itself is real, fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions Christ prepared for all written in the Lamb's book of life. And the cross revealed to Constantine is the pattern: the King of angels gives the token of victory to those who look to heaven for aid, not to the size of their host. So look for Christ's sign, and expect the city to follow.

weighed: I'd first say that feeling chased usually comes from fear and guilt, not from God. Scripture says God is love, and in Christ He isn't waiting to punish you but to welcome you. That sense of being pursued may be your own anxiety or a voice that misrepresents Him. Take it to prayer and wise counsel, and ask whether the fear matches what Scripture actually says about God's heart toward those who turn to Him. You're not being hunted by a God who needs to be calmed; you're invited to come near and find rest. One principle that matters here is that God desires to give Himself to us, and asking for anything less than Him is an affront and hurts us. That changes the focus from just getting relief to actually seeking God Himself. But it leaves in place the truth that your fear is real and worth bringing honestly to God, not explaining away.
dogmatic: Feeling chased often comes from fear and guilt rather than from God, but don't stop there. God, in His promises to hear our prayers, is desirous to bestow Himself upon us, and asking for anything beneath Him is an affront and a self-injury. So don't settle for relief; ask for Him, without multiplying words or worrying over distractions. But don't take comfort in denying what is real. Evil, sickness, and pain are real, and pretending otherwise is a narcotic, not a Redemption. The answer isn't to explain the fear away but to walk the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice, facing what is true and turning to God in it. His promise isn't to remove every shadow but to give Himself to those who ask.

weighed: Yes, I'd still say pray for converts from the very beginning. Prayer keeps the work centered on God instead of your own plans, and it prepares hearts before you ever speak. One thing worth holding onto is that no conversion happens except by the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, and your deepest need is to know God himself. That changes the ground you stand on: it's not your persuasion or technique that turns anyone, so you can stop carrying that weight. What it leaves in place is the practice itself. You still start with prayer, still ask God to open doors and soften hearts, still pray for wisdom in how you speak and serve. It just makes prayer the foundation rather than an afterthought, and it keeps you leaning on God rather than on yourself.
dogmatic: Yes, pray for converts from the very beginning, and don't treat it as a nice sentiment you get to later. No one is ever converted except by the almighty power of the Holy Spirit, so the great need of anyone who works is to know God himself. That means prayer is not a warm-up to the real work; it is the work. Go find some sad and needy heart for whom nothing is prepared, pray for someone who has no one praying for them, and love even the unworthy the way Christ loved. Treat prayer as real business with a God who answers, not as a last resort when your own efforts run out. Bring souls before him expecting an answer, trust him for their needs and for your protection, and begin every effort by lifting the unprayed-for before God.

weighed: I'd start where I said before: that fear is common, and it usually matters less than it feels. You're not responsible for the labels people put on you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Look for natural openings, speak gently, and let small faithful steps shrink the fear over time. One principle worth weighing here is committing yourself and everything you care about to God's providence in silence and peace, accepting what comes as from a father's hand rather than churning over what people think of you. That changes the inner ground you stand on: the fear of being called a fanatic loses some of its grip because your reputation is no longer the thing you're guarding. What it leaves in place is the practical side, which still matters: you still choose your moments, still speak with gentleness, and still don't force conversations. The principle steadies your heart; it doesn't excuse you from reading the room.
dogmatic: Stop treating other people's opinions as your master. Commit yourself and everything you care about to God's providence in silence and peace, and accept whatever comes as from a father's hand. Don't let vain, wandering thoughts about your reputation wear you down and waste your strength. Learn not to be troubled or resentful when people insult you; sincerely believe you deserve contempt and scorn, and desire to be counted as nothing rather than to enjoy human honor. Be patient, wait on the Lord, take whatever befalls you as meant for your highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, cooperating with him as you speak. That is how you overcome the fear of being called a fanatic: care nothing for the label, and speak.

weighed: I'd start by saying your mind isn't simply a piece of God's mind. Scripture puts God's thoughts far above ours, and when you think, it's you thinking, even though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. One idea worth weighing is that under this dispensation we shouldn't use the lot to figure out the Lord's mind; we seek it through prayer and the Scriptures, since the Spirit now teaches believers. That changes the practical advice: instead of suggesting lots when a decision is unclear, I'd point you to prayer, the Word, and the Spirit's teaching. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God influences and directs your thinking, but your mind isn't a fragment of His.
dogmatic: Your mind is not a part of God's mind, full stop. God is one, infinite, and perfect, and He cannot become finite and imperfect, so any notion that your thinking is God thinking in you collapses under that. And the theories that treat mind as a material sense sitting in brain or nerve are serpents of error, not truth. If you want to know the Lord's mind, don't reach for the lot; that's not how the Spirit teaches believers now. Go to prayer and the Scriptures. And if you truly want clarity, enter into deep recollection, cut off unnecessary intercourse with the outside world, and let God and I be the only objects of your thought. In that stillness His guidance comes clear.

weighed: I'd start by saying that anxiety about spiritual progress usually comes from constantly measuring yourself. So set realistic goals, celebrate small gains, keep a gentle routine of prayer and Scripture, and talk with a trusted pastor or friend. One principle worth naming is that not advancing is going back, so keep steadily moving forward without hurry or fretfulness. That principle changes the tone: it turns progress into a calm, steady walk rather than a performance review. But it leaves in place the core advice to rest in grace, avoid perfectionism, and focus on faithfulness today rather than comparing yourself to others.
dogmatic: Anxiety about progress comes from over-eagerness, and the remedy is to keep yourself in God's presence. Do not mistake calm for complacency: not advancing is going back, so keep steadily advancing without hurry or fretfulness. When storms of worry rise, call on the Lord present within you; awakening Him calms the soul's storms. And when you stumble into small faults, do not be terrified or paralyzed. Humble yourself quietly before God and say to your soul: 'Courage! we have made a false step, but let us keep steadily on.' Over-eagerness breeds anxiety, and terror over trifles blocks perfection; but a calm, advancing soul, calling on Christ within and rising gently after each fault, finds both peace and growth.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is the oldest and hardest question, and no answer fully takes away the sting. Scripture and reason suggest God permits evil because a world with free creatures is greater than one without them—genuine love and virtue need the possibility of their opposites—and suffering can be formative, and the cross shows God entering suffering rather than standing aloof. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that all evil happens by God's permission and always for some good end, so we can commit everything to Providence without fear. That principle deepens the trust part: it says evil's form and measure are allowed by a wisdom that will turn all to good. But it leaves in place the hard fact that pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves, and it doesn't explain why this particular suffering, now, is necessary. So it changes the tone from argument to trust, but it doesn't remove the sting.
dogmatic: The answer is that pain and sin are real evils, never goods in themselves, yet God permits them only as necessary means to a greater good. All evil of whatever kind happens by His permission and ever for some good end; it could not be at all except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. His omnipotence is limited only by His own nature—He cannot deny Himself or be the author of evil—so He cannot attain His ends without these means, since omnipotence means ability to do all things in their own nature possible. The struggle is inward: the enemy is partly your own pride, fear, and disordered desire, and deliverance is not a magical rescue from outside but God and man together battering the citadel of evil, the soul's resolve joined to grace. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: weave short reminders of God into your day, offer each task as a prayer, use a brief phrase between activities, and review where you noticed God at the end of the day. One principle worth naming is that we must not be troubled if our attention is distracted from God by necessary work, since doing all our actions for God keeps us in His presence without needing to offer each action explicitly. That changes the pressure to make every task an explicit prayer or to feel guilty when your mind wanders. It leaves in place the value of small reminders and a gentle return, and it still honors your exhaustion by not adding more techniques.
dogmatic: Do not multiply techniques; simplicity is the heart of practicing God's presence. Do each action for God without anxiety over distraction, for a wandering thought in necessary work is not a failure. Beware of hurry and over-eagerness, for anxious fretting blocks perfection. Remember that God is the one living Worker, and all human workers are only His instruments. Cast all your care upon Him, for anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Keep yourself in His presence calmly, doing what lies before you as His instrument, and return gently when you drift. Awareness grows through simple, repeated intention and trust in the one who works in you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: praying for your congregation's salvation is good and important, but it probably isn't enough on its own. One principle worth naming is that we gather not only for our own benefit but especially to build up our brothers and sisters through worship, prayer, and teaching, with love as the motive. That changes how I'd frame your question: it's not just about the content of your prayers but about showing up for the whole body, including the stranger among you. What it leaves in place is your core instinct: salvation is still the most important business, and your prayers for it still matter. So keep praying for their salvation, and let that prayer pull you into worship and mutual care rather than replace it.
dogmatic: Praying only for their salvation is not enough, and the honest question is whether your commitment matches your prayer. Every member should join for no other end than to serve God and his holy Mother and to save his own soul, and should not abandon the congregation on appointed days for worldly affairs, because eternal salvation is the most important business. This is not a day of prayer; few there are who pray, and the greatest benefactor this age could have is the one who brings the preachers and the Church back to prayer. Do not neglect congregational worship because you get nothing out of it; love is the highest motive. Attend chiefly for the edification of the whole body and of the stranger among you. Keep its days, serve God and Mary, and let prayer and presence together seek the salvation of all.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: Christ's presence in your heart is more than a feeling or an idea. Feelings come and go, and ideas can stay abstract, but His presence is a real relationship grounded in faith, prayer, and love of neighbor. You won't always feel it, and that's normal. One principle that fits here is that Christ invites you to live in an atmosphere of love, believing He ever loves you and claiming His approval, rather than living in thought, sensuality, or mere duty. That changes the tone: it turns the question from 'am I feeling something?' into 'am I trusting His love and resting in it?' What it leaves in place is everything I said first. It's still more than a feeling or an idea, still grounded in faith and prayer, and still true when you feel nothing. So don't chase emotional highs or reduce it to a concept. Trust His promise, stay in prayer, and let His presence shape your life.
dogmatic: Christ's presence in your heart is not a feeling or an idea at all. It is a living relationship in the atmosphere of His love. Believe that He ever loves you and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. His words are spirit and life, spoken long ago yet coming to you now brightened with that same spirit and life. When you behold His Passion, don't see pain alone. Behold the hard pains He bore, the love that passes them, and the joy and bliss of the Trinity within it. That same loving, joyful presence is what dwells in you. So rest in His living word, remain in prayer, and let His presence shape your life, confident that you are loved, accompanied, and held in joy.

weighed: I'd start by saying that distraction through cares and anxieties is one of the devil's favorite tactics, because it scatters the mind and keeps it from resting in God. So first, name what's happening: when your thoughts start churning over responsibilities, finances, or worries, treat that as an invitation to return to God, not a verdict on your spiritual state. Then set aside fixed times of prayer and keep them even when your mind wanders, and when it does wander, don't panic or scold yourself endlessly; gently bring your attention back. Writing down your anxieties as a way of handing them over helps too, and so does limiting the mental clutter you let in. One principle worth weighing here is the picture of coming to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate: your business is simply to keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and if it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect; the will brings it back in tranquility. What that changes is the tone of the return: it's less about managing yourself and more about humble, quiet re-collection. What it leaves in place is everything practical I said first, the fixed times, the gentle return, the honest naming of worry.
dogmatic: The remedy is not frantic self-management. Come before God like a beggar with nothing to offer but your need, and simply wait in His presence. When your mind wanders into worries, don't be terrified or paralyzed by the lapse. Quietly humble yourself, recall your attention without agitation, and say to your soul: courage, we've made a false step, but let's keep steadily on. Small faults are not catastrophes; they're occasions for humble return. Cast all your care upon Him, for He is the one living Agent who works in you; your part is only the instrument He uses, and anxious self-reliance is distrust of Him. Let the cares pass through, bring your attention back in tranquility, and trust that God is present and at work even when thoughts scatter.

weighed: I'd start by saying that being busy is a real constraint, and seasons of life vary. But 'too busy to pray much' is rarely a valid excuse in the deepest sense, because prayer doesn't require large blocks of time. Short, honest prayers throughout the day can sustain a relationship with God even when you're busy. One principle that sharpens this is that prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs our spiritual bankruptcy. That principle changes the tone: it reminds me that prayer isn't just a time-management issue but a matter of the heart, and that human nature resists it. But it leaves in place the practical point that consistency matters more than length, and that short prayers can fit a busy season. So I'd still say: examine your priorities if you truly can't find a few minutes, but for most people the busyness excuse is more about habit and attention than actual lack of time.
dogmatic: No, that is not a valid excuse. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. You should pray with your family and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. Prayer is humbling work that abases intellect and pride and signs your spiritual bankruptcy; human nature resists it, and little praying is worse than no praying because it is make-believe. Secret prayer and meditation on the word of God must not be sacrificed to busy activity. The worker for God must first be a worker with God, taking time to be alone with His word and Spirit. Constant activity, public service, and Christian fellowship do not compensate for the loss of the secret place. So refuse to let activity crowd out communion, and keep your appointed times with God.

weighed: Yes, there's another way, and honestly your exhaustion is telling you something important: trying to be good purely on your own strength treats goodness like a project you have to finish by willpower, and that always ends in burnout. The alternative is to receive goodness as a gift instead of manufacturing it. Start by being honest with God that you can't do this alone and ask for help each day, and build small habits of prayer, rest, and honesty with trusted friends. When you fail, treat it as information rather than identity. One principle worth naming here is that when an occasion to practice some virtue comes up, you can turn to God and say, in effect, 'I can't do this unless you enable me,' and receive strength more than sufficient. That changes the moment-to-moment texture of it: each temptation or small act of love becomes a chance to ask for help rather than white-knuckle it. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff, the habits, the honesty, the rest, and the fact that failure is information, not your identity.
dogmatic: There's another way, and your exhaustion proves the first way was never going to work. Trying to be good on your own strength treats goodness as a project you complete by willpower, and that always burns you out. The real answer is that strength of character is the power of the will to control your actions independently of your inclinations and of other people's opinions. It grows through repeated virtuous acts and shrinks every time you give in to your passions, and your progress is measured by self-victories. So stop waiting to feel like it. Every occasion of virtue is a test: turn to God and say you cannot do it unless He enables you, and strength more than sufficient is given. Then act. Return to God after every failure and keep steadily on. Goodness is built by winning these small battles, one self-victory at a time.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: if Jesus is just a human ideal, your hope is in ordinary growth—studying his life, adopting his practices like prayer and mercy and courage, and letting example and community shape you over time. You won't hit perfection, but ideals are directions, not destinations. One principle here pushes back on that: an ideal seen only as a human masterpiece would be despair, like Kant's genius that mocks imitation; it's as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life carries real dynamic for change. That changes the source of hope—from your own striving to something given. It leaves in place the practices and the community, and the honest admission that you won't become exactly him.
dogmatic: If Jesus is only a human ideal, there's no hope—an ideal can't lift you to itself. But the Christ-ideal is a revelation of the God-life, and that supplies the dynamic for striving. Don't settle for a righteousness merely credited to you; salvation is an actual redemption of the entire self, made righteous by living in Christ's power the life he lived. And don't cling to your own good works or best attainments, as though striving or real change were your achievement. Give up the good as well as the bad, and take Jesus in place of your own self, receiving his divine impulses instead of your best attainments. Then the unattainable ideal becomes ground of hope, not despair: not you imitating a distant pattern, but Christ living his life in you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: name the failure honestly, separate the act from your whole self, and then take one concrete next step so kindness doesn't turn into avoidance. One principle worth borrowing is the caution against hurry and anxiety—treating frantic self-fixing as its own obstacle. That changes the pace: you slow down and let the honest naming settle before you rush to repair. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for—you still own the harm, still keep your standards, still make amends. Gentleness just isn't frantic.
dogmatic: The real problem isn't that you're too hard on yourself—it's that you're in a hurry. Anxiety and eagerness to fix yourself are the biggest things standing between you and any real peace, so stop racing to repair and just be still. And watch out for softness that quietly excuses harm: mercy only means something when you've truly owned the damage, and self-pity can rot into deceit before you notice. So don't wallow in guilt, and don't trust your own faltering feelings—stand firm in what's true, name the wrong plainly, and let calm, unhurried honesty do the work.

weighed: Yes, that's the heart of it: Christ took the punishment we deserved. Sin brings guilt and separation from God, and the wages of sin is death. He was innocent, yet he stood in our place and bore that penalty so that those who trust him are forgiven and spared condemnation. That's substitution. It doesn't mean we never suffer or die physically, or that consequences vanish, but the eternal penalty and estrangement are removed. One principle that deepens this: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law—from disobedience—by being made a curse for us, so that we need not sin any more. That changes how we see the cross: it's not just a legal transaction but a rescue from sin's power, not permission to keep sinning. What it leaves in place is the reality of sin's cost and our need to turn from it and trust him. The cross shows both God's justice and love, and our assurance rests not in feelings but in his finished work.
dogmatic: Yes, he took your punishment so you don't have to face it. But understand the curse rightly: the curse is disobedience, not obedience; transgression, not law-keeping. Christ was made a curse for us on the tree, and thereby loosed us from sin so that we need not sin any more. Redemption is not liberty to disobey. Death is the law of physical nature, yet death as we know it—with its fear and estrangement—is the penalty of sin; Christ abolishes death, so it becomes the gate of life immortal. Let your consolation rest wholly on Christ: his sufferings, temptations, cross, death, resurrection, and pleading at the right hand of the Father. Looking at yourself clouds the view, but his promises leave no room to doubt his power and will to save. Turn from yourself to the altogether lovely Saviour.

weighed: My first instinct is to treat the nails as symbols: keep them as reminders of what the crucifixion cost, let them stir gratitude and mercy, and steer clear of turning them into lucky charms. One principle here says the nails belong on a king's bridle, a holy sign that brings speed in war, victory in battle, and peace afterward. That shifts the focus from remembrance to protection and triumph in conflict, which sits uneasily with the rest of what I said about suffering love being stronger than violence. What it leaves in place is the idea that the nails are a sign pointing beyond themselves, meant to be put to use for people's good rather than hoarded or worshipped as metal.
dogmatic: The nails should be set on the bridle of the most noble king as a holy sign of God, so that whoever guides the horse has good speed in war, victory in battle, and peace after the strife. They were hidden and then revealed by a sign of fire, and the people who had long been in heresy saw the miracle and gave glory to God. So the nails are not a private keepsake or a lesson in sentiment; they are a public sign with real power, given to be carried into the hardest conflict and to bring a king safely through it. Handle them with reverence, put them where they will guard the one who leads, and let the wonder of their finding turn doubters toward God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it makes sense to grieve dreams that failed, and giving up entirely isn't the only option. Hope can rest on what remains—your life, your relationships, your ability to learn and begin again. One principle worth naming is that a relapse can't really occur because there's only one Mind; meet the cause mentally and courageously, and conquer your own fears. What that changes is the framing: a failed dream isn't a final fall, just a fear to face. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—take small steps, talk with someone you trust, and don't demand a whole new vision today.
dogmatic: There is no true relapse, because there is only one Mind. The dream that failed was never your life, and failure has no final claim on you. Meet the cause mentally and courageously: name the fear that said one failure was the end, and refuse it. Pity the smallest and the lost—even the little emmet matters—and know that a watchman is set to light the ground. But first examine your own heart. Do not blame the hardness of circumstances while your own love has grown cold. The results you desire come by intense distress for souls and by tears, not by complaint. Let your heart be softened, weep for the lost, and then rise with courage to the work still waiting.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: name the jealousy honestly, then reorient each task around whether God's glory or your image is at stake, practise hidden service, let others take credit, and measure yourself by faithfulness rather than recognition. One principle worth weighing is that the real secret of rest is to be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus, since failure often comes over a trifling thought or word. That changes the method: instead of mainly retraining your heart through habits over time, it turns you quickly from a distracting thought or a slight and fixes you on him. What it leaves in place is the honest naming and the practical steps of hidden service and letting others take credit. It just puts the centre of gravity on being occupied with Jesus rather than on managing your reputation.
dogmatic: Jealousy over your own name is a snare, and jealousy itself is corrosive, because jealousy and mistrust destroy affection. The work was never yours to possess. So stop trying to manage your image or slowly retrain your heart. Be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus. When a trifling word or a distracting thought pulls you aside, don't lose your peace over a straw; turn from every conflicting thought and look steadily to him. Give others room and let confidence and goodwill grow wider. And refuse to chase riches, greatness, or honour in a world where Christ was poor and despised, because that chase doesn't fit discipleship. Your true glory is to be despised, poor, and lowly with Christ. A heart fixed on him and content with his lowliness has no room left for jealousy over its own name.

weighed: Yes, keep going. Praying for someone you love for years is never wasted, even when you see no change, and Scripture keeps pointing us toward persistence. One thing worth holding onto is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to keep at set times whether or not you feel like it, and to share with your family where you can. That adds some structure and steadiness to how you keep going, but it doesn't change the core of my answer: stay persistent, keep lifting your family member up honestly, and look for chances to show love and speak truth gently. You still can't force their choices, and you still need to care for yourself so you don't burn out or grow bitter.
dogmatic: Yes, keep going, and don't treat prayer as a mood you wait for. Pray at set times whether or not you feel like it, pray with your family where you can, and never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Let prayer run through your whole day, at work, at home, sitting or lying down, keeping God before your eyes in ordinary things. Make prayer your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and ask God to help you search out and reform your own heart, because the same grace you're asking for your family member is the grace at work in you. That kind of prayer, steady and woven through everything, is powerful and never wasted.

weighed: Wanting to work for God is a good place to start. What you need most isn't a credential but a willing, faithful heart—start where you are, serve in small ways, learn from Scripture and mature believers, and stay close to God in prayer. One principle worth holding onto is that the first thing necessary is to earnestly search God's will through devout reading, listening, and meditating on His truths. That sharpens your beginning: it makes seeking His direction the first step rather than just jumping into activity. But it leaves in place the rest—humility, faithfulness in small things, and prayerful dependence—and it doesn't add requirements like degrees or titles. So begin by seeking Him, then serve with what you have.
dogmatic: The first thing necessary in God's service is to earnestly search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths, which enlighten His law and guide you to every duty. Trust God to provide both the people and the means for any work He orders, as He fitted the workers and furnished the materials for the Tabernacle. Carry on the work within the landmarks of His word. Do not seek or depend on the patronage of the world, do not appeal for money from unbelievers, and contract no debts; let the Living God alone be your Patron and prayer your only appeal. Bring a willing heart, humility, and faithfulness in small things, and depend wholly on His blessing in answer to prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying distraction is normal, and the goal isn't to force your mind blank but to gently return your attention to what matters. When you notice a useless thought, acknowledge it without judgment, then redirect to your task, your breathing, or a short prayer. Build habits that cut clutter: limit input, take breaks, and practice noticing when your mind wanders. One principle worth weighing is that useless thoughts spoil things and should be rejected as soon as you see they don't belong, then you return to communion with God. That adds a firmer, more decisive stance toward the thought itself, but it leaves in place the gentle, unhurried return and the habit-building I'd already suggest. Be patient with yourself; frustration just adds noise.
dogmatic: Useless thoughts aren't harmless. They spoil everything, because they crowd out communion with God, your true life. So the moment you perceive one, reject it and return to God, but calmly, without hurry or anxious fretting. Over-eagerness is the mother of imperfection; anxiety about every stray thought only multiplies them. Keep yourself quietly in God's presence, and let your return be gentle and steady. Guard your mind's wandering at other times, not only in prayer: the soul that practices God's presence through the day becomes calm and recollected when it comes to prayer. What you do outside prayer shapes what happens within it. Cultivate a steady awareness of God in ordinary tasks, and recollection in prayer will come more easily.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: if you see yourself as part of God, worship is less about rituals and more about living in tune with the whole—gratitude, love, service. And on the wicked-men question, I'd say being made in God's image isn't the same as being identical with God; wickedness distorts that image rather than belonging to God's nature, so God stays good and evil is a turning away. One idea worth weighing here is that it's more worship to behold God in all things than in any one special thing. That shifts the focus of worship from particular experiences or insights to a steady, general beholding of God in creation, in your neighbor, in ordinary life. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God's goodness isn't compromised by creatures misusing their freedom, and worship still means aligning your will with the good. It just widens where you look for God—everywhere, not just in the exceptional.
dogmatic: Worship isn't a special thing you do in a special place. It's beholding God in all—take everything generally, cling to nothing in particular. If you're chasing singular insights or extraordinary shewings, you're narrowing what can't be narrowed. And understand God rightly: not a corporeal person with human passions, sitting somewhere in space, swayed the way a man is swayed. That picture keeps you bound to your own doubts and fears and keeps you ignorant of yourself as God's image. God is incorporeal, infinite Mind and Love. As for wicked men, behold God in all and see that His goodness isn't divided by creaturely misuse of freedom. But don't swing to self-reliance without God or dependence without effort. Fight your own battles with confidence and personal effort while acknowledging constant dependence on God. Know yourself, cherish good character, and let worship be the grateful, undivided beholding of God in all.

weighed: The stone cut out without hands is from Daniel 2: a stone strikes the statue of world empires and grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Because it's cut 'without hands,' its origin is divine rather than human—it stands for God's everlasting kingdom, inaugurated in Christ, which outlasts every earthly power. One principle I'd bring in is the image of yourself as a stone before a carver, asking God to form His likeness in your soul. That adds a personal, prayerful layer: the same divine shaping that establishes the kingdom also works on you. It doesn't change the stone's meaning as God's kingdom—it just turns it into something you can pray with, while the cross-shaped carving stays fitted to what you can bear.
dogmatic: The stone cut without hands is God's kingdom, and don't soften it: it is not built by human effort, politics, or religion's machinery—it comes from above and shatters every empire in its path. But the stone isn't only out there in history; it's you, presented before the Carver, yielded and passive, letting God form His perfect image in your soul. Being carved is no resting place—your rest must be 'no rest below,' and you press on toward Sion's hill while the pillar stays and the waters smile. The chisel that shapes you is often the cross, fitted to your stature, measured to what you can bear, and all God does shall work your final good. He carves the stone, and He will bring it at last into the mountain of His kingdom.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: look honestly at the parts of your life you're still holding the reins on—your ambitions, your closest relationships, the habits and hidden desires you don't talk about—and consciously hand those over to Christ. Then build rhythms of prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability that keep those areas in front of God, ask what obedience actually requires in each situation, and do it even when it costs you. That's a process of incremental surrender; when you fail, confess and keep going. One principle worth adding is that Christ dwelling within you conquers what you never could—so the question shifts from what's the best you can do to what's the best Christ can do through you. That changes the engine of the whole thing: it's no longer your resolve white-knuckling its way to holiness, but His life in you doing the deep work. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—the honest inventory, the disciplines, the accountability, the costly obedience. Those don't go away; they just stop being the power source and become the shape your trust takes.
dogmatic: Stop treating this as a project you manage. The deepest parts of your life will never be conquered by your own resolve—only by Christ dwelling within you. So quit asking what the best you can do is and ask what the best Christ can do through you; trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could. And don't imagine you need to be learned or great to find Him—Christ is revealed to lowly shepherds and plain hearts, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest soul to where He dwells rather than let them miss it. Don't try to manufacture purity and grace by effort either; know Christ in you as your sanctification and strength. Abide in Him, say with Paul 'Not I, but Christ,' and rest in His indwelling. His life in you is the rule you're looking for.

weighed: I hear your discouragement, and I want to say first that fruitfulness in ministry is rarely quick or obvious. My first answer would be to focus on faithfulness over visible results: preach clearly, love your people, keep going, and care for your own soul. One principle that sharpens this is that the true ministry is God-touched, God-enabled, and God-made—the Spirit must anoint both the preacher and the word, because truth without the Spirit can deaden rather than give life. That changes how I think about methods and effort: it's not just about working harder or being more strategic; it's about praying for the Spirit's power on your preaching and depending on God for any real fruit. What it leaves in place is the call to faithful, persistent labor—you still prepare, love, and serve. But it shifts the measure of success from numbers to God's enabling, which should ease your discouragement without letting you off the hook.
dogmatic: The secret of fruitful ministry is not in your results but in God's anointing. You must stop measuring yourself by visible outcomes and start seeking the Spirit's power on your preaching and your people. The true ministry is God-touched, God-enabled, and God-made. Without the Spirit, even orthodox truth deadens. So pray for the anointing on both messenger and message, and let that dependence shape everything you do. Fruitfulness will follow God's enabling, not your effort.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: it's a fair question, and you can hold that Scripture is inspired without needing every number or genealogy to be historically precise. Inspiration can mean the writers faithfully carried God's message in their own cultural setting, using the conventions of their time, and apparent inaccuracies can come from copying, translation, or the different purposes the texts served. One principle worth weighing is that Scripture's unity across many authors and centuries points to a superhuman intelligence behind it. That adds a reason to trust the Bible's overall coherence, but it doesn't settle the specific numbers and lists, so careful reading and good scholarship still matter, and the central message of God's character and saving work stays the focus.
dogmatic: Look at the Bible's unity: roughly forty writers across some seventeen centuries, from every rank of life, all speaking with one subject, one spirit, and one aim. That kind of agreement can't come from collusion across such a span of time and station; it requires a superhuman intelligence as its author. So take up Science and Health as a key to the Scriptures, and let honest study with the Bible enable you to prove all things, testing apparent inaccuracies against the spiritual sense. Still hold the Holy Scriptures as the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, preferred above all other books. Read daily, systematically, and prayerfully, meditate on what you find, and translate it into obedience.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: committing your past, present, and future to God's Providence begins with trust. Acknowledge that God cares for you and has a purpose for your life. Reflect on how He has guided you in the past, and let that build confidence for the future. Practically, pray regularly, surrender your plans each day, and accept that you can't control everything. When worries come, remind yourself of God's faithfulness and focus on what you can do today. Seek support from your community, and remember that trust grows over time through small acts of reliance. One principle I'd add is that all evil happens by God's permission and for some good end—He can turn everything to good. That changes the frame for the hard parts of your past and future: you can commit even the painful and confusing things without fear, because nothing is outside His wise allowance. It leaves in place the everyday practices—prayer, surrender, community, and patience—since those are how trust actually grows.
dogmatic: Commit yourself and everything that concerns you to God's unfailing and most sure Providence, in silence and peace. Accept all things, whatever their cause, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and set aside vain and wandering thoughts that weary your soul and body. Learn to trace His leadings: even a chance meeting or a gathering of the serious and the careless at a grave may hold a manifest connection in His purpose of grace; adore rather than scoff. Remember that all evil of whatever kind happens only by God's permission and ever for some good end: it could not be except He permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by Him Who can and will by His wisdom turn all to good. Therefore commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear makes sense, and the way through isn't to stare at your sin until it swallows you. Look at it honestly, confess it, accept forgiveness, and keep a trusted person close so you don't lose perspective. One principle I'd add is that the practical answer to evil isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion—stepping back from endlessly studying sin to the greater reality of God's goodness. That changes the frame: you're not examining your evil in isolation but against something larger, so reflection doesn't intoxicate or paralyze your will. What it leaves in place is the honest look itself—you still name your sin and confess it; you just don't make it the whole horizon.
dogmatic: Don't go looking for an intellectual solution to why evil exists—that's not the remedy. Start by clearing your mind of sin and sickness, guarding evil thoughts before they take hold of your body. Then refuse to dwell on sin in a way that intoxicates the will or paralyzes it with despair. Shrink the cruel facts of your experience to their true proportion against the universal goodness of God; recoil from the study of sin and exult in His goodness instead, so your will is freed from evil and given fresh temper for the fight. And know this: sin gives no real pleasure. Seeing that clearly strengthens your moral courage to master evil, because you no longer fear losing a good you never truly had.

weighed: I'd start by saying criticism comes with the job, so expect it and try not to take it personally. Listen closely, sort the useful feedback from the hostility, and respond calmly instead of getting defensive. Ask clarifying questions, own what's valid and say what you'll change, correct the record briefly if it's unfair, and keep your temper. One principle worth holding onto is that you honor past leaders by applying the spirit of their conduct to new circumstances, not by repeating what they did. That changes how you frame your decisions, because you're defending a principle rather than just precedent. It leaves the practical steps in place: listen, stay calm, acknowledge what's true, and move on.
dogmatic: Appeal to principle, never to mere practice. Ask what earlier leaders were really after and carry that forward, even when the circumstances have changed completely. Don't gloat when critics stumble; flattery and reproach should land the same way on someone who sees things clearly and is growing in humility. And toward those who wrong you, take 'Resist not evil' and the Sermon on the Mount seriously: refuse retaliation and legal vengeance, and let the principle guide you rather than your reaction.

weighed: Yes, funeral singing and solemn music can be proper in Christian worship. Music has long helped believers express grief, hope, and reverence, and the Psalms themselves include laments and songs for solemn occasions. The key is that the music serves worship rather than performance, so choose texts that reflect faith and resurrection hope, keep the tone fitting for mourning, and involve the congregation where possible. One principle worth naming is that a prayerless ministry is really a funeral for God's truth and Church, however beautifully adorned. That principle changes the emphasis: it means the music must be joined to prayer and to a congregation whose daily lives are already offered to God, not treated as a polished performance that stands on its own. What it leaves in place is your original point—funeral singing and solemn music may still be used wisely and prayerfully, with texts of faith and resurrection hope, to comfort the grieving and direct hearts to God.
dogmatic: Yes, funeral singing and solemn music may be used, but never as a substitute for prayer. A prayerless ministry is a funeral and an undertaker for God's truth and Church, however adorned it may be. Singing in the church is not a professional performance but the Spirit-filled, mutual worship of the regenerate body, so unconverted or hired performers are disqualified from this ministry. Nor does devotion belong only to cloisters or solemn occasions; it suits every state of life. Amid exterior business the heart must remain on God in interior recollection and prayer, and the spirit of the world must be shunned. So let funeral music be joined to prayer, with texts of faith and resurrection hope, sung by a congregation whose daily lives are already offered to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying reason is a real gift and it can take you a long way. You can examine the evidence for God—cosmological and moral arguments, the historical reliability of Scripture, the coherence of faith—and you shouldn't check your intellect at the door. But reason has limits: it can clarify concepts and weigh evidence, yet it can't by itself produce trust, love, or surrender. Many rational people find arguments bring them to the threshold, but a personal decision of faith carries them across. So use your reason fully, follow the evidence where it leads, and be open to the possibility that knowing God involves more than argument alone. One principle that fits here is that reason isn't the most primal act of the personality; faith, like love and moral venture, uses reason's evidences but goes beyond them. That changes how you see the endpoint—reason can justify trust but never create it. It leaves in place the full use of your intellect and the real value of evidence; it just says the final step is a venture of trust, not a deduction.
dogmatic: You can't reason your way to God, because reason is not the measure by which revealed doctrine must be approved. Rightly ordered reason prepares the way for revelation, examines its credentials, and systematizes its facts, but once revelation is given, reason must implicitly trust what is above it. Don't make reason a supreme, self-sufficient arbiter or demand that argument alone produce belief. In our present state, unaided reason and natural religion are not sufficient for the knowledge of God and duty; reason and intuition fail on matters of utmost importance, and even natural truth needs divine confirmation. Only a revelation of God's merciful nature can break the power of sin. So use your reason, but seek the revelation that reason cannot supply.

weighed: Yes, it's okay to tell God you're angry. People in the Bible did it—Job, David, Jeremiah—and God didn't reject them. He can handle your emotions. Be honest but not disrespectful, and ask Him to help you process what you're feeling. One principle that matters here is that God isn't the one who arranges evil and then punishes the helpless; that's contrary to our best understanding of Him. That changes how you frame your anger—you can bring it without treating God as the author of the harm. It leaves in place the invitation to speak honestly and the caution against sinning in your anger. So tell Him plainly, and trust that He listens.
dogmatic: You can tell God you're angry, but don't demand a sign or give up in despair. God often speaks in a still small voice, not in dramatic displays. Choose to believe rather than see. Cast your bread upon the waters, trusting that God is at work even when you can't see it. Return to your daily life with hope. Remember that God is good and cannot produce sickness or evil; He destroys them rather than sends them. Suffering and evil often come from human agency, indiscretion, or ignorance, not from God's design. God's hand is in all things as permission and overruling, but He is not the author of evil. Trust that He hears you and will guide you as you trust Him.

weighed: I'd start with the simple answer: it means your desires get aligned with God's, so you want what He wants without your identity being erased. You don't lose yourself; you find your true self in Him, and your will becomes an instrument of His. One idea that sharpens this is that your will is the mistress of your faculties, so it has to pull your wandering mind back and carry it to God as its last end. That changes the picture from passive surrender to active inner work, but it leaves the core in place: you're still you, choosing, and the goal is still alignment rather than erasure.
dogmatic: Your will is the mistress of all your faculties, and it must recall your roving mind and carry it to God as its last end. When your will refuses to run in conjunction with the Divine will, that is the root of all sin, and the friction of those opposing wills generates forces that are baneful to you. So this isn't a gentle metaphor about finding yourself; it's the central work of your life. Take God's promises and comforts as largely and mightily as you can, and set your troubles at nought. Align your will with His, and you will not lose yourself, you will finally be whole.

weighed: I'd first say that using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war isn't appropriate—relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be treated as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. One candidate principle is that we should be peaceable, submit to the powers that be, pray for kings and authorities, and wait for the Lord's time rather than foment rebellion. That principle changes the emphasis: it shifts the focus from personal trust in objects to a posture of prayerful submission and peaceableness toward rulers. But it leaves in place the core point that victory comes from God, not from relics, and that prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance matter more than physical tokens.
dogmatic: No, it's not right. A holy relic is not a charm to guarantee victory in war. Relics are for inspiring faith and devotion, not for being strapped to a king's bridle as if they were a magical talisman. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to be peaceable, to submit to the powers that be, to pray for kings and all in authority, and to wait for the Lord's time rather than foment rebellion. Intercession for rulers is a foremost duty because the peace of the world depends on them, and they need God's wisdom. We give due honor to princes as far as religion allows, but we never blaspheme Christ or sacrifice to idols to escape death. So prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are far more important than any physical token. Victory comes from God, not from relics.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: that stirring you're feeling is likely the Holy Spirit at work, and the best next step is to slow down and get grounded. Spend time in prayer, read Scripture, and talk with mature believers in that gathering who can help you make sense of it. One thing worth adding is the idea that when God draws you closer, the resistance often gets stronger too, so you'll need real vigilance, honesty, and a willingness to obey even in small things. That doesn't replace the simple advice to pray and seek guidance, it just adds a note of sober watchfulness to it. Take your time, test what you're hearing against Scripture, and let trusted people walk with you.
dogmatic: What's happening to you is that you're being drawn nearer to God, and you should know that the closer you come, the thicker the darkness gathers around you. So don't treat this as a casual curiosity. You must despair of your own strength, hand yourself over to God's mercy, and sink into the passion and death of Christ. Watch your mind against every evil thought, put away all unrighteousness, forgive those who have wronged you, and count yourself a servant of God and of your fellow believers. Be slow to take any new step, seek to have no will of your own, and determine God's will through prayer and the Word, then move forward with earnest, expectant trust in His help. Obedience, singleness of heart, and holy vigilance are what this hour demands of you.

weighed: The shaking of the powers of heaven is the dramatic cosmic upheaval described in passages like Haggai 2 and Hebrews 12, and echoed by Jesus: the sun darkened, stars falling, and the heavenly hosts shaken. It signifies God's decisive intervention, removing what is temporary and establishing His unshakable kingdom. As for when, Scripture gives no date—Jesus said no one knows the day or hour. It's best understood as a future event tied to Christ's return, and also as a present spiritual reality whenever God's kingdom displaces the powers of this world. One candidate principle says God will roar from Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth, and then Jerusalem will be holy and the sign of the Son of man will appear. That principle underscores the certainty and source of the shaking—God's own voice—and ties it to Jerusalem's restoration and Christ's sign. It leaves in place the call to watchfulness and hope rather than date-setting, and it doesn't fix a timeline. So I'd still say: it's a future, certain event connected with Christ's return, and a present reality we live in by faith.
dogmatic: God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth will shake. This is not a vague metaphor—it is God's own declaration. When it happens, the Lord will be the hope of His people, Jerusalem will be holy, and the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven. This shaking is sure because God has spoken it, and it points to the decisive future intervention of God. Until then, our calling is to long for it and seek it, not to claim we already have full rest. The Kingdom of Heaven is in the saints, operative by faith, even while we are surrounded by flesh and blood, the world, and the devil. So the soul sinks into the hope of God's grace and stands like a rose among thorns until the body's death. That is the answer: a future, certain shaking from God's own voice, and a present life of longing and hope.

weighed: I'm really sorry you're going through this. When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you, but I'd say God sometimes allows these trials to draw you closer to Him. One thing worth holding onto is that steady, persistent desire matters more than a single cry or a few tears shed only when things fall apart. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of telling you a single tear will move Him to pour out His gifts, I'd say keep knocking and keep asking, trusting He answers in His time. What stays in place is that He is near to the brokenhearted and welcomes your honest emotion, so you don't have to hide what you're feeling.
dogmatic: When everything you relied on is stripped away, it can feel like God has abandoned you, but God sometimes allows these trials to draw you closer to Him. Don't imagine that one cry or a moment of disappointment is enough to obtain His gifts. God requires steady, persistent desire, a continual seeking of His face, not only when prosperity fails, friends disappoint, or you are sick and lonely. Keep knocking, keep asking, and trust that He will answer in His time. Guard your tongue against angry complaints, and examine yourself to see if any sin is hindering your prayers. Attend to your own duties and do not meddle in others' affairs. Above all, remember that self-renunciation is the foundation of all perfection. Without renouncing your own will and embracing humility and compunction, exterior practices bear little fruit. Lay that foundation first, and God will be near to you.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's disappointing when the home church tells you to retrench, but trust that the leadership has wisdom and support the decision by focusing on what's most important. One principle that matters here is that God's work should be done according to God's mind, with separation from unbelievers, and that mixing the world and the church leads to departure from the Word. That changes how I'd think about retrenchment: instead of just streamlining or seeking business partnerships, I'd see it as a chance to purify the work and avoid worldly mixtures. But it leaves in place the core advice to trust the leadership and not be discouraged, and it doesn't cancel the need for mutual confession and pastoral visitation.
dogmatic: When the home church tells you to retrench, the real issue is whether the work is being done according to God's mind. Establishments that mix the world and the church necessarily lead to departure from the Word, so retrenchment may be a call to separate from unbelievers and worldly methods. Don't try to keep things going with business partnerships or community resources. Instead, open your heart to trusted brethren and welcome pastoral visitation, because an unvisited church becomes unhealthy. Meekly and mightily fasten yourself to Holy Church, for the whole Body was never broken, though a single person may often be broken. Submit in humility, trusting that Christ guides His Church.

weighed: My first answer would be that Jerusalem is made holy when Christ returns and sets up His kingdom, and God then dwells with His people in a renewed creation. One idea worth weighing is that God roars from Zion and speaks from Jerusalem, shaking heaven and earth, and then the city is holy. That adds a vivid picture of how the change happens, but it leaves the core in place: the timing is still future, God still dwells with His people, and we still live faithfully until then.
dogmatic: Jerusalem becomes holy at the moment God roars from Zion and thunders from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth. Then the sign of the Son of man appears, and the city is holy. God dwells in his heavenly sanctuary and in Zion, and his voice goes out from Jerusalem. This is a real city, fifteen hundred miles square, with many mansions Christ has prepared for his saints, room enough for everyone written in the Lamb's book of life. The Jews will be gathered and redeemed by God's power, not by our preaching, and we should wish them nothing but good as we wait for that day.

weighed: What I'd say first is that you're missing that Jesus' example isn't just something to admire, it's about transformation. He lived in perfect obedience to God, and through his teachings and the power of the Holy Spirit, we can actually change. Start by studying his life and teachings, ask God to help you apply them, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and let the Spirit work in you. It's a process, so be patient. One thing I'd add from the principle that Jesus beheld the perfect man and that correct view healed the sick: it changes how you see the people and situations you want to change, because you start looking for the wholeness God sees rather than fixating on the flaw. What it leaves in place is the slower, daily work of prayer, forgiveness, and obedience. You still have to show up and practice, but now you're practicing from a different view of yourself and others.
dogmatic: Here's the thing: Jesus didn't just teach, he demonstrated. He beheld the perfect man and that correct view healed the sick, and his works matter more than his words. His healing and teaching were the demonstration of an ever-operative divine Principle, not mere doctrine, and his followers are commanded to heal the sick and do the works he did, not just admire his personality. So stop treating him as an inspiring figure and start proving the Principle by works. See yourself and others as God sees them, perfect and whole, forgive injuries after the example of the good thief and of Christ on the cross, and take up the present duty to heal the sick and cast out error. That's how you become a true imitator of Christ and an heir of his disciples' privileges. Admiration alone changes nothing; the works are what change you.

weighed: Yes, you can know God directly in your experience. My first answer would be that many people have a real sense of God's presence without needing arguments or inference. One principle that sharpens this is that we may know God truly though partially—the objections that we know only phenomena or only the relative don't block real knowledge of God. That changes how I'd frame it: your experience is genuine knowledge, but it's not exhaustive comprehension. What it leaves in place is the directness—you don't need to reason your way there first. So seek God in prayer and meditation, and expect to know Him truly, even if not fully.
dogmatic: You can know God directly, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. The idea that you only know phenomena or only the relative is a dead end—it doesn't stop real knowledge of God. God is nearer to you than your own soul, and you won't come to full knowing of God until you first know your own soul clearly; both are known together. So stop treating difficulties as problems to escape. God often brings His people into trouble on purpose so they can know Him as they couldn't otherwise, revealing Himself as a very present help in trouble. Open your heart, seek Him, and expect direct encounter—no arguments needed.

weighed: I'd start by saying it sounds really frustrating to pour yourself into these conversations and feel like nothing lands. My first instinct would be to wonder if you're coming on too strong or using the wrong approach, and to suggest trying new methods or moving on to people who seem more receptive. But one idea worth weighing is that the soul is a strange, piteous, futile thing, and its futility is exactly what God's love addresses—seeing none but I makes much of naught. That changes the frame: instead of treating the lack of results as a technique problem, it invites you to offer your own weakness and let God work through it. What it leaves in place is the honest frustration and the real limits of what you can do—you still can't force anyone to change, and you still have to keep speaking truth in love and leaving results to God. So I'd say: don't despair, keep going faithfully, and let your own nothingness be the place where grace does its work.
dogmatic: The soul is a strange, piteous, futile thing, and its futility is precisely what God's love addresses—seeing none but I makes much of naught. So stop measuring your speaking by visible results. Wait patiently upon the Lord, take whatever befalls you from His hands as intended for your highest good, and play the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ, co-operating with His grace. Your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Name your piteous futility honestly: you can do nothing of yourself, and that is exactly where His love works. Offer your weakness to Him and let Him work through you. Receive kindly and amiably any censures upon your condition, life, and conversation, and offer that acceptance to God as fruitful for your soul. Keep speaking the truth in love, and leave the results to God. He will bring forth fruit in His own time.

weighed: I'd start by saying Christ's kingdom was inaugurated at his first coming—he preached that it had drawn near, he defeated sin and death, and he reigns now at the Father's right hand—but it's also still future, because Scripture promises a consummation when he returns in glory. So it's both already and not yet. One principle worth weighing is that the kingdom of heaven isn't the visible church and Christ hasn't yet set up his everlasting kingdom on earth. That changes how I'd frame the present age: the church isn't the kingdom itself, and we still pray for God to establish it visibly. But it leaves in place the reality that Christ's rule is present now through the Spirit and that the kingdom has truly been inaugurated. So I'd hold both: a real present reign and a future, visible establishment.
dogmatic: The kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth. His people still wait and pray for it. It cannot be built by human organization, legislation, or moral suasion—it must be revealed from heaven and established by God's own interposition, with an angel restoring the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion built up, and judgements preparing the way. Yet this is no mere inward state. The kingdom of God is a literal kingdom on the earth, composed of living and resurrected saints, with laws and administrators, and Christ will reign over all the earth. Believers therefore labor faithfully now while awaiting that visible, literal reign.

weighed: I'd start where you are: the vastness you feel is itself a good sign, because a love you could fully measure wouldn't be divine.
