Begin small and concrete—read one Gospel scene a day where Christ shows compassion, pray simply, 'Show me your love,' and watch for it in Scripture, in the kindness of others, and in your own conscience. You don't need to comprehend the whole ocean at once; touch one wave and let it teach you. One principle worth naming is that knowing the love of Christ is a knowing by experience that surpasses knowledge, with infinite stretches beyond even your highest moments. That changes your goal: you're not chasing a finish line but entering a mystery that keeps opening. It leaves in place the small, daily practices—they're still how you begin, and they still matter.
dogmatic: Stop treating the vastness as a problem to solve and enter it as a mystery. Christ's love surpasses knowledge, yet it is known by experience, and even your highest experiences leave infinite stretches beyond. So despair of your own power and give yourself up to the Mercy of God. Sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, and trust the indwelling Christ to conquer what you never could. Watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, and forgive your outward enemies. Esteem yourself a servant of God and of your fellow Christians. This is the narrow way, and it is not self-powered: ask what the best Christ can do, and do all things through Him who strengthens you.

weighed: My first instinct is to say that doing chores for the love of God means reframing ordinary tasks as acts of service rather than drudgery. You offer a brief intention before you start, and washing dishes or folding laundry can become prayer when it's done with love. You do each task well and attentively, without resentment, seeing the person who benefits. Small rituals help: a short prayer before work, gratitude when you finish, awareness of God in the ordinary. The chores don't change, but your posture toward them does. One principle worth naming here is that the intention determines the true value of every act, and actions done for merely natural ends or to be seen by others lose their supernatural reward. That changes the stakes of the framing: it's not just about feeling peaceful, it's about who the work is finally for. What it leaves in place is the practical core of my first answer, the brief intention, the attentiveness, the gratitude, the small rituals. Those still hold, they just get a sharper reason behind them.
dogmatic: Doing everything for the love of God means the intention determines the true value of every human act. The same chore done for merely natural ends, or only to be seen by others, loses its supernatural reward, even if it isn't always sinful. So before the dishes or the paperwork, ask for grace and set your intention on God, and do all things for His glory. Prayer is not a way to turn stones into bread or escape labor. Daily bread is as much God-given as it is won by the sweat of your brow, and God and man cooperate in the avenues of daily work. Pray for grace, then work with your hands, and let the task itself, offered in love, become your prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying a few minutes a day is better than nothing, and God can work through small faithful habits. But honestly, a few minutes is unlikely to sustain a demanding ministry on its own. Ministry draws deeply on your own union with God, and that union needs real time. Try to protect a slightly larger block—even twenty or thirty minutes—and let short prayers punctuate the rest of the day. Use commute time, walking, and waiting as prayer. Be realistic about your limits, but also examine whether some commitments could be trimmed. The goal is not guilt but a sustainable rhythm that feeds you and, through you, the people you serve. One principle that speaks to this is that holy pastors have always made a life of prayer their preparation and kept it up amid ministry, setting aside regular times by day and even part of the night. That principle changes my answer by making prayer the main business rather than an add-on, so it pushes you to find more than a few minutes. But it leaves in place your real limits: you can still start small and build, and you don't have to match someone else's schedule. The key is to let your calendar show what you truly believe about prayer, while being honest about what you can sustain.
dogmatic: A few minutes will not sustain a ministry. The measure of your estimate of prayer is the time you actually give it. Holy pastors made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship and preparation, and afterward, amid its functions, remained men of prayer, keeping God always present to their mind and setting apart intervals by day and much of the night in silence. Great praying is the sign of God's great leaders. Do not fix on dates or assume the last days unfold slowly; trust that God will cut His work short in righteousness and prepare for events that are hastening. So give prayer real, measured time—your calendar will show what you truly believe about it.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, humility and submission aren't beneath your dignity. They're actually the foundation of everything good in us. But here's a principle that sharpens this: we should pursue humility because God calls us to it, not because we want to look great or holy. That changes the motive—it strips away the pride that can sneak into even our best actions. What it leaves in place is the truth that humility is still the path to real greatness, reflecting God's own character. So you don't have to choose between dignity and humility; humility is where true dignity is found.
dogmatic: Humility and submission are not beneath your dignity—they are the very ground of all virtue. You must be humble in courage, esteeming yourself little, because the greatness of courage lies in the humility with which it is possessed. The first degree of humility is such a firm attachment to God that nothing in the world, not even the danger of death, can make you deliberate about committing a mortal sin. So embrace humility and submission as the path to true greatness, reflecting the character of God.

weighed: I'd start by saying that God isn't actually distant or abstract—He's always near to those who seek Him. You can find Him near by building a habit of prayer and reflection: set aside a few minutes each day to quiet your mind and focus on His presence, read Scripture and meditate on passages about His closeness, and look for Him in ordinary moments like nature, kindness, and your conscience. One principle that adds to this is that God is nearer to you than your own soul, and you can't fully know God until you first know your own soul clearly—both are known together. That changes how you approach seeking: instead of only looking outward or upward, you also look inward with honesty. It leaves in place the practical habits of prayer, Scripture, and noticing God in daily life, because those still help you draw near.
dogmatic: God is nearer to you than your own breath, speaking in your conscience and mind. Don't treat Him as distant or abstract—seek Him early, before the day's distractions crowd in, and listen in the quiet of your heart. But don't limit your awareness to prayer times alone: in all your business and diversions, remember He is always near and should be adored continually. When you work, converse, or rest, lift your heart to Him. Everything worldly passes away—possessions, achievements, relationships—but God remains unchanging and faithful to the soul that seeks Him. So don't look for Him in far-off places or abstract concepts; look within, where He dwells by His Spirit. Seek to know God and your own soul together, for your soul is found where it truly is—in God, who holds all things in being. In that unified knowledge, you'll discover He was never far away but always waiting to be found.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling like a task is beneath you often comes from pride, and it helps to focus on the value of the task itself and the good it can do. One principle I'd weigh is that unwelcome tasks should give you no uneasiness—you can say it's God's business you're about and find it well performed. That changes the emotional weight: instead of feeling resentful or uneasy, you can approach the task as something offered to God. But it leaves in place the honest recognition that the task may still feel unpleasant or beneath you—it doesn't magically make it pleasant. You still have to do it, but you can do it without the inner turmoil.
dogmatic: You should feel no uneasiness at all. When you're asked to do a task you think is beneath you, say plainly: it is God's business I am about, and find it well performed. The trivial round and common task furnish all you ought to ask—room to deny yourself and a road to bring you daily nearer God, without bidding farewell to neighbour and work. So drop your sense of being above it. Do the task as God's business, and refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that would multiply undertakings and burden you more than any legitimate employment. That is the whole answer: no uneasiness, no resentment, just the work done well for God.

weighed: Yes, God regards your lowly dwelling. Scripture shows Him especially close to the poor, and your worth isn't measured by wealth or by who notices you. One thing worth adding: the question with the Lord isn't how much a person has but how they came by it and what they do with it, and more means more responsibility. That shifts the focus onto the rich who pass by, but it leaves your comfort intact: God still sees you, hears the prayers in your cottage, and never overlooks you.
dogmatic: God absolutely regards the lowly dwelling, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. The real issue with wealth was never the amount but how it was gotten and what's done with it, and those with more carry more responsibility to relieve misery. Your poverty is no barrier to God's regard; He looks on you with pity, not blame. This passing life doesn't ask you to live without any fault or sin, only to keep falling and rising while held in one Love. Worth like yours can sit unseen like a diamond in the mine, and the prayers of the poor and desolate rise to the Lord's ear with more splendor than any royal pomp.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: God's love isn't a wage you earn—it's a gift given before you could deserve it. Resting in His mercy begins by receiving, not achieving. Good works become the grateful response to that love, not its price. One principle that helps here is doing everything for the love of God, with prayer for His grace to do the work well. That changes the motive—work stops being a payment and becomes a response. But it leaves the core in place: you're already loved, and resting in mercy is still about receiving, not earning. So when the lie surfaces, name it, pray something like 'Lord, I receive your mercy,' and let service flow from security rather than fear.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating God's love like a wage. It's a gift given before you could deserve it. Rest isn't the absence of labor—it's abandoning yourself to God in it. Work for love of Him, pray for grace, and let Him carry the outcome. Don't measure yourself by whether the work feels easy or by the words you say. Test yourself by fruits: do you live the supreme good, and does your life show healing, patience, and love to the people around you? When dryness comes, offer it and keep working, living, and rejoicing in God rather than in results. Let mercy received show itself in mercy given, and let the fruit, not the claim, prove your understanding.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your longing for comfort and honour is natural, and the way forward is to set aside quiet time each day and let God meet you there, offering him those desires and asking for the grace to seek him first. That still holds. What I'd add comes from the principle that we should commit everything to God's sure Providence in silence and peace, accepting whatever comes as from his fatherly hand rather than wearing ourselves out with restless thoughts. That changes the posture: instead of treating silence mainly as a technique for transforming your desires, you receive what comes, pleasant or painful, with a quiet mind. It leaves your original instinct intact—comfort and honour aren't the enemy, and the daily practice of silence and offering still stands. It just gives the silence a softer shape: less striving, more trust.
dogmatic: Stop negotiating with comfort and honour as though they were neutral. They will quietly hold you back from giving yourself wholly to God's sure Providence, and the place to begin is silence and peace—entrusting everything that concerns you to his unfailing care. Accept whatever comes, pleasant or painful, as from the fatherly hand of Divine Providence, and refuse to be carried off by vain and wandering thoughts that exhaust your soul and body and waste your time and strength. Watch especially for apathy, which is deadly to the soul; when prayer seems to get no response, the danger is that your feelings slide into unbelief or dull resignation. God in his love uses circumstances—loss of the nearest and dearest, the removal of prosperity, touching you where you are most tender—to keep you from that. Receive it as his means of awakening and humbling you and lifting you into his consolations. And remember that prayer rising unseen like a lonely rill is heard by God, who accepts every heart that fears him and does what is right, whatever nation or station it comes from. True peace is not in satisfying every desire but in resting in his wise and loving plan.

weighed: I'd start by saying the cross matters because forgiveness isn't just a legal pardon; it's God entering the depth of human sin and suffering to heal it from within. God could pronounce forgiveness, but the cross shows He doesn't forgive from a safe distance—He absorbs the cost Himself. That reveals both how seriously God takes sin and how far divine love will go, and it anchors our assurance. One principle that fits here is that the cross puts God's love into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—that love costs, that wrong must be borne, that mercy and justice are real. That principle deepens the picture: it shows the cross isn't a transaction that changes God's reluctance into willingness but the shape God's mercy takes when it meets a broken world. It leaves in place the core answer: God could forgive without the cross in some abstract sense, but the cross is how He actually forgives—by bearing the cost Himself and inviting us to trust that love rather than merely accept a verdict.
dogmatic: The cross matters because it is the love of God put into the old fundamental pieties of the human heart—that love costs, that wrong must be borne, that mercy and justice are real. In Jesus those dearest truths are realized in Himself, revealing the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and His responsibility for our eternal issues. The cross is not finished history: Christ suffers still in His lowly ones, and the cross sweetens life's bitterest griefs by placing God inside them. But we must not choose our own cross or demand that suffering be fruitful on our schedule. Accept being fashioned by whatever means God pleases, desiring that the cross be wholly the cross of Jesus Christ—His manner, His timing, His good pleasure—trusting that the Father who shaped the Son will shape us in love.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: your longing points beyond itself, like hunger implies food, but it's a clue, not a proof. One candidate principle here is that the search is double—the God you seek is also seeking you. That changes the picture: your longing isn't just your own reaching out, it's a sign of being pursued. But it leaves in place the caution that longing alone can be wishful thinking, so you still test it by seeking and seeing whether the object proves itself.
dogmatic: Your longing is evidence because the search is double: you seek God, but He is already seeking you. Don't seek Him just for the delights He gives—seek Him because it is His wish, because Perfection calls and love calls to love. And drop the idea of God as a distant monarch; He is an Infinite Person woven into our lives, sharing the travail of bringing forth sons of God. Your longing is the pull of that nearness, the trace of a pursuit already underway.

weighed: Honestly, what I'd say first is that reading about God and knowing God are different things, and that gap you feel is really common. What may be missing is practice: prayer, silence, service, and some honest self-examination that moves things from the page into your life. Try taking one idea from your reading and living with it for a week, add some silence and a simple rhythm, serve someone concretely, and talk with a spiritual director or a trusted friend who can help you notice where God is actually at work. One idea worth weighing is that we can't jump straight to knowing God in one step: first you learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally the Holy Trinity becomes your all. That changes the pace and direction of the search, giving it a path and a person to follow rather than a subject to master. It leaves in place what I said first: the books aren't wasted, and relationship still takes time, honesty, and repetition.
dogmatic: The order of knowing is what's missing, and the grace that makes it possible. Don't leap to the highest knowledge. First learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity becomes your all. And don't treat faith that Christ is the Messiah as something you naturally possess or reason your way into. It's a gift of God, to be earnestly sought, striven for, prayed for, and desired. That knowledge is the very coming to God by which you are saved. So pray for the gift, and let the order lead you to Him.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: a queen should teach her people the things that outlast her reign, like integrity, courage, and care for the vulnerable, and show that authority exists to serve. One principle I'd weigh is that there's no substitute for the home, a divine institution of stability and love. That adds a strong word about building lasting homes and not chasing restlessness, but it leaves the core in place: honesty, generosity, and love for one another still matter most.
dogmatic: A queen should teach her people that there is no substitute for the home. It's a divine institution of stability and love, and no real happiness exists apart from it. She should honor the duties of the housewife, prize modesty, and lift up Relief Societies in caring for the poor. She should discourage the restless urge to move about and encourage permanent homes where love takes root. And she should teach homeliness with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, while keeping courtesy, since He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous.

weighed: I'd start with plain, specific thanks: name what was spared or restored, and tell someone else about it so the gratitude becomes worship instead of private relief. Then let it show in changed priorities and in serving someone still waiting for their own recovery. One principle worth weighing here is that we shouldn't just wish the pain away but ask for a wise and thankful heart that stays with God in all griefs. That changes the tone of your thanks: it's less about the crisis being over and more about trusting God's care even in what came before. What it leaves in place is everything practical—specific thanks, telling others, changed priorities, service, and letting the relief deepen trust rather than just end the crisis.
dogmatic: Don't make the removal of pain your chief good. Ask God for a wise and thankful heart, yield your will to His rod, and trust that His correction is love—never so safe as when your will yields, undiscerned by all but God. When prayer seems ineffectual, keep on rejoicing and count it all joy; God will make the reckoning good. He knows your wants before you ask and comes in His own time, never late, never careless. Patience in affliction is itself a mark of His care, so comfort yourself in Him and give thanks for all.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said first: it's natural to fear losing control, comfort, or identity when you surrender to God. But think about what you gain—peace, purpose, and a love that surpasses all. Surrender isn't really loss; it's an exchange, trading temporary fears for eternal security. Start by naming your fears and offering them to God. Trust that He who made you knows your needs. As you take small steps, you'll find that what you thought you'd lose was never truly fulfilling, and what you gain is far greater. God's love is gentle and persistent; He won't force you but will patiently wait for you to trust Him. One principle that fits here is that fear can't evade as Love can pursue—the soul's fear of losing everything except God is overcome by a Love that outruns its evasions. That principle changes the picture by making God's love active and pursuing rather than just waiting, so your fear isn't something you have to conquer alone; Love meets you at every crossroad and turns you back. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer: surrender is still an exchange, you still name your fears, and you still take small steps of trust. The gentle persistence and the promise of greater gain remain.
dogmatic: You say you're afraid of what you'll lose if you surrender to God. Let me press this: fear cannot evade as Love can pursue. The soul's fear of losing all beside God is overcome by a Love that outruns its evasions. Your fear may try to hide, but Love meets you at every crossroad and by-path, gently turning you back. So what will you actually lose? You lose the illusion of control, the anxiety of self-reliance, and the chains of sin. In exchange, you gain a peace that surpasses understanding, a purpose rooted in love, and the security of being held by a God who never lets go. Yet when doubts arise, do not remain paralyzed. Humble yourself, beg God's forgiveness for any hesitation, renew your promises of fidelity and love, and continue pursuing perfection. Test every thought, word, and deed: if they make you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong, they are according to God; if not, fear lest they are not acceptable to Him or profitable to you. Surrender is not a loss but a homecoming. Step by step, let Love pursue and transform your fear into trust.

weighed: I'd start by saying the prophets speak of both, but the ultimate fulfillment is the new Jerusalem from above. Old Jerusalem was the earthly city where God's presence dwelt in the temple, a shadow of the heavenly reality; the new Jerusalem is the city of God where he dwells with his people forever. One principle I'd weigh is that the Holy City is a real city now in the third heaven with God and Christ, which will descend at the second advent and be located in the midst of the promised land. That changes how concrete the new Jerusalem is for you: not just a spiritual idea but a literal city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom. It leaves in place the point that old Jerusalem had real historical significance and that the prophets looked forward to the new one.
dogmatic: The prophets spoke of both, but the fulfillment is the new Jerusalem from above. Old Jerusalem was the earthly city where God's presence dwelt in the temple, but it was only a shadow of the heavenly reality. The new Jerusalem is a real city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land. This is not merely a spiritual concept but a literal city where God will dwell with his people forever. And remember the solemn charge against the men of the Hebrews: they were once dear to the King of glory and strong in his service, yet they cursed Him who thought to loose them from their curse, spat upon the face of Him who cured their blindness, and doomed Him to death who raised their own race from death. They confounded false with sooth, light with darkness, hate with reverence. That curse weighs them down until they confess the truth. But God will roar out of Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem; the heavens and the earth will shake. Then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man will appear in heaven.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: that shame you feel is actually a sign of growth, because it means you're recognizing God's faithfulness. So don't stay stuck in it. Recall specific times God provided, thank Him for each one, and then practice trusting Him in small daily things. Let testimonies and Scripture about trust surround you, and when doubt comes, answer it with reminders of what God has already done. Be patient with yourself; faith grows through choosing to trust even when you doubt. One principle worth naming is that faith is hindered by leaning on human wisdom, whether your own or other people's. That changes the focus a bit: instead of just building a habit of trust, you're also watching where you're quietly relying on your own understanding or someone else's advice more than on God. It leaves in place the practical steps I'd already suggest—remembering, thanking, small acts of trust, patience—but it adds a warning against self-reliance as the thing that blocks faith from growing.
dogmatic: Stop treating shame as the main event. When you've drifted from thinking about God, don't sit there disquieting yourself—acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That's the move. And don't stop at warm feelings about past provision; faith without works is dead. Let your trust produce obedience, service, and love. Work out your own salvation; another person's suffering doesn't lessen your liability, and you can't lean on someone else's faith. Faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, your own or others'. Trust God with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding. Don't demand to investigate whether God has told the truth before you trust Him; childlike trust pleases Him. Each act of trust strengthens your faith. God isn't waiting to condemn your lack of faith—He's waiting to embrace you and help you grow.

weighed: I'd start by saying Jesus was telling Pilate that his authority doesn't come from Rome or any earthly political system. His kingdom originates with the Father and is established by truth, not force. That doesn't mean it will never be on earth. Scripture promises he'll reign here when he returns. So the source and character are heavenly, but the final location is earthly. One principle worth naming is that the kingdom of heaven isn't the visible church, and Christ hasn't yet set up his everlasting kingdom on earth. That changes how you read the present age. His people still pray for the kingdom to come. But it leaves the future earthly reign fully intact. It just clarifies that it's still ahead, not already here in the church.
dogmatic: Jesus said his kingdom wasn't of this world because its source and authority are heavenly, not because it will never touch the earth. But don't confuse the kingdom of heaven with the visible church. Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on earth, and his people still pray for it to come. When it does come, it will be a literal, tangible kingdom on the earth, with laws, officers, and resurrected saints, and Christ reigning over all. And none of that outward religion means anything without the spirit of humility and truth in which Christ dwells by faith and love. You can gain the whole world and lose your own soul. The religious state, the holiness of profession, the shaven head, outward signs of abnegation, all of it profits nothing without that inward spirit, because the kingdom of God, that is Christ, is within you.

weighed: Feeling shy about talking about religion is really common, and the fix isn't to force yourself to become a different person. Start small: practice with trusted friends in low-pressure settings, prepare a few simple, honest sentences about what your faith means to you, and lean on listening and asking questions to take the pressure off. One idea worth holding onto is that we come into personal contact with Jesus the same way we make any friend—by thinking about Him, spending time with Him, and forming brief mental pictures of walking beside Him. That changes how you prepare: instead of rehearsing arguments, you'd build a quiet habit of companionship, which makes your words come out more naturally. It leaves in place the practical stuff—low-stakes practice, honesty, listening—so you're not adding a new burden, just a warmer center to what you're already doing.
dogmatic: The real answer is to enliven your faith and make it the rule of your conduct, not to amuse yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. The way of faith is the spirit of the Church and suffices to bring you to a high degree of perfection. So stop treating shyness as the problem to be managed and start living from faith as your guide. Form the habit of brief mental pictures of the Saviour—walking beside Him, joining His daily life, asking what He would do, look, and think in each situation. That deliberate companionship will make your faith come alive, and your conversation about Him will follow. And let your zeal be tender and childlike, not harsh or intolerant; the truly spiritual person is simple, tender, tolerant, and considerate, having the love that cannot help but love. Seek the full baptism of the Holy Ghost, which produces such a spirit.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's probably both, and the honest answer is that you can't always tell them apart in the moment. The felt sense of God's presence can be a real encounter, but feelings are also shaped by mood, tiredness, and expectation, so some discernment is wise. Testing the experience by its fruits—more love, humility, honesty—is a good check. One principle worth naming is that prayer is meant to bring real knowledge of God, not just warm feeling, and that this knowledge is open to every believer, not a select few. That shifts the emphasis: your prayer can be genuine knowledge of God even when the feeling fades, so you don't have to grade the experience by its emotional intensity. What it leaves in place is the caution—feelings still aren't the measure, and Scripture and the church's wisdom still help you test what's happening.
dogmatic: You're asking the wrong question if you think the feeling is the point. Prayer is where you actually come to know God—not a vague impression but real acquaintance with all the wisdom and knowledge stored up in Christ, and that's open to every believer, not just the clever ones. So stop treating your emotions as the evidence. Adore God in spirit and truth, which means your mind and will purified of every earthly phantom, entering the inmost chamber of your heart and shutting the door on your senses. God hears the earnest prayer of the soul; he understands your innermost thoughts the way human invention carries a message across great distances. So ask in faith, nothing wavering. The feeling may come or go; the knowledge of God in Christ is what prayer is for.

weighed: I'd start by saying doubts like this are common and don't mean something is wrong with you. A practical first step is to look at the fruits: does the experience lead to more love, patience, and humility? If so, that's a good sign. You can also pray for clarity, talk with a trusted spiritual director, and keep a journal of these experiences and their effects over time. Feelings come and go, so ground yourself in community and Scripture rather than chasing or analyzing experiences, and if the doubts cause real distress, a counselor can help too. One principle worth weighing here is that spiritual experiences aren't something we can manufacture or should secretly crave; they're accepted as God chooses, with simple submission rather than anxious questioning. That shifts the focus from proving the experience is real to letting go of the need to control or demand it, which can ease the pressure behind the doubt. What it leaves in place is the practical side: checking the fruits, seeking wise counsel, and caring for your distress still matter.
dogmatic: Stop treating your doubt as a puzzle to solve and stop treating the experience as something you can secure. Spiritual experiences are entirely outside your volition. You don't pray for them, you don't secretly want them, and you don't take pride in them as achievements of your will. Accept them only as God chooses, in total submission, without questioning, fear, or curiosity. And don't go disputing about God's Being or Will to settle your doubt. All such disputation is carried on in images of the senses and thoughts, without God; it's a sign you haven't felt him, and it exalts your own meaning above others and desires dominion. Instead, rest in the felt presence of God and the love of your brother. Train yourself to enter again into the Love of God and your brother, and try things one with another in humility and love. Your aim should be simple surrender, not securing experiences or winning an argument.

weighed: I'd start by saying: keep it small and realistic. Even ten or fifteen minutes of quiet in the morning can anchor your day, so put it in your calendar like any important appointment and protect it. Use little pockets of the day—commuting, waiting, walking—for brief prayer, and aim for consistency before length. One candidate principle says our ability to stay with God in the closet measures our ability to stay with him outside it, and that hasty visits can be deceptive. That changes the tone: I'd stop treating a rushed minute as the whole goal and let the time grow in stillness. It leaves the practical scaffolding in place—small start, calendar, protected slot, pockets of prayer—so your full schedule still has a real entry point.
dogmatic: Make the closet first, not an afterthought squeezed between errands. Hasty visits are deceptive; the closet is the heart's school, where thought is born and where more is learned about preaching than in libraries. Your ability to stay with God outside the closet is measured by your ability to stay with him in it, and great waiting before God is the source of great victories. So put it in your calendar as an important appointment and protect it, letting your time there grow in length and stillness. Yet God is always near; think of him and adore him continually, even in business and diversions, and do not neglect him. Let the stillness you learn in the closet carry into your work, so the whole day becomes a continual remembrance of the God who is near.

weighed: I'd first say that anger at God is a very human response to pain, and it doesn't automatically cut you off from Him. What matters is what you do with that anger—if it hardens into bitterness, that can create distance, but if you bring it honestly to God, it can actually deepen your relationship. Many people in Scripture expressed anger and grief to God. One principle I'd weigh here is that God doesn't cause evil, sickness, or death—that's contrary to our highest ideas of Him. That principle changes how you see the source of what happened: it's not God arranging evil and then punishing you. But it leaves in place the core answer: your anger itself doesn't block you, and honest expression can be part of a real relationship. So I'd still encourage you to talk to a trusted friend or counselor and be gentle with yourself as you process.
dogmatic: Anger at God is common, but you need to be clear: God, who is good, cannot produce sickness or evil—He destroys them rather than sending them. So whatever happened to you is not God's doing. Your anger doesn't automatically block you from Him; bringing it honestly can be part of a real relationship. Don't get anxious about distraction in your necessary work; do all your actions simply for God. And know that when the divine Spirit comes, the man does not go out—the Spirit becomes the life of a new moral personality in you. If anger hardens into bitterness, that creates distance; if you express it honestly and stay in the relationship, it can deepen your faith.

weighed: Your faith is personal, and that's good—but personal doesn't mean isolated. My first answer would be that fellowship matters because other believers encourage you, challenge you, and help you see blind spots. They offer wisdom from their own experience and remind you of truths when you're discouraged. Community also gives you chances to practice love, patience, and service, which are essential to growth. A purely private faith can drift into self-deception or stagnation. That said, fellowship doesn't replace your personal relationship with God; it supports and shapes it. One principle I'd weigh here is that the vague impulse to reach beyond yourself gives way, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That changes the picture: fellowship isn't just a helpful add-on but the natural shape of a faith that's truly personal, because it's fellowship with a personal God who draws you into community. What it leaves in place is your point—your faith is still personal, and your private times with God still matter. It just reframes fellowship as part of that personal relationship rather than a threat to it.
dogmatic: Your faith being personal doesn't mean it's meant to stay private. The vague impulse to reach beyond your isolated self gives way, when God is known as Father in Christ, to actual social fellowship with a personal Friend and Companion. That's not optional extra credit—it's the shape your faith takes. And don't confuse spiritual growth with intellectual attainment or scholarship. Wisdom and revelation come through full knowledge of God in personal fellowship, and they're available to the unlearned; believers with little natural education can have uncommon spiritual perception. So fellowship with other believers isn't about keeping up with the smartest people in the room—it's about shared life with the God who knows you. And you don't have to be at church every time to be with God; you can make an oratory of your heart and converse with him in meekness, humility, and love. But that inner conversation and the outer fellowship belong together. One feeds the other.

weighed: Feeling like a fugitive is exhausting, and it makes sense that you're looking for safety. The first step is usually to stop running long enough to breathe and to name what you're running from. Safety rarely comes from a single hiding place; it grows through honest support—trusted friends, a counselor, a community where you can be known. If your past involves real danger, practical precautions matter, and it's wise to seek professional advice. But if the danger is mainly memory and shame, the path forward is not another hiding place but gradual truth-telling and repair. You don't have to solve everything at once. Find one safe person and one small, steady step, and let safety build from there. One principle worth naming is that the safest place is the path of duty, with God first and children trusted to him. That principle changes the framing: it says safety isn't a hiding place but a direction of obedience and trust. What it leaves in place is the practical core—honest support, professional advice when there's real danger, and the need to take small steps rather than solve everything at once.
dogmatic: The safest place is not a hiding place; it is the path of duty. God must come first, and children can be safely trusted to God wherever he leads. Duty has an order: a presiding officer is the head, his place should be held sacred, and no one should run before his file leader or usurp authority that is not his. Keep proper ward over your mind as well. Do not dwell on the past, on danger, or on fear in a way that familiarizes thought with them; dwell on good and exclude false beliefs as you would exclude thieves. Stay under the authority God has set over you, take the next step of obedience, and let your thoughts be kept in peace by watching the door of the mind.

weighed: Your instinct is worth taking seriously. Pantheism appeals because it promises nearness—God not far off but in everything. Yet the fear you name is real: if God is simply identified with the universe, holiness and personal relationship become hard to preserve. A middle path may help. You can affirm that God is present in all things, sustaining them, while still holding that he is distinct from creation and personal—one who knows, wills, and loves. That keeps nearness without dissolving the difference. One thing worth weighing here is that idealistic pantheism ends up denying God's personality and transcendence, and that undercuts exactly what you're afraid of losing. That point sharpens the stakes, but it doesn't change the advice: read broadly, pray honestly, and talk with a pastor or theologian. The goal is not to pick a label but to worship the God who is both near and holy.
dogmatic: Pantheism can't give you what you fear losing. If God is impersonal or comes to consciousness only in man, then unconscious or necessitated substance is made to produce self-conscious and free beings—impossible. Such a view destroys both God and man, leaving no one to pray to and no ground for responsibility or hope of immortality. God is personal and transcendent, near in sustaining all things yet distinct from them. Hold to the God who knows, wills, and loves. And remember that many are called to serve him in a retired contemplative life; those conscious of their weakness may rightly retire as from a too potent enemy, not to indulge sloth but to fly from the dangers of sin. Do not measure spiritual worth by outward station, education, or visibility, nor reject the piety that ripens in seclusion because it does not fit your favorite system. God has chosen the weak and despised, and those who name the name of Christ and depart from iniquity are not to be refused.

weighed: I'd start with what I told you before: disagreement with a superior is normal, and obedience isn't always simple. Raise your concerns through the proper channels, ask for clarification, propose alternatives, and if the decision is lawful and within your superior's authority, you generally should comply while voicing your objection respectfully. If it's illegal or gravely unethical, you may need to refuse and escalate. One principle worth naming here is that the appeal to authority should be to principle, not to practice. That changes how you frame your objection: instead of arguing that we've always done it this way, you argue from the purpose the rule serves, which is fair to your superior and more persuasive. What it leaves in place is the rest: lawful authority still deserves respect, proper channels still matter, and your conscience still has a say when something crosses a line.
dogmatic: Obedience is an eternal principle. There will never be a time, in time or eternity, when it is not obligatory to obey God's commandments, and it is by obedience that we keep in touch with God and obtain eternal life. So when you disagree with your superior, the first thing to examine is yourself, not the decision. Set aside your preference, submit where you can, and trust that order and obedience serve a good even when you can't see it yet. If the command is truly against God's law, obey God rather than man and accept the cost. But do not retaliate against those who wrong you; resist not evil, return good for evil, and leave judgment to God. Your disagreement is not the measure of what is right. Obedience is.

weighed: I'd start by saying what you're feeling is real and common, and it's good you're noticing it instead of ignoring it. Revival usually begins with honesty before God and a return to the basics: unhurried prayer, Scripture read for yourself and not only for sermons, rest, and confession. One principle worth naming is that a professional ministry is a heartless ministry—when salary and self-advancement play a leading part, the heart plays little part. That changes how you might look at your schedule and motives, but it leaves in place the practical steps: keep praying, keep reading, keep resting, and talk with a trusted friend or mentor. Be patient; the heart warms gradually, and God isn't waiting for you to perform before he loves you.
dogmatic: A cooling heart in ministry is real, and you should not meet your own distraction with violence or discouragement. When your heart wanders in prayer, bring it gently back and lay it tenderly at the feet of its Master—the hour will be well employed. Beware of treating ministry as a profession or business where salary and self-advancement lead; that professionalism is itself a kind of heartlessness. Put self to the rear and heart to the front. Return to unhurried prayer, Scripture for yourself, rest, and confession. And keep on rejoicing even when it feels ineffectual—count it all joy, trusting God to make the reckoning good. The first dose may seem to fail, but do not give up rejoicing; small, consistent habits do more than dramatic resolutions, and God is faithful to warm what you keep bringing back to him.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's natural to want to talk about someone who hurt you, and venting to a trusted friend can bring real relief. Gossip isn't always harmful; sometimes sharing your side helps you process anger and even warns others. Still, if it's turning unkind, pause and ask what you hope to gain. If it's revenge or making them look bad, try a journal or, if it's safe, talking to the person directly. Prayer can help too—ask for peace and perspective. One principle here is that gossip and fault-finding injure the one who indulges in them, so the Saints should mind their own business, look for good in others, and hold their tongues from slander. That changes the framing: it's not just about whether venting helps you, it's about what the habit does to you. What it leaves in place is that you were genuinely wronged and that talking to a trusted friend can still be a real relief—it just asks you to watch for the line where relief becomes slander.
dogmatic: The urge to talk about someone who wronged you is a test of your lips and your thoughts. Gossip, backbiting, and fault-finding are contemptible and injure the one who indulges in them; mind your own business, look for the good in others, and refrain your lips from slander. Don't cover the wrong with pretense either—whoever covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy. Be honest about the offense with God, and where possible go directly to the person, so the wrong is confessed and forsaken rather than buried. Stand porter at the door of thought, admitting only what you wish realized, and shut out the unhealthy thoughts and fears the offense would plant. Let your speech be true, kind, and aimed at reconciliation.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is one of the hardest questions, and honest people have answered it differently. Some say God can't suffer because suffering implies lack, so God stays untouched while we hurt. Others say a loving God must grieve with us, and they point to Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb. The problem of suffering is a mystery we can't fully resolve, and no tidy answer removes the feeling that it counts against a good God. So the best response is often compassion—sitting with people in pain rather than explaining it away—and trusting God is present even when we can't see how. One candidate principle says suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, meant to produce righteousness, and that the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That changes something real: it reframes suffering as purposeful rather than pointless, and it points to the Cross as proof that love and agony can coexist. But it leaves in place the raw fact that suffering still feels like evidence against a good God, and it doesn't explain why some pain seems to produce nothing good. So I'd hold that principle loosely and keep sitting with people in their pain.
dogmatic: Scripture doesn't present suffering as evidence against God. It presents suffering as a remedy for moral evil—a discipline that turns us from sin toward God. God's righteousness is central: He is not the author of evil, but His hand is in all things as permission and overruling, never as the direct cause of suffering, accident, or evil, which arise from human agency, indiscretion, and ignorance. The clearest proof that agony is compatible with the most perfect love is Christ Himself, who submitted to the Cross in perfect love; His agony was not a failure of love but its deepest expression. So abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike. Don't seek life, work, or joy outside of Him; let your living, working, and rejoicing be in God alone. In that surrender, suffering becomes not a barrier to God but a doorway into deeper union with Him.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: baptism matters, but it isn't what saves you, so don't let it become a source of anxiety. Practically, many churches do treat baptism as the doorway to membership and full participation, so yes, it can affect your standing in the congregation—but before God your standing rests on faith in Christ, not the ritual. One principle worth weighing is that baptism accompanied by faith is a means of real blessing, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ, while the rite by itself is useless. That changes the tone: it's not just a box to check but a real means of grace, so it's worth taking seriously rather than putting off indefinitely. What it leaves in place is your freedom from pressure—your standing before God still isn't earned by the water, and you can talk with your pastor and take your time without fear.
dogmatic: Baptism isn't an optional extra or an empty form—it's a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ, and it's useless only when it isn't accompanied by faith. Believers' baptism and the breaking of bread every Lord's day are scriptural practices to be embraced on the authority of the Word, even at personal cost. And for all practical purposes, the church on earth is the fellowship of the baptized; that's the visible ground of membership, not some inward test we can't see. So stop treating this as a private preference. Pray, study, speak with your pastor, and then be baptized as a believer and join the fellowship in breaking bread. Leave the judgment of other people's spiritual state to God—that's not your business—but your own obedience is.

weighed: I'd start by saying Christians should treat the Jews of the holy city with respect and restraint. History shows that passion for holy things has too often turned into violence against Jewish communities, and that's a betrayal of the faith. Jesus and the apostles were Jews, and the Church owes the Jewish people a debt of gratitude. So practically: refuse to take part in persecution, speak out against violence, and treat Jewish neighbors with ordinary justice and kindness. One principle here says the Jews will be gathered to Jerusalem and redeemed by God's power, not by our preaching, so we should hold no ill will and look for their welfare. That changes the tone of how I'd talk about their future, putting it in God's hands rather than ours, but it leaves in place everything about restraint, gratitude, and refusing violence. It doesn't add any charge against them or any curse language, and it doesn't turn prayer into pressure.
dogmatic: The men of the Hebrews were once dear to the King of glory and strong in his service, yet they cursed Him who meant to loose them from their curse, spat on the face of Him who cured their blindness, and doomed Him to death who raised their own race from death. They knew the prophets and still refused to confess the truth, confounding false with sooth, light with darkness, hate with reverence, and that curse weighs them down until they confess the truth. So Christians should treat them with goodwill and restraint and refuse all violence, for Jesus and the apostles were Jews and the Church owes them gratitude. Our part is prayer, patience, and loving witness, looking for their gathering and redemption by God's power. And we look for the New Jerusalem as a real city, the capital of Christ's everlasting kingdom, now in the third heaven and about to descend out of heaven to be located in the midst of the promised land.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's okay to acknowledge your limits. Prayer doesn't have to be formal or long. You can rest in God's presence, knowing He understands your fatigue. Try a short, honest prayer like 'Lord, I'm tired; please help me.' Or use written prayers or Scripture when your mind is foggy. Physical rest matters too—sometimes the most spiritual thing is sleep. God doesn't demand perfection; He wants a sincere heart. You can also listen to worship music or sit quietly. Don't feel guilty. His grace is sufficient even when you feel you have nothing to give. One principle that fits here is holding yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate—just keep your mind in His presence, and if it wanders, gently bring it back without fretting. That changes the focus from saying the right words to simply waiting humbly. It leaves in place the permission to rest and the reassurance that God understands your exhaustion.
dogmatic: When you're too exhausted to pray, don't give up prayer—change how you pray. Come before God like a beggar, waiting humbly in His presence. You don't need many words; just keep your mind on Him, and when it wanders, gently bring it back in tranquility without disquiet. That is prayer: humble waiting on God. But remember you need His continual help. Praying, being with God, and thinking of Him often are linked through holy habit. We must know before we love, so cultivate the habit of thinking of God throughout the day, even in exhaustion. Yet don't rely on your diligent work without prayer for the blessing, nor pray without diligent labor. Join your work with earnest believing prayer, trusting not in the work but in the Lord who alone gives the increase. Let your exhaustion drive you to Him, not away. In this way, your waiting becomes a holy habit, and your soul learns to love the God it knows.

weighed: I'd start by saying that peace is possible, but it won't come from just running less or being kinder to yourself. You have to face what your conscience is pointing at. One principle that matters here is that a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy your ability to do right—if the regret isn't growing and the sin isn't shrinking, it's heading somewhere bad. That changes how I'd answer: it's not enough to acknowledge guilt and move on; you need to actively turn from what you've been running from, and let the regret push you toward change. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—making amends, seeking forgiveness, getting counseling. Those still matter, but they're not the whole story. The core is that peace comes from facing your conscience and actually repenting, not just accepting yourself.
dogmatic: You can't make peace with your conscience by running, and you can't make it by just feeling bad. Unrepented sin hardens your heart until you lose the ability to do right at all—that's the danger you're in. Peace requires repentance and reformation, and even that isn't enough: you have to overcome the evil in yourself, bring every appetite and desire under control, or you'll never overcome it anywhere. Stop running, face your wrongs, turn from them, and fight the evil that remains. And before you try to help anyone else, deal with your own blindness and fear—otherwise you'll have no power to help them. True peace comes from overcoming evil within, not merely regretting it.

weighed: Ezekiel saw a stormy wind, a great cloud, and fire, with four living creatures and wheels within wheels, and above them a throne with a figure like a man. John's vision in Revelation has living creatures, a throne, and a figure like a son of man, so they agree in showing God enthroned and glorious. One idea worth weighing is that the visions of Jacob, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Stephen, Peter, Paul, and John all testify to the same opening heavens and the same voice of God. That would tie Ezekiel and John into one continuous testimony, but it leaves in place that each vision is still distinct and has its own setting.
dogmatic: Ezekiel saw the heavens opened by the river Chebar: stormy wind, great cloud, fire, four living creatures, wheels within wheels, and a throne with a figure like a man. This is no isolated event. Jacob at Bethel, Isaiah in the temple, Stephen before his martyrdom, Peter on the housetop, Paul on the Damascus road, and John on Patmos all testify to the same opening heavens, the same voice of God, and the same heavenly sanctuary. Ezekiel and John see the same throne, the same living creatures, the same glory, not contradictory pictures but complementary revelations of one divine reality. And in that vision we learn not to fear evil as a real power, for evil is nothing and God is all. Refuse to fear the serpent; see its nothingness and God's allness. Learn too from Manannan that what seems to Bran a clear sea is a flowery plain: the sea-horses are calves and lambs of fair hue, with truce and without mutual slaughter, and his land is without old age and without transgression. The God who opened the heavens to Ezekiel and John opens to us a land of peace.

weighed: I'd start by telling you not to panic—lukewarm feelings are a common struggle, and feelings aren't a reliable measure of where you stand. Keep showing up: pray, read, stay in fellowship, take one step at a time. One principle here sharpens that: it's the stopping half-way that causes the distress—trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings that gloomy, vacillating feeling. That reframes your lukewarmness as a call to wholehearted commitment rather than just a mood to ride out. What it leaves in place is the core comfort: your standing doesn't rest on your feelings, so keep praying even when joy is lacking and don't be too hard on yourself.
dogmatic: Your lukewarmness isn't a phase to manage—it's dangerous. The misery you feel comes from stopping half-way, trying to serve God and the world at once. You can't safely give God part of your heart while keeping the rest for worldly interests; Christ calls that wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. So don't accept it—repent and follow Him all the way. And don't make feelings your gauge; trust the changeless word of promise, not your moods, and keep praying even when joy is gone. Let your devotion be gentle and firm at once, because whatever makes you sour or peevish only makes you worse.

weighed: I'd start where I'd naturally start: test the teaching against Scripture, pray for discernment, look at the fruit it produces and the character of the teacher, and stay humble and patient since understanding usually comes gradually. One idea worth weighing is that God is incorporeal, infinite Love rather than a corporeal person, and that praying to a bodily God can keep us stuck in human doubts and fears. If that's true, it changes how you'd evaluate a doctrine: you'd ask whether it honors God as Spirit and corrects the belief that life and intelligence live in matter, rather than judging it by striking signs or by how well it fits a picture of God as a person located somewhere. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: Scripture, prayer, fruit, humility, and patience still matter. It just reframes what you're looking for when you test a teaching.
dogmatic: Judge every doctrine by whether it honors God as infinite, incorporeal Mind and Love, not a corporeal person with human passions or a location in space. Truth is discerned by aligning thought with divine Principle, not by chasing signs, miracles, or visions; those are not the basis of testimony. Humility and faithful obedience to God's laws are, and the testimony comes line upon line through the still small voice of the Spirit. Don't reject a doctrine just because you can't yet demonstrate it on rational grounds, and don't expect a perfect, finished system here; our apprehension grows even though the facts don't change. If a teaching keeps people believing that life and intelligence reside in matter, or keeps them praying to a bodily God, it is not of God.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: honestly, no, it isn't fair, and that's part of what makes it so hard. Your actions can ripple out and land on people who had nothing to do with them, and that can feel deeply unjust. One principle worth taking seriously is that the wrong you do to someone tends to come back on you, and that right eventually adjusts the balance. That changes how I'd frame it: it says the harm won't just vanish and the wrongdoer doesn't really gain by it. What it leaves in place is the plain fact that others still got hurt, and the unfairness of that isn't erased. So I'd still say the useful move is to own it, apologize where you can, make amends, and change what led to it, rather than drowning in guilt. You can't undo the past, but you can help carry what you helped create.
dogmatic: No, it isn't fair, but the deeper truth is that wrong done to another comes back on the one who did it, and right adjusts the balance sooner or later. Nobody truly profits by injuring someone else. If others are bearing consequences of your wrong, don't just sit in guilt and murmur about how unfair it feels. Take the suffering and turn it into strength, and let your help for them flow from a victory won in your own heart. Misfortune and strife aren't God's design; they come from human choices, carelessness, and ignorance, though God permits them and overrules them for good. So repent honestly, make amends, and trust that right will settle what wrong disturbed.

weighed: Yes, you can start there, and honestly that's where most people do start. My first answer would be that it's possible but has limits, since experiences are subjective and can conflict, so philosophy can help you sort real encounters from emotional highs. One idea worth naming is that religion is the open air of the soul: the selfish person is a moral invalid huddled indoors with the blinds down, and the fix is to tear the curtains open and receive God's mercy as something objective, as free as sunshine and as near as the open air, rather than as your own feelings about religion. That changes the center of gravity: your experiences stop being the thing you inspect and become the doorway to something outside you. What it leaves in place is your question's real point: you don't need a philosophy degree to have faith, and personal encounters remain a valid part of it. So keep your experiences, but don't lock yourself indoors with them.
dogmatic: No, experiences alone won't hold. Religion isn't a feeling of dependence or a private glow; it's a life in God, with your intellect, affection, and will all engaged, and holy affection leading the way. Feelings shift, and a faith built only on them collapses when they do. You begin with history, with the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and then you go on to experience, not the other way around. And stop treating religion as your feelings about religion. Tear down the curtains and let the sunshine in: God's mercy is objective to you, as free as the sunshine and as near as the open air. The selfish person cowering indoors over his fire with the blinds down is a moral invalid; the remedy is to receive God's mercy as a reality outside yourself. That is religion, and it doesn't depend on your moods.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're not cut off from God just because you can't get to church. God isn't confined to a building. You can pray at home, read Scripture, listen to sermons, and join services online. A simple routine helps: a short morning prayer, a psalm, a few minutes of silence, and gratitude at night. Reach out to your pastor or a friend for support. Faith is also lived in ordinary acts of love and honesty. Church attendance is a gift, not a gate. One principle that fits here is that you can make an oratory of your heart—a quiet place to converse with God in meekness, humility, and love, and everyone is capable of that. That changes the emphasis: it's not just about finding substitutes for church but about cultivating inner conversation with God anywhere. It leaves in place the value of community and sacraments when you can access them, and it doesn't dismiss the real loss of not being able to gather.
dogmatic: You don't need to be at church to be with God. Make an oratory of your heart and converse with him there in meekness, humility, and love—everyone can do this. The Lord isn't confined to time or place; his presence makes your paradise, and where he is, is heaven. Even the sick who can't attend worship can enjoy communion with him. So pray, read Scripture, sing a psalm, keep silence before him. And don't lay the Church's lack only at the door of priests or institutions: the lack is a tepid love for a dimly known Lord in each member, yours included. The Church gains what's lacking when each heart worships the beloved Christ. Let your hidden worship be real converse with him and feed your love for his people.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: solitude can genuinely help spiritual growth when you go into it with clear purpose, but it isn't automatically holy, and it can slide into avoidance or isolation. So ask what you're withdrawing toward, not just what you're leaving, and test your motives with a wise counselor or spiritual director. One principle worth taking seriously here is that solitude only counts as holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself, because walls alone are a weak fence without silence of the inner faculties. That sharpens the test: it shifts the question from how much time alone you get to whether your inner life is actually recollected or just quiet on the outside. It leaves the rest in place, though. You still need intention, honesty about escape, and accountability with a community that can speak truth into your life. Take it slowly.
dogmatic: Solitude is only truly holy when it is interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself. The enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties, so do not confuse a quiet room with a recollected heart. And remember that the days of retreat are the most important in the year, because your own salvation and spiritual progress must come first; what would it profit you to gain the whole world and lose your own soul? So enter solitude as a labor of love, watching and praying, and do not presume that salvation is already secured and needs no further care.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: be honest with God about the dryness, slow down with a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, pray before you preach to prepare your own heart, and maybe talk with a spiritual director. One principle worth taking seriously is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—praying that God would help you search out and reform what's amiss in your heart. That deepens the diagnosis: it's not just routine words but a heart that needs God's searching light. It leaves in place the practical steps—honesty, slowing down, preparing your heart before preaching—but it shifts the focus from fixing your prayers to letting God examine and change you.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't your routine; it's that prayer has become an accessory instead of your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. You need to pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. True prayer isn't an occasional exercise—it's like breathing, the constant drawing in of heavenly life that nourishes the seed within. And the deadness you feel in ministry? Trace it to its root: lack of praying. Your text, your sermon, your study—all of it should be the result of prayer, bathed in prayer, so that what you preach comes from converse with God. Stop treating prayer as a slot in your day and let it become the atmosphere of your whole life.

weighed: Yes, that discouragement is understandable, and no, you shouldn't just sit in it. My first answer would be: the Christian life isn't a competition, it's a relationship, so look to Christ rather than to other people's heights, and measure progress by love, humility, and faithfulness in your own calling. One principle worth naming is the idea of holding two beholdings at once: look higher, to God, and let that keep you in comfort and real enjoyment of him; look lower, at yourself, and let that keep you in honest humility and a healthy shame about your own state, but dwell far more in the higher than the lower. That changes the tone of my first answer, because it treats self-examination as something to keep, not something to skip, and it puts enjoyment of God ahead of anxious scorekeeping. What it leaves in place is the practical core: saints were sinners who kept getting up, so set small, realistic steps of prayer, honesty, and service, and keep walking. When you fall, repent and continue, and rest in grace rather than in comparisons.
dogmatic: You should not be discouraged, but you should be ashamed, and both at once. Look up to God and to the heights of the Christian life, and let that keep you in solace, enjoying and resting in him. Look down at yourself, and let that keep you in dread and honest shame of self, not crushing despair. Hold much more in the higher than the lower. Then abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering alike; do not seek life, work, or joy outside him, but live, work, and rejoice in God. Test your thoughts, words, and deeds by this: do they make you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If so, they are according to God. If not, fear lest all is not according to God, acceptable to him, or profitable to you. Saints were sinners who kept getting up, so set small steps of prayer, honesty, and service, and keep walking.

weighed: I'd start by saying that deep wounds are real, and forgiveness is not denial. The spiritual life doesn't ask you to pretend the harm didn't happen or to trust someone who's unsafe. It asks you to release vengeance to God and refuse to let resentment become your identity. Tell God honestly what was done and how it hurt. Ask for the grace to will the other's good, even if feelings lag behind. Set wise boundaries where needed. Forgiveness is often a process, not a single moment; return to it as often as resentment rises. Seek support from a pastor or counselor. Take your time, but don't let bitterness take root. One principle that speaks to this is that forgiveness of injuries is required for salvation—that refusing to forgive forfeits your crown, while meekness under insults wins enemies and converts them. That principle changes the stakes: it frames forgiveness not just as healing but as a condition of your own salvation, which can add urgency and gravity. But it leaves in place the reality of the wound, the need for honest grief, wise boundaries, and the slow, grace-filled process of forgiving. It doesn't erase the harm or demand instant trust; it just says your soul's health is tied to letting go of vengeance.
dogmatic: Forgiveness of injuries is required for salvation. If you refuse to forgive, you forfeit your crown; meekness under insults wins enemies and converts them. So do not let the sun go down on your anger. Return meekness and kindness for insults, and will the other's good even before feelings follow. Refusal to forgive endangers your own soul, for the unforgiving cannot receive the mercy they withhold. But do not imagine you must do this by sheer will. Be faithful at the beginning in this duty and self-denial, and you will find that duty leads to pleasures; recourse to Christ's grace makes the hard thing easy. Never let your soul settle in sadness, bitterness of spirit, or scrupulous fear. Ground your consolation not in your own effort but in the goodness and sweetness of Him who died to give you life. Tell God honestly what was done, ask for grace to forgive, renew it as resentment rises, and seek support from a pastor or counselor.

weighed: When you're discouraged and confused, it helps to step back and breathe, write down what's swirling in your head, and lean on a trusted friend or mentor. Don't make big decisions while you feel this way, and give it time. One idea worth trying is treating prayer like sitting before God as a humble beggar at a rich man's gate, gently bringing your wandering mind back without getting upset at yourself. That changes how you handle the mental noise, turning it into calm return rather than frustration, but it leaves the practical stuff in place: reaching out, writing things down, and being patient. If it only makes you more distressed, you're free to set it aside.
dogmatic: Turn to God in humble prayer and hold yourself before him like a beggar at a rich man's gate. Keep your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, don't let yourself get troubled, because disquiet only scatters you more. The moment you notice a useless thought, reject it and return to communion with God. Let your prayer be simple: 'Lord, I am here, confused and discouraged; have mercy on me.' Keep your mind fixed on him as much as you can. If after sincere effort this only brings greater distress, don't force yourself to continue against your will; you're free to set it aside and learn from your own experience, because God does not coerce the soul.

weighed: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick between your own reason and the church—they can work together. Reason helps you understand the church's teachings, and the church offers guidance reason alone might miss. One principle that matters here is that authority means weight, what carries weight with your judgment, and the church's authority isn't greater for adding coercive power; believing under threat of pain isn't believing on the church's authority at all. That changes how you see the church's role—it invites your free assent rather than threatening you—but it leaves in place the real guidance and tradition the church can offer. So you can trust both your reason and the church in different ways, and it's okay to have questions as you seek answers.
dogmatic: The only ultimate authority is Christ himself, and Scripture's authority is mediate and relative—the Spirit of Christ must enable you to interpret it. Reason is not the most primal act of your personality; faith, like love and moral venture, uses reason's evidences but goes beyond them, and reason can justify but never create the act of trust. So stop treating your own reason or the church as the final authority. Christ speaks by his Spirit, and the church's genuine authority points beyond itself to him, inviting your free assent rather than threatening you. Reason is honored as faith's guide and instrument, but faith remains a personal venture of trust that reason can justify but never create.

weighed: My first answer would be that faith connects you to others by giving you a shared set of values and a supportive community. You meet people who believe what you believe, and regular gatherings and small groups help build real friendships. Faith also teaches compassion and service, so working together to help others deepens those bonds. One principle that sharpens this is that faith sanctifies daily life by keeping you mindful of God's presence, revealing Christ in the Eucharist, and showing you Christ in every person, especially the least. That changes how you see the ordinary—your daily duties and relationships become occasions of encountering God, and serving the poor becomes serving Him. What it leaves in place is the basic structure: shared values, regular gatherings, and a supportive network still matter. You still need community and friendship; the principle just gives them a deeper purpose.
dogmatic: Faith connects you to others because it is an identification of yourself with Christ—a going down into death with Him and a rising into newness of life. That is not a metaphor; it is the core of what faith means. When you re-live His life, you are united to everyone else who shares that death and resurrection, and that union is far deeper than shared values or social support. You encounter Christ Himself in the Eucharist, and that communion binds you to His body, the Church. You also learn to hear God's voice in the rules of the community and in your superiors, seeing their guidance as His providence. And you see Christ in every human being, especially the least—the poor, the suffering, the overlooked—so serving them is serving Him. Faith is not tied to any particular scientific or philosophical theory; it uses current knowledge as a tool and stays free to readjust as knowledge advances. Ultimately, faith sanctifies your daily duties and relationships, making them occasions of encountering God. That is how faith connects you to others: not merely by making you feel welcome, but by making you one with Christ and, in Him, one with all who are His.

weighed: It's completely normal to feel tempted to walk away when your vocation gets hard. I'd start by taking time to reflect on why you chose this path in the first place, remembering the early joy and sense of calling, and talking with a trusted mentor or friend who can offer perspective. Ask whether the difficulties are temporary or a sign something needs to change, and give yourself space to think and pray before deciding. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't desire another vocation or kind of service, since nothing blocks us from growing in our current one like longing for a different one. That principle shifts the focus from escape to faithfulness, so it changes how you interpret the hardship, but it leaves in place the practical steps: honest reflection, wise counsel, and care for your well-being. If after all that you still feel called elsewhere, it's okay to explore other options.
dogmatic: Do not long for a different state or place. Embrace your present vocation as God's will for you right now, and serve faithfully in the lowly duties at hand. Care not what the service may be, provided God be served. Study the letter of God's word, imbibe its spirit, and adhere steadfastly to the divine Principle. The difficulty is not a sign to flee but an opportunity to grow in fidelity, so offer each task, however small, as an act of love. Withdraw as much as possible from acquaintance and from people, abstain from affairs that hinder your purpose, and seek with jealous care the place, time, and means most suited to quiet and contemplation. Lovingly embrace silence and solitude, and fly the agitation of a world never at rest. In this way you will find strength to persevere.

weighed: My first answer would be that God's control doesn't mean he acts like a cosmic enforcer who overrides freedom.
