A lot of evil comes from human choices, and stopping it by force would mean wiping out the freedom that makes love and moral goodness possible. God works patiently instead, restraining evil, bringing good out of tragedy, and inviting people to choose the good. One idea worth weighing says that if you hold back force when you could prevent evil, you'd better be able to show that your suffering offers real hope of redeeming the wrongdoer, or else you're just being idle and cowardly. That sharpens things: it rules out passive standing-by and pushes us to resist preventable evil where we can. But it leaves my core point intact, that God's power is persuasive and redeeming rather than coercive, and that we're called to resist evil ourselves rather than wait around.
dogmatic: God's control doesn't mean he's a cosmic enforcer overriding freedom, yet nothing escapes his providence. All evil of whatever kind happens by his permission and always for some good end. It couldn't be except he permitted it, and its form and measure are allowed by him who can and will by his wisdom turn all to good. Refusing force is justified only where there's real hope that the suffering borne will prove redemptive for the evil-doer, as Christ's suffering was. Where we simply stand by while evil proceeds, that's idle cowardice, not Christian patience. So resist preventable evil where you can. And when pressure and trial come, don't flee them; they're God's way of generating spiritual force and power. Receive the trial and rise above the painful cause rather than running from it. Because every evil is bounded by his permission and bent toward good, commit all things without fear to the Providence of God.

weighed: Here's what I'd say first: patience is a skill you build with practice. Notice the early signs of frustration in your body—tight jaw, quickened breath—and use them as cues to pause and count to five before you respond. Set realistic expectations, since people are slow for lots of reasons and your irritation often says more about your schedule than their worth. Try reframing delays as small gifts of unstructured time. Keep a journal of your triggers and track how you're doing. When you do lose your temper, apologize quickly and move on instead of spiraling into shame. Now, one idea worth adding: the secret of patience is love—if you live in the love of God, patience comes as its fruit, and peace comes from patience. That changes the root of the thing: instead of white-knuckling your reactions, you're resting in being loved first, and patience grows out of that rather than out of willpower. What it leaves in place is everything practical—the body cues, the realistic expectations, the quick apologies. Those still matter; they just stop being the whole engine.
dogmatic: Stop treating patience as a technique you can manufacture. Willpower only tightens the knot. The secret of patience is love: live in the love of God and you will find the grace of patience, for patience is the fruit of love and peace is the fruit of patience. Avoid hurry and anxiety above all—they are the greatest obstacles to progress—and keep yourself faithfully in the presence of God. When a slow person frustrates you, don't rush to fix your reaction or fret about how fast you're improving; that over-eagerness is itself the mother of imperfection. Be long-suffering the way the Lord is with you, pleading gently again and again rather than passing a quick, harsh verdict. Deal out kindness, not cursings; a kind smile does more than a hundred cures. Lose your temper, apologize without spiraling, and return to the source. The source, not your vigilance, changes you.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not selfish to pray for your own needs. Scripture invites you to cast your cares on God, and bringing your needs to him is an act of trust, not greed. The real danger isn't in having needs but in how you pray—if your requests turn into demands, or if you only pray for comfort and never for others, that can slide into selfishness. A healthy pattern is to pray honestly for what you need, then widen your prayer to include others and the world. One candidate principle here is that the only obstacle to effectual prayer is individual selfishness—you may ask only what can be shared. That principle sharpens the boundary: it says private advantage or blessings that can't have a universal implication aren't really prayer but selfishness. What it changes is that it makes the test of selfishness stricter and more objective—not just your attitude but whether your request could be prayed by everyone. What it leaves in place is the core answer: praying for your own needs is fine, as long as you're open to others and not seeking gain at their expense. So ask honestly for what you need, but let your asking be something others could join.
dogmatic: No, it's not selfish to pray for your own needs—but the only real obstacle to effectual prayer is your individual selfishness. You may ask only what everybody can share. Prayer for private advantage, for the injury of others, or for blessings that can't have a universal implication is not prayer but selfishness, and it severs your soul from the very source of blessings. So don't dress up self-seeking as devotion. Ask honestly for your needs, yes, but widen your prayer to others and let your asking be something all could pray with you. If it can't be shared, it isn't prayer.

weighed: I'd start with my first answer: yes, a yearly festival of the cross can be a good practice, because annual celebrations give shape to the church's memory and give us a regular occasion to reflect on Christ's suffering and what it means for us. It doesn't have to be mandatory to be valuable; it works as a helpful tradition that families and congregations can adopt. The cross is central to the Christian faith, so setting aside a day to remember it is reasonable, as long as the observance stays meaningful and focused on gratitude and discipleship rather than empty ritual. One principle worth naming here is that the cross of Christ is to be carried as a crown, and no one should blush at the ensign of salvation. That principle changes the tone of the answer: it pushes the festival from a reasonable option toward something we should embrace with confidence and even joy, not treat as an embarrassment or a mere custom. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of my first answer: the festival still needs to be kept thoughtfully, as a yearly remembrance that points beyond itself, and it still doesn't have to be mandatory to be valuable.
dogmatic: Yes, a yearly festival of the cross should be kept, and kept rightly. The cross is not a mark of shame to be politely managed but the crown of the Christian life. We carry the cross of Christ as a crown, sign ourselves with it in prayer, and find it at the heart of every sacrament and devotion. Nor is the cross a remedy patched together after an unexpected fall: it stands as the consummation of an elemental spiritual movement, organic with the entire process of the making of men and the divine-human travail for a redeemed humanity. So keep the festival, not as mere custom, but as holy remembrance. May hell's portal be closed and heaven's opened; may the eternal kingdom of the angels be revealed with joy unceasing; and may their part be assigned with Mary to each man who keeps in memory the most sacred festival of the cross beneath the heavens. Never blush at the ensign of salvation.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: feeling unworthy of love is a common human experience, but your worth isn't determined by your feelings. God's love is unconditional and not based on your performance. Acknowledge these feelings without judgment, practice self-compassion, and remind yourself that you're inherently valuable. One principle that fits here is that we shouldn't doubt God looks upon us with love, since in His goodness He looks down with love even on the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. That principle changes the tone of the reassurance—it grounds it in God's character rather than just in self-esteem advice. But it leaves in place the practical steps: self-compassion, supportive people, prayer, patience. It doesn't replace those; it gives them a deeper reason to keep going.
dogmatic: You need to stop doubting that God looks upon you with love. In His goodness He looks down with love even on the most terrible sinner who has any true desire to be converted. So humble yourself before God, beg His forgiveness, and renew your promises of fidelity and love. Then keep pursuing perfection, staying in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience. That trust and obedience will make hard things easier and line your sorrow with hope. Don't wallow in unworthiness—turn to God, trust His mercy, and keep going.

weighed: My first answer would be no: the uncertainty of what happens after you're gone shouldn't stop you. Every lasting work passes into other hands, and its worth isn't measured by how completely you can control its future. You're responsible for faithful stewardship now, not for guaranteeing outcomes you can't see. Take it on if it's good, do it well, build in structures that let others carry it forward, and release it. One principle worth naming is that death is a door to a higher state, that identity is preserved, and that the body will be raised. That changes the tone of the question: it means the work isn't the only thing that continues, and you can trust that what you are doesn't simply dissolve. What it leaves in place is the practical point: you still can't see or control what happens to the work, so you still plan for others to carry it and let go of the outcome. It steadies you; it doesn't hand you a guarantee about the work itself.
dogmatic: No, don't let the uncertainty stop you, but don't lean on a false comfort either. Death works no miracle. We are after death exactly as far advanced as before; dying doesn't suddenly complete what was never begun in us. Being baptized and calling yourself a Christian doesn't by itself guarantee paradise; that's a delusion to be warned against. What matters is that the seed of divine love be planted and consciously growing in you here. And the continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection: by keeping that memorial present and meditating on it, we learn to die daily. Yet death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state. We don't mourn hopelessly for the righteous dead: identity is preserved, and the body will be raised. So let the thought of death steady you rather than frighten you. Take on the work if it is good, do it faithfully, build in structures that let others carry it forward, and release the outcome to God.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: figure out your needs, ask trusted friends and church members for recommendations, interview caregivers, check references, and make sure they share your values. One principle worth naming is that you should bring every matter, great and small, before the Lord in prayer, seeking guidance and waiting until His will is clear. That principle changes the tone of the search — it adds a deliberate, prayerful pause before you commit to anyone, and it reminds you not to rush. But it leaves the practical steps in place: you still need to ask around, interview people, check references, and communicate openly with your children. So pray first, then do the legwork.
dogmatic: Bring this decision before the Lord and wait for clear guidance before you take any step. Don't lean on your own planning or rush to hire someone; seek counsel from Scripture and prayer until God makes His will plain. The safest place for you and your children is the path of duty — put God first, and trust your children to Him wherever He leads. Also honor the family structure He established: involve your parents and your children's father in the decision, and respect their wishes. Only after that should you ask for recommendations or interview anyone.

weighed: I'd start with what's in the text: in Ezekiel's vision the four living creatures are symbolic figures of God's creation and presence, and the wheels suggest God's freedom to move in any direction; in Revelation they're often read as all creation worshiping God, and together they're taken as signs of divine wisdom, power, and majesty. One principle I'd weigh here is that the hermit's shieling is small but not too small, with familiar paths, a bird singing from its gable, stags leaping, and clear spring water. That principle nudges me to keep the imagery grounded and modest rather than grand, but it doesn't change the core reading of the creatures and wheels as symbols of God's presence and creation.
dogmatic: The four living creatures and the four wheels are symbols of God's creation, presence, and movement, and in Revelation they show all creation worshiping him. But the deeper point is this: anyone who says life, substance, and intelligence belong to matter breaks the brotherhood of man right from the start. And remember the four wise men at Alexander's grave: yesterday the whole world was around the king, today he is alone; yesterday he rode the earth, today the earth rides on his neck; he owned everything and now has only seven feet of earth, and his gold is here and counts for nothing. So don't rest on worldly power or wealth, because they don't outlast death.

weighed: My first answer would be: no, a strong feeling doesn't automatically make something a revelation from God. Feelings come from lots of places, including emotions, experiences, and our own desires, so they need testing. One principle worth naming is that no one can know the things of God except by the Spirit of revelation, and every faithful person may receive that witness for themselves. That principle changes the picture by saying the real test isn't how intense your feeling is but whether the Spirit is actually giving you light, and it leaves in place the caution that raw emotion alone proves nothing. So pray for that witness, check it against Scripture, and talk it through with wise believers.
dogmatic: No, a strong feeling by itself doesn't make something a revelation from God. Feelings shift with moods and desires, so they can't be your measure of what's true. The only sure test of the things of God is the Spirit of revelation, and that witness is available to every faithful person directly, not just to leaders or experts. So don't rest on how strongly you feel something or on human argument alone. Ask the Holy Ghost to make the truth known to you, and trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods. Keep praying even when the joy isn't there, and keep living so that your fruits show what the understanding of God brings.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: as a Christian, you're called to honor God, and while parties and dressing like the world aren't automatically sinful, they can lead to compromise. The Holy Ghost is given to those who obey and seek holiness, so ask whether these things draw you closer to God or away. One principle that matters here is that missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually and return as pure as white paper. That principle changes the tone: it makes holiness a daily pursuit, not a later cleanup. But it leaves in place your freedom to examine your motives and the wisdom of mature believers—so you still get to decide, with the Spirit's guidance, what honors God in your actual life.
dogmatic: You ask if you can have the Holy Ghost while keeping your parties and worldly dress. The answer is no—not if you want the Holy Ghost continually. You must start with clean hands and pure hearts, live so as to enjoy the Holy Ghost every day, and return as pure as white paper. Do not think you can begin pure only later. Remain in a holy nudity of spirit, assuming no care, desire, affection, or pretension, resting on no breast but God's. The Holy Ghost is the special gift of the Father, given according to God's discretion and your faithfulness. Going to parties and dressing like the world may not be inherently sinful, but they clutter your spirit and lead to compromise. Seek the Spirit continually and surround yourself with mature believers who can advise you.

weighed: I'd start by saying I get why you're worried—it's hard to watch someone you love drift spiritually. My first instinct would be to pray for him and just live your faith sincerely; your example can speak louder than words. One idea that stands out from what you shared is that true love means seeking the Saviour first, then going to win your brother with hope and good thoughts together. That changes the focus: it's not just about your effort but about drawing closer to Christ yourself before you try to reach him. It leaves in place the practical stuff—prayer, patience, gentle conversations, and not nagging. So I'd still say be a loving sister, but start by seeking God first, then look for his leading before you speak or act.
dogmatic: You need to seek the Saviour first, then go win your brother. Don't rely on fading human efforts—give him wreaths of hope instead. Be slow to take new steps, have no will of your own, and find God's will through prayer and the Word before you do anything. If you hold back from delivering him, you sin against your own soul—you are your brother's keeper. So pray earnestly, trust Christ to save, and act when he leads.

weighed: I'd start by saying: before you criticize, check your own heart, pray for your minister, and if you have a real concern, go to him privately and kindly, following Matthew 18. Avoid gossip and public fault-finding, and look for ways to support and encourage him. One principle worth weighing here is that ministers are ambassadors for Christ and messengers of God, so they're called to reprove sin faithfully and fear God rather than people. That principle shifts the focus: instead of just criticizing from a distance, you'd pray for him and encourage him in that costly work. But it leaves the core of my first answer in place—private, humble conversation, no gossip, and support rather than tearing down.
dogmatic: Don't fall into either trap—hiding away from people to be with God, or turning ministry into busy activism where prayer has no place. Time with God only matters as you spend it on others. Your minister is an ambassador and messenger of God: he must reprove sin sincerely, visit the sick, value a person's immortal soul above present favor, and fear only the One who can destroy both soul and body. So instead of criticizing from a distance, pray for him and back him in this costly work. And where Scripture speaks plainly, don't soften it: clergy living under the same roof with deaconesses or spiritual sisters, under the pretext of piety, is an occasion of evil and a scandal, even if they claim it's safe. Hold to that, encourage your minister toward faithful obedience, and let your own time with God flow into love for His people.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: make love concrete. Speak kindly, serve quietly, forgive quickly, show up when it's inconvenient, and do the loving action even when you don't feel like it. One principle worth adding is that self-love never really dies—it sleeps and springs up again—so staying watchful matters. That changes the tone: instead of just building habits, you also notice when self-interest is quietly steering you. But it leaves the core in place—you still attach love to real deeds, and you still act your way into love rather than waiting for a warm feeling. The watchfulness just keeps the habits honest.
dogmatic: Love becomes real when you stop trusting warm feelings and start treating love as a decision you make over and over. Speak kindly, serve quietly, forgive quickly, give generously, and show up when it costs you something. And be honest about the engine underneath: self-love never dies—it sleeps like a fox and springs up suddenly—so constant watchfulness is not optional. Don't wallow in it, but don't pretend it isn't there either. When trials come, meet them with stronger faith and purer love, because perfect love casts out fear. The harder the situation, the stronger your faith and the purer your love should be. Feelings will follow the actions, so act your way into love.

weighed: My first answer would be that the divisions come from a mix of history, culture, and conviction. Fights over authority, sacraments, and how to read Scripture hardened into separate traditions, often propped up by politics and national identity, and because each side thinks it holds the truth, the disputes feel like life or death. Pride makes it worse, though a lot of the bitterness is needless since many groups agree on the core about Christ and differ on secondary things. One principle worth naming is that people who slander and persecute each other over religion haven't really known Christ, and that kind of prideful quarreling is just self pushing the kingdom of darkness forward. That changes the tone of my answer: the problem isn't disagreement itself but the venom, and it puts a sharp question to anyone who fights dirty in Christ's name. What it leaves in place is that real differences still matter and some things shouldn't be shrugged off as mere preference.
dogmatic: The bitter quarreling between the sects of Christendom is itself the evidence. Anyone who slanders and persecutes others over the kingdom of Christ has not yet known Christ; that swelling pride over opinions is the image of Self, and it helps the Kingdom of Darkness along. So don't treat this as a harmless family spat. And don't answer with a lazy tolerance either, because tolerance can be a deadly sin. Toward the works of the Nicolaitans, only hatred was in place, and merely enduring that guilty sect drew the Lord's rebuke. Some teaching excuses immorality, and blessing that is fatal, as the letters to Pergamum and Thyatira make plain. Look at the Elkesaites: they demanded circumcision and Sabbath, repudiated Paul, appealed to a new revealed book that supposedly completed Christ's Gospel, and carried strong Asiatic heathen influence, so they barely deserve the name Christian. Bear with secondary differences, yes, but never surrender the truth or bless what corrupts.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: to love God alone, you don't need to cut people off—you detach by seeing friends as gifts that point to God, not rivals. Limit unnecessary socializing, keep your heart recollected in conversation, and offer brief prayers. Detachment isn't coldness; it's freedom to love others in God. One principle that sharpens this is that God is always near and should be adored continually, even in business and diversions. That changes the method: instead of withdrawing from friends, you practice God's presence right in the middle of your interactions. It leaves your goal intact—loving God alone—and your constraint of not becoming cold, because you stay engaged while keeping God first.
dogmatic: To love God alone, stop worrying about staying warm toward friends. Each heart's bitterness is its own, and God alone knows your secret throbbings. Accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will for some seasons. Don't fear living alone—the Lord who dwells on high knows all yet loves you better than He knows. When you forget God, don't be disquieted; return with greater trust. Detachment means creatures never take God's place, but you can enjoy them as His gifts. Keep your mind fixed on His nearness, and let every encounter be an occasion to adore Him. That way you remain loving, not cold, because His love overflows into charity.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Your sense of fragmentation is real, and it points to a need for wholeness that ultimately comes from union with God. One principle that matters here is that personality means the power of self-consciousness and self-determination, and God is personal in the highest degree. That changes how I'd frame things: your own self-awareness and freedom aren't obstacles to God but the very ground on which you can know and relate to a personal God. What it leaves in place is the practical path—prayer, Scripture, community, inner healing—and the promise that God is faithful to complete the good work begun in you. So seek Him, and He will make you whole.
dogmatic: Yes, an infinite personal God can complete you, and the reason is that personality itself is the power of self-consciousness and self-determination. God is in the highest degree self-conscious and self-determining, so denying spirit in man actually bars you from recognizing that attribute in God. God's attributes are objective qualities inhering in His divine essence, not mere names, and God is not a being of absolute simplicity but infinitely complex. The Spirit of God does not suppress your human self but identifies itself with the human me whose life it becomes, creating a new moral personality. So as you grow in self-awareness and self-determination under God, you become more truly yourself, and God, who is infinite personality, calls you to become a person in the fullest sense.

weighed: I'd start by saying: ground yourself in solid reasons for belief—study apologetics, read Scripture, and engage with thoughtful Christian thinkers. Build a community of believers who can support you. Develop spiritual disciplines like prayer and Bible reading. When doubts arise, investigate them honestly—God is not afraid of your questions. Remember that faith is not blind; it is trust based on evidence. Also, limit exposure to cynical voices and fill your mind with truth. Finally, focus on serving others; faith grows when it is exercised. One candidate principle says faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, whether our own or others'; we must trust God with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. That principle changes the emphasis: instead of leaning heavily on study and evidence, it calls you to trust God more directly and not let endless investigation become a substitute for simple reliance on him. But it leaves in place the value of community, prayer, Scripture, honest questions, and serving others—those still matter. So hold on by trusting God deeply while still using the good supports he gives you.
dogmatic: Trust God with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding. Human wisdom and endless investigation can hinder faith; instead, simply believe that God is true and that he rewards those who seek him. But do not stop at the first act of faith: hold fast your confidence firm to the end. Follow up your faith with perseverance, enduring trials as victorious testing until the blessing comes. Yet faith must be demonstrated in works and spiritual understanding; each must work out his own salvation with fear and trembling, and another's suffering cannot lessen your own liability. Fill your mind with his promises and recall his faithfulness. When cynicism surrounds you, turn to God in prayer and refuse to rely on the wisdom of others. Let your faith rest on his character, not on arguments. Hold on by fixing your eyes on Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will direct your paths.

weighed: Yes, it matters, and I'd start there. Small critical thoughts do shape your heart and eventually your words and actions, so it's worth taking them seriously and redirecting them toward something more charitable. One idea that adds to this: useless thoughts spoil everything, and the trouble starts right there, so reject them as soon as you notice they don't belong and turn back to God. That sharpens the timing of what I'd say first. Instead of only examining a critical thought and weighing whether it's fair, you'd also learn to drop it quickly once you see it's just noise, then return to prayer. What stays in place is the core: notice the thought, don't let it grow, and replace it with kindness and gratitude for the person who annoyed you. So yes, it matters, but the fix isn't only analysis. It's also a quick turn away from the thought and back to God.
dogmatic: Yes, it matters far more than you think, and the real danger is that hard, critical thoughts get planted in you by evil suggestions and by the subtle pull of evil companions, and you barely notice it happening. Useless thoughts spoil everything, and the mischief begins there, so the moment you perceive a thought is impertinent to the matter at hand or to your salvation, reject it at once. Don't analyze it, don't linger over it, don't turn it around in your mind. Turn immediately and return to communion with God. And don't be troubled about the imperfections of others, because dwelling on them only holds back your own perfection. Look upon others simply, kindly, and amiably. Gather honey from every flower and refuse to fix your attention on their flaws. When annoyance rises, reject it promptly, pray briefly, and choose to see the person with charity. That is how hard thoughts are not merely fought but replaced by a kind and simple gaze that returns you to God.

weighed: I'd start where you'd expect: pick a set time and place for prayer and reading, keep sessions short at first, confess the neglect, and lean on the Holy Spirit rather than willpower. What I'd add from the beggar-at-the-gate picture is this: don't treat wandering thoughts as failure. When your mind drifts, bring it back calmly instead of scolding yourself, because fretting just scatters you more. That changes the tone of the whole thing, from a task you're scoring yourself on to humble waiting. It leaves the practical scaffolding in place: fixed time, short starts, confession, grace. Keep it simple and keep returning.
dogmatic: Stop treating prayer as a corner of your schedule. The best of your time and the heart of your strength belong to the closet, and study and everything else come second and get refreshed by it. Enter that closet, shut the door, silence the noise, and wait before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in His presence and bringing it back in tranquility when it strays. Don't measure yourself by techniques or perfect focus; prove your sincerity by putting your desires into practice. Confess the neglect, ask for grace, and give God the first and best, not the leftovers.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said first: renew your prayer life by setting aside daily time for prayer and Scripture, examine your conscience and repent, seek accountability from a trusted friend or mentor, engage in service and charity, consider a retreat, read inspiring books, and remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again, and don't rely on feelings—act in faith. One candidate principle I'd name is this: the narrow way of continual ascension means despairing of your own power, giving yourself up to the Mercy of God, sinking into the Passion and Death of Christ, watching your mind against evil, putting away unrighteousness, forgiving outward enemies, and esteeming yourself a servant of God and of fellow-Christians. That principle changes the starting point: instead of beginning with disciplines and accountability as the engine, it begins with surrender and mercy, and it reframes the struggle as dying to self rather than self-powered effort. What it leaves in place is the practical core of my first answer—daily prayer and Scripture, repentance, watching your thoughts, forgiving others, and serving—so those habits still matter, but they become responses to grace rather than the source of renewal.
dogmatic: The narrow way of continual ascension is the answer: despair of your own power, give yourself up entirely to the Mercy of God, sink into the Passion and Death of Christ, watch your mind against evil, put away all unrighteousness, forgive your outward enemies, and esteem yourself a servant of God and of fellow-Christians. In the beginning of the spiritual life, be faithful in doing your duty and denying yourself; afterward unspeakable pleasures follow, and in difficulties you need only have recourse to Jesus Christ and beg His grace, with which everything becomes easy. Quicken and enliven your faith, taking faith as the rule of conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily; the way of faith is the spirit of the Church and suffices to bring you to a high degree of perfection. This is not self-powered effort but surrender, and grace makes the hard way easy. Persevere, and you will experience the warmth of His love again.

weighed: It's not wrong to want proof before you commit to praying. Honest questions deserve honest answers, and God isn't offended by a searching mind. But notice what you're asking: prayer isn't a transaction that needs a verified counterpart first. You can start honestly—'God, if you're there, help me'—and let the practice itself become a place of testing and discovery. One idea worth weighing is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and proofs are how faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not how it's created. That changes the order of things—you don't have to settle the evidence question before you pray—but it leaves your desire for evidence fully in place. So keep asking, read the Gospels, weigh the historical case, talk with thoughtful believers, and don't demand certainty as a precondition for any step of trust. Commit tentatively and let evidence and experience grow together.
dogmatic: Wanting proof before you pray gets the whole thing backwards. Belief in God was never meant to be the conclusion of a demonstration; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are simply the modes in which faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation—they don't create faith. The fullest argument is your own moral nature: it yields not merely an infinite cause or a designer, but a personal and righteous Lord, the proper object of supreme affection and service. So begin praying honestly—'God, if you are there, help me'—and watch what follows. Don't dismiss answers as coincidence, chance, or natural law: the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance, and they compel belief in a God who hears and answers prayer.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: feeling empty in service is common and worth taking seriously, not something to push through on willpower alone. Name the weariness honestly to God and to a trusted friend. Check whether you're serving from depletion—too little rest, no receiving, no real sabbath—and rebuild rhythms of rest and gratitude. Remember your worth isn't the output; you're loved before you do anything. Ask whether this particular service still fits your gifts and season, and feel free to step back or change commitments. Let others serve you too. One principle here says we should be indifferent to the nature of the service God chooses, satisfied with anything as long as God is served. That's worth weighing: it can loosen your grip on needing the service to feel meaningful or impressive, and it can make small, hidden duties feel just as worthy as visible ones. But it doesn't erase the practical question of depletion or fit—it doesn't mean you ignore rest, gifts, or season, or that you never step back. It shifts the focus from what the service looks like to who it's for, while still leaving room to care for your limits and receive from others.
dogmatic: You're not your own—your life and strength belong to the Lord, and your commitments are held before Him, not set by your preferences. So bring the weariness to God, yes, but don't let it become an excuse to negotiate down what He asks. Be indifferent to the nature of the service He chooses: be satisfied with anything, provided God is served, and ask only what He would have you do. Accept even the lowliest duties of the house without caring what the service is. See self-denial and simplicity not as loss but as privilege—the less you spend on yourself, the more you have to give, and cheerful giving brings a fuller joy than comfort ever could. Your worth rests in God's love, not your output, so stop measuring the service by how it makes you feel. Let the joy of the Lord be your strength, and keep yourself free from binding engagements, because you don't know when He may call.

weighed: My first answer would be that God doesn't overwhelm everyone with proof because compelled belief isn't the kind of trust Scripture praises. Evidence can inform your mind, but it can't convert your heart; belief involves trust, love, and willingness, which proof alone can't produce. God has given plenty of evidence, yet people suppress or read it differently, and God respects your freedom instead of forcing agreement. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are how faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not how it's created. That changes the framing: the question becomes less about why God withholds proof and more about what problem faith is answering in your life. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: evidence still matters, the heart still needs more than information, and freedom still matters.
dogmatic: Belief in God was never the conclusion of a demonstration. Religion existed before argument, and the proofs are simply the ways faith expresses itself and looks for confirmation; they don't create faith. So stop treating the absence of overwhelming proof as a problem God has to solve. The real evidence of God's presence is the adversary's opposition; power is developed by resistance, and you should take the enemy's attack as a token of salvation. Where resistance arises, claim double blessing, victory, and power. And when it comes to miracles reported by grave and pious authors, take the safer course: rejecting them savors of infidelity or presumption, while there is less risk in believing what is related with probability by honest persons and not rejected by the learned. Attend to the light already given, to opposition, and to credible testimony.

weighed: I'd start with what Scripture plainly says: Christ returns, the dead are raised, judgment comes, and then a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world isn't just thrown away; it's purified and renewed, and believers wait for creation itself to be redeemed. Before that there's tribulation and deception, but the gospel still goes out to all nations, and since the timing is unknown we're called to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful mission rather than date-setting. One principle I'd weigh here is that the judgments of the last days—war, plague, famine, nations gathered against Jerusalem—purify the earth and prepare the way for Christ's reign. That adds a sharper picture of how God clears away wickedness and gets the world ready for His rule. What it leaves in place is the core hope: judgment is real, Christ reigns, and the end is renewal rather than escape. It doesn't settle the timing, so watchfulness and faithful mission still stand.
dogmatic: Scripture says the end of time brings Christ's return, the resurrection, and final judgment, and then a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world won't be abandoned; it will be purified. The judgments of the last days—war, plague, famine, the gathering of nations against Jerusalem—are God's means of purging wickedness and preparing the earth for Christ's reign. And the Lord's work will keep growing and spreading until it fills the earth with the glory of God and the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem shall be holy, and the sign of the Son of man will appear. So watch, pray, and labor faithfully, for the timing is unknown.

weighed: I'd start where you're already leaning: pray for the specific children you know, name their situations, and ask God for protection, provision, and healing. Then put legs on it—foster care, mentoring, safe housing, schools, giving, advocacy—and pray for the people who care for them too. One thing worth adding is that God's names are pledges you can actually lean on in prayer. He calls Himself the Father of the fatherless, so you can say, 'You said You are their Father—be a Father to them now.' That gives your praying a firm footing without changing anything else: keep it simple and sincere, and keep pairing prayer with concrete love.
dogmatic: Plead the name. God has chosen titles for Himself—the Father of the fatherless, the LORD who provides—and those aren't decoration, they're promises He means for you to stand on. Come to Him and argue from His own word: 'You have said You are the Father of the fatherless; be a Father to these children now.' He is near to the lost child, leading him by the hand, and no weeping is beyond His reach. And don't rest your confidence on how well you pray—rest it on the Spirit who intercedes for you and on the sheer goodness of God. Then go do the work: foster care, mentoring, safe homes, schools, giving, advocacy, and praying for families and churches to welcome these children.

weighed: What I'd say first is that you're probably not doing anything wrong. Trying hard to be good and still feeling no peace is really common, and it usually means the problem isn't your effort but what you're expecting goodness to do for you. One idea worth weighing is to ask yourself whether your life is actually moving toward the supreme good and showing the healing power of Truth and Love, letting your fruits prove it rather than your intentions. That shifts the focus from keeping score to noticing real effects, which can ease the pressure. What it leaves in place is your honest effort and your longing for peace. It doesn't tell you to try harder or to stop caring. It just moves the question from am I good enough to is my goodness bringing healing, to you and to others. And be gentle with yourself while you sort that out.
dogmatic: You're asking the wrong question. Peace was never going to come from being good enough, so stop measuring yourself and start asking whether your life actually approaches the supreme good and demonstrates the healing power of Truth and Love. Your fruits will prove what your understanding of God brings to you, not your intentions or your effort. Drop the hurry and the anxiety, because those are the biggest obstacles to progress, and keep yourself faithfully in God's presence instead. Rejoice evermore, even when it seems to make no difference, and trust that God will make your reckoning good. Peace follows that, as fruit rather than prize, in God's own time.

weighed: Yes, God can help you with this fear. Many people struggle with public speaking, and it's not a sign of weakness. Start by practicing in front of a mirror or a small group, and remember the audience wants you to succeed. Take deep breaths and focus on your message. Prayer can calm your nerves—ask God for courage and clarity. Consider joining a group like Toastmasters, and if the fear feels overwhelming, a therapist can help. One principle that fits here is to speak so you're heard and understood, say what you have to say, and then stop. That changes the focus from performing to being clear, but it leaves in place the practical steps like practice and support. God often works through those steps and through people.
dogmatic: Yes, God can help you, but first learn to talk to God for your hearers before you talk to them for God. Talking to God for men is greater than talking to men for God; you will never speak well to people unless you've learned to speak to God for them. So before every occasion, ask God for enabling grace, and receive strength more than sufficient. When you speak, speak plainly so all can hear and understand. Say what you have to say and then stop. Do not darken counsel with many words or try to impress with eloquence. Your fear grows from trying to perform; instead, focus on the message and the hearers. Prepare simply, then trust God to give you the words. If your voice fails, pause, breathe, and continue quietly. The goal is not to be impressive but to be understood. God can calm your fear as you commit to speaking simply and briefly, leaving the results to Him.

weighed: I'd start by saying God wanted the tabernacle built to the exact pattern because it was meant to be his dwelling place among his people—a place where his holiness and order were reflected, and where Israel's worship was set apart from the nations. That's the answer I'd give first. One principle worth naming is that the earthly tabernacle was a pattern and shadow of heavenly things. That changes the focus: the pattern isn't just about precise construction, it points beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary where God truly dwells. But it leaves in place the original point—that approach to God must be on his terms, not our own invention, and that the tabernacle ultimately points forward to Christ.
dogmatic: God commanded Moses to build according to the pattern because the earthly tabernacle is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary. The pattern shown on the mount wasn't a mere blueprint for a tent—it was a revelation of the true heavenly reality. The wilderness tabernacle and the later temple were shadows, not the substance. Building by that pattern reminded Israel that their worship pointed beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary where God actually dwells. And this isn't arbitrary: it reflects God's power fixed to a moral purpose and held under moral responsibility, as shown at the cross, where Christ's bearing was active self-control rather than passive surrender. The Almighty doesn't resort to revengeful violence under outrage; he holds to his moral purpose, sending sun and rain on the just and unjust alike.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: look at your motives, whether you give cheerfully or to be seen, whether it's consistent and sacrificial, and whether it draws you closer to God or feeds pride. One principle worth naming is that charity is the light—God's own love, our soul held in God, and the virtue it becomes. That deepens the picture: your giving isn't just a moral habit to inspect, it's a share in God's own love that keeps you in faith and hope. What it changes is the focus, from mostly checking your intentions to asking whether your giving keeps you rooted in God and leads you further into love. What it leaves in place is the practical self-examination—motives, consistency, humility—and the call to keep giving and ask God to purify your heart.
dogmatic: Here's the heart of it: charity is the light. Charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. Charity keeps us in faith and hope, hope leads us in charity, and in the end all shall be charity. So the real question isn't whether your giving measures up to some standard of motives—it's whether it's rooted in God's own love and keeps you in faith and hope. And be scrupulous with gifts: decline questionable or encumbered donations, refuse funds tied to endowment or personal provision, and give an honest account of your stewardship to those who give. Remember too that the more generous we are toward God, the more generous we find God toward us, and the more fit we become to receive his graces and spiritual gifts in greater abundance. That's how your charity stays pure and of God.

weighed: I'd start by saying: test the idea against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community, look at its fruits—does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control?—pray for discernment, seek wise counsel, and be patient rather than acting hastily. One principle worth naming is that belief in God isn't the conclusion of a demonstration; religion existed before argument, and proofs confirm faith rather than create it. That changes how much weight you give to trying to prove or disprove the idea intellectually—it shifts the emphasis toward the kind of life the idea produces and the habit of turning toward God. What it leaves in place is the practical testing: Scripture, community, fruits, counsel, and patience still matter. So I'd still say don't rush, and if the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may well be from God.
dogmatic: You should stop treating this as a puzzle to be solved by argument. Belief in God is not the conclusion of a demonstration—religion existed before argument, and the proofs are just the ways faith expresses and confirms itself, never the means of creating it. So the real question isn't whether you can prove the idea is from God. It's whether you are cultivating the habit of rising after falls and renewing acts of faith and love until thinking of God becomes as natural as it first was difficult. That habit is what attunes your mind. Test the idea against Scripture and your faith community, yes, and look at its fruits—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control—but don't make your religion depend on proof. Pray, seek counsel, be patient, and if the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may be from God.

weighed: I'd start by saying that stagnant love is really common, and it usually grows through faithful practice more than sudden feeling—so pray daily, read Scripture, serve others, and let obedience carry you when affection feels cold. One principle that shifts this is the idea that we fail to love Christ more ardently mainly because we don't think enough about Him—that spare moments like train rides or waiting rooms can be filled with thoughts of Him. That changes the tone from duty to attentive reflection, but it leaves in place the need for steady habits and repentance where sin or distraction is quenching love. So keep showing up, and also use those small gaps to think often of Christ's character and what He has done.
dogmatic: Love grows when you stop treating it as a duty and start living in the atmosphere of Christ's love—believing He ever loves you and claiming His approval as your daily portion. The only reason you fail to love Him more ardently than any human being is that you don't think enough about Him. Use the hours on trains, waiting for appointments, and restless rests to think about Jesus, for no one is so restful to think of, and every quality you admire is found in Him. Don't settle for a little love as though it were enough. Seek love in abundance and continual increase, with the motto 'more and more,' since abundant love is the measure of abundant life. Love is not a fixed quantity but a living growth; abide in the sense of being loved, fill the small spaces with thoughts of Him, and press on to more.

weighed: No, it's not wrong to ask your people to pray for you. Scripture shows leaders depending on the prayers of others, and Paul himself asked the churches to pray for him. Asking is humility, not weakness, and it draws your congregation into partnership in the gospel. One principle worth naming is that prayer is a duty and privilege to be kept at set times whether or not you feel like it. That changes how you wait on this: don't hold back your own praying until the spirit of prayer comes. Pray at your appointed times even when you feel dry, lead your family in prayer, and don't ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. What it leaves in place is your asking: it's still right to request your people's prayers, and it still invites them into the work. Keep it simple too, like a child asking a father, not a formal procedure.
dogmatic: It is not wrong to ask your people for prayer, but don't stop at asking. Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. Pray with your family. Never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. The Apostle would not have prayed these prayers unless he had been certain God would answer them, and they will assuredly be answered as you resolutely, humbly, lovingly, and trustfully fulfil the required conditions through Jesus Christ. So set yourself to those conditions and expect the answer. At the same time, keep prayer simple and natural, a child asking a Father, not a formal procedure governed by human rules. God as Father delights to be sought for everyday needs, so ask Him plainly and constantly, and don't hedge prayer about with man-made rules.

weighed: I'd start by saying the fear comes from a misunderstanding: giving yourself completely to God doesn't erase your individuality, it purifies and fulfills it. The self you're afraid of losing is often the self built on pride and self-will, not your true identity. One principle worth naming is that self-denial has to flow from inward joy in God and the work of the Spirit, not from custom or just copying other people, or you'll regret it and it won't last. That changes the tone of surrender: it's not grim self-erasure but something alive and joyful. What it leaves in place is the core answer: God is a better keeper of your identity than you are, so you don't have to fear becoming no one.
dogmatic: The thing standing between you and God isn't your personality, it's the creaturely will, the self built on pride and self-will. That will can only be broken by the grace of self-denial and removed by perfect conformity with the Divine Will, and you can't do that by your own effort or technique. It happens by the light and grace of God received into your soul, and you must not resist it. So stop treating your individuality as something to protect. We are nothing, and every man at his best is vanity; only in humility and self-emptying can God fill you and work through you. Surrender isn't loss. It's the only way to become the person God intended you to be.

weighed: I'd start by saying the fear of death is common and it helps to name it honestly rather than deny it. Then I'd point to one idea worth keeping: fear is often a cause of disease, so warning people against death and describing disease can frighten them into it, while changing your thought about disease restores health. That changes how you talk to yourself and others — no rehearsing worst-case scenarios or predicting illness. What it leaves in place is the practical side: calm the fear first, then take sensible steps, and keep steady rather than rushing. Turn your thought toward health and toward Life as God, the source of all being, and let faithful steadiness matter more than quick results.
dogmatic: You should handle the fear of death by mastering it rather than cultivating it. Calm the fear first: silently reassure yourself that you are exempt from disease and danger, and remove fear as the first step toward healing. Do not rehearse symptoms, describe illness, or predict disease, because that thinking only strengthens fear of death and illness. Turn your thought decisively toward health and toward Life as God, the source of all being. Keep yourself steadily in God's presence, free from hurry and anxiety, since over-eagerness is the mother of all imperfections. Let faithful steadiness, not anxious striving, govern your days. Calm the fear first, lift thought to Life, and walk quietly before God; in that stillness fear loses its hold and healing has room to work.

weighed: I'd start by saying that humility isn't really about working up contempt for yourself—it's about seeing yourself honestly and choosing to serve. So take time each day to look at your actions, own your faults, and stop comparing yourself favorably to others. Serve quietly where no one notices, and when praise comes, redirect the credit. That's the answer I'd give first. One principle worth naming is that true humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares that can quietly poison your affections and cost you grace. What that changes is the emphasis: it makes you wary of praise and keeps you from preferring yourself to anyone, placing yourself below others. What it leaves in place is the steady, honest self-examination and quiet service—it doesn't turn humility into self-hatred. It just adds a real caution about praise and a deliberate choice to put others first.
dogmatic: Start by accepting that of yourself you are nothing and that every good thing in you comes from God, not from you. Distrust your own judgment, expect nothing from yourself, and don't be surprised when you fail—you're just seeing what you are apart from grace. Serve unnoticed and put yourself below everyone, counting others as better than yourself. Above all, dread the esteem and praise of others, because praise is a snare that can slip a mortal poison into your affections and rob you of divine grace. Don't measure your growth by feeling capable or by any self-assessment, since even your best state is vanity. Empty yourself so God can fill you and work through you. Courage here isn't confidence in your own strength—it's a low esteem of self that leaves room for God alone to act.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, God acts—often quietly and on a different timetable than we expect. Keep praying persistently; the persistence itself shapes your heart while you wait, and it helps to look for small signs of grace, like a peace that steadies you or a person who shows up at the right moment. One principle I'd weigh in is that God is an ever-present help in trouble, always near though not always known. That changes the tone more than the substance: instead of mainly urging you to make each request explicit and leave nothing unasked, it lets your prayer be a simple turning of your heart to him amid your work, and it means distraction doesn't have to trouble you—you can return quietly and keep going. What stays in place is the core: keep praying, watch for his hand in ordinary things, and trust he's already at work.
dogmatic: Yes, God acts—he is an ever-present help in trouble, always near, though often not known. So stop treating prayer as a checklist where every request must be spelled out and nothing left unasked; that anxiety isn't faith. Do all your actions for God and let prayer be the simple turning of your heart to him in the middle of your work. If your attention wanders, don't be troubled—just return quietly. And make prayer your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: pray that God would enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. He isn't far off or slow to hear; he's nearer than your own breath, steadying you, opening doors, sending help at the right moment. Trust that he's already at work in ordinary things—he never leaves you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your being overwhelmed is itself a sign you're seeing your need, and God's mercy is bigger than your sin. Christ's work is enough for anyone who turns to Him, so bring it honestly, confess it, and receive forgiveness—you're not defined by your failures. One principle I'd weigh in is this: if your confidence is sinking under the sheer number and size of your sins, remember that all things are possible to God, and it's as easy for Him to blot out countless heinous sins as to forgive one. That changes the tone—it lifts the despair and turns your eyes to how freely God forgives. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: confession, repentance, and resting in mercy. So take one step at a time, turn from the sin, make amends where you can, and let the burden lighten as you grow in trust.
dogmatic: Don't soften this: a single mortal sin left unrepented is enough to damn the soul forever. So cultivate an intense, abiding fear of sin and eternal loss—if love of God is too weak to hold you back, fear of hell must restrain you. And don't let your confidence sink over the number or magnitude of your sins: all is possible to God, and it's as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable heinous sins as to forgive one. Of ourselves we can't even think what is right; everything comes from God. But salvation isn't a verdict merely credited to you—it's the actual redemption of your whole self, being made righteous by living, in Christ's power, the very life He lived. So confess, turn, and let Him transform you from within.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, you shouldn't be discouraged. Getting stuck in the same spot is common, and it doesn't mean you're beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up, look at what sets off the failure, and adjust. One principle worth naming is that you can be faithful in your exercises while staying untroubled and unastonished when you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That changes the tone: instead of treating each stumble as a verdict on you, you expect weakness and let it deepen your dependence on God. What it leaves in place is the honest effort itself, prayer, Scripture, accountability, and the steady work of learning from what triggers the failure. So keep going, and don't be surprised when weakness shows up.
dogmatic: No, don't be discouraged, and don't let fear get a foothold. Be brave and true to your convictions from the beginning, because cowards always get hurt and those who stand firm from the start face the fewest tests. Be faithful in your exercises, prayer, Scripture, and the study of the textbook, and stay completely untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes failure. Failure is common and doesn't mean you're beyond hope, so expect weakness and let it deepen your dependence on God. Material remedies and physicians may have done their best, but without avail; the healing comes through the study of the textbook. Stand firm, trust God to stand by you, and keep returning to your exercises without fear or dismay.

weighed: Yes, you may hope. I'd say that first and mean it: God cares about your parents, and your prayers for them are not wasted. One principle worth weighing is that prayer can go wrong when it's really about our own comfort rather than God's glory, and that's a good check on my first answer. What it changes is the focus of your hope: pray for their souls and for God's glory, not just for your own peace of mind. What it leaves in place is the main thing: you may still hope, keep praying, share your hope with them while you can, and leave the timing and results to God, who wants their good even more than you do.
dogmatic: You may hope, but your hope needs to be purified of selfishness. Don't pray mainly for your own comfort or reputation; pray for God's glory and for the salvation of their souls, for what your parents could become for God and His kingdom. Make prayer your main helper in every step of spiritual progress. Pray that God would help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is wrong in it, so that your intercession comes from a purified heart. Keep entrusting your parents to God, who is ever-present and omnipotent, and share your hope with them while you still can.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, God doesn't force anyone to be saved. Scripture shows God drawing, convicting, and enabling, but never coercing the will—the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Grace is resistible, yet persistent. One candidate principle says that in every soul that will be saved there is a Godly Will that never consents to sin. That changes how I'd frame it: salvation isn't just a neutral choice but the awakening of a will God preserves. It leaves in place that no one is saved against their will and no one is saved by their own effort alone.
dogmatic: No, God does not force anyone to be saved. In every soul that shall be saved there is a Godly Will that never assented to sin, nor ever shall—so we are that which He loveth. The order matters: first we set our purpose and will toward God, we make the effort, and then God stabilises it and brings it to fruition. Without the willing will God gives no grace, and without God's grace no will of man reaches attainment. Grace does not override the will; it heals and strengthens it, and the saved freely turn to Him.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's completely natural to fear your family's judgment, so look at your beliefs honestly, talk with them openly, listen to their concerns, find common ground, set gentle boundaries, and lean on supportive friends or a faith community. One principle worth weighing here is that faith gets hindered when we lean too hard on human wisdom, our own or others'—we're called to trust God with all our heart. That changes the center of gravity: instead of making your family's approval the test of whether your faith is sound, you anchor yourself in God and let their concerns inform you without ruling you. What it leaves in place is everything practical—you still talk openly, listen, set boundaries, and keep loving your family. It just means the fear of being judged doesn't get to be the judge.
dogmatic: Fear of family judgment is real, but the answer is not to put your faith on trial before human wisdom. Trust God with all your heart and refuse to lean on your own understanding, because that leaning hinders faith. Faith must be quickened—made alive and taken as your rule of conduct—rather than replaced by trivial, shifting devotions that rise and fall with approval or mood; the way of faith suffices to bring you to perfection. Do not let comfort or safety become your master. Be ready to endure discomfort and even rejection for Christ's sake, and regard this trial not as pointless but as given for God's glory and the strengthening of your faith. Speak gently, love your family, and let a living faith, not fear, govern your choices.

weighed: My first instinct is to say that Christ's suffering was complete and sufficient, so you don't suffer to earn salvation—He suffered so you could be spared. Your part is gratitude and obedience: share the gospel, serve the poor, forgive, give generously, and let your life commend the message. One principle worth naming is that the believer's true glory is to be despised, poor, and lowly with Christ, and it ill becomes a servant to seek riches and honor where his Lord was poor and despised. That changes the picture: instead of pursuing influence so your witness carries weight, you'd embrace being overlooked and lowly as your real glory, standing with the poor and suffering. What it leaves in place is the core—redemption is finished at the cross, and your task is still to live it out and announce it, just without chasing greatness along the way.
dogmatic: Christ's suffering is on your behalf, not instead of you. He bore what you could not, and now He invites you into the fellowship of His sufferings and His ongoing work of redeeming the world—not to add to your salvation, but to share His life. You share in it by dying to self, bearing burdens, forgiving enemies, and standing with the suffering and poor. Don't seek riches, greatness, or honor where your Lord was poor and despised; embrace being despised and lowly with Christ as your true glory. And don't be too anxious for sensible devotion, sweetness, or tears; your chief care should be to stay inwardly united to God by good will, denying yourself to follow Christ, who was truly poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. Redemption is accomplished at the cross yet applied through His body, and your life becomes its embodiment.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: the Lord will come back visibly and personally at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. That's what the creeds say, and Scripture paints Christ coming in glory with the angels, raising the dead, and separating the righteous from the wicked. It's a final, universal judgment. Believers don't need to fear condemnation because they're in Christ, while the unrepentant face eternal separation. The timing is debated, but the main thing is to be ready—live faithfully now, trust Christ, and share the gospel so others can be ready too. One principle worth naming is that we're judged by the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and as death leaves us, so judgment finds us. That sharpens the stakes: it's not just outward actions but the heart's hidden intentions that are laid bare, and there's no changing our account after death. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—Christ's visible return, the resurrection, the final separation, and the call to be ready. It just makes the call to readiness more searching.
dogmatic: The Lord will return visibly and personally to judge the living and the dead, and that judgment runs deeper than anyone likes to admit. It's according to the deeds done in the body—what you've done, said, and even thought—and the thoughts and intents of the heart are laid bare before Him. Death leaves you as it finds you; judgment isn't something you can defer or amend afterward. Yet death isn't the end of identity but a door to a higher state. The righteous dead aren't lost, so don't mourn them hopelessly—the body will be raised and the person preserved. God will honor and magnify His servants, sustain them in righteousness, lift them on high, exalt them into His presence, and let them share His glory forever. Their service is not in vain. So be ready, trusting Christ, doing good, and guarding the heart's hidden intentions.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, loneliness is a common cost of following your conscience, and it's healthy to acknowledge it. One principle worth naming is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior—walls are a weak fence without inner silence. That changes how I'd frame the loneliness: it's not just a social gap to fix but an invitation to quiet your imagination, memory, and will and dwell with God and yourself. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—build new friendships, pursue hobbies, stay connected with family where possible, and don't isolate indefinitely. So the loneliness is expected, but it can become a school of interior silence rather than just a void.
dogmatic: Loneliness after obeying conscience is to be expected, but don't mistake exterior solitude for true solitude. Walls and physical separation are only a weak fence; without interior recollection they are not true solitude at all. True solitude requires silence of the interior faculties—quieting imagination, memory, and will—and employing the mind on God and on yourself. Keep yourself in the love of God by constant trust and constant obedience, so that hard things become easy and sorrow is silver-lined with hope. And do not expect romance, family, business, pleasure, or art to fill the emptiness within; every substitute for God leaves an emptiness unfilled and ends in disillusionment. Only the finding of God is a permanent success. Let your separation become a school of interior silence and abiding love, where loneliness is met by His presence.

weighed: I'd start by saying that moving to a new country with plenty of food and land can bring real relief, but peace and happiness are interior realities that travel with you rather than living in a place. One principle here says this world is a touchstone and finding-place for God, and that true happiness comes from finding God from this world rather than waiting for the next. That changes the frame: the move becomes a setting for seeking something deeper, not a cure-all. It leaves in place the practical advice to think about community, legal stability, and work before you go, and it still warns that happiness isn't guaranteed by geography or abundance.
dogmatic: Your desire for happiness is God-given, and God is to be found here in this world, the touchstone and finding-place for Him. Do not expect a new country, abundant food, or land to produce peace by itself: forms of government and external arrangements do not materially alter the people's condition, and happiness and peace are gifts of God. So receive peace as His gift where you are, and let any move be a place of finding Him rather than escape. When your interior states shift, do not be curious about their causes; accept the diversity of consolation and dryness without inquisitive inquiry, and show love by patiently enduring them.

weighed: I'd start by saying guilt is a normal human emotion, and it can be useful—it signals that something in your life is out of alignment with your values. But being chased by it sounds exhausting, and that suggests the feeling has become disproportionate. It's worth asking whether the guilt is tied to a specific action you can address, or whether it's a more general anxiety that's attached itself to religious themes. Talking with a counselor or trusted pastor can help with persistent guilt. God is often described as merciful and forgiving, so if the guilt feels condemning rather than corrective, it may not be coming from God at all. One principle I'd weigh in here is that when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, you should humble yourself, ask forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That principle changes the practical next step: instead of only analyzing the guilt, it gives you something to do—bring it honestly before God, ask forgiveness where it's needed, and begin again. What it leaves in place is my original point: persistent, condemning guilt still isn't the same as God's voice, and it's still worth talking to someone you trust if it won't let go.
dogmatic: Guilt that chases you is real, but it isn't your master, and managing it alone isn't your job. God is the one living Worker; counselors, friends, and your own efforts are only instruments—useful when they lead you to Him, harmful when they replace Him. Cast all your care on Him, because anxious self-reliance is distrust of the God who promises to hear. If you've offended Him—by hiding, by preferring a creature to Himself—don't stay paralyzed in doubt. Humble yourself, beg His forgiveness, and renew your promises of fidelity and love. Then begin again and keep pursuing perfection, for He desires to give Himself to you, and asking for anything beneath Him insults Him and hurts you. The chasing isn't condemnation; it's His drawing. Run to Him.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: notice the pride without turning it into a shame spiral. Remember the message matters more than the messenger, and that any skill you have is a gift you grew into over time. Deflect compliments graciously, jot down what worked so you can improve, and ask a trusted friend for honest feedback. It also helps to remember that a talk lands differently with different people, so 'successful' is partly circumstance. Over time, focusing on serving your listeners rather than your performance will loosen pride's grip. One idea worth adding is that the greatest sermon is your practice, and that you need the Spirit to give each heart a word in due season. That shifts your measure of success from how the talk was received to how you lived and prayed beforehand, and it makes a short word fitly spoken better than a long impressive one. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff: noticing pride, receiving feedback, and serving your listeners.
dogmatic: The real remedy isn't managing your feelings about a good talk; it's reordering what you count as success. The greatest sermon is your practice. A life lived in obedience preaches louder than any eloquence, and fine language without it is empty noise. Before you prepare, seek the Spirit for a word in due season, and prefer a short sermon fitly spoken to a long one that shows off the speaker. And don't fool yourself that sermon-making and study keep your spirit in trim. Sermon-making without prayer hardens and estranges the heart from God, and much prayer is needed to keep your spirit in harmony with your calling. Yet don't despair at the temptation. God permits such inclinations to humble us. Despise the temptation while embracing the trouble it brings, and let it drive you to prayer rather than to shame.

weighed: My first instinct is that the phrase shows up in several biblical traditions, and interpreters genuinely differ. Some read it as a symbol of God's presence or the community of believers, others as a literal place. Hebrews talks about a true tabernacle set up by the Lord rather than by humans, which points to something more than a metaphor, though 'real' in ancient thought could include heavenly realities that aren't physical buildings the way we mean it. One idea worth weighing is that the sanctuary is a real building in heaven, the pattern shown to Moses, pitched by the Lord and not by man. If you take that seriously, it shifts the emphasis from symbol to substance and makes the earthly tent a copy of something that actually exists. What it leaves in place is the point of the image in each text: it still assures believers that God's saving work rests on something more enduring than earthly institutions. So I'd say the question is worth holding open, but that reading gives real weight to the heavenly side.
dogmatic: It's not a figure only. The heavenly sanctuary is a real building, the true tabernacle the Lord pitched and not man, and the wilderness tabernacle was just a pattern and shadow of it. Moses was shown the pattern on the mount so the earthly tent could image the heavenly reality, not replace it. The priest at that altar holds Christ himself, angels attend it, and the sacrifice demands a purity becoming heaven. And the opened heavens aren't a mere figure either. Where the cherubim and the flaming sword guard the way of the tree of life, the heavens are literally opened. That's the gate of heaven, and by that way the Holy City will come down. The earthly was the shadow; the heavenly is the substance.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this is a hard spot, and kindness matters. Before you say anything, ask whether it's clearly sin or just a personal preference, and whether you're the right person to bring it up. If you do speak, do it privately and gently, with humility, making it about your care for her rather than about being right. Invite her to talk instead of issuing a correction, and be open to correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest thing is to pray and wait. One idea worth weighing is that there's no real pleasure in sin, that what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives. That can give you courage to speak rather than stay silent out of fear of hurting her feelings. What it changes is your resolve to say something loving instead of nothing. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: privacy, gentleness, humility, and not wanting to wound her.
dogmatic: Silence isn't the safe choice you think it is. Sin offers no real pleasure; what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs far more than it gives, and once you see that clearly, you'll have the courage to help her escape it. So speak, and speak plainly. If she's swearing, treat it as a serious habit to break and put a penance on every oath. Don't settle for gentle hints; severity is what actually breaks a habit like that. And know your limits: it isn't your place to point out the supposed faults of church leaders. God will judge them. Correct what's yours to correct, and don't give the world a reason to speak evil because of careless words.
