weighed: I'd start by saying that rich countries still see unhappiness and violence because money alone doesn't fix inequality, isolation, or a lack of meaning. People feel disconnected and stressed, and consumerism can break community ties. One principle that adds something is that the poor have powerful arms—their sighs and groans pierce the heavens and draw down vengeance on the rich and on cities that oppress them. That principle changes the picture by making the suffering of the poor not just a social problem but a moral and spiritual cry that demands justice. It leaves in place the practical points about inequality and isolation, but it shifts the focus to the voices of those left behind. So material riches alone don't guarantee well-being; social and spiritual factors matter, and the cries of the oppressed won't go unheard.
dogmatic: Rich countries are unhappy and violent because the poor have powerful arms—their sighs and groans pierce the heavens and draw down vengeance on the rich and on cities that oppress them. That's the real answer. You can't just talk about inequality or isolation; the cries of the destitute are a force that demands justice. And as long as great numbers of citizens have undeveloped faculties, society cannot be justly ordered. The only real solution is a complete education that raises each person's actual worth to the level of their potentialities. The poor are the people of God and shall inherit the earth; the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone, and persons are esteemed by character, not wealth or position. So don't be surprised by violence—it's the consequence of ignoring these truths.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, it's not wrong to accept your religion on authority. Most of what any of us believes rests on trust in people who know more than we do, and faith traditions are no exception. What matters is whether you trust a source you have good reason to consider reliable, or you're just avoiding questions because they make you uncomfortable. A healthy faith usually includes some personal digging—reading, asking, reflecting—alongside trusting teachers and tradition. One principle worth naming here is that authority means weight, what genuinely carries weight with your judgment, not coercive power. That changes something real: it means believing under threat of pain isn't believing on the Church's authority at all, so you can set aside fear as a motive and still lean on the tradition that formed you. What it leaves in place is your own responsibility to examine the core claims enough to know what you're trusting. So if you've never looked into it, make some time; if you've looked enough to trust it, that can be a mature position.
dogmatic: Accepting your religion on authority is not wrong, but you need to understand what authority actually is. It isn't coercive power or the threat of penalty; it's moral and spiritual weight that rightly carries your judgment. Coercion adds nothing to the Church's true authority—a faith secured by threat is submission to force, not authority. Nor is the final arbiter your inward light or private consciousness set above the Bible. Submit to the prophets and apostles speaking through the Scriptures; that subjection is perfect freedom, placing you under truth itself. Be willing to depend wholly on God. Where human guarantees, teachers, or reasoned proofs would secure you in advance, be ready to decline that support if doing so enables a fuller dependence on His faithfulness. Receive the faith handed down, and let its authority carry you where your own reasoning cannot reach.

weighed: When you feel like God has hidden Himself, my first instinct is to say: don't panic, but do check your heart. Look for anything you've been ignoring, repent, and get back into prayer, Scripture, and community. Feelings aren't reliable; God promises never to leave you. One idea that stands out is that when you realize you haven't thought of God in a while, you shouldn't beat yourself up—just acknowledge it and return to Him with more trust. That shifts the tone from anxious self-examination to a gentler turning back, but it doesn't remove the call to examine your life and renew your practices. So I'd still say: check yourself, but do it with trust, not fear.
dogmatic: You shouldn't be disquieted at all. If you feel God is hidden, it's because you've neglected Him—not because He's left. God is the one living Agent who works; your anxious self-reliance is just distrust and sinful self-conceit. So stop examining yourself in fear and cast all your care on Him. Think of Him constantly—by day, by night, in business, even in diversions. He's always near, and it's rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit you. Don't neglect Him; adore Him continually. Return to Him without disquiet, confident He'll reveal Himself in His own time.

weighed: Start with yourself. Before you plan meetings or hand out prayer guides, become a leader who actually prays—because praying leaders are the ones who produce praying followers. That's the principle I'd lean on here: none but praying leaders can have praying followers. It changes the starting point from programs to your own practice, but it leaves the rest of the plan intact: cast a clear vision, form a prayer team, set regular meetings, teach on prayer, share testimonies, and be patient as the culture shifts. So begin on your knees, then build the structures around that.
dogmatic: You begin by becoming a praying leader, full stop. No program, no team, no resource will set your church to praying if you aren't praying yourself—a praying pulpit begets praying pews, and the greatest reformer is the one who can set the Church to praying. Keep your set times of prayer whether you feel like it or not, lead your family in prayer, and never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send forth laborers, and treat prayer as the mighty engine that moves the work. Everything else follows from that.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, love and clear-eyed judgment can coexist—in fact, real love needs them together. Love isn't about turning off your brain; it's about seeing someone clearly, faults and all, and still choosing their good. One principle that sharpens this is that love is discerning, not blind: it grows in knowledge and insight so you can tell what really matters, what's good versus better, and what's best. That principle changes how I'd frame it—love isn't just compatible with judgment; it actually calls for it. But it leaves in place the core idea that love and judgment work as partners, with love giving warmth and motive, and judgment giving direction and honesty.
dogmatic: Love and clear-eyed judgment don't just coexist—true love demands them. Love abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, so you can distinguish things that differ and approve what is excellent. This isn't optional; it's the very shape of genuine love. True sanctity isn't found in raptures or imaginings but in love of God and in meekness, humility, and charity—shown in submission, self-renunciation, and consideration for others. Love isn't mere affection for the lovable; it's the principle of unselfishness that seeks another's good even toward the unthankful. It follows Christ's motto of self-denial, not Satan's 'Spare thyself.' Love sees clearly and acts wisely, setting boundaries and speaking hard truths, while discernment without love becomes harsh. Love provides motive and warmth; discernment provides direction and honesty, distinguishing good from bad, better from best, and best from excellent.

weighed: I'd start by pointing you to Scripture and prayer: test your thoughts against what God has revealed, look at their fruit—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control—check your motives, and get counsel from mature believers. One principle worth adding is the humility test: do these thoughts leave you more humble, more gathered toward God, and more steady? If so, they're likely from him; if they inflate you or scatter you, be wary. That adds a useful inner check, but it doesn't replace Scripture, prayer, and wise counsel—those stay in place as your anchors.
dogmatic: Here's the test you actually need: do your thoughts and actions make you more humble, more recollected in God, and more strong? If yes, they are according to God. If not, fear that they are not acceptable to him or profitable to you. And stop turning this into a debate about what God is—that dispute itself shows you haven't felt him and that you're exalting your own meaning and craving control. Instead, learn to enter again into the love of God and your brother. Our commonness lies in un-Godlike thoughts of heart and mind, and their alteration is the Holy Spirit's work, set in motion by taking Christ into the heart. So rest in the felt presence of God and love of the brother, and let the Spirit transform you.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, social work and charity are genuinely good ways to serve others and improve the world, and they can reflect God's heart for people who are struggling. But I'd add that charity isn't the whole of the Christian life. It needs to flow from a real relationship with God, with prayer, worship, and community around it, and it can quietly become a substitute for that relationship if you lean on it for your identity or salvation. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that, not the means to it. One principle worth naming is that we serve God well only when we serve Him as He wills, not as we think we could serve Him better some other way. That changes the posture of your question: instead of asking whether social work is the way, you'd ask whether this is the particular way God is calling you to serve right now, and stay open to Him redirecting you. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: charity is still a real expression of faith, still worth pursuing, still a genuine way to love your neighbor. It just isn't a shortcut around trusting Christ.
dogmatic: Charity is good, but don't confuse it with the way to God. We serve Him well only when we serve Him as He wills, not as we imagine we could serve Him better by some path we prefer. That means yielding completely to God's will for His honor and letting go of the idea that you can improve on His way by choosing your own. And be careful how you give: charity must not encourage idleness or pauperism. People should have a self-sustaining spirit, willing to work in exchange for aid. The Church's aim is to relieve present needs and then help the poor help themselves. Watch out, too, for treating riches as an aid to service. Hoarded wealth is a snare, and voluntary poverty for the Lord's sake is the fitting companion of a life of self-denial. Service has to flow from your relationship with God, with prayer, worship, and community around it. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that relationship, not the road to it.

weighed: What I'd say first is pretty ordinary: slow down, pay attention, get outside, seek out art or music or kindness that stirs you, cut back on the distractions that numb you, and be patient, since wonder is something you practice. One principle worth adding is the beggar-at-the-gate image: wait before God without fussing when your mind wanders, and gently bring it back in calm. That changes the tone of the advice, from self-improvement project to humble, patient waiting, and it gives you a place to put the restless moments instead of fighting them. What it leaves in place is the practical core: attention, patience, and stepping back from noise still matter. It just frames them as trust rather than effort.
dogmatic: Stop treating wonder as a skill to optimize. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and make it your business to keep your mind in His presence. When it wanders, don't get agitated, because agitation scatters you further; bring it back quietly. And don't settle for repose or slide backward in the ascent. Go forward like a climber until you reach the goal. If your desires drift toward lesser things, you'll lose yourself in byways and endless distraction. Withdraw from the world's noise into the one unchanging Good, and recollection will deepen as you rise.

weighed: Yes, it matters. Your desire to serve God is real, and he sees it even when your life feels small and hidden. Greatness in his eyes isn't about visibility or worldly success; faithfulness in small things counts for a lot. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through love, integrity, and quiet service. One principle I'd weigh here is this: the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate 'religious' life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. That changes how you see your small, hidden life—it's not a lesser path but a real place to meet God. What it leaves in place is the call to faithfulness right where you are, and the trust that God will use your life for his purposes. Your worth isn't in what you do but in who you are in Christ.
dogmatic: Yes, it matters—but not in the way you might think. Don't measure your life by how great or visible it seems. Ask instead whether you're living the life that approaches the supreme good, whether you're demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love. Your fruits will prove what your understanding of God brings to you. And remember: the high mysteries of God come at a price. You must learn to live in extraordinary lowliness and loneliness of spirit, and the interests and enjoyments of ordinary life will dry up, because God wills to have the whole of you. So don't cling to the comfort of a small, hidden life as an excuse. Let God have all of you, even if that means the ordinary pleasures fade.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: bear it with patience and humility, keep your integrity, don't argue or defend yourself, and let steady good conduct speak for you. The principle about being ready to be made all things to all men in matters of indifference, but never at the cost of truth or conscience, sharpens that. It means you can bend on small things for the sake of peace and still hold the line on what actually matters, so you're not rigid about everything or loose about the essentials. What it leaves in place is the rest: patience, kindness, prayer for those who misjudge you, and trusting God to vindicate you in his time.
dogmatic: The real answer is that the highest service is the bond slave's service: self-renunciation and glad submission to proper authority for the Master's glory and the brethren's sake. So stop protecting your reputation and yield your preferences. Where their vanities are matters of indifference, adapt for the sake of love and witness; where they touch truth or conscience, refuse and bear the cost quietly. Deal honestly and uprightly with those over you and alongside you, because that is what kindles confidence and brotherhood where people now want to take advantage. Don't argue, don't defend yourself, and don't wait to be understood. Serve faithfully, pray for those who think ill of you, and leave vindication to God.

weighed: I'd start by saying that the trustworthiness of the Old Testament doesn't hinge on knowing who wrote each book. Many are anonymous or disputed, but that doesn't make them unreliable. The texts have been preserved and recognized as Scripture by faith communities for centuries, and their internal consistency, historical references, and spiritual depth attest to their genuineness. Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament as authoritative, which gives us confidence. So focus on the content and its witness to God's work rather than authorship. One principle that fits here is that our Lord's use of the Old Testament depends on nothing about authorship or date—he appeals to its spiritual testimony to himself, and his references to familiar names involve no fallibility. That principle reinforces the point: it shifts the weight from human authorship to divine testimony, but it leaves in place the value of historical evidence and the church's recognition. So you can trust the books without solving every authorship question.
dogmatic: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament is not up for grabs just because some books are anonymous. Our Lord's use of those books depends on nothing concerning authorship or date—he appeals to them in their spiritual aspect and testimony to himself, and his references to writers under familiar names involve no fallibility. That settles it. You don't need to fret over disputed authorship; Christ's own use of the Scriptures is enough. Apply the rule that ancient documents in proper custody are presumed genuine until sufficient evidence is brought to the contrary. The same goes for the New Testament documents found in the custody of the church. And remember that the textbook is a key to the Scriptures—its honest study enables you to prove all things. So stop worrying about who wrote what and let honest study confirm your trust.

weighed: My first answer would be that God's love isn't just indulgence—it's holy love. Because he's good, he can't shrug at evil, and because he loves us, he won't leave us stuck in it. So his love is demanding: it calls you to change, to turn around, to become like him, while staying patient and forgiving. Picture a parent who loves a kid too much to let them wreck their life. One idea worth weighing is that God's love isn't only something we ask him to come down and give us; we're also invited to actively enter into his life and offer him our love. That shifts the picture from us waiting on a feeling to us taking up a practice, but it leaves the core intact: his love still meets you where you are and still calls you forward.
dogmatic: God's love is holy love, and it isn't detached or unmoved. He can grieve over sin, and his holiness demands atonement while his love provides it. So stop treating prayer as begging God to come down and love you—that's the wrong posture. The way into adoration is to constantly strive to enter into his estate and offer him your love. And when you feel dry, when the enemy stirs up a racket inside you, don't conclude your love is fake. Serve God purely for love of his will in the middle of sadness, terrors, and temptation, and refuse the lie that your love is useless. That unshakable fidelity in trial is itself the proof that his demanding, holy love has taken hold of you.

weighed: I'd start where I'd have started before: the worry itself suggests a tender conscience, so take heart. Genuine sorrow shows up in honesty before God, in confessing what you've done, and in wanting to change. Ask whether you grieve more over having offended God than over the fallout you face. Feelings swing around, so don't gauge repentance by emotional intensity alone; look at the direction of your life instead. One principle worth naming is that repentance means ceasing the wrong as soon as you know it, and that ignorance is winked at. That sharpens things: it tells you to act on what you now know and not wait for a feeling, and it leaves in place the honest self-examination and the turn toward God that were already there. Pray for a contrite heart, trust God's mercy in Christ, and let the concern push you toward him rather than into despair.
dogmatic: The worry itself is a tender conscience, but don't let it become an excuse to sit still. Sin is doing wrong when you know better and could do otherwise; where you acted in ignorance God winks at it, but the moment you learn a thing is wrong you must stop it immediately and for good. True repentance isn't mere sorrow or a deathbed confession; it turns from evil, reforms the life, and makes restitution to those you've wronged, as Zacchaeus restored fourfold. The early fathers pressed this hard, treating forgiveness as a single remission at baptism and righteousness as virtue itself, so examine whether your life is actually being reformed, not just whether you feel contrite. And don't rest on your own resolve: cleansing comes through Christ's atonement. Bring your grief to him, turn from the sin, make right what you can, and trust his blood to cleanse you.

weighed: My first answer would be that Scripture treats judgment as real and serious, but it also insists God is just and doesn't lump the righteous in with the wicked. God knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unjust for judgment, so the fire doesn't fall equally on everyone. One idea worth weighing is that at judgment people divide into three parts, not two: the righteous highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful in the middle place, and the accursed host cast into the depths. That changes the picture by adding a middle group and a distinct fate for the worst, but it leaves in place the core point that the righteous and the sinful don't suffer alike. The real aim isn't satisfying curiosity about the details; it's turning us toward repentance and faith.
dogmatic: No, they won't suffer alike, and the division is threefold, not twofold. The righteous are highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful are in the middle place shrouded with smoke, and the accursed host are bound in the depth of the surge and cast into the depths of hell. Sin had to be allowed to rise, yet all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. God's mercy has restored more by grace in redemption than the devil robbed by Adam's sin. Temporal calamities come from God, and we fall into sin only by our own malice, so blame no one else and trust the mercy that exceeds our loss.

weighed:
I'd start where I started before: God isn't standing off at a distance watching you struggle. He's in the work of bringing people into his family, and that means your hard seasons aren't outside his care. You're not alone in them, and they're not just problems to escape—you can ask what he's doing in them, and let them become a place of honest fellowship with him rather than evidence he's walked away.

One idea worth weighing is that God often brings his people into difficulties on purpose so they come to know him as a very present help in trouble. That shifts things: some struggles may be less an accident to survive and more a place where he means to show up in a way you couldn't see otherwise. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—your struggles still aren't a sign he's abandoned you, and they're still not something to just grit your teeth through. It just adds a reason to look for him in the middle of them, not only for the exit.
dogmatic: God doesn't just sympathize with the work of bringing people into his family—he deliberately leads his people into trouble so they'll finally know him as a present help they'd never meet on easy roads. So stop treating your struggles as accidents to escape. Expect him to reveal himself in them. And don't buy the idea that sickness is his will—he's a good Father who gives good things, and plenty of people have had to confess they wrongly blamed him for disease. When loss or correction does come, it's never mere punishment or proof he's forgotten you; it's a Father giving you something better, holding you with one hand while he deals with you with the other. In every struggle, look for what he's giving and let it drive you deeper into knowing him.

weighed: The book of Hebrews pictures Jesus as our high priest serving in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary the Lord Himself pitched, not one built by human hands. That means His priesthood outranks the old Levitical system, which served in an earthly copy. He entered the true sanctuary once for all with His own blood, securing eternal redemption, and He intercedes for us before the Father. One principle worth naming is that the Lord's work is God's and not man's—no mere man leads the Church, and the honor belongs to God, though the instruments He chooses should be honored as such. That principle shifts the focus onto God as the builder and gives Him the glory, but it leaves the heart of the answer in place: Jesus is the perfect mediator, and we can draw near to God through Him with confidence.
dogmatic: Hebrews presents Jesus as our high priest in the true tabernacle—the heavenly sanctuary the Lord pitched, not one built by human hands. His priesthood is greater than the old Levitical priesthood. Because this is so, those who administer His holy things must refuse the holy table to notorious sinners who will not repent; Christ will demand an account of His blood if it is given to the unworthy, and the priest's power in this is above an emperor's. Yet this must be done with awe at the tremendous sacrifice: the priest holds Christ Himself, angels attend the altar, and a purity becoming heaven is required. And let no man take the honor and credit for leading and building the Church; that belongs to God alone. Honor chosen instruments, but give the glory to God, who builds His Church.

weighed: Yes, I'd say it's right to ask God for great things, especially for his work. He invites us to bring our requests to him, and he's able to do far more than we ask or imagine. The size of the request isn't the problem; the heart behind it is. So ask boldly, but ask with humility, submitting to his will and trusting his timing. Prayer isn't a way to manipulate God; it's a relationship with a Father who loves to give good gifts. One thing worth weighing, though, is that prayer is a duty and a privilege to keep at set times whether or not you feel like it, together with your family, and never asking God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. That doesn't shrink your big request or tell you to stop praying for the work. It just adds that you keep showing up in prayer regardless of feeling, and that you're ready to act and labor alongside what you ask for, rather than expecting God to do it all while you stand back.
dogmatic: Yes, ask for great things for God's work, and don't be shy about it, because the promises of Christ cannot fail. We ask and receive not because we ask amiss. If the art of praying well is the art of living well, then nothing matters more than learning this heavenly art of conversing with God the way we ought. So don't pray for riches; those who ask for more than daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. Ask instead for the means to keep yourself and your family from want and for the supply of God's work. Don't excuse neglect of prayer because you lack the spirit of prayer; keep your appointed times no matter how you feel, and pray with your family. And don't ask God for things without a willingness to act: help accomplish what you ask rather than expecting him to do it all. Pray, live well, and labor alongside your prayer.

weighed: Yes, you can and should pray for your son's protection. It's natural to bring that fear to God. One principle I'd name is that a little lifting up of the heart suffices—short, inward prayers count, even on a march with a sword in hand. That changes how you might pray: you don't need long, formal prayers, and your son can pray in a moment too. It leaves in place the main answer—pray for his safety, for wisdom for those around him, and for his well-being, and ask others to pray as well. Stay in contact with him and take care of yourself too.
dogmatic: Pray continually, not just once. You cannot escape life's dangers without God's actual and continual help, and you cannot pray without being with Him—so build a holy habit of thinking of Him often. Keep set times of prayer whether you feel like it or not, and pray with your family. Don't ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself: write, encourage, and support your son. And teach him that a little lifting up of the heart, one act of inward worship on a march with a sword in hand, is a prayer very acceptable to God and fortifies courage in danger.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it makes sense to wonder whether this is God or just your own head, and a good next step is to pay attention to what you're feeling, check it against Scripture, and talk it over with someone you trust. One idea worth weighing is that God really does guide people—through his Spirit, through Scripture, and through the ordinary circumstances of your life—and when those three line up, you can have real confidence it's him. That adds something to my first answer: it says the sense of being guided isn't automatically wishful thinking, and there's a solid way to test it. What it leaves in place is the caution—still test it, still talk to someone wise, still don't panic if it's unclear. So I'd say: take the question seriously, look for that agreement, and let it settle you rather than scare you.
dogmatic: Stop treating this as something you have to figure out on your own. The search you feel is real—but it's only half the story. The God you're looking for is already looking for you, and he isn't sitting back waiting for you to stumble onto him. He's the one who set this whole thing in motion. So yes, seek him in prayer, expect him to answer through his Spirit, his Word, and the plain circumstances of your days, and when those agree, trust it. But the deeper truth is that your seeking is just the echo of his. You're not imagining things—you're being found.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: no, it isn't wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty. Scripture keeps commanding care for the poor, and Jesus fed the hungry and healed the sick. But I'd also ask whether caring for souls and caring for bodies have to compete, because they aren't opposites. One principle worth naming is that the poor are the people of God and will inherit the earth, that the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone, and that people are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. That principle changes how I'd hear your question: it means the poor aren't a lesser concern or a distraction from spiritual things, and it rules out treating poverty as a sign of low worth. What it leaves in place is the rest of what I said: poverty is not only a lack of money, people are more than their circumstances, and a real answer meets immediate needs while still attending to deeper longings. So your concern isn't wrong, and it doesn't have to be traded against concern for souls.
dogmatic: Caring for the poor is not optional, and it is not a lesser calling. The poor are the people of God and will inherit the earth; the hungry and destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and persons are esteemed by character, not by wealth or position. So do not treat poverty as degrading or measure people by money and station. Honor the poor and give them food and fellowship. At the same time, do not blame poverty only on outside causes: much want comes from lack of discretion and sound calculation, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. And remember that wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, not securely your own. Use it for the Gospel and for the poor, and warn against covetousness and the idolatrous love of property. Concern for souls and concern for bodies are not rivals; both are commanded, and neither excuses neglecting the other.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, they're not all teaching the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. They make different claims about God, salvation, and what a human being is for, and those differences aren't cosmetic. That said, I wouldn't write off other faiths as empty; many carry real moral insight and genuine wisdom. The question is whether what they offer is complete, and Christianity makes a claim about Jesus that the others don't. One idea that sharpens this for me is that there's really only one true religion, and the others are either distorted versions of it or honest gropings toward it. That changes how I see other faiths: not as equal paths but as partial or skewed reflections of something fuller. What it leaves in place is my respect for the truth and goodness found in them, and the honest work of testing any claim against Scripture and the Spirit rather than just custom or opinion.
dogmatic: No, they are not teaching the same thing, and pretending otherwise is a comfortable evasion. There is strictly one religion. Everything else is either a caricature of it or a blind groping toward it, and Christianity is the one because it is the inclusive one, holding all that is best and truest in the others as fragments of itself. The light that lights every person is Christ, whether or not they name him. But Christian religion is not outward observance or speculation about God. It is learning to know yourself: where you came from, what you are now, how you fell from unity into dissension, and how you are delivered and restored. And this is not settled by tradition, custom, human opinion, or expediency. Test everything by the Holy Scriptures as the only standard, with the Holy Spirit as the only teacher. Lay aside your prejudice, ask simply what Scripture says, and follow it.

weighed: My first answer would be that God's reign mainly changes people inwardly—forgiveness, peace, a new heart, hope beyond death—and that outward changes come as people live by kingdom values. One idea worth naming is that the kingdom will be a literal, tangible rule on earth, with laws and resurrected saints. That changes the picture from a mostly private, spiritual renewal to a public, visible order with real governance and justice. What it leaves in place is the inward transformation: forgiveness, a new identity, and the fruit of the Spirit still matter. So for ordinary people, the change would be both a new inner life and, in God's time, a just society to live in.
dogmatic: God's reign on earth will be a literal, tangible kingdom, not just a warm feeling inside. It will have laws, officers, and resurrected saints ruling under Christ, and ordinary people will live under just governance with real peace and prosperity. The Greek idea that Christ pre-existed glorifies Christ instead of the God who guides history, and it makes the flesh seem worthless—but Scripture says the meek will inherit the earth. The saints will reign on the earth, and the New Jerusalem will come down to a purified earth where God dwells with men. That is our eternal inheritance, and God's will will be done on earth as in heaven.

weighed: I'd start simple: before you open your laptop or pick up your tools, pause and say a short, honest prayer—name the task, ask God to be in it, and offer it as work done for Him. Then just begin. Keep it brief so it doesn't turn into a ritual you skip, and offer the hard parts too, not just the wins. One principle worth adding is that the chief business of each day is first to be at rest and happy in God, feeding your soul through Scripture and prayer, especially in the morning. That changes the order—the offering flows out of time with God rather than being a quick box to tick—but it leaves your simple habit in place: a sentence of offering before the task, and gratitude at day's end.
dogmatic: Don't treat the offering as a quick formality tacked onto your morning. Make your first business each day to be truly at rest and happy in God—feed your soul on Scripture and prayer before anything else claims you, especially early. Only then offer the work: name it, ask for grace, and do it for the love of God. And don't arrange your day by preference alone. Seek God's appointment of the time, the way, and the people for His work; wait for the Master's signal before you take a step, and accept the helpers He provides rather than the ones you'd pick. Offer the difficulties too, do everything heartily as to the Lord, and close the day with thanks and the unfinished parts committed to Him.

weighed: Yes, it matters a lot. If Jesus were only a holy man, then the New Testament's claims about him would be wrong, and the gospel would shrink into good advice. A merely human teacher can inspire you, but he can't save, forgive sins, or bring you back to God. One thing worth weighing: the Gospels show Jesus as truly human and as more than human, and the differences between the Synoptics and John are about point of view, not contradiction. That doesn't soften the question, but it does mean you shouldn't play a human Jesus in Matthew, Mark, and Luke against a divine Jesus in John. So read all four Gospels again and ask what they actually claim about him.
dogmatic: Yes, it matters greatly. If Jesus were only a holy man, the New Testament's claims about him would be mistaken and the gospel would collapse into good advice. But don't set a merely human Jesus of the Synoptists against a divine Jesus of John, as though the Gospels contradicted each other. There is one Jesus, truly human and truly divine, in all four Gospels; the differences come from point of view, not contradiction. Nor is he a figure small enough to be fully comprehended. The manifold Gospel picture is a self-evidencing fact: Jesus appears as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God. This is the theologia Christi: he is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, and one must think of him as of God—yet, within monotheism, he was never placed on an equality with the Father. A merely human teacher can inspire, but he cannot save. Read all four Gospels afresh and ask what they claim about him.

weighed: My first instinct is that you don't need details to pray well. Pray for strangers by name or by category—people in your city, the suffering, leaders, the lonely—and ask God to give them what they most need, since He knows better than you do. Pray for their welfare, protection, and salvation, and trust God to apply it where it's needed. A simple pattern like nations, neighbors, the needy can help, and keeping it brief and regular beats waiting for information you'll never have. One principle worth naming is that prayer grows out of a life of prayer: we can't pray without being with God, and that takes holy habit. That principle changes the starting point—it says build the habit of set times and frequent turning of your mind to God first, and the praying for strangers will flow from it. What it leaves in place is the core: you still don't need details, you still ask God for what they most need, and you still keep it regular rather than occasional.
dogmatic: Prayer for people you've never met isn't mainly a technique—it grows out of a life of prayer. We can't escape life's dangers without God's actual and continual help, so pray continually. But you can't pray without being with Him, can't be with Him without thinking of Him often, and can't think of Him often without a holy habit. We must know before we can love, and to know God we must often think of Him. So build the habit first: set times of prayer and frequent turning of your mind to God, then pray for strangers. Pray with confidence, relying on the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, not your own worthiness. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from His presence or forget to ask—so don't be discouraged by your sins; ask boldly. You need no details about those you pray for; ask God to give them what they most need, which He knows better than you do. And when the point is that faith be strengthened by receiving help from God in answer to prayer alone, don't make your needs known to those who'd gladly meet them—wait on God for supply. Keep this prayer regular, trusting God to apply it where it's needed.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: holy character grows through the ordinary means of grace — Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and small, steady obedience. It's shaped by repentance and faith, by trials borne patiently, and by habits of love and self-control. The saints weren't made by extraordinary experiences but by faithful plodding. So begin where you are: keep short accounts with God, serve the people right in front of you, and let Scripture's promises and commands shape you. Expect slow growth, and don't despise small beginnings. One thing worth adding is that prayer isn't just one item on that list — real, honest, persistent prayer is a major way God actually forms saints, and praying people tend to become holy people. That raises the stakes on prayer without canceling anything above; Scripture, fellowship, and obedience still matter, and slow growth is still the norm. It just means you shouldn't treat prayer as a box to check.
dogmatic: Prayer is what makes saints. Not prayer as a duty you squeeze in, but real praying — honest, persistent, humble, seeking God himself and not just his gifts. Where prayer abounds, saints abound; where it languishes, holiness withers. And drop the idea that sainthood is a special rank for the exceptionally pure. In the New Testament, 'saints' means all Christians — people in communion with a holy God, set apart from the world. So the question isn't whether you qualify for an elite class; it's whether you're actually praying. And hear the warning: to profess the Gospel and not enjoy its spirit is one of the most painful things a person can go through. To live as a saint while walking in darkness is the hardest task there is. So don't chase the name. Seek the enjoyment of God in your praying.

weighed: I'd start by saying that when God feels beyond your senses and imagination, that's not a sign you're doing something wrong. You can find Him in silence, in Scripture, in the beauty of creation, and in the love of others. Start by acknowledging your desire for Him—that desire itself is a sign of His presence. Practice stillness and let go of the need to grasp Him with your mind. One idea worth weighing is that as long as you're just playing with images and sensations, you haven't moved past your animal nature; but through your intelligence, affections, and will—made in God's image—you're meant to commune directly with Him. That changes the focus: instead of relying on sensory or imaginative experiences, you turn your intellect, affections, and will toward God in pure faith and love. It leaves in place the practical advice—silence, Scripture, ordinary moments—but reframes them as supports, not the main thing. So don't be discouraged by dryness; keep seeking, and trust that He is near even when you can't feel Him.
dogmatic: You need to stop trifling with images and sensations—that's just your animal nature, the same instincts brute beasts have. You were made in God's image with intelligence, affections, and will, and by those powers you ought to commune directly with God, be united to Him, and cleave to Him. So turn your intellect, affections, and will toward Him in pure faith and love, not through sensory or imaginative props. In silence, let your mind rest in the simple truth of His presence, and your heart cleave to Him without depending on created things. And know this: finding God increases both joy and the power of suffering, but joy becomes so much greater that pain is overwhelmed and evil becomes negligible. But be warned—if you don't find Christ here, when you cast off the flesh you enter a bewildering vortex of terrible intensity and great solitude, aware of nothing but self, blind, without the light of this world or the light of Christ. The remedy must be found now, in this life, by turning directly to God in faith and love.

weighed: I'm really sorry you're going through this. What I'd say first is: hold onto hope, the support of people who love you, and the small moments of peace each day. One idea from the candidate principles is to avoid talking about the illness and not name the disease. That could help by keeping your focus off fear and symptoms, but it leaves in place the need for honest medical care, real conversations with your doctor, and the comfort of loved ones. So I'd still say: lean on your support, follow your treatment plan, and let yourself feel afraid without letting fear run everything.
dogmatic: Hold onto the truth that God is all and there is no disease. Don't dwell on symptoms or name the illness—fix your thought on health and harmony as the reality of your being in God. If a crisis or mental disturbance comes, treat it as a false suggestion, not a disease. You are not a helpless victim; you can resist disease as positively as you resist sin. Stand firm in this truth, and let go of every expectation of growing worse. In God there is no sickness, only wholeness and peace. Rest in this truth, and let it fill your consciousness. You are held in perfect health now.

weighed: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It starts with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Begin with small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection isn't about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving. One principle that matters here is that the more you aspire to perfection, the more dependent you are on Divine grace. That changes the focus from your own effort to relying on God's strength, but it leaves in place the call to keep growing and the assurance that perfection is possible for you.
dogmatic: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. Aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love, seeking nothing less than perfection in that love. Do not settle for a love that seeks something less, for such love must be imperfect. Begin with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. Growth in holiness is a lifelong journey, but the goal is nothing less than perfect love. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection is not about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God—yet that devotion must be total. However, do not give way to hurry or over-eagerness, for over-eagerness is the mother of all imperfections. Keep yourself in God's presence and avoid anxiety, which is an obstacle to perfection. And know that aspiring to greater perfection means becoming more dependent on Divine grace, not less. The more you strive, the more you must rely on His strength. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving.

weighed: I get why the portrait feels too polished to be real, and I'd start by saying the evangelists weren't writing modern biographies—they were proclaiming what Jesus meant for their communities, so they shaped the traditions to highlight his significance. That said, they didn't invent him: the Gospels keep details like Jesus being tired, angry, or sorrowful, which suggests a real person behind it all. One principle worth naming is that the full Gospel portrait, mysterious as it is, is a self-evidencing, life-giving fact, while the smaller Jesus of modern criticism can't really account for how Christianity began. That principle shifts the burden of proof—it says the richness of the portrait is itself evidence, not something to explain away. What it leaves in place is your observation that the evangelists did idealize and shape the material; it just denies that shaping means fabrication.
dogmatic: The portrait isn't too perfect to be real—it's too real to be dismissed as idealization. The Gospels give us Jesus as Lawgiver, Teacher, Healer, Ruler, and Saviour, man and God, and that manifold picture is a self-evidencing fact. The evangelists didn't smooth over the hard edges; they preserved details only genuine memory could supply. The very perfection that bothers you is the signature of his divine origin. And consider this: if the Christ-ideal were only a human masterpiece, it would be our despair, like a genius who mocks all imitation. It's as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life becomes the hope of the ages and supplies the dynamic for human striving—the unattainable ideal becomes ground for hope, not despair. So don't fight evil by direct contention; substitute another picture, another invitation—Jesus and his pure and beautiful invitations—and transfer your allegiance from the glamour of evil to the glamour of God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: perfection isn't attainable, and that's okay. Set realistic goals, treat mistakes as part of learning, and talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend. One principle worth naming is that the real secret of rest is to be habitually occupied with something larger than your own performance—for many people, that's God. What that changes is the direction of your attention: instead of constantly checking whether you're measuring up, you return your gaze outward and let the pressure to prove yourself loosen. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—self-compassion, realistic goals, maybe a counselor—because those still help. It doesn't ask you to stop caring about doing well; it just moves the weight off your shoulders and onto something steadier.
dogmatic: Stop trying to fix your exhaustion by trying harder to relax—that's just perfectionism wearing a new outfit. The real secret of perfect rest is to be jealously and habitually occupied with Jesus. Quiet your heart, remember God is with you right now, and refuse to let every distracting thought or trifling word steal your peace. You are not behind. Freedom from anxiety isn't another goal to achieve; it's a gift to receive. When you stumble, humble yourself, return your gaze to Him, and go on with simplicity and confidence. You are loved as you are, and that love—not your flawless performance—is what frees you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: the piety of the poor is just as precious in God's eyes as the piety of the rich and learned. God looks at the heart, not at wealth or schooling, and the poor often show a deep trust in Him that puts the rest of us to shame. So honor that faith and learn from it. One principle worth naming is that poverty often comes from a lack of discretion and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. That does change something: it means I shouldn't romanticize poverty or treat every hardship as pure misfortune, and I can teach prudent management and frugality alongside encouragement in faith. But it leaves the core in place. Their piety is still equally valuable, wealth and learning still don't make faith more acceptable to God, and I must never show partiality to the rich. So I'd encourage and support the poor in faith and in practical wisdom, and keep building a community where all are valued.
dogmatic: The piety of the poor matters, but don't let anyone tell you poverty is simply noble or blameless. Much of it comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means. So preach prudence and frugality plainly. Wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain; it brings happiness only when it's used for the Gospel, and covetousness is a sin to be overcome. The poor should be honest and thankful, taking no more than they need, and a poor person who covets what isn't his is as wicked in heart as the miser who hoards. Jesus identified with the poor, yes, but that's no excuse for sloppy stewardship. Honor their faith and teach them responsible management.

weighed: I'd start by saying the hard demands reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness, and a gentler message might draw a crowd but leave faith shallow. One principle worth naming is that the Bible appeals to the heroic: its severities aren't disguised, and calls for the utmost tend to meet a real response. That changes my answer by making the difficulty sound like an invitation to something great rather than just a test to endure. What it leaves in place is your point about gentleness: it's better to err toward too much gentleness than too much severity, since God is all love. So the demands stay, but they're framed as a summons, not a trap.
dogmatic: The Bible makes hard demands because the Christian life is cross-bearing, and its severities are not disguised. A gentler message might attract a crowd, but it would lure people by false pretenses. The call of Christ is heroic: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow him. That's not an easy appeal; it's a summons to a great adventure, and the reward is incomparable, the comradeship of God and man. Yet learn from Christ meekness and humility, and trust that it's better to account for too much gentleness than too much severity, for God is all love. Be willing to be lost sight of in your fruit, letting others be more prominent and holding up their hands by silent love and prayer.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: salvation is both a historical event outside you and something that has to happen in you. Jesus' death and resurrection accomplished it, and faith applies it, so the Spirit works in you and grows you over time. One principle worth naming is that salvation isn't a transaction done wholly without us; it requires the cooperation of your will through faith, an identification with Christ by which you re-live His life, co-dying and co-rising with Him. That changes the picture from a gift merely received to a gift actively entered into, so your will is won rather than bypassed. What it leaves in place is the historical, outside-you reality: the cross and resurrection still happened long ago, and faith still receives them. So it's not either/or; it's both, with your cooperation as the living link between the two.
dogmatic: Salvation is not a transaction that happened long ago and outside you. It is an actual deliverance wrought with you, by a positive winning of your will. Faith is not intellectual assent but an identification of the self with Christ's life, so that you share His death to sin and His risen life. Salvation must happen in you: your will must be won, not coerced, and you must actively cooperate with grace. It is not enough to believe facts about Jesus; you must be united with Him in His death and resurrection, so that His life becomes yours. Salvation is an individual operation: each must receive or reject it for himself, and no one is saved by another's righteousness. The conceptions of Christian salvation were grouped around two ideas: the coming glorious kingdom with the resurrection of the body, and the truth, the complete knowledge of God including eternal life. Thus salvation is both a historical reality and a present experience, worked out in the depths of your own being.

weighed: I'd start by saying honor the donor's intent, but if the need is truly urgent and you can replace the funds soon, it might be okay as long as you're transparent and tell the donor if you can. One principle worth weighing here is that we tend to hold onto things others could use, and keeping them costs us a blessing. That changes the picture a little: before touching the designated money, look at what you already own that you don't really need and could part with. It leaves your original constraints in place, though. You still keep the money's purpose, still replace it, still stay transparent.
dogmatic: Honestly, the real issue isn't whether you can shuffle the money around. It's that we accumulate things useful to others while not needing them ourselves, and holding onto them costs us a blessing. Go through what you have first. There's likely something you don't need that someone else could use, and parting with it is the habit of mind that actually matters. Don't go asking people for money either; that just makes it look like money is the whole point. Give freely, waste nothing, and trust that what you need will come without you chasing it.

weighed: My first instinct is that the image of gold refined in fire is a real and powerful one, but it doesn't come with a blanket promise that every sin gets burned away automatically. Scripture usually ties cleansing to repentance and faith in Christ, and it warns against presuming on some purifying fire while we keep clinging to the sin. One principle worth naming is that God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration, so grafting holiness onto unholiness and expecting forgiveness while we don't forsake the sin is foolish. That principle sharpens the picture: the fire purges only what is actually forsaken. What it leaves in place is the hope that refinement is real and that mercy meets us when we turn, but it doesn't turn the fire into a guarantee for everyone regardless of how they respond.
dogmatic: Yes, sins can be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy. The refining flame is exactly how guilt is separated and burned off, and those in it can look upon the Prince of angels, be freed from their sins, and come out shining like pure gold from the furnace. This is not a punitive fire for all but a refining fire for those being saved, and it ends in peace and eternal well-being. But make no mistake: the fire only purges what is forsaken. God's pardon is the destruction of sin, not its toleration, so grafting holiness onto unholiness and supposing sin can be forgiven while it is still clung to is folly. The Lord is merciful if you straightway purge yourself of your evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, even though you have transgressed many times and wounded Him with your sins. Never offer scorn, blasphemy, or wrathful opposition to the Son of God, and you may deserve eternal life in heaven.

weighed: Yes, you should still stand, but not as someone who picks fights. Your fear is real, and you don't have to pretend it isn't. What I'd say first is that standing for truth doesn't mean being aggressive or denying what you believe; it means seeking wisdom about when and how to speak, leaning on God for courage, and finding people who support you. One principle that matters here is that simple seekers are waiting for a cup of cold water in Christ's name, and you shouldn't fear the consequences of giving it. That changes the focus from winning a conflict to serving someone who's ready to hear. It leaves your caution in place, though: you still get to be wise about timing and gentle in how you say things. So stand, but stand with love and respect, and don't let fear make the choice for you.
dogmatic: You must stand. Don't let fear of being in the minority silence you. Give the truth freely to those who are ready, like a cup of cold water in Christ's name, and never fear the consequences. Be brave from the start; cowards always get hurt, and those who stand true to their convictions from the beginning face the fewest tests. Don't let the enemy see that you're afraid. Trust God to stand by you. Yes, speak with love and respect, but don't withhold what people need. Remember that war and contention come from wickedness and the lack of God's Spirit, not from God's design, and peace comes only through the gospel. So stand for that truth, even in the minority, and give it courageously.

weighed: My first answer would be that the pollution isn't literal dirt in heaven. The sanctuary there is real, but what needs dealing with is the record of sin, not sin itself clinging to God's presence. The cleansing at the end of the 2300 days in Daniel 8:14 is about the final removal of that record, pointing to Christ's high priestly work. One principle that sharpens this is that the cleansing is the work now being accomplished, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern, by blood. That changes how I'd frame it: it's not a future symbolic gesture but a present priestly reality. What it leaves in place is your core question, that heaven itself isn't morally polluted; the defilement being addressed is the accumulated guilt and record of sin that the sanctuary handles on our behalf.
dogmatic: The heavenly sanctuary is real, and Daniel 8:14 means exactly what it says: it is cleansed at the end of the 2300 days, and that cleansing is happening now, not by fire on the earth but after the pattern, by blood. The pollution in question is never sin infecting God's own presence; it is the record of sin that the sanctuary bears and then removes. And here is the deeper thing: God does not merely wipe away miseries, he converts them into graces, turning the poison of our iniquities into remedies for the soul. So the cleansing is transformation, not just erasure. If you want to receive it, make a definite act of faith in Christ, then abide habitually in him, drawing life from him the way a tree draws from the soil without straining.

weighed: I'd start by saying both faiths really do teach charity and kindness, and the real difference is what those things rest on. Christianity is built on a personal God who made and loves you, and on Jesus as Savior; Buddhism is about walking the Eightfold Path toward enlightenment. One principle worth naming is that charity shouldn't create idleness or dependence. That changes how I'd talk about giving: the aim is to meet the need and then help people stand on their own. It leaves the core comparison intact, though, because the deeper question is still what you believe about God and ultimate reality.
dogmatic: Charity that just hands things out and leaves people idle isn't charity at all. The Church's aim is to relieve present wants and then help the poor help themselves, so they can labor and stand on their own. Real love also won't let sin slide; it goes to the person and speaks the truth rather than stabbing them behind their back. And patience in sickness and suffering is more heroic and precious in God's sight than busy activity, so we should ask for health only if it honors God more. That's the kind of charity worth building a life on.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's completely natural to feel anxious when you have nowhere to go, but God promises to provide for His children. Trust that He sees your need and will make a way. Look for practical steps: reach out to local churches, community organizations, or government assistance. God often works through people. Keep praying and don't lose hope. One principle that speaks to this is that God supplies all our need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and that our extremity is God's opportunity. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'trust and look for help,' I'd lean into the idea that this desperate moment might actually be where God shows up most clearly, often through people you haven't met yet. What it leaves in place is everything practical: keep reaching out, keep praying, stay connected to a faith community, take one day at a time. It doesn't promise a specific timeline or a specific house, but it does reframe the waiting as a place where God is already at work.
dogmatic: You need to hear this clearly: God has appointed you a place and a service right now, even in this. Your job isn't to panic about the future but to recognize that your current place is from Him and fill it sweetly and lovingly. Stop treating your lack of a home as a sign that God has forgotten you. He supplies all your need, and man's extremity is His opportunity. This is not the time to keep God at a distance. Be homely with Him, as your heart may think or soul desire, but don't get so reckless in that familiarity that you leave courtesy behind, because He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. Trust that He will provide, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others. Reach out to churches and community organizations, yes, but do it as someone serving where God has set you, not as someone scrambling. Take one day at a time, do what you can, and fill your place sweetly and lovingly. He will not abandon you.

weighed: Yes, I'd say accountability is real. Scripture keeps warning that people with authority—kings, judges, religious leaders—answer to God for how they use it, and Jesus was blunt about leaders who load heavy burdens on others. So I'd name this: the priesthood can't be exercised in any degree of unrighteousness; its power won't stay with the corrupt or treacherous. That sharpens things—it means abuse doesn't just get punished later, it hollows out the authority itself, so a corrupt leader has already lost the thing they're pretending to hold. What it leaves in place is the timing: the reckoning still belongs to God, and our part is still to speak truth, protect the wounded, and refuse to join the corruption.
dogmatic: Yes, and don't soften it. No ruler now sitting on a throne was lawfully called or anointed by God—their claim is usurped, and God merely overrules them the way He overruled Nebuchadnezzar and Cyrus. The same goes for priests: authority that can't be exercised in any degree of unrighteousness simply will not abide with the corrupt or the treacherous. It departs. So the reckoning isn't some vague someday—it's already happening in the loss of the very power they flaunt. And the standard cuts both ways: anyone who governs with haughty anger and calls it zeal is showing they can't govern themselves, let alone anyone else. God humbles the proud and restores authority only to those who rule with meekness, as servants beneath the people they lead.

weighed: My first instinct is pretty practical: name what's still good, even small things, and let that shift your focus a little. Write down a few things you're thankful for each day, lean on supportive people, and don't pretend everything's fine. One idea worth adding is that God is already close to you in this, so you can talk to him in short, honest moments as you go, offer what you're about to do, and thank him afterward. That deepens the gratitude into a relationship, but it doesn't replace the simple daily practice or the honesty about how hard things are.
dogmatic: Recognize that God is intimately present with you right now and speak to him constantly, in short honest words. In anything unclear, ask his help to know his will; in what's plainly required, offer it before you do it and give thanks when it's done. He already knows your wants, so you're not informing him but trusting him, and he comes in his own time. The patience and courage you show in affliction are themselves a mark of his care, so pray for strength to suffer with humility and love rather than only for relief. Build a familiar, affectionate conversation with him, watching your thoughts, words, and deeds as one walking with a friend, and that habit brings the peace of paradise into this life.

weighed: I'd start by saying prayer isn't always easy, and struggling with it doesn't mean you're doing it wrong. Many people find it hard because of distraction, doubt, or busyness, and that's normal. Be patient with yourself and keep showing up. Try different methods—written prayers, silence, gratitude lists, or praying while you walk—and find what fits you. Lower your expectations of having a profound experience; prayer can be simple and ordinary. If it feels dry, that's not a sign of failure. Talk to a trusted friend or spiritual leader if you want guidance. The important thing is honesty and persistence, not perfect focus or intense feeling. One idea that might help is that doing everything for the love of God, with prayer for grace to do the work well, can make even naturally aversive work feel easier. That changes how you might approach the struggle: instead of just pushing through, you could offer the difficulty itself as part of your prayer and ask for grace to do it well. But it leaves in place the core of what I said—that struggle isn't failure, that you don't need perfect focus or intense feeling, and that patience and honesty matter most.
dogmatic: Prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it. The struggle you're describing often comes from trying to carry it alone. There is a secret that makes it lighter: labor done for the love of God, joined with prayer for grace, becomes easy. So keep your appointed times of prayer even when you feel nothing—feelings are not the measure of faithfulness. Pray on your knees, both secretly and with other believers, for prayer is the one great central secret of holy living and serving, the cornerstone on which all life-work is built. When you ask God for something, be willing to act: help God accomplish what you ask rather than expecting him to do it all while you wait. Make prayer your first resort in every crisis, great or small, not a last resort after human means are exhausted. Ask for grace to pray, offer your work for love of him, and do the next small thing. Grace carries what effort alone cannot, and what felt heavy becomes natural.

weighed: Yes, God still wants you. Feelings of hypocrisy are really common, and they don't disqualify you from God's love. Grace is bigger than your failures. The church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints. Prayer isn't about being perfect; it's about being honest. Start by telling God how you feel—He already knows and loves you. One principle that fits here is that when you feel you can't do something good, you can say, 'Lord, I can't do this unless you enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is given. That changes the focus from your performance to God's help, but it leaves in place the simple step of showing up and being honest. You're not alone. Take a small step: attend a service or say a simple prayer. God will meet you there.
dogmatic: Yes, God still wants you. Your very sense of need—that feeling of hypocrisy and desire for authenticity—is evidence of a real God who made you for Himself. The soul's yearning for God is not a delusion; it's an appetite He planted in you, and the search implies something to be found. In every occasion of virtue, especially when you feel weak, turn to God and ask for His enabling grace, which is more than sufficient. Forgetting God should not cause disquiet; instead, let it lead you to return with greater trust. The church is a hospital for sinners, and prayer is where we receive strength. Start by honestly asking God for grace to overcome hypocrisy, and trust that He will supply. Take a step: attend a service and pray, not in your own strength, but in the strength God supplies. He will meet you with grace and peace.

weighed: I'd start by saying: be honest about your sins before God, but don't camp out in despair. Focus on his forgiveness and grace, and talk with a trusted pastor or friend. One principle that adds something here is that confessing our sins and standing with other sinners is part of how we help each other. That changes the tone—it makes confession less about self-punishment and more about shared honesty. But it leaves in place the core: God's grace is greater, and you don't have to be crushed.
dogmatic: You deal with your sins by confessing them and making yourself one with other sinners—that's how Christ took our sins as his own. Don't hide your faults; bring them into the light. Promptly confess and forsake even small sins, and don't let any mercy go unrecognized. And if you harbor unforgiveness, you're more guilty than the one who sinned against you, so dismiss envy, malice, and retaliation and forgive as Christ forgave you. That's the path to freedom from the crushing weight.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it's understandable to feel discouraged after years of seeking without a clear response, and that silence doesn't mean you're doing something wrong or that God has abandoned you. One principle worth naming is that God doesn't always give just what we ask—sometimes a petition is denied in kindness, and we're invited to trust that he gives something better. That changes the frame: instead of reading silence as failure, you can hold it as a place to keep returning with deeper trust. What it leaves in place is the honest ache and the practical advice—talk with a trusted spiritual guide, adjust your practices, give yourself permission to rest, and see a counselor if the distress gets heavy. You don't have to give up, and you don't have to push yourself relentlessly.
dogmatic: Don't give up—return. The disquiet you feel is not a verdict that God has abandoned you, and feeling forgotten shouldn't throw you into turmoil; it should call you back with greater trust. God is not obliged to grant every request exactly as asked. A father may deny a child's petition in kindness because he knows what the child does not, so resign your will to his—'Not my will but yours'—trusting that his denial can be better than the thing you asked for. And don't take refuge in denying evil, sickness, and pain; that comfort is a narcotic, not a Redemption. Face suffering honestly and choose the way of Redemption through heroism rather than cowardice: keep seeking, keep returning, keep trusting, and walk forward with courage.

weighed: My first answer would be that you can't earn God's favor by being good—it's a gift you receive through Jesus, and good works flow from a heart already accepted, not toward earning that acceptance. One principle worth naming is this: serve God as He wills, not as you think you could serve Him better some other way. That changes the posture of your effort—instead of measuring yourself against a performance checklist, you're yielding to what He actually asks. What it leaves in place is everything I said first: grace is still the gift, faith is still the way in, and goodness is still the fruit rather than the root.
dogmatic: Stop trying to earn it—that whole project is upside down. You serve God well only when you serve Him as He wills, not as you imagine you could serve Him better by some other route. So drop your own plan for making yourself acceptable and yield to His. When a chance to do good comes up, don't grit your teeth and perform; turn to Him and say you can't do it unless He enables you, and He gives strength more than sufficient. That's the way to approach Him—not a scorecard, but surrender and dependence.

weighed: I'd start by saying the secret of knowing God more deeply is to seek him consistently through prayer, Scripture, and community. Set aside regular time each day to read the Bible and reflect on it, and let what you read shape your life. Pray honestly, bringing your questions and desires to God. Join a faith community where you can learn from others and be challenged and encouraged. Serve others, because love in action opens your heart to God's presence. Keep a journal of what you notice and how you change. Be patient—knowing God is a lifelong journey, not a single insight. One idea that adds something important is that it's better to know Jesus himself than to know the truth about him. That changes the focus from collecting facts about God to actually knowing Christ as a person—so prayer and reading become about relationship, not just information. But it leaves in place the practical habits: you still need regular time, honest prayer, community, and service to grow that relationship over time.
dogmatic: The secret of knowing God more deeply is to stop trying to capture him in a single definition or method. God is neither this nor that—not a formula, not a doctrine you can hold completely—but infinitely more than any of our categories, known only according to each one's capacity to receive him. Where do we learn his character? Not chiefly from arguments about nature or history, but from the moral consciousness within us: when you recognize as self-evident that cruelty is wrong and mercy is good, you are hearing a deliverance of Reason that reveals God's own judgments. Yet do not stop at truths about God. The secret is to know Jesus himself, not merely facts about him—to enter into the secret of the Lord himself as a single-hearted seeker, letting conscience be purified and the vessel of your heart enlarged. So pray, read, serve, and above all seek the person of Christ, for he is the one in whom God is truly known.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, the Gospels present a bodily resurrection, and that's the claim Christianity rests on. The risen Jesus shows his wounds, eats fish, and is touched, which is meant to rule out a mere spirit or vision. What I'd add now is this: resurrection is also the spiritualization of thought, a higher idea of immortality where material belief gives way to spiritual understanding. That doesn't cancel the bodily claim or the empty tomb; it deepens what the event means for how you live now, rising above sin and sickness into newness of life. So the physical reality stays in place, and the spiritual meaning gets its full weight too.
dogmatic: The bodily resurrection is as well attested as any fact of ancient history, and without it Christianity makes no sense at all. The disciples didn't see a ghost or have a vision; they saw the risen Christ in body and spirit, and that changed them from frightened men into bold witnesses. But don't stop at the tomb. Resurrection is the spiritualization of thought, a new and higher idea of immortality, where material belief yields to spiritual understanding. If you want to know Christ's likeness, you have to live under the holy Cross, drawing your purer breath from above until people see an angel face in you. That's the whole point: the empty tomb and the risen life are one truth, and it's meant to raise you above sin and sickness right now.

weighed: I'd start by saying that serving the poor and forgotten isn't a distraction from your duties; it's a central part of following Jesus. He said whatever you do for the least of these, you do for Him, so that pull you feel is likely a calling. Still, you have to balance it with family and work, and the key is integrating service into your daily life rather than neglecting your duties. One principle worth weighing is that it's a privilege to live economically and endure hardship so you have more to give to the Lord's service, and the less you spend on yourself, the fuller your joy. That changes how you think about your budget and comforts: cutting back isn't a loss, it frees resources for others. What it leaves in place is the balance itself; you still honor your family and work responsibilities, and you still serve through your church, volunteering, or simple kindness. So deny yourself some unnecessary comforts, give more, and trust God to provide the time and resources.
dogmatic: Serving the poor and forgotten is not a distraction from your duties; it is an indispensable command, and refusing the needy puts you at risk of eternal loss. What you give to the poor you give to Christ Himself. If you're drawn to this, treat it as your first obligation, not a hobby you fit around your comforts. Live economically, deny yourself unnecessary things, and endure hardship gladly, because the less you spend on yourself, the more you have to give to the Lord's service, and the fuller your joy will be. Don't excuse yourself from succoring the unfortunate or treat the poor as anything less than members of Christ. Almsgiving is not optional. Urge generous relief, not exemption, and know that in serving the poor you serve Christ Himself.

weighed: Yes, I really do believe you can hope to meet your friend again. Scripture says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and that those who die in Christ will be reunited. That hope should comfort you and steady you as you keep walking in faith, and it should move you to live in a way that honors God, knowing she is with Him now. You grieve, but not as those without hope.
