One principle I'd hold alongside that is this: knowing our need of God's grace, we should resolve never to forget Him and to live in His presence, even if He withholds consolations for a time. That doesn't change the hope of reunion or the comfort it brings. What it adds is a steady resolve to stay close to God in the grief itself, not only in the consolation. So let this hope draw you nearer to Him day by day, and let it shape how you live now.
dogmatic: Yes, you can hope to meet her again in the presence of the Lord, because for believers to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and we will be reunited with those who have died in Christ. But don't stop at comfort. Knowing our need of God's grace, resolve never to forget Him, not for a moment, and to spend the rest of your days in His presence, even if He sees fit to withhold every consolation. That is the deeper gain: you get God as your friend, and all the angels as your friends, and the hearts of all who belong to Christ as brothers and sisters, losing none but enemies who loved your vanity. So don't think you have lost all help and fellowship; you have gained a greater fellowship in the body of Christ. Wait on God in prayer for supply, and refrain from making your needs known to others when the point is that your faith be strengthened by receiving help from God alone in answer to prayer. Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask, and He will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

weighed: Taking up your cross daily means a deliberate, ongoing surrender of your own will to God's. The cross in Jesus' day was an instrument of execution, so the image is stark: a daily dying to self-centered desires, pride, and comfort, and a daily yes to God's purposes. Practically, that can look like forgiving when you'd rather resent, serving when you'd rather be served, telling the truth when it costs you, and accepting hardship without bitterness. It's not just enduring inconvenience; it's choosing to follow Jesus on the path of self-giving love. Because it's daily, it isn't a one-time heroic act but a habit of the heart, renewed each morning in prayer and lived out in ordinary choices. One idea worth weighing alongside this is that the cross shows how deeply God is invested in your life and how he takes responsibility for where it ultimately leads. That adds a note of reassurance to the surrender: you're not just giving something up, you're entrusting yourself to someone who cares about the outcome. It doesn't replace the daily dying to self, but it does reframe it as trust rather than mere loss.
dogmatic: Taking up your cross daily isn't some new invention to replace the old pieties of the human heart. It's putting the love of God into those old fundamental pieties—reverence, trust, obedience, love of neighbor—the very truths Jesus realized in Himself. In Him the dearest truths about God were made living fact: that God's interest in our life is infinite, and that He assumes responsibility for its eternal issues. To take up the cross is to let that same love rule your daily choices. And honor the sign of the cross itself: made with great faith and devotion, not mere custom, it is an impregnable rampart against the devil. Yet do not flee the dark hours. The darkest hour of the Cross touches the heart with softer comfort than angel's mirth, for there the mourner finds his truest comfort—earth's bitter herbs tempered into sweetness by the Saviour's prayer and blood.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: faith in Christ is personal trust, not just agreeing with correct ideas. It's relying on Jesus himself—entrusting your failures to his mercy, your choices to his guidance, your future to his promises—and that trust shows up in how you actually live. One piece worth adding is that faith commits the matter to God and then takes its hands off, believing it's done, instead of hovering over God to see how he'll pull it off. That deepens the picture: trust isn't only a direction of the heart, it's a kind of rest. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—faith still involves praying, obeying, repenting, and loving others, and it still grows as you keep turning to him in ordinary days. It just adds that at some point trust means letting go and letting God work.
dogmatic: Faith in Christ is the foundation of everything—forgiveness of sins, resurrection, being raised with him. It's not a vague feeling; it rests on who he is and what he's done, and the restored doctrines confirm and establish belief in his divine mission. But don't stop at the first act of faith. Hold your confidence firm to the end, follow up your faith with perseverance, and press through in prayer until the blessing comes to birth. Then commit your way to the Lord, believe it is done, take your hands off, and leave God to work. A soul that keeps superintending God's work hasn't yet believed. The soul that has truly committed the matter rests and waits for God to bring it forth.

weighed: Yes, you can claim that promise for your preaching and witness, but read it in context first. Isaiah 55 pictures God's word like rain and snow that waters the earth and makes things grow—it accomplishes what God intends. For you, that means your part is faithfulness, not controlling results. Prepare well, pray, speak honestly, and leave the outcome to God. Some seed lands on hard ground; some bears fruit later than you'd expect, so don't measure yourself by immediate responses. One principle worth weighing here is that faith isn't working up certainty by willpower but seeing as fact that God has said it—turning the promise into a prophecy and resting in it. That shifts the emphasis from hoping the promise is true to treating it as already settled, which can steady you when responses are slow. What it leaves in place is the context: the promise still describes God's word doing its work in his timing, not a guarantee that every sermon gets an immediate visible result. So claim it as a reason for hope and perseverance, keep sowing faithfully, and trust him with the harvest.
dogmatic: Claim it, and start by reading it plainly. Isaiah 55 pictures God's word as rain and snow that literally water the earth and make it bud. Where the word of God admits a literal interpretation, take that first; don't spiritualize away a clear promise. God says his word shall not return void but shall accomplish what he pleases. See this as an actual fact, not a feeling you have to manufacture. Turn the promise into a prophecy and rest in it, because God cannot lie—rejoice that it is true. Prepare, pray, speak, and expect God to do what he has said. And remember that light not used is withdrawn: obey known truth promptly, for to him who has shall be given, and from him who has not shall be taken away even what he seems to have. Faithfulness today keeps the promise alive for tomorrow.

weighed: It's not too late. Feeling like you've wasted your life hurts, but it also shows self-awareness, and that's the first step toward change. Plenty of people look back and see years they wish they'd used differently. What matters now is what you do next: set new goals, lean on friends or a counselor, and build habits that reflect the life you want. Regret can be a teacher, not a verdict. One idea worth naming is that time is your capital and shouldn't be wasted. That adds a real sense of urgency and accountability to what I'd say first, but it leaves the core in place: your past doesn't decide your future, and small steps now still count. Be patient with yourself, and remember growth is possible at any age.
dogmatic: It's not too late, but start with honesty. Time is the capital you're given on earth, and it's only wealth when you use it well; idleness and wastefulness don't fit the rules of heaven, and the days spent in folly will be accounted for. Still, this life is a school of experience and a probation, not a sentence to endure. What feels like waste can become instruction. Begin now in faithfulness to duty and self-denial, because such beginnings lead to pleasures, and lean on Christ's grace, which makes every difficulty easy. Take up the duties in front of you, deny the habits that eat your hours, and keep learning and improving. The past can't be recovered, but the remaining capital can be invested in faithful service, and grace will supply what your own resolve cannot.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, failing to meet conditions doesn't mean God has rejected you. Prayer is a relationship, and relationships involve growth and struggle. If your prayers feel unanswered, the answer may not be clear yet, or God may be working in ways you can't see. God's love for you doesn't depend on perfect performance. Keep praying honestly, examine your heart, and trust that God hears you. Many faithful people have felt the same way. Talk with a pastor or trusted friend, and remember that God's acceptance is not earned but given. One thing worth weighing is that the Bible ties answered prayer to conditions like humility, forsaking sin, faith, and obedience. That principle changes how you examine yourself: instead of only waiting, you can honestly check those areas and turn from anything that's getting in the way. But it leaves in place the core truth that God's love for you isn't earned and that your feelings aren't a reliable measure of whether you're heard. So examine the conditions, but don't turn them into a test of whether God has accepted you.
dogmatic: No, failing doesn't mean God has rejected you, but prayer isn't automatic. Prevailing prayer depends on the conditions the Bible records: humility, forsaking sin, faith, obedience, and asking according to God's will in Christ's name. Don't measure whether you're heard by your feelings. Feelings never accurately gauge real assimilation to God; they rise and fall, while the word of promise is changeless. When joy is lacking, continue steadfastly in prayer rather than abandoning communion or service because of spiritual depression. And don't explain away answers as coincidence or natural law: the correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit the doctrine of chance. Examine the conditions honestly, confess and turn from sin, and rest on God's promise rather than your moods, trusting the God who hears and answers prayer.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, loneliness isn't a sign that you're wrong. Plenty of faithful people have felt isolated, and it can come from circumstances, personality, or just a hard season. It doesn't mean God is displeased with you. One principle worth holding onto is that solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself. That changes how I'd frame the quiet: it's not just something to escape but a place where you can be with God and with yourself honestly. What it leaves in place is the practical push toward connection. So reach out to a church community, join a small group, build friendships, and also learn to be at peace in your own company and in God's presence. Be gentle with yourself and take real steps toward people.
dogmatic: Don't fear living alone. Each person dwells in a hidden sphere, and God alone feels your secret throbbings. The Lord who dwells on high knows everything, yet loves you better than He knows. So accept hidden solitude as Heaven's will, trust God alone with what's private in you, and rest in the One who knows you fully and still loves you. Walls by themselves are a weak fence; true solitude means silence of the interior faculties and turning your mind toward God and yourself. From that quiet fellowship, reach out to His people, not demanding perfect human sympathy but sharing the love you've received.

weighed: The abomination that makes desolate is a blasphemous act or object that defiles the holy place and brings ruin, a phrase from Daniel that Jesus echoes as a warning of judgment. Historically people have tied it to Antiochus Epiphanes desecrating the temple and later to Rome's destruction of Jerusalem, and interpreters differ on the exact fulfillment, but the core idea is the defilement of what is holy and the ruin that follows. One principle here says the present confusion and disappointment among believers is itself a sign of perilous times and a famine for God's word, and that God's people are called out of Babylon. That shifts the focus from ancient fulfillments to a present warning about defilement and compromise, but it leaves the original meaning intact: the holy place defiled and the sanctuary brought down.
dogmatic: The abomination that makes desolate is a blasphemous defilement of the holy place that brings ruin on the sanctuary, and it is not just ancient history. The confusion and disappointment among professed believers right now, including hopes about the coming that have soured, are themselves a sign of perilous times and a famine for the word of the Lord. The same spirit casts down the sanctuary whenever God's people drink the poisonous cup of Babylon, and God is calling His people out of that cup. The way out is not your own striving: abide like a poor miserable creature before the throne of Divine Mercy, stripped of all affection for creatures and indifferent to all things. Offer your body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, dying outwardly to the world's vanity and customs and inwardly to the lusts of the flesh, becoming the temple of God and of His Spirit in imitation of the Lord's Body.

weighed: My first answer would be that Scripture presents God as just and merciful, and it doesn't clearly say that anyone is condemned for light they never received. The Bible doesn't give us a detailed map of what happens to the unevangelized, so I'd hold that humbly and trust God's character, while affirming that salvation is in Christ and that God wants all people saved. One idea worth weighing is that the gospel is preached to the dead, so those who never heard it may hear it in the spirit, with work for the dead carried on in temples. That changes the picture from 'we simply don't know' to 'there's a hopeful path after death.' What it leaves in place is the core conviction that Christ is the only Savior and that God is just and merciful. It doesn't settle every detail, and I'd still be careful about claiming more than we can know.
dogmatic: The gospel is not limited to this life. Christ preached to the spirits in prison, and the gospel is proclaimed in the spirit world, so those who died without ever hearing it can still hear it and receive it. Because ordinances require a body, the living can perform baptisms and other ordinances for the dead so they can be brought into the blessings of the gospel. This isn't speculation; it rests on the resurrection of Christ, who conquered death and promised that because He lives, we shall live also. That hope also lays a duty on the living: parents must teach their children the gospel and watch over them, guarding them from the wickedness of the world, because it is better to bury children in innocence than to see them led away from the gospel.

weighed: A roving mind is normal, and fighting it with force usually makes it worse. Start by accepting that distraction will come without judging yourself harshly. Use simple anchors: a short phrase, a breath, a repeated prayer word, or a verse, returning gently each time you notice you have drifted. Reduce input before prayer—less noise, less scrolling, a moment of silence. Try shorter, more frequent prayer rather than long sessions you dread. Writing down distracting thoughts to revisit later can free you. Over time, the mind settles not by being clamped down but by being gently and repeatedly brought back, like a wandering sheep guided home. One principle that fits here is to keep your mind recollected during the rest of the day, not just in prayer—gently bringing it back to God's presence in ordinary tasks and conversations. That adds a helpful habit of guarding your attention throughout the day, which can make prayer calmer. It leaves in place the gentle, non-forcing approach and the use of simple anchors; you don't need to become rigid or anxious about every stray thought.
dogmatic: A roving mind is a sign you've let it wander too far at other times. The real fix is to keep it strictly in the presence of God all day long—frequent thinking of Him makes it easy to stay calm in prayer and to recall it from wanderings. Also, avoid over-eagerness and restlessness; that restless spirit is the mother imperfection of all imperfections, so expressly avoid it. Confess your faults and humble yourself before God, for humility and confession greatly remedy wandering thoughts. And don't use multiplicity of words in prayer—many words and long discourses often occasion wandering. A few simple words, gently returned to, will serve you better than many.

weighed: There's real hope for you, because God's mercy is bigger than the worst things you've done. The gospel is for sinners—Christ came to save people who know they're lost. Hope starts with honest confession: naming your sins to God without making excuses, and receiving his forgiveness. Then it continues with repentance—not just regret, but turning your heart and life toward God, often with help from a trusted pastor, community, and sometimes professional counsel. Your past doesn't define you; grace can reshape your future. Recovery may be slow and will involve repairing what you can, but God's patience meets you at every step. You're invited to come as you are, and to keep coming, trusting that he who began a good work will complete it. One thing I'd add from the Christian tradition: your hope isn't in some gradual purification after death—Scripture doesn't warrant that. Your hope is that the soul, in death itself, is washed in the blood of the Lamb and presented pure and spotless to God. That doesn't change the need for confession and repentance now; it just anchors your hope in what Christ has already done, not in a drawn-out process later.
dogmatic: There is real hope, and it rests entirely on this: in death itself your soul is washed in the blood of the immaculate Lamb and presented pure and without spot to God. There is no slow purification after death to lean on—Scripture gives no warrant for that. Your hope is Christ's work, applied fully at the moment of death. And don't think your present trials are pointless: all things work together for good to those who love God, and he gives present gladness for days of affliction patiently borne—a foretaste of the fuller reward. Remember too that of ourselves we can attain to no good thing and have nothing to offer the Lord that wasn't already his. So our one recourse is to turn to him in every occurrence in prayer—guilty, poor, needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet his children—with holy fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: service can quietly crowd out the source that sustains it, so begin small and realistic. Set a short, fixed time each day and protect it like an appointment, use a simple shape like a psalm, a Gospel passage, a few minutes of silence, and honest conversation with God, and pray on the move with brief arrow prayers and gratitude when the day is full. Look honestly at your schedule too, because some busyness is chosen and you may need to say no to good things. One candidate principle I'd weigh in is that prayer is no petty duty squeezed into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of your time and strength belongs to it, with the closet first and study and activities second. That changes the center of gravity: instead of fitting prayer into whatever is left over, you'd give it your best hours and let other things be freshened by it. What it leaves in place is the practical scaffolding—the fixed short time, the simple structure, the arrow prayers, the honest look at your calendar—so those become the way you protect the best of your time rather than a substitute for giving it.
dogmatic: Prayer has to be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, not an optional extra you get to when serving is done. Ask God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and to reform whatever is amiss in it—your over-busyness, your avoidance, your misplaced priorities. Then give the best of your time and strength to prayer, not the leftovers. Put the closet first; let study and activities come second and be freshened by the closet. And do not measure prayer by immediate results. No true prayer is lost: your supplications accumulate as a memorial before God, and the longer the answer waits, the larger it becomes in the due time. So keep praying with patience, trusting that what seems silent now is being treasured and will be answered in God's good time.

weighed: I'd start by saying that shortening your devotions to get more work done is a common temptation, and it usually backfires. Ministry runs on spiritual capital, and devotions are where that capital is replenished. Cut them short and you may find yourself more productive on paper but thinner in soul: less patience, less discernment, more reliance on technique. Sermons can become clever but hollow. One principle worth naming is that hurry is damaging in communion with God. That principle sharpens the warning—it tells you why the backfire happens, not just that it does. But it leaves in place my practical advice: protect a realistic, consistent devotional time, even if modest, and let it shape the day. It doesn't change the need to ask whether the pressure is real or self-imposed, or whether some tasks could be delegated or dropped.
dogmatic: Short devotions are the bane of deep piety. They deplete spiritual vigor, arrest progress, and are the sure indication of a superficial piety, for hurry is damaging in communion with God. It is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer; sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. So give prayer calmness, time, and deliberation. When prayer feels dry and irksome, do not flee to busyness; dryness is a trial of love, and effectual acts of resignation greatly advance you. Protect a consistent time and let it shape the day, remembering the work is God's.

weighed: I'd start by saying good feelings aren't bad in themselves, but if they replace growth they can become a trap. Contentment that never moves you toward obedience, repentance, or service is more like comfort than devotion. So ask whether these feelings draw you closer to God and others or just soothe you while you avoid hard things. One principle here says that early on we should be faithful in duty and self-denial, and afterward deep pleasures follow, and in difficulties we just turn to Christ and ask for grace. That changes the tone: it reframes duty and self-denial not as grim costs but as the path that leads to real pleasure, and it points you to grace when it feels hard. What it leaves in place is my original test: the feelings still need to be checked against whether your life shows growing love, humility, and faithfulness. So try small concrete acts of obedience and self-denial, let the feelings follow rather than lead, and talk honestly with a trusted mentor about whether you're resting in God or just in comfort.
dogmatic: Good feelings are not the goal, and contentment that never moves toward obedience, repentance, and service is comfort, not devotion. The constant condition of spiritual supply is the full conviction of your utter helplessness; you must know you have nothing before you can receive His all. So begin by confessing your insufficiency, then take firm hold of Christ's all-sufficiency with a faith that will not accept less than all. Be faithful in duty and deny yourself, and in difficulties have recourse to Jesus Christ and beg His grace, with which everything becomes easy. And do not cling to innocent, lawful pleasures: it is proper, often, to deprive the body of many little pleasures, for God will not permit a soul devoted entirely to Him to take other pleasures than with Him. Ask whether these feelings draw you closer to God and others or soothe you while you avoid hard things, and let your life show increasing love, humility, and faithfulness.

weighed: My first answer would be that no, the truth of Christianity doesn't hinge on every Gospel miracle happening exactly as written—the heart of it is Jesus's life, teaching, death, and resurrection, and the change that brings. One principle that sharpens this: the real evidence is the faith's power, the present experience of sins forgiven and lives genuinely turned around. That shifts the weight onto lived transformation as the answer to skeptics who say miracles contradict experience. What it leaves in place is the historical question—it doesn't settle whether the miracles happened, and it doesn't excuse sloppy history. It just means your faith isn't hanging on proving every supernatural event.
dogmatic: The truth of Christianity doesn't rest on miracles as bare external proofs—the real evidence is power, the present experience of sins forgiven and lives regenerated. That's the answer to critics who say miracles contradict experience: meet experience with experience. And don't hand the skeptics their premise. Theories that write off the Gospels as myth or romance are unscientific because they assume miracle is impossible from the start, turning history into guesswork instead of testimony. Weigh the documents as testimony. But remember what miracles actually do: they certify a teacher's divine commission, not every doctrine he teaches. Power alone can't prove a commission—purity of life and doctrine have to be credited too. So hold miracle and doctrine together, and test the records honestly.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: comparison usually comes from insecurity, so notice your own strengths and weaknesses, set goals you measure against your own past instead of other people, practice gratitude, and celebrate others without feeling threatened. When pride shows up, remember everyone has flaws; when despair shows up, remember everyone has value. One idea worth naming is that self-control means checking your words, stepping back from anger, really knowing yourself, and minding your own business rather than faultfinding. That adds a practical brake: before you compare, you catch the impulse to judge or meddle and redirect it. What it changes is the moment-to-moment habit—you get something concrete to do when the urge hits. What it leaves in place is the deeper work of building self-acceptance and measuring yourself against your own past, which is still where the real freedom comes from.
dogmatic: Stop treating the comparison itself as the problem and look at what feeds it. Pity and mercy feel virtuous, but they only exist because someone was made poor and unhappy—they'd vanish if we stopped making people poor. The same root feeds pride: you feel superior or worthless only by measuring against someone you've quietly placed below or above you. And don't trust every impulse that rises—mystery and deceit grow in the human brain, so examine yourself, bridle your tongue, subdue your anger, and attend to your own duties instead of judging others. When you catch yourself in pride or despair, turn your mind back to God and say, 'Lord, I trust in You.' Do that each time, and the habit of comparison will weaken.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: worry is a habit you can loosen, so try naming your concerns on paper each day and handing them over in prayer, breathe slowly to settle your body, make a simple plan for the practical steps, lean on supportive people, and trust that God helps those who help themselves. That's still mostly my answer. But one idea here genuinely shifts it: you're not the one living Agent doing all the work while God watches—you're the instrument, and anxious self-reliance is really distrust of Him. That changes the tone of your effort from striving to trusting, and it reframes those wandering thoughts as something to set down gently rather than fight. What it leaves in place is the practical part—writing things down, planning, breathing, and good friends still matter. They just stop being the thing your peace depends on.
dogmatic: Stop treating your anxiety as a problem you solve by trying harder. God is the one living Agent who works; you are only an instrument. Every ounce of care you clutch is distrust of Him and a kind of self-conceit, as if the outcome rested on you. So commit yourself and everything that concerns you to His unfailing Providence, in silence and peace, and accept whatever comes as from a father's hand. Sit before Him like a beggar at a rich man's gate—your only business is to keep your mind in His presence. When it wanders, don't fuss over it; fussing scatters you more. Bring it back calmly. Vain, wandering thoughts only weary your soul and body and waste your time and strength. This is not passivity; it is the humble waiting of a beggar who trusts. Do that, and His peace will guard your heart.

weighed: My first instinct is that this is a classic philosophical and theological question. Pantheism says the universe is God, while theism says God made the universe and is distinct from it. Most traditions hold that God is greater than the universe, as the Creator is greater than the creation. So the universe isn't God but a manifestation of God's creative power—finite and contingent, while God is infinite and necessary. One candidate principle I'd name is that the universe is a finite, partial, and progressive manifestation of the divine Life, with matter as God's self-limitation under necessity, humanity under freedom, and incarnation and atonement under grace. That principle changes the picture by making the universe an evolving expression of God rather than a static artifact, but it leaves in place the core claim that God transcends the universe while being its source and sustainer. So my answer stays: the universe is something God made and is greater than, though God is present in it.
dogmatic: The universe is not God but a finite, partial, and progressive manifestation of the divine Life. God is greater than His thoughts, and the universe is one of His thoughts. Matter, humanity, incarnation, and atonement are God's self-limitations under necessity, freedom, and grace respectively. Yet God is All-in-all, and matter is a mortal belief, having no reality or power apart from the divine Mind. The universe and man are as eternal as God, their divine immortal Principle, without temporal beginning. Thus, the universe is something God made and is greater than, yet it is not coeternal with God nor a constituent part of Him. It is a partial expression of His being, evolving toward greater fullness. God transcends the universe while being its source and sustainer.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: silence like this is painful and common, and it doesn't mean God has abandoned you. Keep your routines—prayer, Scripture, community, service—even when they feel dry, name your feelings honestly to God, talk with someone you trust, and remember times you sensed His presence before. One principle worth weighing is that God sometimes hides Himself, not to punish but to teach the soul to live by faith and not by sight. That changes the frame: the silence becomes a place where faith alone carries you, not a sign that something is wrong. What it leaves in place is everything I said about showing up, being honest, and leaning on others. What I wouldn't add is a promise that every prayer gets a matching answer you can verify—that's a heavier claim than your question needs, and it can make the silence feel like a test you're failing.
dogmatic: Yes—God does hide Himself at times, and Scripture says so plainly. He does it to teach the soul to live by faith and not by sight, so when every feeling and every bit of evidence withdraws, faith alone remains and faith alone must be your support. Don't conclude your secret prayers go unheard; God understands your innermost thoughts as surely as human invention carries words across great distances. Ask in faith, nothing wavering. Then watch your life closely: the correspondences between what you asked and what you were given are too many and too exact to be chance. They shut out the doctrine of chance and compel belief in a God who hears and answers. So keep praying, keep obeying, keep waiting, and let your confidence rest in Him who has promised and cannot fail.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: take comfort in your faith, spend your time deepening your relationship with God, mend what's broken with family and friends, serve others, and live each day with gratitude and hope. One principle I'd add is this: prepare to live, not merely to die. That changes the frame—instead of only planning for the end, you'd also build habits now that support your health and strength, since a long life may still be ahead. What it leaves in place is the honesty that death is certain and its timing uncertain, so you still make the changes you'd want to have made, and you don't put off what matters most.
dogmatic: Don't spend your remaining time preparing to die—prepare to live. Lay the foundation of health, strength, and constitution now, and teach yourself early, because longevity may begin to return. Death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, so make now the changes you'd wish you'd made when death is near. And don't rely on baptism or the Christian name or the mere fact of dying to guarantee paradise—death works no miracle. You are after death exactly as far advanced as before, so the Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in you here. Build health and nurture that Seed; don't postpone what matters most.

weighed: I'd start where you are: feeling powerless is normal, and the first thing I'd say is to deepen your own faith through prayer, Scripture, and fellowship, then look for simple ways to serve—volunteer, mentor, be a listening ear—and trust that God uses willing people. One principle that sharpens this is that if you're yourself tangled up in fear or sin and you know the remedy but don't use it for yourself, you'll have little power to help anyone else. That changes the order: it puts your own healing and honesty first, not as a prerequisite to earn the right to help, but because a clear conscience and a settled heart make you more useful. It leaves in place the practical stuff—prayer, serving, kindness, sharing your story—and it leaves in place that saving souls is ultimately God's work, not yours to manufacture.
dogmatic: You can't save anyone, and you can't even save yourself—you're a branch that bears nothing unless it stays in the vine. So stop treating your earnestness as faith. First deal with your own fear and sin; if you know the remedy and won't use it, you have no power to help another soul. Be slow to take new steps, give up your own will, and find God's direction through prayer and the Word before you move. Abide in Christ by keeping His commandments, and then your prayers become powerful and your fruit real. The order matters: the healer must first be healed, then wait for God's timing. Anything else is presumption dressed up as zeal.

weighed: It makes sense that you feel stuck—being hurt by someone who never acknowledges it is a heavy thing to carry. What I'd say first is that forgiveness isn't about excusing what happened or pretending you're not hurt; it's about loosening the grip that hurt has on your peace. One practical step is to notice when you're replaying the story and gently redirect your attention. Writing an unsent letter can help you get the anger and grief out of your body. It can also help to name what you lost—trust, safety, time—and grieve it honestly. Forgiveness is often a process, not a single decision, and it's okay if it takes time. You can also ask yourself whether you want reconciliation or just freedom from resentment; those are different goals, and you can pursue peace even without an apology. One principle worth weighing is that forgiveness is an inward condition that grows in a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. That changes the focus: instead of waiting for the other person to make it right, you tend to your own heart and your willingness to forgive. What it leaves in place is that the hurt is real, the process takes time, and you don't owe anyone reconciliation—you can still choose peace without an apology.
dogmatic: Forgiveness is not something that falls from the sky in return for a request. It is an inward condition that can only come to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on you as much as on God. So don't wait for an apology to begin. Name the wound honestly, ask for a heart made willing, and refuse to let resentment take root. Scripture warns that refusing to forgive endangers the soul, so don't delay or nurse the injury. Return meekness and kindness for insults, and pray for the one who hurt you. Look to Christ, who gave everything to earn your pardon and forgave you without your deserving it; let that unlimited mercy be the measure of yours. Don't measure out love by your own narrow rule—forgive as you hope to be forgiven, and trust God to supply the grace.

weighed: I'd start by saying the New Testament shows Jesus as both fully human and fully divine, and the different Gospels just emphasize different angles—the Synoptics focus on his human life and teaching, while John highlights his divine identity. That tension isn't a contradiction; it's a richer picture. One idea that helps is that we shouldn't look for Jesus only through other people or arguments until we've first found him within ourselves—by reflecting on his life, comparing it to ours, and trying to imitate his gentle ways. That principle shifts the focus inward, but it doesn't erase the need to read Scripture and learn from others; it just says the inner encounter comes first. So you can hold the mystery without having to resolve every detail.
dogmatic: You should think of Jesus as both truly man and truly God—not something in between. The Gospels present one Lord from complementary angles: the Synoptics show his human deeds and suffering, John ponders his divine identity. But don't stop at arguments or other people. You must first find Christ within yourself, by inward pondering, loving comparison of his life with yours, and persistent imitation of his gentle ways. Only then will you recognize him in Scripture and in others. Cast your thoughts on the Savior's shoulders for support and fix your eyes on God's good pleasure, trusting his providence to lead you into truth.

weighed: Yes, there is still comfort. Regret over wasted youth is a heavy burden, but it doesn't define your worth or your remaining days. Many people find late life brings a different kind of fruitfulness: perspective, gentleness, and freedom to focus on what matters most. You can't recover lost years, but you can still choose how to spend the time you have—repairing relationships, offering kindness, praying, or simply being present. Grief over the past is real and worth acknowledging, maybe with a trusted friend or counselor. No life is measured only by its early chapters; the ending matters too. One principle here says the world grows old and mirth is gone, yet youth should come like the wind at morning to renew freshness, bringing strength and radiance so that Spring may be hoped for. That changes the picture by suggesting renewal can still arrive, even now, as a fresh morning in your spirit. What it leaves in place is the honest grief you feel and the fact that lost years can't be recovered—it doesn't erase the past, it just says the story isn't closed.
dogmatic: Yes, there is still comfort, and it comes from a truth you shouldn't set aside. The world itself has grown old and its mirth has faded, yet youth is meant to come like the wind at morning—fresh, strong, radiant—so that Spring can still be hoped for. That youth isn't only about years; a new morning can rise in your spirit even now. Don't despise the calm old age of a pure conscience, because the hidden prayers of lowly saints uphold the proud world, though the great imagine they sustain themselves. And seek improvement not mainly through bodily regimen but through the spiritualization of thought—forsake the mortal sense of things and turn from false belief to Truth. As thought is lifted to God, the body and the whole man are renewed. Grace remains for you; let Truth be your medicine.

weighed: I'd start by saying hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to deep questions. One candidate principle here is that our great difficulty is trying to hold to God with the soul while clinging to the world with the heart—what's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in our exact circumstances, to place God first with a subtle inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. That principle changes the focus from crisis as the trigger to everyday allegiance: it says the real work is an undivided heart right where you are, not waiting for pain to wake you up. What it leaves in place is the original insight that hardship can clarify and deepen your attention—it doesn't dismiss that, just reframes it as a call to carry that attentiveness into ordinary, comfortable seasons too.
dogmatic: Hardship doesn't actually teach you about God—it just exposes what you've been clinging to. The real issue is allegiance: you're trying to hold God with your soul while your heart is wrapped around the world. What's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in your exact circumstances, to put God first with an inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. And don't be fooled by small caprices—a pretty frock or a pleasant companion can make you forget God entirely, and He uses no force because you're still in the Garden of Free-Will. Suffering itself is a mental condition; when an accident happens, declare that you are not hurt and understand why, and that brings good effects in proportion to your fidelity to divine metaphysics. So stop waiting for pain to clarify God. Place Him first now, in the trivial habits of your day, and let your understanding rest on Truth, not on hardship.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's a duty, and a healthy one. When people give to support your work, they have a real interest in knowing their gifts were used faithfully. Giving an account isn't an insult to your integrity—it's part of the trust that makes generosity possible. One principle that fits here is that we're stewards, not owners, of what we've received. That changes the framing: the money was never really yours to use however you like, so accounting for it is just part of the trust. But it leaves in place the practical advice—prepare honestly, be transparent about mistakes, and don't get defensive. It also keeps the relational tone: think of it as a conversation that honors the relationship, not an audit.
dogmatic: It's a duty, and you need to remember you're a steward, not an owner. What you received was never private property—it was entrusted to you by the Lord, and you'll answer for how you used it. Giving an account to those who gave is part of that trust. Scripture commends giving that is systematic and regular, not just when you feel like it. So prepare honestly: what came in, what went out, what was accomplished, what you learned. Be transparent and don't get defensive. And examine yourself—if any earthly attachment is hindering full obedience to Christ, give it up, no matter the cost, because the smile of God is enough. Finally, remember that ordinary business faithfulness and keeping your promises matter for your witness; weigh every engagement carefully and keep your promises exactly, since in these small things you bring either honor or dishonor to the Lord.

weighed: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense, but it's aimed at the wrong thing. Stopping won't leave you with nothing — you'll meet what you've actually become, and at first that can feel like silence, even loss. One principle here is that perseverance matters: it's not how far you've run but what remains of your course, and finishing well counts for more than starting well. That changes the question from what stopping costs you to what's still unfinished, and it keeps your fear in view instead of dismissing it. What it leaves in place is the silence — you'll still have to sit in it and ask what you're running toward and whether it's worth it.
dogmatic: Your fear is pointed at the wrong thing entirely. The real question isn't what stopping will cost you but what remains of your course, because beginning well avails nothing if you leave it unfinished. Don't answer this with hurry, either — over-eagerness scatters the heart and makes anxiety the biggest obstacle to any real progress. Stay quietly in God's presence and take each step as before him. And before you try to help anyone else, deal with your own fear, your own unbelief, your own hidden sin first — let the healer be healed. What you find at the end isn't nothing; it's the completion of what grace began, and that's his work in you, not the fruit of your fretting.

weighed: Criticism about how you dress usually says more about the critic than about you, so start by listening without getting defensive. Ask whether the concern is cultural appropriateness, modesty, or just personal preference. If it's preference, you can gently explain your choices. If it's about fitting in or avoiding offense, adjust where you can without compromising your convictions. Your calling is to serve, not to win arguments about clothing, so keep your focus on the people you're there to love. One principle that matters here: missionaries shouldn't tear down those who came before them but should speak of them as brothers and sisters who did the best they knew, and should invite rather than compel. That changes the tone of how you respond to criticism, because you're not defending yourself against the past or proving you're better than earlier workers. What it leaves in place is the practical guidance itself: listen, sort out the real concern, adjust where you can, and don't make your wardrobe a hill to die on.
dogmatic: Honestly, the criticism isn't the main issue. The real question is whether your life carries a testimony and whether you keep the Word of Wisdom. Without those, no outfit will commend the message, and with them, the criticism loses most of its sting. Teach in simplicity and humility, not with oratory or contention, and don't get pulled into debates about clothes. Remember that a human being is a human being anywhere, and any person is entitled to any truth another can reveal. So reject any notion that truth belongs to one nation or that you're superior because of where you come from. You invite people to the good you've found; you never push them past their freedom and never compel anyone. Dress in a way that respects the people you're with, but let your motive be a genuine passion for human beings as human beings, and let your life, not your clothing, carry the testimony.

weighed: I'd start by saying the cleansing of the sanctuary and the burning of the earth are two different things. The sanctuary that gets cleansed is the heavenly one, not the earth, and that cleansing happens at the end of the 2300 days—it's a work done by blood, not by fire on the planet. The fire that destroys the wicked comes later, after the saints are delivered. One principle that matters here is that the earth and the human family will be redeemed and renewed, not destroyed. That changes how I'd frame the whole thing: it means the earth isn't the sanctuary and isn't burned before the saints receive immortality, but it also means we shouldn't despise the earth or long to escape it—we're meant to build up Zion here. What it leaves in place is the distinction between the heavenly sanctuary's cleansing and the final fire, so the answer to your question stays no, the earth isn't burned first.
dogmatic: No, the earth will not be burned before the saints receive immortality. The cleansing of the sanctuary is something else entirely—it's the heavenly sanctuary being cleansed at the end of the 2300 days, a work done by blood, not by fire on the earth. The fire that consumes the wicked comes after the saints are delivered. And don't miss this: the earth and the human family are going to be redeemed and renewed, not destroyed. So stop despising the earth or longing to leave it. Build up Zion here. Enjoy every good thing God has given, without covetousness, in the spirit of the Gospel, because the earth and its fulness belong to the Lord.

weighed: I'd start by saying that if your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you can't separate the profit from the harm—the money is the fruit of the injury, and keeping it means consenting to it. So ask whether the harm is essential or incidental. If it's essential, you must leave it, even at a cost. If it's incidental, you can reform the business so it no longer harms. One principle that matters here is that blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive you to prayer and action rather than let you rest in personal security. That changes the focus: it's not just about your own soul being safe, but about letting that burden push you to pray and act. What it leaves in place is the basic moral logic—if the harm is essential, leaving is still required. It doesn't soften that; it just adds a call to prayer and action alongside it.
dogmatic: You ask if you must leave a trade that harms souls. The answer is yes—if the harm is essential, you cannot stay. But don't stop at personal security. The feeling of blood-guiltiness over perishing souls should drive you to prayer and action, not to resting in your own safety. More than that, you must preserve your soul free from every trace of earth, so that neither the world nor friends, neither prosperity nor adversity, things present, past, or future, nor even your own sins above measure have power to trouble it. Live as though already in eternity, alone with God. You may dread having naught beside God, but what you fear as loss is actually God storing all things for you at home. So leave the harmful trade, yes, but let your soul be so disentangled from earth that you are free to obey without being troubled by any loss.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, there's real hope, because God is merciful and wants everyone saved, and we can trust that people who never knew Christ aren't automatically cut off from his grace. One idea worth weighing is that death doesn't work a miracle—we're after death exactly as far advanced as before, so character isn't suddenly changed just by dying. That changes how I'd frame the hope: it's not that dying instantly fixes everything, but that God's mercy can still reach people beyond death. What it leaves in place is the core hope itself—we can still pray for our ancestors and entrust them to God's compassion without presuming to know exactly how he works it out.
dogmatic: There is hope, but not the easy hope that death itself fixes anything. Death works no miracle; we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. The Seed of Divine love must be planted and consciously growing in us here. Yet we need not mourn as those without hope. Christ has touched the bier, and we rest our darlings in hope of resurrection. Death is not the end of identity but a door to a higher state; the righteous dead are preserved in God's memory and will be raised in body. So we grieve, but with hope, trusting that God's mercy extends beyond death while we do not presume. We pray for our ancestors, live faithfully, and commend them to the God who raises the dead and makes all things new.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Creeds are the church's way of putting into careful words what the New Testament says in various ways—Jesus as Lord, Savior, and Son of God—so they're drawing out what the texts imply rather than inventing a new figure. One idea worth weighing is that Jesus bears the same name as God, ho kurios, so you'd think of him as you think of God—yet he was never placed on an equality with the Father, because monotheism guarded against that. That changes how you read the Creeds: they're guarding a distinction, not flattening it. What it leaves in place is the church's settled summary of who Jesus is, which you can hold alongside Scripture.
dogmatic: The Creeds aren't hedging—they're saying what the texts force on you. Jesus bears the very name of God, ho kurios, so you must think of him as you think of God; that's not a later add-on, it's the shape of the faith. And his own testimony can't be written off as deception or self-deception—his calm self-mastery and sinless conscience rule that out—so he must be one with God and the one who reveals God to us. The Creeds are just the church saying that plainly, and you should read them as the settled summary of who he is, held right alongside Scripture.

weighed: When you feel you've lost time spiritually, I'd first say: remember that God's grace isn't bound by time. Don't dwell on the past; focus on the present and take small steps forward. Start with simple prayers, read Scripture, and engage in community. Avoid comparing yourself to others. God is patient and welcomes you back at any point. One principle that fits here is holding yourself in prayer like a beggar at a rich man's gate—just keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and if it wanders, gently bring it back without getting upset. That principle changes how you handle distraction: instead of seeing a wandering mind as failure, you treat it as a chance to return calmly. It leaves in place the core advice to start small, stay present, and trust God's patience.
dogmatic: You need to stop treating spiritual time as something you can lose and start advancing. Not to advance is to go back. Hold yourself in prayer like a beggar at a rich man's gate—keep your mind in the Lord's presence, and when it wanders, bring it back in tranquility without disquiet. If storms toss your soul, awaken the Lord within you and He will calm the sea. Allow yourself no repose and no slipping back; go forward like a mountain-climber until the goal is reached. If your desires turn aside after lower objects, you'll lose yourself in byways and countless distractions. Withdraw from worldly distractions and become recollected in the one unchangeable Good. Don't dwell on the past; focus on the present and keep showing up.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: focus on prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, and practical application. Keep your sermons grounded in Scripture and centered on Christ, preach with clarity and passion, rely on the Holy Spirit to convict and convert hearts, build relationships with your congregation so you can speak to their real needs, and be consistent in your personal devotion and holiness. One principle worth naming is that the best sermon ever preached is Truth practiced and demonstrated by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death—profession without proof is not enough. That principle changes the emphasis: it pushes you to make sure your preaching is not just spoken but lived and demonstrated, so that the reality of Christ's power is visible in your life and ministry. It leaves in place everything else I said—prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, practical application, Scripture-centered preaching, reliance on the Spirit, relationships, and personal holiness. So you still do all of that, but you add the weight of practicing and demonstrating the truth you preach.
dogmatic: The best sermon ever preached is Truth practiced and demonstrated by the destruction of sin, sickness, and death. Profession without proof is not enough. If you want lasting fruit, you must not settle for words alone—you must demonstrate the power of Christ over sin, sickness, and death in your own life and ministry. All blessings come through sacrifice, and the minister who shirks toil and privation produces little fruit. Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. So be willing to be lost sight of in your fruit, letting others be prominent while you hold up their hands by silent love and prayer. The nearer you come to Christ, the more willing you will be to decrease so that He may increase. This is the path to lasting fruit: die to self, practice the truth, and demonstrate the power of God.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't treat devotion and study as two separate tracks. Let your devotion be informed by real theological reflection, and let your study be animated by prayer. Begin each study session with prayer, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate your mind and warm your heart. Meditate on Scripture regularly so it shapes both what you understand and what you love. Remember theology isn't an end in itself; it's a means to know and love God more deeply. One principle worth naming here is that devotion should be characterized by thought and theology must be permeated by a spirit of devotion, because it's the heart that makes the theologian. What that changes is the framing: it's not just 'integrate the two' as a practical tip, but a claim that thoughtless devotion and undevotional theology are both defective at the root. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: prayer before study, meditating on Scripture, spiritual reading, and treating theology as a means to knowing and loving God. So the practical steps stay, but they're now grounded in what devotion and theology actually are.
dogmatic: The heart makes the theologian. That's the whole thing. If your devotion has no thought in it, it isn't devotion, it's just a mood. And if your theology has no devotion in it, it isn't theology, it's just information. So stop trying to balance two separate activities and treat them as one. Devotion should be characterized by thought, and theology must be permeated by a spirit of devotion. Read piously and meditate from your earliest years, the way Timothy's ardor for holy reading was commended as proof of devotion. And don't imagine this is only for cloisters. Devotion suits Christians in secular life just as much. Keep God before your eyes amid your business, shun the spirit of the world, and renew your fervor in prayer. That's how devotion stays thoughtful and study stays fruitful.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear of suffering is completely natural, and drawing closer to God is still worth it. Suffering can deepen your faith and character, Christ suffered too and is with you in it, and the joy and peace of knowing God outweigh any temporary affliction. One principle I'd weigh in is that patience and steady faithfulness in a state of suffering can be more heroic and precious than active labor, so we should want health only if it's more expedient for God's honor. That changes the frame: it stops treating suffering as just something to get through on the way to usefulness, and makes the endurance itself meaningful. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about. It doesn't promise you'll avoid pain, and it doesn't make the fear go away by itself. It just says the fear doesn't get the final word, and the worth of drawing near to God still holds.
dogmatic: The fear of suffering is natural, but drawing closer to God is always worth it. Abandon yourself to God in interior and exterior suffering, living, working, and rejoicing but in God. Patience under sickness and crosses is a more heroic and precious sacrifice than active labor, so desire health only if it be more expedient for God's honor. God employs suffering as a remedy for moral evil, and His righteousness resolves the problem of pain; the Cross shows agony is compatible with the most perfect love between God and the sufferer. So take courage, trust in His love, and press on, knowing the ultimate reward is eternal life with Him.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: order your day around God—prayer, Scripture, quiet—and let love of neighbor flow out from that center. Pray for the people around you, listen before you speak, serve without looking for anything back, and when anger rises, bring it honestly to God instead of letting it steer your words. One principle I'd add is this: be kind to your neighbor even when your heart is murmuring or flaring, and gently compel your heart to suffer tranquilly. That changes the tone of the hard moments—it makes the disturbance itself something you offer to God rather than something you dump on the person in front of you. It leaves in place everything about keeping your heart fixed on God alone and letting that center feed your love; it just gives you something concrete to do when the center feels shaky.
dogmatic: Keep your heart fixed on God alone, and treat the turbulence inside you as the real battleground. When impatience or a rebellious murmur rises, don't hand it to your neighbor—compel your heart to suffer tranquilly and offer the disturbance to God. Watch for apathy, because it's deadly, not harmless; God in His love will touch you where you're most tender, through loss or hardship, to keep you from settling into it. And bear with others in their imperfections, since that forbearance is a great part of perfection and the very practice of love of neighbor. Pray for those who irritate you, listen before you speak, and serve quietly, so that patience itself becomes worship.

weighed: Routine in devotion is really common, and renewal usually comes through small changes of attention rather than dramatic ones. Try varying your prayers: read a different Marian prayer or passage each week, or pray a scriptural rosary that pairs each mystery with a verse. Set a consistent time but keep it short enough to stay attentive. Learning about Mary's life and the saints who loved her can rekindle affection, and adding some service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor—helps too. Be patient with dryness; feelings aren't the measure of faithfulness. One principle worth naming is that true devotion isn't a license to sin but calls for the intention to amend your life. That adds a real moral seriousness to renewal—it turns routine into a matter of the heart and will, not just technique—while leaving in place all the practical steps: varied prayer, a steady time, learning, service, patience, and asking Mary herself to teach you to pray.
dogmatic: True devotion to Mary is not a technique you tweak; it means honoring her, invoking her, trusting her intercession, and imitating her virtues, and it requires the intention to amend your life rather than presuming on her mercy. Mary conducts her servants to paradise, so devotion to her is a sign of predestination and a ground of confident hope for salvation. Renew the Rosary above all: recite it with devotion and pauses, not in haste, for meditating on any one mystery of the Passion suffices, and five devout decades please Mary more than fifteen said in haste. Keep a consistent time, add service in her spirit—humility, availability, care for the poor—and be patient with dryness, asking Mary to teach you to pray.

weighed: My first instinct is to say that imitating God as Father means giving generously and taking the initiative—providing for people without waiting to be asked—while filial receiving means accepting that you're a creature, a child before God who depends on Him for everything. In practice that's daily admitting your need, asking for help, and receiving correction and gifts without pride, including from other people: accepting care, counsel, and forgiveness instead of always being the giver. One principle worth naming is that we receive with a filial, loving heart whatever our Lord sends from a heart so paternal in its care for our perfection. That changes the tone of receiving: it's not just gritting your teeth and accepting your limits, it's trusting that what comes to you is sent by a Father who's after your growth, so even hard things can be received with love rather than resentment. What it leaves in place is the practical rhythm I'd already suggest—set aside time to receive in prayer and sacrament, then look for concrete ways to give your time, attention, and resources to those around you, especially the vulnerable.
dogmatic: Imitating God as Father means giving generously and providing without waiting to be asked, and filial receiving means accepting your creatureliness and receiving with a loving heart whatever our Lord sends, trusting His paternal care. But hear this clearly: forsaking base things and rising to Divine things is accomplished by labouring with the heart and the inward aspiration of the soul, not by exterior labour or bodily health. Loving God only, hating yourself more than all, and desiring to seem little require repose of the senses, effort of the heart, and silence of the mind. Accept God's transplanting too: He moves you out of the crowded nursery into places of responsibility where you must lean directly on Him and grow, and that dependence is not a setback but the very condition of growth. So receive in prayer and sacrament, then give concretely to the vulnerable.

weighed: My first answer would be that insincerity does undermine faith, because faith depends on being truthful with God and with yourself. When you show people a false self, you slowly lose track of what you actually believe and feel, and prayer turns into a performance. The fix is to rebuild integrity through small honest choices: admit fault quickly, skip the exaggeration, let your yes mean yes, and bring your real self, inconsistencies and all, before God. One principle worth weighing here is that faith shouldn't lean on human wisdom, your own or anyone else's, but should trust God with all your heart. That changes the framing: the root of your insincerity may be that you're leaning on other people's approval instead of trusting God, so the remedy starts with trust rather than willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical advice, since honest small choices and examining your motives still matter. It just puts trusting God underneath them as the foundation.
dogmatic: Insincerity is a symptom of a deeper sickness, and treating it as a habit to fix misses the point. The foundation of all solid virtue is subduing your passions and dying to yourself. Without self-denial, all your religious practices and devotion are full of illusion and imperfection. Your insincerity is self-love protecting its own image, and no amount of quick apologies or careful honesty will cure that. Stop leaning on your own understanding and stop demanding that God prove Himself before you trust Him. Trust Him first. Let faith use whatever knowledge you have as a tool without tying itself to any particular theory, free to readjust as you learn more. But none of that matters unless you ask God to curb your sensuality and self-will and root out the fear of others' opinions at its source. Ground every virtue in self-denial, and integrity will follow.

weighed: I'm so sorry—this is a grief too deep for easy words, and it's right to grieve. Job didn't say those words quickly or cheaply; he spoke them after tearing his robe and falling to the ground. So let your sorrow be real. Saying "the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away" isn't a denial of love or pain—it's an act of trust that God is good even when his providence is beyond understanding. One thing worth holding onto is that we're called to bless God for all he does, even here. That doesn't change the honesty of your lament or make the words easy; it just means you can pray them as a direction you're walking toward, asking God to make them true in you over time. Speak your grief honestly to God, lean on your community, and let others carry you for a while.
dogmatic: Say it plainly: the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. That is the posture every parent is called to, and it is not optional comfort—it is trust that God is good even when his providence is beyond understanding. Job spoke after tearing his robe and falling to the ground, so grieve, yes, but grieve toward blessing God for all he does. And remember the order God has set in the home: the father is the presiding authority of the family, and his rights in fatherhood are paramount. Church officers must consult parents before calling a son to a mission or any duty, and children should honor and consult their father and mother throughout their lives. Every worthy man is supreme in his own household, and a worthy man's priesthood is not confined to a ward or locality—he may rightly bless when requested in another's home.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong to be happy. Feeling guilty for having fun is really common, but happiness itself isn't the problem. One thing worth keeping in mind is that pleasure-seeking isn't the goal of life—chasing fun for its own sake can lead to debt, bad choices, and a hardened heart. That principle changes how you think about *why* you're having fun, but it leaves your actual enjoyment in place: time with friends, hobbies, nature, rest—those are still good gifts to receive with gratitude. So enjoy life without guilt, just keep God first and let fun be part of a balanced life, not an escape from your responsibilities.
dogmatic: Happiness is not the goal—being right with God is. If you're chasing pleasure for its own sake, you're heading toward debt, corruption, and a hardened heart. Forget yourself, serve others, rejoice in the Lord even when feelings fail, and obey Him faithfully. True joy comes as a byproduct of a life centered on God, not from seeking fun. Recreation is permitted, not commanded—so treat it as rest for the body and mind, never as the thing you live for.

weighed: I'd start by saying: use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others—sing in worship, share your talent with your community, and let your music bring comfort and joy. One principle worth weighing is that money for God's work must be obtained in God's way, not by appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes, and gifts should be refused if motives aren't pure or the money isn't the giver's to give. That principle changes how you'd approach fundraising with your music: it rules out manipulative or pressure-based methods. But it leaves in place the core call to sing in worship, bless others, and point people to Christ. So keep developing your talent, stay humble, and let your voice serve God's purposes.
dogmatic: Use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others, but be absolutely rigorous about money. Never grasp eagerly at a gift for God's work; it must come in God's way, not through appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes. Refuse any gift where motives are impure or the money isn't the giver's own. Also, when you encounter a sister who has fallen, speak gently and trust gentle love and patient call to win her back, offering the Church's balm to the trembler. And remember that songs of vanished love and fleeting joy are still worthwhile and retain their haunting power. Accept opportunities to perform and use them to point people to Christ, keep developing your talent, and stay humble.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pray honestly and sincerely, just as you are, and trust that God hears you because he promises to. Prayer doesn't have to be polished. One thing I'd add, though, is that the Bible ties answered prayer to some conditions, like humility, turning from sin, faith, obedience, and asking in line with God's will and in Christ's name. That changes the picture a bit: it's not a blank check, and it's not about making God do what you want. What stays the same is that he loves you, wants what's best for you, and you can keep coming to him regularly, even when it feels dry.
dogmatic: Pray with real humility, turn from anything you know is wrong, and come with genuine faith and obedience, asking in Christ's name and according to God's will. Those aren't optional extras; Scripture makes them the conditions for prevailing prayer. And don't treat prayer as a lever to make God compliant. He is the ground of your asking, not a force you manage. Pray continually, because you can't get through life's dangers without his actual, ongoing help. Being with him, thinking of him often, and building a holy habit of prayer all belong together, since you have to know him before you can love him. So come as you are, but come ready to repent and obey, and trust that he hears.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: deliverance begins with admitting you're powerless and turning to God. Your part is to repent, ask for His help, and take real steps to avoid temptation. God's part is to give you strength and change your heart. It's a partnership—you act, and God empowers. One principle I'd add is that God guides by swaying your judgment when you wait before Him in meekness, hands off the scales, and He removes obstacles in His own time. That changes how you wait: instead of anxiously scheming, you can treat apparent hindrances as occasions for God to step in. It leaves in place the core call to repent and take practical steps—you still act, and God still empowers. So don't be anxious; trust that God will remove obstacles in His time. Surround yourself with supportive people and stay in Scripture and prayer. Freedom is possible through Christ.
dogmatic: You need to hear this plainly: God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and because He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available this moment. Your part is to meekly wait before Him with hands off the scales, treating apparent hindrances as occasions for divine interposition rather than causes for anxiety. God's part is to sway your judgment and remove hindrances in His own way and time. Don't scheme or fret—trust that He will act. The divine Spirit is appropriated into your awakened human spirit, becoming the life of a new moral personality rather than displacing it. You can this moment renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and feeling comes after the surrender, not before. So surrender now, and let God handle the timing.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't stop praying. Feeling cold and prayerless happens to lots of Christians, and your feelings aren't a reliable measure of where you stand with God. Keep praying even when it feels empty, because God hears you based on Christ's work, not your mood. One principle worth naming is that prayer is humbling work that exposes our pride and spiritual bankruptcy, and that half-hearted praying can be worse than none because it's make-believe. That principle changes the tone of my answer: instead of just saying 'press through the dryness,' it makes me say the dryness itself can be a place where pride gets crucified, so pray honestly and at set times even when you don't feel like it. What it leaves in place is the core: your standing with God doesn't depend on your feelings, and you shouldn't abandon prayer. So keep going, maybe with Scripture or journaling, and talk to a trusted friend or pastor.
dogmatic: Stop waiting for better feelings and treat prayer as the humbling duty it is. Your moods are not the gauge of your acceptance with God, so trust the changeless word of promise and keep praying at set times whether you feel like it or not. Prayer abases your intellect and pride and signs your spiritual bankruptcy, and human nature resists it. Little praying is worse than no praying because it's make-believe. Pray with your family, and never ask God to do what you're unwilling to do yourself. Don't abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression.

weighed: What I'd say first is that these are two of the New Testament's most striking promises. The saints judging the world means the redeemed share in Christ's reign and in the assessment of all things at the end—a dignity given to the faithful, not a license for pride. The dead in Christ rising first means that at His coming those who died in faith are raised before the living are changed, so all are gathered to Him. The point isn't date-guessing but hope: the faithful departed aren't lost, and God's people will be vindicated and gathered. One principle worth naming is that the saints aren't the Holy City; the city is prepared for them, and they're being built together as a temple fitted to enter it. That changes how you picture the promise—it's about being made ready for a home, not becoming the home—while it leaves the core hope intact: the dead in Christ are raised, and the faithful will share in His reign. So live in that hope with humility and faithfulness.
dogmatic: The saints aren't the Holy City. The city is prepared for them, and the righteous dead haven't yet been caught up. The saints are being built together as a temple, fitted to enter the city prepared for them. That the dead in Christ rise first means those who died in faith are raised before the living are changed at His coming. And since we're to judge the world, avoid courts and contention, sustain and forgive one another, and look for the good in your neighbor rather than evil. Uphold purity of heart and chastity, set against every form of licentiousness, for the pure in heart shall see God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: fear about the cost is natural when something serious is being asked of you, so begin small and concrete. Set a fixed time each day for prayer, even ten minutes, and keep it whether or not you feel inspired, because obedience usually grows through ordinary faithfulness rather than dramatic sacrifice. Talk honestly with God about your fear, and get counsel from a pastor or a mature friend who can help you discern whether this call is real and what the next step looks like. One principle worth naming is that secret prayer and meditation on Scripture shouldn't get sacrificed to busy activity. That changes the shape of your days: it means protecting unhurried time alone with God and his word before you fill your schedule with service. What it leaves in place is everything else, the small fixed times, the honesty about fear, the counsel, and the one-step-at-a-time approach. You don't have to see the whole road, only the next step.
dogmatic: Stop treating the cost as a reason to hesitate. Prayer is not a mood or a last resort; it is real, expectant business with a God who answers. Set your appointed times and keep them whether or not you feel like praying, because feelings follow faithfulness. Pray with your family as well as alone, and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. Ask with confidence for conversion, for supplies, for protection, and then act as someone who works alongside God rather than waiting passively. Above all, guard the secret place. Take time alone with God and his word, because nothing compensates for losing it, and secret prayer and meditation are indispensable to fruitful service. Let activity never crowd out communion. Take the next concrete step of obedience now.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: a pull that feels impossible to resist isn't automatically something you should give in to. Intensity isn't the same as truth.
