So before deciding anything, get specific about what's pulling you, and notice whether it moves you toward patience, honesty, and care for others or away from them. One principle worth holding onto here is that God won't let you be tempted beyond your strength and always provides a way through, and that enduring temptation patiently is what counts. That changes the tone of the question: it's less about whether to stop resisting and more about resisting gently and steadily, without white-knuckling it or endlessly analyzing yourself. What it leaves in place is the rest of my first answer: don't decide today, talk to someone wise and trustworthy, and keep your ordinary routines, rest, and prayer steady so time can show you what this pull really is.
dogmatic: No, you shouldn't stop resisting. A pull that feels irresistible proves nothing except that it's strong, and strength is not truth. Error of every kind is opposed to Life and has no real power over you, so resist it firmly and it will flee. God doesn't tempt anyone, and he won't let you be tempted beyond what you can bear; with every temptation he provides a way out, and temptation endured patiently is crowned with life. So don't tolerate it, don't bargain with it, and don't sit around dissecting your motives. A quiet refusal repeated a few times a day is enough. Turn away from the thought, refuse the small yes, and go back to your duties, your rest, and your prayer. If it keeps pressing, get wise counsel and keep resisting to the end.

weighed: I'd start by saying: God is with you right in the middle of the noise, so don't wait for perfect silence. Look for small moments—while washing dishes or folding laundry, breathe a prayer. Make a quiet corner if you can, put a verse on the fridge, play a worship song, and involve your family in brief devotions. One principle that fits here is that secret prayer and meditation on God's word shouldn't be sacrificed to busy activity. That changes things by making sure you still carve out time to be alone with God, even if it's short and imperfect. It leaves in place the idea that God meets you in the mess and that little moments of turning your heart toward Him throughout the day really matter.
dogmatic: You need to recognize that your place in this household is from God, so fill it faithfully and sweetly, like a small screw in a great machine. Don't fight the chaos or try to escape it. When temptation or irritation arises, don't answer it or even appear to hear it—just prostrate yourself before God and stay at His feet while the noise swirls around you. And you must insist on taking time to be alone with God and His word. Secret prayer and meditation are indispensable; don't let activity crowd out communion. The worker for God must first be a worker with God. In the small, loving service of your home, you please Him right where He has set you, and His presence becomes your constant reality.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: live with intention, since the kingdom is near. Build habits of prayer, generosity, and integrity, take responsibility for your growth, mend relationships, and stay awake to what matters rather than passively waiting. One principle worth naming is that unless you become like a little child, hanging on Christ for everything, you can't enter the kingdom. That changes the footing of everything I just said: the habits and goals stop being a project you pull off and become a way of depending on him, so your effort rests on his grace instead of your willpower. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of the life: prayer, generosity, integrity, mending what's broken, using your gifts for others. You still act decisively; you just act as a child holding on, not as someone building a résumé.
dogmatic: Become like a little child and hang on Christ for all things, because that is the only way in. Don't treat the kingdom as a self-improvement plan where you set goals and shape a life worthy of your calling; that puts you at the center. Depend on him as the source of every good thing, seek first God's will and glory rather than your own blessing, and even claim his promises for him, not for yourself, trusting that everything else gets added and never comes first. And don't expect the kingdom without judgment: God judges evil, present struggles sit under the control of the one on the throne, and he works through those judgments toward making all things new. So watch, repent, and trust his sovereign hand, knowing he will finish the work of renewing all things.

weighed: I'd start by saying that Christian faith has always been tied to real claims about who Christ is—truly God and truly man, crucified and risen—so rejecting many traditional doctrines isn't just a style choice; it touches the substance of the faith. But honest people do wrestle with this, and the real question is whether you're engaging those doctrines to understand them more deeply or setting them aside without examination. One principle that matters here is that Christian doctrine, especially about the Logos and Trinity, is the Church's attempt to express the unique value of Christ, and it needs re-interpretation and development—the old expressions aren't worthless. That changes how you might hold your objections: you can treat the tradition as something to dig into and reinterpret rather than something to toss out. What it leaves in place is that the great verities still matter; toleration in the Church is about methods of work, not indifference to doctrine. So talk with a thoughtful pastor or theologian, read the classic texts charitably, and be patient with yourself.
dogmatic: No—if you reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ, you're not simply expressing a different spirituality; you're questioning the substance of the faith. Christian faith has always been bound up with claims about who Christ is: truly God and truly man, crucified and risen. Doctrine isn't a magic formula, but it isn't disposable either. The Church's teaching on the Logos and Trinity is its attempt to express the unique value of Christ, and that teaching requires re-interpretation and development—the old expressions are not valueless. So don't discard them; give them the maximum of meaning and let them be further developed. Remember that theology progresses in our apprehension of unchanging facts, not in the facts themselves, and a complete system is impossible this side of heaven. But toleration in the Church concerns methods of work, not matters of doctrine—there's room for many kinds of workers, not indifference to the great verities. Hold firmly to those verities, and don't reject a doctrine merely because you can't rationally demonstrate it.

weighed: What I'd say first is that this looks like a daily rhythm of prayer, obedience, gratitude, Scripture, serving your family and church, and quick confession when you fail—not perfection, just a steady direction toward Him. One principle worth naming is that Christ in you is your hope of glory, your purity, grace, and strength. That changes the center of gravity: instead of white-knuckling your own goodness, you rest in His indwelling life and let Him live through you. It leaves in place the practical habits—prayer, obedience, service, confession—but reframes them as abiding rather than striving, so the day-by-day shape stays the same while the engine becomes Him in you.
dogmatic: Day by day, this means abiding in Christ and knowing Him as your purity, grace, and strength—not you trying harder, but 'Not I, but Christ' living in you. Make the cross of Christ your constant theme and sole ground of glory: Jesus tasted death for you, in time and in eternity. Let that be the one thing you boast in. And don't expect full rest now—longing and seeking are your common work until fulfillment in Heaven, and that holy discontent keeps you pressing on, trusting He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Christ.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: set fixed times of prayer—morning, evening, before meals—and protect them, then carry a short prayer or a single word through the day, returning to it whenever you notice you've drifted. Offer ordinary tasks with attention and gratitude, keep a simple journal, and review it weekly. One principle worth adding is that prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress—asking God to help you search out and reform what's amiss in your heart. That shifts the emphasis from building a habit to letting prayer do interior work, but it leaves the structure in place: fixed times, short aspirations, ordinary tasks offered, patience over months.
dogmatic: Make prayer the one great central secret of holy living and serving—the cornerstone your whole life is built on, the first resort in every matter, great or small. On your knees, in secret and with other believers, begin by asking God to enable you to search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. Don't treat prayer as an occasional verbal exercise; it's the constant drawing in of heavenly life, like breathing or feeding—the air by which the divine seed within you is nourished from without. So let your whole day be one continual turning and drawing in, and let God search and reform your heart as the unbroken life grows.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: you're both, and you're neither—you're the one who chooses, and your identity gets shaped by what you do with those desires. One candidate idea sharpens that: we have two wills, the natural will to live that seeks comfort and never finds peace, and the will to love and gladly please God, which is the only will by which we truly live. That changes the stakes—it's not just two appetites to balance, one of them has to die so the other can live. But it leaves your question intact: you're still the one who has to surrender the natural will and nurture the other, and God's grace still meets you in that struggle.
dogmatic: You are not two equal selves. One is the natural will to live—your comfort, your security—and it must be broken and bruised until it dies. The other is the will to love and gladly please God, and that is the only will by which you truly live. So stop asking which one you are and let the natural will die; live by the will to love God. This isn't choosing which appetite to feed, it's a death and a resurrection. And know this: your search for God is matched by God's search for you—He spares no cost to bring you into fellowship. God and man are conjunct, mutually organic; your personality is formed only in fellowship with Him, His life opening into yours and yours into His. In Christ, you die to self and live to God.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: give your best hours to Scripture and sound theology, and let that study feed your own walk with God. One principle worth naming is that theology is the favorite study of the elders, and they should become profound theologians while also learning every branch of science. That changes the scope of your study—it tells you not to narrow your reading to Bible and doctrine alone, but to take seriously history, science, and the wider world as fields where truth belongs to God. What it leaves in place is the priority: Scripture and theology stay central, and your study still has to fuel devotion and pastoral care, not just fill your head.
dogmatic: Give your best hours to theology, and don't apologize for it. The elders' favorite study is theology, and every elder should become a profound theologian—so let that be your aim, not a sideline. Study the letter and imbibe the spirit; adhere to the divine Principle and follow the behests of God, abiding steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, and you will progress most rapidly. Learn every branch of science too, since all truth serves the gospel, but keep theology at the center. Bring a disciplined mind, an intuitional habit of mind, acquaintance with science, knowledge of the biblical languages, holy affection, and the enlightening influence of the Holy Spirit to the task. That is the study that makes a minister.

weighed: I'd start with something small and doable. Pick one area—sleep, honesty, or a relationship—and set a change you can actually keep this week. Build a routine around it, tell one trusted person who can check in, and clear out the cues that pull you back. Expect setbacks; they're normal, so treat them as information and begin again. One principle here says to prepare to live, not just to die, and to teach children early about health and strength. That principle shifts the focus from just avoiding old patterns to actively building a life—so it adds a forward-looking, long-term view. But it doesn't replace the practical steps: you still need small, concrete changes and a support person. It leaves the core advice in place.
dogmatic: The first thing is to deny that a relapse can really happen—there's only one Mind, so meet the cause mentally and courageously. Conquer your fears instead of managing them. Victory over lower passions isn't won by willpower or common-sense discipline; it's a Living Power transforming you from fleshly to spiritual, teaching you higher pleasures. Cooperate with that Power: choose one area, keep a change this week, tell one trusted person. And teach the young early to lay a foundation of health and strength, so longevity may return. When the old pull appears, refuse it with a clear mind and begin again at once if you stumble.

weighed: My first answer would be: no, God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned. You chose it, and you're still responsible. God permits and overrules evil without being its author, so the decree isn't an excuse and it isn't fate either. One principle worth naming here is that God's commands always imply promises, so the call to walk worthy of the Lord isn't held out unless grace can actually realize it. That changes the tone of the answer: instead of only saying "you're guilty, repent," it says the power to turn is available right now, and feeling follows surrender rather than coming first. What it leaves in place is the main point: your choice was real, your guilt is real, and you still need to confess and turn. So don't wait to feel more before you renounce it, and don't despair as if your sin were fixed fate.
dogmatic: No, God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned. You chose, and you remain responsible, and God permits and overrules evil without being its author. But hear this: God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and where He commands, He promises the power to obey. The ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not set before you unless it can be realized by grace. So stop waiting to feel more, weep more, or receive greater power first. This moment you can renounce sin in will and purpose; God supplies the strength, and the feeling comes after the surrender, not before it. Sin is real, and it had to be suffered to rise, but it is not final: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Renounce it now in will and purpose and trust the God who commands your holiness to supply what He commands.

weighed: I'd start by saying that love grows through knowing God and practicing it—spending time in Scripture and prayer, recalling his mercies with thanks, serving others, and asking him to change your heart. Feelings often follow faithful obedience, so duty isn't the enemy; it can become the channel. One idea worth weighing is that the way into adoring God isn't begging him to come down and make you feel something, but steadily entering into his estate and offering him love. That shifts the focus from waiting on an emotion to actively giving love as an offering. It leaves in place the practical habits—Scripture, prayer, gratitude, service—and the patience that affection often deepens over time.
dogmatic: Stop begging God to come down and make you feel affection. That's the wrong entry point. The way into adoration is to constantly endeavor to enter up into his estate and offer him love. Learn who he is in Scripture and prayer as one ascending to offer. His love isn't mere sentiment or a bargain; it's rational, voluntary self-communication that seeks your true good, regulated by and subordinate to holiness—so it wills your good, not merely your comfort. Then let love be the outgoing of your entire nature in self-sacrificing service, because that is the supreme proof of the reality of your Christian profession. Recall his mercies, thank him specifically, serve others at cost. Duty done steadily as an offering becomes the channel through which love grows. Keep showing up and offering, and affection deepens in time.

weighed: I'd have said first: feeling glad when someone who hurt you falls is a very human reaction, but it's worth looking at. Love doesn't delight in another's downfall; it grieves even over an enemy's harm. That gladness may show the wound is still raw and forgiveness is unfinished. It doesn't make you a hypocrite—it makes you honest. Bring it to God and name it plainly. Ask for a heart that wants your enemy's good, and pray for them, even briefly and reluctantly. Over time, prayer reshapes what you want. Forgiveness is usually a process, and growth in love shows in what you begin to want for the other person. One principle I'd weigh is that love believes all things and covers imperfections—as God doesn't see iniquity in His people, so we should be gentle with others' faults. That principle changes the tone: it adds a call to gentleness and to cover faults rather than expose them, which softens how you look at your enemy's failure. But it leaves in place the honest diagnosis: your gladness still points to a raw wound and unfinished forgiveness, and the core direction—praying for their good—stays the same.
dogmatic: Gladness at an enemy's fall is common, but love does not delight in another's downfall. Love is not blind; it abounds in full knowledge and all discernment, so you can tell the difference between what is good and what is better. Examine your gladness honestly—it may show the wound is still raw and forgiveness unfinished. Bring it to God, name it plainly, and ask for a heart that wants your enemy's true good. Remember that love is never without pity, and that Christ alone keeps the charge when we fall; for reverence and kindness, turn hastily and do not leave Him alone. Do not be eager to see or expose another's faults. Believe all things, clothe others with the graces faith can claim for them, and be gentle with their imperfections as God is with ours.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: chasing signs can turn into a distraction fast, especially when it becomes date-setting or guesswork, and Jesus warned against trying to calculate times. The better focus is living faithfully now, loving God and neighbor, growing in character, staying ready in heart. One idea worth weighing is that Christ's return will be literal and personal, as real as the events of the first advent. That changes the tone of watchfulness: it's not about decoding the news, it's about trusting a promise that will actually happen. What it leaves in place is my main point, that the healthy posture is faithful living now rather than obsessive sign-hunting.
dogmatic: Christ will literally and personally come again in the clouds, just as he literally ascended, and any spiritualizing that shrinks his coming to an inward experience clouds the whole thing and leaves believers with no tangible ground to stand on. So yes, watch for the signs he gave, not as idle speculation but as confirmation that the promise is real. But don't put off finding Christ to some later comfort. If you don't find him here, when you cast off the flesh you enter a bewildering, terrible solitude, aware of nothing but yourself, blind, without the light of this world or the light of Christ. The remedy has to be found now. Look to heaven for aid rather than trusting in the size of your own host, and the King of angels gives the victory.

weighed: I'd start with what I actually think: fear of suffering is natural, and avoiding it is a sensible instinct, so the goal isn't to stop caring but to face it in manageable pieces when it comes. Acknowledge the pain honestly, lean on steady routines and people you trust, deal with what's in front of you today, and accept help. One principle worth naming is that fear must be overcome for healing to be realized, that perfect Love casts out fear. That changes the inner posture—you don't have to let dread run the show, and trust can steady you before and during hard times. What it leaves in place is the reality of the pain itself and the practical steps: it doesn't erase grief, the need for support, or the wisdom of not pretending nothing hurts. So let trust calm you, but still take the day in small pieces and let others help.
dogmatic: The core thing to see is that suffering is a mental condition, and fear is what gives it power. When something happens, don't rehearse the symptoms or picture harm; declare that you are not hurt and understand why, because the effect follows your fidelity to that truth. Fear causes disease, and dwelling on danger or describing illness only frightens you into it, while changing your thought restores health. Perfect Love casts out fear, so let trust in God's allness govern you and refuse the belief that man is hurt. Man is God's image, whole and free, untouched by matter, and nothing can separate him from divine care. Abide in that, and dread dissolves before the healing appears.

weighed: My first answer would be that wealth and the beauty of the field are both temporary—gold rusts, fields wither, and you can't carry any of it past the grave. So hold it loosely and put your heart into what lasts. One idea worth weighing is that hoarded wealth brings leanness of soul and darkness of mind, and that property is meant to be used, not salted down. That sharpens my answer: it's not just that things fade, but that keeping them unused damages you now. What it leaves in place is the main point—creation is good but not ultimate, so enjoy the field and use wealth responsibly without setting your heart on it.
dogmatic: Wealth isn't the problem—the earth is full of wheat, meat, wool, and everything you need, and it's your job to mold it to your wants through knowledge and labor. There's enough for everyone if you stop contending over it. But hoarding is poison: riches kept unused bring leanness of soul and darkness of mind, and the heart that trusts in abundance doesn't just go soft—it turns tiger, strengthening itself in active wickedness. So put every dollar and every ability to work for the good of the community. When this world passes away, what passes is your misuse of God's provision, not the provision itself.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to weigh shared values, emotional compatibility, attraction, and financial stability, and to treat godliness as a nice bonus if it fits your beliefs. But one principle I'd want to name is that marriage should be entered upon prayerfully, with true godliness as the absolutely needful qualification, and with calm weighing of suitableness rather than being prompted by beauty, age, money, or mental powers. That changes the order: godliness moves from bonus to foundation, and the other factors get weighed calmly instead of driving the choice. It leaves in place the practical work of knowing someone, observing how they handle conflict, and discussing expectations openly. So I'd still say take time and be honest about compatibility, but make godliness the first thing you look for, not the last.
dogmatic: True godliness is the first and absolutely needful qualification; without it, no beauty, wealth, or brilliance can make a marriage right. Begin with prayerful waiting on God for guidance, and understand marriage as a serious vocation with sacred duties, not merely a means to private happiness. Its end is the mutual enrichment of personality and mutual freedom to fulfil the true ideal of human life. Make no terms with lax views of divorce. Commend mutual tender love and the bearing of each other's faults, for forbearance is the daily bread of marriage. Beware of making marriage a matter of traffic or a money job; a union formed for gain is no true marriage. Make godliness the foundation, let love and forbearance be its walls, and let the rest be weighed in calm, prayerful judgment.

weighed: I'd start by being honest: I don't know why God spared me and not them, and I won't pretend to explain it. I'd avoid any hint that I was more deserving, acknowledge the grief, and point to Christ who shares our death and promises resurrection. One principle that fits here is that a true convert holds nothing back and asks, 'Lord, what will you have me to do?' That adds a posture of open-handed surrender and gratitude, but it doesn't fill in the mystery or give you a reason for who lived and who died. So you can say you don't know, grieve with them, and let your life answer too.
dogmatic: Don't soften it with 'I don't know' and leave it there. The real answer is that you were spared so you could be given entirely to God, with no secret exception held back, asking, 'Lord, what will you have me to do?' And don't stop at the minimum you owe to save your soul. Look at Christ mocked, scourged, crowned with thorns, and dying for your sins, and ask what sacrifices you can make out of gratitude. Your spared life is meant to be that offering, not an explanation.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's good you recognize the pattern. Lasting love usually begins with knowing yourself and choosing relationships slowly, with honesty and shared values. Look for people who are consistent, kind, and willing to grow. Set boundaries, communicate clearly, and don't expect any human relationship to be perfect; every love has flaws and requires patience. Community, service, and faith can also give your life a stable center so you're not desperate for affection. Give it time, and let trust build through small faithful acts rather than grand gestures. One principle here is that true love is never weak or unconcerned about the character of the beloved; it's intense love that wields the rod, and it's superficial to set up a schism between love and justice. That principle changes how you might think about patience and boundaries—it says love isn't just tolerant but actively cares about who someone is becoming, so you can be honest and even corrective without seeing that as unloving. What it leaves in place is the core advice: know yourself, choose slowly, build trust through small acts, and don't expect perfection. So you still do the slow, grounded work, but you hold it together with a love that's serious about character.
dogmatic: Do not settle for a love that merely tolerates flaws; aspire constantly to the perfection of holy love. True love is strong and concerned with character: it corrects, purifies, and refines, and in God justice and mercy are one. Yet love cannot rest until it has sounded all the depths and learnt the perfections of its Beloved and become one with Him. It suffers nothing to intervene between itself and God, springing forward and finding no peace till it has overcome every obstacle and reached the Beloved, for love is strong as death and carries the lover out of himself into the heart of the beloved. Seek first that love; let every human affection be ordered toward it, and no lesser love will finally satisfy you.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: readiness is a life turned toward God—prayer, repentance, love of neighbor, and faithfulness in small things. Keep your conscience clear, lean on grace, and let hope shape your choices, because the city comes as a gift, not something you earn. One idea worth weighing is that the opened heavens are a real place, the gate of heaven where the cherubim and flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life, and that the city will come down from there. That adds a vivid sense of a real doorway and a real guard, but it doesn't replace the everyday practices—it just gives them a setting. So you still pray, repent, love, and trust; you just do it with your eyes on that gate.
dogmatic: You need to see that the opened heavens are a literal place—the gate of heaven, where the cherubim and the flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life—and that the Holy City will descend from there. God will roar out of Zion and utter His voice from Jerusalem, shaking the heavens and the earth; then Jerusalem will be holy and the sign of the Son of man will appear. So don't be tossed around by every new teaching or go looking for Christ here and there. Come into God's rest now: a settled conviction of the truth, freedom from doubt and fear, and a refusal to chase every fresh claim. That is how you get ready—settle it, stand at the gate, and stop wavering.

weighed: Start by noticing when your mind drifts, then gently bring it back to God without beating yourself up. Set aside a daily time of prayer and Scripture, cut down on the obvious distractions like screens, news, and clutter, and let gratitude for good earthly things keep them from becoming your center. Memorize a verse you can call on when you drift, and look over your week to see what pulls you most so you can adjust. Repeated turning builds a habit, and your affections gradually shift upward—be patient, this is a lifelong practice. One idea worth adding: keep your heart occupied with God as the one you love rather than turning back to inspect yourself. That changes the tone of the drifting—instead of monitoring your performance, you're turning toward someone. It leaves your practical steps in place, but it makes the daily prayer and the cutting of distractions a way of being with Him rather than a scorecard.
dogmatic: The aim isn't to watch yourself but to be occupied with God, the object of your love. Live in the atmosphere of Christ's love: believe that He ever loves you, and claim His sweet approval and tender regard. When your mind drifts, don't examine the drift; turn to Him and delight in pleasing Him above any pleasure in your own performance. This calls for deep recollection: keep 'God and I' as the only objects of thought, and avoid unnecessary intercourse with the outside world—unnecessary conversation, screens, news, and clutter—so your attention is free for Him. Keep your daily time of prayer and Scripture, not to grade yourself but to be with Him, and let gratitude for earthly good rise to the Giver. The more your heart rests in His love, the less the things of earth pull, because you are occupied with a greater and loving object.

weighed: My first answer would be that the Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it still speaks to modern people. It says God isn't a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship sit at the heart of reality, which resonates in a world that values connection. You don't need to fully understand it to find it fruitful; it's a mystery to be lived more than solved. One idea that sharpens this is that the Persons express mutual inclusion, not mutual exclusion, so wherever the Spirit comes, He brings the Son and the Father. That changes the picture from three separate figures to one shared life, and it leaves in place the core claim that God is love and that the doctrine can still mean something today.
dogmatic: The Trinity isn't a meaningless formula, and it isn't a riddle to shrug off either. It's inscrutable but not self-contradictory, and it's the necessary complement to what we say about God's attributes, giving God an eternal object of knowledge, love, and will within Himself. The Persons aren't three separate individuals like three Gods; they express mutual inclusion, so wherever the Spirit comes He brings the Son and the Father. Christian doctrine is the Church's reflection on the unique value of Christ, and it calls for the maximum of meaning and further development, not discard. So approach it prayerfully and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.

weighed: I'd start by saying your doubt is understandable and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Don't wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins. One principle that speaks to your doubt is that God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and since He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available right now—the feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. That changes the timing: you don't have to wait for a better feeling or greater strength before you act. But it leaves in place the lifelong process and the need for patience and community; it doesn't promise instant perfection or remove the slow work of growth.
dogmatic: Your doubt is misplaced. God commands you to repent now, and because He commands it, the power to renounce sin is available this very moment. Stop waiting for a better feeling or greater strength. The feeling follows the surrender, not the other way around. Do not languish over the number and magnitude of your sins. All is possible to God, and it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one. Of yourself you cannot even think what is right; all comes to you from God. With Jesus, affirm that God is the Life of man: individualized existence is restored, not lost in death, which is only a seeming vanishing that Truth restores. So pray, obey, and trust that He will complete what He begins. Your doubt is not humility—it is a refusal to accept the power God offers you right now.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: waiting on God is trust, not sitting still. Forcing change usually comes out of anxiety and self-will, and patience lets God work in his timing while you pray, obey what's already clear, and keep your hands open. One idea worth adding is that the Lord's work should be done in the way, at the time, and with the people he appoints, so you wait for his signal before you take a step. That sharpens things: it makes you slower to launch out and more careful about who you partner with, and it keeps the active side of waiting, the praying and obeying, right where it was.
dogmatic: Waiting on the Lord starts with wanting no will of your own. Be slow to take new steps, and don't assume a strong desire or an open door means it's faith. Bring every step to God in prayer and test it by his Word, then wait for the Master's signal in the time, the way, and the people of his work, taking the helpers he gives rather than the ones you'd pick. And don't despise just being present before him. Like a statue set in the King's palace for his pleasure, stay before God content to wait on his will even when you can do nothing. Prayer isn't measured by what it produces but by devotion. When he signals, move with patient, believing expectation; until then, stay.

weighed: I'd start by saying your peace is worth taking seriously, and there's nothing wrong with enjoying a settled life. But I'd ask what your peace is actually resting on, and whether there's a longing in you that the world's goods can't finally satisfy. One idea that shapes how I'd put this: we're not isolated selves who just happen to need God alongside us. Human personality is formed in fellowship, and God's life opens into ours as ours opens into his. That changes the picture from "why would I need God" to "what am I made for"—but it leaves your peace in place as something real and good, not an illusion to be dismissed.
dogmatic: Your peace is real, but it's a truce, not a homecoming. You were not made to be a self-sufficient unit; personality itself is impossible in isolation, and God needs us as we need him. So the question isn't whether you need God—you do, whether you feel it or not. And don't come to him only when prosperity fails or sickness comes, as if one cry or a petulant demand could obtain his gifts. He asks steady, persistent desire. Ask what your peace rests on, and whether there's a longing in you that only fellowship with him can finally meet.

weighed: I'd start by saying that loving God equally in pain and pleasure begins with recognizing both as gifts from the same loving hand. In pleasure, receive with gratitude and let joy turn you toward the Giver. In pain, remember that God is near and that suffering can deepen trust and compassion. Practically, keep a steady rhythm of prayer, thanksgiving, and service regardless of how you feel. Don't measure your love by emotional highs or lows; measure it by faithfulness. One principle that fits here is that we should practice the presence of God not from the motive of pleasure but from a principle of love and because God would have us. That changes the focus from seeking good feelings to choosing love as the reason for your practice. It leaves in place the practical rhythm of prayer and service and the idea that both seasons can be offered to God.
dogmatic: Loving God equally in pain and pleasure means settling why you come to him: not for comfort or pleasure, but from love and because God wills it. Worldly pains and pleasures aren't comparable to spiritual ones, so don't weigh them against each other or bargain for relief. Be careful for nothing and fear nothing; desire only not to offend God. This is possible because God is not a distant sovereign sitting apart in ease: he is passible, grieved over sin, and his holiness requires and his love provides atonement. The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world expresses an eternal fact in God's nature. In pleasure, receive the gift and turn it into obedience; in pain, don't let it purchase your devotion. Keep a steady rhythm of prayer and service, and let blessedness—God's own joy—be the controlling element of your love.

weighed: I'd start by saying your fear makes sense—the past can feel like a weight that follows you. The Christian answer is that God offers forgiveness and a new beginning. When you confess your past to him, he doesn't hold it against you; he forgives and restores. That doesn't mean consequences vanish, but your identity is no longer finally determined by what you did. One principle that matters here is that the temporal and spiritual aren't separate—God has as much right to guide your everyday affairs as your inner life. That changes how practical this gets: it's not just a private spiritual transaction but something that touches your work, relationships, and daily choices. What it leaves in place is the core promise—God's forgiveness and the fact that your past doesn't have the final word on who you are.
dogmatic: Your past does not get to define you, because God himself steps between you and it. The temporal and the spiritual are not separate—with God nothing is merely temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct your work, your relationships, and your daily affairs as your inner life. So this is not a private feeling you manage alone; God's claim runs through every part of your life. The soul's flight is inward too—down the labyrinthine ways of your own mind—and God follows there as surely as through the years and the world. And the testimony of the Spirit of God in your heart exceeds all other evidence, bearing record of the living Redeemer. You are not dependent only on the history of your past for knowledge of him. Confess, receive forgiveness, and let his witness in you outweigh every other voice.

weighed: I hear that fear, and it makes sense. Giving yourself to God doesn't mean erasing who you are—it means finding your true self in relation to him. Start with small acts of trust, set healthy boundaries, and talk with a trusted pastor or spiritual director about what's genuinely yours to give. One principle that speaks to this is that God supplies all your need, often through unexpected and timely gifts from others, and that your extremity is his opportunity. That changes the picture of surrender: it's not you emptying yourself into a void but trusting a Provider who meets you in your need. It leaves in place your responsibility to discern and give freely—it doesn't erase your personality, gifts, or needs, and it doesn't ask you to skip the slow work of growing in trust.
dogmatic: Your fear assumes you have something of your own to lose. Of yourself you can attain to no good thing, and you have nothing to offer God that was not already his. So surrender cannot impoverish you—all you give was his gift first. When you forget God, and we all do, don't let that lapse disquiet you; let every lapse become a return with greater trust. God supplies all your need, often through unexpected and timely provision, and your extremity is his opportunity. Your one recourse is to turn to him in every occurrence in prayer—guilty, poor, needy beggars, weak and miserable, yet his children—with humble fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection.

weighed: I'd start where I usually do: distraction in prayer is normal, so don't panic. When images or fantasies show up, just notice them and gently bring your attention back to God, maybe with a short phrase or a line of Scripture as an anchor. It also helps to set things up beforehand—a quiet spot, fewer screens, a moment of stillness first. One principle I'd add here is the picture of coming to prayer like a beggar at a rich man's gate: you have nothing to offer and everything to receive. That changes the tone—it means when your mind wanders, you don't scold yourself or fight it; you just quietly bring it back, because the disquiet itself is what scatters you. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff: the quiet place, the anchor phrase, the gentle return. So the technique still matters, but it's no longer the point—the point is simply staying with God, calmly, like someone waiting at a door.
dogmatic: Prayer is humbling work, and that's exactly why it's hard. It abases your intellect and your pride and signs your spiritual bankruptcy—human nature resists it, and a little praying is worse than no praying because it's make-believe. So stop treating distraction as a technique problem to be managed. Come to prayer like a beggar at a rich man's gate: you have nothing to offer and everything to receive. Keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself—trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. Bring your will back in tranquility. And know this: you can't pray without being with him, can't be with him but by thinking of him often, and can't think of him often but by holy habit. You must know before you can love. So pray continually, ask for his actual and continual help, and stop imagining prayer should feel easy or naturally congenial. It isn't. Do it anyway.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, this is a legitimate and very common way to believe. Plenty of people are raised in a faith and then find that arguments—cosmological, teleological, moral—confirm what they already hold. Belief usually starts in nurture and community, and reason can come along afterward to examine and support it. What matters is that you don't just inherit it passively: test it, ask honest questions, let evidence and argument actually shape your conviction. If the arguments genuinely support your belief, that's a strength, not a weakness; if some of them fail, your faith doesn't have to collapse. So long as you're reflective and open to correction, being raised in belief and finding it confirmed by reason is entirely legitimate. One idea worth weighing is that belief in God isn't really the conclusion of a demonstration—religion existed before argument, and the proofs are more how faith expresses and confirms itself than how it gets created in the first place. That shifts things a bit: it means you shouldn't expect the arguments to carry the whole weight, and you shouldn't panic if they don't. What it leaves in place is the main point—keep testing, stay open to correction, and let the arguments do the confirming work they can do.
dogmatic: No—stop treating the arguments as if they were the foundation. Belief in God was never the conclusion of a demonstration. Religion existed long before anyone formulated a proof, and the proofs are simply the modes in which faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation; they do not create faith. The arguments are not a bridge reason can fully cross: both ends are wanting, since all logic already presupposes God, and finite premises can only yield a finite conclusion. Their real use is to awaken, explicate, and confirm a conviction that is the most fundamental of all. So don't fret about whether the arguments confirm what you were raised to hold—that is exactly what they are for. And don't imagine faith must clash with science: God organized the earth from existing matter, and evidence and demonstration remove ignorance and prejudice rather than threaten the truth. Rest your belief on that deeper ground, not on the proofs.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your frailty is real, and God doesn't overlook it. He promises to be with you and strengthen you, to carry you even to gray hairs. Dim sight and failing strength are an invitation to rest in Him, not to strive, and your worth before Him doesn't rest on vigor or eyesight. One of the principles you've raised adds something worth keeping: the calm old age of a pure conscience, and the hidden prayers of lowly saints holding up the world. That changes the tone—it says your quiet prayers are not idle but a real gift, and your remaining days have weight even when your body is weak. What it leaves in place is the promise itself: God's grace is sufficient, and your hope still rests in the life to come, where weakness and dimness pass away.
dogmatic: Hear this plainly: do not prepare to die—prepare to live. Teach the young in the morning of their days to lay a foundation of health, strength, and constitution, so that longevity may begin to return. The aged world has lost its mirth, but Youth must come joyously like the wind at morning, bringing freshness, strength, and radiance, keeping alive the hope of Spring. And do not despise your hidden place: the calm old age of a pure conscience and the hidden prayers of lowly saints uphold the proud world, which cannot sustain itself. So tend what strength remains, welcome the renewing spirit, and let your quiet prayers and clear conscience be your lasting gift.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: the Bible promises resurrection, judgment, and eternal life for those in Christ—passages like John 11:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 15 point to a transformed body, and Revelation speaks of a new heaven and new earth. The emphasis isn't on disembodied souls floating forever but on God renewing creation and raising the dead. Now, one candidate principle says that if God aims at an end not fully realized here, we have ground for postulating immortality—belief in a righteous God carries the idea of a future life. That principle changes the tone: it shifts the focus from death as an enemy to death as a door to a higher state, and it encourages comfort rather than despair for the righteous dead. But it leaves in place the concrete biblical hope—resurrection of the body, identity preserved, and God's promise to raise the dead. So the central promise stays clear: death is not the end for those who trust God.
dogmatic: There is no such thing as mortality, nor properly any mortal beings, because being is immortal like Deity, and being and Deity are inseparable. So the question of life after death is already answered in the nature of things: you cannot be separated from God, and your identity is preserved. Death is not an end but a door to a higher state—we should not mourn for the righteous dead. The Bible's promise is not about escaping death but about the resurrection of the body and the continuance of being that was never truly mortal. Immortality is a corollary of belief in a righteous God, not a mere wish. So rest in this: your being is immortal, and God's purpose for you is not exhausted by this life.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: caring about your community is a good sign, and the way forward is usually to look at your gifts, your passions, and the time you actually have, then find concrete needs nearby and serve in small, steady ways. One principle worth weighing here is that restlessness and ambition can multiply undertakings and burden you more than legitimate work does. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of just adding service, I'd say guard against piling on commitments out of anxiety, and let the plain duties already in front of you count. What it leaves in place is the rest—asking trusted people where you're useful, praying and reflecting without waiting for perfect certainty, setting limits so you don't burn out, and remembering you don't have to do everything, just your part.
dogmatic: Stop measuring yourself by how much you're doing and start with the truth that you have nothing in yourself to meet this need. Confess your insufficiency plainly—that conviction is the very condition for receiving God's all-sufficiency, and you must take hold of it with a faith that won't settle for less than all. Watch your prayers too: don't ask God for what you should do yourself with ordinary wisdom, and don't demand signs. Use the light you've already been given, and let your asking be for grace to do faithfully what's already in your hands. And be careful of curiosity, ambition, and restlessness—they multiply occupations and create more impediments than works. Limit yourself to legitimate employments, the plain duties before you, and refuse to add more out of anxiety.

weighed: Yes, I'd start where you're starting: unbelief may well be part of it, since Jesus often ties receiving God's gifts to faith, and doubt can shut a door He wants open. But don't turn that into self-condemnation—be honest with God about the fear, ask Him to help your unbelief, and then gather with others and pray expectantly, resting on His character rather than your feelings. One principle worth naming is that the Holy Ghost within enables us to detect and expel evil at the command of faith, though He won't do it when the will consents. That adds something real: when fear whispers that nothing will happen, you can refuse to agree with it and call on the Spirit instead of passively accepting the lie. What it leaves in place is everything I said first—faith matters, honesty about doubt matters, and gathering expectantly still matters. It doesn't turn the Spirit into a technique or make your mood the measure; it just gives you something to do with the fear itself.
dogmatic: Unbelief is the problem, and you need to deal with it as such. When fear says nothing will happen, that is a suggestion from the enemy, and you must not consent to it in your will—call on the indwelling Holy Ghost to expel every evil suggestion at the command of faith. Stop seeking power as your own possession; you have none of your own. Receive the Holy Spirit within and upon you, letting Him be the power that causes you to walk in God's statutes. Your spirit naturally loves truth and virtue, but it will be overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. So gather with others in expectant prayer as an act of obedience, ask in faith, and trust God to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

weighed: I'd first say that feeling dry in prayer doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. It's a common season, and feelings aren't a reliable measure of your spiritual state. Keep showing up, be patient with yourself, and don't assume God is displeased. One principle that adds something here is that feelings aren't the gauge of your acceptance with God—you should trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods. That changes the focus from self-judgment to resting on God's promise, but it leaves in place the practical advice to keep praying simply and care for yourself. So you can keep the original reassurance and also lean on God's word when your feelings are numb.
dogmatic: Feeling dry doesn't mean you're doing something wrong, but don't measure your standing by feeling. Feelings are variable and never accurately gauge your real assimilation to God; the changeless word of promise is your ground. Continue steadfastly in prayer even when joy is lacking, and don't abandon communion or service because of spiritual depression. Understand prayer not as an occasional verbal exercise but as the constant drawing in of the heavenly life—like feeding or the unconscious drawing in of air—by which the life from without nourishes the heavenly seed within. Yet refuse complacent security: let the burden for perishing souls drive you to prayer and obedience, since multitudes still perish for lack of knowledge. Let dryness send you, not inward to self-pity, but outward to intercede and serve.

weighed: My first answer would be to tie short prayers to daily routines—morning, meals, commutes, bedtime—and use reminders to build awareness over time. One principle that sharpens this is that we can't think of God often without a holy habit, and we can't love what we don't know, so knowing Him through Scripture feeds the conversation. That changes the starting point: instead of just adding prayer slots, you let what you're learning about God spill into the day. It leaves in place the practical scaffolding—routines, reminders, small consistent steps—because habit still needs repetition.
dogmatic: You can't pray continually without being with God, and you can't be with Him without thinking of Him often, and that takes a holy habit. So don't just tack prayers onto your schedule—make knowing God in Scripture the fuel, because you must know before you can love. Learn from the holy pastors: they made retirement and a life of prayer their apprenticeship, then carried God always present in their work, setting apart intervals by day and much of the night in silence. God is always near; it would be rude to leave a friend alone who came to visit. So adore Him continually—in business and even in diversions—and never neglect Him.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, Christianity has developed a lot over the centuries, and that's a sign of something alive, not something on its way out. The core has held steady—Christ, grace, Scripture—even as the forms kept changing, so your confidence can rest on him rather than on customs staying frozen. One principle worth naming is that doubt is a nearly inevitable stage for thoughtful believers and deserves sympathy plus a clear, orderly look at the history, not a brush-off. That changes the tone: your question gets treated as a doorway to maturity rather than a threat. What it leaves in place is the substance of my first answer—development still means growth, not obsolescence, and the center still holds.
dogmatic: Look, the honest answer is that Christianity isn't a human product that can simply wear out. It's a new beginning in history, an immediate exercise of divine power, even though it always works through ordinary people in ordinary conditions. So stop treating the question as though the faith were a natural artifact of its environment that might get outgrown like an old tool. Growth comes through growth, not by piling up more reading or more arguments—you have to do the real work of proving God for yourself. Do that, and the worry about being outgrown loses its grip, because you won't be resting on customs or on anyone else's conclusions.

weighed: I'd start by saying distraction is really common, so don't beat yourself up about it. Build a few short, regular times of prayer, use reminders through the day to turn your attention back to God, and when you notice you've drifted, gently bring your mind back without guilt. Cutting down on clutter and screen time helps too, and so can jotting down what tends to pull you away. One principle worth naming is the beggar-at-the-gate image: you wait before God with empty hands, and when your mind wanders you don't get agitated, you just bring it back calmly, because fretting scatters you more than it gathers you. What that changes is the tone of the whole thing: instead of treating distraction as a technique problem to solve, you treat it as a return to be made quietly, again and again. What it leaves in place is the practical side: short set times, reminders, less clutter, and honest notes about what distracts you still matter. It also keeps your ordinary work and duties in view rather than setting them against your time with God.
dogmatic: The real answer is that you should stop treating prayer as a task to optimize and start treating it as a quiet, habitual conversation of the soul with God. Hold yourself before Him like a beggar at a rich man's gate, with nothing to offer, and make it your business simply to keep your mind in His presence. When it wanders, don't get worked up about it; disquiet is what scatters you, so bring your attention back in calm. And don't imagine your chores and ordinary duties are obstacles to this. The trivial round and common task are exactly the ground where you deny yourself and draw nearer to God, so meet Him there. Beyond what your state obliges, let go of fussing over forms and set prayers and instead persevere in simple attention and a steady fond regard toward Him, keeping that silent secret conversation going all day and returning gently whenever you've quit it for trifles.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, you shouldn't be discouraged—failing at the same faults is frustrating, but it doesn't mean you're hopeless or that God has given up on you. Growth is rarely a straight line, and plenty of people struggle with the same patterns for years. What matters is that you keep trying, stay honest about your weaknesses, ask for forgiveness, and look at what triggers these faults and whether practical steps like accountability or counseling could help. One principle worth weighing here is that small faults you commit on purpose are dangerous, because the most dreadful falls often start from them. That changes how I'd frame things: I'd add a real distinction between failure that comes from weakness and failure you chose, and I'd urge you to take the deliberate ones seriously and repent where you actually chose the fault. What it leaves in place is the main point—don't be too hard on yourself, God's grace is bigger than your failures, and He is patient with you.
dogmatic: No, you shouldn't be discouraged—but don't let that turn into lowering your effort either. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises, and remain untroubled and unastonished when infirmity causes you to fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from weakness. At the same time, do not make light of small faults you commit on purpose: deliberate minor sins are dangerous beginnings from which the most dreadful falls arise. Distinguish infirmity from presumption, repent seriously where you chose the fault, and amend. But do all this without hurry, over-eagerness, or anxious fretting. Keep yourself in God's presence, because anxiety is an obstacle to perfection and over-eagerness is the mother of all imperfections. Strive calmly, return quietly, and stay present to God.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: get practical—make a budget, build a small emergency fund, and set aside savings so you feel secure. Then pray and trust God to help you follow the plan. One principle worth naming is that believers shouldn't lay up money as a fund for old age or future emergencies, but live from day to day on the Lord's bounty. That principle changes the savings part: it would have you stop hoarding a reserve and instead trust God day by day, giving to His work and the poor. It leaves in place the budgeting and planning—you still track needs and avoid waste—and it leaves prayer and trust central. So the practical stewardship stays, but the long-term stockpile gets rethought.
dogmatic: Handing over money worries means trusting God rather than securing yourself. Don't lay up money as a fund for old age or future emergencies—that stored provision becomes a snare. Live from day to day on the Lord's bounty, and make your only investment in His work and the poor. Offer yourself and your substance cheerfully for His work, trusting Him to supply. In prayer, hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate; keep your mind in His presence, and when it wanders, bring it back gently without disquiet. That's the way to hand over your worries.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's normal for prayer to feel irksome or pointless sometimes, and it can help to try different forms—written prayers, music, walking—and set realistic expectations instead of forcing long sessions. One principle worth naming is that prayer should be continued patiently and believingly until the blessing is granted, without fixing God a time or manner for the answer. That changes my earlier advice in one real way: it removes the permission to step away from prayer for a season, and it replaces a deadline with patient perseverance. What it leaves in place is the honesty about dryness and the practical flexibility—you can still change how you pray and keep your expectations realistic. So keep praying, but don't treat the silence as a verdict or set God a schedule.
dogmatic: Prayer that feels irksome is no reason to stop. Keep asking, keep believing, keep coming back—importunate perseverance is the mark of effectual prayer. Don't fix God a time or a manner for the answer; wait expectantly while you wait patiently. Prayer is not a transaction or a utility; it is an elemental attitude of the soul, older than any city, and it refuses to be reduced to a bread-and-butter basis. And don't explain away the answers you receive as coincidence or natural law—the exact and repeated correspondences between request and supply are too many and too exact to admit chance. They compel belief in a God who hears and answers. So keep asking, and watch for His replies.

weighed: I'd start by saying: offer the work to God each morning, ask for strength to do it well and honestly, break the day into manageable pieces, take short breaks to reset, look for practical improvements, accept what you can't change, and keep rest and relationships in the mix so the job doesn't define you. One principle worth naming is that unwelcome tasks should be given no uneasiness, since it's God's business you're about. That changes the inner tone: instead of gritting your teeth, you set the task down as something already handed to you and get on with it calmly. It leaves your practical steps in place, the small chunks, the breaks, the honest effort, the search for improvements, and the check on whether the work is harmful to your conscience.
dogmatic: Treat the job as God's business, not yours, and refuse to let it make you uneasy. Come to God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, with nothing to offer, and make it your one task to keep your mind in His presence. When it wanders, don't scold yourself or fuss; quietly bring it back, because trouble and disquiet only scatter you further. Do the dull and distasteful parts steadily and honestly, and let everything be done in the name of the Lord. And if any part of the work can't be done in His name, don't excuse it, change it.

weighed: I'd start by saying your fear is real and worth taking seriously, not something to brush aside. You can examine yourself honestly—do you trust Christ, love God, want to obey? Assurance often grows as you see grace at work in your life. If you see little fruit, that's a reason to seek God more earnestly, not to despair. Talk with a pastor who can help you assess your faith and understand the gospel clearly. Remember that salvation rests on Christ's work, not your perfect performance. One principle I'd weigh is that fear itself can be a greater enemy than the fault you fear—like Peter sinking in the water until Christ caught him. That principle shifts the focus: instead of letting terror rule you, you can cry out 'Lord, save me!' and trust the hand He extends. But it doesn't erase the value of honest self-examination or the need for a pastor's help; it just keeps fear from becoming the master of your soul.
dogmatic: You need to hear this plainly: fear is born of Satan and is the great enemy of faith. Every fear is a falsehood, and trust is the only remedy. Do not let small faults or impatience paralyze you—quietly humble yourself before God and keep steadily on with watchfulness. Fear is a greater evil than the evil you fear. Think of St. Peter: he would have perished in the waters had not his Master saved him. So stop letting terror rule your soul. Cry out, 'Lord, save me!' and clasp the hand He extends. Trust God for goodness and mercy all the days of your life, and let trust, not terror, direct your path.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's good that you want to repay this kindness. A small creature that helped you deserves your gratitude, and you can show it by protecting it, looking out for its needs, and speaking well of it to others. If it belongs to someone, thank that person too, and let the memory of its help make you more willing to help others who are small or overlooked. One principle worth naming here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, and you shouldn't despise help that comes from the small or humble. That adds a layer of respect and humility to how you see the creature, but it doesn't change the practical advice: be gentle, be grateful, and pass the kindness on.
dogmatic: You should honor the small creatures whose help saved the great, because small things can save the great and no help from the humble should be despised. So repay this creature with real respect, not just a passing thank-you. But remember this too: a debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor comes to possess your dignity, so rather go without than borrow. Don't let gratitude turn into a chain around your neck. Do with the favor what you will, but never forget the giver.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling lost and wanting to go home is something many people go through. To find your way, first figure out what 'home' means to you—a place, a feeling, or a relationship. Then reach out to trusted friends, family, or a counselor who can help you see things more clearly. Talking it through often makes the path clearer. If it's a physical place, use maps or ask for directions. If it's emotional, think about small steps you can take to feel like you belong. One principle that might help is to hope and keep busy—work can be a real comfort. That doesn't change the need to define home or seek guidance, but it adds the idea of staying active and not just fretting. So keep moving forward, even if the way isn't obvious yet.
dogmatic: You need to turn around and walk the other way. Don't just head straight for what you think is home—sometimes the real way is the opposite direction. Confess your sins, repent of the past, and avoid future wrongdoing. Don't try to make your flaws worse. Hope and keep busy; work is a blessed solace. Follow this advice and you'll find the help you need.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't rush to use a gift you don't understand. First figure out what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, read up on it, or try it in small, safe ways. Then weigh the risk: if using it could hurt you or someone else, saving it until you understand it is wise. If it's harmless and the giver meant it for your good, using it honors the gift and the relationship. Saving it forever out of fear or confusion may just waste it. One principle worth considering is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you most want—so don't let confusion turn into paralysis. That principle pushes you to act rather than sit idle, but it doesn't change the need to understand the gift first or to check for harm. The core questions stay: what is the gift for, what could misuse cost, and what did the giver hope you'd do?
dogmatic: A gift you don't understand is no excuse to sit idle. Clarify what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, test it in low-stakes ways—but don't let confusion become self-pity or paralysis. If disappointment has left you listless because you can't have the one thing you most want, rouse yourself and do something splendid; it's wicked to throw away so many good gifts just because one desired thing is out of reach. Use the gift freely, yet remember the giver. And hold both truths: a gift offered in gratitude may be valueless to the giver compared with her liberty and honor, pressed on you as nothing—while its great consequence may rightly make you hesitate. Neither condemn it as a bribe nor accept it as a trifle; receive it thoughtfully, use it well, and remember who gave it.

weighed: Feeling undeserving can be honest humility or corrosive guilt, and the difference is what it does to you. If it makes you grateful and generous, it's healthy. If it makes you withdraw, punish yourself, or refuse good things, it's turned against you. You don't have to earn every blessing; a lot of what we receive comes from luck, other people, and grace. The right response isn't to insist you deserve nothing, but to receive with thanks and pass the good along. Ask yourself what you'd tell a friend in your place: accept the good, acknowledge the help that brought it, and let it make you kinder rather than smaller. One principle worth weighing is that you should be grateful for kindness shown and repay kindness with kindness. That adds a forward-looking pull to the answer: gratitude isn't just a feeling you hold, it's something you act on toward the people who helped you. What it leaves in place is the core point that you don't have to earn good things to receive them well.
dogmatic: You should feel grateful, full stop. Every good thing that's come to you arrived through someone's kindness, and the honest response is to repay that kindness with kindness and to mourn anyone who did you good and is gone. Where you've done wrong, don't stiffen into pride or rebellion against your circumstances; feel remorse, repent, and acknowledge that a wiser judgment, tempered with mercy, is at work. If you've been shaken by some great crime, take the lesson that an honest life is best: turn your back on the past and start fresh in a new sphere. Gratitude, humility, and honesty are how you receive the good without shrinking from it. Stop auditing whether you deserve it and get on with living rightly.

weighed: Feeling like a fraud is exhausting, and pretending indefinitely usually costs more than it saves. Impostor feelings often stick around even when your competence is real, so first check whether the fear is accurate or just loud. If you've genuinely misrepresented yourself, keeping the act going multiplies risk and anxiety. Consider confiding in one trusted person, correcting small misstatements where you can, and building competence openly rather than performing certainty. You don't need to confess everything to everyone, but you can stop adding new deceptions. One principle worth naming is that deceiving people by making believe is a fault, not a harmless trick, and being found out brings trouble and shame. That principle sharpens the case for stopping new deceptions and correcting what you can, but it leaves in place the practical point that you don't owe everyone a full confession, and it doesn't mean you should hand over your private worries to people who might use them against you. Honesty, even partial and gradual, tends to relieve the dread of exposure and lets others relate to the real you rather than a performance.
dogmatic: Stop pretending. Making believe and deceiving people is a fault, not a harmless trick, and being found out brings trouble and shame. If you've destroyed something that belonged to someone innocent, or suppressed the proofs they needed, that's a fraud you have to confess and undo by making restitution to the person you wronged. Don't tell yourself it's just a small act or that everyone does it. Confess the facts before witnesses and repair the harm. At the same time, don't be naive: don't needlessly reveal your plans, letters, or secrets to an adversary who has no right to them. Keep your own game concealed and set yourself to discovering the other side's designs. Stop adding new deceptions, correct what you can, and confide only in the trustworthy. Where real harm was done, repair it openly; where you face an adversary, be discreet rather than defenseless.

weighed: I'd start by asking whether your prayers feel like a habit or an actual conversation. A dead conception of God often shows up as praying to an idea, like a distant force or a rule-keeper, so the words never seem to reach anyone. One principle worth weighing here is that God is a Spirit, and those who adore Him must do so in spirit and in truth, with a mind and heart purified from every phantom of earth. That adds something real: it says the problem isn't just technique but the picture of God you're praying to, so it pushes you to shut out distractions and come honestly, with a free conscience. What it leaves in place is the practical side I'd still suggest: slow down, pray Scripture, confess specific sins, and ask trusted believers to help you see blind spots. Living faith carries expectation and honesty, and it produces fruit, while a dead conception leaves you unchanged.
dogmatic: The emptiness isn't a technique problem at all, it's a revelation problem. A dead conception makes prayer empty because you're talking to a figure of your own making, and no amount of raised voice or refined method will make that figure answer. Prayer rises or falls with the quality of your faith, so when prayer sinks into mere words, it's a sign you're trying to get along with a dead God. God is a Spirit, and those who adore Him must adore Him in spirit and in truth, with intelligence and will purified from every phantom of earth. So enter the inmost chamber of your heart and shut the door of the senses, coming with a pure heart and unfeigned faith. God hears the earnest prayer of the soul and understands your innermost thoughts, so ask in faith, nothing wavering, and your prayer will not be empty.

weighed: What I'd say first is that contentment usually doesn't come from getting back what you lost. It comes from turning your attention to what's still here and what you can still build. Grief takes time and won't disappear on command, so be patient with it, lean on people, keep some small routines, and notice the good moments when they show up. One idea worth weighing is that the deepest happiness comes from being sure you're loved for who you are, not for what you do or have. That doesn't erase your loss or make the sadness go away, and it doesn't replace the practical steps like gratitude or talking to someone. What it does change is where you look for steadiness: not only at what's missing, but at the people who value you as you are. So keep doing the everyday things that help, and let that kind of love be part of what holds you up.
dogmatic: The supreme happiness of life is the certainty of being loved for your own sake, loved in spite of yourself. Where there is that certainty, there is no blindness, and you do not lose your sight when you have love. Don't take this on trust from what most people say or from books; think it over for yourself and come to understand it. And remember that happiness is not enough on its own: being happy can make you forget the true object of life, so duty must not be forgotten in the midst of joy. Let love supply what your loss takes away, reason it through for yourself, and hold duty alongside delight, so that contentment does not become forgetfulness.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: since you worry about being cruel, build habits that don't depend on feeling. Pause before you act, ask what the other person needs, and deliberately choose the kinder option. The Tin Woodman feared he had no heart, yet he was consistently gentle, and his choices, not his feelings, defined him. One of the principles you're weighing says that someone without a heart must take great care never to be cruel, helping anyone who needs a friend. That sharpens the stakes and gives your worry a useful direction, but it doesn't change the core: kindness is something you practice, not something you feel. It leaves in place the practical steps, the feedback from people you trust, and the idea that your character is shaped by what you do.
dogmatic: If you have no heart, then take the greatest care never to be cruel or unkind to anything, and help everyone who may need a friend. That's the whole of it. Don't waste energy fretting over evils you can't avoid or making them bigger with anxiety; do your duty, do the kind thing in front of you, and leave the rest. And don't let anyone intimidate you into things that are wholly unreasonable, or push you around with claims of duty, honor, or gratitude that don't actually apply. Act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, choose the kinder option on purpose, and let trusted people give you honest feedback.

weighed: My first answer is that it's not automatically unfair for a powerful person to tie help to a favor first, but you should be careful. Ask whether the task is reasonable, whether you can trust them to keep their word, and whether the cost is worth it. One principle that applies here is that you should keep your promises and stay loyal to friends who've done you good turns. That principle doesn't change my basic answer, since I already said to weigh the cost and be wary of being exploited, but it sharpens it: if the favor means betraying a friend or breaking a promise you've made, that's a strong reason to say no, even to someone powerful. It leaves the rest in place, so the decision is still yours to make based on whether the task is fair and the person is trustworthy.
dogmatic: You should keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who've helped you, and that settles it. If a powerful person asks you to do something first, your duty is to honor your existing commitments and not abandon the people who've shown you kindness. Don't trade loyalty for a promised favor. Do your duty, work while you hope and wait, and leave the future to be as God wills rather than neglecting what you owe for the sake of pleasing someone powerful.

weighed:
I'd start where I always start: prayer and honest self-examination. Ask whether your desire to stay is rooted in fear or in real fruitfulness where you are, and whether the pull to move is ambition or calling. Seek counsel from mature believers and denominational leaders—they often see what you can't. Look at the evidence: is there fruit, affirmation, and provision in one direction? Are doors opening with confirmation from others, or are you forcing them? Consider your family, health, and gifting. Write down what you sense God saying and test it against Scripture. Don't rush; give decisions time and let peace and confirmation grow. In the end, the Spirit's leading usually becomes clear through a combination of inner conviction, outward confirmation, and the counsel of the church.
