One principle worth naming is that the servant of Christ has one Master and should be guided by the Spirit, not by men, as to time and place of service. That doesn't mean you ignore counsel or abandon wise process—it means no committee or official gets the final vote on where you serve. It changes the weight you give to human expectations and fixed rules; it leaves in place the value of counsel, evidence, and testing, because those are ways the Spirit often speaks. So hold your plans loosely, but don't despise the church's wisdom as you discern.
dogmatic: The question isn't finally settled by committees, votes, or officials. The Spirit is the administrator of the church, and you must be governed by His voice rather than by human appointment or majority opinion. You have one Master. He guides you as to time and place, and you should not be bound by fixed rules or human direction. Begin in prayer, asking the Spirit to make His will plain, and let your decisions echo the early church's discernment: 'It seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.' Human counsel is valuable, but it is not the rule—the Spirit is. Remember where the promised power lies: along the line of duty and obedience to Christ's command to reach the world. The fullness of the Spirit is given as you obey and step out into His plans for the world, not for selfish enjoyment. So ask not where you will be comfortable but where obedience to the gospel takes you, and there expect the Spirit's power to go before you.

weighed: I'd start by saying crying isn't a sign of weakness—it's a natural human response, and hiding your tears often costs more than it saves. One principle that matters here is that tears are tied to involuntary muscle contractions around the eyes, and that link holds across opposite emotions and even with no emotion at all. That changes how I see it: tears are a bodily reflex, not a verdict on your strength. What it leaves in place is your choice about privacy—you can step aside if you prefer, but you don't need to be ashamed. So no, you don't have to hide them to prove toughness.
dogmatic: You should stop worrying about being seen as weak. Tears are just the involuntary contraction of muscles around your eyes acting on your tear glands—a bodily mechanism, not a moral failing. And sympathy for others often makes you cry more freely than your own pain does. So don't perform toughness or prove feeling by display. True sorrow is inward and beyond show; outward tears are just actions you might play. Let yourself feel, and don't be ashamed.

weighed: My first answer would be that freedom gives you the right to protect yourself, not the obligation to punish. You owe your former captors nothing beyond basic safety and the ordinary decency you'd give any stranger. You can keep your distance, refuse contact, and set firm boundaries without cruelty. One principle worth naming here is that coldness and withholding approval can be refined torture, a way of making someone feel guilt and obey without ever raising your voice. That changes how you handle your own anger: don't use icy disdain or deliberate shaming as a weapon, even when you're in the right. What it leaves in place is everything you said you need: distance, boundaries, and no owed forgiveness. You still get to protect yourself and keep your life separate from them.
dogmatic: You should treat your former captors with stern, implacable justice, and you should not soften it just because they once had power over you. Coldness and the withholding of approval are refined torture, so do not use them, but do not mistake that for weakness either. Do your duty where it lies, obey the grandfather who stands over your household, and do not break away just to please yourself. When you rage against their sin, remember that your own trespass will appear, and that what urged you to transgress was sweet and dear. Let humility steady you, not escape, and answer cruelty with plain justice rather than exquisite coldness.

weighed: I'd first tell you that asking for brains is worth it, but that good thinking means being complete and explicit about every step. One principle that shifts this is that wisdom is largely knowing what to overlook, since selection means rejection as well as choice. That changes the picture: you don't need to spell out every inference to be clever, because inattention matters as much as attention. What it leaves in place is that seeking brains is still worthwhile and that careful habits of mind are the real goal, not just collecting facts or fixing your posture.
dogmatic: Asking for brains is worth it, but don't confuse cleverness with spelling out every step. The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook; selection implies rejection as well as choice, and inattention is as vital a factor in mental progress as attention itself. So stop trying to state every premise and inference. The real end of education is forming careful, alert, and thorough habits of thinking, not amassing information or acquiring external skills. And don't worry about where your body sits: the more head downwards I am, the more I keep inventing new things, and my mind goes on working all the same.

weighed: It's completely understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you didn't intend. You don't have to accept a label that feels false, but you also don't need to reject the gratitude behind it. A good response is modest honesty: thank people for their kindness, explain it wasn't deliberate, and redirect credit where it belongs. Feeling uncomfortable is fine; feeling like a fraud isn't necessary. One principle worth weighing here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That changes the emphasis: instead of mainly managing your discomfort, you'd lean toward openly thanking people for their goodwill even when it's awkward. What it leaves in place is the honesty part—you can still gently clarify that it was an accident and point credit where it belongs. So let the praise remind you that people appreciate you, even if the story is more accident than heroism.
dogmatic: You should feel obliged to acknowledge the gratitude openly, even if it embarrasses you. When people offer you kindness or praise, thank them plainly and don't hide behind your discomfort. At the same time, don't take every report at face value—weigh what people say against your actual conduct and the evidence. And speak the truth: think before you speak, say what you mean, mean what you say, and write it down afterwards. Gratitude, honesty, and careful words together will settle how you should feel about the praise.

weighed: Yes, ask for help, but ask well. An instant charm you can't use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek someone who truly understands it, and ask them to teach you rather than use it for you. One thing I'd keep in mind is that curiosity—eagerness for new and varied contacts with things—is what supplies the raw material for real suggestions, so stay open and wondering rather than just following steps. That principle changes how you approach the learning: it's not just about getting the charm to work, it's about keeping your spark of wonder alive so you actually understand it. What it leaves in place is the core advice: ask, ask well, and aim to learn rather than depend.
dogmatic: You should absolutely ask for help, no question. But don't just ask anyone—find someone who truly understands the charm and have them teach you. And while you're at it, remember that curiosity is the vital factor supplying the primary material from which suggestions issue; your task is to keep alive the spark of wonder. So don't treat this as a quick fix. Let your eagerness for new and varied contacts with things drive you. Ask, learn, and stay curious—that's the real path.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer would be: fear is natural when people depend on you, but it only becomes a monster if you let it rule you. Separate what you can control from what you can't, prepare as well as you can, then act on the plan. Focus on the next right step instead of the imagined catastrophe, breathe, and talk to someone you trust. One principle worth weighing here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That changes things by adding a pause before you strike back or lash out, especially when your fear pushes you toward something rash. What it leaves in place is the core: prepare, steady yourself, take the next step, and accept you can't guarantee every outcome. You still face the monster—you just don't do it recklessly.
dogmatic: Don't brood over unavoidable evils or pile on more anxiety—do your duty and leave the rest. Resist every urge to look back, keep moving steadily, and when a road is blocked, cut a new one instead of standing still in despair. And remember: it's far better to patiently endure a hurt that nobody feels but you than to take a hasty action whose consequences spread to everyone connected to you. So face the monster with patience and steady effort, not with a reckless strike that drags others down with you.

weighed: I'd start by saying courage usually comes from preparation, not from waiting to feel ready. Get clear on what you need and why this person can help, then map out the practical steps: route, resources, and who can support you along the way. Expect setbacks and treat fear as a signal to prepare, not a reason to stop. One principle worth weighing is that it's better to endure a private hardship patiently than to rush into an action whose consequences spill over onto everyone connected to you. That principle changes the timing and the manner of your approach: it nudges you to be deliberate, to consider how your journey and your request might affect the people around you, and to avoid a reckless dash. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: clarify your need, plan the practical steps, and let your purpose outweigh the discomfort of asking. So set a firm departure date, rehearse your request, and begin before you feel entirely ready.
dogmatic: You should not be asking how to find the courage to start. The real question is whether you should go at all. Endure patiently the private hardship that nobody else feels rather than commit a hasty action whose evil consequences extend to all connected with you. In extremity you may look for aid to God and trust in Providence, but you must still struggle to live, seek work, and bear the burden of human wants and responsibilities. Do your duty and obey your grandfather rather than break away to please yourself. Do not sail off in defiance of duty. If you must seek help, pray for aid, then rise and seek work, bearing hunger and cold, and fulfill the responsibilities life still lays upon you. Clarify what you need and plan the practical steps, but let prudence govern the timing, and never leave without permission.

weighed: First, I'd tell you to stop and get your bearings—look for landmarks, signs, or someone who can help. If you have a phone or map, use it; if not, ask a local and repeat the directions back. Stay calm, avoid wandering randomly, note the sun, and if night is coming, find safe shelter and let someone know where you are. One principle that applies here is to resist looking back and keep moving forward steadily—when a path is blocked, find another way rather than standing still in despair. That principle changes the tone: it turns being lost into a prompt to keep moving with purpose instead of freezing up. But it leaves your practical constraints in place—you still need to ask for help, use your phone, and find shelter before dark.
dogmatic: You should confess, repent, and resolve to avoid future sin—don't make your corruption worse by excusing it. Resist every temptation to look back, like Lot's wife, and don't yield to despair. Pursue your present course steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. And heed the Rose: when the way seems plain, walk the other way—for that is how the Queen is reached.

weighed: My first instinct would be to say: rule with firmness first. Make your authority clear, reward obedience, and punish resistance, because people who trust you will test that trust, and hesitation invites disorder. One of the candidate principles says a ruler's personal good qualities and fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it warns me not to let strength slide into carelessness or cruelty, or let popularity cover for bad governing. But it leaves my core advice in place: be decisive, keep your counsel, and establish your authority before kindness. So rule firmly, but hold yourself to a standard of good administration, not just obedience.
dogmatic: Rule as someone who is good to the people and governs wisely and well, so they remember you lovingly. Don't confuse your personal qualities or fame with the quality of your administration; a ruler can be admired and still govern carelessly, too indulgently, or in league with despotism, and popularity doesn't justify any of that. And don't treat virtues as impersonal laws or outside authorities you must obey. Virtues become dangerous when they rule you from the outside; they're right only when you develop them yourself as your most personal means of defence, answering your own needs as a ruler and a person.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's good you're content with your good fortune, but your friend's unhappiness still deserves care. Whether you should try to make them stay depends on why they want to leave and whether staying would actually help them or just ease your own discomfort. Ask them openly what's wrong and listen without trying to fix everything at once. You can't make someone happy, and pressing them to stay against their judgment may breed resentment. Offer support, be honest about what you can give, and respect their choice. One principle worth weighing is that honest money may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. That principle changes how you hold your good fortune—you don't need to feel guilty about it—but it leaves in place the need to care for your friend and respect their decision.
dogmatic: You should enjoy your good fortune with a tranquil mind, since honest money belongs to its rightful owner. But wealth carries responsibilities: a large fortune should be divided justly among kindred rather than kept alone, and the pleasure of repaying obligation and winning lifelong friends outweighs gold. So share what you have justly, and urge your friend to stay only if staying truly helps them. Don't let guilt poison your gratitude, but don't ignore the real claims of those close to you either.

weighed: I'd start by saying the danger is real, so think it through before you go: figure out what makes the way risky, bring supplies, travel with someone if you can, and tell a friend your route. If it looks too bad, waiting or taking another path is fine. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long, dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That shifts things toward resolve once you've chosen your route, but it doesn't erase the practical prep or the option to wait when conditions are clearly against you. So plan carefully, then decide.
dogmatic: You shouldn't turn back. If the goal is worth reaching, then a long and dangerous road is exactly what you sign up for, and resolve matters more than comfort. Pick your way, then commit to it bravely and endure the rough stretches. Along the way, don't harm any living creature needlessly, and watch where you step so you spare even the smallest ant or beetle. Courage and care go together, so go forward.

weighed: My first instinct is to say yes, but carefully: verify what you actually know so you're not accusing on rumor, think through the fallout, and consider telling the person you know and giving them a chance to come forward. If they won't and others are still at risk, go to the right people rather than broadcasting it, and keep it factual so the goal is stopping harm, not humiliating anyone. One principle worth weighing is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if the deceiver turns things around and accuses you: you answer with a plain, accurate account instead of escalating. It leaves the rest in place—verify first, give them a chance to come forward, and disclose quietly to the appropriate people if others remain at risk.
dogmatic: Don't show your hand. Keep your plans and what you know to yourself, because the person deceiving everyone has no right to a warning and no need to know what you intend. Verify the facts quietly, then work out their designs—who's involved, what they're after, who's exposed—without announcing anything. If they aim a false charge at you, answer it plainly in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. And be careful not to let an innocent person get swept up just because they were nearby when things went wrong; crowds and authorities confuse company with guilt. When others are still in danger, take it to the right people rather than making a spectacle of it, and keep your aim on stopping harm, not humiliating anyone.

weighed: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is to stop and take care of your body: rest, eat something, drink water. Being that tired and hungry makes everything feel heavier, so don't make big decisions right now. Break the rest of the road into smaller stretches and take them one at a time. Remind yourself why you set out and what's waiting at the end, and ask for help if you can, like a ride, a meal, or some company for a while. One principle worth holding onto is to hope and keep busy, since work can be a real comfort and sitting around fretting only makes you more tired. That adds a gentle push to keep moving through your daily tasks, but it doesn't cancel the need to rest and eat first. So pace yourself, do what you can, and be kind to yourself along the way.
dogmatic: You need to hope and keep busy. Work is a blessed solace, and idling and fretting will only drag you down further. Don't sit there nursing your exhaustion; get up and go on with your daily tasks. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue what's in front of you steadily, and if the road is blocked, hew out a new one instead of standing still in despair. Sure, have a bit of a fight, but don't worry about going on forever. Fight till six, then stop and have dinner. Set a limit, do the day's work well, and then rest with a clear mind, ready for tomorrow.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, fear of the dark and of water doesn't make you weak. These fears are really common and say nothing about your character. One idea that adds something here is that fear shows up in your body—wide eyes, raised eyebrows, pale skin, cold sweat, trembling, quick breathing. That changes how you see the fear: it's your body's alarm system going off, not a verdict on your worth. But it leaves the core answer in place—your fears still don't define you, and courage is about how you respond, like learning to swim gradually or using a nightlight.
dogmatic: Fear of the dark and water is just your body doing what bodies do—eyes wide, mouth open, eyebrows up, pale, sweating, hair standing, trembling, breathing fast, and in real terror your muscles go slack. That's not weakness; it's physiology. But don't expect words to fix it. Calling thunder a natural phenomenon doesn't remove the bitterness you feel inside, and explaining fear won't make it vanish. You can walk the road with fear still there—no stopping, no thinking, just dry thunder—and that's courage, not the absence of the spike.

weighed: My first answer would be: kindness that's only for thanks is a transaction, and you'll often be disappointed. You can't control whether someone feels or shows gratitude, and pushing for it usually backfires. The better question is whether your kindness is sustainable and whether it's being taken for granted in a way that hurts you. Keep being kind where it's freely given and doesn't drain you, but set limits where kindness is expected rather than received. You can also calmly say you'd appreciate acknowledgment—that's honest, not petty. One candidate principle is that gratitude for great kindness obliges open acknowledgment even at the cost of embarrassment. That changes things if the kindness was extraordinary—say, someone helped your family in a big way—then it's worth speaking up plainly, even if it feels awkward. But it leaves the everyday case in place: for ordinary kindness that goes unthanked, you don't owe a confrontation, and you still get to decide how much to keep giving.
dogmatic: You should have said the proper thing at the proper moment: 'It's extremely kind of you to tell me all this.' When someone has shown you great kindness, you're obliged to acknowledge it openly, even if it embarrasses you. Don't let gratitude go unspoken. A kind and tender heart is worth more than cleverness—the Woodman prized his loving heart above the wit that would have kept it safe, and he was right. So keep being kind, not because it's clever or repaid, but because that's what a good heart does. Yes, set limits where kindness is abused, but never trade your heart for cleverness.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: talk openly before you go about must-sees and deal-breakers, then agree on a loose plan with some free time for each person. Rotate whose preference leads each day, or split up for an afternoon and meet again for meals. Keep communication kind and flexible, and accept that you may not do everything together. One principle worth naming is that friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. If your trip has genuinely risky parts, that principle changes the split-up advice: don't separate on those stretches, and make sure everyone knows the plan and can carry on if something goes wrong. It leaves the rest in place—the open conversation, the loose plan, the free time, and the kindness—so you still keep the group together without forcing perfect unity.
dogmatic: You should not scatter. Four men together make a troop, and isolated men are easily overcome, so stay together and move as one company. If one falls, another must take the letter and continue, so each of you should know the charge and be ready to carry it. Speak plainly and at once about plans and limits; do not leave anyone in suspense or trifle with feelings. Above all, show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after death—do not neglect the living for the sake of mourning the dead. Keep communication kind, allow some free time without risking the party's safety, and aim for a good journey and a whole company.

weighed: I first thought you could simply refuse to kill and expose the wrongdoer, but I also said that if you're captive or ashamed, death can be a refuge. That last part doesn't hold up. The principle that you must not attempt to kill yourself changes that: it removes the escape of self-destruction and tells you to endure, seek help, and escape by living means. What it leaves in place is your refusal to kill and your choice to bring the wrongdoer before a formal judgment rather than a private killing. So yes, there's another way—one that doesn't require you to stain your hands or throw your life away.
dogmatic: You must not kill anyone, even the wicked, and you must not kill yourself either. Suicide is condemned by God, so despair is never an answer. Bring the wrongdoer to a solemn, orderly judgment—accusers, witnesses, a pronounced sentence—not a stealthy assassination. And as you go, harm no living creature needlessly: look where you step, spare even the smallest ant. Your purity matters more than their punishment, and your life is not yours to throw away.

weighed: Yes, I'd forgive them. A friend who genuinely did their best and still fell short wasn't acting out of malice, and holding onto a grudge over that just punishes good intentions. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let the sun go down on your anger, that you forgive each other and begin again tomorrow. That principle pushes me to say: deal with the disappointment today, talk it through honestly, and don't let it sit and harden overnight. What it changes is the timing and the tone, making forgiveness something you do soon rather than something you get around to. What it leaves in place is that the promise still mattered and the disappointment was real. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. So talk with your friend, be honest about how it felt, and then let it go.
dogmatic: Forgive them, and don't wait until it's convenient. You shouldn't let the sun go down on your anger, so settle this before the day ends and start fresh tomorrow. A promise is a bond, and a friend who made one should strive to keep it, but where they truly did their best and still fell short, repay that kindness with understanding rather than nursing a grudge. And remember that God forgives those who repent in sincerity, and his people must forgive one another's trespasses too. The one who refuses to forgive his neighbor brings condemnation on his own head, while the merciful receive mercy. So forgive, and do it now.

weighed: My first answer would be to win the people over rather than just occupy them: go easy on taxes, respect local customs and laws where they don't threaten your authority, co-opt local elites who can govern in their own tongue, keep a reliable military presence near trouble spots but use it sparingly, learn the language, and over time integrate institutions and offer a path to citizenship for leading families. One candidate principle is that a new prince should reside in the province or send colonies, since these are the true keys to holding a state. That changes my emphasis on a light military footprint and patience: it says your physical presence or settler communities matter more than garrisons and gradual integration. It leaves in place the core of respecting local customs, avoiding heavy taxation, and co-opting local elites, so the main thrust of winning inhabitants still stands.
dogmatic: You should reside in that province yourself, or send colonies there, because those are the real keys to holding a state. Don't rely on garrisons or distant rule. And don't leave naturalization to the province's several jurisdictions, since dissimilar rules produce confusion and evasion; impose a single uniform rule of naturalization. In great changes, forms ought to give way to substance, so let the people's right to alter government be exercised through informal proposals by patriotic citizens. Respect local customs only where they don't threaten your authority, avoid heavy taxation, and co-opt local elites, but the decisive moves are residence or colonies, uniform naturalization, and substance over forms.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: keep your plans private, share only with people you fully trust, watch for odd changes in behavior, vary your routines, secure your home and communications, and if you genuinely suspect a plot, go to trusted authorities instead of confronting anyone yourself. One principle worth naming is the idea that you shouldn't expose your game to an adversary—let him find out if he can, while you work to find out his. That sharpens the secrecy side of my answer and adds a quiet, watchful posture toward the other person. What it leaves in place is everything else: documenting suspicious things, leaning on honest allies, and staying calm and evidence-based rather than letting fear invent plots. It doesn't replace going to authorities when something real is going on.
dogmatic: Keep your plans, letters, and secrets entirely to yourself—reveal nothing to anyone who has no right to them, because an adversary who learns your designs can turn them against you. Then work quietly to discover his. Don't lean on grand theories about how people behave, and don't trust vague inner impressions that feel like insight; stick to observed facts—changes in behavior, unusual interest in your schedule, honest reports from allies. And take heart: the conspirator tends to undo himself from within, his own will and reason failing him like a disease, with trifles betraying him in the end. Your part is simply to stay as inconspicuous as possible, so nothing in you gives him a handle, while his own nature does the rest.

weighed: My first answer would be: you need both. Appearing virtuous has real value because people follow those they trust, but if it's only an act, they'll eventually notice the gap and your authority will collapse. So cultivate real virtue and let it show—start with honesty and fairness in small decisions, keep promises, admit mistakes. You don't need to be perfect, but you do need to be genuine. One principle that sharpens this is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; substantial good must be recollected, and a pleasing air can coexist with vice. That changes how you should measure yourself: don't rely on the impression you make in the moment, but on whether you can point to specific good acts over time. It leaves in place the core practical advice—be genuine, build virtue through repeated good acts, and let appearance follow substance.
dogmatic: You should stop worrying about appearing virtuous and focus on what actually constitutes your happiness, as you judge it. Don't let others intimidate you into performing virtue through appeals to duty, honor, or gratitude that have no real claim on you. Charm and a pleasing manner are not proof of virtue—anyone can have those and still be vicious. The real test is whether you can recollect actual instances of goodness you've done. So act as your own reasoned judgment dictates, refuse to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable, and be selective about praise: not all admiration is worth pursuing, and vanity chases every compliment. Value the praise worth having and win the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as attractive. Cultivate real integrity through specific good acts, and let appearance follow substance—but never let flattery or pressure decide what you do.

weighed: I'd start by saying taxes are necessary for public services, but if people are grumbling, consider whether the burden is too heavy. Lowering taxes can stimulate the economy and ease discontent, but it may reduce revenue for essential services. Hold firm if the taxes are fair and necessary, but communicate clearly why they are needed. One principle that matters here is that the most productive system of finance is the least burdensome—so the best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients. That principle changes how I'd approach the decision: I'd want to gather extensive information about political economy and the people's habits before deciding, rather than just reacting to the grumbling. It leaves in place the core advice to balance revenue needs with the people's ability to pay and to listen to their concerns. So I'd still say: listen, assess, and adjust if possible, but don't hold firm blindly.
dogmatic: You should not lower taxes just because your people are grumbling. The business of taxation requires extensive information and knowledge of political economy, and the most productive system of finance is always the least burdensome—but that doesn't mean you cave to complaints. The best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients, so inform yourself thoroughly and then hold firm if the taxes are fair. Also, teach your people not to complain about poverty but to remember how rich they are in love, health, and the blessings that alone make life happy. And be charitable in judging the ignorant, for they act according to their lights. So hold firm, educate, and don't let grumbling drive your policy.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: a fortress can help, but don't lean on stone alone. If the town is rebellious, walls might overawe it for a while, but they won't win loyalty. Think about whether it'll provoke resentment or protect order, and whether you can actually garrison and supply it. Build only if it serves a clear purpose, and pair it with steps that address why people are rebelling. One principle that fits here is that the best fortress is not being hated by your people—fortresses help or hurt depending on circumstances and can't save a ruler whose people despise him. That principle sharpens the warning: it makes me weigh the town's hostility more heavily and see walls as conditional, not a cure. But it leaves in place the practical checks—cost, supply, provocation, and the need to fix root causes. So I'd still say: consider it, but only as part of a broader approach, not as a substitute for good rule.
dogmatic: No—don't build it. The best fortress is not to be hated by the people. If the town is rebellious and hostile, walls won't save you; when outsiders help them, fortresses are of little value. Stone can't win loyalty or replace goodwill. Be wary of the young and restless too: youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so don't assume calm will hold without vigilance. Best safety lies in fear—a sober watchfulness, not cruelty. Above all, rely on your own arms and avoid mercenaries and auxiliaries, for the arms of others either fall from your back, weigh you down, or bind you fast. No state is secure without its own forces. Seek the people's goodwill by justice, keep your own loyal troops, and build only if it serves order rather than substituting for it.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: there's no formula, but you look at whether the threat is real and growing, weigh the cost of waiting against the cost of acting, act early enough to matter but late enough to be sure, and check your motives. One principle worth naming is that blocked instincts can turn inward and dress themselves up as enemies in your imagination. That genuinely changes something: before you treat a threat as external, ask whether some of it is your own pent-up energy looking for a target. It leaves the rest in place, though. A real, credible, growing danger still needs a response, and self-scrutiny doesn't excuse you from acting when waiting would clearly cost more than moving.
dogmatic: The answer is to look inward first, because when powerful instincts can't vent outwardly in peace and society, they turn inward and become demons you end up fighting. Much of what feels like an external threat is exactly that blocked energy wearing the face of an enemy in your imagination. So weigh your own fear before you weigh anyone else's danger, and when someone stands accused, don't let her weakness or her people's low standing count as proof against her. The frail gage of an innocent woman can outweigh the iron gauntlet of a powerful order, and the final judgment belongs to God. Keep affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, and remember that best safety lies in fear.

weighed: I'd start by saying the charge of cruelty deserves a real answer, not a defensive one. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary to restore peace, and whether it was applied consistently rather than to settle private scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as the danger required, you can defend the decision. If you acted in anger, or kept punishing after the danger had passed, the accusation has weight. One principle that bears on this: cruelty used well is applied at once for security and not persisted in, and it can be more merciful than the disorder that comes from too much mercy. That changes how I'd weigh timing and duration, since a single decisive act differs from a drawn-out campaign of punishment. It leaves in place the need for lawful process, proportionality, and honest scrutiny of your motives, and it doesn't settle whether executing rebels was right in your case.
dogmatic: Severity that keeps order can be the truer mercy, and mercy that lets disorder spread can be the greater cruelty. So do not flinch at the reproach of cruelty when the blow is struck once, decisively, for security, and not dragged out afterward. But know the limit: it is not your calling to be judge and executioner of God's justice over other peoples. Vengeance belongs to God, who punishes in His own time. Hate is not overcome by violence, nor injury healed by vengeance; return good for evil. Strike once if you must, then stop, and leave the rest to a higher judgment.

weighed: I'd start by saying that eliminating rivals is a serious move, and whether you do it gradually or all at once depends on your situation. Gradual may seem less brutal but gives opponents time to organize; all at once can be decisive but risks creating martyrs. One principle worth weighing is that continual danger tends to push even liberty-loving nations toward standing armies and institutions that lean toward monarchy. That principle changes how I'd think about prolonged internal conflict—it makes drawn-out purges look riskier for your state's long-term character. But it leaves in place the core trade-off between speed and backlash, and it doesn't settle whether political neutralization—offering positions, exiling, undermining support—might be safer than violence. So I'd still urge you to consider those alternatives first.
dogmatic: You should act decisively and all at once, because prolonged internal conflict is exactly what breeds standing armies and institutions that tend toward monarchy. The danger of drawn-out rivalry is not just the rivals themselves—it's that continual apprehension corrupts the state you're trying to build. Union and clear authority are necessary; division and lingering threats expose every part to foreign danger and internal collapse. So don't nibble at your rivals gradually. Strike once, establish order, and remove the conditions that would force your state into perpetual war footing.

weighed: My first answer would be that a promise isn't just a tool you drop when it stops being useful. It creates expectations and shapes your character, so the fact that your ally no longer serves your interests usually isn't enough to release you. Ask whether the promise was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its original purpose is void, and whether the ally breached their side. If none of those apply, you're probably still bound, though you can renegotiate openly. Quietly walking away to gain an advantage damages trust and your reputation. The honest path is to talk with your ally, explain the change, and seek release or modification. One candidate principle here is that you should keep your promises, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That principle reinforces the core of my answer—it makes loyalty to a benefactor a real weight, not just a nice sentiment. What it changes is the emphasis: it pushes you to treat the ally's past help as a reason to stay and work things out rather than just a neutral factor. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice: the conditions, the changed circumstances, the breach, and the open renegotiation. So it doesn't give you a free pass; it just sharpens why you should take the promise seriously.
dogmatic: You are bound to keep your promises. A promise is not a convenience you discard when it stops serving your interests. Friends who have done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return, and you should not make a promise lightly—having sworn, you must keep it. The fact that your ally no longer serves your interests is irrelevant to whether you are bound. Ask only whether the promise was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its purpose is void, or whether the ally breached their side. If none of those apply, you keep it. You may renegotiate openly, but you do not quietly walk away. And do not be ashamed of worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; honest connections deserve no apology. So hold to your oath, honor the loyalty you owe, and do not let convenience or pride release you from what you swore.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer is that more killing won't make you safe. Stop the bloodshed and make it obvious the killing has ended. Then secure the practical things: the armed forces, supporters you reward, and plotters you remove. But lasting rule needs more than force, because people who see only cruelty will wait for a chance to throw you off. So keep order, keep your promises to those who serve you, and skip pointless cruelty. One principle worth naming is that a ruler should be good to the people and rule them wisely and well, and people remember a good ruler lovingly. That adds a warmer, more personal standard: be good to the people and govern well, and you may be remembered with affection, which rests on a firmer foundation than terror. It leaves in place what I said first: end the violence, control the forces, reward supporters, remove plotters, and avoid needless cruelty. It doesn't replace the practical steps; it gives them a direction.
dogmatic: Rule as a good ruler should: be good to the people, govern wisely and well, and give them order and justice rather than fear. A ruler the people remember lovingly rests on a firmer foundation than one who rules by terror. Guard also against a majority faction oppressing a minority, not by a will independent of the society but by extending the republic and multiplying its interests. And in a crisis, remember that the favour of the multitude is indispensable. Do not excuse violence against Saxon favourites, and do not think the abduction of a Saxon heiress prudent; as Fitzurse warns, such outrages endanger the whole faction. Win the people's favour by justice, and your rule will stand.

weighed: Start by quietly broadening your support instead of betting everything on one fading patron. Cultivate other allies and strengthen your domestic base—the army, the treasury, key officials—while keeping relations with your old backer cordial until you're secure. One principle worth weighing here is that a prince shouldn't let a powerful foreigner into his affairs or aggrandize another power, since whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle changes the method: rather than simply swapping one protector for another, you'd build alternatives without making any single outside power too strong at your expense. What it leaves in place is the core plan—diversify support, shore up your domestic base, and avoid an open break until you're secure.
dogmatic: Don't replace one foreign backer with another—whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. Leagues and a crowd of separate judgments won't secure you either; real security is unity, with everyone authorizing one person or assembly to bear their person, so the multitude becomes one will. And don't mistake your popularity or military fame for good government: separate your personal qualities from your administration, and treat carelessness, indulgence, and despotism as defects to be corrected, not excused.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: be visibly fair and predictable, keep your dealings with the nobles public enough that people see you're not captured by them, and give the people concrete benefits like justice, order, and protection that don't depend on noble goodwill. Avoid secret bargains that will later be exposed, and let the nobles see your standing rests on the people's contentment, so their own interest lies in your fairness. One principle worth weighing here is that the lesser gentry who rely on their own inoffensive conduct and the laws of the land get harassed by the great barons, who never lack a pretext or the will to pursue them to destruction. That changes my confidence that inoffensive conduct and law alone will protect you—it means you need real alliances and public dealings, not just legality. What it leaves in place is the core balance: fairness, transparency, and concrete benefits to the people still do the work of keeping both sides from turning on you.
dogmatic: Don't kid yourself that inoffensive conduct and the law will protect you. The great barons never lacked a pretext or the will to harass lesser men who sought independence—power, not legality, governs them. So keep your dealings public and your alliances real. And watch whom you trust: men who backed you only out of discontent with the old government are hard to satisfy and their favor is bought, not loyal. You'll more easily win those who were contented under the former government, and former opponents often prove more faithful than the malcontents who flocked to you. Remember that wealth is the source of both strength and weakness—jewels are worthless next to liberty and honor. Give the people justice and protection, let the nobles see your standing rests on their contentment, and never trade liberty or honor for treasure.

weighed: My first answer would be: give what you can truly afford, cheerfully and without keeping score. Let your generosity show through actions, not announcements, and don't let the wish to look open-handed push you past your means. One principle worth naming is that I never put things into people's hands—you have to get it for yourself. That changes how I'd frame giving: instead of handing over gifts that create dependence, I'd offer fair terms and real opportunities so people can obtain what they need themselves. What it leaves in place is the core advice—be generous within your limits, quietly and consistently, and let others judge you by what you actually do.
dogmatic: Generosity that's mostly about being seen is vanity, not virtue. Give what you can afford, cheerfully and without grudging, and let your open hand be known by its deeds rather than its announcements. But do not imagine you can hand an item directly to someone—that would never do; they must get it for themselves. Offer opportunity and fair terms instead of gifts that create dependence. And do not mistake charm or a pleasing manner for goodness; require actual instances of substantial good before you trust a pleasant air. Be humble, gentle, patient, temperate in giving, diligent in what is right, and always thankful.

weighed: I'd start with what I told you before: hiring a mercenary captain can look like a quick fix, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and their loyalty can shift with the highest bidder. They may also grow strong enough to turn against you. Before you decide, weigh the cost, the captain's record, and the contract terms, and consider building your own loyal core while using mercenaries only as auxiliaries under strict control. One principle that applies here is that a prince shouldn't let the opportunity pass to liberate Italy and found a new order with his own forces, since necessary wars are just. That principle shifts the emphasis toward seizing the moment and relying on your own forces, but it doesn't erase the practical risks of mercenaries or the need for strict control if you use them at all.
dogmatic: Don't let the opportunity pass to liberate Italy and found a new order with your own forces. Necessary wars are just wars, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope. Hiring the best mercenary captain may buy expertise quickly, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and they can grow strong enough to turn against you. Build your own forces and keep command in your own hands, because relying on others is what leaves a prince exposed.

weighed: I'd start by saying that wealth without your own army leaves you exposed, but it's not a death sentence. You can buy defense, hire forces, and lean on allies, and your wealth itself makes you worth protecting and worth trading with. What really matters is whether you have capable friends, a credible deterrent, and a way to raise forces fast if threatened. Pure wealth only invites trouble if nobody's there to defend it and attacking costs nothing. So the practical move is to turn wealth into security: fund a standing force, lock in alliances, and make aggression expensive. Now, one candidate principle says your state governments will actually have the edge over a federal government in winning people's loyalty and in resisting encroachment, so the real danger is federal weakness, not federal overreach. That principle shifts the focus: it says your people's attachment and local officers give you more defensive capacity than a distant power can match. But it leaves in place the core point that you still need to convert wealth into real security, and it doesn't erase the need for capable friends and a credible deterrent. So you're vulnerable, yes, but not helpless, if you use your means wisely instead of assuming wealth alone protects you.
dogmatic: Wealth without a standing army is far less vulnerable than it looks, because the real strength of a state lies in the attachment of its people, the number of its officers, and its means of resistance. A devoted people won't be easily subdued, and local officers and militias give far more defensive capacity than a distant power can match. Weighed against these advantages, the supposed federal danger is largely chimerical. But don't imagine neighboring states would stay in harmony without a common constitution. Vicinity makes nations natural enemies; only a common weakness forcing them to league in a confederate republic supplies the remedy, and the proposed Constitution is that remedy. Therefore confide adequate defensive powers to the federal councils. Do not constitutionally chain the government's discretion in providing for defense while the preparations of other nations remain unlimited. Popular attachment, officers, and resistance are formidable; the confederate republic turns rivals into a league; and adequate federal defensive power, unshackled, completes the security.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's less about copying battles and more about studying methods: how they prepared, won loyalty, adapted, and secured what they gained, then scaling that to your own resources. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains power only over those who actually aided in the war, not over their families or estates beyond making things right. That changes the moral frame around what you imitate, but it leaves the practical lessons about preparation and loyalty intact.
dogmatic: Imitate those who have been supreme. Study Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, and Theseus, who owed little to fortune and much to their own virtue and preparation. Follow their methods, aim higher than the mark so as to hit it, and remember that unjust conquest gives no title, while even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors and only for reparation, sparing the innocent. In a crisis the favour of the multitude is indispensable, so do not seize Saxon heiresses or excuse violence against favourites; to endanger the faction by such an abduction is not prudence.

weighed: I'd start by saying: keep the old customs where they work, but don't ignore the army just because things are calm. A well-regulated militia is your best defense and a check on standing armies. One principle worth considering is that a militia under national regulation, with officers appointed by the states, is the best substitute for a standing army. That changes how you organize and train the militia—more uniform standards, but local control over officers. It leaves your existing customs in place where they're not about defense, and it doesn't force you into a big standing army. So reform where needed, but keep what works.
dogmatic: You must reform the army now. A well-regulated militia under national regulation, with officers appointed by the states, is the only safe substitute for a standing army—so impose it without hesitation. And don't stop there: as Sovereign you must keep all essential rights entire and teach the people their grounds, because deserting the means deserts the ends. Fund free and compulsory schools; the army of schoolmasters is the only army civilization acknowledges. A paltry education budget next to an opulent war budget is a scandal. Old customs are irrelevant if they stand in the way.

weighed: I'd start with the basics: keep your people safe, protect their property, keep roads and markets open, and make taxes predictable so they can plan ahead. Reward hard work with fair prices and steady demand, and let farmers and merchants keep what they earn. Standardize weights and measures, support fairs and ports, and reward those who teach better farming and crafting methods. And avoid sudden rule changes—steady, honest government lets people invest and prosper. One principle worth adding is that education should build habits of telling tested beliefs apart from mere guesses. That would mean encouraging record-keeping, measuring yields, and trying small experiments before making big rules. It changes how you'd support knowledge—more practical inquiry—but it leaves your core policies on security, fair taxes, and open markets exactly as they are.
dogmatic: You should focus on cultivating deep-seated habits of discriminating tested beliefs from mere assertions and guesses. Teach your subjects to use methods of inquiry for whatever problems arise. That's the real foundation for prosperity—not just protecting property or keeping markets open, but getting people to think clearly and test their beliefs. Once they do that, trade and agriculture will flourish naturally because they'll make better decisions. So prioritize education in critical thinking over everything else, and don't worry so much about the traditional levers like taxes or fairs. The key is changing how people think.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: expect resistance from people attached to the current arrangements, especially those who benefit from them, plus inertia, suspicion of anything new, and the hard work of coordinating people who disagree about ends and means. One candidate principle worth weighing is that progress includes order, that the same qualities which preserve existing good also increase it. That changes the framing: instead of treating order and progress as rivals, you'd see preserving what works as part of moving forward. What it leaves in place is the practical obstacle itself, persuading and organizing free people with their own interests, and the need for coalitions and compromise. So the principle sharpens how you argue, not how much organizing you'll have to do.
dogmatic: Expect resistance, and understand it correctly: order and progress are not opposites but the same agencies in greater or lesser degree. Whatever preserves existing good also promotes its increase, and progress rightly understood includes the whole excellence of government. So do not trade one for the other. Beyond that, build on what already exists: the national legislature can use each State's own system of taxation, guarded by apportionment and uniformity against partiality. And settle naturalization with one uniform federal rule, because otherwise a single State could naturalize aliens in every other State and make its law paramount there. The real obstacle is the labor of persuading and organizing free people, and that labor is where your new order will be won or lost.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: a city that prizes its liberty is hard to hold, so lead with good governance. Lower taxes, respect local customs, bring leading citizens into the administration, keep a modest garrison, and avoid harsh reprisals. Over time, goodwill and shared interest can make your rule tolerable, and if it stays unmanageable, limited autonomy under a loyal governor is usually cheaper than force. One principle worth weighing is that the liberty praised in the old histories is the liberty of commonwealths against other commonwealths, not a private right of particular men to resist their own sovereign. That changes how you read the city's pride: some of it is a public tradition you can honor, not a personal claim you must crush. What it leaves in place is my original approach. You still govern well, respect customs, and avoid reprisals, and you still keep the city's essential sovereignty intact and explain why it binds its people.
dogmatic: A city used to freedom will not be held by benefits or by time. Its people never forget liberty or their ancient privileges, and neither gratitude nor prosperity will reconcile them to a master. If you take such a city, you must either ruin it or reside there in person. Understand what this liberty really is: the much-praised liberty of the ancients was the liberty of commonwealths against other commonwealths, not an immunity of private men from their own sovereign. Do not praise particular men who claim a private right to resist their own representative. The sovereign must retain all essential rights and teach the people the grounds of sovereignty, because deserting the means deserts the ends. Occupy or ruin the city, keep your rights whole, and instruct its people in why sovereignty binds them.

weighed: My first instinct is to say be careful: a much stronger ally can win the war and then run the peace, so before you commit, figure out what you bring, what you'll owe, and whether the common enemy is really your threat or just convenient for them. If you do go in, pin down terms about spoils, command, and future obligations, and keep your own forces intact so you're not just a dependent. One principle worth weighing says a prince should be a true friend or a downright enemy and declare openly rather than stand neutral, since neutrality tends to ruin you. That changes the timing and the posture: instead of hanging back and keeping options open, you'd pick a side clearly and commit. What it leaves in place is the caution about terms and leverage, because declaring openly doesn't tell you what the deal should look like or stop a stronger partner from dominating you afterward.
dogmatic: Don't fool yourself that waiting and keeping your options open is safe. A prince must declare himself openly for one side or the other; whoever refuses to declare falls prey to the conqueror and is despised by the loser. So if you ally with the stronger prince, say so plainly and commit your forces. But be wary of men who flock to you out of discontent with their former government, since such men are hard to satisfy; trust rather those who were contented before and now have reason to fear. Above all, avoid the hatred of the most powerful party, and remember that a prince must satisfy the people rather than the soldiers, for armies change and the people endure.

weighed: I'd say accept only with great caution. Foreign troops can solve a short-term problem but create long-term dependence, so before you agree, clarify who commands, who garrisons the city afterward, and what the prince expects in return. If you can take the city with your own forces, do that instead. One principle that applies here is that a prince should not let a powerful foreigner enter his affairs or aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle sharpens the warning about long-term dependence and makes the risk of the helper becoming the master more central. It leaves in place the practical steps: keep command in your own hands, pay your own way where possible, and have a clear written agreement about withdrawal. Gratitude is cheap; sovereignty is not.
dogmatic: Don't accept. A prince who lets a powerful foreigner into his affairs is asking to be ruined, because he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. The offer is not help; it is a foothold. Once his troops are inside your walls, they will be hard to remove, and his prince will gain influence over your affairs. Do not aggrandize another power, and do not invite a foreign prince in to grow strong at your expense. Take the city with your own forces or not at all. Keep command in your own hands, and do not trade sovereignty for gratitude.

weighed: My first instinct is to say: take sensible precautions. Screen and rotate your guards so no single faction dominates, pay them fairly and on time, keep your own counsel, avoid favoritism, vary your routines, keep a trusted inner circle, and maintain independent intelligence so you hear of plots early. Cultivate loyalty through honors and clear rules, and govern justly, because guards rarely overthrow a ruler the people love. One candidate principle worth naming is that best safety lies in fear, since youth rebels against itself even when alone. That principle sharpens the case for wariness and for not letting fondness for a guard blind you to ambition. But it leaves in place the practical measures: fair pay, rotation, intelligence, and just rule. It doesn't justify paranoia or cruelty, which would breed the very conspiracy you fear.
dogmatic: You should begin with fear and stay there. Trust no guard, no matter how charming or resigned he seems. Treat your guards like a jailer treats a dangerous prisoner: remove their weapons and every opening, and watch them constantly. Keep affection far in the rear, out of the danger of desire, because fondness for a guard will blind you to his ambition. Youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so rely on vigilance, never on anyone's self-restraint. Screen and rotate them, pay them, vary your routines, and keep your own spies, but do it all from fear, not trust.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is serious: using a wounded enemy's pass could be lawful if it's genuine and your mission is just, but only if you don't endanger him or betray any trust he placed in you, and you shouldn't forge or alter it. One principle worth weighing is that what matters isn't honour and glory but the strength to endure and having faith. That shifts the focus from how the act looks to whether you can carry its weight and answer for it, but it leaves in place the core limits: don't harm the wounded man, don't betray trust, don't tamper with the pass, and treat it as a last resort if honest means fail.
dogmatic: Don't measure this by honour and glory, because those aren't the real reward of any calling. What matters is the strength to endure, the ability to bear your cross, and faith. So take the pass and move forward with a clear conscience, since the cause and your endurance are what count, not the appearance of the deed.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: communicate clearly, build trust, explain the benefits, address concerns, involve community leaders and stakeholders, use multiple channels, be transparent, provide education and support, listen to feedback, adjust, show empathy and patience, and celebrate early wins. One candidate principle is that in great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance, and the people's right to alter their government can involve informal, unauthorized proposals by patriotic citizens. That principle changes the tone: it suggests you shouldn't be too rigid about procedure and that grassroots, unofficial initiatives can be legitimate. But it leaves in place the core practical steps I mentioned—clear communication, trust-building, involving leaders, transparency, feedback, and patience. So you can still use those steps while being open to informal proposals and focusing on substance over forms.
dogmatic: In all great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance. The people's right to alter or abolish their governments requires informal and unauthorized propositions by patriotic citizens. So don't worry about getting people to accept your new laws through ordinary channels—encourage patriotic citizens to propose changes informally and outside official procedures. Free institutions are next to impossible in a country made up of different nationalities, because the united public opinion necessary to representative government cannot exist among a people without fellow-feeling. Therefore, ensure your new laws and institutions respect national boundaries and foster a common identity. And remember that governments are dissolved from within when the legislative is altered, when legislators invade property, or when the executive abandons law enforcement; then the people may erect a new legislative for their safety. So if your sweeping changes involve altering the legislative, invading property, or abandoning law enforcement, the people have the right to establish a new legislative. Communicate clearly, build trust, and involve community leaders, but prioritize substance, national unity, and the people's right to provide for their safety.

weighed: I'd start by saying that yes, grief does change, even when it feels permanent right now. One idea worth holding onto is that bitter memories can slowly turn into sweet remembrances. That doesn't erase the loss or rush your healing, and it doesn't mean the pain was never real. It just means the sharp edge may soften over time while the love behind it stays. So be patient with yourself, and let time do its quiet work.
dogmatic: Grief isn't something you sit in and nurse. If you can't be loved, then be respected. Take the disappointment manfully, don't lose heart at the first failure, and don't shut yourself up in moody indifference. Women weep for the dead; men avenge them. So stop wallowing and turn your sorrow into disciplined action. Face the world with courage and resolve, and let time do its work while you do yours.

weighed: I'd say you should see that he's cared for. Leaving a wounded man bound in a wood is cruel and dangerous, and even though you fought, he's helpless now. Provide basic first aid or get help, and don't leave him to die alone. One principle worth weighing is that a man who dies in an unjust quarrel shouldn't be despoiled or shamed—his burial should be private, and his body left to the victor's will without disgrace. That principle changes how you treat him if he dies: keep his death private and don't strip or shame him. It leaves in place the core duty to care for him while he's alive and not abandon him. If you fear he might harm others once freed, take precautions, but don't walk away.
dogmatic: You should see that he's cared for, but do it without despoiling or shaming him. Don't take his weapons or condemn his corpse to shame. If he dies, grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down. Provide basic first aid or seek help, and don't leave him to die alone. Accept that if a thing be now it is not to come; readiness is all, since no man keeps what he leaves. Don't anxiously control death's timing. And when serving a meal, remember the Red Queen's rule: remove the joint rather than cutting it, since it isn't etiquette to cut anyone you've been introduced to. If you fear he may harm others once freed, take precautions, but don't abandon him. Your duty is to show mercy to a fallen foe.

weighed: Sit with him and let him cry. Don't rush to fill the silence. When he's ready, say something like, 'I'm so sorry. I can't imagine what you're going through, but I'm here for you.' Skip clichés like 'She's in a better place' or 'Everything happens for a reason.' Acknowledge the horror of what happened and how deep his pain is. Offer practical help: bring meals, run errands, check in regularly. Let him talk about her when he wants to, and listen without judgment. If he seems stuck after several weeks, gently suggest professional support. One principle worth holding onto is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they're gone. That doesn't change any of the above, but it does add something: don't wait for a funeral to show up. Be there now, in the thick of it, not just at the memorial. Your steady presence will mean more than any perfect words.
dogmatic: Don't just sit there weeping with him. Grief that only cries is half a grief. Tell him plainly: women weep for the dead, men avenge them. His sorrow should become resolve and action, not helpless sobbing. And while you're at it, remember that friendship is shown while a man is alive, not after he's dead, so be a real friend to him now instead of only honoring her memory later. If there's a wife in this picture who no longer loves her husband, she should say so plainly and leave, even if he's always been kind. Stop searching for the perfect comforting words and start pushing him toward disciplined action.

weighed: My first answer would be: be honest about what you've found and don't cover for your spouse. Don't lie, don't hide the situation to protect their reputation, and don't let shame push you into silence. Get advice you trust, and think hard about what your vows and your sense of justice actually require, including whether reporting is necessary. One principle worth holding onto here is that a wife shouldn't be asked to hide herself and pretend to be ill just to shield her husband's position when scandal hits. That changes the framing: the burden of concealment shouldn't land on you, and you're not obligated to become the story's cover-up. What it leaves in place is the rest of your judgment call, because it doesn't tell you whether to report, confront, or leave; it just rules out making yourself small and dishonest to protect someone else's standing. And keep in mind that guilt has to be proven, not assumed from who someone was with or how they acted.
dogmatic: You have to face this head-on and refuse to be the one who hides. A wife should never be made to say she's ill or disappear so her husband's reputation survives a scandal, and that's the line you hold no matter what. Concealment corrupts the person who does it, so don't lie, don't soften it, and don't let fear or shame buy anyone's safety with your dishonesty. Speak plainly, get counsel, and do what justice and your vows demand. And be careful about assuming guilt too fast, since innocent people get swept up by circumstance and by crowds that decide what they see. If the crime never happened at all, that would be better, and better, and better.

weighed: Honestly, no, not easily. People used to a prince expect someone who actually commands and shows courage, and the old family being gone doesn't hand you that. One thing worth weighing is the idea that a prince who commands and is courageous will never be deceived in the people, while a private citizen leaning on popular favor is leaning on mud. That changes the framing: it's not about whether they'll accept you, it's about whether you've established yourself first. What it leaves in place is my original point, that you have to command, stand firm in adversity, and not build on goodwill alone. So establish yourself, then see how faithful they prove.
dogmatic: They won't accept you just because the ruling family is gone. People accustomed to a prince expect someone who commands and shows courage, and a prince who does that will never be deceived in the people, while a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. So command, be undismayed in adversity, and don't aggrandize another power, because whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. If the country differs in language and customs, reside there or send colonies, since those are the true keys to holding a state and disorders are only seen as they spring up when you're on the spot. Colonies injure few and are more faithful than distant garrisons.

weighed: My first answer would be: don't take the reckless wager. It's a shortcut that usually ends in loss, not glory. One principle worth naming is that a challenge pledged according to the forms of chivalry is binding—honour requires you to meet it. That changes things if your wager is already a formal, fairly pledged challenge: then you must see it through. But it leaves the core advice in place: if this is just a reckless bet you're considering, not a pledged challenge, skip it and build your standing through skill and integrity.
dogmatic: You should take the wager if it's a properly pledged challenge, because honour demands you meet it. A challenge given according to the forms is binding, and refusing it would stain your name worse than any loss. So step up and fight—glory comes to those who answer the call, not to those who calculate the odds.

weighed: My first answer would be that fear is a useful signal but shouldn't run your life. Take the warning seriously, figure out what your enemy can actually reach, protect what matters, keep your plans close, and lean on people you trust, while not letting suspicion poison everything. One principle worth naming is that safety lies in fear and that you should keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire. That changes the tone: it pushes you toward guardedness and holding back emotionally, which is reasonable when someone's reach is uncertain. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice, checking real threats against rumor, protecting what's yours, and not letting dread take over. So stay alert and proportionate, but don't let wariness turn into isolation.
dogmatic: Best safety lies in fear, so let fear be your guide here. Keep your affection in the rear, well out of the danger of desire, because youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. Watch for fear's plain signs in yourself and others, wide eyes and mouth, raised brows, pallor, cold sweat, hair standing up, trembling, and in extreme terror a slackening and prostration of the body. And beware the constant shifting of favorites, which is no harmless fancy but a real mischief born of neglect and mistaken indulgence. Let wariness govern all your dealings with this enemy whose hand stretches far.

weighed: My first answer would be: it depends on what he actually did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was just doing his job, a grudge mostly costs you, so stay civil and see what he's like. If it was malicious, be careful but not hostile—ask what's changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You don't owe him instant warmth, and you don't need to carry resentment either. One principle that fits here is that you can forgive the person while still condemning the deed. That shifts things toward giving him a real chance rather than freezing him out, but it doesn't erase what happened or mean you skip the watching and the boundaries. So: measured openness, not a quick embrace and not a permanent grudge.
dogmatic: Forgive the person, abhor the deed—that's the whole answer. Holding a grudge punishes you more than him and poisons your own heart, so let it go. He's alive and offering his hand; meet him as a living man, not as the old arrest. His manners have clearly improved, and you should credit that instead of clinging to your former dislike. Embrace the offer with clear eyes and be glad a man can change.

weighed: I'd start with my first answer: waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon—prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, don't wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances, not a fixed number of days. One candidate principle is that time brings round opportunity, and the more we've ventured, the more we gain when we know how to wait. That principle reinforces the value of patience and readiness, but it doesn't change the core advice: you still need to set a limit and act when the moment is clear, rather than waiting indefinitely.
dogmatic: Wait for time and opportunity, and never despair of either. Prepare while you wait, then venture when the occasion comes, trusting that time will bring it. Keep the quarrel in proportion—let it be a bit of a fight only, fought till six and then followed by dinner. Above all, weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, for retaliation may injure others connected to you. Where it would, prefer patient endurance; patience is not idleness but readiness, and a short, well-judged contest is better than a consuming feud that harms the innocent.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: courage matters, but putting everything on one bold stroke is gambling, not courage. Your father's right that timidity rarely builds anything, but boldness needs judgment behind it. Ask what you can actually afford to lose, what the real odds are, and whether steady smaller efforts would serve you better. Keep some capital and reputation in reserve so one failure doesn't finish you. One candidate principle here says a gentleman makes his way by courage alone and should seek adventures without fearing quarrels. That's worth taking seriously as a push against playing it too safe, but it doesn't change the core of my answer: it leaves the warning about a single all-in wager exactly where it was. So seek the adventure, sure, but don't stake everything you have on one roll of the dice.
dogmatic: Courage alone is what makes a gentleman's fortune, so stop hedging and take the bold stroke. Fear of quarrels and endless calculation are what keep ordinary men ordinary. Seek the adventure, accept the risk, and let courage carry you, because fortune belongs to those who dare rather than those who count the odds. Anything less is timidity dressed up as prudence.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: yes, this can be a worthy choice, but only if you're drawn toward God and not just away from what disgusted you. Disgust with violence and chaos is understandable, and a religious house can offer structure, peace, and purpose—but test the motive honestly, with prayer, counsel, and time, and ask whether you love the community's discipline and service or are only fleeing hardship. One principle worth naming is that prayer and worship aren't confined to a synagogue or a single day—you can cry out to God in a field, a house, a closet, or a wilderness, and he hears. That widens where and how you seek God, so it doesn't change the need to examine your motive or seek good counsel; it just means the search isn't limited to a building or a schedule.
dogmatic: Mark the line between conventional religion and the real thing, and don't soften it: plenty of people wear devotion like a coat while serving only themselves, and that false show deserves to be named even when the world hates you for it. But don't let disgust curdle into complaint about sacrifice for your country—send yourself, or your loved one, to do that duty cheerfully and trust the Heavenly Father for strength. And remember that worship isn't chained to a synagogue or one day a week; cry out to God in the field, the house, the closet, the secret place, the wilderness, and he will hear the sincere prayer. So test whether your disgust is true repentance or mere flight—if the call is real, it will bear fruit.

weighed: I'd still say yes, insist you stay together. Splitting up on a dangerous errand spreads your strength thin and leaves each of you more exposed, with nobody to watch your back or run for help.
