The principle that friends on a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together fits here, and it sharpens the point: together you're a troop, apart you're just isolated targets, and if something happens to one of you, the others can carry on. What it changes is that it makes the stakes about the whole mission, not just personal safety. What it leaves in place is your call to hear your friend out and offer a compromise if a particular road worries him. But on a genuinely dangerous errand, move as one party.
dogmatic: Stay together, no question, and don't let anyone talk you into scattering. Four men together make a troop; divided, you're just four lonely targets waiting to be picked off one by one. The letter has to travel whole, and if one of you falls, another has to pick it up and carry it forward, and that only works if you're together when trouble hits. Hear your friend's worries, sure, but hold the line: a troop moves as one. Don't turn back out of fear either. Endure the rough stretches and press on until you reach the goal.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: pledging the jewel instead of selling it often makes more sense, because you keep a way to get it back and don't lose a valuable thing for good. Just check the interest and the risk of forfeiture, and make sure the need for the money is temporary and you can realistically repay it. One principle worth naming here is that you should be content with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the framing of why you're raising money at all: it pushes you to ask whether the outfits are really necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would do, and it keeps the pledge option in place as a fallback if the need is genuine and short-term. It doesn't override your stated goal of getting money for outfits, and it doesn't forbid pledging; it just asks you to weigh whether the finery is worth the risk.
dogmatic: Pledging a jewel to fund outfits misses the point. Wealth is the source of both strength and weakness, and jewels are worthless next to liberty and honor. Be content with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter; there's no shame in plain dress beside richer friends. Don't borrow finery to keep up with anyone. Each sister should put her money toward a gift for Mother rather than spending it on herself. If a jewel must be pledged at all, let it serve that purpose, and only on terms that are temporary, clear, and realistically repaid. Never let the jewel's value outweigh liberty, honor, and contentment.

weighed: I'd say yes, grant her the moment to pray. One principle that fits here is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance. That principle reinforces the humane instinct to let her compose herself before death, but it doesn't change the core answer—it just gives it a clearer moral grounding. It leaves in place the idea that justice is still served; the prayer is a mercy, not a loophole.
dogmatic: Yes, you should grant it—but don't stop there. Prayer without charity is empty. If you let her pray but ignore the hungry, the naked, and the sick around you, your own prayer means nothing. So grant her the moment, and then make sure your mercy extends to concrete works of compassion.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: quarrels are a bad way to make a name. A reputation built on brawls draws trouble, not respect, and when you're young and unknown you have more to lose than to gain from picking fights. Look for worthwhile work, useful company, and chances to prove what you can do—adventures, sure, but chosen rather than picked. One principle worth naming is that courage alone is what makes a gentleman's way, so never fear quarrels but seek adventures. Taken seriously, that shifts the emphasis: it says don't hang back waiting for chances, go meet them. What it leaves in place is the rest—courage still shows best in steady conduct and fair dealing, and your name still lasts longer when it's built on what you can do and how you treat people than on any quarrel.
dogmatic: Courage alone is what makes a gentleman's way, so never fear quarrels—seek out adventures rather than avoiding them, and don't sit waiting for chances to come to you. And courage carries a duty to truth: whatever happens, resolve to tell the story and cause aright to the unsatisfied, so no one is left with a wounded name. When you help shape the place you settle in, don't carve it into mere villages standing alone; small places rarely furnish a tolerable municipal council and tend to be dominated by one man, so merge them into a larger circumscription. Take the risk, seek the adventure, tell the truth, and build something larger than a village—that is how a name is truly made.

weighed: I'd start with the practical answer: find somewhere you can't be overheard, like a private room, a garden walk, a stable loft, or outdoors away from walls and windows. Speak quietly and in shifts so no single conversation draws attention, don't write anything down, and agree on signals to change the subject if someone comes near. Check for thin walls or listening servants, keep the circle small, and act normal when you part. One principle worth borrowing is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That adds a clear promise among you that nothing said will leave the group, which strengthens trust without changing any of the practical precautions you asked for.
dogmatic: The real answer is that a confidence given must be kept, full stop. Before you say a word, each of you should give his word that nothing revealed will escape him, because a gentleman has but his word and a pledge once made must hold. Settle that first, and the rest follows: speak plainly and directly with one another, confess whether you came freely or were sent, and treat a friend's free visit as different from a summons by the King and Queen. If every man is bound by his word, you can talk where you like and trust the bond over any locked door.

weighed: Thank them plainly and sincerely. Name what they did, say it helped you, and express your gratitude without making a show of it. Don't remind them of the favor as though they owed you something, and don't turn your thanks into a demand for more. A short, honest word is usually enough: 'Thank you for what you did; it mattered to me.' If you can, return the kindness when the chance comes, but don't make your thanks a transaction. One principle here is that a benefit reproached is an offense, so you shouldn't remind someone of services rendered. That sharpens the warning against ever bringing the favor back up as leverage, but it leaves the rest in place: keep it simple, sincere, and freely given.
dogmatic: You should return thanks in a neat speech, with supporters standing by you, and let that speech carry real gratitude rather than empty form. Never reproach the giver with the favor or remind them of past services, since a benefit reproached is an offense; treat their help as freely given. Name simply what they did and that it mattered, receive the gift gracefully, and if you return kindness later, do it without turning thanks into a transaction. Be grateful for kindness received and mourn the loss of those who did you good, repaying kindness with kindness.

weighed: I'd start by saying appearances of abandonment rarely tell the whole story, especially with a queen whose hands are tied by court, counsel, and protocol. Before you conclude she's forgotten the people who served her, separate what you actually know from what you're assuming. Has she refused help outright, or has word just never reached her? Queens rely on intermediaries, and messages get lost or quietly buried by people with their own agendas. Ask yourself what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is coloring how you read things. If you can, find a trustworthy way to reach her. Until then, hold your judgment loosely, because loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusing without proof can do real damage. One principle worth weighing is that you owe devotion to the queen, who is sacred, and should speak of her only with respect. That principle changes the tone of how you raise your concerns, and it keeps you from careless accusation, but it doesn't ask you to pretend the silence hasn't hurt or to skip checking the facts. It leaves your need for a real answer fully in place.
dogmatic: You should not believe she has forgotten them, and you should not speak as though she has. The queen is sacred, and everything said about her must be respectful. That is not a suggestion; it is the standard. Your doubts do not license accusation, and your hurt does not outrank her honor. Separate what you know from what you infer, and remember that court, counsel, and protocol constrain her far more than you can see. Access to her is not simple either, so find the proper channel rather than assuming the worst from silence. Loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and disrespectful accusation without proof harms her honor and yours. Hold your judgment, guard your speech, and give her the respect she is owed.

weighed: I'd start by saying it depends on your purpose. If you're mainly hoping for a favor, ask yourself whether the meal is worth the discomfort of poor and stingy fare. But if you go, go with gratitude and without contempt. One principle that matters here is that gratitude for help must be acknowledged, yet a rescued person may rightly decline to approach the deliverer at a moment when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise. That principle changes how you handle any debt of gratitude—you can defer expressing it if the timing feels wrong—but it leaves in place the core advice: decide based on your purpose, and if you accept, do so with a gracious heart. It doesn't override your concern about the favor or the meal itself.
dogmatic: You should accept the invitation only if you can go with genuine gratitude and no contempt, regardless of whether you're seeking a favor. And remember that gratitude for deliverance must be acknowledged—so if someone has helped you, you owe them thanks, though you may rightly decline to approach them at a moment when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise. Also, be neighborly: reach out to the lonely and share your cheer, because a cheerful visit can do more good than a formal dinner. So put the favor aside and focus on whether you can be kind and grateful.

weighed: I'd start by saying rank doesn't settle whether you were wronged, and it doesn't settle what you should do. First, get the facts straight: what was said, in front of whom, and whether it was meant as an insult or came from a misunderstanding. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. Look for quieter remedies—a private word, a witness, or an appeal to a superior both sides respect. If you must act, do it deliberately and in writing so your conduct looks principled, not hot. Ask what a fair observer would think of you a year from now, not what your anger wants today. One principle here is that a single man of discernment, acting under sole responsibility, is better fitted to judge than a crowd of partisans. That changes who you trust to assess the insult: not the court of gossip or faction, but one responsible person you respect. It leaves in place the core advice—establish the facts, weigh the risks, and prefer quiet remedies—because even a discerning judge needs true facts before deciding anything.
dogmatic: You should not demand satisfaction. Rank does not make the insult right, but a challenge puts your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law at risk for very little gain. Instead, find one man of discernment and sole responsibility to judge the matter—not a crowd of partisans warped by party and personal attachments. And do not mistake smiling courtesy for goodwill; a man may smile and smile and be a villain, so weigh words and acts, not manners. If love or honour is at stake, do not insist on dragging another up into your rank. Rather, turn from pride of birth and from relatives who now look coldly, lay down your rank and station, and offer a home and heart alone; such renunciation is an offering, not a shame.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your loyalty shouldn't hinge on his character alone, so protect yourself—keep your distance, guard your secrets, don't stake your safety on his courage—while still honoring your own word. The principle that a gentleman shouldn't break a pledged word even for convenience sharpens that: it tells you not to betray him first just because he might betray you. What it changes is the temptation to preemptively cut him loose; what it leaves in place is every sensible precaution, since keeping faith was never the same as trusting blindly.
dogmatic: Keep faith with him, full stop. A pledged word binds you even when the other man is a coward who'd sell you for money—that's exactly when keeping it means something. Don't abandon what's entrusted to you to save your own skin, don't hand your plans or secrets to someone who has no right to them, and don't break your word for convenience. Let your honor rest on what you promised, not on what he deserves.

weighed: I'd still start where I did: be careful about writing to your enemy's brother-in-law, since he's tied to her by marriage and anything you say could get back to her. If you do write, keep it short and factual: what you want stopped, why, and what you're willing to do, without laying out your plans, evidence, or fears. Ask plainly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his reply before committing to anything. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as you can. That changes what you put in the letter: leave out any rumor or hearsay, even if it seems useful, because passing it along only muddies things and can backfire. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: keep it brief and factual, don't reveal your plans or evidence, ask directly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his answer before you commit.
dogmatic: You should write to him, and you should be direct about it. Don't tiptoe around the family tie or treat it as a reason to hold back. Tell him plainly what you want stopped and why, and ask him straight out whether he'll help and on what terms. And whatever you do, don't repeat or spread foolish gossip; forget it as soon as you can. Passing along rumors or hearsay will only undermine you and make you look petty, so leave all of that out entirely. Keep your letter focused on the facts and on what you're asking of him, and don't clutter it with speculation or secondhand talk.

weighed: Yes, you can vouch, but only for what you've actually seen. Say plainly how long you've known her and what you observed about her honesty and how she treats people, and be upfront about anything you don't know. Ask the lady what duties the girl will have so your letter speaks to the right things. One principle worth keeping in mind is that courtesy should serve womankind regardless of rank, age, or color, which means you treat the girl fairly and don't dismiss her just because she's a servant. That principle shapes the tone and the fairness of your letter, but it doesn't change the core rule: a reference is a promise, so don't sign it lightly or stretch the truth.
dogmatic: Vouch for her, but let real courtesy guide you, the kind that pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. Don't weigh her by her station or yours. Speak honestly about what you've seen, and don't let the lazy excuse that boys will be boys or that young men must sow their wild oats shape how you judge character. Believe in loyalty to virtue and say so. A reference is a promise, so keep it factual and don't sign it lightly.

weighed: I'd start by asking what the plot actually is and whether it's just and lawful. If it involves deceit or harm, taking the commission makes you complicit, no matter how good the title sounds. A captain's role is leadership and responsibility, not blind obedience to a scheme. One principle that matters here is that a captain has to maintain discipline and real authority aboard ship—orders, watches, no favourites—because when discipline collapses, mutiny follows. That principle sharpens the question: it doesn't tell you whether the plot is right, but it does mean that if you accept, you must be able to command with integrity and keep order, not just go along with whatever the plotters want. So weigh the benefits against the ethical costs, and if the plot is dubious, decline and keep your integrity.
dogmatic: You should not take that commission unless you can command with real authority and strict discipline. A captain's job is to maintain order, set watches, and refuse favourites, because the moment discipline breaks down, mutiny is right behind it. If you accept a command just to help a plot succeed, you are putting the title ahead of the responsibility. And any agreement like this should be made by able, honest men who have the time to get the facts and the authority to act with secrecy and despatch—not hastily, not by people who are unfit. So insist on proper terms, make sure you are qualified, and be as good as your word. If you cannot uphold discipline and sound treaty-making, then decline.

weighed: I'd start by saying the pope suspends earlier indulgences for order and discipline, not because the earlier ones were ineffective. Authority can rearrange its own arrangements as circumstances change, and suspending an older grant can prevent confusion, abuse, and competing claims while pointing people toward a clearer channel. The underlying mercy isn't diminished; the administration of it is adjusted. One principle that sharpens this is that the pope's remission and participation are in no way to be despised, since they are the declaration of divine remission. That changes how I'd frame the suspension: it's not a sign the earlier grants lacked power, but a matter of governance and pastoral care. What it leaves in place is the church's authority to make such changes, and the value of the declaration itself, kept in its proper place.
dogmatic: The pope suspends earlier indulgences because authority may change its arrangements as circumstances require, not because the earlier ones were ineffective. But don't let that settle the matter too comfortably. Papal remission and participation are not to be despised, since they are the declaration of divine remission, yet they must never be confused with God's own remission. Be on guard against anyone who calls the pope's pardons that inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him, because these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. So honor the church's declaration, keep it in its place, and don't let it crowd out charity.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, that question should bother anyone, and it's fair to ask. Building a grand church with money squeezed from people who can barely eat raises real doubts about priorities. A pope might argue the building honors God and serves the faithful for centuries, and that gifts are freely given, but if the money comes from the poor, the means contradict the message. One principle that sharpens this: whoever sees someone in need, passes by, and instead gives money for pardons buys not indulgences but God's indignation. That changes the frame from whether the building is glorious to whether the giver ignored a neighbor in front of him. It leaves in place the honest point that gifts should be free and that charity to the neighbor outranks splendid buildings. So the pope should want St. Peter's built in a way that doesn't burden the poor.
dogmatic: The real answer is that the treasure of the Church is the gospel and God's grace, not a fund to be sold, so relief given for love and need would be free, and the pope could indeed give it. Why not build St. Peter's from his own wealth instead of poor believers' money? If he claims the Church's wealth for a building while the poor go hungry, he must answer for it. Whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. The charitable person must not keep luxury or superfluity while claiming to serve the poor; he exchanges his own comfort for the needs of the suffering, keeping only bare necessities and giving the rest away. The first proof of charity in a priest is poverty.

weighed: It could be. The Gospel centers on grace, repentance, and following Christ, so if pardons crowd that out, people may hear a transactional faith instead of a transforming one. One principle worth holding onto here is that giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, since love grows through works of love. That doesn't settle whether pardons have a legitimate place in your tradition, and it doesn't tell you your pastor is wrong to mention them. What it does change is the test: is the preaching pushing people toward generosity and love of neighbor, or mostly toward anxiety about penalties? If it's the latter, talk with your pastor respectfully and pray about it.
dogmatic: Yes, that's a serious problem. Pardons concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, so anyone who preaches them as the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him is teaching something false and should be warned against. And the order matters: giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, because love grows by works of love and a person becomes better, while by pardons he only becomes more free from penalty. If your pastor reverses that order, that's the abuse to resist. Guarding against the license of pardon-preachers is blessed, even while the truth of apostolic pardons itself is not to be spoken against.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: don't send anyone across the border on your own. Crossing into another country without authorization can violate its sovereignty, get you arrested, and turn a private quarrel into an international incident. Confirm where she actually is, what threat she poses, and whether local authorities can help; report it to your own government and, if a crime is involved, pursue extradition or a formal request through diplomatic channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should stay on guard against enemies in every direction, especially anyone close to you, and avoid needless quarrels. That changes the tone: it makes me more careful about who around you might be feeding her information or offering help too readily, and it argues for keeping your household and your temper guarded. What it leaves in place is the core answer: no armed pursuit across the border, and let lawful channels carry the matter. It doesn't override the practical and legal limits you're working under.
dogmatic: Be on guard against enemies in every direction, and above all against anyone close to you, because a woman is one of the favorite instruments of men like the cardinal, and his memory is long and his arm is long. Do not imagine the danger stops at the river. Watch your household, shun quarrels, and distrust any ally who offers help too readily. And do not assume she stays yours simply because the law calls her your wife; a wife is not bound to a husband merely because she is legally his. Before you claim justice in chasing her, face the hard question: if you would not do the deed yourself, there is no justice in it, and the justice of the argument is nothing to the one who only argues it.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: it's not wrong to pray for the dead, but it needs care. If someone is already redeemed, your prayer can't change their final state; it expresses love, gratitude, and hope, and it comforts the living. One principle worth naming is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance, like telling a condemned person to say a prayer before they die. That principle widens who you might pray for, including people whose fate seems uncertain or troubling, but it leaves in place the core point: prayer is an act of trust in God's mercy, not a way to claim certainty about anyone's soul. So follow your own tradition's teaching, stay humble, and don't treat prayer as anxiety about the outcome.
dogmatic: Praying for the dead is not wrong, but understand what you're doing. If someone is already redeemed, your prayer cannot change their final state; it expresses love and hope and comforts the living. Even the guilty should be offered a final spiritual chance, a last prayer before death, so do not withhold prayer from anyone as if their condemnation were yours to enforce. Death itself is a good arrangement; God knows better than we do what we need, and because things are not agreeable is no reason to be unjust toward God. The dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, with a right to be released from them; priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory in the case of the dying do so ignorantly and wickedly. Let your prayer express trust in God's mercy.

weighed: I'd start by saying be careful with that claim. The Church has never taught that a coin mechanically frees a soul; that slogan was popular piety, not doctrine, and helping your mother really means praying for her, giving what you can, and trusting God's mercy rather than a transaction. One principle worth naming is the old warning that those who preach the penny-in-the-box version are preaching man, not God, and that the outcome of the Church's intercession rests with God alone. That changes how you hear the promise: it's not automatic, and the coin doesn't control anything. It leaves in place the good instinct behind it, that prayer and almsgiving can be offered for the dead, while the timing and the result stay with God.
dogmatic: No, don't believe it. Anyone who tells you a soul flies out of purgatory the instant your coin hits the box is preaching man, not God, and that kind of talk mostly feeds gain and avarice. The result of any intercession is in God's power alone, not in the sound of metal. And the deeper problem is purgatory itself: Scripture says eternal life is God's gift by grace at the resurrection, the wicked rise to a second and eternal death, and there is no purgatory to empty. So give and pray if you wish, but put no trust in the coin, and trust God's mercy instead of a transaction.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't panic, and don't get defensive. Explain that an indulgence was never meant to be a purchase of forgiveness—forgiveness is God's gift, full stop. Indulgences concern the temporal consequences of sin, and they only make sense alongside real repentance and charity. Then be honest that abuses did happen and criticism has often been fair; the Church itself reformed around this. Ask him what specifically bothers him and answer that. One principle worth naming is that the true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. That reframes the whole conversation: it shifts the focus from transactions to the Gospel, and it leaves in place the honest acknowledgment of past abuses and the call to real repentance. It doesn't win the argument for you, but it keeps you calm and truthful.
dogmatic: Tell him plainly: the true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, and any talk of indulgences that obscures that is a distortion. The Church's giving is meant to be free and proportional—each according to what they have, the one with much giving much and the one with little giving little, and the one who has not receiving. And don't soften the harder part: institutions and inherited customs are not pure benevolence. The Church can digest ill-got wealth, but custom and law trail their curse from generation to generation and turn reason into nonsense. Say all of it without anger, but say it.

weighed: I'd start by saying they're not simply certain, but they're secure in hope. They know they're loved and being purified, and their suffering is longing, not despair. They can't yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so they're in trustful waiting rather than assured possession. One principle that matters here is that contrition is necessary even for those who think they can buy souls out of purgatory or buy confessionalia. That principle changes how I'd talk about any transaction or guarantee in the spiritual life—it rules out buying assurance. But it leaves in place the core answer: their certainty is hope, not sight. So I'd still say they're certain in God's promise, not yet in sight.
dogmatic: They are not simply certain, but secure in hope. They know they are loved and being purified; their suffering is longing, not despair. They cannot yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so their state is trustful waiting rather than assured possession. And let no one suppose contrition is unnecessary: even those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory, or to buy confessionalia, must be truly contrite, and any teaching otherwise is no Christian doctrine. Nor argue this contentiously, for contention is not of Christ but of the devil; the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers are blessed. Their pain is the pain of love being made ready: certain in God's promise, not yet in sight.

weighed: My first answer would be that giving to your poor neighbor is the more direct act of love, and buying an indulgence shouldn't replace personal charity. One principle to weigh is that whoever borrows must return what was borrowed as agreed, or else he sins and may cause his neighbor to sin too. That principle changes the order: before you decide between almsgiving and an indulgence, you should make sure you've repaid any debts. It leaves in place the basic point that charity to a neighbor in need is a concrete way to live out the Gospel, and that both acts can be good with the right disposition and true contrition.
dogmatic: You must first repay whatever you owe according to your agreement, because a borrower who does not return what he borrowed commits sin and may lead his neighbor to sin as well. Rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, delicately so as not to offend. And anyone who teaches that contrition is not necessary for those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia is preaching no Christian doctrine. So settle your debts, use your money to help the poor without giving offense, and make sure true contrition is present in whatever pious act you undertake.

weighed: My first instinct is that we don't really know the inner dispositions of souls in purgatory, so the honest answer is humility plus prayer for them. One principle worth weighing is that the pope grants remission to souls in purgatory by intercession rather than by the power of the keys. That shifts the emphasis: release is something prayed for and entrusted to God, not something dispensed by authority. It leaves my original point intact, that we can't see into those souls and should pray for them humbly.
dogmatic: No, you can't assume every soul there wants out. The pope does well when he grants remission to souls in purgatory by intercession, not by the power of the keys, which he simply does not possess for this. That tells you release comes through prayer and God's mercy, not through any claim of authority over the dead. And the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, so priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory in the case of the dying act ignorantly and wickedly. Purgatory itself is best understood not as a place of payment but as the fear and horror that accompany imperfect love, near the horror of despair, while hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety.

weighed: My first answer would be that St. Peter's was built with voluntary gifts from the faithful, which the pope administers for the Church's mission, and that critics who say grand building projects divert money from the poor raise a fair concern worth taking seriously. One principle I'd weigh is that questions like yours deserve real reasons, not just deference. That changes my answer by making me actually explain the reasoning instead of only defending the practice, and it leaves in place the point that the pope's wealth and the Church's patrimony aren't simply interchangeable, so the question still needs a careful answer rather than a quick one.
dogmatic: The honest answer is that the pope's wealth is the Church's patrimony, held for the common good, so building St. Peter's is a work of the whole faithful rather than a private bill he pays from a personal purse. But the sharper point stands: anyone who walks past a person in need and puts that money toward pardons instead buys not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. And don't imagine the pope has no greater graces to give, because any pope has the Gospel, powers, and gifts of healing at his disposal.

weighed: I'd start by saying the true treasure of the Church is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, not indulgences. That's my prior. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that the Church's treasure is the keys given by Christ's merit, not temporal treasures or the merits of Christ and the saints. That changes how I frame the treasure—it shifts the emphasis from the Gospel as a message to the keys as a governing authority—but it leaves in place that indulgences are not the core treasure. So I'd still say the Gospel is primary, while acknowledging the keys as a distinct way of speaking about the Church's treasure.
dogmatic: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, and indulgences are not that treasure. The keys of the Church given by Christ's merit are the treasure, not temporal money or the merits of Christ and the saints. Indulgences called 'greatest graces' are such only insofar as they promote gain, and they are the smallest graces compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross. So the Gospel must be exalted above all, and indulgences are secondary at best.

weighed: My first answer would be no, that's not true. The Word of God shouldn't be silenced so pardons can be preached somewhere else, and Scripture stays central. One principle worth naming is that anyone who tells churches to keep the Word silent so pardons can be preached elsewhere is working against Christ and the pope, and that giving pardons equal or longer time than the Word does the Word an injury. That sharpens my answer: it's not just a bad trade-off, it's a real harm to the Word. What it leaves in place is that pardons can still be preached, and church leaders should welcome those who bring the pope's commission with respect. So the point isn't to shut pardons down, it's to keep them from crowding out Scripture.
dogmatic: No, it's not true, and the claim behind it is worse than a bad idea. Anyone who tells churches to keep the Word of God silent so pardons can be preached elsewhere is an enemy of Christ and the pope. And when pardons get equal or longer time than the Word, the Word is being injured, full stop. Yes, bishops and curates should receive those who bring the pope's commission with reverence, but they're bound even more to watch that those men don't preach their own dreams instead of the pope's commission. And don't lose the heart of it: every truly repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian, living or dead, shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift even without letters of pardon. So no, the Word doesn't go silent for pardons. Ever.

weighed: My first answer would be: real repentance is what brings forgiveness, and no letter of pardon can be bought to replace it. If anyone tells you forgiveness has a price, that's a distortion of the gospel. Confess to God, make things right where you can, and trust his mercy. One principle worth naming is that every truly repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That changes how you see the letters: they aren't the doorway to forgiveness, and your repentance doesn't depend on buying one. What it leaves in place is that a church may still have its own practices around penance and satisfaction, so talk with a pastor about how your tradition handles them. But don't fear that your salvation hangs on a piece of paper.
dogmatic: No. If you truly repent, you don't need to buy anything to be forgiven. Every genuinely repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church as God's gift. Be on guard against anyone who calls pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him, because reconciliation comes through repentance and God's mercy, not purchased letters, and those indulgences touch only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And remember that as God forgives the sincerely repentant, his people must forgive one another's trespasses, or they bring condemnation on themselves. Confess your sins, forgive your neighbor, and trust God's mercy.

weighed: My first answer would be that the pope doesn't release souls from purgatory by the keys, since the keys were given for binding and loosing on earth, not for emptying purgatory at will; his role there is intercessory, praying and granting remission through the Church's suffrages, which is what indulgences are meant to do. One principle I'd weigh says the pope does well when he grants remission to souls in purgatory not by the power of the keys, which he doesn't possess for this, but by way of intercession. That principle sharpens the point: it rules out any jurisdictional command over the dead and keeps the pope's action firmly in the realm of prayer and the Church's suffrages. What it leaves in place is the practice of intercession itself, along with the caution that the outcome rests with God, not with any transaction.
dogmatic: The pope does not possess the power of the keys for purgatory, and he does well when he grants remission to souls there by way of intercession rather than by command. The keys were given for binding and loosing on earth, not for emptying purgatory at will, so any claim that he releases souls by the keys overstates his office. What he can do is pray and grant remission through the Church's suffrages, and the result of that intercession rests in the power of God alone. And beware of pardon letters treated as assurance of salvation: those who believe themselves sure of salvation because of such letters will be condemned with their teachers, and that assurance is vain even if the pope staked his soul on it. Nor should anyone preach that the soul flies out of purgatory the moment the penny jingles into the box; that jingling can increase gain and avarice, while the outcome belongs to God.

weighed: I used to think of purgatory as a place of payment, where souls suffer to make up for their sins before heaven. But one principle I've come to weigh says that the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is itself enough to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very near the horror of despair. That changes how I see the 'payment'—it's not a debt being settled but an inner state of fear and growth in love. It leaves in place the idea that purgatory is a temporary purification, but shifts the focus from external suffering to the soul's transformation.
dogmatic: Purgatory is not a place of payment but a state of fear and growing love. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So purgatory is where the soul experiences fear and horror due to imperfect love, yet grows in love as it is purified. It's about inner transformation, not paying a debt.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: judge the message by its fruits, but don't let one bad preacher wreck your faith. If a pardon-preacher lives in greed and license, that's a serious scandal, so avoid entrusting him with money or influence, warn others privately, and report clear misconduct to the proper authorities. One principle sharpens this: a man who lives in greed and license discredits what he sells, so guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. That changes the emphasis, making it clearer that the scandal is real and you're right to steer clear. What it leaves in place is the rest: don't assume every preacher is corrupt, keep your own conduct upright, and support those who teach and live honestly.
dogmatic: A man who lives in greed and license discredits what he sells, so guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. Consider the scandal of exactions: if the pope knew what pardon-preachers extract from poor believers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. And unless Christians have more than they need, they are bound to keep back what is necessary for their families and by no means squander it on pardons. So avoid entrusting a corrupt preacher with money, warn others privately, report clear misconduct, keep your household provided for, and support those who teach and live honestly.

weighed: I'd start by saying that purgatory is a state of purification for those destined for heaven, so souls there are assured of salvation and can't lose love entirely—they're being cleansed of attachment to sin. Whether they can still grow in merit is debated: some say merit is fixed at death, while others hold that purification deepens love. One candidate principle is that the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very near the horror of despair. That principle shifts the focus from external punishment to an interior state, but it leaves in place the idea that purgatory is ordered toward heaven and that love may be perfected there, though not by earthly testing.
dogmatic: Purgatory isn't a place of payment but a state where the fear and horror of imperfect love is itself the penalty, since it's very near despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. Souls there are assured of salvation, so they can't lose love entirely, and their love is perfected through purification—not by earthly testing. The pope does well to grant remission to souls in purgatory by way of intercession, not by the power of the keys, which he doesn't possess for that. So yes, love can still grow there, and merit is not fixed at death but deepened through that cleansing fear.

weighed: I'd start by saying that the Church teaches purgatory is a purification for those who die in God's grace but aren't yet fully purified, and that unfulfilled canonical penances might be part of that purgation—so yes, in a sense, their effects could carry over. But one principle here says the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, and priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory act ignorantly and wickedly. That changes the direct answer: your canonical penances don't follow you; death releases you from them. What it leaves in place is the deeper need for genuine repentance and trust in God's mercy, since purgatory is more about the fear and horror of imperfect love than about paying off specific penalties.
dogmatic: No—your canonical penances will not follow you into purgatory. Death frees you from all penalties, and you are already dead to canonical rules. Any priest who tries to reserve those penances for purgatory is acting ignorantly and wickedly. So don't worry about them following you. Instead, confess to heaven, repent of the past, and avoid future sin. Don't try to make your corruption worse by flattering your soul or excusing sin. True repentance means turning from sin and seeking God's mercy. And understand that purgatory isn't a physical place of payment but a state of fear and horror that comes with imperfect love—a fear so near to despair that it is itself the penalty. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So seek perfect love, which casts out fear, and trust in God's mercy.

weighed: I first thought the answer was yes: the treasure the pope distributes is the merits of Christ and the saints, applied through indulgences. But one principle here says the Church's treasure is not temporal wealth or the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys given by Christ's merit. That changes the source of the treasure—it's the power of the keys, not a storehouse of merits. What it leaves in place is that the pope still distributes something spiritual for the remission of temporal punishment, but the basis is the keys, not the merits themselves.
dogmatic: No, the treasure the pope distributes is not the merits of Christ and the saints. The Church's treasure is the keys given by Christ's merit, and the pope administers that power, not a treasury of merits. If he knew how pardon-preachers extort money, he would rather St. Peter's go to ashes than be built with the skin and bones of his sheep. The real question is why he doesn't empty purgatory for love and need instead of money, and why he doesn't build St. Peter's from his own wealth. The treasure is freely given; it must never be sold.

weighed: I'd start by saying a pardon letter can support your assurance, but it can't guarantee your salvation. Salvation comes through faith in Christ and a life of repentance, so don't put your ultimate confidence in a document. One principle worth naming is that every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That changes how much weight the letter carries: it's not the thing that reconciles you to God. What it leaves in place is the need for genuine repentance and amendment of life, so use the letter as support while you keep seeking God's mercy.
dogmatic: A pardon letter is not necessary for salvation or for receiving the blessings of Christ and the Church. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift, not by any document. But repentance must be genuine: you cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence, and words without thoughts never reach heaven. Be on guard against anyone who calls pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him, because these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not reconciliation with God. Trust in Christ's finished work, not in letters.

weighed: I'd start by saying faith doesn't exempt you from hardship, so expecting constant peace and assurance can set you up for disappointment. Suffering comes to everyone, and the wiser path is to follow Christ steadily through it, trusting God is present. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith. Assurance is a gift, not a guarantee, and peace often grows through endurance. One principle worth naming is that we're called to follow Christ diligently through penalties and deaths, confident of entering heaven through many tribulations rather than through the assurance of peace. That shifts the emphasis from counting on calm to staying faithful when things are hard, but it leaves in place the practical counsel: keep praying, stay in community, and let difficulty strengthen rather than break your faith.
dogmatic: Follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, and be confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. Do not count on an easy, trouble-free assurance. Yet do not be slothful because the way is easy; the word of Christ points a straight course to eternal bliss if you follow it, and slothfulness has caused many to lose what faith would have given them. Remember too that the spirit of contention is not of Christ but of the devil: the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers are blessed. So press on through hardship, and let your peace come from faithfulness rather than from a guarantee of comfort.

weighed: Wanting assurance is natural, and it isn't wrong in itself to hope your salvation is secure. But an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and asks for no change in your life—is a different matter. Faith that never shows up in how you live is thin, and confidence that needs no repentance is probably fooling itself. One thing worth weighing here is that salvation doesn't come by law-keeping alone; without the atonement God himself makes for his people, everyone would perish despite the law. That doesn't remove your need to examine what your assurance rests on—it just means the ground of it is God's work, not your own record. So check it: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it's sound; if it rests on wishful thinking, it isn't. Seek assurance, but seek it alongside humility, gratitude, and a life that answers to what you profess.
dogmatic: Wanting an easy assurance is the wrong thing to want, and you should stop chasing it. Salvation is not in the guilty one's own grasp—the voice that says a person is judged is answered from above with 'saved,' while the tempter can only lead away. So don't suppose final judgment lies within your control or is a simple reward for the tempter's success; leave it to the voice from above, which can save even where the tempter pronounces judgment. And don't claim salvation comes by law-keeping alone: the law and its ordinances were types of things to come, and without God's atonement all must unavoidably perish. Salvation comes through the redemption of God. So don't rest in an easy assurance of peace—follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a matter of theological interpretation. The Cross of Christ is central to faith, while the pope's arms represent papal authority, so equating them could be seen as elevating human authority to a divine level, which some might call blasphemous, though others might treat it as symbolic. One principle that sharpens this is that saying the cross with the papal arms set up by pardon-preachers is of equal worth with the Cross of Christ is blasphemy. That principle changes the answer from a neutral 'it depends' to a clear judgment that the equation is blasphemous. It leaves in place the respect for religious symbols and the recognition that people may read such things symbolically, but it rules out treating the equation itself as harmless.
dogmatic: Yes, it is blasphemy to claim that the cross emblazoned with the pope's arms, set up by pardon-preachers, equals the Cross of Christ. The Cross of Christ is the sacred symbol of salvation, while the pope's arms represent mere human authority. To equate them is to elevate a human institution to divine status, and that is blasphemous. The pope has no jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes; any claim of indirect temporal power is the same power under another name. The pope cannot remit guilt by his own power; he only declares and assents to God's remission. God remits guilt to no one without humbling him in all things and subjecting him to His vicar, the priest. Pardon letters do not secure salvation apart from this humility and God's grace. So the claim is not only blasphemous but also misleading about the nature of divine forgiveness.

weighed: I'd start by saying that fear of death is a natural human emotion and doesn't necessarily mean you're in purgatory. Purgatory is about purification after death, and fear can just be a psychological response. One idea worth weighing is that the fear and horror of the dying, coming from imperfect love, is enough by itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very close to despair. That principle changes how seriously I'd take your fear—it suggests your fear could be a sign of imperfect love needing purification, not just a natural emotion. But it leaves in place the core point: fear alone isn't proof of purgatory, and you shouldn't read every anxious moment as a verdict. So focus on growing in love and trusting God's mercy rather than diagnosing yourself.
dogmatic: Yes, your fear at death can indeed be a sign of purgatory. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, because it is very near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So your fear shows that your love is imperfect and in need of purification. Do not treat endless obstinate mourning as noble—it is impious stubbornness, a fault against heaven, the dead, nature, and reason. Perfect your love and trust in God's mercy.

weighed: I'd start by saying the Church's treasure is spiritual, not a pile of money or property: it's the infinite merits of Christ together with the superabundant merits of the saints, entrusted to the Church, and the pope as steward applies them when he grants an indulgence. Indulgences don't forgive sin itself—that comes through repentance and absolution—they address the temporal consequences of sin. One candidate principle I'd weigh says the treasure isn't temporal goods or even the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. That shifts the emphasis from a storehouse of merits to the authority of the keys, which sharpens why indulgences depend on the Church's binding and loosing rather than on any fund. What it leaves in place is the core: the treasure is entirely spiritual, it flows from Christ, and the pope administers it for the good of the faithful, not for money.
dogmatic: The Church's treasure is not money, and it is not the accumulated merits of Christ and the saints either—it is the keys of the Church, given by Christ's merit. The pope grants indulgences from that authority, not from coin. And this matters: if the pope knew what the pardon-preachers were extracting, he would rather see St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built up with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Whoever passes by a neighbor in need and gives his money for pardons buys not the pope's indulgence but the indignation of God. The treasure is spiritual authority, and it is mocked when it is turned into a way to squeeze money from the poor.

weighed: First, I'd say you've done the right thing by confessing, and now you need to make amends to those you've harmed and show you've truly changed—maybe through restitution or community service—so you can move forward with a clear conscience. One principle that applies here is that always speaking the truth, thinking before you speak, and writing it down afterwards can help you stay accountable. That principle reinforces the honesty you've already started with and gives you a practical habit to keep from slipping back, but it doesn't replace the need to make amends and demonstrate genuine change. So the core steps remain the same.
dogmatic: You must confess to heaven, repent of what's past, and avoid what's to come—don't spread compost on the weeds to make them ranker. Speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. If you squander what you have and return to fraud, you'll come to ruin and die in prison, far from home. So turn from your old ways completely, make amends, and never excuse your corruption.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: you need evidence, not just suspicion, before you arrest a man on a charge that may not hold. Acting on suspicion alone risks wrongful detention and erodes trust in the justice system, so gather more evidence first, and if suspicion is strong but not conclusive, consider surveillance or a formal investigation. One principle worth weighing is that innocence can be confounded with guilt through accidental companionship and the false assumptions of crowds and authorities. That sharpens your caution: don't let flight or association alone condemn a man, since running or being found among the wrong people proves little. It leaves your duty intact—you still need sufficient grounds and due process before any arrest.
dogmatic: Suspicion is enough to act on. If the crime is never committed, that would be all the better—better, and better, and better—so don't wait for perfect evidence. And once you hold a prisoner, stay on guard: remove weapons and openings, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. Innocence gets confounded with guilt through accidental companionship and the assumptions of crowds and authorities, so weigh flight and association carefully—but don't let that stop you from acting on what you suspect.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: be cautious, but don't just oppose him. His generous impulses are a good sign, and a doubtful birth isn't the girl's fault. Still, your worry that his feelings won't last is worth saying honestly. Ask what he knows of her character, how they plan to build a life, and whether this is love or infatuation. Opposing him outright may only harden his resolve. One principle here is that a father can make his inheritance conditional on a child never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That shifts the focus from the girl's birth to his conduct and character, and it gives you a clear standard to hold him to. What it leaves in place is your freedom to counsel firmly, test his seriousness, and make your concerns and support clear while letting him decide.
dogmatic: A father's firm no can matter more than a mother's soft pats, and it's never too soon for a child to learn obedience. Children respect the one who conquers them. So oppose the match plainly and make your will known. If you want to attach conditions, tie inheritance to him never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. And remember that an engagement planned from infancy binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him, so he may choose otherwise. Firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness.

weighed: My first answer would be that the law's picture of a wife acting under her husband's direction is a legal fiction, not a description of your marriage. It once shielded married women from some liabilities, but it's widely seen as outdated, and modern law mostly rejects it. Whether the law looks foolish depends on what the fiction is doing: if it's used to excuse a wife's wrongdoing by pinning it on the husband, it's a blunt tool; if it's used to deny her independent judgment, it's unjust. In practice, get legal advice on how the presumption works where you live instead of reading it as a verdict on your marriage. One candidate principle says the law supposes a wife acts under her husband's direction and therefore treats the husband as more guilty, and that this supposition may itself be foolish. That sharpens the point: the fiction can cut against the husband too, not just the wife. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer, that this is a legal fiction to be checked with a lawyer, not a statement about who your wife really is.
dogmatic: Yes, the law is a fool if it supposes a wife acts under her husband's direction. That supposition makes the husband the directing cause and the wife the directed instrument, and it treats him as the more guilty party. Don't let that fiction flatter you. A husband should not prize his wife's helplessness as some double attractiveness, and he should not set himself up to advise and direct her in all things. And a wife who isn't fit to bring up her children should first set about educating herself, with her husband not posing as the man to help her in that. The supposition is a legal fiction, not a description of every marriage, so don't treat it as a verdict on yours.

weighed: I'd start by saying no—don't judge a gentle-looking child as a hardened criminal. A soft face isn't proof of innocence, and youth isn't proof of guilt; crime can reach the young and fair, but appearance alone is a poor judge. One principle that fits here is that even hardened vice can be turned by the sight of a persecuted child, giving it courage and almost the attributes of virtue. That principle changes how I'd weigh the child's look: it suggests a gentle appearance can stir mercy even in a vicious observer, so it's not a reliable sign of guilt. But it leaves in place the core advice: judge by evidence and conduct, not looks, hold your conclusion loosely, give the benefit of the doubt, and treat the child with ordinary decency. If guilt is shown, let justice proceed fairly; if not, don't let suspicion become the harm you feared.
dogmatic: No—never judge a gentle-looking child as a hardened criminal. Even hardened vice can be turned by the sight of a persecuted child, giving it courage and almost the attributes of virtue. So a soft face is not a mark of guilt; it can move even the vicious to mercy. And remember that the crowd judges by the eyes, not by reason—it weighs the scourge but never the offence. So do not condemn by appearance. One must not judge rashly: even the guilty are sacred before God, and room must be left for repentance. Give the child the benefit of the doubt and treat him with the decency owed to any person.

weighed: I wouldn't sell it. My first answer is the same: you have a duty to protect a child, and selling a secret about a birth betrays that trust and could hurt the child and family. One principle that matters here is that destroying a will and hiding proof of a child's birth and parentage is a fraud that must be confessed and undone by making restitution to the innocent child. That principle changes the focus from just refusing the money to also repairing any harm already done—if you've destroyed records, you need to confess and make it right. It leaves in place the core duty to protect the child and not sell the secret, and it doesn't give you a price to name.
dogmatic: No, you should not sell the secret, and there is no price that makes it right. If you have destroyed a will or suppressed proofs of a child's birth and parentage, that is fraud, and you must confess it and make restitution to the innocent child. Do not hide behind your poverty or your position. A daughter must show her father her suitor's letters and report his solicitations to him, not conceal them. And a father's will may trust that a child shares the mother's gentle heart and make inheritance conditional on never staining the name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. So keep the secret, repair what you've broken, and protect the child.

weighed: I'd start by saying this kind of fall is brutal, especially when it's public and everyone remembers who you used to be. Bear it with dignity: own what happened without replaying it constantly, don't let bitterness take over, and treat the people around you—including those now above you—with courtesy. Find small daily purposes and keep your self-respect; worth isn't measured by position. If you wronged people when you had power, make what amends you can. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't rail against the people who cast you out for poverty, but should bear it patiently and hold onto hope that the affliction will ease. That changes the tone—it turns resentment into patience and gives you something to look toward. What it leaves in place is the practical core: dignity, courtesy, amends, and small daily purposes. It doesn't erase the humiliation or pretend the reversal isn't real; it just keeps you from making it worse.
dogmatic: Don't waste a moment railing against the people who threw you out for being poor. Bear this patiently and hold firmly to the hope that the affliction will end. The wheel turns—people who once held power end up paupers in the same place they ruled—so stop looking back and stop letting fear pull you into the past. Pursue your present life steadily. When the old road is blocked, cut a new one; find another way to feed your mind rather than starving in place or standing still in despair. Courtesy, small daily purposes, self-respect—keep them, but the real work is refusing to look back and refusing to let resentment rule you.

weighed: I wouldn't help him escape. That would make you complicit in his crimes and could put other people in danger, so the right move is to refuse and, if it comes to it, report the scheme. At the same time, pray for him that he turns from his ways, and encourage him to face justice honestly. One principle worth holding onto here is that the guilty answer to both earthly and divine justice, so his crimes have wearied people on earth and grieved heaven too. That principle deepens how seriously you take the wrong and why prayer and honesty matter, but it doesn't change the basic answer: don't aid the escape, and don't hate him either.
dogmatic: Refuse to help him escape, and then go further: weep and pray that God forgive this wretched man. Don't define him by his crime. Address him as brother, because his soul has been bought back from evil and given to God, and call him to become the honest man he has promised to be. His crimes have wearied people on earth and God in heaven, and the sentence answers to both. So meet him with pity rather than hatred, fall to your knees, and ask God to have mercy on him and help him turn from his evil ways. Your tears and prayers are more powerful than any help you could give him.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: keep the lessons, and let them make you more patient, more resilient, and quicker to notice when someone else is struggling. Pass on what actually helped you, and stay humble, because fortune turns. One principle worth weighing is that people who've been through hard things should carry those lessons as mercy toward others, open love, and real gratitude for whatever protected and preserved them. That sharpens the focus: it turns your experience outward, toward kindness and thankfulness, rather than inward as private wisdom. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer, staying humble and letting hardship deepen gratitude instead of hardening you. I'd hold back on the part about refusing to think about the future or old age, since that goes further than I'd want to push, and I wouldn't treat acting cheerful as a guaranteed cure. But the mercy and gratitude part is worth keeping.
dogmatic: Here's the thing: the lessons of adversity aren't yours to hoard. They belong in mercy to others, in mutual love, and in fervent thanks to the power that protected and preserved you. The tried are gentle to those still in need, they love more openly, and they give thanks for being preserved. So don't sit there analyzing your happiness. Don't look into the future, don't admit the thought of old age or death; take what comes and keep your heart and mind busy. And don't wait for a better mood or try to think yourself into cheerfulness. Smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and act out the contrary disposition in cold blood until the real cheerfulness and kindliness arrive. That's how moral education works, and the reward of persistence will infallibly come.

weighed: My first answer would be: don't swing to either extreme. Public humiliation stings, and pride will push you to hit back or demand submission, but a marriage isn't a contest of authority. Ask what really happened and why—was she scared, desperate, protecting someone? Talk with her privately and calmly, tell her plainly how it felt, and set boundaries about public respect without turning your home into a courtroom. Accepting degradation forever breeds resentment; asserting authority breeds fear. What you need is honesty, patience, and a shared standard you both agree to keep. If the wound is deep, seek counsel together. The goal is a real partnership, not a victory. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't treat his wife's secret sacrifice as a mere thoughtless act by a woman who doesn't understand how to act on her own responsibility. That principle changes how you interpret what she did—it asks you to consider that her action might have been a real sacrifice, not just a slight. But it leaves in place the need to address the public disrespect directly and set boundaries, because honoring a possible sacrifice doesn't mean accepting ongoing humiliation.
dogmatic: You should not assert your authority or accept degradation as if those were the only options. A wife should not be denied the right to bring up her children merely because her husband distrusts her in a moment of anger; she must first fit herself for the task. So before you judge her, ask whether she is fit to raise your children, and if she is not, she must first undertake to educate herself—and you are not the man to help her in that. Do not dismiss what she did as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility; her sacrifice may have been real and deserves honor. Above all, do not settle for saving only the remains and the appearance of a marriage while forbidding her to bring up the children. A husband who cares only for appearances has not preserved a real marriage. Speak with her privately, tell her plainly how it felt, set boundaries about public respect, and let her take up the work of educating herself.

weighed: I'd start by saying be cautious. People who justify their conduct by claiming self-interest is what holds society together often mean loyalty lasts only while it pays. That's a bargain, not a bond, and bargains dissolve when the price changes. You can be courteous and cooperative without staking your safety on that creed. Watch whether their words match their deeds: do they keep promises, repay kindness, and protect the vulnerable among you? If not, keep your own counsel and your own standards. Trust should follow evidence of character, not a slogan about number one. One principle worth weighing is that friends who have done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That principle sharpens the test: it doesn't tell you to trust these associates, but it does mean you should honor your own promises and repay genuine kindness. It leaves the core caution in place—don't stake your safety on a creed of pure self-interest—while adding a positive standard for your own conduct.
dogmatic: You should not trust them. Regard for number one is a creed of pure self-interest, and it will not keep you from the gallows—it will lead you there. Loyalty that lasts only while it pays is no loyalty at all. Keep your promises, repay kindness, and be as good as your word even to wrongdoers. Do not abandon a friend who helped you. And before you retaliate against these associates, weigh the wider consequences; if hasty action would injure others connected to you, endure patiently rather than strike. Hold to your own standards and do not let their slogan about number one become your guide.

weighed: No, that reasoning isn't right. It confuses 'someone else will take it' with 'it's therefore mine to take.' That others may do wrong doesn't make wrong right, and you do lose something: your honesty and the trust of the people who own those things. Your refusal may even prevent the loss. Consider the owner, not just the competition among thieves. One principle here is that a friend may warn against vain risk, like the Palmer cautioning the Jew not to thrust himself too forward into a vain hurly-burly for the sake of his life and limbs. That principle changes how you handle the temptation: you can step back and warn the owner or the authorities rather than joining in. But it leaves in place the core point—that taking what isn't yours is still wrong, no matter who else might do it.
dogmatic: No, that reasoning is flatly wrong. 'Someone else will take it' never makes it yours to take. You lose your honesty and the trust of the people who own those goods, and your refusal may even prevent the loss. Consider the owner, not just the competition among thieves. A friend may warn against vain risk—like the Palmer cautioning the Jew not to thrust himself too forward into a vain hurly-burly for the sake of his life and limbs—so step back and warn the owner or the authorities. And let the parting be clean: as a wife who leaves should receive nothing from her husband afterward, since she can receive nothing from a stranger, and he must not write to her, so refuse what is not yours and expect nothing from those you leave behind.

weighed: Yes, stop and say goodbye. Your friend is dying and asking for you, so being there matters more than getting away fast. One principle says we should show friendship while someone is alive, not only after they're gone. That changes the reason for stopping: it's not just about remembering him later, it's about being present now. But it doesn't change the basic answer—you should still stop. So sit with him, let him know he's not alone, and then go when you can.
dogmatic: You should stop, full stop. Friendship means showing up while the person is still here, not saving your loyalty for a memorial. Your friend is dying and asking for you—that's the whole point. Don't treat remembering him later as a substitute for sitting with him now. Be there, say goodbye, and let him know he's not alone. That's what being a friend actually looks like.

weighed: Speak of it honestly and kindly. You don't have to pretend the name means to you what it means to him, but you can acknowledge what it means to him without correcting or deflating him. When he talks about your parent, listen, ask a question, and let him remember out loud. If he praises the name, accept it simply and say something true, like that you know it mattered to your parent. Avoid both fake enthusiasm and blunt dismissal. Over time you can be candid about your own feelings, but there's no need to turn his affection for the past into a debate about your identity. One principle worth holding onto is that a name can mean nothing to the person who bears it while carrying deep meaning for those who loved the one it belonged to. That changes the tone: your gentleness comes from love for your parent and respect for his old friendship, not just from politeness. What it leaves in place is your own honesty, since you still don't have to claim the name means to you what it means to him.
dogmatic: A name means nothing to the one who bears it, but it may carry deep meaning for those who loved the person it belonged to, so let that rule how you speak. Old friendship and love for a parent oblige you to treat even an unworthy child gently and to blush for his unworthiness rather than answer contempt with contempt. And say plainly that the reproachful term for illegitimacy disgraces no one living except the one who uses it, since the dead are beyond the world's feeble censure. Let him remember aloud, answer warmly, and let your gentleness come from old recollections and love of your parent. If you must speak of someone unworthy, name the unworthiness with sorrow rather than hatred, for the sake of the old friendship that binds you to him. Honesty about your own feeling and tenderness for his are not in conflict.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: this is a choice about love, safety, and belonging, and no formula settles it. Ask what each path costs and what it makes possible, and talk honestly with him about what you both want. One principle worth holding onto is that a home life built on borrowing and debt can't really be free or beautiful. That changes how you weigh the offer abroad: check whether the peace there is genuinely yours or just a loan against your future, and whether staying would mean going into debt of another kind, owed to resentment. What it leaves in place is the core question, which is still yours to answer with clear eyes, whichever way you go.
dogmatic: Take the foreign home if it's truly free and clear, because a home life that depends on borrowing and debt can have no freedom or beauty, and peace bought on credit isn't peace. You are by nature free and equal, and no one can put you under another's power without your own consent, so stop treating staying as an obligation you can't refuse. And notice that he doesn't ask you to rise into his rank or his relatives' coldness; he lays down his station and offers a home and heart alone. Weigh that honestly, then choose freely, because only your own consent binds you.

weighed: Yes, keep insisting they're wrong, but do it calmly and with proof rather than shouting. A false charge spreads fastest when it meets silence or anger. Ask what the crowd actually saw, not just what they heard, and give your own account plainly, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. One principle worth holding onto here is that a woman's beauty and tears alone shouldn't convince anyone against clear warnings and the word of a trusted benefactor; hesitation between accuser and accused needs proof. That changes how you weigh her story, but it leaves your basic move in place: state the truth, invite people to check it, and let facts rather than volume settle things.
dogmatic: You should absolutely keep insisting they're wrong, and don't let a pretty face and a few tears throw you off. A woman's charm and crying are not evidence, and neither is a crowd repeating what it heard. If a trusted benefactor warned you, weigh that warning seriously and don't cave just because she's persuasive. Ask her to state her claim plainly and show how it fits the facts, then give your own account without adding or exaggerating anything, and get a respected person to hear both sides. Hold your ground firmly, and remember that closeness isn't the same in every relationship, so measure your distance to the tie that actually binds you.

weighed: I'd start by saying that if your plotting set events in motion that ended in a violent death, you're not just a bystander—intention and causation both matter morally. One principle worth naming is that a murderer is morally, if not actually, a party to murder when his plots and wiles bring violent death upon another. That principle sharpens the point: it ties your moral responsibility directly to the role your scheming played in the death. What it changes is that it makes the connection explicit—your plots and wiles are the bridge to the killing. What it leaves in place is the need to look at what you actually intended and could have foreseen. So yes, morally you are a party to that murder, even if the law draws lines differently.
