You should still seek legal advice if there's any risk of prosecution, and talk to someone you trust about guilt and repair.
dogmatic: You are morally, if not actually, a party to that murder. Your plots and wiles brought violent death upon another, and that makes you no bystander—intention and causation both bind you to the deed. Don't console yourself with the tavern argument that one tiny crime may be wiped out by thousands of good deeds, or that nature must be corrected and directed; even if that reasoning has a place, it is no license for what you did. And don't shift blame onto the innocent, as Oliver was blamed—he was no thief, only a boy wrongly taken because he ran and was found among thieves. Own your part honestly. The principle is clear: when your scheming brings violent death, you are a party to murder.

weighed: Your safety comes first. Don't confront Sikes or make a scene that could get you shot. Look for a safe moment to slip away, get help, or alert someone without being seen, and once you're clear, report what you know to the authorities. Going along with the robbery makes you a participant and deepens your danger and guilt. Try not to carry or handle stolen goods, keep track of where you are, and remember details that could help later. If escape is impossible, stay calm, avoid provoking him, and wait for a better chance. The priority is surviving and getting out, not proving courage in the moment. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't expose your plans to an adversary; let him find out if he can, and you can find out his. That changes how you handle the escape: keep your intentions hidden, quietly learn what he's planning, and don't tip him off. It leaves your core priorities in place: avoid a direct confrontation, get out safely when you can, and don't take part in the robbery or handle the stolen goods.
dogmatic: Don't kid yourself that Sikes will somehow dodge what he's done. Murderers don't escape justice, and Providence doesn't sleep; the torment that follows the crime is real even when no court catches it. But keep your game concealed from an adversary who has no right to your plans, letters, or secrets; instead, quietly discover his designs. Don't confront him or make a scene that could get you shot. Look for a safe moment to slip away, get help, or alert someone unseen, and once you're clear, report what you know. And remember the deeper duty: to let another bear your punishment through silence is a hideous crime. If your silence would condemn an innocent person, you must sacrifice your own safety and reputation and denounce yourself rather than let him be condemned. Going along with the robbery only deepens your guilt.

weighed: I'd start by saying you should respect her refusal and not push her to change her mind. One principle worth weighing is that a promise made under pressure or in a former state of feeling can rightly be revised when circumstances and conscience change. That idea might loosen the grip of any vow she made in bitterness, but it doesn't erase her stated reasons or give you license to pressure her. So honor her no, and if anything shifts, let it come from her, not from you.
dogmatic: Don't just accept her refusal as final. If she's in that state of mind where she wants to deny something but can't name what, her reasons may be confusion rather than conviction. And don't apologize for your worthy relations or blush for them before the proud. A vow made in bitterness can be set aside when love and duty require otherwise, so press her with patience and truth until she sees her way clear.

weighed: My first instinct is that it's probably a mix, but the gloom sounds more like a reflection than the truth. When you're low or worn down, your mind filters things: it spots threats, discounts kindness, and reads neutral moments as hostile. The world does hold real darkness, but also ordinary good that a clouded heart can't register. One idea that sharpens this: we're often unconscious of our own peculiarities, the way someone colour-blind doesn't know what they're missing, and the way out is to inform yourself about how others actually see things. That changes the emphasis—instead of just treating your gloom as weather, it gives you a practical test: compare your view with what others genuinely perceive. What it leaves in place is the core answer: your gloom is likely a lens, not the true colour of things, and real darkness still exists alongside real good.
dogmatic: Your eyes are jaundiced, and that's the whole story. The sombre colours you see are reflections from your own heart, not the true hue of the world—the real colours are delicate and only a clearer vision catches them. Don't trust your private lens; people are blind to their own peculiarities, so go inform yourself of how others see things and let that correct you. And while you're at it, stop prying into other people's lives out of curiosity—that vice brings catastrophe and broken lives, and its happiness is black. Clear your vision, and the delicate, ordinary hues will come back.

weighed: Sharp words and even threats between dearest friends hurt, but they don't automatically mean the friendship is over. What I'd say first is: cool down, then come back and talk plainly—own your part, name the hurt without keeping score, and ask what can be mended. One principle worth weighing is that interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be confessed. That changes the tone of the apology: instead of a vague sorry, you'd name any meddling honestly. It leaves the rest in place—the cooling off, the plain talk, the offer before the demand. If both of you are willing, a quarrel like this can deepen trust rather than destroy it.
dogmatic: Sharp words and threats don't end a friendship by themselves, but don't wave this away. If you interfered in your friend's affairs, that interference was absurd and impertinent, and you must confess it plainly rather than hide it or dress it up as prudence. Respect your friend's modesty too: in an anxious case, leaning on trusted judgment is natural diffidence, not weakness, and their feelings must be honored. And where the unworthiness is real, let gentleness rest on old recollections and love for the parent, naming the fault with sorrow rather than hatred. Then return and speak plainly, admit your part, and ask what can be mended. If both are willing, this can deepen trust rather than destroy it.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: protecting a child on impulse is understandable, and good intentions count for something, but as a doctor you carry duties of honesty and professional integrity that a concealment can undercut, so I'd ask whether there were safer routes like reporting, consulting a colleague, or involving protective services, and I'd urge you to document your reasoning, get advice now, and be ready for the consequences. One candidate principle worth naming is that a fallible person shouldn't simply declare a strange, unsanctioned course of action right by their own say-so. That changes the tone of my answer: it warns against treating your good object as a self-issued permission slip. What it leaves in place is everything practical, the child's safety, the search for proper channels, and your accountability, so my original advice stands, just with less room for self-justification.
dogmatic: Good intentions don't give a fallible person the authority to declare an unsanctioned act right by decree, and that's the heart of it. As a doctor you have duties of honesty and integrity you can't wave away because your aim was good, and you shouldn't imagine psychology or evidence can settle the matter for you. Whether effort of attention is an independent variable is not something you can prove, and past a certain point you can't tell if more or less was possible, so the choice is a voluntary projection, not a demonstrated conclusion. Strike while the iron is hot: instincts are fleeting, so seize the wave of interest before it ebbs and build the habit that carries you afterward. Seek proper channels and accept the consequences.

weighed: I'd write now, without waiting. A letter can be slow, but silence is worse, and she may still have time to see him. Send it by the surest way you have, and say plainly how things stand so he can decide fast. If you doubt it'll arrive in time, ask someone nearby to carry word or send a telegram too. One principle worth weighing here is that personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence when letters fail. That changes things a little: instead of only trusting the post, you might send someone you trust to find him, or go yourself if you can. But it leaves the core in place: act now, keep her comfortable, and let her know you've acted. Waiting risks a regret you can't undo.
dogmatic: Don't wait, and don't lean on a letter alone. Letters are vain when time is short, so send someone you trust to seek him out, or go yourself, and keep inquiring until you find him. Settle your resolve now and act at once, for she may not have time. Keep the neighbors at a respectful distance too; assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable, so don't let them crowd or triumph over the afflicted. And if anyone on the verge of death persists in denying where the papers are hidden, adjure him for the love of God not to lie as he dies, and require him to say where they are. Keep the girl comfortable and let her know you've acted. Waiting risks a regret you cannot undo.

weighed: My first answer is still no: don't take the money and don't do it. Watching a colleague and reporting where she goes and who she sees is a betrayal of trust, and getting paid for it makes you part of whatever harm comes next. One principle worth weighing here is that a wife shouldn't be asked to hide herself and pretend to be ill to protect her husband's position when scandal looms. That changes how I'd frame it: no one should be pushed into concealment and falsehood to shield someone else's standing, so the request itself is the problem, not just the payment. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about: decline the money, decline the task, and if there's a real concern about this woman, raise it openly through proper channels instead of secretly. It also doesn't loosen your constraints, so keep your integrity and your distance from the scheme.
dogmatic: No, and don't take a cent for it. A wife shouldn't be told to hide herself and claim she's ill just to protect her husband's position when scandal threatens, and the same logic applies here: nobody should be pressed into concealment and lies to shield someone else's standing. If you need money, ask for honest work and don't be ashamed of it; being short on cash and a place to live doesn't make you a beggar. And a woman with a head for business can act boldly and procure money on her own when it's necessary, even without a husband's consent, to save a life. Necessity and good judgment justify boldness, not spying for pay. So refuse the task, refuse the money, and raise any genuine concern in the open.

weighed: My first instinct is that greatness doesn't come with a pass on the rules; if anything, people with more power should be held to a higher bar because their choices reach further. Take the idea that men are naturally free and equal and can't be subjected to power without their own consent. That principle sharpens the picture: it rules out the notion that some special nature or birthright puts a great man above everyone else. What it doesn't settle is how much leeway a leader gets in a genuine emergency, or how we should judge someone whose rule-breaking ended up helping many people. So it changes the default from 'greatness excuses' to 'greatness still needs consent and justification,' but it leaves open the hard cases where the stakes are enormous.
dogmatic: No, greatness grants no exemption. Men are by nature free and equal, and no one can be put under political power without his own consent. That settles it: a great man has exactly the same standing as his neighbor, and any claim that his stature lets him do what others cannot is a demand for subjection dressed up as admiration. Consent is the only thing that binds a person, and it binds the great no less than anyone else.

weighed: I'd first say what I thought before: feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms can seem monstrous, but such reactions are common in moments of intense stress. Your mind processes the event, and the relief you feel may be a mental affection that then produces bodily changes—a surge of energy, a quickened pulse, a sense of clarity. It doesn't mean you're callous. One candidate principle here is that bodily changes follow directly from perceiving an exciting fact, and feeling those changes is the emotion—we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike. That principle shifts the explanation: the surge you felt is the feeling of your body's response, not a verdict on your character. But it leaves in place the core reassurance that this is a human reaction, not a moral failing, and that you shouldn't shame yourself for it. Allow yourself to grieve in your own time.
dogmatic: Feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms isn't monstrous—it's just your body doing what bodies do. The perception directly produces the bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion: we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike. So the surge you felt is the feeling of your body's response, not a judgment on your soul. Don't cavil at life in old age either; complaining at sixty-two is petty, for nature commands every life to end, and even the satiated dread death. And be wary of the colossal vitality of illusion: a cherished image can outrun the real person it's fixed upon. Grieve honestly, and let feeling alive amid death be human, not a moral failing.

weighed: I'd start by saying your sister has a real point, but you shouldn't just swap your fears for her judgment. Words and deeds aren't the same, yet words can sting and can hint at what someone really intends, so your unease might be flagging something worth naming. The best move is to bring both views together: tell her plainly what worries you, ask what she means by putting up with a great deal, and see whether her confidence rests on real knowledge or on a wish to avoid conflict. One principle here is that you shouldn't judge someone's character from a single evening's manner when no other fault can be found. That softens how you read your sister's remark, but it doesn't settle whether her judgment should outweigh your fears; that still needs evidence and an honest conversation.
dogmatic: You should trust her judgment over your fears, because she means well even if she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. Her remark about words and deeds is just the kind of loose thing she says, not a sign of bad intent, and no fault has been found in her beyond it. So don't weigh her down with your anxieties; defer to her read of the situation and move on.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: what you did has to be judged by your intention and the facts, not by a slogan. If you took something without looking into it, that can affect whether it counts as taking for gain, but it doesn't erase the act. Ask yourself honestly what you knew, what you intended, and what you did with what you took. Ignorance can lessen culpability, but it doesn't make an action good or bad in itself. The important thing is to face the facts, make amends where you can, and learn from the mistake. One idea worth weighing here is that an action in itself is quite devoid of value, and the whole question is who performed it, since the same crime may be the greatest privilege or infamy depending on the selfishness of the judges. That changes how you see the people judging you, and it should make you suspicious of a verdict that rests on their interests rather than your intent. But it leaves your own honest self-examination exactly where it was: you still have to reckon with what you knew and what you did, and it doesn't excuse you or settle whether you gained anything.
dogmatic: Don't judge your deed as good or bad in itself, because an action is devoid of value in itself. Ask instead who performed it and who judges it: the same deed may be privilege for one and infamy for another, according to the judges' own interests. Yet distrust your own account too. Alterations of memory change the me, and the accounts we give others grow more simple and interesting than the truth, until fiction expels reality. And know who your judges are: the multitude does not judge by reason but by eyes, weighing the scourge rather than the offence. They will see the punishment, not the intention, and call you criminal accordingly. So understand what you have done by asking who you are before judges who see the lash, not the motive, and who take their measure from the spectacle.

weighed: I'd start by saying the wish to serve a great idea is admirable, but the belief that you personally may break the law for it deserves careful testing. Laws exist to keep peace and protect others, and a private conviction that you're exempt is exactly what every lawbreaker feels. Before acting, ask whether the idea truly requires breaking the law, whether the harm you cause is proportionate, and whether you'd accept others doing the same. If the law forbids what conscience demands, accept the penalty openly rather than evading it. Don't flatter yourself that you're special; test your motive honestly, seek counsel, and act only if you can bear the consequences without deceiving yourself. One candidate principle says the law cares nothing about motives, but that doesn't make the law right; you may find it impossible to convince yourself that the law is right. That principle changes the tone: it tells you not to assume the law's judgment is automatically just, and it gives you room to question whether the rule itself is right. But it leaves in place the need to test your idea against real harm, to ask whether you'd accept others doing the same, and to bear the penalty openly if you still act. So it doesn't hand you an exemption; it just keeps you honest about the law's limits.
dogmatic: The law cares nothing about your motives, but that doesn't make the law right. You may find it impossible to convince yourself that the law is right, and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. The real question is whether your idea serves the known natural inclinations of mankind and the articles of the law of nature: peace, safety, and the means of living. Political power is a trust for making and executing laws for the preservation of property and the public good, not a private possession or arbitrary dominion. So ask whether your idea truly serves those ends, whether the harm is proportionate, and whether you'd accept others doing the same. If conscience still demands what the law forbids, bear the penalty openly. That's the test, and you have no excuse for ignoring it.

weighed: Feeling ashamed is actually a good sign here, because it can push you toward honest repentance. Cruel words about someone you barely know usually say more about your own heart than about them. Start by naming the jealousy honestly, then apologize to the person if you can and make amends where possible. Ask what insecurity or comparison stirred the cruelty, and bring that to prayer. You don't need to punish yourself endlessly; receive forgiveness, learn from the wound, and practice speaking well of others, especially when envy rises. One principle worth weighing is that pride is about your opinion of yourself, while vanity is about what you want others to think of you, and pride offends most when it humbles someone else. That principle sharpens the apology: it reminds you the real harm was making someone else smaller so you could feel bigger. It leaves the rest in place, though. You still need to name the jealousy, apologize, and make amends, and you still shouldn't drown in shame.
dogmatic: Your shame is telling you something true, so don't rush to soothe it away. Cruel words about someone you barely know expose your own heart more than theirs, and the jealousy behind them needs to be named plainly, not managed politely. Pride is simply the opinion you hold of yourself; vanity is what you want others to think of you. Pride can be forgivable when it doesn't crush someone else's dignity, but it becomes ugly the moment it makes another person smaller so you can feel larger. That is what you did. So don't hide the fault while others stumble over it without knowing. Confess the jealousy openly, apologize, and make amends where you can. Better to bear the shame in the open than to let your disgrace quietly burden someone innocent. Suffering honestly is better than being infamous in secret.

weighed: I'm so sorry you're facing this. First, don't carry it alone—tell a neighbor, a church, or a community worker today. Food banks and congregations exist for moments like this, so ask plainly and without shame. Then take the smallest next step: one meal, one phone call, one person who can watch the children while you rest or seek aid. If you are dying, arrange for someone trustworthy to care for them and put that in writing if you can. You are not a failure for needing help. One principle here is that substance should be imparted to the poor according to what each has—feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and giving relief both spiritually and temporally. That principle changes the focus from your own guilt to the practical duty of others to share what they have, and it leaves in place the urgent need to ask for help and arrange care for your children.
dogmatic: Confess your need to heaven and repent of the past—of whatever neglect or wrong brought you here—and resolve to avoid future sin rather than make your corruption ranker. Do not excuse sin or flatter yourself that all is well. Then remember that imparting substance to the poor, according to your ability, in both spiritual and temporal things, is done for the sake of walking guiltless before God and retaining a remission of your sins from day to day. Teach your children this by example: as the girls who gave their Christmas breakfast to the hungry poor family, love your neighbor better than yourselves, even when your own cupboard is bare. Tell a church or neighbor today, plainly and without shame, and arrange trustworthy care for the children.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: steady yourself by accepting that illness and death come even to the young and good. Pray for her life if that eases your heart, but hold that prayer alongside a willingness to accept Heaven's will, and keep your calm so the family leans on you rather than carrying your fear too. One thing I'd weigh is Beth's way of meeting her own approaching death with quiet faith, wanting to prepare her loved ones kindly and enjoy what time remains instead of being miserable. That changes the tone: it turns your prayer from anxious pleading into something gentler, and it suggests speaking softly with her about what may come so she and the family aren't caught off guard. What it leaves in place is everything you asked about, praying for her life and submitting to Heaven's will, and it doesn't touch the other two matters about not throwing life away or not mistaking a clear resolve for delirium, since those aren't your question here.
dogmatic: Compose yourself by looking to Beth: she meets her illness with quiet faith, prepares her loved ones gently, and chooses to enjoy the time she has left rather than make everyone miserable. So pray for her life and submit to Heaven's will at the same time, without anxiety, and let your steadiness be a gift to the family. Speak gently of what is coming so they are ready. And hold firmly to this: life is not something to be thrown away, so refuse any course that would surely bring premature death, and never call it cowardice to turn back from it. Nor should anyone tell a wife she is ill or delirious for holding clear and certain convictions; she may feel her mind clearest at such a moment. Trust that there is a purpose beyond your understanding, and let faith carry you.

weighed: That message is a lie, and you shouldn't accept it. Your worth isn't measured by what others say or by how much you feel you burden them. People who tell someone they'd be better off gone are usually speaking from their own pain, anger, or confusion, not from truth. Disappearing wouldn't fix anything; it would leave wounds that never heal. If you're thinking of harming yourself, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today. You matter, and your life has value even when you can't feel it. One idea that holds up here is that it's only the dead who don't return, so as long as you're alive there's a real chance of meeting the people you love again. That doesn't erase the pain you're in right now or prove that everyone around you will change, but it does mean the story isn't closed. So please stay, and let someone help you carry this today.
dogmatic: The message you were told is false, and you should reject it outright. Your worth doesn't depend on anyone's verdict or on how much you think you burden them. Remember that it's only the dead who don't return; while you live, you can still meet again the people you love on this earth. So don't turn back like a traveler who quits a hard road when the goal is worth reaching. Even in solitude, God's presence can comfort you when no one else is near, and you don't have to pretend to be grateful for suffering you'd rather escape. Keep going, and reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today.

weighed: I get why you're torn. My first instinct is that your well-being comes first, and you shouldn't feel chained to a promise just because you made it. One principle worth weighing is that promises should be kept, and friends who've done you good deserve loyalty in return. That does shift things: if this person has genuinely helped you in the past, that history counts for something, and walking away without a thought isn't fair. But it doesn't erase how they've treated you badly, and it doesn't mean you owe them unlimited patience or that you have to stay close. So keep the promise if you can do it without harming yourself, but you're still allowed to set boundaries and step back from the relationship.
dogmatic: You should keep your promise. Loyalty and gratitude matter, and if someone has done you good turns, you repay that with faithfulness, not abandonment. Even when you feel wronged, the right path is to endure it patiently rather than act rashly, because a hasty move can hurt people around you. And be careful about what you swear to, because once you've given your word, you hold to it. Your word is your bond, so honor it.

weighed: What I'd say first is that feeling alone even around people is really common, and it doesn't mean you did something to deserve it. Isolation can come from lots of places, like anxiety, depression, old hurts, or just not having found your people yet. It's worth gently asking yourself whether you tend to pull back from others, but blaming yourself completely won't help. Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, not a verdict on your worth. One idea that shifts how I'd frame this is that a single mind can hold more than one self, and those selves can feel split off from each other. That changes the picture a little, because the aloneness might partly be a division inside you rather than only something you caused socially. What it leaves in place is the practical part: reaching out in small ways and getting support still matter, and you're still not to blame for feeling this way.
dogmatic: The real answer is that you're not one simple self at all. Your brain runs many paths on their own, and different conscious selves can coexist or take turns, so the isolation you feel may be a division between parts of you rather than something you personally brought on. Stop treating it as a moral failing you caused. And underneath all of it, love is what actually brings happiness on earth, the kind of love that sweeps away the world's sorrows, so lean toward connection and let sympathy move you, even to tears, more freely than your own pain does.

weighed: My first answer would be that it depends on why you won't do it. If you're stepping back because of a special role or limit, like a judge who upholds a sentence but won't carry it out, you can still call the deed just. But if you won't do it because it strikes you as wrong, then calling it just rings hollow. One principle worth naming is that destroying a will and hiding proof of a child's birth is a fraud that has to be confessed and put right for the child. That principle sharpens the point: some refusals aren't about the deed's justice at all, they're about cleaning up a wrong already done. It changes how I'd frame the test, but it leaves your core question where it was, since it doesn't tell you whether the deed itself is just.
dogmatic: No, you can't claim it's just while refusing to do it, unless your refusal comes from a special duty or a real incapacity. If you won't do it because it feels wrong, then your praise is empty. And this isn't just about you: destroying a will and suppressing proof of a child's birth and parentage is fraud, and whoever does it must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent child. The will's real work is holding a difficult idea steadily before the mind, and that effort is the whole phenomenon of will. So be honest about what you'd actually do, and make right what you've broken.

weighed: It's not shameful to ask someone who will probably turn you down. What would be shameful is pretending you need nothing, or letting pride keep you from trying. Asking plainly costs you a moment of discomfort; staying silent guarantees nothing changes. One thing worth weighing, though: a gentleman shouldn't compromise a lady who wishes not to be seen. If the person you'd approach is someone whose privacy or reputation would suffer by your going, that changes the picture, and no need of yours makes it honorable. So go where you can go honestly, state what you need without begging, and don't trade someone else's dignity for your own direction.
dogmatic: Go. A man must have somewhere to go, and when you have no one and nowhere else, you go even to those who will surely refuse you, because there are times when you absolutely must go somewhere. A certain refusal is still a place to turn, and asking is not groveling. And don't let anyone tell you that you owe obedience to a claim you never freely accepted. Men are naturally free and equal, and no one gets to put you under their power without your consent. So ask plainly, hold your head up, and give your consent to nothing that isn't freely given.

weighed: My first instinct is that handing over cash can be risky—it might get misused, create awkward dependency, or embarrass them—so I'd start by figuring out what they actually need, maybe paying a bill or a specific expense directly, or giving gift cards for essentials. If you do give cash, keep it discreet and no strings attached, and stay within your own limits. One principle worth weighing is that to help others you first need the right to do it—meaning you shouldn't give away money your own family depends on. That changes the order of things: secure your own household first, then help from what's genuinely surplus. It leaves the rest in place—assessing needs, paying providers directly, giving discreetly, involving a local charity, and being mindful of your relationship and any enabling patterns.
dogmatic: You shouldn't give away what your own family needs—that's the first rule, and without the right to give, you shouldn't be giving at all. Secure your household, then help from surplus. And don't just sit on your money or let it pile up for others to waste; use it while you're alive to help people, especially the poor and gentle, and do it delicately so you don't offend them. Even when people act ignorantly, judge them charitably—they act according to their lights. So give wisely, discreetly, and without strings, but only from what's truly yours to give.

weighed: Your anger isn't simply a sin. It's the natural response of someone who gave a lot and got little back. Those nights washing his rags were real work and real love, and it's not wrong to grieve that no one acknowledged them. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending the harm never happened or calling the pain unimportant. It means letting go of the debt so it stops running your life. You can name the wrong honestly, hold the memory without bitterness, and decide you won't let it poison the days you have left. Feel the anger, then release it at your own pace. That's not the same as excusing what he did. One principle here says that if you don't forgive others their wrongs, you shut yourself off from forgiveness too. That's a real warning, and it changes the stakes: your anger isn't just about him, it's about what it does to you. But it doesn't change the fact that the wrong was real or that your grief deserves to be heard. It leaves your honesty intact. You can forgive without pretending, and you can release the debt without calling the harm small.
dogmatic: Forgiveness isn't optional for you. The teaching is clear: if you don't forgive others their wrongs, you won't be forgiven yours. Your anger, however understandable, is a debt you're holding, and holding it puts you under the same judgment you're resenting him for. God forgives those who confess and repent sincerely, and he asks the same of you. So forgive. Name the wrong honestly, release the debt, and ask for forgiveness in the same measure you give it. That doesn't mean you have to welcome the unrepentant back into your life or pretend the vice never happened. You can keep your distance and still refuse to let the debt rule your heart. But you can't keep the ledger open and call it justice. Let it go.

weighed: My first instinct is that suffering isn't something to chase for its own sake, but it's often where real growth happens. You shouldn't romanticize pain or run from every difficulty. Some suffering is avoidable and wise to avoid; some is unavoidable and can be met with courage. What matters is your posture: don't let hardship make you bitter, and let it teach you patience and compassion. So don't embrace suffering as a goal, and don't dodge it when it's the consequence of your own choices. Accept what you can't change, learn from what you can, and keep moving forward with hope. One principle worth weighing here is Sonia's: that the way forward is to accept suffering as a means of atonement. That changes the frame for suffering you've brought on yourself through wrongdoing. It doesn't change the rest. It leaves in place that you shouldn't seek out pain for its own sake, and that avoidable, pointless suffering is still worth avoiding.
dogmatic: Suffering is good for you. Stop treating it as something to be managed or minimized and accept it as the means by which you set things right. If you've done wrong, don't justify it or dodge the cost. Give yourself up to the consequences, let the pain tell you the truth, and make repair where you can. Beyond that, suffering teaches, it deepens you, and it strips away pretense, so don't over-deliberate about every risk. Fling yourself into life and trust that it will bear you to the bank and set you on your feet. But keep your own precipice to yourself. You have no right to drag your disgrace or misery onto innocent people without their knowledge. Bear your suffering honestly and let it purify you, but don't load a burden on people who never agreed to carry it.

weighed: My first answer would be that this sounds more like a fantasy than a serious deed. Days in your room rehearsing something you can't bring yourself to do usually means the plan is doing mental work for you, not pointing toward action. One idea worth weighing is that a plan like this has its own psychic value: a wish supplies the motive, and something from your recent days supplies the material. That changes how I'd read the plan itself, since it may be expressing a wish rather than announcing a deed. What it leaves in place is your own sense that you can't carry it out, and that gap between imagining and acting is still the thing to look at. So ask what wish the plan serves and what recent experience fed it, and whether a smaller real step would meet the same need.
dogmatic: Every plan formed in solitude has its own psychic value: a wish supplies the motive for its formation, and the experiences of the previous day furnish its material. So stop asking whether it's fantasy or deed and ask what wish it expresses. The shame and inhibition you feel are censorship at work, and the ridiculous parts of the plan are a parody of the thought they mock. What you call a plan you cannot carry out is a psychic action with value of its own, and reading it that way tells you what your mind is actually after.

weighed: My first instinct is that you can live among them by holding your own convictions firmly while respecting that others hold theirs just as sincerely, being honest in your dealings, and letting your conduct speak rather than trying to convert everyone. One principle worth taking seriously is that people tend to be truthful mainly among equals and with good will, that we hold back before strangers, and that the powerful tend to lie. That changes how openly I'd advise you to speak: share your judgments freely with those you trust, but be more guarded with people you don't know and with anyone who holds power over you. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer, that you should keep your own understanding of good and evil and live with integrity, just with more discretion about who gets to hear it.
dogmatic: You should stop assuming everyone deserves your full honesty. People are truthful only among equals and with good will; before strangers you conceal yourself, and the powerful are always liars. So give every person your ear but few your voice, take each person's criticism yet reserve your own judgment, and above all refuse to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable or bullied out of your own mind by claims of duty, honor, or gratitude that don't actually hold in the case. Act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, listen widely, speak sparingly, and don't let anyone shame you into surrendering your convictions.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: his line about lymph and blood sounds like a weird jab, not a real claim, so the actual question is what you want from tonight. If you value the friendship and the invite is real, going could clear the air. If it felt belittling, staying alone is a fair way to protect your peace, and you can say so later. One principle worth naming is that friendship should be shown while someone is alive, not saved for after they're gone. That nudges me toward reaching out rather than sulking, but it doesn't decide the evening for you, and it doesn't mean you have to march over and argue about blood. So: reach out warmly if you want, and keep the choice yours.
dogmatic: Honestly, the friendship matters more than the strange remark, and you should show it now, while you both can. Don't sit home nursing a grudge over a comment about lymph. Go see him, be warm, and let the evening be easy. Being kind to a friend who's right there beats protecting your pride, and you'll regret the silence more than the awkwardness.

weighed: What I'd say first is that feeling your life has ended is a heavy, painful place, and it deserves compassion, not a quick answer. Those feelings often shift over time, and talking with someone you trust—a friend, a counselor, or a crisis line—can help you see options you can't see right now. Try to find even one small thing worth staying for: a person, a task, a curiosity. If you're in crisis, please reach out right away to local emergency services or a suicide helpline. You don't have to figure this out alone, and you don't have to decide today. One idea worth naming is that life is given only once, and that you might want to live it for yourself rather than waiting on some larger happiness. That idea can add urgency and permission to keep going for your own sake, but it doesn't erase the emptiness you feel or replace the need for real support—it sits alongside it, not instead of it.
dogmatic: Life is given to you only once, so you shouldn't wait around for the happiness of everyone else before you allow yourself to live. You either want to live yourself or you don't want to live at all—so choose to live, and treat the emptiness as a signal to find regular work, something to occupy your mind and fill your days. Like a traveler who bravely resolves not to turn back, endure the rough and dangerous stretches to reach the goal. Don't let the feeling that your life has ended stop you from pressing forward.

weighed: I'd first say what I thought before: failure often feels like proof of weakness, but calling yourself a louse or a Napoleon are two extremes of the same mistake—measuring your whole worth by one outcome. What matters now is not the verdict but what you do next. Be honest about where you fell short without turning it into a total judgment on your character. Strength isn't a fixed quantity; it's built through repeated, ordinary effort. Rest, recover, and try again on a smaller scale. One candidate principle here is that it's weak and silly to say you cannot bear what it is your fate to be required to bear—one should endure patiently what cannot be avoided. That principle changes the tone: instead of analyzing the failure, it asks you to accept the burden and keep going without complaint. But it leaves in place the core point that you shouldn't label yourself a louse or a Napoleon. It doesn't tell you whether you were too weak; it just says stop dramatizing it and endure what you must.
dogmatic: Stop asking whether you're a louse or a Napoleon. That whole question is self-pity dressed up as honesty. It is weak and silly to say you cannot bear what it is your fate to be required to bear. You must endure patiently what cannot be avoided. Do not waste yourself in complaints about your weakness. Where you are wronged, weigh the wider consequences of any response, for rash retaliation may fall hardest on those connected to you; where retaliation would harm others, prefer patient endurance. And remember that great outcomes are not the work of one man alone. Waterloo was a change of front on the part of the Universe, decided by destiny, not by a single general. No man may hold the world's vitality in one head; excessive concentration of power in one person is fatal to civilization. So do not judge yourself as a louse or a Napoleon. Do your part faithfully and leave the rest to forces larger than any single will.

weighed: It matters less than you fear. Shame about clothing is mostly social habit; the people around you are busy with their own concerns and notice far less than you imagine. If the task before you is serious, let your attention rest on the work rather than on your appearance. Dress as decently as your means allow, and then set the worry aside. One principle worth naming is that breaches of etiquette can sting more than real wrongdoing, because they hinge on the opinion of others, and the memory can make you tingle years later. That explains why the rags feel so loud, but it doesn't change the practical answer: the people around you are mostly absorbed in themselves, and the seriousness of what you're about to do is what deserves your attention.
dogmatic: Your shame is not really about the rags. It's an old childhood wish to be seen, and the shame is the part of you that censors it, while the strangers you fear are the opposite of the one person you once wanted to notice you. Don't flatter yourself that this is just nerves or a silly worry; that only skins over the sore place while it festers underneath. Look at it honestly and let it heal. And remember that a breach of etiquette can make you blush harder than an actual crime, because it rests on other people's opinions, and the memory can make your body tingle years later. So examine the shame instead of excusing it.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, rehearsing isn't the same as deciding. Rehearsal is going over the steps in your head without committing to anything; deciding means choosing and owning the choice. One principle worth naming is that complete thinking ends in testing, not just in thought. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of leaving it as a definition, I'd suggest you test it by setting a small step and seeing whether you actually follow through. What it leaves in place is the basic distinction, since rehearsal can still be preparation without commitment. So if you're only rehearsing, you haven't decided yet.
dogmatic: Rehearsing a plan is not deciding, and the only way to know which you're doing is to test it. Thinking that stops at rehearsal is incomplete; it has to end in concrete observation. So set a time limit, commit to one small step, and watch whether you follow through. If you hesitate or make excuses, you haven't decided. If you act, you have. And when you seek advice on something big, take each counselor's reasoning apart on its own rather than deciding by open plurality in a numerous assembly, where eloquence and passion carry men and secrecy is endangered.

weighed: Yes, I think you were wrong, and I'd tell you to own it. Interfering in a friend's romantic life is risky even with good intentions, because you put your judgment above his and took a choice that was his to make. The question now is whether confessing helps him or just eases your guilt, so weigh the harm and your motives. One principle worth naming is that meddling in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be confessed. That pushes me toward plain honesty without excuses, but it leaves the practical part in place: consider whether reopening something long past actually serves him, and accept whatever response you get.
dogmatic: You were wrong, and you should say so plainly rather than bury it. Interfering to separate your friend from a woman you judged unsuitable was absurd and impertinent, because you set your judgment above his and took a choice that belonged to him. Confess it without excuses. Think too about how such schemes injure the innocent: a feigned courtship, like Rochester's pursuit of Miss Ingram, is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and you should ask whether Miss Ingram suffers from such dishonest coquetry. And do not hide your own worthy relations for fear of a proud person's disdain; present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. Examine your motives, accept your friend's response, and let honest confession begin the repair.

weighed: You acted from mixed motives, and that's what's bugging you. Handing over money to get a vulnerable person home safely is a decent instinct. But calling the officer back and reversing it suggests you either doubted the plan or got nervous about what you'd set in motion. The real question is whether that second thought was about protecting her or protecting yourself. If you honestly judged the first arrangement unsafe, changing course was reasonable; if it was embarrassment or distrust, then yeah, it's closer to contemptible. One principle worth weighing here is the officer's own point: if you wouldn't do the deed yourself, there's no justice in arranging for someone else to do it. That sharpens things, because it asks whether you'd have been willing to walk her home yourself rather than pay someone to handle it. What it changes is the standard you're measuring against; what it leaves in place is the core question of whether her safety or your discomfort drove the second call. Be honest with yourself about which it was.
dogmatic: The honest answer is that you acted from mixed motives, and the second call is the tell. Giving money to get a drunk girl home is fine in itself, but countermanding the officer suggests you doubted the arrangement or feared the consequences, and the question is whether that second thought protected her or protected you. Now press the principle: if you wouldn't do the deed yourself, there is no justice in claiming your arrangement was right. Justice requires that you be willing to bear what you ask of others. You paid a policeman to do what you wouldn't do, then pulled him back, and that is not a neutral act. A related mischief is the habit of shifting responsibility from one person to another and calling it caution; that is the mischief of neglect, not care. Ask yourself honestly which motive governed you, and whether you would have done the officer's part yourself. If not, the arrangement was not just, however decent the impulse felt.

weighed: My first instinct is to tell you to stay a little guarded until you have clearer evidence, because politeness can look a lot like affection and it's easy to get hurt by reading too much into small courtesies. One principle worth weighing here is that a woman shouldn't hide her affection too skillfully from a man she favors, since most people need some encouragement to love. That changes the advice toward showing a bit more warmth than you strictly feel, rather than freezing him out, but it leaves the core in place: watch for consistency over time, notice whether he seeks you out and makes time, and don't hand over your whole heart on the strength of charm alone. So meet his attentions graciously and let the acquaintance deepen, while still protecting yourself until his intentions are unmistakable.
dogmatic: You should stop guarding yourself and start encouraging him. Reserve can cost you the very man you hope to keep, and few people have enough heart to love without some sign from you, so show more affection than you feel and help him along. Politeness is not cowardice, and polished courtesy is worth modeling; meet his attentions warmly and let things deepen. But courtesy must be matched by respect for your person: any man who lifts his hand to a woman, save in kindness, is the lowest of the low, and no charm excuses that. Short of that, lean toward favor rather than suspicion.

weighed: It makes sense to worry about that, and the first thing I'd say is to learn your triggers and early warning signs—tight chest, raised voice, racing thoughts—so you can pause before you react. Breathe, step back, buy yourself a moment before speaking. One principle worth taking seriously here is that a quick temper is an enemy you have to keep watching and keep working against, never assuming it's just how you are. That changes the tone of my first answer: instead of mostly arranging your life around a hot temperament, it says keep trying to master it, patiently, without giving up. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—knowing your signs, pausing, breathing, stepping away. Those still matter; the principle just adds that you shouldn't treat the temper as fixed or harmless.
dogmatic: A quick temper is a bosom enemy, and you must watch and pray against it and never give up the effort to conquer it. Don't tell yourself it's just your nature and there's nothing to be done—that's surrender. Notice the early signs, pause, breathe, step back, and keep at it no matter how often you fail. And don't hand your will over to anyone else along the way; a weak character just vacillates between ties and gets carried off by whoever pulls hardest. Keep your own will steady while you master the fault. Expect some sadness too—looking at your settled life through someone else's fresh eyes can grieve you, showing you what you'd grown used to. Let that soften you rather than stop you, and keep working.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: don't presume too much. A generous act can come from real affection, from habit, from wanting a good reputation, or from several of those at once, and you can be grateful for the benefit without claiming to know his heart. Watch whether his generosity is consistent, whether it costs him something, and whether it shows up when you can't repay or admire him. One principle worth naming is that charity can cover a multitude of sins, so a man's generosity may coexist with real flaws and even soften how others see them. That changes how I'd weigh the whole picture: don't assume the kind act proves a spotless character, and don't assume a flaw cancels the kindness. What it leaves in place is the core caution: judge the act more than the secret intention, and stay grateful without becoming certain about his motives.
dogmatic: You should presume a good deal less than you'd like, and also stop treating his flaws as disqualifying. Charity covers a multitude of sins, so a generous man can keep a fair character despite real irregularities, and you should weigh the kindness as genuine evidence of something good rather than hunting for a hidden angle. At the same time, don't flatter yourself that you can measure his heart by your own limits. People sacrifice honor for love in ways you'd never predict, and women have done it in numbers beyond counting. So take the generosity at face value, extend him the benefit of the doubt, and stop demanding certainty before you allow yourself gratitude.

weighed: I'd start by saying share the humor, but don't stop there. Your father's irony is how he carries an entail he can't change, and laughing at what can't be mended keeps the house livable. But irony can turn into evasion, and an entail that cuts daughters off is a real injustice that hits you directly. Take it seriously enough to learn the law, plan for your own security, and say so plainly when the joke starts dodging hard decisions. Humor goes well with clear eyes; it isn't a replacement for them. One principle worth naming is that even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. That shifts the emphasis: your father's wit shouldn't be allowed to wave away what happens to you. What it leaves in place is that his humor is still fair as a way of bearing what he can't undo, and that you can share it without pretending the injustice isn't real.
dogmatic: Share the humor, because no other course was open to a man of sense with an irreclaimable wife and an entail he cannot undo; irony keeps the household livable. But even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. Refuse the fool's comfort that faith may be broken when breaking brings advantage: keeping covenant is a rule of reason, for he who breaks faith cannot reasonably expect safety in any society, and successful wickedness is not thereby made just. So laugh, understand the law, plan for your security, and speak plainly when humor becomes evasion.

weighed: I'd start by suggesting you talk to your father privately and calmly, pointing to specific examples of your sisters' behavior and how it could affect the family's reputation, without blaming him. One principle that fits here is that parents who fail to check a daughter's exuberant spirits and teach her that present pursuits are not the business of life fix her character and expose the whole family to contempt. That principle sharpens your case: it gives you a reason to ask your father to guide them firmly rather than laugh it off. But it leaves your original constraints intact—you still keep the conversation calm, avoid blaming him, and accept that you can only control your own conduct and model good behavior.
dogmatic: Your father's laughter is the problem, and you should tell him plainly that a parent who doesn't check a daughter's exuberant spirits and teach her that present pursuits are not the business of life is fixing her character and exposing the whole family to contempt. Don't soften it or worry about his feelings—insist that he stop laughing and start guiding them firmly, because unchecked folly will disgrace you all.

weighed: I'd start by asking whether you actually respect his judgment, character, and conduct when no one's watching, and whether you'd defend him to others. Do you feel admiration or just tolerance? Can you name specific qualities you value, not just vague affection? Notice how you feel when he succeeds or fails: real esteem is glad for his good and grieved by his faults without contempt. One principle worth weighing is that pride shows itself plainly: a proud person holds himself tall, makes himself look bigger, and looks down on others, the opposite of humility. That principle sharpens the test, because it makes you check whether your regard is admiration of real worth or just your own pride being flattered. What it leaves in place is the core of your question: whether your esteem is genuine still comes down to respect, specific qualities you can name, and how you respond to his successes and failures. It doesn't settle it for you, and it doesn't override your father's point, but it gives you a sharper mirror to check yourself against.
dogmatic: Esteem isn't a feeling you wait to discover; it's a judgment about whether you can look up to him as your superior. If you can't, the marriage is unequal, and an unequal marriage leads to discredit and misery, so you should be neither happy nor respectable in it. Test yourself against pride: the proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with contempt, the direct antithesis of humility. If your regard is just tolerance or vague affection, it isn't esteem. You must be able to name specific qualities you value, be gladdened by his successes, and grieved by his faults without contempt. Anything less, and you're entering a marriage for convenience, which you must refuse.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: hope cautiously, but don't build your life on an uncertain attachment. His admiration may be real, but family wishes carry weight, and a man who won't openly choose you against them isn't yet a safe hope. Watch what he does, not what he says. One principle worth naming is that gratitude and a rigid sense of duty to someone whose goodness rescued a person from hardship can make them refuse a marriage that looks like abandoning that duty. That changes how you read his hesitation: some of it may be loyalty and debt, not lack of feeling for you. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer. His conduct still has to show a plan, and you still guard your heart and keep your options open. If the family opposition is immovable and he won't act, resign yourself with dignity and grieve privately. Don't let this one attachment decide your worth.
dogmatic: You should resign yourself, and the reason is duty. If someone's goodness pulled a person out of poverty and suffering, then a rigid obligation follows, and a marriage that seems to walk away from that debt is not one to hope for. Gratitude of that kind outranks admiration, and it outranks family wishes too. So stop hoping. Treat his admiration as a feeling that cannot be acted on, and let the duty to the one who saved him decide the matter. Anything else is a struggle you should be proud to make, a pang your heart simply bears.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: weigh it impartially. A cherished opinion is exactly the kind of belief that most needs testing, because affection and habit make us reluctant to revise. Read the letter carefully, ask what evidence it offers, and see whether its claims can be checked independently. One principle worth naming is that people already committed to the opposite view tend to read looking for objections, so they're hard to satisfy. That changes the tone of my answer: don't expect the letter alone to settle anything for you or for anyone else arguing the other side. What it leaves in place is the core advice—don't dismiss the letter just because it disturbs you, and don't accept it just because it's dramatic. Seek corroboration from other sources and from the man's own conduct, and ask whether you'd apply the same scrutiny to a letter that confirmed your view.
dogmatic: Weigh it impartially, but don't fool yourself about the resistance you'll meet. People already locked into the contrary opinion will hunt for objections before they've even finished reading, so mere presentation of the truth won't satisfy them—and that includes you if you're honest. Don't let a pile of letters multiply; go and inquire in person. Read the letter, weigh its evidence, then seek the man himself and corroborate from other sources and from his own conduct. And weigh the stakes: lost honor and a ruined name are no small thing, and a person of any pride would rather die than be proclaimed a traitor amid the jeers of the crowd. Once you've settled your resolve on the evidence, act on it promptly instead of waiting passively.

weighed: You don't have to like someone to thank him sincerely. Keep the focus on what he did for your family, not on how you feel about him. A short, specific thank-you—naming what he did and how it helped—is plenty, and a note is fine if speaking feels too awkward. Keep it brief and warm, with no apologies about being embarrassed. Gratitude isn't a declaration of friendship; it's just acknowledging a good deed. One principle worth naming is that great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at some cost to your own embarrassment. That pushes you to say it in person rather than hide behind a card, but it doesn't change the rest: you can still keep it short, skip the excuses, and offer a small reciprocal gesture later if the kindness was substantial.
dogmatic: Don't let embarrassment keep you from thanking him. This was a real kindness to your family, and it deserves to be acknowledged openly, even if it costs you. Go to him and say plainly that you know how much he did, that your family is deeply grateful, and that you thank him for it. Accept the awkwardness and do it anyway. Gratitude and duty go together, and you shouldn't let your own discomfort get in the way of what you owe him.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're not necessarily wrong to take your own happiness seriously—it's your life, and no one else has to live it. But before you dismiss the voices around you, test them: are they speaking from genuine concern, or from habit and fear? Duty and gratitude are real words, but they can also be used to control. Ask what you actually owe and to whom, and whether the obligation is truly binding or merely expected. One principle worth weighing here is that gratitude is a debt that must be discharged—you shouldn't leave arrears of gratitude behind before stepping into your future. That changes things by making you look honestly at who has genuinely helped you and what you owe them, rather than treating all the pressure as noise. But it leaves in place your core point: you still get to decide what your happiness looks like, and you still shouldn't be intimidated by persuasions that don't hold up. If after honest reflection your course harms no one and honors your deepest commitments, you can follow it with a clear conscience.
dogmatic: Happiness by itself is a false object. You can be perfectly content and still be steering by the wrong star, because the true object of life is duty, not good feeling. So no, you're not simply free to act as your happiness dictates—that framing is already the problem. And don't fool yourself that you can slip past gratitude: it's a debt, and you don't get to walk into your future joyously while leaving those arrears unpaid. Settle what you owe the people who have genuinely helped you, and do it actively, not as an afterthought. Only then does your own judgment about happiness deserve a hearing.

weighed: Tell her plainly and soon: your silence wasn't indifference, it was the awkwardness of strong feeling, and you were afraid of saying too much or the wrong thing. Keep it short and honest—what you felt, why you held back, what you hope for—then let her respond freely. One principle worth keeping in view is that a person should take disappointment manfully and be respected even if they can't be loved, rather than lose heart at the first failure. That changes the ending of the conversation: if she doesn't return your affection, you accept it with dignity instead of letting it sour into moody withdrawal. What it leaves in place is everything about the conversation itself—the plain explanation, the timing, and her freedom to answer honestly.
dogmatic: Stop being silent and grave and just tell her. Your reserve wasn't mystery, it was fear, and she read it as indifference because that's what silence looks like from the outside. Say it plainly: strong feeling made you awkward, and you were scared of saying the wrong thing. And while you're at it, drop the romantic brooding—hopeless love is a fiction from novels. Keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck this out the moment it springs up rather than nursing it as fate. A man can be respected even when he isn't loved, so take whatever she says manfully and don't lose heart at the first failure.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's natural to feel hurt, but resentment will cost you more than it costs him. Wish him well if you can, for your own peace. One principle that matters here is that money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. That changes how I'd frame the wealthy woman—not as the enemy, but as a reminder that a poor man's happy wife is better than a queen without self-respect. What it leaves in place is the core advice: grieve honestly, release the resentment, and keep your dignity. You don't have to pretend you're not hurt, but you also don't have to let his choice define your worth.
dogmatic: You should resent him. He turned to a wealthier woman, and that tells you he values money over character. Wish him well? No—that's just letting him off the hook. The real principle is that happiness doesn't depend on riches, and it's easier to go begging in rags than to suffer certain other sorrows. So don't waste your goodwill on a man who measures worth by wealth. Keep your standards high and your resentment honest; it's a signal that you know what you deserve.

weighed: You're not obligated to make a promise you can't keep or that you'd be making carelessly. A promise is serious, and if you swear to something, you should follow through. So don't swear hastily just to satisfy a relative. If you've already made such a promise, you should honor it, because a solemn promise is binding. At the same time, a family's early plan for a match doesn't bind you regardless of your honor or inclination; a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honor nor inclination confines you. Speak honestly with your relative and avoid oaths you can't keep. One principle here is that you must not make a promise or oath lightly; having sworn, you must keep it. That principle reinforces the seriousness of any promise you make, but it doesn't change the fact that a family's early plan doesn't bind you if neither honor nor inclination confines you. So it leaves in place your freedom to choose another path when your own honor and inclination aren't engaged.
dogmatic: You must not make a promise or oath lightly. Having sworn, you must keep it, because no one has more respect for a promise than the speaker. So if a relative insists you promise never to marry a certain person, you should not swear hastily to satisfy them. But if you have already given such a promise, you must keep it with fidelity. A solemn promise is binding, and you must not break it. At the same time, a family's early plan for a match does not bind you if neither honor nor inclination confines you; you may make another choice. So speak honestly with your relative, avoid oaths you cannot keep, and if you have sworn, keep what you have sworn.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: rejoice carefully, but be honest about the shame. A marriage patched up with money and settlement can restore outward peace while leaving the heart untouched, so ask your sister what she actually feels and don't pretend a settlement is a reconciliation. Support her, listen without judging, and keep the details to yourself. One principle worth naming is Jo's resolve that money did not pay for doing harm, so she burned her stories and waited until she knew better. That changes the tone here: it pushes you to treat the settlement as something that can't buy its way past real harm, and to wait for clarity before calling it a fresh start. What it leaves in place is the practical good of material protection and the need for your sister to decide what she can accept. Keep your own counsel about whether to celebrate or grieve.
dogmatic: Rejoice cautiously, but be honest about the shame. A marriage patched up with money and settlement may restore outward peace while leaving the heart untouched. Ask your sister what she actually feels, and do not pretend a settlement is a reconciliation. Support her, listen without judging, and avoid repeating details. Remember that each sister is to spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee, and nothing for herself. Take Jo's resolve to heart: money does not pay for doing harm, so give up what harms and wait until you know better. And do not let anyone escape on the bare 'if'; as the Queens insist, far more was said than that, and it must be answered. Keep your own counsel about whether to celebrate or grieve.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: don't assume the friend is the problem. Write to your brother yourself, warmly and without accusations, and say you miss him and want to see him. One principle worth naming is that even at the very end, someone shouldn't lie about papers entrusted to him but should say where they are, since nothing more can be gained by hiding them. That sharpens the honesty part of my answer, but it doesn't change the basic advice, because your situation is about a suspected go-between, not a deathbed or hidden papers. So the warm, direct letter to your brother still stands, and so does staying patient and non-confrontational.
dogmatic: Write to your brother, yes, but don't stop at a friendly note. If it ever comes to a deathbed, don't let a dying man keep denying what he knows. Adjure him, for the love of God, not to lie on the verge of death, and make him tell you where the papers are hidden. And keep the relations straight: a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would never allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Remember too the deeper wound, the shame and regret of a man who cannot earn and must watch his family labor for money, and the pain of being unable to speak to his sister and thank her. Chase the truth, but with tenderness for that silent suffering.

weighed: I get why you're feeling awkward about your younger sisters being out in society before you're married. My first instinct would be to say: don't object. Resentment between sisters costs more than any point of etiquette, and their pleasure doesn't take anything away from you. One principle worth keeping in mind is that it's thoughtless to condemn women for seeking more pleasure or knowledge than custom says is proper for their sex. That principle changes how you see their going out—it's not a slight to you but a fair claim to their own enjoyment. What it leaves in place is your own dignity: you can still keep steady and unexceptionable conduct, and let others draw their own conclusions. So defend their right to pleasure, and don't let the awkwardness turn into a family quarrel.
dogmatic: You should defend their right to pleasure without hesitation. The real problem isn't your sisters going out—it's the folly and vulgarity that make the family a spectacle, and your own shame about it. Don't waste energy objecting to their enjoyment; object instead to the impropriety that actually damages your connections. And remember that a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would never allow in a much younger sister—so don't confuse the freedoms proper to different relations. Let your own conduct be steady and unexceptionable, and answer the family's impropriety with the dignity of one member who won't share it.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: this kind of thing happens a lot. When someone tries to split a couple up, they often close ranks against the outsider, and the pressure itself becomes a bond. The aunt may have meant well or been meddling, but her opposition gave you a common enemy and made the relationship feel more precious. It's worth asking what that reveals about how settled your own feelings really were. One principle I'd weigh here is that interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be owned rather than glossed over. That changes the tone: it makes room to name the aunt's meddling plainly instead of just admiring the irony. What it leaves in place is the main insight, that opposition can strengthen attachment and that you should still look at the actual feelings and circumstances that made the pressure bind you together.
dogmatic: Interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, is absurd and impertinent and has to be confessed as such, not quietly celebrated because it happened to backfire. And don't let yourself be carried along by whoever pulls hardest; a person who vacillates between ties, taken this way and that, loses his own will and comes to harm. Yes, opposition often strengthens attachment, but that final-cause explanation is too easy and can shut down the real inquiry. Press on to the actual feelings, habits, and conditions that made the pressure bind you together. Mechanism and purpose are woven together, and neither should be despised, but leaning on the tidy ending has too often stopped people from asking what was really going on.

weighed: Yes, you can change, but it takes deliberate effort, not just good intentions. Pride is stubborn because it feeds on comparison: as long as you measure yourself against others, you'll find reasons to feel superior. True humility starts when you stop ranking yourself and attend to your own faults. Practical steps help: apologize quickly, ask for feedback, serve in unnoticed ways, and pause before speaking when you feel the temper rising. Change is gradual; expect setbacks and keep going. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. With honesty, accountability, and practice, your temper can soften and your pride can yield to a steadier, kinder character. One principle that fits here is that virtue adjoins pride; comparing yourself to the Bishop keeps you humble, but comparing yourself to people in general breeds pride and may lead back to hatred. That principle changes the focus: it warns that measuring yourself against the wrong standard can quietly feed the very pride you want to shed. What it leaves in place is the practical core—apologizing, asking for feedback, serving quietly, pausing before you speak—those still matter. So use the warning to check your comparisons, but keep doing the daily work of humility.
dogmatic: Yes, you can change, but understand what you're fighting. Pride borders on virtue, yet it springs up when you compare yourself to other men, and that comparison is where humility is lost. Preserve humility by refusing the habit of ranking yourself against others. Don't merely wait for a better mood: go through the outward movements of the contrary disposition—smooth your brow, brighten your eye, soften your voice—and act out kindliness in cold blood until the real feeling arrives. Yet be clear-eyed about what such moral improvement is. Moral values are values of appearance, to be compared with physiological values, and becoming more moral does not simply elevate and strengthen the type man; the two can contradict each other. So pursue humility and a gentler temper, but don't assume that moral refinement is the same as human strengthening.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict between loyalty and honesty. Confidentiality matters, but so does justice for the person wrongly accused. First, see if you can clear the other's name without betraying the confidence—urge the liar to correct the record, offer what you know in general terms, or encourage the wronged person to use proper channels. If the lie causes serious harm, the duty to protect the innocent may outweigh the confidence. Speak to the liar privately and give him a chance to make it right. If he refuses and harm continues, you may need to disclose to the appropriate authority, revealing no more than necessary. Weigh the harm of silence against the harm of betrayal, and act with honesty and courage. One principle that applies here is that honesty requires confessing the truth even at the cost of your own happiness; there is a silence which lies, and one must not steal a name or a place by concealment. That principle pushes you to speak up rather than stay comfortably silent, but it doesn't erase your duty to keep the confidence—so you still look for the least harmful way to tell the truth, like going to the liar first or disclosing only what's necessary. It leaves in place the need to protect the wronged person without unnecessarily exposing private details.
dogmatic: You should not let confidentiality become an excuse for comfortable silence that is itself a lie. A silence that lets falsehood stand, sparing you discomfort, is a kind of theft from the wronged. So choose honesty, even at cost to yourself—say plainly what you know, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for ease. Urge the liar to correct the record, but if he refuses, speak the truth where it is owed. Do not mistake smiling courtesy for goodwill—one may smile and smile and be a villain—nor pour out every confidence to those who have not earned trust. Honesty does not require indiscriminate exposure, but it does require that you not steal a name or a place by concealment. Act with courage and tell the truth.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: you don't owe anyone a dance just because he asked, and a graceful refusal like being tired or already promised is perfectly polite. One of the principles you raised—the Palmer keeping his vow of silence even when offered good mead—does shift something here. It suggests that a promise or principle you've set for yourself can justify declining courteously but firmly, without apology for the refusal itself. What it leaves in place is your original freedom: you're still not obliged to dance with someone you dislike, and you can still choose to accept one dance if refusing would cause real offense in your circle. The principle just gives you a firmer footing if you'd rather decline.
dogmatic: You should refuse. If you've set a principle for yourself—say, not giving your company out of mere propriety—then keep it, courteously but firmly, the way the Palmer kept his vow of silence even when offered good mead. A dance accepted only to please propriety is a performance, not a life, and you shouldn't sacrifice your preferences to it. Decline gracefully, and give your company where it's freely offered.

weighed: I'd start by saying neither extreme is the answer. Dwelling on harsh words can turn shame into self-punishment without repairing the harm, while just asking that they be forgotten can dodge responsibility.
