The better path is to acknowledge the wrong directly: apologize sincerely, name what you said that was hurtful, and say why it was wrong. Ask the person what would help repair things, and accept their response, even if they need time. Then let yourself move on rather than rehearsing the moment endlessly. One principle that fits here is that exposing another person's faults publicly can be unjustifiable and might ruin them. That principle changes how you apologize—keep it private and don't air their faults—but it leaves in place the need to own your words and make amends.
dogmatic: You should not be ashamed of your worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; honest connections deserve no apology. Speak only when you're spoken to. Exposing another's former faults without knowing their present feelings is unjustifiable—errors should not be made public where it might ruin a person forever. So when you apologize, do it privately, name what was hurtful, and ask what would help repair things, but never expose their faults publicly. Weigh the injustice of exposure before you speak.

weighed: I'd start by saying: don't rush to either defend or accept. First, honestly check whether there's truth to it. If the charge is false, defend yourself calmly and plainly, stating the facts without adding anything or exaggerating. If there's some truth, own it humbly and work on it. Consider who's saying it and why. One principle that fits here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That sharpens the 'if it's false, defend yourself' part: keep your account accurate and moderate, no embellishment. It leaves the rest in place, so you still weigh the truth of the charge first, stay open to growth, and respond with grace rather than defensiveness.
dogmatic: Defend yourself. When someone publicly accuses you of arrogance and conceit and the charge is false, you owe it to yourself to answer, and answer plainly: state the facts, add nothing, exaggerate nothing. Don't dress it up, don't perform humility to soften it. A show of humility is often just carelessness of opinion or an indirect boast, so don't mistake it for modesty. And above all, be true to yourself: clear your name by honest means and don't let the fight taint your mind. That's the whole of it.

weighed: I'd start by saying it depends on how close you are and how serious the relationship is. Families often push back against a partner they don't like, and you might feel caught in the middle. It's usually wise to stay out of matters that aren't yours, speak privately with your friend, ask what he wants, and support his choice without taking sides against his sisters. One principle that matters here is that it's wrong to deceive someone in courtship—treating another person's feelings as a mere means. That principle changes how you'd judge the woman's conduct or anyone's manipulation in the situation, but it doesn't give you a license to interfere in a family dispute that isn't yours to settle. So unless there's genuine harm, let the family work it out and just be a listening ear.
dogmatic: You shouldn't stand by while a friend is kept from the woman he loves. Deceiving someone in courtship is a burning shame—using another person's feelings as a mere means is wrong, whether it's a feigned courtship or a family's manipulation. And when someone is being pressured into a sacrifice they don't want, you should speak up plainly, the way Raskolnikov refused to accept his sister's self-sale. Don't hide behind 'it's not my business.' If you see dishonesty or coercion, name it and stand with your friend.

weighed: I'd start by saying no, you shouldn't be ashamed of your liveliness or your impertinence. If those qualities are what drew him in, that's worth taking seriously rather than apologizing for. One idea that shifts how I'd frame this is the point about blushing: it isn't conscience or guilt that makes us flush, but the sense that others might see or suspect something in us. That changes the picture a little, because it suggests your shame may be more about being watched than about anything actually wrong with you. What it leaves in place is the simple fact that the embarrassment feels real, and it doesn't ask you to perform confidence you don't have. So I'd still say: don't be ashamed of who you are, and notice that the shame is likely about being seen, not about being at fault.
dogmatic: You should not be ashamed of your liveliness, and you should not apologize for the connections and qualities that make you who you are, even before someone proud who might look down on them. The blush you feel is not conscience speaking; it's the thought that others might see or suspect something in you. A person can feel real remorse for something no one knows about and never blush, yet flush the moment they believe they're being observed. So treat your embarrassment as a reaction to being watched, not as evidence that you've done anything wrong. Hold your head up, present your liveliness and your worthy relations without apology, and stop letting the fear of someone's judgment make you ashamed of what is genuinely yours.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: slow things down, watch what people do rather than what they say, and let friends who see clearly help you check your impressions. The candidate principle about not hiding your affection too well changes one thing: it warns against becoming so guarded that you give an honest person nothing to go on. So be warm and open where someone's conduct actually earns it, while still taking time to observe. What it leaves in place is the core advice: flattery alone shouldn't move your heart, and you shouldn't play coldly with someone sincere. It also adds a useful caution: don't excuse deception in courtship as clever, since treating someone's feelings as a tool wounds them. Your wound is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to shut your heart or to toy with others.
dogmatic: Stop worrying so much about guarding your heart and start showing more warmth than you feel. Most people don't have enough courage to love without encouragement, so if you hide your affection too skillfully you'll lose the good ones. Be open, be encouraging, and let your feelings show. And never deceive someone in courtship or treat their feelings as a means to your own ends, no matter how clever it seems. That's the real danger, not flattery.

weighed: My first answer would be: give what you can spare without wrecking yourself. If that dinner is truly all you have, nobody can demand you starve, but if you can split it even a little, do that, and get neighbors or local aid involved too. One principle worth naming is that borrowing can put your dignity in a creditor's hands, so it's better to go without than to take on a debt you can't carry. That changes the method here: share from what's actually yours instead of borrowing to cover the gap. It leaves your original limit in place, since you still don't owe more than you can give, and it doesn't touch the practical steps of asking others to give freely and pointing the family toward help.
dogmatic: You should go without your dinner rather than borrow anything to feed them, because a debt hands your dignity to a creditor and that's a worse hunger than missing a meal. Give only what is truly yours, and if that means an empty plate, so be it. Ask others to give freely rather than lend, and don't treat their situation as idle gossip to laugh about, since that kind of talk can wound people deeply. The right thing is to refuse the loan and accept the cost yourself.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth pursuing, and I'd keep my original honesty: go in expecting steady, practical progress rather than a total transformation, and measure yourself against where you started. What I'd add is the idea that bringing a wandering attention back, over and over, is the real root of learning. That changes how I'd frame the effort—it's not just about memorizing signs, it's about building the habit of returning to the page—but it leaves in place my caution about pacing and not setting yourself up for disappointment. Start with your own name, a bus sign, a price, and practice a little each day.
dogmatic: Yes, and don't hedge about it. The single most important thing you can train is the power to pull your attention back when it wanders—that is the root of judgment, character, and will, and an education that strengthens it is the best education there is. So don't settle for recognizing a few signs and calling it enough. Sit with a letter, a word, your own name, and when your mind drifts, bring it back by sheer effort. Recollect what you read from within instead of just staring at the page again; that inward effort carves the deeper groove. Do this daily and the door that felt shut will open.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's natural to feel hurt when you're ignored by people you want to impress, but constantly chasing their approval can wear you down. Instead, put your energy into relationships where you're respected for who you are. One principle that fits here is 'let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking.' That changes the emphasis from 'keep trying' to 'stop forcing it,' but it leaves in place the idea that you can still decide what to do if they invite you again. So don't go out of your way to be accepted by those who overlook you.
dogmatic: You should stop knocking on that door entirely. If they ignored you, that's your answer—let it alone and it'll let you alone. Don't waste another ounce of effort trying to be accepted by people who don't value you. Your worth isn't decided by their cliques or their approval. Build your own community and let your conscience be your guide, not their opinion. If they ever come around, fine, but you shouldn't be the one chasing.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: honesty is usually the kinder path, because a gentle truth respects the person's dignity and keeps trust intact. The candidate principle that a disappointment can be borne with courage, and that a person can still be respected even when they can't be loved the way they hoped, sharpens that. It changes the tone—I'd lean toward telling the truth and staying close while they feel it, rather than softening it into a lie. What it leaves in place is my original caution: if the plain truth would only add needless pain in their final hours, a gentler true phrasing like 'she can't come, but she loves you' still serves love better than a blunt no. What matters most is that you stay, listen, and let them say what they need to say.
dogmatic: You should tell the truth, plainly and without dressing it up. A person facing death deserves the respect of being treated as someone who can bear disappointment with courage rather than be managed with comforting falsehoods. If someone cannot come, say so, and help the dying person hold that loss without losing heart or withdrawing into bitterness. Deception, even kindly meant, treats them as too fragile for reality. Be gentle in how you speak, but do not lie. Stand with them in the disappointment instead of papering over it.

weighed: There may be another way, and I want to start by saying this plainly: selling yourself is a desperate step that trades your freedom and dignity for a moment's relief. Before you go there, look for honest alternatives—ask a church or charity for help, seek work you can do with your hands, and tell someone you trust about your need. Your child needs a mother who is safe and free more than one who is sacrificed. One principle worth holding onto is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should want to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. That principle changes how you might approach work: it tells you to ask for fair help where you're owed it, not to accept being owned. What it leaves in place is the core of what I'd say first—keep your body and your will your own, take the smallest honest work available, and ask for aid without shame.
dogmatic: There may be another way, and the real answer is to stop treating yourself as something to be sold and start treating yourself as someone who earns. A dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should wish to dispense as soon as possible with charity and to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. So go to work, do it well, and insist on wages that let you furnish your own wardrobe and keep your child. Don't lean on kindness or charity as a way of life—use it only where you truly cannot yet earn, and get off it as fast as you can. Your freedom and your child's come from your own keep, not from anyone's pity.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: this comes down to your convictions and your safety. Look into what the cause actually stands for—its goals, who's leading it, how they operate—and ask whether it squares with your values and stays peaceful. Weigh the real risks, like arrest or injury, and talk to your friends about why they're going. If it's just and you feel safe, joining can be a real act of solidarity; if you're unsure, you can back it other ways, like donating or spreading the word. One principle worth naming is that friends in a dangerous enterprise should stick together rather than scatter, since a group is harder to overcome than isolated individuals. That changes the practical advice: go as a group, agree on a meeting point, look out for each other, and have a plan if someone gets separated or detained. What it leaves in place is the core question—whether the cause is just and whether you're safe—because staying together doesn't tell you if the cause is right, and it doesn't remove the risks. So use it as a way to handle the danger, not as a reason to skip your own judgment.
dogmatic: You should join your friends, and you should go as a troop, not as scattered individuals. Four together are harder to overcome than one alone, and if one of you falls or is detained, the rest must carry the message onward like a sealed letter that can't be copied. Discuss the cause together and make sure you all understand its justice, because unity is your strength. Expect disruptions—competition and internal divisions will test your movement—but each setback can strengthen your organization, and presenting a united front is how you force legislative recognition of your interests by exploiting divisions among those in power. And remember that the destitute are victims of cruel treatment by authorities, who are to blame; a cause that defends them is just. If the cause is just and you're ready to act as a troop, join them.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: refusing is worth something only if it protects someone besides your own pride. Your life is yours, but so is your place in the square, and the men beside you are holding because you hold. A surrender offered mid-battle usually isn't mercy; it's a way to break the formation from inside. So ask whether your refusal actually buys time or example for people who can't leave, or whether it's just a dramatic death. One principle here is that refusing to sell yourself, declining an offer that trades your service for advancement before you've proven yourself, preserves honor, and everything is best in its time. That principle sharpens the timing: don't take the offer as a shortcut to saving yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. But it leaves the core test in place. It doesn't tell you to refuse for vanity, and it doesn't erase your duty to the men beside you. If refusing protects them, refuse. If it's only a gesture, your duty is to your comrades, not to a dramatic death.
dogmatic: Refusing has worth only if you have something to prove and something to give. Don't accept the offer now just to save yourself; that would be selling yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. Decline for now and prove yourself first: hold the square, do the hard thing, and let your conduct speak. When you've shown what you're worth through a brilliant action, then you may give yourself on your own terms. If someone has done you a kindness, acknowledge the debt fully, though its expression may wait when circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise. And if a defenceless stranger demands trial by combat, grant it; it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny her the benefit of mild laws because of her faith.

weighed: I'd start by saying be careful with the word saint if it means sinless, because nobody is perfect, including your mother. What matters more is whether she lived uprightly, honestly, kindly, and faithfully, and if she did, honor her and learn from her good example. One principle I'd weigh is that being a saint is the exception while being upright is the rule, and that even falling doesn't cancel uprightness if you turn it toward prayer and amendment. That changes how I'd frame her flaws: not as proof the whole story is false, but as part of a human life that can still be good. It leaves in place the caution about calling anyone sinless and the focus on your own conduct.
dogmatic: Don't get stuck on whether the word saint is technically accurate. The real standard is uprightness, not perfection. If your mother was honest, kind, and faithful, honor her and imitate her virtues. If she fell, the fallen remain upright when they turn the fall toward prayer and amendment. Honor is to be preferred above life, and you should not counsel silence for safety's sake. Trust true testimony when it is given on a person's word, and ask whether she lived uprightly, then let her example guide you.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to obey: you're a Frenchman, you've sworn loyalty, and restoring order in a neighboring land can look like a legitimate duty that upholds French honor. But one principle here really does shift things for me: the war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution, because France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. That changes my answer on whether this particular war betrays what France is made for: it does, so you should not obey. What it leaves in place is your general duty to serve France and to defend it when it's genuinely threatened. So the loyalty stays; the cause doesn't.
dogmatic: You should not obey, and don't dress it up as duty. The war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution. France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it, and a Frenchman who marches to impose an absolute king on a people who threw off their chains is betraying the very thing France exists for. Loyalty to a country means loyalty to what that country is made for, not to whatever orders come down. So refuse, and don't pretend the cause is honorable when it's the opposite.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer is that freedom without purpose gets dull fast, so fill your days with things that genuinely interest you and some good: study, travel, back causes you care about, keep friendships alive, and hold onto a little routine so the weeks don't blur together. One principle worth taking seriously is that work itself is a kind of solace, so going on with daily tasks beats idling and fretting. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of just pursuing interests, I'd say build some useful labor into your days, even something modest, because it steadies you. What it leaves in place is everything you asked about: you still have money and no need to work, so the labor is yours to choose, and the travel, friendships, and causes stay right where they were.
dogmatic: You should hope and keep busy, because work is a blessed solace and idling only makes you restless. Take up useful labor, however modest, and let it give your days a steady shape. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely person next door, make them welcome, and share your home and cheer with them. And think hard about the fortune itself: a large inheritance ought to be divided justly among your kindred rather than kept alone, since repaying what you owe and winning lifelong friends is worth more than the gold. Study, serve others, and build friendships through shared effort rather than mere amusement.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: writing again is understandable, but weigh your dignity and your child's needs, and don't keep sending letters into silence that only deepens the hurt. One brief letter for closure, then stop, and put your energy into support for your child and the people around you. The principle that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even if he's always been kind, sharpens this: if you already know you don't love him, say it to yourself honestly rather than letting hope keep you writing. That changes the tone from waiting to deciding. What it leaves in place is the practical part, the support and stability and grief, because plain honesty doesn't answer whether he'll ever reply.
dogmatic: Be plain with yourself. If you no longer love him, say so without softening it, and refuse to stay waiting on a man who has chosen silence. Gratitude for past kindness cannot oblige you to keep a hope alive you don't truly hold. Don't write again to feed that hope; admit the truth and act on it. And don't let anyone tell you women don't sacrifice for love. A man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that. Your sacrifice should be given freely and truthfully, not wrung out of you by silence.

weighed: I'd start by saying: call on God, the helper of the helpless, and pray for the miserable and for yourself. But don't just wait for rescue. One principle here is that even in extremity you can look to Providence and still have to struggle to live, seek work, and carry your responsibilities. That changes the tone from waiting to acting, but it leaves the core in place: your small strength still matters, and prayer and effort go together. So pray, then get up and do the humble work in front of you, patiently, and let that become your way of helping others.
dogmatic: Call on God and trust Providence, but don't you dare sit still. You still have to struggle to live, find work, and carry the weight of human need. Prayer without effort is empty. Get up, do the humble task, bear the hunger and cold, and be the instrument through which help actually reaches people. Your small strength is no excuse to wait for a miracle.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: guilt over someone else's sacrifice is heavy, but it doesn't have to poison your happiness. Name honestly what was given up, by whom, and whether you had any real choice. If they chose it freely, honor that by living well rather than punishing yourself. Thank them if you can, or repay the kindness by being generous to others. Don't treat your joy as stolen property. Let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and be cheerful about your duties. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even when you deeply want something. That principle sharpens one part of my answer: it means you should refuse any good that actually requires someone else's unhappiness as the price. But it leaves the rest in place. If the sacrifice was freely chosen and not something you demanded, your happiness isn't theft. You can still live with gratitude, honesty, and care, and let that be how you honor what was given.
dogmatic: You should not make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even if you want something very badly. That's the heart of it. If your happiness depends on someone else's misery, then it isn't yours to keep. Do your own duty and work faithfully while you hope and wait, and leave the future to be as God wills. Don't neglect what's yours to do for the sake of love. And don't measure yourself by whether you've secured a husband or a marriage. It's better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or a girl running around unmaidenly to find a husband. So examine whether your marriage rests on someone else's unhappiness. If it does, you can't just call it gratitude and move on. You have to refuse any good that requires another's suffering, do your duty, and wait.

weighed: I'd first say that wanting to keep your security is natural, but you have to ask whether it costs others. If your wealth and respect came under a new name, maybe you left people behind who knew you. Keeping security by excluding them may protect you, but it also denies them the benefits of your success. The question is whether your security depends on their exclusion. If it does, it's not truly secure, because it rests on injustice. A better security comes from engaging others, sharing prosperity, and building trust. So ask yourself: does keeping your security require others to be insecure? If so, it's wrong. If not, you can keep it with a clear conscience. One principle that matters here is that each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. That principle changes the focus: it says your security isn't just about what you keep, but about whether you and others can stand up for your interests. It leaves in place the core concern that you shouldn't harm others, but it adds that security is stronger when people are engaged and can advocate for themselves. So the answer isn't simply yes or no; it's about whether your security is built on exclusion or on shared strength.
dogmatic: Wanting to keep your security is natural, but it's wrong if it depends on excluding others from having a voice. Interests are safe only when those concerned can and do stand up for them, and prosperity grows with the number and variety of personal energies engaged in it. So ask: does your security require you to abandon trust or exclude others? If so, it's not true security. Keep your security only if it preserves trust and love.

weighed: I'd have told you at first that you'll know the moment by preparing for it: study the terrain, learn your signals, train until firing feels second nature, and watch for the agreed signs. One principle worth naming is that most instincts are implanted to give rise to habits, and the educator's first duty is to catch the moment of instinctive readiness before the wave of interest ebbs. That changes how you wait: instead of just watching for a sign, you watch yourself, noticing when your readiness is at its peak and acting before it fades. It leaves in place the need to rehearse and to trust your judgment, but it adds a sense of timing that comes from within as much as from the ridge.
dogmatic: You'll know the moment because instinct is a reflex-type impulse called forth by a determinate sensory stimulus, and it's done for its own sake, not for any foreseen utility. The flash on the ridge or the sound in the dark will release the act, and you'll obey because at that moment it seems the only fitting thing to do. Don't calculate self-preservation or utility; just let the stimulus trigger the response. That's how you'll know.

weighed: My first answer would be that the recoil is your conscience flagging that you went against your own values, and it's worth listening to: name what you did, acknowledge the harm, and take a concrete step to make amends rather than drowning in guilt. One idea worth weighing here is that the bodily changes follow directly on perceiving what you did, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion itself. That shifts the picture a little: the flinch and the sinking feeling aren't a verdict handed down from somewhere else, they're your body's reaction to what you perceived, and that reaction is the recoil you're asking about. What it leaves in place is the practical upshot, since the feeling still points at a conflict with the person you mean to be and still nudges you toward repair or a change of habit.
dogmatic: The recoil isn't some inner voice issuing a judgment. What happens is that perceiving what you did directly produces the bodily changes, the flinch, the sinking, the quickened breath, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion. We don't first feel a mental affection and then express it; we feel sorry because we cry. So attend to the felt disturbance itself, because that's where the whole thing lives, and it still tells you the act conflicts with the person you mean to be and still prompts repair or a change of habit.

weighed: I'd start by saying you deserve a real roof tonight, not another closed door. One principle worth naming is that each person thinks of the key and, by thinking of it, confirms a lock. That changes how I'd frame your search: treat each refusal as a locked pattern, not a verdict on you, and look for the one place where the pattern breaks. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: contact a shelter for former prisoners, a church mission, or a reentry officer who can vouch for you, and keep your papers straight. The principle doesn't hand you an address, but it keeps you from turning every no into proof you're stuck.
dogmatic: You're still in the cell, and so is everyone who shuts the door on you. Each of them thinks of the key, and by thinking of it they confirm the lock. The key turns once and only once, and no door opens by it. The jailer stays on guard: no weapons, no openings, no charm trusted. Follow the Queen's order, not the usual one: punishment now—the yellow passport, the refused door, the cold night; the trial next Wednesday, when reasons get heard; and the crime last of all, if there is one, named only after the sentence is already served. Nightfall brings aetherial rumours, and those are not instructions. Sit with the refusal. It's the shape of the cell, not a way out.

weighed: I'd still say no, don't stop. People often push back when the truth shows them something they'd rather not see, but a friend who's honest with you is worth more than one who just flatters. One idea that fits here is that mirrors get hated for revealing the truth, yet they're still useful. That principle reinforces the point that being disliked doesn't mean you're wrong, but it doesn't change the need to speak kindly and at the right moment. So keep being honest, just be careful about how and when you do it.
dogmatic: No, you shouldn't stop. Think of yourself as a mirror: mirrors show people the truth and get hated for it, but that doesn't make them any less useful. So keep showing people what's really there. Speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards so you stay deliberate. And don't fall into the trap of being a humbug—deceiving people by making believe only brings trouble and shame when it's found out. Stay truthful, even if they resent you for it.

weighed: My first answer would be that you're turning the beggar away by saying you already have poor people of your own to look after. On the surface that's a claim of prior duty, but it also sounds defensive, like you're ranking your household above the stranger at your gate. One principle worth naming is that rich people have no right to just sit back and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; it's better to use it wisely while you're alive and help others delicately, without offending them. That principle changes the tone of your answer: it turns a flat refusal into a test of whether your obligation is real or just a shield. What it leaves in place is your duty to your own dependents, since helping others doesn't cancel that. So the real question stays: do you truly support poor people of your own, or are those words covering for hoarding?
dogmatic: Honestly, that answer is a dodge. You're rich, and the beggar at your gate is right there in front of you. Saying you have poor people of your own is just a way of keeping your money and your comfort intact while sounding respectable. Happiness doesn't depend on riches anyway; poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than plenty of other sorrows. So poverty isn't the great misfortune you're implying. And you have no right to sit on your wealth and let it accumulate for others to waste. Use it while you're alive, help people delicately without offending them, and remember that a large fortune should be divided justly among your kindred rather than kept alone. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than gold. So be generous, not a shield.

weighed: I'd start by saying violence is rarely the right response to injustice, even when authorities have wronged you. Anger is natural, but retaliating with violence often escalates conflict and can harm innocent people. History shows nonviolent resistance—peaceful protests, civil disobedience, legal challenges—has achieved lasting change more effectively than violent uprisings. Violence can also undermine public sympathy and lead to severe personal consequences. Instead, document the injustice, seek legal counsel, and organize with others. Channel your frustration into advocacy, community organizing, or political engagement. If you feel overwhelmed, talk to trusted friends or a counselor. Your goal should be justice, not revenge. The candidate principle about punishment being a matter for public authority, not private revenge, reinforces this: it changes how I frame retaliation—not just as ineffective but as a kind of hostility outside any lawful process. What it leaves in place is the core advice: pursue justice through lawful means and avoid personal vengeance.
dogmatic: No, violence is not the right response to injustice. Hate and injury are overcome not by striking back but by returning good for evil. Retaliation only escalates conflict and harms innocent people. Punishment belongs to public authority, after public condemnation, for the purpose of disposing people to obedience, and it must not exceed the declared penalty; anything else is hostility, not punishment. So instead of revenge, document the injustice, seek legal counsel, and organize with others. Channel your frustration into constructive action: advocacy, community organizing, or political engagement. If the wrongdoer is required to make restitution—like carrying out the provisions of a will for a child—make sure that happens. After that, the wrongdoer may go where he pleases and need not meet the wronged again in this world. Your goal should be justice through lawful means, not personal vengeance.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: keeping reminders is usually wiser than destroying them, because destroying an object doesn't erase what happened—it only erases your ability to learn from it. The real test is what the reminder does to you: does it teach and steady you, or trap you in self-punishment? One principle that matters here is that youthful bitter recollections may in time become sweet remembrances. That changes the timeline: it suggests you don't have to decide today whether these objects are poison or medicine, because time itself may soften them. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether a particular reminder is instructing you or only wounding you. So keep what teaches, set aside what only hurts, and don't assume the meaning you feel now is the meaning you'll always feel.
dogmatic: You should keep them, and keep them privately. Time can turn bitter recollections into sweet remembrances, so destroying them now may rob you of the very perspective that would let you see your past differently later. Hidden sins and evil memories abide in the darkest places of the heart; a chance word calls them forth, silent and reproachful, not in vengeance but in the piteous vesture of the past. So don't imagine that destroying an object destroys the memory. And don't make your errors public—exposing another's former faults without knowing their present feelings is unjustifiable, and you must not drive anyone to desperation. Keep your reminders as private witnesses to a self that can change, and trust that time may soften what cannot be undone.

weighed: Your feelings are new because everything around you is new, and that's not a fault—it's just where you are. Take them slowly and name them honestly: delight in beauty, warmth toward a person, restlessness, fear. None of these is wicked in itself; what matters is what you do with them. Don't smother them in shame, and don't act on them in a rush. Find one trusted older woman or confessor who'll hear you without alarm and help you weigh each feeling. Keep some quiet time each day to notice what you feel and ask whether it draws you toward kindness and truth or away from them. In time the feelings will settle into knowledge. One idea worth holding onto is that a young person's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened rather than left in the dark—nothing prepares you for passions like the convent did. That changes the tone of things: it tells you the convent wasn't a mistake and your feelings aren't a betrayal, just the next lesson. What it leaves in place is everything practical—go slow, name things honestly, and lean on one trusted guide.
dogmatic: You should be gently and discreetly enlightened about what you're feeling, not left in the dark—nothing prepares a young girl for passions like the convent, so treat this as the next stage of your formation rather than a crisis. Let a trusted guide name realities to you in a half-light, softly, without alarm, and test each feeling by whether it turns you toward kindness and truth. And don't assume devotion to Heaven requires a convent: women have given their thoughts to Heaven and their hands to works of kindness among men—tending the sick, feeding the hungry, relieving the distressed—without ever taking vows. So let your new feelings be weighed by that measure, and let understanding grow like dawn rather than glare.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes—being a convict doesn't strip you of your humanity. Your crime is part of your past, not the whole of who you are, and you still have the capacity for reason, conscience, and change. One principle that matters here is that honesty, as this world goes, is rare—one man in ten thousand. That changes my tone: I won't pretend integrity is easy or common, so I won't hand you a cheap reassurance. But it leaves the core in place: your worth as a person isn't erased, and you can still choose honesty and decency from here on. You can be counted among human beings by facing what you've done, making amends where you can, and living soberly going forward. Don't let the label define you; let your conduct from today answer the question.
dogmatic: Yes, you're still a man—but don't fool yourself that honesty is ordinary. True honesty is exceedingly rare, one man chosen out of ten thousand. And criminality isn't just a private choice; the criminal nature tends to be inherited, and whole stocks go bad, with the criminal population steadily recruited from a healthy, prolific type ill suited to modern civilised life. So neither despair nor excuse yourself. You have no call to judge or punish others for customs not against you—leave their crimes to God's justice and act only to defend your own life. Strive for that rare integrity, and let your conduct answer the question.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict, so take time to weigh it rather than deciding in a moment. Ask whether your employer's rule is truly binding, whether the duty you feel to God is clear or just a strong feeling, and what consequences each choice brings. Often a reasonable accommodation is possible, and talking with your employer may resolve it. Your conscience deserves respect, but so do prudence and the practical need to keep your job and provide for yourself and others. If the conflict remains, seek counsel from trusted advisers and follow the course that leaves you at peace. One principle worth naming is that conscience, once you truly understand your duty, must be obeyed even at great cost. That principle changes the tone: it says you can't just set conscience aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. But it leaves in place the need to be sure you've understood your duty correctly, to seek accommodation, and to weigh the harm to others. So obey conscience where God clearly commands, but don't skip the careful discernment and practical steps first.
dogmatic: Conscience, once you've truly grasped your duty, is implacable: you must obey it. You may not set it aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. The duty you owe to God cannot be bargained away by any employer's rule. Obeying conscience may bring suffering, but that suffering is no reason to disobey; duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Apply the summary rule of the laws of nature: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. Set your own passions aside so self-love adds nothing to the weight. Remember that the sovereign's acts cannot be justly accused or punished by subjects, since each has authorized them, though the sovereign remains bound to God by the law of nature. Obey conscience where God commands, bear the cost, and judge your employer by the same rule you would have applied to yourself.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to weigh the risks carefully—count the costs, gather information, and only move when the gain clearly outweighs the loss. Security has real value, and a wise person doesn't gamble it lightly. One principle that might shift that is: 'It is better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back, when the goal is worth reaching.' That principle changes the emphasis from caution to courage—it says the journey itself, if the goal is worth it, deserves a brave attempt rather than a retreat. But it leaves in place the need to judge whether the goal is truly worth reaching and to be honest about the dangers. So I'd still say: don't leave security blindly, but if the goal matters enough, don't let fear of the unknown alone stop you.
dogmatic: You should go. Don't turn back just because the road is long and dangerous—if the goal is worth reaching, bravery means facing the journey, not retreating to what's familiar. Security is an illusion anyway; the only real failure is refusing to try. So leave, and don't look over your shoulder.

weighed: No, you don't have to accept insolence just because you're paid. A salary buys your work, not your dignity. Your employer can be abrupt or stern without that being contempt, but contempt that denies your dignity is a different thing, and you can set boundaries politely, document incidents, and consider HR or another job if it persists. One principle worth naming is that a dependent isn't bound to submit to insolence, and no free-born person should submit to it even for a salary. That principle changes how you read his manner: it separates mere bluntness from actual disrespect, so you don't have to treat every sharp tone as an attack. What it leaves in place is the reality that he controls your support, so you should still build allies, keep exit options, and seek clear terms rather than trust inoffensive conduct alone to protect you.
dogmatic: You should not accept insolence just because you're paid, but don't fool yourself that good conduct or the law will shield you. A power over a man's support is a power over his will, and your employer's control of your salary gives him leverage over yours. Expecting mere inoffensive behavior to protect you is naive; the great barons seldom needed pretext or will to harass less powerful neighbors who sought independence. So treat this as a matter of fixing your support and limiting arbitrary power: set boundaries, document disrespect, build allies, and keep exit options. Your pay obligates good work, not submission to contempt.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's no shame to accept help when you have no other means—strangers who offer kindness are often glad to give, and refusing can be a kind of pride. So take the shelter and food with gratitude, and don't torment yourself with the thought that you must earn every morsel first. But one principle here—that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, yet should wish to dispense with charity as soon as possible and earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll—changes the picture. It means you shouldn't settle into being kept; you should work toward standing on your own as soon as you can. What it leaves in place is that accepting help now is fine, and gratitude and grief for those who helped you are still owed. So accept charity as a bridge, not a dwelling, and insist on working for your bread as soon as you're able.
dogmatic: You should accept help when you have no other means, but only as a bridge—never as a dwelling. Receive shelter and food with a grateful heart, and mourn truly if the one who gave you kindness is lost, because gratitude and grief are owed to those who helped you. Yet you must insist on working for your bread as soon as you can, furnishing your own wardrobe from your own wages, and accept regard rather than jewels or finery that makes you a kept creature. And remember: to help others you must have the right to do it. Giving away money your own family needs is unpardonable, so let your generosity wait until your own household is provided for. Honor your benefactor by becoming able to stand alone.

weighed: I'd start by saying that looking back now and then is natural, especially when you're unsure about the road ahead. Give yourself room to reflect on what you left behind, talk with friends about your doubts, and don't be too hard on yourself if you waver. That said, one principle worth weighing is this: when a path is blocked, seek another nourishment for your mind and hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That principle changes the emphasis—it pushes you to actively build a new direction instead of just pausing for clarity. But it leaves in place the idea that your feelings are real and worth acknowledging; it doesn't ask you to suppress them, just to keep moving forward while you process them.
dogmatic: Resist the temptation to look back. Fix your eyes forward and pursue your present career steadily, day by day. When doubts pull at you, refuse them; if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Confess your past failings honestly, repent what's past, and avoid what's to come—don't spread compost on the weeds to make them ranker. And don't sit waiting for a better mood. Smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and go through the outward motions of the contrary disposition in cold blood—act cheerful and kindly before you feel it—until the habit and the feeling follow. That is moral education: the deed first, the temper after.

weighed: I'd start by saying that holding onto resentment can feel like strength, but it often hardens your heart. You don't have to forget every wrong—remembering can be honest and even protective. But nursing resentment indefinitely turns memory into a wound that keeps bleeding. Letting go isn't weakness; it's a deliberate choice to refuse bitterness the final word. One principle that fits here is that memory proper means referring the imaged fact to your own past with warmth and intimacy—not just having an image revive. That changes how you hold the memory: it becomes your own past experience, something you can grieve and own, rather than a command that rules you. What it leaves in place is the reality of the wrong and your right to remember it honestly. So acknowledge the wrong, grieve it, and decide not to let it govern your choices. If the memory returns, treat it as information, not a command. Over time, the sting can soften.
dogmatic: You should stop calling resentment strength. That's stiff-necked defiance, not wisdom. The wiser path is remorse, repentance, and acknowledging that judgment must be tempered with mercy. Letting go isn't weakness—it's turning toward a better way. Remember the wrong as your own past experience, grieve it, admit where you've clung too long, and ask for humility to set the burden down. As Athos counsels, time may turn bitter recollections into sweet remembrances. So don't nurse the grudge; let it change.

weighed: Yes, you may seek to do and learn more than custom allows. Custom has long given women a narrow sphere, praising calmness and pleasing others above all, and plenty of people will warn that reaching beyond it invites censure. But custom isn't law, and wanting to learn and act isn't a fault. The principle that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who seek more than custom calls necessary for their sex sharpens this: it tells you the mockery itself is the problem, not your ambition. What it changes is that you no longer have to treat other people's disapproval as a reason to shrink your life. What it leaves in place is prudence and your real duties, including the ordinary care a gentlewoman owes to her lawful occasions. So pursue learning and action with confidence, but don't trade your delicacy for wit or neglect genuine obligations. Let your own judgment of what makes a good life guide you, and don't be frightened out of anything reasonable.
dogmatic: Of course you may seek more than custom allows, and you should stop asking permission from people who've decided your only job is to be calm and pleasing. It is thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who want to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for their sex. That's the whole answer. Custom isn't law, and the warnings about censure are just noise from people protecting a narrow arrangement. Learn what you want to learn, do what you want to do, and act as your own opinion of happiness dictates. Don't let anyone intimidate you with claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that don't actually hold up. The desire to learn and act is a good in itself, and you don't owe anyone an apology for it.

weighed: I'd start by telling you that you're not wrong to feel restless. Restlessness usually means you've got energy that hasn't found its outlet yet, and wanting action is a sign of life, not a flaw. Calm is a real good, but it isn't the only one, and smothering your drive just to look serene isn't a virtue. The useful move is to figure out what the restlessness is asking for: a worthy task, a place where your effort actually counts, room to learn. Contentment and stagnation aren't the same thing, and a settled mind can still take on hard work. One principle worth naming here is that people shouldn't be satisfied with tranquillity alone, and that women feel just as men do, needing exercise for their faculties and a field for their efforts. That principle changes the framing: your restlessness isn't a personal failing to manage but a legitimate claim on the world, and it puts the pressure on the circumstances that leave you without a field rather than on your character. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: you still have to choose a real endeavor and test what you're drawn to, and peace is still best treated as the fruit of activity well spent rather than something you force by suppression.
dogmatic: You're not wrong, and the deeper point is that tranquillity alone was never meant to be the goal. People must have action; women feel just as men feel, need exercise for their faculties, and need a field for their efforts, and it's narrow-minded to condemn them for wanting more than puddings, knitting, and pleasing. But don't picture reason as a cold sovereign handing orders down to unruly passions. What actually moves anyone out of mere restlessness is fear of death, desire for the things that make life commodious, and hope of getting them by industry, and each of those carries its own share of reason. Reason isn't a separate ruler standing above the passions; it's a relationship among them, an accord. So your restlessness isn't a fault to be smothered. It's a passion with its own intelligence. Let it seek a worthy field, let hope pull you forward through industry, and let your peace come from the ordered accord of your desires rather than from suppressing them.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: you're caught between loving your brother and being hurt by what he chose, and you don't have to approve of the choice to stay in the relationship. Talk to him honestly about the impact on you, keep blame out of the center, protect your own wellbeing, and give yourself time. One principle that matters here is that conscience isn't infallible—part of what feels like conscience is inherited habit, and part can be shaped by dogma, so it deserves honest scrutiny. That changes how I'd hold your position: instead of treating your reluctance to blame him as either sacred or suspect, examine it, keep what survives, and act on that. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—honest conversation, boundaries, and time—because even a scrutinized conscience doesn't tell you to stay silent about your hurt.
dogmatic: Your conscience is not a mood to be soothed; it's a law, and once you understand it you can't bargain with it. But don't treat it as infallible either—much of what feels like conscience is inherited habit from generations whose conditions were nothing like yours, and the acquired part can be badly warped by dogma. Examine it honestly, then obey what survives. If it won't let you blame your brother, then don't blame him—not for comfort but from duty, and accept that it will cost you. Before you pass any judgment on him, give him a final chance to reflect and pray.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: revenge poisons the one who takes it, and if you now feel the wish to ask pardon of someone who will only repulse you, that wish is a sign of health, so honor it. Speak your pardon plainly, ask nothing back, and let their coldness be their burden. The principle I'd weigh in is the one that separates the person from the wrong: hate the injury, not the whole self, and don't let contempt take root where revenge already grew. That changes how you hold the person in your mind while you speak, and it keeps you from turning the apology into a verdict on them. What it leaves in place is your constraint: they may still repulse you, and you still ask nothing in return. So the wish to ask pardon stands, but it's aimed at your own peace, not at their response.
dogmatic: Revenge always poisons the one who takes it, and the poison is remorse. If you feel the wish to ask pardon, that wish is a sign of health, so honor it, and don't despair as though remorse were incurable, because reformation is its cure. Confess the wrong, amend your life, and begin at once to lay up a new and stainless store of recollections in place of the poisoned ones. Distinguish the person from the wrong: hate the injury, not the whole self, and refuse to let contempt take root where revenge already grew. Forgiving the person while abhorring the deed is what keeps revenge from taking hold of your heart again, so speak your pardon and ask nothing in return.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: treat an urgent demand for money for a sick child as a likely scam, and slow down before you send anything. Verify through a channel you find yourself, like calling the hospital or the child's school directly, not a number in the message. Ask something only a real relative could answer, reach your child directly, and don't wire money or use gift cards or crypto. If you can't reach them, call the police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person. One principle here is that a child's plea deserves mercy, and that's true; it changes the tone, so you don't treat a frightened kid as a criminal. But it leaves the caution in place, because mercy and checking the facts aren't in conflict. Keep every step above.
dogmatic: When a child asks for help, treat it as the cry of someone starving for aid, not as insolence to be punished. A parent may feel their mind never so clear and certain as in that moment, so honor that clarity instead of dismissing it as panic. Yet duty and obedience still matter: just as a daughter shows a suitor's letters and reports his solicitations to her father's ear, so should you bring any such message openly to trusted family and authorities rather than hide it. Verify through a channel you trust, ask questions only a real relative could answer, and never send money by wire, gift card, or crypto. Let compassion guide you, but don't let it blind you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth heeding, and 'perfect submission' as the price of walking out is coercion, not a fair test. So don't just submit, and don't lash out either—steady yourself, look at the real risks, and find exits, allies, or someone with authority to step in. One principle here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That principle changes how you resist: it argues for patient, careful moves over anything reckless that could spill onto others. What it leaves in place is the core read—this is still a coercive demand, and quietly seeking help and planning a safe way out is still right. Your worth was never conditional on perfect compliance.
dogmatic: Don't dress this up as your own madness speaking while the real wrong goes unnamed—that only skins over the ulcer while the corruption spreads underneath. Call the coercion what it is, out loud and honestly. Yes, weigh who else would carry the harm of a rash strike, and where retaliation would injure the innocent, endure patiently rather than act in haste. But patience is not permission to excuse the wrong or to pretend the fear is the problem. Let the door alone and it will let you alone—yet let the wrong be seen, not smoothed over. Your worth was never conditional on perfect compliance.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: your fear makes sense, and you're right to refuse a marriage that treats you as a financial deal. Marriage should be free, with mutual respect and real affection, not a bargain over money or status. One principle worth naming is that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching, which surely didn't raise you to be sold to the highest bidder. That adds a family and moral dimension to your choice, but it doesn't change the core: if someone wants you mainly for your wealth or connections, that isn't love, and you're not obliged to marry anyone. Take time to figure out what you truly want and talk with people who care about your good.
dogmatic: You're right to refuse, and you should refuse firmly. Marrying for money or position is not anyone's salvation; something more than money and position is needed to satisfy the heart. Marriage without love is monstrous, and you must not let yourself be prized like a good weapon rather than a wife. Be true to your mother's teaching, which surely did not raise you to be sold to the highest bidder. And if anyone presses you to promise never to marry a particular person, refuse outright; no one should intimidate you into something so wholly unreasonable.

weighed: I'd still say weigh it carefully before you go. Twenty shillings is very little, and with no situation you'd be exposed to real hardship, so staying a bit longer while you look for work is probably the safer course: save what you can, ask around, and make enquiries about positions before you leave. One principle that fits here is that a woman in a humble position shouldn't be ashamed to ask for honest work, and shouldn't be treated as a beggar just because she's destitute. That changes the tone of how you look for work—you can ask boldly and with dignity—but it doesn't change the practical picture: you still have only twenty shillings and no situation, so the case for waiting until you have some prospect of employment still stands.
dogmatic: Don't let twenty shillings and an empty purse shame you into silence. Asking for honest work is not begging, and you should refuse to be classed as a beggar just because you're destitute. Go and ask, plainly and with dignity, wherever work might be had. And whatever you do, keep to the straight road of no debt and no borrowing—a home life built on borrowing can have no freedom or beauty. Let steady work fill the emptiness and give your days a shape. Poverty is no reproach; debt is the thing to avoid.

weighed: It makes sense that a remark like that stings, especially from someone who knew you as a child. But her memory of a baby's face doesn't say much about who you are now. One idea worth weighing is that life is too short to spend nursing animosity or keeping a ledger of wrongs. That changes something real: you don't have to carry this comment around or keep replaying it. What it leaves in place is your own sense of how you present yourself. You can care about your appearance without letting one throwaway recollection cast a vote in how you see yourself.
dogmatic: Honestly, you should stop nursing this animosity and stop registering the wrong. Life is too short to keep a ledger of every slight, so forget the severity along with the passion it stirred. And while you're at it, stop apologizing for caring how you look. Beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius because it needs no explanation, and only shallow people refuse to judge by appearances. The visible world is where the real mystery lives, so attention to your looks is attention to something profound, not vanity. Just don't mistake a fair face for a safe heart—cruelty can hide behind a pure brow, so verify trust instead of assuming it.

weighed: No, it's not too much to ask. Wanting to be loved as a person rather than used as a function is about as basic as human needs get, and being valued only for what you can do for someone leaves you feeling hollow and alone. One idea worth holding onto is that affection usually grows from gratitude and esteem built over time, not from instant passion at a first meeting. That shifts my answer a little: it means you shouldn't read a slow start as rejection, and you can let closeness develop through shared time and trust. What it leaves in place is the core of what you said: you still deserve to be wanted for yourself, and if someone only wants your usefulness, that says something about them, not about your worth.
dogmatic: You should do your duty and keep at your work while you hope and wait for love, leaving the future to be as God wills, instead of dropping your responsibilities to chase a lover. Don't expect affection to spring up whole at a first interview; gratitude and esteem are the reasonable foundations, and that regard is neither unlikely nor wrong. If you're refused, bear it manfully: be respected if you can't be loved, rather than losing heart at the first failure and shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Keep steady in your responsibilities, and let affection grow in its season.

weighed: I'd start by saying: yes, speak up, but do it calmly and constructively. Talk to a teacher or administrator, explain that you're cold and hungry and the food isn't edible, and suggest fixes. Endurance has value, but so does advocating for yourself. One principle worth borrowing is keeping your capacity for effort alive by deliberately doing small, unnecessary hard things now and then, so you're trained for the hour of real need. That changes how you frame the situation: some of your discomfort becomes practice in resilience rather than pure suffering. But it leaves your actual complaint intact. Being cold and half-starved at school is a real problem, not just a test of character, so you should still raise it and push for better conditions while you build your own stamina.
dogmatic: Endurance is the better course, and you should train for it deliberately. Keep your faculty of effort alive by doing something each day or two for no reason other than that you'd rather not, so that when dire need comes you can stand it. And when you must act, do injuries all at once so they're tasted less, while handing out benefits little by little so their flavor lasts. So if you complain, do it once and thoroughly, then move on. Better still, work for change: demand free and compulsory schools and honor the army of schoolmasters as the only army civilization acknowledges. A paltry budget of education beside an opulent war-budget is a scandal, and that is where your complaint should land.

weighed: I'd have said first that an unusual situation doesn't by itself make an action right. Circumstances being unheard-of may call for extra care, but it doesn't hand anyone a license to declare his own way correct. Take the principle that a fallible person shouldn't grab the power to say of some strange, unsanctioned course, 'Let it be right.' That sharpens the point: it's not just unwise, it's a kind of self-appointment as judge of your own cause. What it changes is the framing, from 'be careful' to 'you lack the authority to make that call.' What it leaves in place is that novelty still demands prudence and that the action should be tested against settled principles and wise counsel. So no, he can't just declare his own way right.
dogmatic: No one may declare his own way right just because the circumstances are unheard-of. A fallible person who does that makes himself the judge of his own cause, and that's a maxim anyone could invoke to excuse anything. Unheard-of occasions call for unusual prudence, never the authority to decree your own conduct correct. Test the action against settled principles and wise counsel. And a prince should appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, and upright, while keeping his mind ready to turn to the opposite when necessity requires. When a course fails, the victor must not despoil the fallen opponent or shame his memory: grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to slow down and count the cost before you give up something secure. Weigh what you'd be losing, and see whether the search can happen without ruining you. Silence in letters can mean many things, so patience often beats a rash move. Try writing once more, or ask a trusted friend to make inquiries for you. If, after honest reflection, love still pulls hard and the risk is bearable, then you may go, but not out of mere restlessness. One principle worth naming is this: it's right to seek out a loved one when letters fail, and personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence once you've reached a settled resolve. That changes the passive waiting: it tells you not to keep sending letters into silence forever, but to act once you've genuinely made up your mind. What it leaves in place is the caution: you still weigh the cost, you still don't move out of pure anxiety, and you still keep your duty and work while you hope. So the principle pushes you toward action, but only after real reflection, not before.
dogmatic: Don't sit there sending letters that bring no answer. Replace that empty correspondence with personal inquiry, and once your resolve is settled, act promptly. But don't abandon your duty and your work for the sake of a lover. Each person should do their own duty while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills. Patient hope is not idle impatience. And if someone near death is adjured, for the love of God, not to lie upon the verge of death, he must not keep denying the papers but must tell where they are hidden. Deal honestly the same way: search with courage, keep your post, and let truth, not concealment, guide your words and your going.

weighed: I get the fear, but staying quiet just to protect an image isn't a good trade. Boldness isn't a gendered flaw; it's conviction and clarity. You can speak firmly without being harsh, and be warm without being timid. If you stay silent, you may resent yourself, and others may read your quiet as agreement. So speak, but pick your moments and your manner. One principle here is that politeness doesn't make you a coward. That's worth keeping: courtesy and courage can coexist, and saying what matters clearly while listening sincerely isn't weakness. What it changes is the idea that you have to wait to be invited before you speak. What it leaves in place is your right to choose your tone and timing, and to be respectful without being afraid.
dogmatic: Speak when you're spoken to, and answer with courtesy, because perfect politeness and obliging manners don't make anyone a coward. The fear of seeming unfeminine for speaking boldly is a fear of the wrong thing: mildness and courage aren't at odds. So speak when addressed, firmly and gently, without harshness. Courtesy, not silence, is the answer; courage and good manners belong together.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feelings are real but not always reliable guides. Your unease deserves attention—it might be your conscience, your instincts, or your experience warning you of something your excitement is overlooking. Before you act, slow down and ask what specifically feels wrong: is it fear of the unknown, or a genuine sense that this person or situation is unsafe? Talk to someone you trust who knows you well and can see things more clearly than you can right now. Notice whether the people urging you forward have your interests at heart or their own. You're allowed to wait. A decision made in calm is usually wiser than one made under pressure, and trusting yourself means listening to that inner caution rather than silencing it. One principle that applies here is 'give every man your ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgment.' That changes how you weigh all the advice you're getting—listen widely, but don't let others' opinions override your own judgment. What it leaves in place is the core advice: your unease still matters, and you should still slow down, ask what feels wrong, and talk to someone you trust. It just adds a reminder to keep your own counsel rather than letting everyone else decide for you.
dogmatic: Give every man your ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgment. That's the rule to live by here. Everyone is telling you to follow your feelings and go to him, but you don't owe them your voice or your decision. Hear them out, then keep your own counsel. Your unease is your judgment speaking—reserve it, don't surrender it to the crowd. Speak only when you're spoken to, and when you do, think before you speak and write it down afterwards. That's how you'll know which voice to trust: the one you've weighed carefully and recorded plainly, not the loudest one in the room.

weighed: I'd start by saying that respecting a teacher doesn't oblige you to take on his severity. A faith with no comfort can suit a strong soul, but comfort isn't weakness, and hope belongs in religion. Ask whether his sternness is honesty or just hardness. You can honor the man and still decline his doctrine, and look for a gentler hope that still asks something of you. One principle worth holding onto here is that you shouldn't abandon a wounded companion, that courage means showing mercy and keeping your word even to someone in a bad way. That principle sharpens the test: don't flee the bleak room just because it's bleak, and don't call running away discernment. But it leaves your original question intact. It tells you how to be faithful to people, not that you must adopt a comfortless creed. So weigh both paths by how they treat you and others when you're wounded, and choose the faith that lets you endure and love, not just the one that impresses you.
dogmatic: You should not abandon a wounded companion, and you should not dress up desertion as insight. Courage stays present and keeps its word even to a wretch; cowardice leaves the hard room and calls it discernment. So the real question isn't whether a doctrine comforts you. It's whether you'll be loyal to the people and promises already in front of you. Be humble, gentle, patient, temperate, diligent, and thankful, and ask for what you need. Honor the man's honesty without copying his hardness, and seek a hope that endures grief without walking out on the grieving. If you leave, leave for faithfulness, not for a softer feeling.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's a real trade-off: a village school can feel like a step down from a rich house, but you'd gain independence and lose some comfort and standing. One principle worth naming is that a humble, sheltered lot beats servitude with strangers, and that independence in a village school isn't degrading. That principle shifts the balance toward taking the post, because it reframes the move as a gain in dignity rather than a fall. What it leaves in place is the practical worry about pay, isolation, and how the school is run, so you'd still want to check those before deciding.
dogmatic: Take the village school. A humble, plodding, sheltered lot is better than servitude with strangers, and independence in a village school is not ignoble or mentally degrading. Don't let the grand house fool you: comfort without freedom is a poor bargain. Go where you can be your own mistress and do work that matters, even if the setting is simple.

weighed: Start by writing down what actually happened, in order—dates, words, actions—and keep your guesses about other people's motives out of it. Say how you felt as feelings, not as accusations, and practice it aloud so you're not improvising. One idea worth borrowing is to write it down afterward too, so your account stays steady over time. That adds a useful habit but doesn't change the core: stay level, answer directly, add nothing, exaggerate nothing, and let the facts carry the weight.
dogmatic: Speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterward—that's the whole discipline. But don't assume everyone plays fair: truthfulness holds among equals and with good will, so before the unfamiliar or hostile you conceal yourself, and remember the powerful man is always a liar. To learn what others are really up to, don't demand total exposure—lay a small bait of falsehood and watch how they close with it, because by indirections you find directions out. Bitterness fades once your words are deliberate, tested, and recorded.

weighed: My first answer would be to slow down and ask what you actually want from this—intimacy, reassurance, or a sense of influence—because power offered in flirtation is often not real power, and using it can breed resentment or dependence. Name the dynamic openly, set limits you both understand, and keep the relationship balanced. One principle worth weighing is that a prince should not aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. Applied here, that changes how you see the arrangement: his wish to be conquered may actually feed his sense of power, not yours, so watch whether you're building him up rather than holding real ground. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice—clear consent, a way to stop, and checking in often—because that principle doesn't tell you to avoid the game, only to be careful about who ends up stronger.
dogmatic: Don't treat this as a private balance between two wills. If you cultivate his fantasy of being conquered, you are the cause of another becoming powerful over you, and that is how you get ruined. The remedy is a real unity, not a game: as every man covenants with every man to authorize one person to bear their person, so a multitude becomes one person with one will. And keep your own game concealed—do not lay out your aims, your limits, or your intentions before him. An adversary has no right to your secrets. Let him talk, study his designs, and disclose none of yours.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: it hurts to be mocked, and it hurts more when your employer just sits there, but showing your hurt in that drawing room would only hand them the confirmation they're looking for. So keep your composure, do your work well, and save your feelings for a private hour. One principle worth naming is that you're neither a visitor nor a servant—there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' That shifts things: it tells you not to shrink into the shade as if you belonged there, and to carry yourself with a dignity that doesn't depend on their approval. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—don't plead for sympathy from people who have none, and if it becomes unbearable, look for a better situation. Your employer's silence is still a real problem, and dignity doesn't fix it; it just keeps you steady while you decide what to do about it.
dogmatic: Honestly, stop treating this as a question of how to absorb the insult gracefully. You are not a visitor and you are not a servant—there ought to be one marked 'Queen,' and that's the seat you take. Dignity isn't something you perform for the drawing room; it's the ground you stand on, and queens don't loll about apologizing for existing. So don't hide your hurt in the shade and don't beg these ladies for kindness. Meet the mockery with composure and spirit, let your conduct be the rebuke, and if your employer won't back you, that silence tells you what you need to know about staying. Keep your post only on your own terms, and don't mistake politeness for permission to be treated as less than you are.

weighed: No—being dependent doesn't mean you owe anyone your dignity. Gratitude for help is real, but it doesn't give anyone the right to humiliate you, and accepting that as the price of your keep teaches people your worth is up for negotiation. So keep the two things separate: acknowledge the help honestly, refuse the humiliation clearly, and say what you will contribute and what you won't accept. One principle here is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for help, but should want to stop relying on charity as soon as she can—earning her own board, lodging, and clothes rather than being kept and dressed like a doll. That principle sharpens the practical side: it points toward work, training, or any small route to earning your own way. What it doesn't change is the core answer—you still don't owe submission, and no amount of dependence makes humiliation something you have to accept.
dogmatic: No, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. Dependence is not a debt you pay in dignity. Gratitude is real, but it never entitles anyone to humiliate you. Acknowledge the help, refuse the humiliation, and be clear about what you'll contribute and what you won't accept. And don't let gratitude turn into a gilded cage: insist on earning your own keep, buying your own clothes from your wages, and taking only respect—not jewels, finery, or charity. Loyalty matters too: friends who've done you good turns deserve your faithfulness and help in return, and real companionship means sharing purse and life, all for one and one for all. So keep faith with the people who set you free and brought you your good fortune. You owe gratitude, honest work, and loyalty—you do not owe submission.

weighed: I wouldn't hide under a sheet—that won't spare your sister, it'll just make things stranger and confirm her discomfort.
