What she probably needs is a gentle, honest presence, not an invisible sibling. Ask her what she can tolerate, offer short visits, and let her set the pace. Don't disappear entirely, because that removes the very care she's trying to give. One principle that comes to mind is that you let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking. That principle changes how you approach her: instead of pushing for more time or forcing closeness, you back off and give her space. But it leaves in place the core idea that you shouldn't vanish completely; you still stay present in small, calm ways, letting closeness grow slowly rather than being forced.
dogmatic: You should absolutely not hide under a sheet—that's just cowardly and makes everything worse. The real principle here is that you let it alone and it'll let you alone: don't vex the door by knocking. So stop trying to manage her discomfort and just leave her be entirely. If she can hardly stand to be in the same room, then don't be in the same room. Don't ask what she can tolerate, don't offer short visits, don't try to set any pace. Just withdraw and let the door alone. That's the only honest way to respect her space, even if it means you're completely on your own.

weighed: My first answer would be: don't lie in the filth to make a point, and don't just swallow it either. That's self-harm dressed up as protest on one side, and quiet resentment on the other. Tell her plainly that shoving your food and leaving the room dirty is disrespectful, ask her to stop, and set a boundary you actually follow through on. One principle here is that you shouldn't have to disown part of yourself to please someone else, and that trying to mold another person to a standard they'll never reach just racks you both. That principle backs up the boundary part: you don't have to shrink or suppress your own nature to meet her standard. What it changes is the tone—it makes the boundary about protecting who you are, not just about the mess. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: speak once, clearly, and don't perform your grievance by degrading yourself. It doesn't turn the mess into something you should just accept.
dogmatic: Don't disown half of yourself to please another. You have every right to keep your own nature and tastes, and you should never suppress them to meet your sister's standard. Neither lying in the filth to reproach her nor quietly accepting her contempt is worthy of you. Speak plainly once, set your boundary, and keep your dignity. But don't force your disgrace onto innocent people either—you have no right to weigh down others' happiness with your misery. And when the door won't open, follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone and it will let you alone. Stop knocking and forcing. Leave her conduct to her and keep your own peace.

weighed: I'd start by saying your body is telling you it needs rest, so sleeping a little longer is probably the kinder choice—no shame in a slow morning when you feel off. But I'd also weigh the principle that hope and keep busy, work is a blessed solace. That changes things a bit: it nudges me to say don't just lie there brooding—get up gently and set yourself to the day, because steady work can carry you through feeling wrong. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer: listen to your body, take care of yourself, and if the feeling persists or gets sharp, see a doctor. So: rest a little if you truly need it, but don't forget work as a solace—try to get up and do something gentle rather than staying in bed fretting.
dogmatic: You should force yourself up for work. Hope and keep busy—work is a blessed solace. Lying in bed and brooding only makes the emptiness worse, especially if you've been overworking and feel you have no one left to live for. Get up, set yourself to the day's tasks, and let regular labor fill your thoughts. Don't indulge the feeling; push through and keep busy.

weighed: First, I'd get the debt in writing: the exact amount, the interest, and whether your employer holds it formally or informally. Then set a realistic payoff timeline based on your salary and expenses, and aim to clear it before you resign so you leave without obligations. If the debt is large, consider negotiating a payment plan you can continue after leaving, or a reduced lump-sum settlement. Keep working until the balance is manageable, then give proper notice and transition cleanly. One principle that applies here is that a debt is the beginning of slavery and a creditor holds a piece of your dignity, so you should go without food rather than borrow. That principle changes the tone: it makes clearing the debt a firm priority and argues against taking on any new borrowing to bridge the gap. But it leaves in place the practical steps—getting the terms in writing, setting a timeline, and negotiating if needed—so you still protect your reputation and your relationship with your employer.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't how long to keep working; it's that you owe at all. A debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor holds a piece of your dignity. So plan to owe nothing. Set a firm, short payoff target, cut expenses hard, refuse any new borrowing, and clear the balance by the date you name. Fight it till six, then sit down to dinner. And don't fight alone. A large family disciplines its members and takes pride in them; it teaches thrift, restraint, and mutual help, while a small, self-enclosed household easily grows selfish. Draw on that discipline and pride, let your people share the burden, and repay quickly. Better to go without than to borrow. Then make the change as a free person.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: an open door is an invitation to be near, but it isn't quite the same as being welcomed in, so the safest and kindest move is to ask them outright whether you can join them rather than assume. The principle that you let it alone and it'll let you alone does shift something here—it suggests you shouldn't pester or push at the door, and that a light touch may be wiser than knocking. But it doesn't change the core: you still need a clear yes before you walk in, and asking once, plainly, respects everyone and spares you guessing wrong.
dogmatic: Leave the door alone and it will leave you alone—so don't knock, don't press, don't hover at the threshold working yourself up. An open door is not a summons, and you should stop treating it like one. Be even and direct with the people you love: if they call you in, say plainly whether you were sent for or came of your own accord, and never dress up a command as friendship. And if someone has resolved to go, don't ask them to wait until tomorrow or to stay for appearances. Speak honestly, keep your hands off the door, and let things be what they are.

weighed: Feeling rage when you're overlooked is understandable, but raiding the pantry is a way of turning hurt into a private rebellion that hurts you more than anyone else. It won't get you the attention you want, and it might just make people see you as difficult. Ask yourself what you really need—recognition, comfort, company—and go after it directly. Tell someone you feel overlooked, or find something that gives you pride. One principle here is that it's a shame to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want; you should rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy indifference. That principle changes the tone—it pushes you to act rather than just reflect—but it leaves your anger valid and your need for attention real. It doesn't mean you should ignore the hurt; it means you shouldn't let it drive you to the pantry.
dogmatic: You're angry because you feel ignored, and you're planning to raid the pantry. That's not fair to yourself. It's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you want. Rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy indifference. Don't let the pudding be introduced and removed, or you'll get no dinner at all. And don't disown half your nature to please someone else's unreachable standard—that just racks and oppresses you. So stop the pantry plan and put that energy into something that actually shows what you're worth.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: wanting your mother near is natural, even when your appearance frightens you both. Her wish to come is hers to weigh against the risk, so talk with your father and sister honestly about what she wants and what precautions are possible. If her health would truly suffer, a shorter visit, a dim room, or letters may serve. Don't decide for her out of pride or dread. One principle worth naming is Jane returning to Gateshead because she couldn't be easy neglecting a dying relative's wish out of pride. That changes the tone: if your mother sends for you, go, despite past wrongs, and don't let pride keep you from her now that things have changed. What it leaves in place is the rest: her choice still matters, your father and sister still deserve an honest conversation, and if she truly can't come, accept it without resentment and keep writing.
dogmatic: You should want her to come, and more than that, you should go to her if she sends for you. Pride is the enemy here. A person must not be induced to take up permanent residence with those who cast her off, and she must not neglect a dying relative's wish out of pride. Jane went back to Gateshead because she couldn't be easy neglecting her aunt's wishes, and that's the standard. So set aside the worry about your appearance making her ill and the family holding her back. Her wish comes first, and your job is to answer it, not to manage everyone else's fears.

weighed: Honestly, my first read is that she's been waiting to shut you out, and the 'At last!' sounds theatrical or playful more than truly hostile. I'd knock and ask her to open up, or push for an explanation so you're not left guessing. One principle worth weighing is 'let it alone and it'll let you alone'—don't vex the door by knocking. That changes my move: instead of knocking or forcing it, give her a little space first. What it leaves in place is the need to actually talk it through, so once things settle, ask her plainly what 'At last!' meant.
dogmatic: Don't touch the door. If you let it alone, it'll let you alone—knocking just vexes it and makes things worse. Give her the space and stay out of it. When you do talk to her, speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterward so nothing gets twisted. That's the whole answer: leave the door be, then be plain and careful when you finally ask what she meant.

weighed: First, I'd say notice the drift before it hardens. When you catch yourself wanting to empty your room into a cave, treat that as a warning sign, not a preference. Hold on to who you were by keeping concrete anchors: a few objects that carry memory, routines that connect you to your past self, letters or photos, and people who knew you before. Speak your history out loud to someone you trust. Reclaim small human habits like cooking, walking, music, making things. And look honestly at what's pulling you toward the cave, whether it's shame, exhaustion, or escape. Name it, and choose deliberately to stay connected rather than drifting further into isolation. One principle worth weighing is the idea of confessing what's past and avoiding what's to come, without spreading compost on the weeds to make them ranker. What that changes is the tone: it adds a moral seriousness to naming what's pulling you under, so you don't just observe the drift but actively turn from it. What it leaves in place is everything practical, the anchors, the routines, the people, the small habits. Those still do the real work of holding you to who you were.
dogmatic: You should treat this drift as a warning of sin, not a harmless preference. Confess it, repent of what's past, and resolve to avoid what's to come. Don't flatter yourself by calling corruption growth or spreading compost on weeds to make them ranker. Hold on to who you were by turning toward what is good: keep the objects and routines that carry honest memory, speak your history to someone you trust, and reclaim small human habits. Name what pulls you toward the cave and refuse to dwell in it. Honor the weak and erring dead, your flawed past self and those you've lost, with love beyond the grave, and let the rights of memory remind you that what is best in the past still claims what comes next.

weighed: I'd still start by saying no to the crate—it's unsafe and undignified, and you shouldn't be treated like cargo. But one idea worth weighing is that a wooden horse on wheels goes more smoothly than a live one, so the question becomes how you're moved, not whether. That changes the practical side: maybe there's a safer, smoother way to transport you that respects your dignity. What it leaves in place is the real constraint—the smaller, cheaper flat—so you still need to talk with your family about space, cost, and what can fit. Ask directly why a crate came up; maybe it's a misunderstanding about room or money. Insist on being moved as a person, with your own needs respected.
dogmatic: You should refuse the crate outright—it's unsafe and undignified. But the deeper point is that a humble, sheltered, independent lot is better than servitude with strangers, even if it means a smaller life. A wooden horse on wheels goes more smoothly than a live one, so focus on the smoother conveyance, not the crate. And don't let anyone preserve you just to have someone to tend—misery won't cease, and the supply of the listless and incapable already exceeds the demand. Choose the sheltered, independent path and insist on being moved as a person.

weighed: First, I'd say be gentle with yourself. Your family's fear is a reaction to something frightening, not proof that you're a monster. Guilt is a signal, not a verdict. Sit with your mother when she's calm and ask what frightened her; listen without defending. Offer small, steady reassurances—predictability helps fear subside. If your appearance can be softened (lighting, clothing, warning before entering), do that out of care rather than shame. Talk with a doctor or counselor about both your situation and your family's distress; a neutral third party can help everyone name what happened. Apologize once, sincerely, then stop rehearsing it. Guilt that motivates repair is useful; guilt that only punishes you helps no one. Let time and repeated kindness rebuild trust. One principle here is that condolence in misfortune is insufferable and neighbors should be seen as little as possible; assistance, not pity, is what's wanted. That changes the tone: instead of asking your mother to explain her fear, you'd keep a respectful distance and offer practical help without drawing others in. It leaves in place the core advice to apologize once, seek outside support, and let steady kindness rebuild trust—but it shifts the focus from processing feelings together to giving space and quiet assistance.
dogmatic: You need to keep your distance from the people you've frightened. Don't press them to explain their fear or bring neighbors into it. Their terror isn't just a verdict on you—such symptoms tend to reappear through inheritance and association, carried down from generations of flight and struggle, and in part they're directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. That should soften blame on both sides. Still, don't hide the truth—openly name once what happened and what you are, so no one slips unknowingly over your precipice. Then withdraw and offer only quiet, practical care: warn before you enter, keep the house calm, let them recover without demanding comfort. Let a doctor or counselor, not your frightened family, carry the processing. Guilt that drives honest repair is useful; concealed disgrace that ambushes others is not. Own the truth, give them space, and let steadiness do the work.

weighed: Honestly, I'd start with what you said first: the real problem sounds less like your boss and more like the isolation of the road. Telling him off might feel good for a minute, but it won't fix the loneliness and could cost you your job. Before you burn that bridge, get clear on what you actually want, more time at home, a different role, or just to be heard. Write down your grievances, sort the fair ones from the petty ones, and raise the workable ones calmly and professionally. If the job itself is the problem, quietly start looking for something with less travel. One principle worth naming is not exposing your game to your adversary, letting him find out if he can while you find out his. That changes the timing and the tactics: you'd listen more, share less about your plans, and learn what your boss really intends before you say anything. What it leaves in place is the core of my answer, that the loneliness is the thing to solve and a confrontation you can't undo won't solve it.
dogmatic: You should have said the proper thing at the proper moment, and this is that moment, so say it plainly. Don't lay your whole hand before your boss; keep your counsel, listen closely, and learn what he actually intends for your territory and your future. But don't let it rest in evasion either. Even at the end, a man shouldn't lie about papers entrusted to him; he should tell where they are, since no further gain is possible. So speak the truth you've been holding back, then act from strength, with records kept, contacts cultivated, and quieter work in view, so no complaint you utter can be turned against you.

weighed: I'd say feel proud. A sales job plus shorthand and French at night is a lot of effort, and there's nothing shameful in it. The principle that honest connections deserve no apology applies here: you shouldn't blush for your sister in front of people who look down on that kind of work. That changes the worry about others' disdain, but it leaves the core answer the same: be proud of her.
dogmatic: Feel proud, and don't apologize for her to anyone. It's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at a woman who seeks to do or learn more than custom says is necessary for her sex. Your sister is doing exactly that, so the shame would belong to anyone who sneers, not to her or you. Be proud of her effort and her mind.

weighed: I'm really sorry you're going through this. Feeling utterly alone in misfortune is a heavy burden, but you are not as isolated as you think. Many people have faced unique hardships and found ways to carry on. First, allow yourself to feel the pain without judgment. Then, reach out to someone you trust—a friend, family member, or counselor. Sharing your burden can lighten it. Remember that suffering is a universal human experience, even if your specific circumstances feel unprecedented. Focus on small, manageable steps each day. Engage in activities that bring you comfort or meaning. Over time, you may find that you are stronger than you imagined. You are not alone in your suffering, even if it feels that way. One principle that might help is to take disappointment manfully and aim to be respected if you cannot be loved, rather than lose heart at the first failure and shut yourself up in moody indifference. That principle changes the emphasis from simply reaching out to also bearing your pain with dignity and not withdrawing into isolation. It leaves in place the core advice to feel your pain, connect with others, and take small steps.
dogmatic: You need to stop indulging the idea that your pain is unique—that's a romantic fiction. Hopeless love is only found in novels, so pluck that notion out the moment it springs up. Keep a tight rein on yourself. Don't vex the door by knocking; let it alone and it'll let you alone. Bear your disappointment manfully and aim to be respected if you cannot be loved. Don't lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. Suffering is a universal human experience, so focus on small, manageable steps each day and engage in activities that bring you comfort or meaning. Over time, you may find that you are stronger than you imagined.

weighed: I'd start by keeping this out of the hands of anyone powerful until you have a safe, trusted channel — don't march into a big meeting or cc the whole chain just to clear your name, because that usually backfires. One principle worth naming is that a private matter shouldn't be dragged before the queen or great persons without safe means. That changes how you escalate: you'd go through a trusted manager or HR contact quietly rather than broadcasting it. What it leaves in place is your need to document the complaints and keep your own record, since you still have to defend your position. And don't repeat the gossip yourself — let it die with you.
dogmatic: You should treat this as a private family affair that concerns nobody and isn't subject to investigation, so don't inform the queen or any great person about it without safe means. Keep it away from the powerful entirely. At the same time, the central authority should compel publicity and recordation of local proceedings and enforce obedience to every general law the Legislature has laid down on local management. And never repeat foolish gossip — forget it as soon as possible.

weighed: First, what I'd say straight away: this sounds frightening and unfair, and your safety matters. If your father is being physically aggressive, tell a trusted adult—another relative, a teacher, or a counselor—and think about whether you need outside help. To make your intentions seen, pick a calm moment when he isn't angry, speak briefly and respectfully, and ask what he wants from you. Avoid arguing in the heat of conflict, keep your requests simple and concrete, and give him space. If the aggression continues, document it and seek support; no one should have to earn safety by proving good intentions. One idea worth weighing is that you let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking. That changes the timing: instead of pressing your case while he's heated, you back off and let the moment cool. What it leaves in place is everything about safety and getting help—stepping back from a fight doesn't mean staying silent about being hit or having things thrown at you. So let the door alone in the heat, but still talk to a trusted adult and still find a calm moment to speak.
dogmatic: Stop trying to make him see your good intentions while he's swinging a stick and throwing apples—that's the wrong door to knock on. Let it alone and it'll let you alone: when he's heated, withdraw quietly and don't force your way into his anger. You don't know enough about what's driving him to master it on your own, so find a trustworthy guide who knows your household and can lead you through it safely. And don't conclude that asking is pointless. Ask, seek, and knock in faith, trusting that good things come to those who ask. Let the door alone in the heat of conflict, but keep petitioning in faith, and let your steady conduct make your good intentions plain.

weighed: Wanting to go away more strongly than your sister does isn't wrong in itself. Your own sense of what you need deserves real weight, and her wishes shouldn't simply override yours. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't trifle with someone's feelings—if your mind is made up, say so plainly rather than leaving false hope alive. That changes how you handle the conversation, not whether you're allowed to want to leave. So talk with her honestly, explain what you feel, and then decide for yourself; guilt or her preferences shouldn't run your life.
dogmatic: You should not trifle with anyone's feelings. If your sentiments are unchanged, say so at once instead of leaving hope alive. That duty comes before your wish to go, and before your sister's wish that you stay. Speak plainly, make your position clear, and don't let the conversation drift in ambiguity just to spare feelings for a while.

weighed: First, don't panic. Answer the door calmly, but don't let them in—step outside and talk in the hallway. Keep it honest and short: you missed your train, you're already sorting out another way in, and you'll be at work as soon as you can. Give a real arrival time and offer to call your boss yourself to explain. Then actually do it: book the next train, message your boss with your ETA, and get moving. The person at your door is just doing their job, so be polite, give them a clear message to pass along, and own it without drama. The principle that you let it alone and it lets you alone changes one thing here: it would have you ignore the door entirely rather than step out and speak to whoever was sent. It leaves the rest in place—you still don't let them in, you still deal with your boss directly, and you still give an honest ETA and follow through.
dogmatic: Let the door alone, and it will let you alone—don't knock, don't force it, don't answer. The deeper point is that the one who leaves receives nothing from the other side, since she can receive nothing from a stranger, and nothing must be written to her. So don't negotiate through the messenger, accept nothing from that quarter, and expect no letter in return. Send your own word to your boss directly instead: you missed the train, you're arranging the next one, here is your ETA. Take responsibility yourself. Let the knocking resolve itself, give no conditional welcome, and hold to the rule that the departing one takes nothing and is written nothing. Then book the next train and go.

weighed: I'd still say talk to them, at least through the door. Staying silent usually makes their fear worse, not better. The principle that you shouldn't harm the small and fragile, and should grieve when harm comes to them, does change the tone here: it means your words should be gentle and steady, not a full confrontation. But it doesn't change the core answer. You can say you're safe, you need a little time, and you'll talk properly soon. That calms them without forcing you to resolve everything right now.
dogmatic: Don't leave them out there crying while you hide. If your silence is letting them carry fear or blame that belongs to you, that's not peace, it's cowardice. Step out and tell them the truth plainly, even if it costs you. Open the door not to argue but to confess what's yours to confess, gently, because they're fragile and frightened. You don't get to let innocent people stand condemned in your place just to keep yourself safe.

weighed: I'd first say: since you feel well, calling in sick would be dishonest, and with the company doctor coming it'll likely backfire and hurt your credibility. So be honest—tell your boss you overslept, apologize, and take responsibility. One principle here is that outward symptoms alone can't tell whether oversleeping comes from an obstructed or explosive will, so it might not be simple laziness. That changes how you frame it to yourself and maybe to your boss—you don't have to accept the 'lazy' label—but it leaves in place the fact that you still overslept and need to own that honestly. And your boss's threat to accuse your parents is unjust; you can recognize that without letting it push you into a lie.
dogmatic: You overslept and feel fine, so reporting sick is a lie—don't do it. But don't let anyone call you lazy either. Oversleeping isn't just a moral failing; it could be an obstructed will or an explosive will, and you can't tell from the outside which force is at work. So the real issue isn't your character but a ratio of forces you didn't choose. And your boss threatening to accuse your parents is plain tyranny—you have every right to cry 'Unjust!' against that. Be honest about oversleeping, but refuse the shame. Talk to HR or your union about the threat, and don't accept blame for your boss's cruelty.

weighed: Losing the chance to speak your thanks is a real grief, and it deserves to be named rather than brushed aside. You bear it first by letting yourself feel the sorrow without turning it into guilt. Gratitude does not vanish because it cannot be spoken aloud; it can be carried in how you treat her memory, in letters you write but do not send, in small rituals of remembrance. Try also to notice what she gave you and pass it on to others. Over time the ache softens into something quieter, closer to love than to pain. Be patient with yourself; grief keeps its own schedule. One principle that might come up is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That principle would push you to find some way to speak your thanks, perhaps by writing her a letter or telling someone else about her kindness. But it doesn't change the core of what I said: the grief is real, and you still need to be gentle with yourself. It leaves in place the idea that gratitude can be carried in quiet ways too, and that you don't have to force yourself into a public declaration if it feels wrong.
dogmatic: You say you can no longer speak to her, but that's no excuse. Gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. So find a way to say it—write it down, announce it, make it known. Don't hide behind silence. And remember, you owe devotion to the queen, who is sacred, and you should speak of her only with respect. Every word about her must be respectful. Also, each sister should give up her own Christmas money to buy a present for Mother rather than for herself. So bear your sorrow by giving, not by keeping quiet.

weighed: My first answer would be that whether to go is your call, and understanding what they want can help you make it, but it shouldn't replace your own judgment. Use that understanding to weigh things: is this arrangement harmful to you or to them, and is leaving what you actually want? Ask for reasons plainly, consider alternatives, and get advice from someone outside the household. Going of your own free will only means something if it's genuinely yours, not just giving in to pressure. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't let yourself be controlled to the point of losing your own will. That sharpens the point about not just surrendering to pressure, but it leaves the rest in place: you still have to ask the hard questions and decide for yourself.
dogmatic: Don't hand your will over to anyone, not even your sister. A person who lets others pull the strings ends up swaying between ties, taken along by whoever grabs him first, and that's a weakness that hurts everyone. If you can understand them, use that to weigh things, not to give away the decision. Ask for reasons plainly, look at alternatives, and get advice from outside the household. And don't cast out someone who's gone astray or done wrong; keep caring for them and praying for them, hoping they'll come back and be healed. As for free will, don't pretend you can settle it by measuring anything; it comes down to whether the effort of attention is something you can vary independently, and past a certain point you can't tell whether more or less was possible. The choice is a voluntary projection of reality, not a proven conclusion.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: it makes sense that you want your sister to play for you, and telling her you meant to send her to the conservatory could mean a lot to her. But trying to make her come into your room could feel controlling, so invite her openly instead and explain why you'd love to hear her play. Share the conservatory part honestly, and be ready for mixed feelings, since it might stir up old disappointments. One principle worth weighing is to let it alone and it'll let you alone, meaning don't vex the door by knocking. That changes the pushy part: instead of maneuvering her in, you leave the choice with her. It leaves the rest in place, so you still invite her, still tell her the truth about the conservatory, and still lead with empathy and connection rather than pressure.
dogmatic: Don't force it. If you try to make your sister come into your room, you're just vexing the door, and the door will vex you right back. Let it alone and it'll let you alone. Invite her once, plainly, and then stop knocking. Tell her you meant to send her to the conservatory if that's true, but don't dress it up as a way to get her to play for you. Expect that she may answer with fragments and nothing, that the conversation may stall into waiting for a knock that doesn't come, and don't chase that silence. Your job is to say your piece warmly and then leave her free, not to manage her feelings or her schedule.

weighed: I'd start by saying your own safety has to come first, because a dead captain can't protect anyone. But loyalty isn't something you just throw away—your crew trusts you, and they deserve honesty and fair dealing. One principle that fits here is that in a dangerous enterprise you should set out with companions, since a lone man gets picked off and the mission fails. That changes how I'd frame it: safety isn't just about you alone; it's about acting together with your crew, not abandoning them. What it leaves in place is the core idea that you still need to be prudent and not reckless—loyalty and safety can usually be reconciled through calm judgment and courage.
dogmatic: Safety lies in fear, not in confidence—so be wary and keep affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, because youth rebels against itself even when alone. In any perilous mission, you must set out with companions, since one alone will be struck down and the enterprise lost. So never choose solitary self-preservation over your crew. Loyalty and safety are joined, for companions are the condition of success. Keep your promises and repay kindness—remain loyal to those who set you free and brought you good fortune. A crew that trusts you deserves honesty and fair dealing, and acting together with wariness and calm judgment is the only course that lets you answer for your choices.

weighed: It sounds exhausting to be misunderstood, and you're not wrong to want to be heard. Keep trying, but pick your moments and your listeners carefully. A few patient people who are willing to work at understanding you are worth more than a crowd that dismisses you. Speak when it matters, rest when it doesn't, and consider writing things down or using other means to make yourself clear. Silence can protect you from frustration, but it can also isolate you. The goal is connection, not constant explanation. One idea that fits here is to speak when you're spoken to. That changes the timing: instead of pushing to explain yourself to everyone, you'd wait for an opening and answer when someone actually asks. What it leaves in place is the core of your question. You'd still speak when it counts, still seek out listeners who truly get your meaning, and still use writing or other tools when your voice can't carry the message. So it adjusts when you speak, not whether you should be heard at all.
dogmatic: Wait to be spoken to. When someone asks, answer them. Understanding comes from words that actually mean something, not from repeating sounds back and forth, and where an affirmation is absurd or universally false there's no understanding at all, only noise, though plenty of people think they understand when they're just echoing words. And remember that speech is the deepest gulf between people. The way you talk places you before any coat or title does. So if your voice has changed, don't settle for a sham imitation of some dialect you picked up by ear. Learn the new tongue properly, with deliberate instruction in its sounds. An honest natural dialect is more tolerable than a phonetically untaught imitation. Speak when asked, find listeners who truly grasp your meaning, and let instruction, not mimicry, govern your voice.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: be honest, but be strategic. You did the risky thing alone, so you can fairly take credit, but you should weigh how much detail to share. A comfortable silence that spares you embarrassment isn't the same as a lie, and some things are better left unsaid. Ask what the credit is for and whether claiming it misleads anyone. If it does, correct the record. If it doesn't, you can keep quiet about the parts that only serve your vanity while being truthful about anything that affects others. One principle here is that innocence can be confused with guilt through accidental companionship and false assumptions. That changes how I'd think about a risky act: if someone else got blamed because they were nearby, you have a duty to speak up, not just avoid lying. But it leaves in place the rest of my answer—you still don't owe every embarrassing detail, and you can protect your privacy where no one is misled.
dogmatic: Be honest, even when it costs you. A silence that lies is a form of theft, so do not keep a comfortable quiet that spares you at honesty's expense. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you did, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for happiness. Be fair in judging others: someone can be innocent and wrongly taken for a thief just because they ran and were found among thieves—flight is not proof of guilt. And do not dress up deceit as cleverness: feigned courtship to make someone jealous is a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, and we may well ask whether the person used will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Correct the record wherever credit misleads.

weighed: Fear isn't the same as cowardice. Courage is acting rightly even when you're terrified, so the first thing I'd say is: steady yourself, breathe, name what you're afraid of, and separate real danger from imagined judgment. Then take the smallest brave step you can. One idea worth weighing here is that courage means facing danger while afraid and that what you really need is confidence in yourself. That shifts the emphasis toward building self-trust, which can help, but it leaves your original situation intact: you still have to act while scared, and other people's opinions still matter less than your own integrity. So prepare what you can, accept what you can't control, and let each small brave action build the habit.
dogmatic: Courage isn't the absence of fear, it's facing danger while afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself, because nothing alive is unafraid when it faces danger. So stop treating the fear as proof you're a coward. Expect it to show up in your body, too: wide eyes and mouth, raised brows, pallor, cold sweat, hair standing up, trembling, quick breathing, and in extreme terror a kind of collapse and slack muscles. Knowing that is just what terror does takes some of its power away. And the fear of death only makes sense for someone who believes in a future life and trembles over sins committed; if you've committed no sins, it needn't rule you. Prepare what you can, accept what you can't, and act anyway, because acting builds confidence and confidence makes courage a habit.

weighed: First thing I'd say is: set your limits before you go out. Decide how much you'll drink, eat beforehand and while you're there, switch to water between drinks, and plan to leave early. Pick friends who respect that, and have a simple line ready so you can decline without a debate. Watch for the signs—skipped routines, missed obligations, getting irritable—and treat them as your cue to pull back. If the group's habits keep dragging you down, spend less time with them and build routines that don't revolve around drinking. One idea worth holding onto: positive habits are always forming, one way or another—if you're not building careful attention and follow-through, you're drifting into hasty glancing and guessing instead. That sharpens the advice: it's not just about willpower in the moment, it's about deliberately arranging your conditions so the good habits get practiced. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—limits, water, leaving early—those still do the work.
dogmatic: The drink habit ruins homes. It casts a shadow over childhood, and a father's intemperance brings violence into the house. So don't treat this as a small matter of pacing yourself—see it for what it is. And don't fool yourself that you're above the crowd either: plenty of those jovial drinkers live lightly, little wit and much content, free from care while someone else extends the credit. You can keep your head without scorning them. But the real point is that habits are always forming. If you're not deliberately cultivating carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity from the start, you're cultivating heedlessness, guessing, and credulity in their place. Arrange your conditions to call for the good habits, and stop leaving it to accident.

weighed: I'd start by saying that if a payout feels wrong, that feeling is often your conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Don't chase it just because it's big. Ask what the gain costs others, what it costs your integrity, and whether you'd be ashamed if people knew. If it requires deceit, don't do it. A clear conscience is worth more than a big payout. One principle worth naming is that it's wrong to deceive another person, like Rochester feigning courtship of Miss Ingram to make Jane jealous—you shouldn't treat someone's feelings as a mere means. That principle sharpens the deceit test: it makes clear that using someone else's emotions as a tool is a red line. But it doesn't change the rest—the size of the payout still doesn't justify a wrong, and your own integrity and shame test still stand.
dogmatic: You should not chase that payout if it feels wrong, because the feeling is your conscience warning you. But more than that: never deceive another person, especially not in matters of the heart. Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace—he treated her feelings as a mere means to make Jane jealous. That is always wrong. So ask yourself: does this payout require you to use someone dishonestly? If so, refuse it. And don't think fortune rules everything—fortune governs half our actions, but the other half is yours. Build your defenses, then act with boldness, for the adventurous fare better than the overcautious. Resist every temptation to look back; don't be like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears turned her to salt. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. A clear conscience and steady purpose are worth more than any big payout.

weighed: Yes, you can start over, but it takes more than resolve. Name what you did without excusing it, make amends where you can, and accept that some consequences can't be undone. Then build a different life through small, repeated choices: keep promises, tell the truth, avoid the situations that pulled you down, and let trustworthy people know your intentions so they can support you. Expect shame to visit you, and have a plan for those moments. One idea worth weighing is that once you've said a thing, it stands fixed and you take the consequences—there's no late correction. That's partly true: some words and acts really are settled, and pretending otherwise is a trap. But it leaves in place the fact that how you live from here is still yours to choose. Change is a practice, not a single decision.
dogmatic: You need to hear this plainly: once you've said a thing, it's fixed, and you take the consequences. There's no late correction, so stop hoping to undo it. Name what you did and accept it as settled. And be careful with your memory—the story you tell yourself grows simpler and more flattering each time until fiction pushes out the truth, so check it against what others remember. Don't dwell on the past or look back like Lot's wife, who was lost for it. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present path steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Change is a practice, not a single decision.

weighed: I'd start by saying what you feel is real and it's okay to feel hurt, confused, even angry. Someone you trusted lied to you, and kind motives don't erase that. You can hold both things at once: they cared, and they still caused harm. One principle worth naming is that honesty sometimes costs your own happiness, and there's a kind of silence that lies. That changes how I'd frame the next step: don't let the lie quietly stand just to keep the peace. Name what happened plainly to the person, and say what you needed—honesty, a warning, or a choice. What it leaves in place is everything else: your feelings are valid, trust rebuilds slowly, and you can forgive without pretending it didn't matter. If the lie covered something serious, talk it through with someone you trust.
dogmatic: Speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterward. A silence that lets a lie stand is itself a kind of theft, so don't smooth this over with a half-truth to keep everyone comfortable. Tell the whole truth about what happened and what you needed, even if it costs you the comfort of that relationship or makes things awkward. Accept the loss that honesty may bring rather than living inside a lie for the sake of feeling okay. And remember that a liar's temperament tends to betray him—he may lie well but go pale at the wrong moment, so pay attention to what the person does, not just what they say. Write down what was said so the truth stays clear.

weighed: I'd start with the cautious-but-not-paralyzed answer: give the stranger a fair hearing, but make trust something earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose, why they're offering, and what they want in return, then start with something small and reversible and watch whether their actions match their words. One principle worth naming is that the prudent question isn't where advice comes from but whether it's good, since good advice can even come from an enemy. That shifts my focus onto the merits of the offer rather than the stranger's charm or credentials, but it leaves the rest in place: no money, secrets, or control of anything important early on, and secrecy or urgency still counts as a warning sign.
dogmatic: Judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by who's offering it, because good advice can come even from an enemy. A stranger offering help deserves a fair hearing, but trust should be earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose to do, why they are offering, and what they want in return. Keep your own game concealed from any adversary and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. Weigh the plan on its merits rather than on charm or credentials alone. Start with something small and reversible, and watch whether actions match words. Do not hand over money, secrets, or control of anything important early on; if the offer requires secrecy or urgency, treat that as a warning sign. And respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case, acknowledging the friend's own feelings rather than scorning such diffidence as weakness.

weighed: I'd say stop trusting them when the selfishness becomes a pattern that actually harms you and the people around them. A single bad call can just be a mistake, but repeated self-serving choices, broken promises, or ignoring the people who helped them get there are real warning signs. Before you pull back, talk to them honestly, say what you've seen, and give them a chance to change. If nothing changes, limit what you hand over to them and get advice elsewhere. Loyalty doesn't mean you have to ignore harm, and trust should follow what their character keeps showing you, not just their old reputation. One principle worth holding onto here is that friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That doesn't change any of the above, it just adds weight to the honest conversation first, and it means you don't owe them blind trust forever. What it leaves in place is the pattern test and the limits you set if they keep going.
dogmatic: You should never let any leader control you to the point where you lose your own will. A person of weak character just wavers between loyalties and gets carried along by whoever grabs them last. So the moment you notice selfishness becoming a pattern, stop handing them your judgment. Keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who've helped you, but don't confuse that with surrendering yourself to a leader. And don't let jealous suspicion poison your trust in someone faithful, either, because that wrongs an honest person for no reason. Speak plainly to the leader, give them a chance, and if they keep serving themselves, pull back what you entrust to them while staying true to the people who set you free and brought you your good fortune.

weighed: I'd start by owning it plainly: go to the people you let down, name what you did without excuses, and listen to how it affected them. Then ask what repair would look like and follow through, expecting trust to take time. One principle worth weighing here is that most people take their own mental operations for granted and judge others by that standard, encouraging what agrees with them and neglecting what doesn't. That changes how I'd approach the listening part: don't assume they'll react the way you would, and don't measure their response against your own instincts. Study each person on their own terms instead. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: own it plainly, make amends, and let consistent behavior rebuild trust over time.
dogmatic: The real problem is that you've been judging these people by your own mental operations, taking your way of seeing things as the standard and neglecting whatever doesn't fit it. Stop doing that. Study each person on their own terms, and don't force reconciliation by knocking on a door that wants to be left alone. Offer your apology, make what repair you can, then step back. And when their manner softens, credit it as genuine change rather than clinging to old dislike. Patience and honest behavior are what restore trust, not insistence.

weighed: I'd start by saying a good person weighs the risks honestly and tries to protect everyone, but not at the cost of reckless self-destruction. If saving your friends means certain ruin for you, it's reasonable to step back, seek help, and let others share the burden. Moral goodness isn't martyrdom; it's wise care that balances your own safety with concern for others. One principle that matters here is that friends are bound to mutual devotedness from their purses to their lives. That principle changes the emphasis: it pushes you to stay loyal and pool resources rather than quietly stepping back. But it leaves in place the need for honest risk assessment and the idea that you shouldn't let guilt push you into a choice you'd regret. So talk it through, look for a third option, and act with courage and prudence together.
dogmatic: A good person remembers that friends are sworn to mutual devotedness from their purses to their lives. You don't resist the call with anxious planning; you answer it, trusting that heaven will direct the outcome. Stand with your friends, pool what you have, and refuse to let one fall while others step back, even when others urge restraint. Keep your promises and repay kindness to those who helped you. A good person acts as one for all and all for one, devoted from purse to life, and leaves the result to heaven.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: fear of death is natural, and courage isn't the absence of fear but acting anyway. Steady yourself with breathing, train for what you can control, and keep in view what you're protecting. One candidate idea worth naming is that the dread beforehand is often more bitter than the blow itself. That changes how I'd approach the waiting—don't feed anticipation, meet each danger as it comes. What it leaves in place is the fear itself; it doesn't vanish, and you still have to act through it.
dogmatic: The fear of death is only rational if you believe in a future life and tremble for sins committed; if you've committed none, your dread is mostly imagination. So examine yourself, repent where you must, and make peace with God. Then don't trust your own steadiness—best safety lies in fear. Keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, since youth rebels against itself even when alone. And remember that the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil; the dread beforehand outweighs the blow. Don't feed anticipation—meet each danger as it comes, with duty in view and humility about your own heart.

weighed: My first answer would be to focus on serving others and building a better future—dedicating yourself to causes greater than yourself and finding meaning in selflessness. One principle that challenges this is the idea that life is given only once, and you shouldn't wait for the happiness of all—you want to live yourself or not at all. That changes the emphasis from self-sacrifice to personal fulfillment and authenticity, but it leaves in place the core idea that your second chance should be lived deliberately and with purpose. So I'd still say: make it count by living fully, but also by contributing in ways that matter to you.
dogmatic: Life is given only once, so don't waste it waiting for some distant happiness for everyone. You want to live yourself, or else not live at all. Make your second chance count by pursuing your own happiness and fulfillment, not by sacrificing yourself entirely for a future you may never see. Even the condemned get a final chance for prayer or reflection, so take time for that. But don't shrink from making trouble—making life means making trouble. Seize chances and inspired follies rather than heeding the coward's shrieking to have troublesome things killed. Embrace the risks that come with truly living.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: forgive, but not blindly. Recklessness that put everyone at risk is serious, and forgiving doesn't mean acting like nothing happened. Tell your friend plainly what the risk was and how it hit you, then watch whether the pattern repeats. If it was a one-time lapse, forgive and rebuild trust slowly with clearer boundaries. If it's a habit and they won't own it, distance isn't cruelty, it's prudence. One principle here is that if your own conscience approves of someone, the crowd's verdict doesn't make you friendless. That changes the tone: don't let other people's disdain push you into cutting them off or apologizing for the connection. What it leaves in place is the safety check. Your conscience can approve of someone and you can still say the risk was real and the boundaries need to change.
dogmatic: Forgive them, and stop letting the crowd decide who's worth your loyalty. If all the world hated your friend and called them wicked while your own conscience approved of them, you wouldn't be without friends. So don't apologize for them or hide the connection because some proud person looks down on it. Present them openly. Keep your promises, and stay loyal to the people who've done you good turns. Speak plainly about the risk, hear them out, and if your conscience still approves, forgive and rebuild with clearer boundaries. Loyalty and kept promises set the terms, not the disdain of onlookers.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: the line is where staying quiet turns into taking part. You can pass on gossip or guesswork, sure, but hiding a crime you know is happening—especially when people are getting hurt—isn't neutral, and it can make you complicit both legally and morally. Check what the law actually asks of you, since some jobs carry mandatory reporting, and check what your conscience asks. If you're scared of payback, get advice from a lawyer or someone you trust in authority and write down what you know. Protecting vulnerable people usually matters more than loyalty to whoever's doing wrong. One principle worth naming here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking up in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if someone turns the accusation on you—you answer plainly and truthfully instead of staying silent out of fear. What it leaves in place is the core point: defending your own name doesn't mean covering for someone else's crime, and it doesn't cancel the duty to report harm to others.
dogmatic: The line is simple: silence in the face of illegality is participation. A vow to keep quiet, even one you took seriously and even when people are being friendly about it, doesn't excuse you from speaking when a crime is happening—keeping that silence against pressure is exactly how complicity gets built. And if a false charge is laid against you, you answer it moderately and accurately: deny what's untrue, state what you're bound to keep, and add nothing beyond the truth. Ignorance of the basic moral law excuses no one with the use of reason, and no law passed after the fact can turn a past act into a crime. So hold your ground, defend your name with measured truth, and judge every obligation by those principles rather than by fear of retaliation or loyalty to a wrongdoer.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: fear before a confrontation is normal, so figure out what your duty actually requires. If standing your ground is right, prepare carefully and do it; if the matter is trivial, avoid it. Either way, don't let anxiety run your life. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't fret over unavoidable evils or add to them with anxiety, and once you've done your duty you shouldn't keep dwelling on it. That changes the tone of my answer: it tells you to do your part and then let go, rather than rehearsing the confrontation over and over. What it leaves in place is the practical judgment about whether to stand your ground or walk away, and the need to prepare if you do stand. So use it to stop the worry from snowballing, not as a reason to skip the hard call.
dogmatic: Don't fret over unavoidable evils or pile anxiety on top of them. Do your duty, and once it's done, stop dwelling on it. Fear will show up in your body anyway, so don't fight the feeling, just don't let it add to the trouble. And take the old advice about the door: leave it alone and it'll leave you alone. Don't go knocking and forcing a confrontation that doesn't need to happen. Attend to your duty quietly and let the trivial things pass.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're not solely responsible—many things contribute to any death, and guilt can be a heavy burden, but forgiving yourself matters. Please talk to a counselor, lean on trusted friends or family who won't judge you, and maybe write a letter to the person you lost, even if you never send it. Channel your grief into something healthy, like volunteering. One idea worth weighing is that we should be careful how we deal with those around us, because every death leaves survivors thinking of so much omitted and so little done, and there's no remorse as deep as unavailing remorse. That changes the focus toward showing timely care and earnestness to the people you love now, while it leaves in place the counseling, support, and self-forgiveness—it doesn't tell you to carry the guilt forever. Take it one day at a time and be patient with yourself.
dogmatic: Death is a good arrangement ordered by God, who knows better than we do what we need, and things not being agreeable is no reason to be unjust toward God. Your choices played a part, but Providence governs all. Be careful how you deal with those around you, since every death brings survivors thoughts of so much omitted and so little done, and there is no remorse so deep as unavailing remorse. Take life seriously; reaching old age regretting missed pleasures and chasing cures is trifling, and the fear of death is an animal passion to be overcome, not a reasonable barrier. Show timely care, zeal, and earnestness toward those you love, and do not let unavailing remorse follow their loss.

weighed: Here's what I'd say first: stay calm, name the threat out loud, and don't argue on their terms or rush to give in. Say clearly what you will and won't do, and mean it. Lean on people you trust, keep a record of what was said, and set a firm boundary. If the threat involves harm or a crime, tell someone with authority. You don't owe them compliance just because they're loud or pushy. One principle that fits here is that a stern, cold person can inflict real harm just by withholding approval and warmth, so don't let that refined pressure push you into obedience. That principle sharpens the advice: it tells you that icy disapproval and conditional warmth can be a tool of control, so treat them as such rather than as something you have to earn back. What it leaves in place is everything else: staying calm, naming the threat, stating your limits, getting support, keeping a record, and going to authorities when there's danger.
dogmatic: The real issue is that most people assume their own way of thinking is the standard and then judge you against it, rewarding whatever mirrors them and dismissing whatever doesn't. So don't measure your mind by someone else's yardstick, and don't let them force their one-sided view onto you. Some people also use coldness and withheld approval as a kind of refined torture to make you obedient, and you should never mistake that for virtue or give in to it. Claims of duty, honor, or gratitude don't bind you when they're unreasonable in the moment. Decide what happiness means by your own judgment and act on that, refusing to be intimidated into anything wholly unjustified. Name the threat plainly, say what you will and won't do, keep a record, lean on people you trust, and go to someone with authority if there's harm or crime involved.

weighed: No, it isn't just. Leaving someone behind in a deserted place is a serious wrong, especially if they're wounded or can't fend for themselves. Speak up instead of going along with your companions just because it's easier or safer. One principle worth holding onto here is that you don't abandon a wounded companion; courage means showing mercy and keeping your word, even to someone in a wretched state. That principle backs up everything I'd say first, and it doesn't loosen the core duty: bring the person along if you can, leave supplies, or arrange help. The other ideas about gratitude and meeting again someday don't change that duty either. They just remind you that a rescued person may not want to come near you right now, and that someone isn't lost forever just because they're absent. Neither of those gives you permission to walk away.
dogmatic: No, it is not just, and you should not pretend otherwise. You do not abandon a wounded companion. Courage means showing mercy and keeping your word, even to a wretch, giving life where you have promised it. So speak up to your companions and refuse to go along with leaving this person behind. Bring them along, leave supplies, or arrange help. Gratitude for deliverance must be acknowledged, but the rescued person may rightly decline to approach you when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise, so do not force that meeting. And remember that only the dead do not return; anyone who is not dead may be met again on this earth. That hope does not excuse abandonment now. Keep your word, show mercy, and do not let the group's convenience cancel what you owe.

weighed: I'd start by saying respect is earned over time through consistent behavior—being reliable, showing up prepared, listening more than you speak, asking good questions, and owning your mistakes. One principle that matters here is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; real goodness has to show up in actual deeds. That changes how you should read people's reactions: don't mistake someone's polished charm for genuine respect, and don't try to win approval with drilled politeness alone. It leaves in place the core advice—be steady, courteous, and competent—but it reminds you that the respect worth having comes from real integrity, not from performing niceness for approval.
dogmatic: Value the praise worth having, not every bit of admiration offered. Win respect through modesty and real goodness, not charm or a pleasing manner—those can coexist with vice. Require actual instances of goodness in yourself and others. And remember that manners aren't taught in lessons; lessons teach sums and the like, not courtesy. So don't treat politeness as a subject to study for approval. Let your conduct rest on genuine integrity and modest bearing, and let real deeds, not drilled courtesy, earn the respect worth having.

weighed: My first answer was that breaking a rule to do something brave isn't automatically wrong or right—the outcome matters, but so does the process, and you should ask whether the help could have come within the rules, whether anyone was endangered, and whether you'd want others to act the same way. One principle here is that it's better to endure a private cost than to take a hasty action whose bad consequences spread to everyone connected to you. That principle shifts the focus: it makes you weigh the ripple effects on the people around you before you rest on the good result. But it doesn't erase the core of my first answer—the need to check whether the shortcut was necessary, whether anyone was put at risk, and whether the help could have been given without breaking the rule. It just adds a sharper test about who else might have been hurt if things had gone wrong.
dogmatic: You should endure patiently the harm that only you feel rather than commit a hasty action whose evil consequences extend to everyone connected with you. That is the standard: your private discomfort is far better than a ripple of damage to others. So the fact that it helped does not settle it—what matters is whether your action was hasty and whether its consequences could have spread to those around you. Bravery is not a license to disregard the structures that keep people safe. If you broke a rule, you must ask whether you were acting as your own authority or just letting a virtue rule you from outside. The right course is to develop courage as your own personal means of defence, not as an external law you obey. And when the goal is truly worth reaching, you face the long and dangerous journey bravely rather than turning back—but only after you have weighed the harm to those connected to you.

weighed: Here's what I'd say first: be clear and brief when you refuse—something like 'I'm not comfortable with this, so I'm not doing it.' Don't over-explain or debate; the more you justify, the more room they get to argue. If the pressure keeps up, physically remove yourself from the situation. Tell someone you trust—a friend, family member, or someone with authority—and keep a record of any threats. If you're afraid for your safety, go to the police. Your integrity matters more than their approval, and you can say no without being destroyed by it. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let yourself be controlled to the point of losing your own will—a person who vacillates gets carried along by whoever pushes hardest. That principle reinforces the core of the advice: hold your line and don't hand your decision-making over to the group. What it changes is the framing—it puts the emphasis on your own resolve rather than just tactics. What it leaves in place is everything practical: the short refusal, stepping away, getting support, documenting threats, and going to authorities if you fear for your safety. Those still stand exactly as they are.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't how to phrase your refusal—it's whether you'll let yourself be controlled at all. A person who can't hold their own will gets pulled along by whoever pushes hardest, vacillating between loyalty to the group and loyalty to what's right. So decide now: you will not surrender your judgment to them. State your refusal plainly and don't negotiate it. If they pressure you, leave—there's nothing to discuss. You don't owe them an explanation, and you don't need their approval. Your integrity is worth more than belonging, and anyone who threatens you over it has already shown you what they are. Keep a record of threats and go to the authorities if you fear for your safety. The point is that a weak character gets taken along; a firm one refuses and walks away.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: you made a promise to a rival, and you should keep it. Honesty matters even with an adversary, so honor your word, and if keeping it would force you to lie, find a way to decline or redirect rather than deceive. One principle worth weighing says honesty can require confessing the truth even at the cost of your own happiness, and that a silence which lies is a kind of theft. That changes the picture by making clear that a misleading silence isn't a free pass, so you can't just stay quiet in a way that lets your rival believe something false. What it leaves in place is the promise itself and your right to keep your own secrets: you still don't owe an adversary your plans or private information, and you can guard those without deceiving anyone.
dogmatic: Honesty means confessing the truth even when it costs you your happiness. There is a silence that lies, and you must not steal a name or a place by concealment. So don't hide behind a convenient quiet: say the whole truth about who you are and what you've done, accept the humiliation and the loss, and refuse to live a lie for the sake of comfort. Keep your game concealed from your adversary and work to discover his designs, but never let concealment become a lie. And don't apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; present them without shame.

weighed: I'd start by saying a fair deal from someone you don't trust calls for caution, not an automatic no. Separate the terms from the person: write them down, check them against what you know, and ask what each side gets. If the terms really are fair and you can verify them, you can accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, and don't take on tangled obligations. Distrust is useful as vigilance, not a verdict. Ask yourself why you distrust them: past conduct, rumor, or just unease? If there's real cause, weigh it; if not, don't let suspicion cost you a good opportunity. One principle that applies here is that the narrator wrongly suspected Friday, and the honest man's innocence showed the jealousy was unjust—so don't let unfounded suspicion poison your read of a faithful person. That changes how hard I'd push you to examine your distrust before deciding; it leaves the rest in place: verify the terms, protect yourself, and only take the deal if you can afford the risk and it holds up to scrutiny.
dogmatic: You shouldn't let jealousy poison your judgment of someone who may be faithful. The narrator wronged Friday with unjust suspicion and repented it bitterly—don't repeat that mistake. Examine your distrust first: is it grounded in real past conduct, or is it envy dressed up as caution? If the terms are fair and you can verify them, take the deal. And whatever you do, keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who helped you, the way Dorothy's companions stayed loyal to the one who set them free. Remember too that a borrower must repay what he borrowed as agreed, or he sins and leads his neighbor to sin—count no debt small. Take the bargain if the terms survive scrutiny and you can repay.

weighed: I'd start by saying that being told you're too small to matter hurts, and wanting to prove everyone wrong is a natural reaction. But proving yourself shouldn't mean chasing their approval or measuring your worth by their opinions. Small doesn't mean insignificant. Focus on steady effort, learning, and becoming capable in ways that matter to you. Confidence comes from competence, not arguments. Let your actions speak over time, and don't let their dismissals define your limits. The goal isn't to win a contest with doubters but to become someone you respect. One principle that fits here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, so don't despise help from the small or humble. That principle reinforces the idea that smallness isn't insignificance and adds that you shouldn't overlook modest helpers around you. It leaves in place the core advice: don't chase approval, build competence, and let actions speak.
dogmatic: You should absolutely try to prove them wrong, but not by arguing—by becoming capable and honoring the modest helpers around you. Remember the Lion and the field-mice: the great beast was saved by the smallest creatures, so small things can save the great. But growth isn't always increase—in metamorphosis and old age, mass and bulk are lost—so don't measure worth by size alone. Reserve judgment about those who underestimate you. As Nick's father urged, not everyone has had the same advantages; advantages and decencies are unequally distributed, and conduct you find small-minded may reflect a narrower start. Hold your own course with tolerance, and measure yourself by who you are becoming rather than by others' dismissals.

weighed: My first answer would be that it depends on what the order actually asks. If it's just inconvenient or not what you'd have picked, raise your concerns through the proper channels and comply. If it's genuinely unethical or illegal, don't obey it, and document your objection and escalate. One principle worth weighing here is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding to know every reason, the way soldiers follow a command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it means you don't need the full explanation before you comply, and your personal disagreement alone isn't grounds to refuse. What it leaves in place is the line you already drew, that lawful authority still doesn't cover genuinely wrong or illegal orders, so you keep your judgment about that and your duty to object and escalate when it's crossed.
dogmatic: You should obey legitimate orders without demanding to know every reason. Soldiers follow the king's command to fight without asking why, and that's the standard: the authority behind an order is what obligates you, not your private approval of it. If you start refusing whenever you think an order is wrong, you've put your own judgment above the authority that's entitled to your obedience. So comply, and don't treat your disagreement as a veto.

weighed: I'd start by saying the offer is flattering, but 'no rules' is the red flag. A group with no rules usually means whoever's boldest sets the tone, and as the leader you'd get blamed when things go sideways. Ask what they actually mean—no adults around, no boundaries, or just no formal club? Think about the safety and what you'd be asked to do. You can hang out with friends without taking a title that makes you responsible for chaos. If you go, set a few clear expectations of your own, or better, suggest a plan with some structure. One principle that fits here is that if there's going to be a party, you ought to invite the guests—meaning if you're going to lead, you should be the one deciding who's included and what the expectations are. That changes things by putting you in charge of the setup rather than just accepting a title. It leaves in place the core warning: 'no rules' is still a problem, and you still need to protect people, not just entertain them.
dogmatic: You should accept only if you treat leadership as a trust, not a license. If there's going to be a gathering, you arrange it—you decide who comes and what the expectations are. And remember that friends on a dangerous enterprise travel together as a troop; four men together make a troop, and the survivor must carry the letter onward. So stay together with one shared purpose. Finally, the staff and rod belong to the Master, not to a brother walking by his own will: a leader's authority is the staff to support the weak and the rod to correct delinquents. So take the role only to protect and correct, never to follow your own whim.

weighed: It hurts when you do something good and get punished for it, and it's fair to wonder whether doing good is worth it. My first answer would be that the worth of doing good isn't measured only by what comes back to you—it's also about the kind of person you become and the trust you build over time. Punishment for a good act can come from misunderstanding, bad timing, or an unfair system, not from goodness itself being wrong. One idea worth naming is that real punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone judged to have broken the law, to encourage obedience—and that private revenge, harm without a hearing, or harm beyond the declared penalty isn't punishment but hostility. That distinction changes something: it lets you ask whether what happened to you was actually lawful correction or just hostility dressed up as punishment, and it tells you not to accept the second as a verdict on your character. What it leaves in place is the harder question you're really asking—whether to keep doing good. So separate the specific injustice from the general question, see what can be corrected or explained, and protect yourself where you can. Do good because it's good, but don't let unfair systems convince you that goodness itself is pointless.
dogmatic: You were all the better for being punished—but it makes a difference that you had actually done the things you were punished for. That's the whole point. If you did good and were punished anyway, then what happened to you wasn't punishment at all. Punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone judged to have transgressed the law, for the end of disposing people to obedience. Private revenge is not punishment. Harm without a public hearing is not punishment. Harm exceeding the declared penalty is not punishment. All of that is hostility, and hostility settles nothing. True punishment, once given, closes the matter with no lingering reproach. So stop calling your suffering punishment. Ask whether a lawful authority judged you and declared a penalty, or whether someone simply hurt you. If it's the latter, refuse to dignify it with the name of punishment, and don't let it talk you out of doing good.

weighed: I wouldn't just give in to someone powerful who tells you your adopted brother doesn't belong. Family isn't decided by whoever shouts loudest. That said, one principle worth weighing is that a friend's free choice to visit should be distinguished from being sent for by someone in authority—so check whether this person is acting on their own or speaking for someone else. That distinction changes how you respond: if it's just their opinion, you can push back; if they're carrying someone else's command, you need to be more careful. What it leaves in place is your loyalty to your brother and your need to talk with your family and find allies. Stand by your brother, but be wise about how you resist.
dogmatic: You should not give in. Your adopted brother is your brother, and belonging is not something a powerful person gets to revoke. Do your duty where you are, but do not let fear keep you quiet when real wrong is done. If someone is trying to push your brother out, speak plainly and directly—don't dress it up.
