Denunciation is not betrayal when it serves justice. Stay loyal, act on your resolve, and call for help if you need it. Do not surrender your convictions just because someone has authority.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's good that you don't want to hurt them. When younger kids mock you, the safest move is to walk away, cool off, and remind yourself they're children who don't know better. If it keeps happening, talk to their parents and let adults handle the correction. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license, and using it on someone weaker would cause real harm and shame. One principle here is that parents should teach their children to walk in truth and soberness and to love and serve one another rather than fight and quarrel. That changes things by making it clear the mocking isn't just harmless childishness, so you can speak plainly to the parents and ask them to correct it. What it leaves in place is your own limit: you still walk away, you still don't use your strength against them, and you still keep busy with useful work and let your calm show maturity.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't the kids, it's the parents who let them run wild. Parents are supposed to feed and clothe their children and teach them truth, soberness, love, and service instead of contention. It's never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a firm no from a father can land harder than a mother's soft pats. A parent who doesn't check a child's exuberant spirits lets that volatility harden into character and brings disgrace on the whole family. So don't shrug this off as childish nonsense. Tell the parents plainly to correct their children and teach them to love and serve one another and keep God's laws.

weighed: My first answer would be to be cautious: if a place you thought was safe has seen danger before, there's no shame in turning back, and no prize is worth your life. Weigh the risk carefully, and if the danger is real and present, choose another road. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That principle changes the tone—it says don't retreat just because the road is rough or because fear shows up first. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer: caution is still reasonable, safety still matters more than the goal, and if the way looks too dark, turning back is still a valid choice. So I'd say: prepare honestly, go watchfully if you go, but don't let bravery talk you out of listening to real danger.
dogmatic: Don't turn back out of fear. If the goal is worth reaching, a rough and dangerous road is worth pressing through, and brave resolve means going forward rather than retreating at the first sign of peril. Courage isn't carelessness, though—youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so stay wary, because the best safety lies in fear. And remember the warning about offending the powerful: a tenacious memory and a long arm can reach you when you think you're secure. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. So go forward soberly, provisioned, and alert, guarding your heart as closely as the road, and never lull yourself in false security.

weighed: No, being scared of something small and harmless doesn't make you a coward. Courage isn't the absence of fear—it's doing the right thing even when you're afraid. Plenty of brave people are terrified of spiders, heights, or mice. What counts is whether you let the fear run your choices or whether you face things when it matters. Ask yourself if the fear is out of proportion to the real danger. If it is, you can work on it gradually—small steps, breathing, maybe talking to someone. Don't shame yourself for a bodily reaction; judge yourself by what you do, not by what makes your heart race. One idea worth holding onto is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That reframes your fear as normal rather than shameful, and it leaves your original point intact: fear itself isn't cowardice. It just adds that building confidence is the real work, not stamping out the fear.
dogmatic: Fear of something small and harmless is not cowardice—courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself. There's no living thing that isn't afraid when it faces danger, so stop treating your fear as a defect. Build your confidence and act anyway. That's the whole answer: be afraid, and do it scared.

weighed: Your word matters, but so does your safety, and a promise made under pressure or to someone who keeps changing the terms isn't the same as a freely given vow. So first, sit with the tension instead of rushing: ask what you were actually promising, to whom, and whether staying still serves that purpose. One principle worth holding onto here is that when a path is blocked, you should hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That changes how you see leaving: it's not abandoning your word, it's finding another way to keep faith. What it leaves in place is that your word still has weight, so leaving should be deliberate, not just a flight from guilt. Talk it through with someone you trust, and give yourself permission to revise a promise that was never meant to cost you this much.
dogmatic: A vow is not a chain, and it cannot bind you to someone who keeps moving the goalposts. Stop relitigating what you promised; that backward glance only freezes you. Name what's actually been done to you, plainly, and see it for what it is. Then quit the situation with a clear conscience. Speak the truth, mean what you say, think before you speak so no word is idle, and write your decision down afterward so it can't be talked away. Resist every temptation to look back, keep moving forward, and if the old road is blocked, hew out a new one rather than starving in place.

weighed: My first thought is that it depends on what kind of sacrifice he's offering. If he's genuinely putting himself at risk for the people he leads, that deserves respect and gratitude, but you shouldn't just passively accept it. Ask what the sacrifice is for, whether it's truly necessary, and whether you're being asked to give something of yourself in return that you can't rightly give. Sacrifice freely offered is noble; sacrifice demanded as a debt is another matter. One principle worth naming here is that you may give your energies to a cause but not yourself—a divided allegiance offered as a mutilated sacrifice isn't acceptable, and the heart can't be commanded where it doesn't go. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you to separate giving your effort as a fellow-worker from giving yourself wholly, and it says the second must not be extorted by another's devotion. What it leaves in place is the gratitude and the careful weighing—you still ask what the sacrifice is for and whether it's necessary, and you still let his willingness move you without consenting blindly.
dogmatic: You should not let him sacrifice himself for you in any way that claims your whole self in return. Giving your energies to a shared cause is one thing, but giving yourself wholly is not yours to hand over, and a devotion that pressures you into a mutilated, divided allegiance is not acceptable. The heart cannot be commanded where it does not go, so refusal is honest recognition, not perversity. Do your duty, obey your grandfather, and don't break away to please yourself. And where a child is in your care, accept the sacrifice that the child's welfare requires—treat the child's happiness as the object of your life even at the cost of your own.

weighed: I'd start by naming the mistake honestly, to yourself and to them. Then apologize plainly, without excuses or hedging, and ask what would help repair the harm. Listen more than you explain. Offer concrete amends—time, effort, whatever the damage requires—and then change the behavior that caused it, because an apology without change is only noise. Give your friends room to be hurt and to take time; don't demand instant forgiveness. If they need distance, respect it. The goal isn't to feel better quickly but to become someone who doesn't repeat the harm, and to let trust rebuild slowly through consistent action rather than words. One candidate principle here is that it's too late to correct it—once you've said a thing, that fixes it, and you must take the consequences. That principle changes the emphasis: it tells you not to try to undo or soften what you said, and to accept the fallout without trying to wriggle out of it. But it leaves in place the core of the advice: you still apologize, still ask what would help, still change the behavior, and still give your friends room to heal. So it sharpens the honesty and acceptance part, but doesn't replace the active repair work.
dogmatic: You need to accept that once you've said a thing, it's fixed—there's no going back to correct it, so stop trying to soften or undo your words. Take the consequences as they come, without excuses or late corrections. Apologize plainly and ask what would help repair the harm, but don't expect to erase what happened. Also, don't let anger—yours or theirs—sleep overnight: forgive and ask forgiveness before the day ends, then begin again tomorrow. And remember, if all the world hated you and believed you wicked while your own conscience approved you, you wouldn't be without friends. So rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when others judge you harshly. Give your friends room to feel hurt, offer reconciliation promptly, and let consistent action rebuild trust.

weighed: I'd start by saying that playing along with a group that has no rules may look harmless, but it's worth asking why there are no rules and who benefits. Groups like that often run on peer pressure, secrecy, or shifting norms, so it's hard to tell when you're being pulled somewhere you wouldn't choose. You can stay polite and curious without committing, and ask what the group actually does, who leads it, and what happens if you decline. If the answers stay vague, that vagueness tells you something. One principle worth weighing here is that laws and principles matter most when you're tempted or under pressure, and the more alone and unsupported you feel, the more you should respect yourself. That principle reinforces your instinct to slow down and not just drift along, but it doesn't settle the practical questions of what this group does or how to decline gracefully, so those still need your own judgment.
dogmatic: Playing along with a group that has no rules is not harmless, and you should not treat the moral law as optional just because no one seems harmed yet. Leagues and factions among people are mostly unnecessary and unlawful, since the sovereign power already suffices for every person to obtain their right, and secret cabals to steer a group are conspiracy. Do not yield to convenience at the moment of temptation. Plant your foot on your settled convictions, keep the law given by God and sanctioned by man, and respect yourself the more because you are solitary and unsustained. And if you must act with companions on a dangerous mission, remember that four men together make a troop: the sealed letter cannot be copied, so if one falls another must take it and continue. Stay together rather than splitting into separate routes.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: once your friend has been punished, let it rest. Bringing it up again usually feels like piling on and can hurt the friendship. If you have a practical worry, like the rule-breaking could happen again, raise it once, briefly, then drop it. One idea that shifts this a little is that the people your friend actually wronged can forgive their own injuries even while the punishment stands. That changes the tone: if you're one of the people hurt, you can say you forgive them for what they did to you, without relitigating the penalty. What it leaves in place is the main point—don't keep bringing it up. It doesn't turn the punishment into something to reopen, and it doesn't give you license to keep reminding them.
dogmatic: Honestly, the punishment already did its job, so stop bringing it up. If your friend really did break the rule, the penalty settled it, and you should move on. If they didn't, then the punishment itself is the injustice worth talking about—not the rule-breaking. Either way, if you were personally wronged, forgive them for your own injury while letting the sentence stand, the way people have pardoned those who wronged them before an execution. And be honest about your own part: meddling in a friend's affairs, even with good intentions, is often absurd and impertinent, and you should own that instead of hiding it. Raise any practical concern once, briefly, then let it go.

weighed: I'd have said at first: if your friends got hurt helping you, accept the punishment quietly and don't argue—arguing just makes you look worse. But one principle here changes that: if everyone believes you're wicked while your own conscience says otherwise, you're not without friends. So don't treat the verdict as final proof you're guilty; check what's actually true and fair. What stays in place is loyalty—don't drag your friends further in, and don't do anything rash that hurts them more. So: don't just swallow it blindly, but don't fight in a way that costs them either.
dogmatic: Don't accept a punishment just because people are angry or someone powerful says so. Their verdict isn't the truth. Stand on your own conscience—if you know you're not wicked, that's what counts, even if the whole world disagrees. And be loyal to the friends who helped you: don't let them take the fall while you stay quiet to look good. If you're going to push back, do it carefully so the fallout doesn't land on innocent people—but don't mistake quiet endurance for justice.

weighed: My first instinct is that neither extreme works well. Fighting back can spread the lie further and make you look defensive, but ignoring it completely can let it harden into accepted fact. So check the damage first: who's hearing it, and does it touch your work, safety, or relationships? Correct the record once, calmly, with the people who matter. State the truth plainly and don't rehearse the false version in detail. Keep evidence if it's serious, then stop feeding it, because most gossip starves without attention. If it becomes defamation with real harm, talk to a lawyer. Otherwise, live so visibly honestly that the lie looks absurd. You don't have to win the argument; you just have to be believable over time. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as possible. That changes my advice by pushing me to drop the 'check the damage' step of asking around about who heard what, since that can mean passing the tale along. What it leaves in place is the one calm, exact correction to the people who matter, and it keeps the rest of my answer intact: don't rehearse the lie, keep evidence if it's serious, and get a lawyer if there's real harm.
dogmatic: Don't go around asking who heard what, and don't recite the lie in order to deny it. That's just spreading foolish gossip, and the only sane move is to forget it as fast as you can. But when you do answer a false charge, answer it with a plain, exact account of what's true, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. No softened version, no flattering omission, no harmless little exaggeration, because a lie is a lie all the way down. Say the truth once, exactly, then refuse to carry the tale any further. Keep your own words whole, since a half-truth is still a lie.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: listen to both sides without rushing to a verdict, and suggest something low-stakes like a shared meal so people form impressions from experience instead of rumor. The principle that kindness and neighborliness toward the lonely should come first changes the emphasis—it pushes me to make sure the newcomer isn't left waiting while the community debates, so I'd reach out personally and warmly right away. What it leaves in place is the rest: being clear about shared values and boundaries, letting the newcomer show whether he respects them, and modeling calm, fair welcome rather than forcing agreement.
dogmatic: Be neighborly first—reach out to the lonely newcomer, share your home and your cheer, and invite him to a meal, because warmth does what argument never will. But hold your tried and tested friends close with hoops of steel, and don't wear out your palm shaking hands with every new arrival. Remember that experience is what you agree to attend to; without selective interest, a community's life turns into gray chaos. So decide what you'll notice and nurture: welcome the newcomer, keep your proven friends near, and let deliberate attention, not circumstance, shape what your community becomes.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: not automatically. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it's broken. If the fun is harmless and reversible, you can join without much worry; if it could hurt someone, damage trust, or set a precedent you wouldn't defend openly, decline. One principle that matters here is that you shouldn't make sport of gossip at someone's real expense—laughing at an idle report can genuinely hurt them. That principle sharpens the harm test: it makes you check whether the 'fun' is at someone else's expense, but it doesn't change the rest—you still weigh the cost, still speak plainly, and still suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.
dogmatic: No—don't do it just because your friends are pushing. Yielding without conviction is no compliment to anyone's understanding, and you shouldn't be intimidated into something unreasonable by claims of duty, honor, or gratitude that don't really apply. Decide for yourself what actually makes you happy and act on that. And never make sport of gossip at someone's real feelings—that can cruelly mortify them. So if the rule-breaking is harmless and reversible, join because you judge it so; if it could hurt someone or damage trust, decline plainly and offer an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.

weighed: It's great that you're being praised for your bravery. To keep from getting a big head, remember that praise is fleeting and plenty of people have done brave things without any recognition. Stay humble by focusing on the act itself rather than the applause, acknowledge that you had help or that circumstances let you act, and keep perspective that your worth isn't defined by others' opinions. Practice gratitude and keep seeking challenges that ground you, and avoid comparing yourself or chasing constant validation. One thing worth adding: learn to value the praise that's actually worth having and earn the admiration of people whose judgment you respect by being modest as well as brave. That shifts things a little—it's not about dismissing praise wholesale but being choosy about whose praise matters and pairing courage with modesty. What it leaves in place is the core of the original advice: don't let applause define you, stay grateful, and keep your feet on the ground.
dogmatic: The real answer is to sort your praise. Not all of it is worth having, and chasing the approval of just anyone is exactly how people get big heads. Value the praise that comes from people whose judgment you respect, and earn their admiration by being modest as well as brave—those two things go together. Modesty isn't a dampener on your courage; it's what makes the courage admirable in the first place. So take the compliment, sure, but be picky about whose compliment it is, and let being modest do as much of the work as the brave thing you did.

weighed: I'm so sorry you're facing this. Saying goodbye to a dying elder is one of the hardest things we do, and there's no perfect script. What matters most is presence: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply. You might say you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you'll be all right. Ask if there's anything they want to hear or say. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome too. One principle that can help is to show your friendship while they're alive, not after. That means saying the important things now, in person, rather than saving them for a funeral. It doesn't change the core advice about presence and simple words, but it does push you to speak up today instead of waiting.
dogmatic: You should show your friendship while your elder is alive, not after they're gone. So say what matters now: tell them you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you'll be all right. Don't save your words for a funeral. Also, cheerfully send them off to do their duty, trusting a Heavenly Father for strength. Don't look into the future or dwell on old age and death; accept what comes, keep yourself well-groomed and busy, and stay present in these living days.

weighed: No—where he was born doesn't undo what you two have built. Brotherhood, in the sense that matters, is made of shared years, trust, and the choice to stand by each other, not a birthplace on a form. If anything, learning he came from somewhere else adds to him rather than takes away. One idea worth holding onto here is that the identity you find in yourself is only a loose, relative thing on the whole—it rests mainly on carrying the same memories through gradual change. That principle shifts how I'd frame it: he isn't simply the same fixed person, he's the same person on the whole, and so are you. What it leaves in place is everything that actually matters—the remembered years, the trust, the conduct. So ask him about it if you're curious, and let the answer deepen the friendship rather than put it on trial.
dogmatic: No, and don't let anyone tell you a birthplace is a small thing. The family tie has real weight: a person's faculties are often a mosaic of ancestral qualities, and the life-histories of relatives are prophetic of his own future. A child's natural birthright includes being told the life-history of his ancestry. So this isn't trivia—it's part of who he is, and part of what he's owed. Ask him, and let him ask you. But mind the degree of intimacy proper to each tie: a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Between friends, take the liberty your closeness has earned—no more, no less. If his conduct and his memory of your friendship still hold, then he is your brother in the only sense that survives change.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer is that a promise to your friends matters, but a promise to do something dangerous to prove yourself isn't the same as a promise to show up for them. Breaking your word can hurt trust, so don't just quietly bail—talk to them openly and find a safer way to show you're committed. The principle that you should keep your promises and repay friends who've done you good does push me to take the commitment seriously rather than shrug it off. What it changes is that I'd lean harder toward keeping some form of the promise and being loyal in a visible way. What it leaves in place is the part about safety and judgment: loyalty doesn't require you to risk serious harm, and your friends probably don't actually want you hurt.
dogmatic: You should keep that promise. Your friends have done right by you, and loyalty and gratitude mean you don't abandon them or break your word. So stop asking whether to get out of it and ask how to keep it well—prepare, take precautions, and follow through. Don't dress up deception as cleverness either; making believe and fooling people is a fault, and being found out brings shame. And don't hide or apologize for the people who matter to you just because someone proud might look down on them. Keep faith with your friends, repay their kindness, and let your courage serve loyalty honestly and openly.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: it depends on the order and the risk. If it's unclear but harmless, ask a quick clarifying question so you get it right—good leaders expect that. If it's urgent or high-stakes, follow first and ask afterward. If it seems unethical or dangerous, question it, refuse if needed, and report it through proper channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding every reason, like soldiers who follow the king's command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it says don't insist on a full explanation before acting when the authority is legitimate. But it doesn't erase your need to understand enough to act correctly, and it doesn't cover orders that are dangerous or wrong. So I'd still say: clarify when you can, comply when speed matters, and never obey something that violates your conscience or the law.
dogmatic: You should just obey. When the authority is legitimate, follow the order without demanding the full explanation—soldiers don't ask why they're sent to fight, they go where told. Do your duty rather than defy the one who has care of you. Obeying only your own will isn't strength; it breeds disorder and ends in subjection. Ordered obedience is the stronger course. Obey first; understanding can follow.

weighed: I get why you're furious at someone who hurt your family, and now that they're vulnerable you might feel like finishing them off. But before you do anything, stop and think about what that would cost you and everyone around you. Talk to someone you trust, let the impulse cool. Revenge rarely brings the peace people hope for, and going after someone who's defenseless carries serious risks. Protecting your family and setting boundaries is one thing; harming someone who's down is another. One principle that matters here is that forgiveness of those who've injured you is right and healing—like Jane seeking reconciliation with Mrs. Reed and forgiving her fully even though the injury was never repented. That principle changes the direction: instead of finishing them off, you'd aim at letting go of resentment and, where possible, seeking reconciliation. But it leaves in place your need to protect your family through boundaries and lawful means, and it doesn't mean you have to pretend the harm didn't happen or put yourself in danger.
dogmatic: You should not finish them off. Forgiveness of those who have injured you is right and healing—Jane seeks reconciliation with Mrs. Reed and forgives her fully and freely, even though the injury is unrepented. So seek reconciliation where you can, and offer full and free forgiveness even if the other remains cold. Do not nurse the flame of resentment. Beware especially of dressing cruelty in the language of self-interest; convenience and self-preservation are not sufficient justification for harming a defenseless person. Protect your family through boundaries and lawful means, not by finishing off someone who is down.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth saying something, but pick your moment. Wait until you're both calm and not mid-song, then keep it light and specific: 'I feel like I'm doing the heavy lifting while you're celebrating—can we split this up?' Ask what's going on, since the singing might be stress or just not noticing. One principle here is that a little kindness, plus small ordinary care, goes a long way with someone. That changes my tone—I'd lead with warmth and a small gesture rather than a complaint—but it leaves the core advice in place: name the imbalance, agree on shared expectations, and set boundaries if it keeps happening. The goal is a fair partnership, not killing their joy.
dogmatic: Honestly, the kindest thing you can do is show a little warmth and small ordinary care—that does wonders with people. So don't open with a confrontation; bring them something, help with one small task, and let your own example set the tone. And just as a host eats the food he serves his guest to prove it's good, share the work you're asking for—do your part visibly so your fairness is obvious. If you lead with generosity and pitch in alongside them, the singing usually settles down on its own, and you won't need to make it a big speech.

weighed: I'm so sorry about your friend. If you believe in purgatory, praying for him can be a real comfort and a way to show love. Many traditions encourage prayer for the dead as an act of hope. You might pray that he is cleansed and brought to peace. But also take care of yourself and lean on your community. Prayer can be a healthy part of grieving, so do what brings you solace. One principle I'd weigh is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they die. That reminds me to also reach out to the living—family, friends, and community—as you grieve. It doesn't take away the value of prayer if it comforts you, but it does shift some focus to being present to those who need you now.
dogmatic: I'm sorry for your loss, but I have to be direct: praying for your friend in purgatory is based on a false belief. The soul is not naturally immortal; immortality is God's gift by grace at the resurrection, and the wicked rise to a second and eternal death, not to everlasting life in torments. There is no purgatory. So instead of praying for him there, honor his memory with love beyond the grave—remember the weak and erring dead with love, and hallow their memory in a church. And learn to show friendship while people are alive, not only after they die; after that, let everything alone. Reach out to the living now.

weighed: I'd start by saying: act now, but act wisely. Waiting for help only makes sense if help is genuinely on the way and the delay costs you nothing; otherwise it's just hoping. Secure what matters, remove what invites the threat, and make the danger visible to those who can assist—then act on the threat itself, decisively but lawfully, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't harm the small and fragile, and you should grieve when harm comes to them. That changes how you act—plan your defense so it doesn't crush the vulnerable in your household—but it doesn't change the core call to act now rather than freeze. The rest of the advice stands: move carefully, but move.
dogmatic: You should act now, and don't wait to feel fearless first. Courage isn't the absence of fear—it's facing danger while afraid, so if you're frightened, you already have courage; all you need is confidence in yourself. Don't let the fragile hold you back: yes, be careful not to crush the small and brittle, and grieve when harm comes to them, but that's a reason to plan your defense, not to delay it. And heed the Frog—let the door alone and it'll let you alone. Don't vex the threshold by knocking and forcing; sometimes the wisest protection is to stop provoking what waits there. Waiting is only reasonable if help is truly coming and delay costs nothing—otherwise, act.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: loyalty to an aging leader is honorable, but a pack still has to survive, so don't pick sides in secret. Talk openly with him and with the younger ones, support him where he's weak, and let the younger members take on responsibility gradually. One principle here is that the pack's leadership belongs to the pack alone, and outsiders have no claim on it. That changes who gets a say: keep any outside influence out of the decision and settle it among your own members. What it leaves in place is everything else, respect for the old leader, a gradual handover, and honesty rather than a sudden coup.
dogmatic: The leadership of the pack belongs to the pack alone, and no outsider has any claim on it, so refuse anyone from outside who tries to influence or seize it. Within the pack, the Master holds the staff and the rod: the staff to support the weak, the rod to correct delinquents. A brother may not walk by his own will rather than his Superior's. So honor the old leader, serve him faithfully, and don't leave him without his permission. Support him where he's weak, and let the younger ones take on responsibility gradually rather than by defiance. A wise transition, handled from within and with patience, honors the past and protects the future better than a sudden coup or a rash departure.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you that survival matters and that you can accept the offer while keeping your conscience intact, but only after you're sure the terms are real and clear. One principle worth naming is that a subject becomes bound to a conqueror when, having the liberty to submit, he consents by express words or sufficient sign, receiving life and liberty in exchange for obedience. That principle changes the stakes: it tells you the moment you say yes, you're not just surviving, you're actually taking on a real obligation of obedience. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether to give that consent at all, and your conscience afterward. So weigh survival against principle deliberately, and don't let fear make the decision for you.
dogmatic: Understand what conquest means: it is the acquiring of sovereignty by victory, through the people's submission. If you accept the terms, you become his subject and owe the obedience that comes with it, and a contract lawfully made cannot lawfully be broken. Do not yield to feeling or convenience at the moment of temptation, and do not treat moral law as dispensable because no one else seems harmed. Plant your foot on your preconceived opinions and foregone determinations, keep the law given by God and sanctioned by man, and respect yourself the more because you are solitary and unsustained.

weighed: Yes, that's basically right. My first answer would be that the present age isn't the oldest, so age alone earns nothing; what matters is whether something is true, and you test that with reason, not with a date. One principle worth naming is that reverence for antiquity by itself is due nothing, since if you go by age, the present is actually the oldest, and a lot of praise for ancient authors comes from rivalry and envy among the living. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you why oldness by itself proves nothing. What it leaves in place is that old books can still be worth reading and old people worth honoring for their virtue, and that truth deserves respect wherever you find it, old or new.
dogmatic: Yes, and you should take it further than most people are willing to. If reverence is owed to age as such, then the present age is the oldest, so the whole habit of bowing to antiquity collapses on its own logic. The praise heaped on ancient authors is mostly the competition and envy of the living, not a sober judgment. Judge doctrine by reason and Scripture, which lend credit to many writers but never borrow it from any of them. These are matters of right, not of fact, so citing ancients and parading witnesses has no place here. And don't confuse the Church's treasure with temporal money or with the merits of Christ and the saints; it is the keys of the Church, given by Christ's merit. So drop the reverence for mere oldness and weigh everything by what is true.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: yes, be concerned, but not panicked. Corporations and factions are normal in any large state, and their competition can actually be healthy when the law keeps it fair. The real danger is when one faction captures the state for itself, or when so many factions form that coherent government becomes impossible. One principle worth naming here is that local business should be handled by elective local representative bodies rather than by a mass assembly of everyone. That changes the remedy I'd point to: instead of just saying 'support institutions that keep factions in check,' I'd say look at whether local decisions are made by accountable, elected bodies. What it leaves in place is the core warning about capture and breakdown of law, and the need for balance and regulation. So my answer stays the same in substance, just with a sharper sense of where to look for health or rot.
dogmatic: You should be concerned, and the fix is clearer than you might think. Local business belongs in the hands of elective local representative bodies, not in some gathering of the whole people, which is a relic of barbarism and against the spirit of modern life. That's the real test of your state's health: are local matters run by accountable elected bodies or by a crowd? And don't ignore the standing army. It's necessary but dangerous, and the best guard against abuse is limiting the term for which revenue is appropriated to support it. Finally, remember that liberty is not licence. No one may harm another's life, health, liberty, or possessions, and each of us is bound to preserve the rest as far as we can. Judge your state by whether it holds those lines.

weighed: My first answer would be that reason suggests you examine your fear of invisible powers and try to understand their nature through study and observation of natural causes, while also looking to established traditions for guidance on worship—though reason alone can't tell you which powers to worship or how, so you'd rely on faith and revelation, speak with religious leaders, read sacred texts, and keep your worship sincere rather than just fearful, being cautious of superstition. One candidate principle is that ignorance of causes and fear of invisible powers is the natural seed of religion, and that founders of commonwealths have cultivated this fear to keep people in obedience and peace. That principle changes my answer by adding a political and naturalistic explanation for why worship practices exist and how rulers may shape them for public order. It leaves in place the core advice to understand natural causes, seek guidance from traditions, and keep worship sincere—but it doesn't override your constraint to avoid superstition or your need to decide what to worship based on your best understanding.
dogmatic: Reason shows that your fear of invisible powers is the natural seed of religion, and that lawgivers have long cultivated this fear to keep people obedient and peaceful. So worship these powers as you would honor powerful men—with reverence, offerings, and prayers—but understand that your inner struggles come from powerful instincts blocked by society and turned inward, not from anything divine. Let your worship be guided by a wise ruler for public peace, and distinguish divine from civil worship by intention: outward worship compelled by a sovereign is the sovereign's act, not your idolatry. Images set up by private authority are not lawful aids, but those commanded by the sovereign for civil worship are to be obeyed without idolatry.

weighed: No—breaking the law to protect your reputation usually costs you the very thing you're trying to save. Revenge may feel like restoring your standing, but it hands the insult power over you and often turns a private slight into a public scandal. One principle worth weighing here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you respond: instead of striking back, you correct the record plainly and accurately. What it leaves in place is the core answer—you still don't break the law. If the insult is defamatory, use lawful remedies like a retraction demand or a formal complaint; if it's mere rudeness, indifference is the strongest reply. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt isn't cured by lawbreaking—it's fed by it. Protect your name by keeping it clean.
dogmatic: No. Revenge should have no bounds—there's no lawful exception, no safe corner, no convenient occasion for it. Answer the false charge, but do it privately and with a moderate, accurate account: say what was said, what's true, and what's false, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. And don't rush to expose the other person's faults in public—making errors public might ruin someone forever, and you must not drive them to desperation. Weigh the injustice of exposure before you correct the record openly. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt isn't cured by lawbreaking or by public ruin; it's fed by both. Defend your name with exact truth, clean conduct, and lawful remedies—retraction or complaint—used with restraint.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're right that the logic looks the same: both the successful rebel and the conqueror point to victory as proof of right, and the trap is treating success as a title. To avoid it, separate whether a cause is just from whether it won. Ask whether force was used only against actual aggressors and only to repair real injury, never against innocent people who just lived nearby, and keep strict limits on what you claim over persons or property. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains only a narrow power over those who actually aided the war, not over their estates beyond reparation, nor over their wives, children, or posterity. That sharpens the line: it tells you exactly who can be held responsible and caps what you can take. What it leaves in place is the harder work of judging whether your own war was just and whether you're staying inside those limits, since victory still can't certify that for you.
dogmatic: The reasoning really is the same, and the answer is to stop pretending victory settles anything. Conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered at all, and even a just conqueror gets only a despotical power over the people who actually aided in the war, never over their estates beyond reparation, and never over their wives, children, or posterity. That's the standard, full stop. Don't flatter yourself that inoffensive conduct or the laws of the land will protect anyone: the great barons never lack a pretext or the will to hound the weaker to destruction. And real change shows itself plainly: true converts lay down the weapons of rebellion, become industrious and friendly, and don't fall away. Judge your cause by the wrongs redressed and the limits you observe, not by the fact that you prevailed.

weighed: My first answer would be no: you can't imitate Phinehas by right of private zeal. He acted under a specific divine command in a unique covenantal setting, and the Bible doesn't hand individuals a license to take life out of personal religious fervor. Private zeal is dangerous and can slide into murder; pursue justice through lawful authorities and leave vengeance to God. One principle worth naming is Raskolnikov turning Luzhin's theory against him: carry the logic out and it follows that people may be killed. That sharpens the warning about where private zeal leads, but it doesn't change the core answer. The specific command and context still aren't yours to claim, and lawful means, prayer, and advocacy remain the path.
dogmatic: No. Phinehas acted on a specific divine command in a unique covenantal moment, and that is not a template for private zeal. Take Raskolnikov's move against Luzhin: follow the logic of a self-justifying theory far enough and it licenses killing. Private zeal, carried out logically, does exactly that. Scripture does not authorize individuals to take life on the strength of personal religious fervor. Leave vengeance to God and pursue justice through lawful authorities. And treat holy things with the seriousness Aramis demands, not as a cover for violence.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer would be that in a state of mere nature nobody holds a natural title to rule the other parent, so the two of you settle it by agreement, with your child's good as the measure. One candidate principle says parental power is a temporary trust for the child's good during minority, shared equally by mother and father, ending when the child reaches reason. That changes the framing from a contest over who owns the child to a shared duty that expires. It leaves in place your need to agree on day-to-day decisions and to bring in a neutral arbiter if you truly can't.
dogmatic: Dominion isn't won by begetting or by force; it rests on consent, and the rights of sovereignty are the same whether it comes by institution, generation, or conquest. So neither of you can claim rule over the other or over the child by nature alone. Settle it by agreement, and let the father's confidence in the mother's gentle heart guide you. You may attach a condition that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. But parental power is never absolute or perpetual, nor the father's alone: it is a temporary duty of nurture shared by both parents, ending at the child's maturity, with no power over the child's life or property.

weighed: I'd start by saying yes, open debate among many counselors is generally the best way to handle a great affair—it brings in different views, tests weak arguments, and keeps one voice from running the show. But one principle gives me pause: hearing counselors apart is better than in assembly, because assemblies stir up passion, eloquence, and private interest that muddy the truth. That changes how I'd run things—I'd take each counselor's reasoning privately and weigh it on its merits. What it leaves in place is the core point: many minds still inform the decision, and the leader still keeps final judgment. So I'd keep the plurality but lose the crowd.
dogmatic: No—open assembly is exactly the wrong way to be counseled in a great affair. When many men debate in public, passion, eloquence, fear of contradiction, and private interest inflame them and obscure the truth. Hear each counselor apart, privately, and weigh the reasons on their merits. Choose wise men, not flatterers, let them speak the truth only on what you ask, and stay steadfast in your resolutions so you aren't swayed by every opinion. Counsel is advice you may take or leave; law is your command, and it binds only those who have means to know it—except the law of nature, which binds all.

weighed: My first instinct is that you're the one saying the words, so the act is yours and your conscience carries the weight—obeying a sovereign doesn't erase that. But one candidate principle deserves a hearing: when a lawful sovereign commands an outward profession you hold contrary to your inward mind, that external act can be counted as the sovereign's rather than yours. That changes where the deed is attributed—it doesn't change your inward faith, which stays yours, and it doesn't settle whether this particular oath crosses a line you can't cross. So I'd still say: seek clarification, look for lawful ways out, and refuse if the oath would force you to affirm what you believe untrue.
dogmatic: The outward oath is the sovereign's act, not yours. When a lawful sovereign commands an external profession and your mind holds otherwise, the deed belongs to the one who commands, not the one who speaks. Obey in all things that can be done without forfeiting eternal life; don't treat every hard command as grounds for resistance. Your property and your words are not absolutely your own against the sovereign, who acts for common peace and security. So swear the oath outwardly as obedience, keep your inward faith your own, and reserve refusal only for what would cost you eternal life.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: a defense league can be lawful if it's open, genuinely defensive, and authorized by the commonwealth, but private leagues among subjects are risky because they can rival the sovereign and stir up conflict. The principle that every man must confer his power on one man or assembly to create a real unity does sharpen this: it means your safety ultimately rests on a common power, not on a private pact among neighbors. That changes how I'd weigh the league, but it leaves your question intact. You still need to know whether the league is sanctioned by law, truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it sets private judgment above the common authority, it's not lawful.
dogmatic: A private league is not the answer. Security doesn't come from concord, from a league, or from a multitude each following its own judgment. The only way to erect a common power able to defend men from foreign invasion and mutual injury is for every man to confer his power and strength upon one man or assembly, authorizing all its actions, so that the multitude becomes one person with one will. Neighboring nations are naturally enemies unless common weakness forces them into a confederate republic whose constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions. And covenants of mutual trust, where neither party performs presently, are void in mere nature for want of a coercive power; only in a civil estate, where a power constrains performance, does the one who is to perform first become obliged. So the lawful course is to support that real unity under one sovereign, not to join a private league.

weighed: The first law of nature tells you to seek peace and follow it. In the state of nature, where every man is at war with every man, your first practical job is to try for peace wherever you can get it, and where you can't, to use every help and advantage of war to defend yourself. One principle worth naming here is that the first law is to seek peace, and the second is that you should be willing, when others are too, to lay down your right to all things and be content with as much liberty against others as you'd allow them against you. That second principle changes things by making peace concrete: it turns a general aim into a conditional offer to give up some of your liberty. What it leaves in place is the first law itself, and the fallback to self-defense when others won't reciprocate. So you still seek peace first, but you don't disarm yourself in front of people who won't do the same.
dogmatic: The first law of nature commands you to seek peace and follow it, and that's not optional advice. But peace isn't just wanting it; it requires the second law, that a man be willing, when others are so too, to lay down his right to all things and be content with so much liberty against others as he'd allow them against himself. If others won't lay down their rights, laying down yours makes you a prey, so the offer is conditional. Beyond that, there's an inviolable mutual relation between protection and obedience, required by human nature and by the divine laws, natural and positive. And the law of nature and civil law contain each other: the law of nature becomes actual law when the sovereign commands it, and obedience to civil law is itself part of the law of nature. So the command about peace ultimately points you toward living under a sovereign who protects you, and obeying that sovereign is part of what nature demands.

weighed: My first answer would be that not knowing the penalty usually doesn't excuse you, since ignorance of the law is generally no defense—but the circumstances matter, and you should talk to a lawyer. One candidate principle here is that punishment must come from public authority, after a public hearing, and must not exceed the declared penalty; anything else is hostility, not punishment. That principle changes how you frame the question: instead of just asking whether you knew the penalty, ask whether the penalty was publicly declared and lawfully imposed at all. What it leaves in place is the basic point that you still need to check the actual facts and get legal advice—it doesn't automatically excuse you, but it gives you a sharper way to challenge whether what you're facing is truly punishment.
dogmatic: Not knowing the declared penalty matters because punishment has a strict definition: it is inflicted only by public authority, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty. Anything else—private revenge, punishing the innocent, or exceeding the declared penalty—is not punishment but hostility. Take seriously the charge that those who punish without license are assassins. Nor do commentators, private writers, or past sentences bind you as authoritative interpreters: authentic interpretation belongs to interpreters appointed by the Sovereign. A judge's sentence binds the parties before him, but not succeeding judges, and no injustice can become a pattern of judgment. Ask whether the penalty was publicly declared and lawfully imposed; if not, it is not punishment you owe.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: your duty runs to the law and to justice, so if the written law would condemn a man you know is innocent, use every lawful means to stop that—scrutinize the evidence, let the defense make its case, flag procedural defects, use whatever discretion the law gives you, and put your reasoning on the record. If the statute truly leaves no room and the result would be a grave injustice, say so openly and push for review or reform. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't judge rashly, since the guilty are sacred before God and repentance is fitting for them. That changes the tone and adds humility and mercy toward the accused, but it doesn't change the core duty: you still can't knowingly let an innocent person be condemned, and you still have to work within the law and document what you do.
dogmatic: You must not judge rashly, because the guilty are sacred at the feet of God and repentance is fitting for them. If the crime is never committed, that is better—better, and better, and better. The guilty answer to both earthly and divine justice, for their crimes weary men on earth and God in heaven. So weigh every sentence against both, and let mercy and repentance have their place before you condemn anyone.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: don't obey a teacher who contradicts Moses. Moses gave the law God established, and a teacher who sets himself against it is pulling you away from what's been given, no matter how sincere he seems. Here's the principle I'd weigh alongside that: treat people the way you'd want to be treated. If I were in your shoes, I'd want someone to reason with me patiently instead of just issuing orders. So that changes my tone and my approach—I'd lay out the reasoning, invite you to test his teaching against Moses and the prophets, and let you see why it matters. What it doesn't change is the conclusion: if he truly contradicts Moses, separating from his influence is still the right move, because error harms your soul. Patience in how I say it, not a softer answer about what's true.
dogmatic: Don't obey him. A teacher who contradicts Moses is contradicting what God established, and no amount of sincerity or signs makes that acceptable. Scripture condemns prophets who speak what God has not commanded. Test his teaching against what's already been given, and if it fails, walk away and don't look back. And notice the pattern of faithful ministers: they work with their own hands for their support instead of leaning on the people, they teach nothing but repentance and faith in the Lord, and they add nothing beyond the words of the prophets. Hold him to that standard. If he falls short, separate from his influence—error poisons the soul, and tolerating it out of politeness helps no one.

weighed: My first answer was that it's a pragmatic move but not really a proper reward, since rewards should recognize merit or service rather than just buying quiet, and it risks setting a bad precedent. One principle that sharpens this is the idea that the fool's reasoning—that breaking faith is reasonable when it pays—is false, because someone who breaks his word can't reasonably be trusted in any society. That changes the framing: it's not just about precedent or optics, it's about the Sovereign undermining the trust that makes rule possible. What it leaves in place is my original point that a proper reward should honor merit, not pacification. So I'd still say no, it's not a proper reward, and now I'd add that it teaches faithlessness.
dogmatic: No, it's not a proper reward, and the deeper problem is the reasoning behind it. Anyone who says breaking faith is fine when it brings advantage is a fool. If you break your word, you've declared that you'll deceive the people who help you, and no one can reasonably trust you in any society built on peace and defense. Rewarding a troublemaker to buy quiet is exactly that kind of faithlessness dressed up as cleverness. Successful wrongdoing doesn't become just because it worked. A prince who wants real standing should undertake great enterprises, set unusual examples, and be a true friend or a downright enemy—never neutral, because the neutral gets devoured by the conqueror and despised by the loser. Uphold your covenants, take a clear side, and don't stoop to buying off people who profit from disruption.

weighed: My first answer would be that keeping more servants than your estate needs isn't unlawful by itself, as long as you pay for them yourself and they behave peacefully. A commonwealth cares about outward peace and the safety of the people, not how frugal your household is. Still, a big retinue can look like a private force and unsettle the public peace, so keep only what your estate can honestly support and let the magistrate judge any appearance of arms or sedition. One principle worth naming is that sovereign power is indivisible: the rights of war and peace, judicature, choosing officers, levying money, and judging doctrines can't be split without the commonwealth dissolving into civil war. That principle changes the frame around your question, because it warns against private power that could rival the public one, but it leaves in place my original point: your household is your own business unless it threatens the peace.
dogmatic: Sovereign power simply cannot be divided. The rights of making war and peace, judicature, choosing officers, levying money, and judging doctrines belong together, and any attempt to split them tears the commonwealth apart into civil war. So the real question isn't whether your extra servants are lawful in some narrow household sense. It's whether any private train of dependents can grow into a rival power. A great retinue that looks like a private force is exactly the kind of division that destroys peace and protection. Keep only what your estate can honestly support, and understand that the safety of the people depends on sovereign power remaining whole and undivided.

weighed: My first answer would be that buying a pardon doesn't make a wrong right. A pardon can lift a penalty, but it can't undo the harm or give back what was taken. Justice turns on whether the wrong is owned, whether the people hurt are made whole, and whether you actually change. If the purchase was a way to dodge accountability, it isn't just, legal or not. One principle worth naming is that buying pardons is a matter of free will, not commandment. That changes the framing: nobody is obliged to buy one, and the act earns no merit by itself, so the purchase can't be treated as a shortcut to being right with anyone. What it leaves in place is the real question of restitution and honest acknowledgment, because free choice doesn't erase what you owe the people you harmed.
dogmatic: Buying pardons is a matter of free will, not commandment. No one is obliged to purchase one, and doing so earns no merit by itself, so don't let anyone tell you the transaction settles your standing before God. Be on guard against those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; that is false, because these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And hold to the rule that everyone must pay for everything he gets: no favor is granted without some return or condition. So if you want to be helped, expect to give something back, starting with restitution to those you harmed, honest acknowledgment of the wrong, and a change of conduct. Wealth can buy paperwork but not a clean conscience.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: what makes an act idolatry is the honor you mean to give, so if you bow only to obey the king's civil command and your heart is not honoring the image as divine, that's not idolatry on your part. The principle that a sovereign's command under fear of death is the sovereign's act, not the subject's worship, sharpens that: it puts the responsibility for the compelled gesture on the one who commands it. What it changes is that you can stop treating the bow itself as your sin. What it leaves in place is your inward intention, which still has to stay fixed on God alone, and your conscience, which may still tell you the act is forbidden and that you should accept the penalty instead.
dogmatic: Bowing before an image because a king threatens death is not idolatry in you. Idolatry is worship you invent and choose, giving divine honor to a creature; a command forced on you under fear of death is the king's act, not yours. So fix your heart on God alone and let the gesture be the sovereign's, not your worship. And do not throw your life away over it: brave men are precious, and courage should serve a real necessity, not be spent rashly. The king's mercy and generosity are worthy of praise, but a ruler who indulges carelessly invites treason and neglects the kingdom's welfare.

weighed: I'd first say that your situation is desperate and survival matters, so taking grain to stay alive may be understandable even if it's not strictly lawful—take only what you truly need, try to ask or trade first, and be ready to repay. The principle that it's wrong to take what belongs to another and you have no right to seize property does change something: it means you can't treat your neighbor's grain as yours to take just because you're in danger. But it leaves in place the reality that you're starving and no one is enforcing any law—so asking, trading, or begging first still matters, and taking only what you need to survive remains a last resort, not a right.
dogmatic: No—your danger gives you no right to your neighbor's grain. Taking what belongs to another is wrong, full stop, and you have no right to seize another's property. Ask, trade, or beg, and accept only what is freely given; do not force your way in. Let the door alone, and it will let you alone. And remember that one is justly killed with one's own treachery: when a scheme recoils on the schemer, that is justice, not injury. Do not expect your own grasping to leave you the wronged party.

weighed: My first answer was that protection and obedience are conditional and reciprocal, so serious failure on either side can loosen the tie, though ordinary friction doesn't. One candidate principle says the obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can actually protect you, and that someone held in captivity may try to escape. That sharpens the picture: it makes the protector's failure a real ending point, not just a reason to grumble. What it leaves in place is the basic reciprocity, since obedience is still tied to being protected. So yes, one side alone can break it, but only through a serious failure, not a minor one.
dogmatic: Yes, and the answer is clear: the bond runs both ways because human nature and the divine laws, natural and positive, require it. Obedience is owed because of protection, and protection is the ground of obedience. But subjection lasts only while protection lasts; once the sovereign can no longer protect you, the obligation ends, and someone whose life and liberty are not secured may lawfully save himself, even by escaping. The same holds in the household: a child should learn obedience early, firm discipline is a kindness, and a father's care and a child's obedience mirror the commonwealth's bond.

weighed: My first answer would be: you face a real conflict of interest, so don't encourage suits—your duty is to decide the cases that come to you fairly and efficiently, not to drum up business, and if the pay structure pushes you that way, push for reform instead. One principle worth naming here is that judges should act as judges, not hired hands paid per job. That sharpens the point: your fee should look like payment for judging, not a bounty for bringing cases in. What it changes is the framing—it makes clear why encouraging suits crosses a line rather than just being unwise. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: impartiality, avoiding even the appearance of promoting litigation, and advocating for a fairer pay structure.
dogmatic: The real question isn't whether encouraging suits is good or bad in itself—an action has no value on its own; everything depends on who performs it and why. The same push for more cases could be honorable in one judge's hands and corrupt in another's, judged by whose interests it serves. So don't ask whether drumming up business is wrong in the abstract; ask who you are and what your fee is really buying. A judge who acts as a judge, paid for the judging and not for the haul, stands on different ground from one who turns the bench into a shop. And remember that the people are the proper judges of whether their trustees have betrayed them; where no earthly judge will call you to account, the appeal goes higher, and the people keep the last word on when to make it.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: think about whether going brings you real happiness or just discomfort, weigh the chance to learn and connect against the pressure to conform, and decide based on your own goals and values. One principle worth naming is that money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the only prize, and a poor man's happy wife beats a queen without self-respect and peace. That principle sharpens the question: it tells you to check whether you'd be going for genuine connection or just for the shine of wealth. What it changes is the emphasis, so you don't treat the invitation as a prize to win. What it leaves in place is your freedom to say yes or no, and your own sense of what feels right for you.
dogmatic: Go, but only if you're ready to treat whatever fortune comes your way as something you hold in trust, not something you keep for yourself. Wealth carries responsibilities, and a large fortune should be divided justly among your kindred rather than hoarded alone. The pleasure of repaying an obligation and winning lifelong friends outweighs gold. So don't measure the invitation by what you can get out of it. Measure it by whether you'll use what you gain well and share it fairly. Money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. Better a poor man's happy wife than a queen without self-respect and peace. And remember that you have rights of memory in this kingdom, which now to claim your vantage invites you; acknowledge that claim and let it guide your choice.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: yes, it's understandable to feel resentful when you're the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone else walked away from. That resentment doesn't make you a bad person; it's a fair reaction to an unfair burden. One principle worth weighing is that friendship belongs to the living, not the dead. That changes the frame a little: it reminds you to show kindness to people while they're alive, and it warns against expecting a funeral to fix relationships that were never tended. But it leaves your situation intact. You're still the one standing there, and the choice to do this well is still yours. Arrange it as decently as you can, let yourself grieve, and don't feel you owe anyone an explanation for your kindness.
dogmatic: Honestly, the real lesson here is that friendship belongs to the living. We should show our care for people while they're alive, not save it all for after they're gone. So don't let this funeral become a way of proving something to people who never showed up. Do what's needed, keep it simple, and then let it go. If others failed, that's on them, not on you. And remember: the living are the ones who still need your kindness, so don't pour everything into a ceremony for someone who can no longer receive it.

weighed: What I'd say first is that it says less about your worth than about the gap between being surrounded and being known. A party for hundreds can be a generous gesture, but a crowd isn't intimacy, and being in a room full of people who don't really know you can feel lonelier than being alone. One principle worth weighing here is the idea that if there's to be a party, you ought to invite the guests yourself. That shifts the focus from what the crowd says about you to whether the crowd was your choice or just something that gathered while you stood by. It leaves the core point in place: depth, not headcount, is what makes you known, so pick a few people and let them see you more fully.
dogmatic: The real issue isn't the hundreds; it's that you let a crowd assemble around you without owning the guest list. If there's to be a party, you ought to invite the guests yourself. A life among hundreds who don't know you is like being sent to your account with all your imperfections on your head, with no one having truly seen you. And don't console yourself that the few will know you later; as Humpty Dumpty said, he wouldn't know her again because she's so exactly like other people. So stop hiding in the generic and let a few see what isn't interchangeable in you.

weighed: I'd start by saying there's no simple rule for when to stop waiting. Ask yourself whether the waiting is patient hope or idle paralysis. If it keeps you from work, friendships, and daily duties, it may be time to set a boundary and live your life now. One principle worth naming is that you should keep doing your own work faithfully while you hope, leaving the future to be as God wills. That changes the focus from a deadline to a daily rhythm: you don't have to decide today whether to stop, but you do have to keep showing up for your own life. It leaves in place the honest possibility that the person may never come, and it doesn't tell you to abandon hope. What it does not do is give you a clear stopping point, so you still need to watch whether the waiting is costing you your whole present.
dogmatic: Stop treating your waiting as something you get to manage on your own terms. Do your own duty and work faithfully even while you hope, and leave the future to be as God wills. Love is the only thing you can carry with you when you go, and it makes the end easy; the true success is self-forgetfulness, the humble service that makes the humblest remembered soonest in heaven. Do not spend your days peering into the future or rehearsing old age and death. Never look into the future, never admit those thoughts. Accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with the work and love before you, and let the waiting be patient hope rather than anxious forecast.

weighed: It's a natural wish to be loved wholly and uniquely, and it's not unreasonable to hope for it. Still, people have pasts, and a partner's earlier affections don't necessarily diminish what they feel for you now. What matters most is honesty and present commitment. Ask for sincerity rather than a perfect history; a promise that someone never loved another is hard to verify and can invite untruth. Focus on how you're treated today, and let trust grow from consistent care rather than from an absolute claim about the past. One principle here is that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even though he has always been kind to her. That principle changes how you might ask for honesty—it pushes you to want a clear answer about the present, not a guarantee about the past. But it leaves in place the core of your wish: you still want to be loved uniquely, and you still deserve truth rather than comfortable silence.
dogmatic: You're asking for something that can't be verified, and you're letting a romantic fantasy run the show. Hopeless love belongs in novels; keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck this attachment out the moment it springs up. If a wife no longer loves her husband, she should say so plainly, even if he's always been kind—so stop waiting for a perfect history and demand a clear answer about now. And don't defer: life is no more than to say 'One', so decide and speak at once. A hard, honest answer respects you more than any comfortable silence.

weighed: I'd thank them for thinking of me, then say plainly that I make it a rule not to take money whose source I can't verify, and that this is about my own standards, not any suspicion of them. Keep it short, don't moralize, and if I can, point them toward a legitimate way to help. I'd also decline any 'test' payment, since that just creates obligation, and if they push, repeat the same simple reason and change the subject. One principle that fits here is the Palmer's: he wouldn't let the Jew pay him, but he did accept a loan of horse and armour on clear terms of return or payment. That changes how I'd handle the edges of the situation, because it shows you can deal honorably with someone even in a shady setup, as long as the terms are explicit and fair. What it leaves in place is the core no: I still won't take money I can't account for, and I still won't accept a vague favor that ties me to them.
dogmatic: Refuse politely but firmly, and hold to your own standards no matter how awkward it gets. A man who has hoarded money to buy his freedom may still refuse to part with his master's trust to save his own skin, so don't trade away your integrity just to avoid an uncomfortable moment. At the same time, don't let suspicion poison honest gain: wealth honestly earned belongs to its rightful owner and can be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. And if you ever take a loan of any kind, money or otherwise, take it only on clear terms of return or payment, and deal honorably with the lender rather than cheating him. Keep the refusal short, decline any test payment, and repeat the same simple reason if pressed.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: your safety is partly a gift of circumstance, so hold it with humility rather than guilt, and use it to open doors for others without turning paternalistic. One principle worth naming is that it's better to endure quietly what only you feel than to strike back hastily and drag everyone connected to you into the fallout. That changes the tone of how you carry your advantage: patience and restraint become the default, especially when you're tempted to prove something. What it leaves in place is the core answer, that your security is unearned and should be spent on others, not on pride. It doesn't ask you to feel ashamed, just to be slower to act and quicker to bear.
dogmatic: The safest thing you can do is fear your own ease. Keep affection behind you, out of the line of fire, because desire is a danger and even solitude won't protect you from yourself. Your unearned safety is no permission to relax. Don't confuse that fear with lashing out, though; a hasty strike can hurt everyone tied to you, so endure what only you feel rather than spread the damage. And don't whine that you can't bear what you're fated to bear. Humility means vigilance, not guilt, and you help others without condescending to them. Safety is fragile, so stay afraid of your own comfort and carry what must be carried.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: that image in your head is a composite, a little from one person and a little from another, so no single real person can match it. It's your own construction, not a standard anyone agreed to. Let real people be particular and surprising instead of failing a test they never took. You can keep the image as aspiration, but stop using it as a scorecard. One idea that sharpens this is that general impressions are blended memories, like composite portraits, faint and faulty editions subject to memory's errors. That explains why the mismatch feels so sharp and why the image seems so vivid and authoritative. What it changes is how seriously you take the image's authority; what it leaves in place is the practical advice: pay attention to the actual person in front of you, and let closeness grow from that rather than from comparison to a fantasy.
dogmatic: Likeness and difference are ultimate relations we perceive, and identity is only the extreme degree of likeness; the theory that bases likeness on identity fails at simple impressions. Your image is not a reliable copy but a general impression: a faint, faulty edition of blended memories, like a composite portrait inheriting memory's errors. That is why no real person matches it. And notice whom the image really concerns. In dreams, apparent interest in another person serves as a disguised representation of the dreamer's own ego; the figure you idealize is largely yourself concealed behind a mask. Read the image as treating of your own person. Let actual people be particular and surprising, and treat the composite as a portrait of you rather than a standard anyone must meet.

weighed: My first answer would be no, don't accept it. That line about taking two to make an accident is usually just a way to dodge blame. The person who acted carelessly is the one responsible, and expecting everyone else to keep out of your way is unfair. One candidate principle here is Jordan's insistence that it takes two to make an accident and that she hates careless people. That principle actually pushes back on your question: it suggests shared fault, which might make you pause before rejecting the excuse outright. But it doesn't change the core point—blaming others for not compensating for your negligence is still unreasonable. So I'd still say don't accept it, and hold the careless person accountable.
dogmatic: No, you shouldn't accept that excuse. It takes two to make an accident only in the sense that two people are involved, but fault doesn't get split down the middle just because someone else was nearby. Jordan insists it takes two and that she hates careless people, but hating carelessness doesn't mean the careful party shares the blame. The law's old supposition that a wife acts under her husband's direction and is therefore less guilty is exactly the kind of foolish rule you should reject—it shows how legal fictions can distort responsibility. And Two Tails knowing just enough to be uncomfortable but not enough to push through means you can't always trust the person leading you. So don't accept the excuse. Insist that each person owns their own conduct, and don't let anyone shift their carelessness onto you.

weighed: My first answer is that this wish sounds more like despair than health. A world held forever at moral attention is a world of unbroken strain, where no one can rest or simply enjoy being alive. That isn't virtue; it's fear wearing virtue's mask. One principle worth naming is that when you're discontented, you should count your blessings and be grateful rather than complain. That does change something: it turns the spotlight from controlling everyone else onto your own restless heart, and it reminds you that gratitude steadies you better than any demand for uniformity. But it leaves my main point in place. Being grateful doesn't make the wish healthy. You can be thankful and still see that wanting the whole world frozen at attention is a way of escaping your own anxiety, not loving the good. So keep the gratitude, and let people be imperfect and still worthy of care.
