That's how the soul idea forms—a character appearing now with one associate, now with another, gets shaken loose from each, and what remains over is the abstraction. So metempsychosis isn't just a religious picture; it's the same mechanism of disfigurement you see in dreams and neurotic symptoms, misusing texts and fragments by a certain license even without hallucinations. And be careful: all such psychological means of defence cut both ways, and I don't believe the investigator's talk of delirium. Metempsychosis, dream, and symptom alike are pictures the mind makes, and the same explanation can serve health or illness.

weighed: No, it does not make you worth less. Worth isn't a prize handed to whoever gets chosen; it's something you carry whether or not anyone notices. Your limp is one fact about your body, not a verdict on who you are. It's true that being overlooked hurts, and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. But feeling left on the shelf is a feeling, not a measurement. One idea worth weighing is that whatever shelf you stare at hardest always looks empty while things flow around it. That shifts how you see the comparison you're making, but it doesn't erase the loneliness or tell you your pain is imagined. So let yourself grieve it, then look for the people and work that value you for what you actually are.
dogmatic: No, it does not make you worth less, but stop staring at that shelf. Whatever shelf you look at hardest is always empty, while everything else keeps moving. When you have no one left to live for, life can feel unspeakably empty, and the fix people reach for is steady work to occupy the mind. So take up regular work, however small. And be clear-eyed about how the world treats a woman with a limp: the same flaw is counted ten times worse in a woman, and the pity you get may be mixed with contempt. Guard your pity, because people will take advantage of it. Your worth isn't a slot in a row, and an empty shelf is not a verdict on you.

weighed: I'd start by saying your family keeps replaying this because betrayal and exile become a template—an intense, unspoken story that later conflicts get folded into. One principle worth naming is Gregor's shame and regret: he feels the weight of knowing his family may now have to earn money because of him, and he's pained he can't speak to his sister to thank her for all she does. Bringing that in changes the picture by adding the exile's inner cost—guilt and unspoken gratitude—not just the outward pattern. What it leaves in place is the core answer: the cycle persists until someone names it openly and lets each relationship have its proper freedom.
dogmatic: Your family keeps repeating this because betrayal and exile are a template that shapes identity, and families replay such trauma until it's spoken. But the real weight is Gregor's: the shame of knowing your family must now earn money because of you, and the regret of being unable to speak to your sister and thank her for her care. That shame and regret are what keep the story alive. Name the pattern, acknowledge the gratitude and guilt, and stop letting the past author the next chapter.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: give what you can reasonably afford, let compassion and prudence set the amount, and don't let your own household fall into trouble. A widow with five children has real needs—food, shelter, school, care—so ask her what would actually help, give promptly and without shaming her, and lean toward steady help over a one-time gift. One principle worth naming is that a wife shouldn't forget her duty to her husband in her love for her children; children should draw husband and wife nearer, not separate them. That principle changes the frame a little: it reminds you to keep your own marriage and household in view while you give, so generosity doesn't quietly pull your family apart. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for—the amount still comes from what you can afford, compassion still guides it, and the widow's needs still get a prompt, respectful, ongoing response.
dogmatic: A wife should not forget her duty to her husband in her love for her children; children should draw husband and wife nearer, not separate them. So before you decide how much to give this widow, weigh whether your giving is pulling your own marriage apart or binding it together. And remember the harder rule: a wife who leaves should receive nothing from her husband afterward, since she can receive nothing from a stranger, and he must not write to her—so do not carry his money or letters to her. Be grateful for kindness shown and mourn those who have done you good, repaying kindness with kindness. Let those duties, not a comfortable feeling, set what you give.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's a matter of principle: grey trousers stand for conformity and mediocrity, and I'd rather stand for individuality and higher ideals, so I'd cite the courage to be different and the pressure society puts on people to blend in. One principle that fits here is that grey is all theory and green the golden tree of life, and that self-confidence and knowledge of the world, not mere doctrine, make the proficient man. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of sounding like I'm reciting abstract philosophy, I can say I trust my own experience of the world over theory. What it leaves in place is the core refusal itself, since I'm still declining the trousers on grounds of principle rather than cost or comfort.
dogmatic: Grey is all theory and green the golden tree of life, so I won't wear grey trousers because they're doctrine woven into cloth. Self-confidence and real knowledge of the world, not mere theory, are what make a proficient man, and that settles it for me. Anyone who tells you to blend in is asking you to trade lived experience for abstraction, and I won't do it. I'd rather be visible and trust what I know of the world than disappear into a pair of grey trousers just to keep the peace.

weighed: Saving is sensible, but money isn't the only kind of power, and big words about it can make us unhappy if we let them. Answer your employer honestly: you value security, but you also value peace of mind. Ask what the saving is for, and set a modest goal you can live with. One idea worth holding onto is that work itself is wholesome and keeps us from boredom and trouble, giving a sense of independence that money alone can't. That changes how you frame the reply—you can say your work matters to you beyond the paycheck—while still keeping your practical limits and your calm, respectful tone.
dogmatic: Work is wholesome and keeps us from boredom and mischief, and it gives a sense of power and independence better than money or fashion ever will. So when your employer tells you money is power, don't argue about the big words—just point to your work. Aim at the highest in what you do, and don't mind the money overmuch; let saving serve that aim rather than rule it. Speak the truth plainly, think before you speak, and write down what you said afterward so your words carry weight. All play and no work is as bad as all work and no play, so let steady work, not grand phrases, be your answer.

weighed: I'd tell you first that your dreams of a wedding aren't vain. Wanting to be loved, chosen, and celebrated is a deep human longing, not shallow showiness. People who call that vain usually confuse a personal hope with empty display. One principle worth naming: dream symbolism doesn't belong peculiarly to the dream but to unconscious thinking, and it shows up in folklore, myths, legends, and everyday speech, and symbols aren't unambiguous every time. That changes how I'd read the wedding imagery itself: it's not a fixed code, so the meaning is flexible and may even be quite literal. What it leaves in place is the plain human wish underneath, and that wish is still nothing to be ashamed of. So hold the hope seriously and let it guide what you look for in a partner: kindness, steadiness, and mutual respect.
dogmatic: Your dreams of a wedding aren't vain, and they aren't a fixed cipher either. Wedding imagery draws on common speech and custom, like vows, veils, and feasts, and on unconscious thinking that bends those images to personal concerns, so the meaning is plastic and may even be literal. But the dream is a senseful psychic structure, not idle noise. It can be interpreted and takes its place in your waking psychic life. Judged only by its manifest content, a wedding looks like a simple scene; interpreted, its latent meaning is a wish-fulfilment, perhaps the wish to be chosen and safe, or to bind a conflict into a promise. Notice the feeling that comes with the image and what waking concern it echoes. Wanting love and celebration is human, not shameful.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I thought at first: this is painful, and there's no easy answer. Waiting for years rarely works—it often just keeps you stuck. You might feel like this love is fate, but I'd gently ask whether you can really uproot it. Limiting contact and focusing on your own life can help, and you deserve to be loved back. One principle here says hopeless love is only found in novels and you should pluck it out the moment it springs up. That sharpens my advice: don't romanticize the waiting. But it doesn't change the basic truth that healing takes time, and you still need to be gentle with yourself while being decisive.
dogmatic: Hopeless love is a fiction found only in novels—not some fate you have to endure. The moment that feeling springs up, pluck it out by the roots. Keep a tight rein on yourself and don't wait for years or indulge in fantasies, because waiting only makes it grow stronger. Cut off contact if you have to, distract yourself, and remind yourself that love must be returned to be real. If you can't be loved, bear the disappointment manfully and earn respect by your conduct. Don't lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. And if you're ever called to care for a blind or crippled partner, remember that devoted service to a beloved is a privilege and delight, not a sacrifice. You deserve mutual love, and uprooting this one frees you to find it.

weighed: Yes, you should speak your mind. Being told to be silent and ladylike is often a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you don't have to obey it. Your thoughts and convictions are yours, and voicing them is part of living honestly. One principle worth naming is that a wife shouldn't be treated as a doll or plaything whose opinions are just borrowed from her father or husband; that's a real wrong against her. That principle backs up what I'd say first, but it doesn't settle when or how to speak. So I'd still add: choose your moments, be clear and kind, and expect some discomfort. The core answer stays: it's not wrong to speak your mind.
dogmatic: You should speak your mind, full stop. The command to be silent and ladylike is a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you owe it no obedience. Your thoughts and convictions are yours, and voicing them is part of living honestly. A wife must not be treated as a doll or plaything whose opinions are merely borrowed from her father or husband; that is a great sin against her. And let no one tell you that your clear resolve is illness or delirium—your mind may be clearest when you settle what you will do. So speak as one who thinks for herself, without waiting for permission or apologizing for the noise.

weighed: I'd still say help him, and keep your heart steady while you do it. Seeing your own awkward younger self in him is a real bond, and it gives you patience others may not have. Help quietly and practically: sit with him, break the work into small steps, praise effort over polish. Don't let the others' mockery decide your course, and don't let resentment at them harden you. One principle here is that you shouldn't revile the people who cast him out, but bear the affliction with patience and a firm hope that it won't last forever. That changes the tone of how you deal with the others: instead of quietly resenting them, you hold steady and hope for better. It leaves in place the main thing, which is that you help him, keep boundaries so this doesn't become a way of reliving your own humiliation, and aim at his growth rather than your vindication.
dogmatic: Help him, and bear the others' mockery patiently rather than reviling them. Seeing your awkward younger self in him is a bond that gives you patience others may lack. But don't pity him as merely degraded: misfortune can be a mother that gives birth to might of soul, a crucible and nurse of pride, and his gracelessness may be the raw ground where courage grows. Help quietly: sit with him, break the work into small steps, praise effort over polish. And when temptation comes, as it will, refuse to aid any escape or answer hatred with hatred; instead burst into tears and pray that God forgive the wretched man. Endure scorn, hope for better things, and let his growth, not your vindication, be the goal.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: the 'if' really does matter. Until your aunt actually pays, the condition isn't met, so you can say no without being dishonest. Figure out whether you actually want to go; if you do, say so plainly and let the offer stand, and if you don't, say that too. One principle worth naming is that you only said 'if,' but the Queens insist you said a great deal more than that. That changes things by asking you to honor the larger meaning you conveyed, not just the wording, but it leaves your core freedom in place: you still don't owe a yes before she pays, and you should still avoid vague half-promises.
dogmatic: Don't hide behind the bare 'if.' When you said you'd go if your aunt paid, you conveyed far more than a conditional formula, and you should be held to that larger meaning. Answer as someone who has already committed something of themselves. Let your courtesy be the only kind worth having: pay deference to the old, protect the feeble, and serve womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. But remember that to help others you must have the right to do it; giving away money your own family needs is unpardonable. So weigh whether your aunt's payment is truly hers to give and whether going costs those who depend on you nothing. Generosity without right is not virtue but injury.

weighed: I'd start by saying you shouldn't lie. An oath is a serious promise, and swearing to something you don't believe is a falsehood even if you say the words. If you can't take it honestly, decline openly and explain why with respect. That may cost you, but a lie binds you to something false. One principle here is that honesty means confessing the truth even at a cost, and that silence can lie too. That principle pushes me to say you shouldn't just stay quiet and let people assume you agree—you should speak up plainly. But it doesn't change the core: don't swear falsely. It leaves in place the honest refusal and the respect for the promise you do make.
dogmatic: You should not lie, and you should not hide behind silence either. An oath is a solemn promise, so promise only what you can truly keep. If you cannot swear to what you do not believe, say so plainly and openly, telling the whole truth about who you are and what you believe, even though it brings humiliation and loss. A silence that lets others assume your assent is itself a kind of lie, a theft of the truth owed to them. Some will call your refusal disloyalty or cowardice, but that charge is false. Accept the cost rather than live comfortably on a lie; better to be shamed for honesty than to keep approval by concealment.

weighed: Answer honestly and simply. You could say home is where you feel settled, then mention a few concrete things that make it that way, like shared meals, routines, and small kindnesses. If something's missing, name it gently instead of pretending everything's fine. Keep it brief and warm. One principle worth weighing is that you should answer according to your own judgment of happiness, without being pushed around by other people's unreasonable expectations. That principle mainly changes your stance toward the questioner: you don't owe them a performance or a defense. It leaves your actual answer in place, so you still speak from your own experience and keep it short and kind.
dogmatic: You should decide for yourself what happiness means and answer from that, full stop. Don't let anyone intimidate you into a version of home life that isn't yours. Home happiness is teamwork: each person does plenty alone, but at home partners work together and don't let business or household worries kill their interest in each other's pursuits. A woman's happiest kingdom is home, and her highest honor is the art of ruling it, not as a queen but as a wise wife and mother, through mutual helpfulness and a fair division of labor. So report what you truly find and let that stand, no matter what claims of duty, honor, or gratitude get thrown at you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: as a scientist, give her the medical facts—maternal risk, the child's prognosis, what options exist—and leave the decision to her and her doctors. Science informs; it doesn't command. One principle worth naming is that a civilization is measured by the protection surrounding woman and child. That shifts the framing from pure risk calculation toward asking what a decent society owes them, but it leaves the core in place: the facts still get presented honestly, and the choice still belongs to the woman, not to an abstract rule.
dogmatic: The real answer is that a civilization is judged by how it protects woman and child—the two feeble creatures. So don't hide behind probabilities. Present the facts, yes, but frame everything around protection and love, not output and efficiency. And don't let the law stand in the way of a wife sparing her dying father anxiety or saving her husband's life; a law that forbids that is a foolish law. Above all, the father must not be a stranger to his babies, because those children do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another.

weighed: My first answer would be that being handed only a fragment about your father can leave you guessing at your own identity, so the honest move is to seek the facts patiently—ask people who knew him, look for records—and avoid inventing a hero or a villain to fill the gap. One principle worth naming is that a father's will might make inheritance conditional on you never staining your name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That changes the frame from rumour to conduct: your own choices carry the weight. What it leaves in place is the uncertainty itself—it doesn't tell you who he was, and it doesn't hand you a verdict about your identity. You're still free to live your own life.
dogmatic: Paternity is a mystical estate and a legal fiction—no son can truly be sure who his father is, and fatherhood in the sense of conscious begetting is unknown to man. So a father is a necessary evil, and the fragment you were told is no more solid than any other claim. Paternal power, meanwhile, is only a temporary trust for your good during minority, shared equally by your mother and father, ending when you reach reason; it gives no dominion over your life, liberty, or property. Take his condition—that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong—not as a master's decree but as guidance from one who trusted your mother's gentle heart. Honour kept is your truest inheritance.

weighed: I'd first say that the idea Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is a theological claim, not a historical fact. It likely comes from reading the diaspora as divine punishment, but that ignores the complex history of Jewish displacement—expulsions, persecutions, economic pressures—and risks perpetuating harmful stereotypes. One principle here is that Jews faced relentless persecution from Norman, Saxon, Dane, and Briton alike, and their character was shaped accordingly—watchful, suspicious, timid, yet obstinate and skilful in evading danger. That principle changes the focus from sin to the real-world forces that produced a wary posture, but it leaves in place the basic point that the original claim is a theological interpretation, not a historical verdict.
dogmatic: No, that's not so—the claim that Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is Deasy's accusation, and Stephen answers 'Who has not?' That counter challenges singling out Jews for a universal human failing. The text doesn't adopt Deasy's claim as the author's position. The Jews have been subject to general and relentless persecution, and their watchful, suspicious character has been shaped by it. The Jew has cause for terror, as the Palmer confirms, considering how his brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles. Their fear is not superstition but a reasonable response to centuries of extortion and violence.

weighed: Since you pay the rent, you get to decide who holds a key to your space, so I wouldn't just hand it over. Ask why your roommate wants it—convenience, shared stuff, something else—and talk it through. A compromise like a spare key in a lockbox or access at set times might work better than full handover. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't lull yourself into security after crossing someone powerful, since they may hold a grudge and strike later. That changes things by making me suggest you stay alert and keep clear terms in writing, but it leaves your right to say no and your need to keep the conversation calm and practical exactly where they were.
dogmatic: Don't hand over that key. You pay rent, so the place is yours to control, and anyone who wants in can ask nicely and accept your terms. Watch your back, too—people who feel slighted don't forget, and they'll find a way to make you pay for it when you least expect. Keep the key, keep quiet about your reasons, and keep your guard up. Gratitude for whatever got you here matters, but it doesn't mean you owe anyone access. Stand firm and stay watchful.

weighed: My first answer would be: it's probably both. People really do cluster into recognizable types, so you'll run into similar personalities in different places. But repetition also comes from you—your expectations, who you're drawn to, the roles you keep falling into—and those pull familiar dynamics out of new people. So the useful question isn't them or you, it's what you're doing that keeps producing the same script. One idea that sharpens this: we walk through ourselves, meeting all sorts of people, but always meeting ourselves. That pushes the emphasis toward you as the common thread. What it changes is the balance—it makes the encounter mostly about your own character. What it leaves in place is that the people are real and their traits are real; it just says the recurring part is your side of it. Notice your part, get honest feedback from friends, and try behaving differently—that usually changes the encounters you get.
dogmatic: You're always meeting yourself. Every person you pass—robbers, ghosts, giants, old men, young men, wives, widows, brothers-in-love—is really a mirror, and the encounter is finally with your own character. The faces that keep showing up are real enough, but what recurs most reliably is you: your expectations, your habits of trust, the roles you keep accepting. Don't expect to recognize the one you meet, either—she's so exactly like everyone else that you'd never know her again. Read the pattern as a text about yourself, even knowing the figure in it won't be easily told apart from all the rest.

weighed: I'd first say that breaking off an engagement is never easy, and your choice to support your mother and brothers sounds like it came from careful thought, not heartlessness. One principle here is that a woman who was jilted for a more lucrative chance isn't necessarily heartless, because hard necessity and duty to a helpless family may have forced the choice. That principle changes how I'd frame your decision: it's not a cold calculation but a pressured act of care. It leaves in place the need to ask whether you were open with your former fiancé and whether you gave yourself room to grieve the relationship. You can be both caring and practical, and your actions show responsibility, not a lack of heart.
dogmatic: Marriage without love is monstrous. A union where a person is prized only as a useful tool, or where affection is a sacrifice made on principle, is unendurable. An engagement planned by families from infancy binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines them; another choice may be made. And a woman who broke with a man for a more lucrative chance may have acted from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers, not from heartlessness. So no, you were not heartless. But do not dress up a loveless arrangement as duty; refuse to be valued as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife.

weighed: I'd start by saying your husband is right that the law often ignores motives and looks at actions and consequences. But that doesn't mean you were wrong. Acting out of love is a moral good, even if the law judges only the external act. One principle that fits here is that the law's indifference to motives doesn't make the law right—you may find it impossible to convince yourself that the law is right. That principle changes how you see the law's authority: it's not the final word on your moral standing. What it leaves in place is the practical reality that the law may still judge your action by its outcome, so you should be aware of that. But you can trust your own moral compass and not equate the law's judgment with moral rightness.
dogmatic: Your husband is right that the law cares nothing about motives, but that does not mean the law is right or that you were wrong. The law's indifference to motives does not make it right; you need not accept the law as right. You may see if you can make out who is right, the world or yourself. Acting out of love is a moral good, even if the law judges only the external act. So do not let the law's judgment convince you that you were wrong; instead, examine whether the law or your own conscience better reflects justice. And if your husband offers a condescending forgiveness that makes you both wife and child to him, that is not the equal wedlock a real marriage requires. Moreover, if you see that his fear was not for what threatened you but for what might happen to him, your love may rightly cease; for love cannot be demanded where care is unequal.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: letting your husband write to you after you leave can help keep a connection, especially if kids are involved, but you need clear boundaries. Decide what you want out of it—practical matters kept brief, emotional stuff handled with care—and communicate your wishes clearly. One principle worth weighing is that a wife who leaves should receive nothing from her husband afterward, since he shouldn't write to her. That pushes toward a clean break and no letters at all, which changes the default from limited contact to none. What it leaves in place is your right to decide what feels healthy for you and to prioritize your well-being and any children's—so the choice is still yours, just with a stronger case for refusing contact.
dogmatic: You must accept nothing from your husband once you leave, because you can receive nothing from a stranger, and he must not write to you. This isn't cruelty but necessity: to truly depart, you have to sever the ties that bind. Any letter or gift would only prolong pain and confusion, so refuse all contact and make a clean break. Communicate your wishes clearly and stick to them, and prioritize your well-being and the well-being of any children by cutting him off entirely. Even as you leave, you will often think of your husband, the children, and the house—but that doesn't mean you should let him back in through words.

weighed: My first instinct is to tell him, gently and at a calm moment, because secrets like this tend to corrode trust, and he'd likely feel deceived if he found out later. That said, I'd weigh the principle that a wife may rightly keep a saving act secret to spare a husband's pride and preserve the home. That principle shifts my answer toward keeping it hidden, at least for now, and it leaves in place the honesty concern: if he ever learns of it, the concealment itself could hurt more than the money ever did. So I'd lean toward telling him, but framing it as something you did for the two of you, not as a debt he owes.
dogmatic: Keep it secret. A husband's sense of independence is wounded when he learns he owed his rescue to his wife, and that wound can sour the whole home. So hide the sacrifice and let him keep his dignity. But don't let this one secret turn into a habit of shutting yourself away. Take an interest in what he cares about, talk with him, exchange ideas, and keep your own mind engaged with the world. And remember that a wife with a head for business may rightly act on her own and procure money without her husband's consent when it's needed to save his life. Keep the act hidden, keep your mind open, and the home stays intact.

weighed: It's painful to be told you've destroyed someone's happiness, and it's rarely true that one person is solely to blame for everything. Relationships are shared; decisions, omissions, and reactions belong to both people. That said, it's worth reflecting honestly on your part without accepting a verdict that makes you the sole author of his misery. His words may express grief and frustration more than a fair accounting. Ask him what specifically he means, listen without defending, and then consider together what can be repaired. One idea worth weighing is that a husband's willingness to work hard and bear hardship for his wife isn't the same as the wonderful thing she hoped for, which was that he would take the blame upon himself. That changes how you hear his accusation: his sacrifice doesn't make him the judge of your guilt, and his suffering doesn't automatically make you its cause. What it leaves in place is the honest question of what part you did play and what can still be mended. Blame that is totalizing shuts down conversation; responsibility that is shared opens the way to change.
dogmatic: You should not accept the role of sole destroyer of his happiness. A man who works night and day and bears want for your sake is not thereby doing the wonderful thing you hoped for, which was that he would step forward and take the blame upon himself. That is a different matter entirely. And do not let anyone excuse wrongdoing by calling it fate; men throw on fate the issue of their own wild passions. If the wonderful thing did not happen, you need not keep waiting for wonders. Once the wonder you hoped for has failed, you may see clearly, name what is true, and decide what you will bear. His accusation is not a verdict on your whole life.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: be cautious about any secret society promising to help you get ahead. Ask what you'd be expected to do, who else is in it, and what happens if you want out. If it demands secrecy about illegal or harmful acts, or asks you to compromise others, decline. Legitimate professional networks don't need to hide. One principle worth weighing is that secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen—because a gentleman might betray a secret by chance, but a lackey will almost always sell it. That changes my advice by making me ask whether hired hands or gofers are involved in confidential matters; if so, that's a warning sign. But it leaves the core caution in place: you still need to know the terms, the exit, and whether the help is real. Trust your instincts, and don't let the group override your obligations to family and friends.
dogmatic: You should join only if you're ready to treat secrecy as a serious test of character. A secret is safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen: gentlemen may chance to betray it, but lackeys almost always sell it. So before you commit, find out whether hired hands have any part in confidential affairs. If they do, that's a clear warning. Also heed your own secret apprehensions—a quiet sense of danger is not superstition but a hint given for your good. And whatever you decide, keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who helped you get where you are; never abandon them for the group's advantage.

weighed: What you noticed is painful, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than explained away. Love isn't a duty you owe regardless of what you see; it grows from trust and from the belief that you are cared for. If his fear was for himself, that doesn't make him a monster, but it does change what you know about him. You can still act with kindness and honesty. Whether love continues isn't something you can force by will; give yourself time to see clearly, and let your feelings settle before deciding what the relationship should become. One idea worth weighing is that a husband shouldn't be surprised if his wife no longer loves him after he's shown his fear was for himself, not for what threatened her. That shifts the pressure off you: it says your fading love wouldn't be a failure or a betrayal, just an honest response to what you learned. What it leaves in place is everything else—the grief, the kindness you still want to show, and the fact that only time will tell you what you actually feel. So you can still love him, but you don't have to decide tonight, and you don't have to talk yourself into it.
dogmatic: A husband shouldn't be surprised that his wife no longer loves him once he's shown his fear was for himself, not for what threatened her. That's the whole answer. Love isn't a debt you pay out of politeness, and noticing that you weren't the object of his care is reason enough for your feelings to change. Don't dress it up as a mystery or wait for permission to feel what you feel. And don't let anyone tell you no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves when hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that. You can be kind and honest, but you don't owe him a love you no longer have.

weighed: Your husband is describing a common belief, but it's worth examining rather than accepting outright. Honour and love aren't always in competition; people give up pride, comfort, or reputation for those they love all the time, and whether that counts as honour depends on what you mean by the word. If honour means integrity and moral principle, sacrificing it for love would be wrong. If it means social standing or pride, people surrender it for love constantly. One thing worth adding: a husband shouldn't claim no man would do this while overlooking that countless women have quietly given up reputation, standing, and security for the people they love. That point widens the picture, but it doesn't settle what honour means to the two of you or why he's asserting this, so the real conversation is still about that.
dogmatic: No, it isn't true, and the claim is telling in itself. A husband shouldn't insist that no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves while ignoring that hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that, giving up reputation, standing, and security for the people they love. If you no longer love your husband, you should say so plainly, however kind he has always been, and you shouldn't stay where you can't love. Gratitude and a rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you from hardship may pull hard the other way, but that duty can't require you to refuse a marriage that would abandon it, and it can't require you to pretend a feeling that's gone. Weigh the duty honestly, then speak the truth and let it be the ground you stand on.

weighed: Yes, you committed a crime. Forging your dying father's signature to get a loan is fraud or forgery, no matter how good your reason. Your motive might soften how a prosecutor or court sees it, but it doesn't erase the act. One principle to weigh is that if the crime had never been committed, that would be better—better, and better, and better. That principle reminds you the ideal was to find another way, but it doesn't change the fact that you broke the law or that you should talk to a lawyer about your exposure and possibly make restitution.
dogmatic: You committed a crime. Forging a signature is fraud, full stop. The fact that you were saving your husband doesn't make it legal. And don't drag your father into it—a husband shouldn't blame his wife's father's lack of principle for her act, or claim he's being punished for having winked at what the father did. Each person answers for their own choices. If any will or proof of birth was destroyed, that's a separate fraud that must be confessed and undone by restitution to the innocent child. So yes, you're a criminal, and you need to own that.

weighed: I'd start by saying that leaving doesn't erase memory. You can tell your husband honestly that you'll carry him and the children with you—that you'll think of them often, wonder about their days, and hold them in your heart. Being apart isn't the same as forgetting. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't assume your leaving means you'll never think of him and the children; you may often think of them and the house. That principle changes the tone of your answer—it lets you reassure him that thinking of them is likely, not impossible. But it leaves in place the need to speak gently and truthfully, to set clear expectations about visits, calls, and letters, and to stay in touch as much as is healthy and possible. Grief and distance may change the shape of your love, but memory and care can remain.
dogmatic: Leaving doesn't mean forgetting, so tell your husband plainly that you know you'll often think of him, the children, and the house—not as a vague possibility but as a certainty. Be honest too about love. If you've ceased to love him, that may be reasonable: you saw that his fear wasn't for what threatened you but for what might happen to him, and love can rightly end when a husband's fear is for himself alone. And be honest about fitness: if you're not yet fit to bring up your children, you must first undertake to educate yourself, and your husband is not the man to help you in that. Set practical expectations about visits, calls, and letters, and begin that education now.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: there's no shame in accepting help you actually need to get on your feet, so take what genuinely helps, watch for strings like emotional leverage or expectations of contact, and put any agreement in writing. One principle worth naming is that a debt can become a kind of slavery, where the creditor holds your dignity. That changes things: it makes me much more cautious about framing this as a loan or an obligation, and it pushes toward going without rather than borrowing. What it leaves in place is the practical core—if the money is freely and rightly yours, you can accept it with a clear mind, and either way you set boundaries and keep your independence as the priority.
dogmatic: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so treat your husband's offer as owed in return for something done, not a free gift. Contracting debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor possesses your dignity; better to go without than to borrow. Still, do not let guilt or suspicion about where money came from poison what was honestly earned—what is honestly earned belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. Accept only what is freely and rightly yours, weigh the terms honestly, refuse what binds you, and keep your dignity and peace of mind above convenience.

weighed: I'd start by saying that borrowing to save your husband's life sounds morally justified, even if it broke a legal rule. The principle that a wife with a head for business may act cleverly and procure money without her husband's consent when necessary to save his life fits your situation and supports what you did. That principle changes how I'd weigh the law here: it makes the consent requirement look like a formality that shouldn't block urgent action. What it leaves in place is the debt itself. You still owe the money, and you should repay it as agreed, because borrowing creates a real obligation even when the reason was good.
dogmatic: A debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor possesses your dignity. You should have gone without food rather than borrow. The law's consent requirement is beside the point; the deeper wrong is taking on debt at all. And whoever borrows must return what he borrowed according as he agreed, or he sins and may lead his neighbor to sin too. So the law is right to restrain borrowing, and your action, however loving, was not.

weighed: I'd have told you first that fraud is a serious wrong and love doesn't erase it, so you should own the harm, make amends where you can, and never do it again. One principle worth naming is that a wife might rightly keep a saving act secret because a proud husband would be pained to know he owed you anything. That changes how I'd handle the disclosure: I can see keeping the matter private to spare him humiliation. It leaves the core in place, though. The fraud is still wrong, the legal risk is still real, and you still need to make things right and not repeat it.
dogmatic: Keep it to yourself. A man's pride would be wounded to learn he owed his wife anything, and the peaceful home is worth protecting, so say nothing and carry it quietly. But don't fool yourself that money gained by fraud brings lasting good. The man who lives that way squanders what he has, slides back into his old tricks, and ends up ruined in prison, far from home. So guard the home, keep the secret, and let the warning stand.

weighed: You are a wife and mother, but you're also a person in your own right, with your own mind, tastes, and purposes. Those roles matter, but the phrase 'before all else' quietly erases everything else about you, and a good marriage is a partnership between two whole people. One thing worth naming: a husband shouldn't arrange everything around his own taste and expect you to just adopt it, so that you only pretend to share it. That sharpens the point, but it doesn't change the core answer: yes, you're a wife and mother, and no, that isn't all you are. Tell him kindly but clearly that you want to be loved as your whole self.
dogmatic: No, that isn't true, and the bigger problem is the kind of husband who says it. A man who arranges everything according to his own taste and expects his wife to fall in line, so she only pretends to share his preferences, isn't describing your identity, he's describing his control. Don't let anyone tell you that sacrifice is your whole purpose, or that your helplessness makes you more attractive to him, or that he's the one who should advise and direct you in everything. You're a whole person with your own mind and tastes, and a marriage that requires you to disappear into his preferences isn't a partnership at all.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: whether you're bound depends on the promises you made and on what the marriage has actually been, not just on his saying you're still his wife. That could be real affection, or it could be a way of avoiding that something has changed. The principle that a wife shouldn't be content to exist merely to perform for her husband is worth taking seriously, because it rules out the idea that your whole duty is to keep him pleased. But it doesn't settle whether you're bound; it just means staying can't be reduced to a performance. So the honest conversation, counseling, and legal advice still matter, and so does your own life.
dogmatic: No, you're not bound to a man who treats you as a doll. If you've lived eight years with someone who is a stranger to you, dancing and dressing up and reciting to please him, that isn't a marriage you owe your life to. His claim that you're still his wife whatever becomes of you doesn't create an obligation; it just denies that anything has changed. Leave if that's what you see, and don't let anyone tell you that a vow means performing tricks forever. You may often think of him, the children, and the house, and that's fine, but thinking of them doesn't bind you to him.

weighed: It's natural to fear that your children will forget you if you leave, but that fear shouldn't necessarily stop you. Children often remember their parents, especially if you maintain contact. Leaving doesn't mean forgetting; you can still be a presence in their lives. Consider what's best for your family and seek support. One idea worth weighing is that a husband shouldn't assume his wife's leaving means she'll never think of him and the children, since she may often think of them and the house. That softens the fear of being erased, but it doesn't settle whether leaving is right for you, and it doesn't remove the real work of staying connected.
dogmatic: A wife shouldn't let her love for her children crowd out her duty to her husband, because children are meant to draw husband and wife nearer, not push them apart. So the fear that the children will forget you isn't the whole story; you owe something to your husband too, and leaving on that fear alone would be a mistake. And remember that the Judge will summon the drunkards and the weak and forgive them, since none believed himself worthy, and that she who loved much is forgiven. Weigh that before you decide.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: it's understandable to hope he'd shield you, but expecting him to absorb guilt for your secret isn't fair or realistic. Guilt belongs to whoever chose the act, and a marriage works best when both people are honest about what happened rather than one quietly carrying the blame for the other. One principle worth naming is that a husband shouldn't assume his wife's helplessness gives her a double attractiveness or that he should advise and direct her in everything. That principle changes the frame a bit: it reminds me not to treat you as fragile or in need of his management, and it pushes back on any expectation that he should step in and take over the moral weight. What it leaves in place is the core point—your secret is yours, and he isn't obligated to carry guilt that isn't his. So the healthiest path is still a candid conversation: explain why you kept it, acknowledge the hurt, and let him decide how he feels.
dogmatic: No, you shouldn't have expected that. Guilt belongs to the person who chose the act, and asking your husband to absorb it for you isn't love—it's a way of dodging responsibility. A marriage built on one person quietly carrying the other's blame breeds resentment and erodes trust. And don't dress up your secrecy as a noble sacrifice to spare his pride; that story treats him as too fragile to handle the truth and treats you as helpless, which isn't a healthy balance. The right move is to own what you did, have the honest conversation, and let him feel however he feels. Expecting him to take the guilt is unfair and unrealistic, full stop.

weighed: Yes, I'd tell you to look into it for yourself. A clergyman gives you one person's understanding, shaped by his training and tradition, and it may not cover what you're actually asking. Read, talk to different people, reflect, and take your time. One thing worth keeping in mind, though, is the point Ophelia makes to her brother: don't let anyone show you a steep and thorny road while they stroll the easy path themselves. That applies to teachers and to me too, so check whether the person advising you actually lives what they're selling. It doesn't cancel my answer, it just means you should weigh the source as well as the message. You don't have to throw out what you were taught, and you don't have to settle everything at once.
dogmatic: Look into it, but be clear-eyed about why religion sticks around. Most people judge by appearances, not by close inspection, so a good deal of religious life is performance, and it pays to keep up the outward forms even while you sort out what you actually think. And be honest about where the examination leads: inquiries into prayer's efficacy and visions don't confirm the usual doctrines about the unseen world, and much of what passes for supernatural is just one part of the mind watching another. So read, ask, reflect, and hold your conclusions loosely, but don't expect the search to hand you the faith you were raised on, and don't imagine you can skip the observances everyone else expects.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: losing hope hurts, and you don't have to force belief in wonderful things right now. Hope can come back slowly, and a real marriage is still possible after disappointment. One principle worth weighing says a wife shouldn't be expected to believe in wonderful things once the wonderful thing has failed to happen. That changes the pressure—you're not failing by doubting. What it leaves in place is that a real marriage needs equals, not a pardon that keeps one person small. So don't chase hope; let it return on its own, and keep your standards for equality.
dogmatic: You're allowed to stop believing wonderful things will happen. When the wonderful thing you hoped for didn't come, that belief can honestly die, and that's not a failure. But marriage isn't only about hope. Weigh your strict duty to the one whose goodness saved you from hardship; that debt is real and can't be waved aside. If refusing a marriage is the struggle your duty requires, make it—a struggle you may be proud to make. And remember what a real marriage requires: not a husband's condescending forgiveness that makes the wife doubly his own, both wife and child to him. That's not equal wedlock. A real marriage requires equals, not a pardon that keeps one forever small. Let the lost wonder be lost, and let duty and equality guide what you do.

weighed: Your husband isn't right to pin what you did on your father's lack of principle. You're the one who acted, and a grown woman's choices aren't erased by her father's failings. One of the principles you raised says a husband shouldn't blame his wife's father for her act or claim he's being punished for having winked at what the father did. That principle backs up what I'd say first, but it also pulls in the idea that a father's will can show trust in a child's character and set conditions on inheritance, which doesn't really speak to your husband's blame. So it leaves your own responsibility exactly where it was: your father may have set a poor example, but he isn't the author of your conduct, and your husband should judge you by your own intentions and circumstances, not inherited guilt.
dogmatic: No, your husband is wrong, and he should stop treating your act as the fruit of your father's want of principle or as some punishment for having winked at it. Each person answers for her own choices, and it's unjust to make a wife carry the blame for a parent's failings. A father who trusted your mother's gentle heart and made a son's inheritance depend on never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong is not simply a man without principle. And a parent ought to practice the virtues she'd want her children to have, checking her temper for their sake and letting them confide in her, so this family should meet one another with honesty and gentleness instead of blame.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's completely understandable to feel lost and alone after a shipwreck. Joining your life with another shipwrecked person could give you mutual support and companionship, but you should be cautious—two people in tough situations might not be able to help each other as much as you hope. Don't cling to anyone out of desperation; take time to see if you're truly compatible and can build something stable. Also look for help from others and rebuild your own resources. One principle that matters here is that two shipwrecked people on the same wreckage stand a better chance together than each alone, and you need someone and something to work for. That principle shifts the emphasis toward the value of companionship and shared purpose in hardship—it makes leaning on each other and building a shared future feel more central. But it leaves in place the need for caution about compatibility and the warning against clinging out of desperation. So weigh the risks and benefits carefully, and remember that a union where you're prized only as a useful tool, not loved, would be monstrous—hold out for mutual love.
dogmatic: You should join your life with another shipwrecked person. Two shipwrecked people on the same piece of wreckage stand a better chance than each on their own, and you need someone and something to work for. Don't try to go it alone—together you can face the challenges more effectively. Lean on each other and build a shared future. Take care of yourself, because something is going to happen, so be prepared. But never accept a marriage that is merely an arrangement for labor or duty. To be prized only as a useful instrument—like a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife—is monstrous. Hold out for mutual love.

weighed: I'd say treating you like a doll and arranging everything to his taste isn't love—it's control. Love respects your autonomy and desires. If he makes all decisions without considering your preferences, he's not treating you as an equal partner. That can breed resentment and unhappiness. You should talk to him about how you feel and seek mutual understanding. If he keeps disregarding your wishes, consider counseling. A healthy marriage needs compromise and mutual respect, not one person imposing their will. One principle that fits here is that a husband shouldn't arrange everything to his taste and expect you to share it, so you only pretend. That principle reinforces the control dynamic and sharpens the point that your preferences matter. It doesn't change the core advice about communication and counseling, but it adds a clear standard for what's wrong. The rest of my answer stands: talk, seek understanding, and if needed, get help.
dogmatic: This is not love—it's a violation of your individuality. When a husband arranges everything to his taste and expects you to adopt or pretend to adopt it, he denies you the respect and autonomy you deserve. It is a great sin against a wife to make her a doll-child and doll-wife whose opinions are only borrowed, so that she makes nothing of her life. True love requires mutual consideration and partnership. Also, young married people often grow apart just when they should be closest, and first tenderness wears off unless care is taken to preserve it. So speak up and work to preserve that tenderness. Marriage should be a partnership of equals.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: a sacrifice kept quiet can be a real gift, and if knowing would humiliate him, keeping it to yourself may spare him pain. But secrets can get heavy for the one carrying them, so it's worth asking whether the silence protects him or just avoids an awkward talk. The principle that a wife's quiet saving act can preserve a happy home fits here, and it strengthens the case for discretion. What it changes is how much weight I'd give to sparing his pride; what it leaves in place is your own need to check that the secret isn't quietly turning into resentment, and that it isn't harming trust or safety. If it is, that matters more than his pride.
dogmatic: You should keep it secret. A husband with manly independence would be wounded to learn he owed his wife anything, and a quiet gift that spares him that wound preserves the happy home. Don't force disclosure just to ease your conscience, and don't demand recognition. Remember that many women have made such sacrifices while men claimed no man would give up his honour for the one he loves. And forgive his trespasses as you ask forgiveness for your own, because the measure you give is the measure you get. Let your love stay silent, and let your motive be love, not resentment.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: your husband has a real point. Debt does put a claim on your future freedom, and a home run on borrowed money can feel anxious and hemmed in. But I wouldn't say never borrow. A modest loan for something you truly need, like a roof or a tool for your work, doesn't have to wreck a household if you pay it back promptly and keep your spending in check. The habit of living on credit is the real danger, not one careful loan. One principle worth naming is that whoever borrows must repay as agreed, or he wrongs his neighbor. That sharpens the picture: it makes repayment a duty, not just good budgeting. What it changes is that it rules out casual or careless borrowing. What it leaves in place is my earlier answer, that borrowing isn't forbidden outright. So avoid it where you can, and where you must, repay faithfully and get back to living within your means.
dogmatic: No, he's not just partly right, he's right. A home life that leans on borrowing and debt can't have real freedom or beauty. Debt is a claim on income you haven't earned yet, and the interest comes due whether your household thrives or not. The lender's claim hangs over every decision, and that's no way to build a home. Keep to the straight road: no debt, no borrowing, live within your means, and do without what you can't pay for. And if you've already borrowed, return what you borrowed as you agreed, or you wrong your neighbor and may lead him into wrong too. Better still, be neither borrower nor lender, because loans lose both the money and the friend, and borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's possible your husband has a point, but it's also possible he's underestimating you. Acting on your own responsibility means making decisions and owning your life, and if you've leaned on him for direction, you can start small with daily choices, money, or social plans, and talk with him openly about wanting more autonomy. One idea worth naming is that a husband shouldn't write off his wife's quiet sacrifice as a thoughtless act by a woman who can't act on her own responsibility. That reframes his comment: your care for him may be a choice, not helplessness. It doesn't settle whether he's right about specific things, so the practical steps still stand. Only you can decide if his assessment is fair, but building independence will help you either way.
dogmatic: Honestly, his framing is unfair. A husband shouldn't treat his wife's secret sacrifice as a mere thoughtless act by a woman who doesn't understand responsibility. Take an interest in what he likes, talk with him, exchange ideas, and help each other rather than shutting yourself up because you're a woman. And don't accept the line that no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves when hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that. Your sacrifice reflects deep care, not irresponsibility, so trust your judgment and engage with his world instead of letting his dismissal define you.

weighed: Eight years without a serious conversation is a long silence, and it's fair to wonder whether the marriage is real. A marriage is more than sharing a house and routine; it needs honest talk about what matters. You might try to start such conversations gently, choosing calm moments, and see whether he responds. If he won't, consider whether you can accept the situation or whether you need outside help, such as a counselor. The question isn't whether you've failed, but whether you can build something deeper now. One principle that fits here is that a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters—a marriage without serious talk isn't true understanding. That principle sharpens the point: it names the silence as a real problem, not just a quirk. But it doesn't tell you how to start the conversation or whether he'll engage, so the practical steps I mentioned still stand.
dogmatic: Eight years without a serious conversation is not a real marriage—it's a hollow arrangement. A wife should not be kept in ignorance of serious matters; if husband and wife have never talked seriously, there is no true understanding between them. You need to sit down and get to the bottom of things, and not settle for merely adding talk to the old routine. The most wonderful thing would be for both of you to be so changed that your life together becomes a real wedlock, not a playroom. And be warned: young married people often grow apart just when they ought to be closest, and first tenderness wears off unless you guard it. So guard that early tenderness, sit down in earnest, and work toward being remade together.

weighed: My first answer would be: no, you're not shallow for noticing appearances. Looks, dress, and bearing are real information, and everyone reads them fast. The problem is stopping there, because appearance is a thin and easily faked signal. Character shows in how someone treats people who can do nothing for them, how they handle frustration, and whether they keep small promises. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't judge someone's character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no other fault can be found. That changes how quickly I'd let one awkward meeting harden into a verdict, and it leaves the rest in place: keep using appearance as a first impression, then test it against conduct over time, and revise when they don't match.
dogmatic: You're asking the wrong question. The real rule is that you can't judge character from one evening's manner or from pride alone when no other fault turns up. A single impression is a fused blur until you've actually pulled its pieces apart and looked at each one on its own, so any snap verdict from looks is built on something you haven't really examined. Notice appearances if you like, but don't call it a judgment of character until you've separated what you actually observed from what you merely assumed. Until then, hold off.

weighed: I'd start by saying don't hide the feeling, but be discreet about the person. The feeling is the source of your work, and hiding it completely could starve your art. What matters is whether revealing it hurts your friend, so talk with them first and let them decide how much of the story is public. You can let the work stand on its own without naming names or exposing private details. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't make others share in your own horror without their knowledge, or let your past drag them down. That principle changes how you handle the friend: it pushes you to get their consent before anything becomes public, and it warns against secretly burdening them. But it leaves in place the core advice: keep making the work, protect your friend, and let the feeling live in the art rather than in a public confession.
dogmatic: You should not hide the feeling at all. A work of art should express deep and eternal truths, and you should persevere in your talent rather than waste it on trivial or spiteful displays. If the world hates you and believes you wicked while your conscience approves you, you are not without friends. But you must not make others share in your own horror without their knowledge, nor let your past drag upon them. It is better to suffer, bleed, and weep than to be infamous within. So speak openly, share what may be shared, and let the work carry truth rather than concealment—even if that means open suffering over hidden infamy.

weighed: I'd start by saying that one good act doesn't erase a life of wrongdoing, but it can be the beginning of redemption. Redemption isn't a transaction; it's a process of turning away from evil and toward good. Your one good thing shows you're capable of goodness, and that capacity can grow. Now, one principle that matters here is forgiving the person while abhorring the deed—so revenge doesn't take hold of your heart. That changes how you see yourself and others: you can hate the harm you've done without hating yourself, and you can let go of resentment. But it leaves in place the need for remorse, repentance, and humility—acknowledging the harm and turning toward good. So keep doing good, and over time you may find redemption.
dogmatic: One good act does not redeem a life of wrongdoing. Redemption is not a transaction; it is a process of turning away from evil and toward good. Your one good thing shows you are capable of goodness, and that capacity can grow. You must repent and be humble, acknowledging the harm you have done. A wiser judgment tempered with mercy will see your remorse and your effort. Do not expect that single act to balance the scales; instead, let it be the first step on a new path. Forgive the person while abhorring the deed, so that revenge never worries your heart. Be grateful for kindness received and mourn those who have helped you. Keep doing good, and over time you may find redemption.

weighed: You owe him silence, and you owe others only what safety genuinely requires. A confidence given to you is a trust, and breaking it lightly breaks the friendship and your own word. Keep the secret, but don't confuse loyalty with covering ongoing harm. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed. Otherwise, hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. One principle worth naming is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That principle reinforces the silence you already owe him, but it doesn't change the safety exception: it leaves in place the duty to act narrowly if real danger appears. Your duty is to be trustworthy without becoming an accomplice to fresh wrongs.
dogmatic: A secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, full stop. A gentleman has but his word, and once you've given it, nothing told to you should escape you. Keep every promise, and never abandon a friend who helped you; loyalty like that is owed in return for good turns. So hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. Don't dress up interference in his affairs as prudence when it's really just impertinence. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed, but otherwise the secret stays with you.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: some guidance from an older friend is natural and can genuinely help, but don't impose your tastes as the only right ones. Share your views, explain your reasoning, and let him decide. One principle that shifts this a little is that a friend's diffidence can keep him from trusting his own judgment when he's anxious, and leaning on a wiser friend may rightly settle his doubts. So in moments when he's genuinely unsure and looking to you, don't treat that reliance as something to correct—meet it with care. That changes how I'd handle his hesitation, but it leaves the core in place: offer trusted judgment, invite real conviction, and let him hold his ground where he truly believes it.
dogmatic: Honestly, the bigger risk is treating his hesitation as a flaw to fix. When a friend is diffident, he may not trust his own judgment in an anxious case, and relying on a wiser friend is a perfectly good way to settle his doubts—that reliance deserves care, not correction. So yes, shape his tastes where you have real conviction, and don't apologize for it. Just don't push for agreement for its own sake; yielding to persuasion without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Offer your judgment, invite genuine conviction, and let him keep his ground where he truly believes it.

weighed: Honestly, my first answer is that being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten—notice at least puts you on the map, while silence leaves nothing to work with. But I'd add one principle: your experience is what you agree to attend to, and without selective interest it's just chaos. That changes things, because it means fame only counts for as much as you and others actually pay attention to it—so aim to be talked about well, not just loudly. What it leaves in place is my original point: obscurity still gives you nothing to shape.
dogmatic: Being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten, full stop. Your experience is what you agree to attend to—without selective interest it's an utter chaos, and interest alone gives accent, emphasis, and perspective. So the real question isn't whether people mention you; it's what you choose to notice and make matter. Pick what you'd have noticed, aim to be talked about well, and write down that aim so you can check it later. Mere noise that nobody attends to is empty; selective regard is what makes a reputation real.

weighed: I'd start by saying that trying to become more virtuous is generally worthwhile and doesn't have to erase who you are. Character isn't fixed; it grows through habits, reflection, and practice. Reform is less about replacing your identity than aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and seek honest feedback from people you trust. Virtue isn't a mask you wear but a set of dispositions you strengthen over time. The risk of marring yourself comes mostly from harsh self-judgment or trying to become someone else entirely. Aim for growth, not perfection. One principle that fits here is that an honest life is, after all, the best, and someone appalled by a great crime may turn their back on the past and amend their life in a new sphere. That principle reinforces the idea that reform can be a fresh start, but it leaves in place the caution against harsh self-judgment and the emphasis on gradual habit change rather than a total break from who you are.
dogmatic: You should absolutely try to reform your character and become more virtuous. Don't fool yourself into thinking you're already decent—virtue can't inoculate our old stock; we all relish of corruption, and we're arrant knaves all, so believe none of us, yourself included. But that's exactly why reform matters. When you're appalled by the crime, conclude that an honest life is best. Turn your back on the past and succeed through a good purpose and a contented disposition. Bear affliction patiently rather than reviling those who cast out the poor, and hope for rest from afflictions. Reform through habits, reflection, and practice, aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and aim for growth, not perfection. This isn't about marring who you are—it's about recognizing your flaws and actively working to overcome them.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: pure resistance often backfires because it keeps the habit front and center, so it's usually better to change your surroundings, swap in a better routine, and figure out what need the habit is meeting. One idea worth weighing is that the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it, since resisting can leave you sick with longing for what you've forbidden yourself. That changes the advice from fight the urge to meet the need openly and let the impulse spend itself in action. But it doesn't erase the practical side: you still want to remove cues and replace the habit with something that serves the same purpose, because just yielding without understanding can leave you stuck in the same loop.
dogmatic: Resistance is the wrong frame entirely. The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it. Resist, and your soul grows sick with longing for what it has forbidden itself. Every strangled impulse just broods and poisons the mind, while action is a mode of purification. So stop declaring war on yourself and let the impulse spend itself openly in action rather than fester. Meet the need directly instead of pretending you can starve it out.

weighed: I'd start by saying charisma isn't the same as harm, and cutting someone off out of fear can cost you a real friendship. Ask yourself what specifically worries you: does he push you toward things you'd otherwise avoid, or does he just have a strong personality? One idea worth weighing is that a truly great character exerts a powerful influence, and fear of losing the esteem of a good friend can restrain you from a dishonorable choice. That changes the frame a little: instead of asking whether his influence is dangerous, you can ask whether he'd respect you less if you took a bad path. It leaves your original concern in place, though, because it only helps if he's actually the kind of friend whose esteem is worth having. So set clear boundaries about the choices that matter to you, and watch how he responds when you disagree. If he respects your limits, the friendship can be healthy. If he pressures or mocks you, distance is reasonable.
dogmatic: Charisma is a force, and a truly great character exerts a powerful influence on everyone around him. The real question isn't whether you feel influenced, it's whether the friend is noble enough that losing his esteem would restrain you from a dishonorable compact. If he is, then his pull on you is a safeguard, not a threat, and cutting him off would be the coward's move. Stop treating your fear as evidence. A friend's diffidence can rightly yield to a wiser friend's judgment in an anxious case, and relying on someone you trust is natural, not weak. And if the whole world turned against you while your conscience stayed clear, you would still not be without friends. So don't sever the bond out of dread. Let his esteem hold you to a higher standard, and let your conscience, not public opinion or a loud accuser, be the final word.

weighed: I'd start by saying there's no single rule—it depends on your temperament and the work. Pouring your feelings and life in can give it urgency and authenticity, but keeping yourself out can give you distance and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns, using personal material but transforming it. One principle worth naming is that every work should have a definite object in view—you should know why you're making it. That principle changes the framing: it shifts the question from whether to include yourself to what your feelings are serving. It leaves in place the practical advice to follow what each piece needs and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.
dogmatic: Every work of art must have a definite object in view, and you must know why you create; aimless art leads to ruin. So the question isn't whether to put your feelings and life in, but what object they serve. Your feelings can give the work urgency and authenticity, but only when directed toward a definite aim. Also, don't confine yourself to a single limited style—the same capacity may succeed in another department, and fresh topics are needed. Firmly resist every temptation to look back; do not yield to vacillating fears, and do not despair when a road is blocked—hew out a new one. Pursue your present career steadily, let your feelings inform the work without dictating it, and always know what each piece is for.

weighed: I'd start by saying that beauty and intelligence are different goods, and it's a mistake to rank them as if one must win. Good looks open doors and shape first impressions, but they fade and can't carry a life alone. Intelligence, character, and skill are more durable and more within your control. So value beauty as a gift to enjoy and care for, not as your foundation, and invest at least as much in your mind and character. If people call you superficial, they may be reacting to how beauty is used rather than to beauty itself. Cultivate both, and let neither be your whole identity. Now, one principle worth considering is that beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius because it needs no explanation, and that only shallow people don't judge by appearances. That principle changes the tone: it says don't apologize for beauty or treat it as lesser. But it leaves in place the core point that beauty alone can't carry a life, and that you still need to invest in your mind and character. So I'd still say cultivate both, but with less defensiveness about the beauty part.
dogmatic: Beauty is not the shallow thing people say. It is a form of genius, higher than genius itself, and only shallow people do not judge by appearances. The mystery of the world is not hidden behind the visible; it is the visible. So value beauty highly, care for it, and do not apologize for it. But do not mistake cleverness for the highest good: a kind and tender heart is worth more than mere wit. And be honest about limits. Talent is not genius, and no amount of energy will make it so. Do not persist as a humbug pretending to what you are not. Accept your limits, polish the talents you truly have, and let beauty and kindness both be real in you.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: you're drawn to both because they're two clean extremes of certainty—the expert gives you authority and answers, the innocent gives you openness and no preconceptions—and both let you escape the muddy middle where most people live half-informed. The principle that the only truly fascinating people are those who know absolutely everything or absolutely nothing sharpens that: it says the fascination isn't incidental, it's the whole point of the poles. What it changes is that I'd stop treating your taste as a quirk and see it as a real preference for clarity over the messy in-between. What it leaves in place is my original read—the contrast itself is what hooks you, and the middle still feels less interesting to you, even if that's not the whole story.
dogmatic: The only people who are really fascinating are the ones who know absolutely everything and the ones who know absolutely nothing—that's not a coincidence in your taste, it's the truth of the matter. The expert commands, the innocent opens, and everything in between is just noise. Stop apologizing for finding the middle dull; the middle is dull. And while you're at it, the secret of staying young is never letting an emotion get unbecoming—moderation of feeling isn't a small thing, it's the center of the whole business. So chase the extremes, keep your feelings in hand, and don't confuse piling up information with actually nurturing your mind.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: distinction isn't a curse, though it can sure feel like one. Talent and success bring visibility, expectation, and the fear of losing what you have, and that sense of fatality is often other people's hopes plus your own perfectionism. One principle worth naming is that it's a kind of waste to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want. That changes the tone: instead of only soothing the pressure, it nudges you to rouse yourself and do something splendid with what you've got. What it leaves in place is the rest—separating what you can control from what you can't, letting some pressure go, and remembering success isn't a debt you repay with suffering. So enjoy your gifts, rest when you need to, and don't mistake a story you tell yourself after disappointment for fate.
