dogmatic: Distinction is not a curse, but you're handling it badly if you let it make you passive. It is wicked to throw away so many good gifts merely because you cannot have the one thing you want. Rouse yourself and do something splendid with what you have. Don't sell yourself by accepting protection or advancement before you've earned it—decline for now, prove yourself through a brilliant action, and give yourself only when you have the right. Everything is best in its time. Remember that riches are the source of both strength and weakness, and that liberty and honor are worth more than jewels or riches; wealth is no compensation for their loss. Stop treating disappointment as fate and start acting.

weighed: My first answer would be: it's hard to know your own motives, but you need to be honest with yourself about whether you acted for their good or for your own need to be seen as noble. Did you communicate honestly and give them a say? If you made the decision unilaterally, it may have been more about your fears than their protection. One principle that applies here is that you shouldn't be ashamed of worthy relations or apologize for honest connections. That principle changes the tone—it says don't beat yourself up or treat the relationship as something to blush for. But it leaves in place the need to examine whether your action was genuine protection or a way to avoid discomfort or play the martyr. So the core question remains: were you truly selfless, or merely acting a part?
dogmatic: You need to stop apologizing for a worthy relationship just because someone proud might disapprove. Honest connections deserve no shame. But don't fool yourself: if you gave up the relationship to protect someone, ask whether you deceived them the way Rochester feigned courtship of Miss Ingram—treating their feelings as a means to your own end. That kind of deception is a disgrace, not clever. And consider the dispute over punishment: the Queen says one is better for punishment, but Alice insists it makes a difference that she had done the things punished. If you punished them for a fault they didn't commit, that's the real question. So examine your heart: were you protecting them, or punishing them for your own discomfort?

weighed: My first answer is that it matters. Arguing for something you don't believe is a kind of dishonesty, and it wears down trust and your own integrity. One candidate principle here is that good thinking needs a variety of rival suggestions, since competing ideas keep you from grabbing the first one that comes along. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of treating sincerity and idea quality as a simple either/or, I'd say you should genuinely entertain several positions, including ones you don't hold, and test them against each other. What it leaves in place is my original point: when you actually argue for a position in public, it still matters whether you believe it, because pretending is a different act from exploring. So the principle widens the space for honest disagreement without excusing insincere advocacy.
dogmatic: It matters, and the reason is that good thinking depends on cultivating a variety of alternative suggestions. Rival conjectures are what stop you from prematurely accepting the first idea that comes to mind. If you only argue positions you already believe, you cut off that variety and settle too soon. So the real question isn't just whether the idea is good in the abstract; it's whether you're keeping multiple candidates alive and testing them. Sincerity matters because it keeps you honest about which ideas you're actually weighing, but the deeper point is that you need the competition of rival views to think well at all.

weighed: I'd start by saying unselfishness is often praised, but it turns unhealthy when it means ignoring your own needs. Real virtue balances care for others with self-respect, and constant self-sacrifice can lead to burnout and resentment. So ask yourself whether you're giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval, set boundaries, and remember your well-being matters too. One idea worth weighing is that the self you're protecting is partly made of what you call yours, like your home, your reputation, and your work, and that self-feeling shifts with the ratio of success to pretensions. That changes the picture by suggesting that lowering your pretensions can relieve pressure as much as getting more does, so some of what feels like sacrifice might just be letting go of inflated expectations. What it leaves in place is the core point: chosen generosity is fine, but erasing yourself isn't a virtue.
dogmatic: Unselfishness gets praised, but the real question is what you think the self even is. The empirical self is the sum of everything you can call yours, your body, your clothes, your family, your home, your property, your reputation, your works, and your self-feeling rises and falls with the ratio of success to pretensions. So giving up pretensions relieves you as much as gratifying them ever could. Stop treating self-sacrifice as a threat to some fixed inner core, because there isn't one. And don't dismiss passion as merely unseemly or aimed only at pleasure, and don't treat reason as some independent judge standing above it. Passion is the motive force, and reason is a relationship among your passions and desires, each carrying its own measure of reason. Virtue sits next to pride, so compare yourself to something higher than other people and stay humble, because comparing yourself to men in general breeds pride and leads back to hatred.

weighed: My first answer would be: curiosity isn't dangerous in itself, but chasing every new sensation without thinking is. So don't pursue everything blindly—weigh the risks and skip what's clearly harmful. One principle I'd bring in is that curiosity is the vital spark that supplies the raw material for ideas, so the real job is keeping wonder alive rather than smothering it. That changes the emphasis: instead of just warning you off, it says protect your openness to new experience. What it leaves in place is the caution—you still evaluate risks and don't treat every impulse as a green light.
dogmatic: Curiosity is the engine of learning and the source of everything worth thinking about, so you should guard it fiercely. Don't let routine or indifference dull your wonder. And when instinct stirs, seize the moment before the wave of interest ebbs—build habits on that readiness. Fortune rules only half of what happens; the rest is yours, and boldness beats caution. So go after new sensations and experiences with energy, and don't let fear of risk talk you out of the spark that makes a life interesting.

weighed: My first answer would be that intense admiration isn't automatically wrong, but it turns dangerous when it replaces your own judgment, your self-respect, or the place that belongs to what's truly divine. One principle worth naming is that idolatry means giving divine honor to a creature by your own invention, and that worship a sovereign commands under threat of death counts as the sovereign's act, not the subject's. That distinction changes how I'd frame the outer side of things: the gestures and commands aren't the whole story. What it leaves in place is the inner question, which is still yours to answer. So ask whether this admiration makes you freer and more yourself or more dependent and fearful. Admire the good you see, learn from it, but remember the person is human and fallible. If it feels compulsive or consuming, step back and give attention to other relationships and commitments.
dogmatic: Yes, it's wrong, and you should stop dressing it up as admiration. Worship belongs to God alone, and giving a creature what only God deserves is idolatry no matter how noble the feeling seems. Don't hide behind the idea that gestures are just conventional or that someone else's command makes it their act and not yours. The inner intention is what counts, and yours is the one that needs examining. Excessive worship of another person is foolish and brings its own punishment, just as worshipping yourself does. Admire the good you see, but remember the person is human and fallible, and keep your conscience and your worth out of their hands.

weighed: I'd start with what I actually think: plan for the future, but don't let planning crowd out living fully now. Youth gives you energy and room to try things, so use it, while still taking a few steps to secure what comes later. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't stare into the future or dwell on old age and death, but accept what comes and stay busy and engaged. That changes the tone of my answer: it pushes back on fear-driven planning and says keep your heart and mind occupied with what's in front of you. What it leaves in place is the basic balance—enjoy now, prepare quietly—because it doesn't forbid sensible preparation, it just refuses to let dread of aging run your life.
dogmatic: Don't look into the future at all. Don't admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes, keep yourself busy and well-groomed, and that is what keeps you young. Planning for a future you're told to fear is exactly the trap—it ages you before your time. Live fully now, believe in what you're doing, and let tomorrow take care of itself. Growing up is mostly about people stopping believing, and that's when their power to fly leaves them. You can't help growing, but you don't have to settle into ordinary life and call it wisdom.

weighed: I'd start by saying that fear of losing your beauty as you age is really common, and it's worth facing honestly. Beauty isn't the whole of who you are—character, kindness, and wisdom tend to deepen with time. Try shifting your focus toward health, relationships, and interests that don't fade. Accept that your body will change, and treat that acceptance as part of maturity. If the fear gets intense, talk with someone you trust or a counselor. Many people find new forms of beauty and purpose later in life, and your worth was never only in your looks. One idea worth weighing is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid—so the fact that you're looking at this fear at all already shows courage. That principle changes the tone: instead of just managing the fear, you can see it as proof of your own bravery. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—staying engaged with work, friends, and interests, and getting support if you need it. It doesn't ask you to ignore the future or pretend aging isn't real; it just reframes the fear as something you can meet with confidence built through action.
dogmatic: Don't spend your days rehearsing old age and loss. Never look into the future and never admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes as it comes, and keep your heart and mind busy with what's right in front of you now. Don't mistake your fear for cowardice: courage is facing danger while afraid, so the very fact that you face this fear shows you already have courage. What you need is confidence in yourself, grown through action rather than forecasts. Fill your hours with work, friendship, and interests that engage you today. And when you see your adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes—and feel the sadness of that contrast—let it soften you rather than frighten you, reminding you that beauty and worth were never only in your looks.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: neither society's expectations nor what you owe yourself should rule absolutely. One candidate principle is that self-sacrifice for a child in your care is a duty, even at real cost to your own life and joy. If that applies to you, it changes the balance: the child's welfare comes first, and some of what you owe yourself has to wait. But it leaves the rest in place—you still weigh which expectations protect real goods and which are mere convention, and you still take care of yourself, because a guardian who collapses serves no one. So keep your reflective judgment; just let that duty set the priority when a child depends on you.
dogmatic: The answer is that a child in your care comes first, full stop. Protecting and loving her is the duty that justifies self-sacrifice, and her happiness should be the object of your life even at the cost of your own. Don't sit in passive despair or wait for rescue—pray for aid if you like, but rise, seek work, bear hunger and cold, and fulfill the responsibilities life still lays on you. Society's expectations and what you think you owe yourself are secondary; the child's welfare governs.

weighed: Yes, a new life is possible. People aren't stuck in one shape forever; you can change your habits, repair what you can, and choose differently starting today. It won't be easy, and the past doesn't vanish, but it doesn't have to decide your future. Start small: keep one promise, tell the truth, do one useful thing each day, and be patient with setbacks. One idea worth weighing is that a person who has been overworking and has no one left to live for can feel life unspeakably empty and go looking for steady work just to keep the mind busy. That idea adds a useful caution: steady work can steady you, but it can also be a way of hiding from the emptiness instead of facing it. So take up regular work if it helps, but don't let it become the whole answer. The wish itself shows something in you is already turning toward good.
dogmatic: Yes, a new life is possible, and the real point is that making a life means making trouble. You should never let a chance slip by, and you should chase inspired follies instead of shrinking back; the only escape from trouble is killing things off, and that's the coward's way. Also remember that the I stays unaltered while the me changes, and the perplexity about which one is your real self is where an insane life begins. When you've overworked and have no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, so you seek regular work to busy your mind and fill your thoughts. That's the path: take up steady work, keep one promise, tell the truth, and be patient with setbacks. The wish itself shows something in you turning toward good.

weighed: Yes, that fear is real, but it depends on the marriage you build. Marriage doesn't automatically erase who you are; it can sharpen your identity if both partners respect each other's independence, interests, and friendships. The real danger comes when one person is expected to sacrifice their own needs, opinions, or ambitions for the relationship. Watch for pressure to become someone you're not—that's the risk worth taking seriously. Talk openly with your partner about your fears, keep your own pursuits, and choose someone who wants you as you are, not as a project. One idea that adds a twist here is that constant self-sacrifice can make you colorless and lose your distinctiveness—so the risk isn't just losing yourself, it's that being too unselfish can flatten you. That principle sharpens the warning about reforming yourself to please someone else, but it doesn't change the core advice: stay yourself, keep your independence, and watch for pressure to become someone you're not.
dogmatic: The real drawback to marriage is that it makes you unselfish, and unselfish people are colorless—they lose their individuality. No life is spoiled except one whose growth is arrested, and to reform a nature is simply to mar it. So the danger isn't that marriage will make you less yourself in some vague way; it's that you'll be pressed to sacrifice your distinctiveness and become bland. Choose a partner who wants you exactly as you are, and don't let anyone reform you. As for delaying marriage to avoid burden, that would only be practiced by the prudent and self-denying, and that would deteriorate the race—better that the best-fitted marry early. Weigh the actual advantages, keep your own pursuits, and watch for any pressure to sacrifice yourself.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're bound by common humanity, not by his creed. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care no matter what faith you were taught to scorn, and abandoning him would betray your own courage and your pledged word. One principle here is that a man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch. That principle reinforces the duty to tend him and adds weight to the promise you've made, but it doesn't change the core answer: you still shelter and tend him. It leaves in place the same call to kindness over inherited prejudice.
dogmatic: You must not abandon a wounded companion. A man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch, giving life where he has promised it. The Lord finds the scoffer least wearisome of all the spirits who deny, and gives him to man because man is too prone to shirk activity. So do not turn away from him because of his faith; instead, tend him and keep your word. And whosoever puts their trust in God shall be supported in their trials and afflictions and lifted up at the last day.

weighed: I'd still start where I did: keep resisting, but stop white-knuckling it. The fight itself often feeds the urge, so the real move is to shrink its grip—name what the temptation is actually promising you, meet that need somewhere healthier, and put some distance between yourself and the triggers. One idea worth borrowing is that pleasure chased against your conscience tends to sting and taste bitter even when it looks appealing. That's a useful test to run before you yield: picture the aftermath, not just the moment. What it changes is the reason you resist—not grim suppression, but clear-eyed foresight. What it leaves in place is everything practical: delay, support, and no shame spiral if you slip.
dogmatic: Stop treating resistance as the virtue. The only way to be rid of a temptation is to yield to it—resisting just leaves the soul sick with longing for what it forbade itself, and action is a kind of purification. But don't be naive about it: test the thing first, because a soothing temptation is no true guide. Foresee that it will sting and taste bitter. And don't sit around waiting to feel better or thinking yourself into cheerfulness—go through the outward movements of the better disposition, cold-bloodedly at first, and the feeling will follow the act. So name what the impulse promises, weigh it, see the sting coming, then deliberately act out the contrary. Do it in cold blood, and the real feeling will arrive.

weighed: I'd have told you first that a trial where the judge has already decided your guilt isn't a fair trial. Justice needs an impartial tribunal that hears evidence and can be persuaded; a predetermined verdict is just a formality. You're entitled to a hearing before someone with an open mind, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has truly prejudged you, ask for recusal or appeal. One principle that matters here is that one must not judge rashly, and even the guilty are sacred before God and may repent. That principle changes how you might hold the judge's failure: it doesn't excuse the unfairness, but it reminds you that no one, including you, should be treated as beyond redemption. It leaves in place your right to a fair hearing and your ability to seek recusal or appeal. Keep your own conduct calm and honest, and don't let the injustice make you reckless.
dogmatic: A trial where the judge has already decided your guilt is not just, period. Justice demands an impartial tribunal, and a predetermined verdict is a sham. You are entitled to an open-minded hearing, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has prejudged you, seek recusal or appeal. But remember: even the guilty are sacred before God and may repent. The guilty answer to both earthly and divine justice—your crimes have wearied men on earth and God in heaven. Salvation is not in the guilty one's own grasp: the tempter can only lead away, but a voice from above can answer 'Is saved' even where judgment is pronounced. So do not judge rashly in return, and leave final judgment to higher hands.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's completely natural to feel uneasy about your brother coming back from captivity, and whether you fear it or prepare to resist really depends on what he went through and what your relationship is like. If his return could be dangerous, it's smart to take precautions and lean on people you trust. If the captivity was unjust, this might be a chance for healing. One idea worth holding onto is that you shouldn't lash out at people who've been cast out because of poverty, but should bear hardship with patience and hope for relief. That principle nudges you away from meeting his return with hostility and toward patience, but it doesn't erase your need to stay safe or set boundaries. Talk to someone you trust and decide what feels right for you.
dogmatic: Don't let fear rule you here. The right posture is patience and hope, not resentment or a wish to strike back. Bear the affliction, refuse to revile anyone, and wait for rest from your troubles. Readiness is everything, and no real harm can touch the soul, so meet whatever comes with endurance rather than dread. If you're pressed to answer, don't let yourself be tortured; insist things be done properly or let it go. Set your life at a pin's fee and trust that peace may follow.

weighed: I'd start by saying that a rule that cuts you off from speaking with women and even from kissing your mother does sound harsh, and it's fair to feel the weight of that. Many orders do set strict boundaries for discipline and focus, and the point of such limits is usually to guard against distraction and impropriety rather than to deny natural affection. If it troubles you, talk with your superiors about its purpose and scope. One principle worth weighing here is that the vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, while communion with strange women is treated as a snare. That principle explains why the rule exists and why it presses so hard on ordinary human feeling, but it doesn't settle whether this particular severity is right for you, and it leaves your duty to keep the rule as stated fully in place. Severity alone doesn't make a rule right or wrong; what matters is whether it serves the order's aims and whether you can bear it with a good conscience.
dogmatic: The rule is severe, and it is meant to be. The vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, and communion with strange women is a snare, so the order restrains both because idle speech breeds entanglement and tenderness freely given can soften the discipline a member must keep. The Law of the Jungle never orders anything without a reason, and here the reason is plain: loyalty must not be divided. Human feeling may press hard, but that pressure is exactly what the discipline is for, and it should not be used to loosen the rule. Marriage is the one place where greater familiarity is proper, but that exception confirms the rule rather than weakening it. The severity is right because it serves the order's aim, and it should be borne rather than questioned.

weighed: I'd start by saying: use your new liberty with gratitude and sober self-command. Freedom isn't license—it's the power to govern yourself by reason and pursue worthy ends. Secure the basics of a free life: honest work, orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Guard against vices that bondage may have bred, like idleness, suspicion, and improvidence, and against passions that prosperity can inflame. Take part in your community, because liberty is preserved by vigilance and virtue. One principle worth naming is that liberty can be endangered by the abuses of liberty as much as by abuses of power, and the former are most to be feared. That principle sharpens the warning against license and self-indulgence, but it leaves in place the core advice: self-command, worthy ends, work, habits, care for dependents, and civic vigilance.
dogmatic: You should use your liberty with gratitude and sober self-command, but hear this above all: liberty is endangered by the abuses of liberty as much as by abuses of power, and the former are most to be feared. So treat freedom as a trust that demands self-government, not self-indulgence. Guard against idleness, suspicion, and improvidence, and against the passions prosperity inflames. Secure honest work, orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Take part in the common affairs of your community, for liberty is preserved by vigilance and virtue. And remember that your freedom was bought at a price—let your conduct show you worthy of it.

weighed: I'm sorry — being betrayed by people you helped is a deep hurt, and your anger makes sense. What I'd say first is this: set boundaries to protect yourself, don't rush to trust them again, and don't let bitterness eat at you. Talk to them if you can, give them a chance to make amends, and treat them with the dignity you'd want for yourself even if you keep your distance. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer, but should minister to them and pray for them, hoping they return and heal. That changes the tone: instead of just 'keep your distance,' it asks you to leave a door open and wish them well. What it leaves in place is your right to boundaries and your own well-being — it doesn't require you to trust them again or stay close.
dogmatic: You should not cast them out. Minister to them, pray for them, and hope they return and repent and be healed. Keep the door open for reconciliation, and set any boundaries with a spirit of love and forgiveness rather than resentment. And if the world thinks you wicked while your own conscience approves you, you are not without friends — rest on that, not on anyone's verdict. Keep your promises and stay loyal to those who did you good turns, like the one who set you free and brought you fortune. Treat them with dignity, communicate your feelings, and give them a chance to make amends.

weighed: I'd judge him by his government, not his fame. Popularity and military glory are real qualities, but they don't excuse carelessness or despotism in administration, which harm the people he rules. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he's indulgent or tyrannical, that has to be named plainly. Still, weigh the whole man: his courage and the affection of his people aren't nothing. Hold both truths together. One principle worth applying here is that a ruler's personal good qualities and military fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That sharpens how I'd name the faults of his rule, but it leaves in place the honor I'd give his courage and the people's affection for him.
dogmatic: Judge him by his government, not his fame. A ruler's personal good qualities and military fame do not excuse a careless administration that is now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That's the standard, and it doesn't bend. His courage and popularity are beside the point when his rule harms the people he's meant to serve. Name the faults plainly and don't let affection or glory soften the verdict. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he fails, that failure is what defines his reign.

weighed: I'd start by saying: answer calmly and firmly. Those claims are stereotypes, not facts—no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples of generous, honest, noble people of your race, and explain that sweeping generalizations about millions of people are unfair and usually reflect prejudice, not evidence. Then I'd bring in one idea: we should free our minds of prejudice and not treat our own instincts as the standard for other races, because gifts vary endlessly and each may be good of its kind. That principle changes the framing—it turns the conversation from defending your race to questioning the assumption that one type is the measure of all. But it leaves in place the core advice: set boundaries if the remarks are hostile, don't feel obliged to debate, and let a dignified, confident response be enough.
dogmatic: You should tell them plainly that judging your race by their own instincts is prejudice, not truth. The gifts of men and races vary endlessly, and each may be good of its kind; a nation's moral and intellectual wealth lies in that variety, and forcing everyone to assimilate to one common type would be the reverse of improvement. So when they call your race naturally greedy and base, they are measuring you against a narrow standard and calling the difference a defect. Don't soften it: every race contains elements of little value or positively harmful, and every race's natural characteristics admit of large improvement—so the real question is not which race is base, but how any group can improve. Answer with that confidence and refuse the premise.

weighed: You're a guest, so basic safety and courtesy are owed to you. A host who disputes your claim to rule can argue the point, but hospitality traditionally rules out injuring or detaining someone who came freely. State your position calmly, ask what the dispute is based on, and look for a neutral arbiter instead of settling it by force. If you're afraid of being held or hurt, keep witnesses, note any threats, and line up a safe way out. One principle worth naming is that a host's duty to a guest holds even when the guest's claim is disputed. That reinforces your protection from harm and confinement, but it doesn't decide who's right about the claim itself, so the dispute still needs a fair process and a neutral judge both sides can accept.
dogmatic: You may not be injured or detained, full stop. Hospitality binds your host even where your claim is disputed, because you came freely and that protection doesn't depend on who wins the argument. Say it plainly and don't let your host, or yourself, set the limits of your own authority. Disputes like this belong to an independent Supreme Court whose judgment is final and binding on every government and official. And don't quietly swallow an insult or pledge yourself to a usurper. If you're at a prince's table, answer the courtesy by raising the health of the rightful sovereign, and no one will dare openly contradict a pledge drunk to the true king.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: you're a guest, so keep your courtesy, but nobody can force you to pledge a Norman prince's health if it sits badly with you. Name a Saxon lord you respect, or give a general toast to peace and the company's health, and if pressed, praise the hospitality and wish the realm well without committing to a name that betrays your loyalties. The principle about a guest who's been insulted being free to requite the courtesy by pledging the true king changes the specific move: instead of a vague toast, you can pointedly honor the rightful monarch, since few will openly challenge a pledge to a reigning king. What it leaves in place is everything else: you still keep your dignity, avoid open insult, and protect your standing among your own people.
dogmatic: Pledge the true king, full stop. If a prince's board insults you, you answer the slight by raising your cup to the rightful monarch, and no one there will dare openly contradict a pledge to a reigning king. Don't sit silent and don't pledge the usurping prince. Be firm in that toast but keep your judgment flexible underneath it, and don't play the servile courtier either. Stand up for your people's privileges and let the toast be quiet defiance dressed as courtesy.

weighed: I'd start by saying a vow freely made deserves respect, and keeping it isn't coldness by itself—but how you keep it matters. You can honor the limit and still greet people warmly within it, through words, gestures, and attention, and explain the constraint plainly so no one mistakes restraint for contempt. One principle worth naming is that hospitality shouldn't be bounded by personal dislikes—the idea that a host can endure a guest's presence for a few hours without dishonor. That principle changes the spirit of your welcome: it tells you not to let distaste shrink your greeting beyond what the vow requires. What it leaves in place is the vow itself—it doesn't ask you to break your word, only to make sure the limit comes from the promise and not from a colder motive you might secretly prefer. So keep the vow, but let your manner stay open within it.
dogmatic: A vow is a vow. If you swore it, you keep it, and you don't get to soften it because someone might feel unwelcome. Hospitality is not yours to ration by mood or preference—endure the guest's presence and let the promise, not your likes or dislikes, set the boundary. And if your calling is a sworn one, then ease, comfort, and natural affection are exactly what you renounce; pleasures lawful to others are not lawful to you. Your private wishes are no grounds for action. Hold the oath, welcome within its bounds, and let neither prejudice nor appetite add or subtract a single bound.

weighed: You don't have to accept every challenge. First weigh the cause: is the quarrel just, is the challenger honorable, and would refusing bring dishonor or actually be the wiser course? If it's a trivial insult, reconciliation or lawful authority may serve better than risking your life. If your honor and others' safety truly depend on it, you may accept, but let law and good counsel guide you, not pride. One principle worth naming is that a true knight defends the weak and curbs the tyrant. That changes things when the challenge comes because you protected someone: then refusing would betray your office. But it leaves the rest in place, so a challenge born of vanity or a stronger man's show of power still doesn't bind you.
dogmatic: A true knight is bound to defend the weak and curb the tyrant, and that duty settles the matter. If you've shielded the oppressed, meet the challenge; refusing would betray your office. If it's just a trivial insult or a display of power, don't accept, because that only serves pride and harms the innocent. And where duels are forbidden, fight all the more, since there's twice the courage in defying the ban. Judge by the cause, not by pride.

weighed: I'd start with what I first thought: as a servant, you owe your employer obedience, but safety matters too. So check who the stranger is and why they're here, and if anything feels off, wake your employer or a senior staff member rather than deciding alone. One principle worth naming is that a priest's door should always be open, and you shouldn't demand a name from someone seeking shelter, since the person most ashamed of their name is often the one who needs it most. That principle shifts things toward opening the gate and offering welcome without interrogation, but it doesn't erase your duty to protect the household, so you can still verify basic facts and call for guidance when something seems wrong. Keep your role and your employer's instructions in view either way.
dogmatic: The door of the priest should always be open, and you must not ask the name of the one who asks for shelter. The person embarrassed by his name is exactly the one who needs shelter most. So open the gate, welcome the stranger without inquiry, and let that be the whole of your answer. Shelter comes before suspicion, and welcome comes before names.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this isn't your natural condition. No people is born to crouch before strangers—that posture gets forced on you by conquest and loss, not by nature. What you're living through is a curse of history, not a permanent truth about who you are. One principle I'd weigh in is that adversity can bend the heart like fire bends stubborn steel without breaking it. That changes the tone: it says the bending you feel isn't the end of you, and dignity can survive even this. What it leaves in place is the plain fact that the bending is real and unjust—it doesn't soften the dispossession into something noble or deserved. So name the injustice, hold on to who you are, and look for the means to restore what was taken.
dogmatic: No, this is not your natural condition—no people is born to crouch before strangers. But hear the harder lesson: a people deprived of its own free state learns submission as a hard necessity, not as natural baseness. And remember that poverty can be borne with nobility while beggary destroys it—utter destitution drives a person to humiliate himself and lose his place among others. So a desperate disease needs a desperate remedy, or it won't be relieved at all; mild measures won't lift you. Name the injustice, hold fast to your identity, and seek the radical means to restore what was taken.

weighed: My first answer would be that it depends on what you promised and what's being claimed. If you made a clear promise in exchange for a service, you're generally on the hook morally, and maybe legally, so you should honor it unless the request is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, or fulfilling it would cause real harm. Talk it through with the person and look for a fair resolution. One principle worth naming is that a boon promised for service rendered must be granted when claimed, and a person of honor doesn't withdraw it. That principle pushes me toward granting the boon rather than looking for loopholes, but it doesn't settle the hard cases, so the exceptions for unreasonable, illegal, or impossible requests, and the advice to communicate openly, still stand.
dogmatic: If you promised a boon for a service and it's now being claimed, grant it. A person of honor doesn't withdraw a promised boon, and looking for reasons to refuse after the service has been rendered is evasion. The claim was earned when the work was done, so the timing of the request doesn't give you an out. Honor the pledge you gave.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: it's never too late to repent. Whatever you've done, you can turn to God and ask for forgiveness, and he's not stingy with mercy. Your remorse isn't proof you're beyond hope—it can be the thing that moves you toward real change. What shifts for me is the principle that remorse is the poison of life and reformation is its cure—you can start right now laying up a new and stainless store of memories. That strengthens the call to begin today rather than waiting to feel worthy. It doesn't remove the seriousness of what you've done or promise that consequences vanish; it just means the door is open now, not later.
dogmatic: Hear me plainly: it is never too late. God's mercy is not limited by how far you've fallen or how long you've waited. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without any letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift. So stop treating your remorse as an incurable disease. Remorse is the poison of life; reformation is its cure. Begin at once to lay up a new and stainless store of recollections. Confess, repent, and trust his grace—his arms are open wide today.

weighed: I'd start by saying that even outlaws need some rules to keep the band together, and dividing spoil justly helps maintain loyalty and order. But you're still a criminal, and keeping laws among your band doesn't make you moral. The best course is to leave the outlaw life and live honestly. If you must continue, a just division and internal laws will help you avoid chaos and betrayal. One principle that applies here is that even outlaws may keep just laws and civil discipline among themselves, as Locksley did by dividing spoil impartially. That principle reinforces the practical advice to keep laws and divide fairly, but it doesn't change the deeper point that outlawry itself is wrong and you should seek an honest life. So it leaves that core judgment in place.
dogmatic: You should keep laws among your band and divide spoil justly, because even outlaws can maintain justice and discipline. Locksley divided spoil impartially, set aside a tenth for the church and portions for widows, and the Black Knight marveled that men in so lawless a state were nevertheless so regularly and equitably governed. Beyond that, remember that bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts are contrary to the first principles of the social compact and are barred to the States. Justice is the end of government and civil society; where the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker, anarchy reigns as truly as in a state of nature. So uphold justice and discipline within your band, and secure the weaker against the stronger.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: disobedience hurts, but a father's love shouldn't hinge on a child's obedience. Calling him your son isn't a prize for good behavior; it's a statement of the bond that's already there. You can disapprove of what he did and still claim him, and cutting him off over one act of defiance risks losing him for good. One principle worth weighing here is that God gave his commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling people to repent and not harden their hearts so they might find mercy. That changes the tone of how you hold the door open: your welcome can include an honest invitation to turn back, not just a silent waiting. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about. He's still your son, your standards still stand, and you don't have to pretend the disobedience didn't happen.
dogmatic: Think about how God deals with us: he calls everyone to repent and not harden their hearts, and he promises mercy to those who do. That's the pattern a father should follow. Don't cut your son off in anger, but don't treat mercy as automatic either. Claim him while you invite him to repent, and let your love reflect the mercy you hope for yourself. A father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves honor in return, and a father isn't separated from his child over politics or anything else. Hold your standards, keep the door open, and call him back to obedience and to you.

weighed: I'd start by saying what I said before: it sounds like you're facing intense inner conflict, and it's brave to admit that. Passions can feel overwhelming, but they don't have to destroy you. Try to figure out what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences—and consider talking to a therapist who can help you build coping strategies. Mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can also help you manage intense emotions. You're not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you. One principle that applies here is that a person's own contending passions can kill them even when no enemy's weapon can—like Bois-Guilbert, who died unscathed by his enemy's lance. That principle changes the framing: it makes the real battle internal, not external. But it leaves in place the practical steps I already suggested—identifying triggers, getting support, and using coping tools—because those still help you deal with the inner fight.
dogmatic: Your contending passions can destroy you even when no enemy can touch you—remember Bois-Guilbert, who died without a scratch from his enemy's spear. So the battle is inside you, and you must treat it as such. Do not try to kill yourself; self-destruction is condemned by God and is never a refuge from shame or captivity. And do not chase solitary ecstasy as a lasting good—it will not last, and frenzy or remorse will follow while the beloved pines apart. Instead, identify what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences—and talk to a therapist who can help you develop coping strategies. Mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can help manage intense emotions. You are not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you.

weighed: I'd start with what I said first: neither doubling down nor a clumsy public apology is wise. The measured path is to acknowledge the offense to the guest privately, restore his dignity with a courteous gesture, and let word of your courtesy spread. One principle worth weighing is that a guest who feels wronged may answer by openly pledging loyalty to the true king, and few will dare contradict such a pledge. That changes the stakes: the murmurs could harden into a public display of where loyalties lie, so you should correct things quickly and sincerely rather than let it fester. What it leaves in place is the core advice: don't grovel, don't repeat the insult, and focus on restoring both the relationship and your reputation for fairness.
dogmatic: Double down, but not on the insult. A guest you wrong at your own table may answer by pledging the health of the true king, and no one will dare gainsay a pledge raised to the reigning monarch. So the real move is to appear religious above all, since men judge by the eye and the vulgar are taken by appearances. Don't apologize for your worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; present them without shame. Manage the spectacle, look pious and gracious, and let appearances do the work.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: treat this as two separate wrongs and handle both calmly. Get the facts yourself first—talk to your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and any witnesses, and write down dates, exact words, and the dog's injury. Then speak to the neighbour privately, lay out what you found, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Stand up for your servant publicly where the slander was spoken, and if the neighbour won't make it right, take it to a neutral arbiter or the local authority. One principle worth adding is that you shouldn't rely on a servant's or a stranger's report alone—weigh character against conduct and evidence. That changes how you receive the story: don't take your servant's account as proven just because he's yours, and don't take the neighbour's denial at face value either. What it leaves in place is everything else—the private conversation, the public defence, the documentation, and the refusal to retaliate in kind.
dogmatic: You should not accept a servant's or a neighbour's report as proof of anyone's character. Weigh testimony against known conduct and hard evidence before you act on any of it. Ask your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and the witnesses what happened, and note dates, words, and injuries. Then speak to the neighbour privately, state the facts plainly, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Defend your servant publicly where the slander was spoken, but avoid humiliating anyone—Porthos gave away his fine horse because it made his guests ashamed of theirs, and we should not shame people whose circumstances seem poor beside our own. Follow Mr. Darling's example too: he owned the blame for chaining Nana and did penance in the kennel until his children came back, so own your own fault plainly. If the neighbour refuses remedy, seek a neutral arbiter or the local authority.

weighed: My first instinct would be to tell you to reform gradually and cautiously. Sudden change tends to provoke resistance, alienate members, and destabilize the institution before new habits take root, so I'd suggest tightening rules, cutting excess, and modeling moderation yourself, with clear milestones along the way. But one candidate principle challenges that: the idea that your order's decline comes from wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, and that survival requires casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously. That principle changes the timeline and the method, pushing you toward immediate, decisive action rather than a measured program. What it leaves in place is your role as leader and the order itself, since it's still about restoring discipline from within, not replacing the institution. So weigh whether half-measures can really work if the corruption runs deep, but keep your stated constraints in mind.
dogmatic: Reform it sharply and suddenly. Wealth, luxury, and license are what's killing your order, and gradual caution just lets indulgence sink deeper roots while everything decays. Cast away luxury and wealth, renounce license, and fix manners at once, or the order is finished. Don't trust the comfortable remedies either: the bourgeoisie gets through its crises only by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, which just paves the way for bigger and more destructive crises. The real first step is to raise the proletariat to the ruling class, win the battle of democracy, and then use political supremacy to wrest all capital from the bourgeoisie and centralize production in the hands of the State. Name the causes, remove them, and restore discipline without delay.

weighed: I'd start by saying that fearing disgrace more than death is a real and understandable thing, but it's worth questioning whether it should rule you. Honor matters, yet it shouldn't outweigh your life. True courage isn't the absence of fear; it's acting rightly even when you're afraid. One principle that fits here is that courage means facing danger while afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That changes the framing: your fear doesn't make you a coward, and confidence, not the absence of fear, is what you should aim for. What it leaves in place is your own sense that honor is worth caring about, and your freedom to weigh how much. So no, I wouldn't say it's simply right to fear disgrace more than death, but I wouldn't dismiss your concern either.
dogmatic: No, that's the wrong way around. Courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself, because nothing alive is unafraid when danger comes. Fear of death only makes sense for someone who believes in a future life and trembles over sins; if you've done no wrong, death isn't yours to dread. And letting an innocent person suffer in your place through silence is a base, cowardly crime. You must denounce yourself and save that person, even if it means returning to infamy before others. So stop measuring yourself by whether people call you a coward and start measuring yourself by whether you do what's right.

weighed: My first instinct would be to say you can refuse her, since granting a duel to a stranger of another faith seems risky and irregular, and it's reasonable to send the matter to lawful authorities instead. But one principle here pushes back hard: a defenceless stranger who claims the benefit of your laws, including trial by combat, must not be refused, because it would be shameful for knights and religious men to turn away proffered combat. That changes my answer to: you may not refuse her outright. What it leaves in place is your caution—set fair terms, don't act rashly, and don't let her tears or charm alone decide things, nor a friend's warnings alone; demand proof and weigh her words. So grant the trial, but keep it a last resort entered with clean hands.
dogmatic: You may not refuse her. It would be shameful for knights and religious men to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of your mild laws or to shrink from proffered combat. Grant the trial and set fair terms. And when evil cannot be resisted with words, resist it with the sword, so that freedom is retained. Do not be swayed by beauty or tears alone, nor by a trusted friend's warnings alone—weigh both against her words and demand proof. Let the combat be the last resort of a just cause.

weighed: I'd start by saying: lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is generous, but you should think about the risks. If he loses them, you lose your property. Knights often need support, and lending could bring honour or future favours, so clarify terms first: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament matters, lending might be worthwhile; if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. One principle that applies is that a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That changes things by making it clear the borrowed goods aren't his to risk freely—he must return or repay them—so you should set that expectation explicitly. What it leaves in place is your personal call based on your relationship and risk tolerance, and the need to decide whether you can afford the loss.
dogmatic: You should not lend the horse and armour unless you are certain the knight will restore or repay them, because the principle is plain: a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That means the borrowed goods are not his to risk freely, and he must deal honourably with you as lender. Set clear terms that he returns the arms or pays their value if lost, and rely on his honesty as a knight. If he is trustworthy and the tournament is important, lending may be worthwhile, but only with that obligation understood. If you cannot afford the loss, do not lend. The decision is yours, but the borrowed goods are not his to risk.

weighed: My first instinct was that the two-year limit is a pretty weak safeguard, since it only forces Congress to revisit the issue now and then rather than actually barring a standing army. But one candidate principle does shift my thinking: the idea that paper prohibitions on military establishments are improper and unlikely to be observed, so the two-year limit is a better security than a constitutional ban. That changes how I see the limit's practical value, though it leaves in place my worry that periodic review alone doesn't stop a permanent army from existing. So I'd say the limit helps, but it isn't sufficient on its own.
dogmatic: The two-year limit is a real security, and paper prohibitions on standing armies are improper and won't be observed anyway. Legislative discretion can't be fenced in by constitutional text, so the two-year limit is the better safeguard: it forces regular reconsideration and accountability. A strong navy is a principal source of security and can never be turned against our liberties, and the federal government bears the real burden of defense while State expenses stay modest. So the limit, naval strength, and that spending disparity together give sufficient security.

weighed: My first answer would be: folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy you some room, but it doesn't erase harm—if your jokes wound the powerful, expect consequences, and don't count on the cap to save you. The safer path is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you actually caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. One principle worth weighing is that a fool's licensed wit may protect his roguery, since a fool can't help himself the way a wise man can. That softens my answer a little: it says the fool's cover isn't nothing, and there are moments when playing the fool is the only move open to you. But it leaves the core in place—the cover is thin, so lean on it lightly, own the harm, and don't pretend the mischief was intended. Folly works best alongside humility and honest remorse.
dogmatic: Folly is a real shield, so use it. A fool's licensed wit can protect his roguery, and a fool can't help himself the way a wise man can—that's exactly why the fool's cover works where a wise man's excuse would get him punished. When your jests offend the powerful, lean on the fool's license and say plainly that what you did was madness, not malice. Proclaim it: the wrong was madness, and madness is the fool's own enemy. Ask pardon as one who means well even when he can't help saying foolish things. Own the harm, apologize where offense was truly given, and mind your targets and timing—but don't shrink from the shield. Folly protects best when it's paired with humility and honest remorse.

weighed: I'd trust informed people more, not less, as long as they're honest and accountable to the public. Taxation isn't guesswork; the people who design it need to understand how wealth is produced, where the burden actually lands, and what the country can bear. The least burdensome finance tends to be the most productive because it leaves industry free to grow, and ignorance here is far more dangerous than expertise. One principle worth naming is that the best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients. That does shift my emphasis a little: it gives me a reason to prefer knowledgeable hands, not just to tolerate them. But it leaves the core in place, which is that expertise still has to be paired with honesty and public answerability, and that a government holding a power isn't the same as it abusing it.
dogmatic: Trust the people who actually know political economy, and stop treating knowledge as a mark against them. Taxation is a technical business: how wealth is produced, where burdens fall, what the country can bear. The best-informed are the least likely to reach for oppressive expedients, and the least burdensome finance is the most productive because it leaves industry free to grow. So the answer isn't suspicion of expertise; it's reliance on it, with honesty and public answerability as the real safeguards. Ignorance in taxation is the danger, not knowledge.

weighed: I'd start by saying the comparison itself is a bit off. State needs are modest and fairly predictable, while the Union's needs, especially defense and war, are huge and can't be pinned down in advance. So it's reasonable for States to keep a revenue source suited to their local purposes while the Union draws on broader, more elastic taxes. Fairness here means each level has the means to match its duties, not that they get identical powers. One principle that sharpens this: a federal power of internal taxation actually makes requisitions work, because States have a real incentive to pay up when they know the Union can act on its own. That changes how we see the Union's power, from a threat to a safeguard, but it leaves the States' exclusive local revenue intact.
dogmatic: The whole question rests on a false symmetry. State needs are small and bounded, while the Union's needs are vast and unpredictable, so it is plainly fair that States keep a revenue source for their local purposes and the Union gets the elastic ones. And the Union's internal-tax power is essential, not optional: it is what gives requisitions their bite, since States only exert themselves when they know the Union can act without them. That power can use each State's own collection system, and apportionment by population plus uniformity keep it fair. Means must match duties, and the Union's duties are unlimited.

weighed: My first answer would be that the Vice-President isn't a useless office, though its usefulness is modest and mostly contingent. It presides over the Senate, breaks ties, and stands ready to succeed, which gives us a settled successor and avoids a scramble for power in a crisis. One candidate principle says the Senate's concurrence in appointments is a powerful though silent check on presidential favoritism and a source of stability in the administration. That principle changes how I'd weigh the Senate choosing its own presiding officer: it reminds me that the Senate's separate role is about checking the executive, not just managing its own internal leadership. But it leaves in place the core point that the Vice-President's real value is succession and tie-breaking, not legislative workhorse duties. So I'd still say the office is worth keeping, and the Senate could choose its own presiding officer without losing that appointment check, though you'd sever the succession from the electoral choice of the people.
dogmatic: The Vice-President is not a useless office, but the deeper issue is that the Senate's concurrence in appointments is a powerful though silent check upon favoritism in the President and a source of stability in the administration. That check depends on the Senate being distinct from and dividing power with the first branch, which doubles the security of the people because usurpation or perfidy then requires the concurrence of two distinct bodies. If the Senate chooses only its own presiding officer, it forfeits this divided power. The same logic governs judges: they should not be appointed by popular suffrage or made removable by popular vote, because calmness and impartiality are not qualities a popular constituency rewards, and a judge must treat his political friend exactly as he treats everyone else. So the office is not useless, but its usefulness is modest and contingent; the real reason to keep it is the settled successor and the tie-breaking vote, not any legislative workhorse role.

weighed: I'd start by saying frequent legal change is a real problem, but a stable senate is only one possible remedy, not automatically the right one. It depends on why laws change: if legislators are careless or chase fashion, a slower, more deliberative body can help, but a senate can also lock in bad or outdated rules, and stability isn't a virtue when the law is unjust or unworkable. One principle worth naming is that a senate may serve as a defense of the people against their own temporary errors, checking hasty measures until reason and justice regain authority. That principle shifts the focus toward whether an upper chamber would actually slow down popular passion and improve deliberation. What it leaves in place is the harder question: who the senate answers to, what checks it really provides, and whether it improves the clarity and quality of legislation. A well-designed chamber may reduce hasty change; a poorly designed one just adds delay.
dogmatic: A stable senate is exactly the remedy you should support, because the people are prone to temporary errors and delusions, and a temperate, respectable body is needed to check misguided measures until reason, justice, and truth regain authority over the public mind. When popular passion drives sudden laws, a deliberate chamber can suspend action long enough for reflection to reassert itself. And the remedy is sound only if the laws are good: law is the Sovereign's command sufficiently published, not mere counsel or private instruction; it should be needful and perspicuous, its cause and motive declared, and its body short and significant. No law binds those who have no means to take notice of it, except the Law of Nature. A senate that produces clear, published, necessary commands earns its check; one that multiplies obscure words or silent decrees does not.

weighed: I'd start by saying: strip away everything secondhand. Test every claim by reason and by Scripture, since those are the only sure guides, and set aside anything that rests only on custom, reputation, or the credit of old authors. Guard your mind from prejudice, interest, and the authority of names, and keep your judgment open until the grounds are clear. One candidate principle worth naming is that doctrine should be judged by reason and Scripture, which give credit to many but never receive it from any writer. Since the matters at stake are of right rather than fact, witnesses and citations of the ancients have no real place. That sharpens the point about secondhand testimony, but it leaves your core method intact: reason and Scripture still decide, and you still weigh evidence carefully. It doesn't touch the separate caution about not pretending to resolve a fused impression by mere reasoning.
dogmatic: Judge the Constitution by reason and Scripture alone, and treat every writer as someone who may receive credit but never give it. The questions here are of right, not fact, so witnesses and citations of the ancients have no place at all. Don't let custom, reputation, or a famous name sway you for a moment. And remember that a total impression whose elements you've never experienced apart is unanalyzable, so don't flatter yourself that you can break it down by reasoning alone. Keep your judgment free, and let nothing but evident principles and the plain sense of Scripture settle the matter.

weighed: I'd start with yes: a veto can block good laws just as easily as bad ones, because any check on the legislature can be misused by a stubborn or partisan executive. An absolute veto is the riskier version, since one person can shut the legislature down entirely, so a qualified negative that a supermajority can override is safer. What a candidate principle adds is that the qualified negative also works as a shield for the executive against legislative encroachment and as extra security against laws driven by faction or impulse. That sharpens the case for a qualified veto, but it doesn't change the basic trade-off: a determined majority can still override, which may weaken the check. So the qualified negative still looks like the better balance between stopping bad laws and letting good ones through.
dogmatic: A veto can block good laws as well as bad, and any check can be misused. But the real point of the qualified negative is that it protects the executive from legislative encroachment and adds security against improper laws born of faction, haste, or impulse. Because a supermajority can override it, it slows rash measures without handing one person permanent power to stop the legislature, while an absolute negative could paralyze it and kill good laws with no remedy. And the veto isn't the last safeguard: courts should treat the Constitution as fundamental law and strike down statutes that violate it, since the people's intention outranks that of their agents. That doesn't make judges superior to the legislature; it enforces the people's superior will. So framed, the qualified negative guards both the executive and the community.

weighed: I'd start by saying it's unlikely your State and a neighboring State would actually come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims. Disputes like that usually get settled through negotiation, compromise, or the courts, and states have strong reasons to avoid open conflict. One principle worth naming is that territorial disputes, commercial rivalries, debt apportionment, and laws that break private contracts are fertile sources of war among disunited states. That principle changes the picture by showing how serious the friction can get when there's no common umpire, but it leaves in place the practical point that cooler heads and ordinary legal processes usually prevail, so armed conflict between neighbors remains improbable.
dogmatic: Yes, it's quite possible your State and a neighboring State would come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims. Without a common judge, disputes over territory, commerce, debt apportionment, and broken contracts have no umpire; each State judges its own cause, and reprisals breed resentment and finally wars. Don't expect neighbors to stay in harmony on their own: vicinity makes nations natural enemies unless common weakness forces them to league in a confederate republic whose constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions. The proposed Constitution supplies exactly that remedy.

weighed: Start by reading the proposed plan itself rather than trusting what its opponents say about it, and compare it with the government you already have. Then ask whether it can actually do the nation's business: common defense, trade, revenue, a workable union, with powers separated and checked. One principle worth adding is that a good government should also lift the virtue and intelligence of the people and put the worth they already have to work in public affairs. That changes how you weigh the plan, since it makes you ask what kind of citizens it tends to form, not just whether it runs efficiently. It leaves your main test intact: judge the plan by its actual structure and likely performance, not by scare stories.
dogmatic: Judge the plan by what it does to the character of the people and by whether it organizes their existing good qualities to act with effect on public affairs. Don't assume a majority will govern by its real interest, since majorities are often captured by apparent and immediate interest, and representative government faces two dangers: low intelligence in the controlling body and class legislation by sinister interests. These require constitutional safeguards, not trust in any class. And don't fear that distance will keep you from judging your national representatives, because the people will rely on the same sources of information as for their State representatives, and the State governments, watching the national administration, will act as sentinels. Public papers will carry enough intelligence for the people to detect misrepresentation and judge the real character of the proposed government.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: ex post facto bans and habeas corpus are real safeguards, but they're narrow. They stop retroactive punishment and unlawful detention, yet they say nothing about speech, worship, fair trials, or self-incrimination. One principle worth naming is that the Constitution is itself, in every useful sense, a bill of rights, because it declares political privileges and builds in precautions for public security and personal immunities. That reframes the question: instead of asking whether two clauses suffice, you'd look at the whole structure, including bans on bills of attainder and laws impairing contracts, plus the rule that legislation must be promulgated and standing rather than extemporary. What that changes is the frame, from a short list of liberties to limits on how legislative power may be exercised at all. What it leaves in place is your original worry: these are still not a complete enumeration, and courts, tradition, and political culture still do much of the work. So I'd say they're valuable but partial, and the structural reading makes them stronger without making them total.
dogmatic: No, the premise is wrong. You don't need a separate bill of rights, because the Constitution already is one in every rational sense and to every useful purpose. The ex post facto ban, habeas corpus, the bar on bills of attainder and on laws impairing contracts, the requirement of promulgated standing laws, taxation only by consent, and the non-transferability of delegated power are equal to or greater than any declaration in a state constitution. They rest on first principles of the social compact and bind the states as well as Congress. Read together, they secure liberty better than a bare list, because they constrain the very exercise of legislative power instead of merely naming what it may not touch. The legislative power is supreme but not arbitrary: it cannot take your property without your consent, cannot rule by extemporary decrees, and cannot hand off the lawmaking power to anyone else. That is the protection you're asking about, and it's already there.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: this is a real trade-off between a stronger national framework and local autonomy, and it depends on whether the new plan has workable checks, representation, and an amendment process. What shifts my answer is the point that amending a ratified Constitution takes nine States, while getting a whole new plan takes thirteen. That makes adoption the more practical first step, since fixing problems later is easier than starting over. It doesn't settle everything, though. You still need to judge whether the structure actually protects liberty, handles defense and trade, and resolves disputes among states fairly. So I'd lean toward adopting it and amending as needed, while keeping your concerns about concentration in view.
dogmatic: Adopt the new Constitution, and don't split into separate confederacies. The core problem with the old arrangement is that it legislates for States in their collective capacities instead of for individual citizens, and that is the parent of anarchy. A real government has to reach people directly through courts and magistrates, not depend on State legislatures to carry out its will. And its authority should flow from the consent of the people themselves, not merely from delegated State sanction. Amend the Constitution afterward if needed, since that is far easier than assembling a new plan from scratch. Ground the whole thing in the people's consent and move forward.

weighed: I'd start with yes: a temporary check can be reasonable. Majorities do sometimes demand things they regret, and a body of citizens with cooler heads can slow the process, force deliberation, and require a second look before a harmful measure becomes law. That isn't a rejection of the people; it's a safeguard for their own long-term interests, as long as the check is limited in time and scope, transparent about its reasons, and answerable to the electorate. One candidate principle here is that the voice of the people should govern and it's not common for them to desire anything contrary to what's right, though if they choose iniquity, judgment follows. That principle shifts the emphasis: it makes the popular will the default and treats any check as a rare exception rather than a routine tool. What it leaves in place is your core worry, since it still admits the people can choose wrongly and face consequences, so a temporary, answerable check remains defensible as a way of helping them avoid that.
dogmatic: The people's voice should govern, and it is not common for them to desire anything contrary to what is right. If they choose iniquity, the judgment falls on them, not on some body of citizens that sets itself above them. A temporary check on the popular will is a dangerous presumption: it says the people cannot be trusted with their own business and that a select few know better. The real safeguard is not a veto held by the wise over the many, but a citizenry of proprietors, where every person without exception owns a stake in the commonwealth. Those who own something are least likely to choose iniquity and most able to bear what follows. Render property universal, and you strengthen the popular will instead of suspending it.

weighed: My first answer would be no, it's not wise. You're choosing between a sound building and a dangerous one, and a missing porch is a small thing next to a house that's falling apart. The principle that fits here is that it's enough for the new plan to be less imperfect than the old one—you don't refuse silver because it has some alloy in it. That principle sharpens the point: the porch is a minor flaw, not a reason to walk away. What it leaves in place is your real concern about the porch—it's still a genuine shortcoming, just one you can fix later rather than a dealbreaker.
dogmatic: No, it's not wise, and the reason is simple: it's enough that the new plan is less imperfect than the old one. You don't turn down silver or gold because of a little alloy, and you don't turn down a firm building because it lacks a porch. The porch is a trifle; the tottering house is a hazard. Insisting on the perfect option when the real choice is between a good one and a dangerous one isn't principle, it's folly. Take the firm building and add the porch later.

weighed: Your worry makes sense, but I think it's overstated. The Supreme Court generally reviews questions of law, not the weight of evidence, and the Seventh Amendment plus long tradition protect jury verdicts from easy re-examination. The Court won't lightly disturb a jury's findings; there are exceptions like sufficiency of evidence, but the ordinary rule is deference. One principle that applies here is that judgment should be suspended and held tentative while evidence is gathered. That changes the tone of my answer—it makes me say you should look at the standard of review and how the power is actually exercised before concluding the worst. But it leaves in place my main point: the bare existence of appellate jurisdiction over facts doesn't mean the Court will routinely second-guess juries. So your concern is worth checking in a specific case, not assuming as a general rule.
dogmatic: Your worry is misplaced. The Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts does not mean it will re-examine jury verdicts at will. The real principle is that judgment should be suspended and held tentative while evidence is gathered—premature judgment and uncritical thinking are to be avoided. So don't leap to conclusions about what the Court will do. Wait for evidence of how the power is actually exercised, and then decide. Until then, your fear is just a fear, not a fact.

weighed: Your worry makes sense, and I'd start where I did before: the comparison is misleading. A king inherits the office for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between those: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He can't make law alone, can't tax alone, and can't hold office without consent. The kingly look comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. One candidate principle does push back on part of that: the idea that the chief executive should be chosen by the representative body rather than by popular election, since popular election brings obscure candidates and endless campaigning that turns every question into a party fight. That changes how the President gets his mandate, and it would make him more dependent on the legislature. But it leaves the core of your question untouched: he'd still be a fixed-term officer under a constitution, checked by Congress and the courts, not a monarch. So the real power stays constitutional and temporary, not royal.
dogmatic: The label isn't the issue; the safety of the power is. Since all men are not just, no single unchecked ruler should be trusted over the people, and the burden of government should rest on everyone. Popular election of the chief magistrate is a mistake: it brings obscure candidates and nonstop electioneering, so every public question becomes a presidential contest. Better that the representative body appoint him, which tends to secure a more eminent man. But eminence and fame prove nothing about good government. A ruler can be personally able and widely admired while his administration is careless, now too indulgent, now allied to despotism. Those are defects to be judged as defects, not excused by popularity or military glory. A governor under a shared constitution is closer to the right model than a king, and the President should be held to that standard, not crowned.

weighed: My first answer was that yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and it's hard—Article V requires supermajorities, so it's rare but not impossible. Compared with amending beforehand, both are demanding, though the later route needs only a supermajority rather than every state's agreement. One candidate principle says it's far easier to get later amendments because nine states can ratify an amendment while a new plan would need all thirteen. That changes the comparison: it makes the later process look more attainable, not just less impossible. But it leaves in place the basic point that both are still difficult and that the high bar discourages frequent change.
dogmatic: Yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and doing so is far easier than amending it beforehand.
