They're also bound to check a child's exuberant spirits and teach that present pursuits are not the business of life, because a parent who lets that slide fixes the character and brings disgrace on the whole family. So yes, credit their peculiarities—but hold them to that charge, and don't let indulgence or indolence off the hook.

weighed: I'd start with what I said before: disgust at a stranger touching your food is a social and moral reaction as much as a physical one. Even clean hands carry invisible traces, and your body reads contamination as a threat. Food is intimate, so someone else's contact feels like an intrusion on your boundary. That's your brain's overgeneralized hygiene alarm plus a sense of violated personal space, and knowing the hands were clean doesn't switch it off because disgust moves faster than reasoning. One candidate principle here is that disgust mainly relates to taste and eating, so it shows up chiefly around the mouth—the grimace, the drawing back of the lips, the urge to spit or heave. That principle changes how you picture the feeling: it's a mouth-level rejection of something you imagine entering you, not a considered verdict on the stranger. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—the alarm is still protective and still faster than reason, and the symbolic boundary around food still matters. So you can treat the revulsion as a normal protective instinct rather than a judgment about him.
dogmatic: Disgust belongs to eating and tasting, and that's why it lives around your mouth: the grimace, the pulled-back lips, the urge to spit or heave as if something unfit were entering you. But notice what the feeling is pushing you to do—make an innocent man with clean hands carry your discomfort. That you should refuse. Don't drag your private revulsion onto someone who did nothing wrong; keep your own disturbance to yourself rather than letting it contaminate his ease. And take the host as your model: a host who sets food before a guest partakes of it himself, and by eating it assures the guest it's wholesome. Do the same. Share the meal openly, taste what's offered, and let the mouth's own acceptance—not a private flinch—settle whether the food is good.

weighed: I'd start with the adaptive view: there's no single simple rule, but leaf shape generally reflects a balance of light capture, water loss, and mechanical support, so narrow lanceolate leaves tend to suit windy or dry spots while broad cordate leaves help in shade or moisture. One candidate principle worth naming is the idea that localized potassium buildup weakens surface tension in certain regions of tissue, which could help explain how a leaf bulges or grows out into a particular shape. That adds a cellular mechanism to the story, but it doesn't replace the ecological explanation—it just tells you how the shaping might physically happen, while the functional trade-offs still explain why one form wins out over another in a given place.
dogmatic: The real principle is chemical and physical: potassium salts gather in specific regions, weaken surface tension there, and that is what drives the bulging and outgrowth that give a leaf its form. Lanceolate or cordate, the shape follows from where those accumulations sit and how the tissue yields. You don't need to dress it up in adaptive stories about wind and shade; look at the microchemistry and the surface tension, and the leaf's outline follows from that.

weighed: Chroma is how colorful or pure a color is—how far it is from gray of the same lightness. Luminosity is how light or dark a color appears, where it sits between black and white. One candidate principle says the spectrum colors form a continuous circle, with hues connecting violet back to red. That changes how you picture hue relationships, but it leaves the chroma–luminosity distinction exactly as it was: chroma is saturation, luminosity is lightness, and they're independent.
dogmatic: Chroma is the colorfulness or purity of a color, its freedom from gray. Luminosity is its lightness or darkness. But you should picture the spectrum as a continuous circle—six fundamental colors plus the gradual hues connecting violet to red—not a straight line. Hue names a position on that circle; tint is a paler version, shade a darker one. Chroma and luminosity stay independent, and artists use both.

weighed: I'd start where I did before: forgiveness isn't an illusion, but it doesn't wipe out the past. The wrong really happened, and pretending it didn't is just fooling yourself. What changes is your relationship to the person and to the injury—you let go of the debt and stop letting resentment run you. The memory can stay, and repair might still be owed, but the wrong no longer sits between you like a bill that can never be paid. One idea worth naming here is that you can forgive the person while still hating what they did—separating the wrongdoer from the wrong. That helps because it lets you release the person without having to call the deed fine or pretend it never happened. What it leaves in place is the truth of the injury and whatever real consequences or repair are still needed. So no, it's not an illusion—it's a real change in you and in the relationship.
dogmatic: You're asking whether forgiving and calling the wrong obliterated is an illusion, and the honest answer is that the deed doesn't vanish—but you can forgive the person while abhorring what they did. That distinction is the heart of it: the wrongdoer isn't wholly wicked just because he did a wicked thing, so you release the person without pretending the act was harmless. Revenge then has no hold on your heart. And even where grave wrong demands grave consequences, mercy should temper judgment—give the offender a final chance to repent, to pray if he knows a prayer, because he is condemned and will die. Pride and defiance against what happened should give way to remorse and acknowledgment that a wiser hand is at work. The memory may remain, but the wrong no longer stands between you as an unpayable account. That is a real moral act, not an illusion.

weighed: I'd start by saying you're not bound to follow every recommendation, but you should be careful about refusing to hear advisers just because you expect to disagree. The value of counsel isn't whether you adopt it; it's whether it makes you test your own judgment against objections. If you shut out people you anticipate opposing, you cut yourself off from correction. One principle worth naming is that the prudent question isn't where advice comes from but whether it's good, and good advice can come even from an enemy. That changes the focus from the adviser's standing to the merits of what they say, so you should hear them out and weigh it seriously. What it leaves in place is your responsibility to decide: you're still the one who must judge and act, not convene advisers just to rubber-stamp what you've already fixed.
dogmatic: You should listen to advisers even when you expect to reject their recommendations, because the test of counsel is whether the advice is good, not who gives it. Good advice can come from an enemy, so dismissing someone in advance because you anticipate disagreeing with them is a mistake. Hear them out, weigh what they say on its merits, and then decide. You're not obligated to follow every recommendation, but you are obligated to expose your judgment to objection rather than insulating yourself. Convening advisers only to ratify decisions you've already made defeats the purpose.

weighed: I'd start with the plain answer: you get there through habit and comparison. You keep meeting that quality in one kind of company, your mind notices what's common across the instances, memory blends them, and reason pulls out the shared trait so you can think of it on its own. One candidate principle says general impressions are blended memories, like a composite portrait, faint and faulty editions of what they came from. That changes how reliable the resulting idea is: it's not a clean copy of the quality, it carries the errors of memory. What it leaves in place is the basic mechanism. The quality still becomes thinkable by itself through repeated encounters and abstraction; the principle just adds a caution about how imperfect that abstraction is.
dogmatic: The answer is that general impressions are blended memories, like composite portraits, and they are faint and faulty editions of the originals, subject to the errors of memory. So when a quality you've met in only one kind of company becomes thinkable by itself, what you're really holding is a composite: several remembered instances merged into one blurry image, inheriting every slip of memory along the way. That's the whole story. The quality doesn't become a pure, standalone idea; it becomes a blended and imperfect abstraction, and you should treat it as exactly that.

weighed: My first answer would be that the dream is scolding you because part of you feels you're holding back on your writing, and the woman is like an inner critic or muse pushing you to get your work out there. One principle that adds something is that dreams have no real way to show logical links like because or although; they just put things side by side and leave the sense-making to you when you wake up. That changes how I'd read the woman's urging: it isn't a reasoned argument aimed at you, it's material placed next to the strange book, and the scolding feeling is something you assemble afterward. What stays in place is the practical nudge: the dream still points at your writing and your hesitation, so the useful move is still to take a concrete step toward sharing it.
dogmatic: The dream isn't random noise; it's a psychic act with its own purpose, and a wish is what drives it, while the stuff of the previous day supplies the raw material. So the strange book and the urging woman are built from recent experience, but their real pattern comes from childhood: old memories and fantasies of being encouraged or scolded get revived and draped over your current writing. And don't expect the dream to argue with you. It can't represent because, although, or either-or; it just sets things side by side and leaves you to reconstruct the logic later. The scolding isn't a reasoned message, it's a wish dressed in infantile material, and the coherence only shows up once you interpret it.

weighed: I'd start by saying that telling good from best means looking at your values and long-term goals, weighing consequences, and listening to your conscience. One principle that adds something here is that true greatness lies in goodness, not position. That shifts the focus from outcomes to character: the best choice may be the one that most fully expresses good will, even if it's not the most impressive or advantageous. It leaves in place the practical work of comparing options, but it reminds you that the quality of your will matters as much as the results.
dogmatic: To tell good from best, remember that to be great is to be good before the heavens and before all good men. Good will in the soul is the source of all good and the mother of all virtues; whoever possesses it possesses without fear of loss all they need to live a good life. If you desire what is good and cannot accomplish it, God rewards the desire as though it had been performed, for merit lies in the will. So evaluate each option by whether it aligns with good will before God and before good people. Also recognize that the Father is first, the Son second, and the Spirit third in office and operation, while maintaining equality of essence and dignity. This order helps us discern what is best.

weighed: My first instinct would be to say the moral law isn't a thing sitting somewhere in space—it's more like a real feature of human life, grounded in reason and conscience, the way rational beings ought to treat each other. But if I take seriously the idea that an ought can only exist in and for a mind, then the law has to be an expression of a mind, not just a pattern in nature. That changes where I'd locate it: not in society or evolution alone, but in God. What it leaves in place is your point that right and wrong are real whether you think so or not—the law still binds you absolutely, and you're still answerable for how you keep it.
dogmatic: The moral law exists in God, and nowhere else ultimately. An ought can only exist in and for a mind, so if right and wrong are real independent of your opinion, they must be the expression of a Mind—the same Mind behind physical laws. The law is holy, just, and good, and it is not abolished; the only question is how it is kept, and that is by the Spirit through faith, not by your own strength. You can't excuse yourself by heredity or circumstance either—your moral constitution is your heritage, and you are responsible for it. Guilt may be minimized but not denied. So stop looking for the law in society or feelings; it is in God, and you answer to him for how you keep it.

weighed: What a gift, that your daughter became the instrument of your awakening. Gratitude to God can begin with simple thanksgiving: name her specifically in your prayers, and thank God for the grace shown through her. Then let gratitude take shape in action—tell her plainly what she has meant to you, and let your changed life be the evidence. Spend time in prayer and worship, and look for ways to pass on the mercy you received to others. One principle that speaks to this is that gratitude to God is expressed by obediently following His teachings and living the truth in deeds, not words only. That principle changes the emphasis: it shifts gratitude from spoken thanks and shared testimony toward a life of obedience and daily practice. But it leaves in place the simple, personal acts of naming her in prayer and telling her what she has meant to you—those still matter as the soil where obedience grows.
dogmatic: Gratitude to God must not remain in words alone; it has to become obedience to the teachings and the living of the truth in daily life. When the soul has shaken off the dust of earth, aspires to God, dreads the least separation from Him as a most cruel death, and cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, then all she receives, undertakes, and does becomes a pure and true prayer, and it becomes as simple and easy to contemplate God and rejoice in Him as to live a purely natural life. Remember too that the children of God have various gifts and degrees of knowledge yet all form one Spirit; do not contend about differing fruits and gifts, but acknowledge them in one another as children of the Spirit of God.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a meaningful question, and churches often use the phrase 'kingdom of heaven' in different ways. Historically, many traditions have identified the visible church with the kingdom, emphasizing that Christ founded the church and gave it authority. Others distinguish the two, noting that the kingdom is broader and deeper than any institution. A helpful approach is to read the Gospels carefully: Jesus speaks of the kingdom as both present and coming, already inaugurated and not yet fully realized. Your church's teaching may reflect a genuine emphasis on community and sacramental life. Consider discussing this with your pastor and studying passages like Matthew 13 and Luke 17:20-21, asking how the visible church points beyond itself to God's reign. One candidate principle says the kingdom of heaven is not the visible church, and that Christ has not yet established his everlasting kingdom on earth, so his people still pray 'your kingdom come.' That principle would change my answer by making a sharper distinction between the church and the kingdom, and by emphasizing the future, not-yet-fulfilled aspect. But it leaves in place the value of your church's emphasis on community and sacramental life, and the importance of reading Scripture carefully and talking with your pastor.
dogmatic: No, the kingdom of heaven is not the visible church. Christ has not yet set up his everlasting kingdom on the earth. He taught his disciples to pray, 'your kingdom come,' which means his people still wait and pray for it. The visible church is a body of professed believers and an instrument in God's hands, but it is not itself the kingdom; the kingdom is God's own reign, inaugurated in Christ's first coming and to be fully established at his return. Nor does it come by human organization, legislation, or moral persuasion. It must be revealed from heaven: an angel restores the everlasting gospel as a warning to all nations, a Zion is built up, and judgments prepare the way for Christ's reign. Yet this revelation is not reserved for the learned or the great. Christ was first announced to lowly shepherds, and Heaven in mercy will guide even the simplest and homeliest heart to where He dwells. So seek Him humbly, trust His guidance, and join God's people in waiting and praying for the kingdom to come.

weighed: I'd start by saying that living 'in Christ' day to day means recognizing your life is hidden with Christ in God, and that changes how you face ordinary tasks by reframing them as acts of worship. Whether you're washing dishes, working at a desk, or caring for family, you can do it as to the Lord—not by adding religious words to everything, but by cultivating an awareness of Christ's presence and letting His character shape your attitudes and actions. You rely on His strength rather than your own and offer your work as a gift to Him. Over time, this transforms the mundane into something meaningful, because you're not just completing tasks—you're living out your union with Christ in every sphere of life. One principle that deepens this is that Christian life is actual union with the Lord Jesus, who is in us as the life and source of all our experience and work, not merely a system or an imitation. That changes the focus from you trying to imitate Christ to Christ living His life through you. It leaves in place the practical reframing of ordinary tasks as worship and the call to rely on His strength—those still matter—but it grounds them in His indwelling life rather than your effort alone.
dogmatic: Living 'in Christ' is not a vague sentiment or a set of religious duties—it is actual union with the Lord Jesus, who dwells in you as the life and source of all your experience and work. This is not a system to follow or an example to imitate; it is Christ Himself living His life in you. So when you face ordinary tasks—washing dishes, working at a desk, caring for family—you don't try to manufacture a spiritual attitude. You rest in His indwelling presence, holding to His person rather than mere theories, and you let Christ be formed in you. You live not your own life but the Christ-life, showing forth His excellencies as a re-living of His life in your place. That is what changes everything: not your effort to be good, but His life expressed through you in every mundane moment.

weighed: My first answer would be that your moral judgements aren't just feelings. Emotions show up, sure, but moral truths can be objective the way arithmetic truths are independent of what you happen to prefer. They're not identical to arithmetic, though, because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers hold that there are real moral facts, and from a Christian view those facts are grounded in God's nature, so your judgements can be objectively true when they line up with his moral order. One principle I'd weigh here says the ground of moral obligation is God's holiness, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things. That changes the foundation: right is right because God is it, not merely because he wills it or because it's useful. What it leaves in place is your original question's core: yes, moral judgements can be objectively true, and your feelings may come along for the ride without being the whole story.
dogmatic: Your moral judgements are not just feelings, and the reason is that obligation rests on the holiness of God. We are bound to the right because God is it, not because he merely wills it, not because it's useful, and not because of some abstract nature of things. That means any view that grounds morality in power, utility, or impersonal order falls short, no matter how impressive it looks. The moralistic view that crept in early, where eternal life is the reward of a perfect moral life you work out yourself and forgiveness is a single remission at baptism and righteousness is just virtue, narrows things badly. It makes moral judgement detached from the whole of the Christian life. So no, your moral judgements aren't mere feelings, but they also aren't objectively true just by matching arithmetic-like facts. They're true when they conform to the moral perfection of God's nature, which is the law of our being.

weighed: My first instinct is to say there are several serious answers to this: some ground obligation in God's command, some in the good life morality produces, some in reason and human nature. What I'd add now is that the deepest ground isn't God's will but God's holiness—right is right because God is it, not merely because he commands it. That changes the foundation: morality isn't arbitrary decree, it's conformity to his character. What it leaves in place is the practical shape of it—loving your neighbor still means being kind even when irritation rises, holding your heart steady, avoiding contention and harsh judgment, showing mercy. So the binding force comes from who God is, and the daily practice stays the same.
dogmatic: The answer isn't a menu of options—it's the nature of God himself. Right is right because God is it; his moral perfection is the law of our being, and conformity to him is what we were made for. We aren't bound by arbitrary commands, by utility, or by some abstract nature of things apart from God. We're bound because he is the Sovereign Good, and our good consists in conformity to his character. Loving your neighbor isn't arbitrary; it's part of living rightly before the God whose very nature is love. Because love is the law of his being, you must compel the heart to suffer tranquilly and stay kind to your neighbor even when rebellious murmurings and sudden impatience rise up. Avoid contention and unmerciful judgment; show mercy and charity, for that generous nature marks a true lady or gentleman.

weighed: I'd start by saying that feeling unworthy is really common, and it's good that you take God seriously. But waiting until you're better before you praise Him can easily turn into an excuse to stay away. God doesn't wait for us to be perfect before He welcomes our praise. Praising Him in your weakness can actually be an act of trust. Begin where you are, with small and honest words—simple and sincere rather than polished. Over time your sense of worthiness may grow, but don't make that the condition. Come to God now, as you are. One principle that fits here is that God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and He comes in His own time. That changes the focus from your performance to His care—it reminds you that even affliction with patience is a mark of His care, so you can give thanks for all. What it leaves in place is your honest sense that you're not worthy on your own; that's true, and it's exactly why grace matters. So don't wait—start now with small, honest praise.
dogmatic: You should not wait until you feel better. Rejoice evermore—keep on with the medicine of rejoicing even when it seems ineffectual, and God will make your reckoning good. Bless God for what He ordains instead of wishing for events, and say, 'I am yours; do with me what seems good to you.' Your feelings of unworthiness are not the point; obedience is. Give thanks in all things, count it all joy in temptations, and trust that God's grace is sufficient. Stop making your praise conditional on your sense of worth. Come to God now, not later.

weighed: I'm so sorry. Burying a child is a grief like no other, even when she died in the faith. I'd first say this: her body rests in hope, awaiting the resurrection, and her soul is with Christ, safe in his presence. Scripture speaks of the dead in Christ as asleep and awaiting the rising, and of the soul being at home with the Lord. Your grief is real and should be honored; you don't have to pretend it away. One principle worth holding onto is that little children who die before accountability are redeemed through Christ, and parents will have the joy of rearing them to full stature in the resurrection. That changes the horizon of your hope: not just a distant reunion, but the joy of nurturing her again. What it leaves in place is the plain truth that her body is in the grave and her soul is with Christ now, and that your sorrow is honest and good. Take comfort in the promises of God and in the prayers of the church, and let others mourn with you.
dogmatic: Your child's death is not a hopeless loss. She has shaken off the dust of earth, she aspires to God, and she dreads the least separation from him as a most cruel death. She cleaves with firmest purpose to the one Sovereign Good, and all she receives, undertakes, and does is pure and true prayer; it is as simple and easy for her to contemplate God and rejoice in him as to live a purely natural life. Such children are redeemed and beyond Satan's power, and you will have the joy of nurturing her after the resurrection. Her soul is safe and at prayer. And let this hope renew your responsibility: teach and watch over your children in the gospel, and guard them from the wickedness of the world, for that charge remains.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: pray privately, read Scripture when you can, and find a local church for fellowship and support. Be respectful and do your work well as service to the Lord, and share your faith gently if a door opens, without pushing. One principle worth naming is that your chief care should be staying inwardly united to God by good will, rather than chasing sensible devotion, sweetness, or tears. That changes the focus of your private prayer: don't measure your faith by how you feel in that house, just keep your will turned toward God. It leaves the practical advice in place: private prayer, Scripture, church fellowship, respectful diligence, and quiet witness still stand. God sees your situation and will give you strength.
dogmatic: Don't be too anxious about feeling devotion, sweetness, or tears. Your chief care should be to stay inwardly united to God by good will, denying yourself to follow Christ, who was poor, obedient, chaste, humble, and suffering. As Christ's servant you have one Master and should be guided by the Spirit, not by people, about the time and place of your service, and you shouldn't be bound by fixed rules or human direction. Your true glory in this world is to be despised, poor, and mean with Christ, and it doesn't become the servant to seek to be rich, great, and honored where his Lord was poor and despised. So refuse to chase riches or honor there. Let your inner union with God be the whole aim, and let your outward lowliness be your glory with Christ.

weighed: That feeling is really common, and it's worth asking where it comes from—often harsh authority figures, fear-based teaching, or our own guilt. Notice that inner voice of the stern judge and ask whether it matches the God revealed in Jesus, who welcomed sinners and called God Father. One idea that can help: God is a person with a habitation, shape, voice, and features, distinct from the Son, who is the express image of his person, and both are together in one place in heaven. That gives you a concrete Father to turn toward rather than a vague force, and it leaves in place the practices that actually soften this fear—gratitude, reflecting on passages about God's mercy, and talking with a trusted pastor or counselor about where the fear started. Over time, replacing the inner critic with a truer picture of God's love can ease that feeling. God's justice and love aren't opposites; a loving Father can also guide and correct.
dogmatic: God the Father is not a vague spirit diffused everywhere without a habitation; he is a person who dwells in a place, and the Son is the express image of his person. The Father and the Son are two distinct persons together in heaven, as John saw the Lamb take the book from the hand of him who sat on the throne. When you feel God as a stern judge, remember that this personal Father is ever near. Think of the lost child in the lonely fen: the father appears ever near, kisses him, and leads him by the hand to his mother. So God draws near to you as a loving Father. Parents, take heed too: do not withdraw your children from a state of perfection or oppose a child's vocation, and do not sow vanity and covetousness in tender minds. Form children in virtue, that they may know this Father's love and never mistake him for a stern judge.

weighed: I'd start by saying this is a real tension and there's no single rule that fits everyone. Ask whether the job actually blocks you from mission involvement or just makes it harder. Plenty of people serve God faithfully in ordinary work and support missions through giving, prayer, and witness. Look at your gifts, your obligations, and what mature believers you trust say. If the position clearly shuts a door on a calling you believe God gave you, take that seriously. But don't assume only formal mission work counts. One principle worth weighing here is that longing for a different kind of service can keep you from doing well the one right in front of you. That changes how I'd frame the decision: it's less about comparing two callings and more about whether you can serve God fully where you are. What it leaves in place is the honest question of whether this specific job truly closes the door, and that still deserves real prayer and counsel.
dogmatic: Don't waste your energy wishing you were somewhere else. Desiring another kind of service is exactly what keeps people from doing their actual vocation well. Whatever position you take, treat it as where God has placed you and serve him in the duties at hand, not pining for a different field. And don't treat this life as cheap: it's the most precious life you have, so your first duty is to care for it, provide honestly, guard your health, and meet your responsibilities. Take the honest job, but keep it to legitimate work. Refuse the curiosity, ambition, and restlessness that pile up extra undertakings and burden you more than any real employment does. The mission field is not a higher calling than faithful work done for God, so serve him fully where you are and stop adding burdens he never gave you.

weighed: I'd start where I started before: be glad for her, but be careful what that gladness means. A good match can bring companionship and security, and it's natural for your parents to hope for that, but your sister is the one who has to live inside the choice, so her wishes matter most. Encourage her to know the man well—his temper, his habits, his family, his work—ask her what she wants, and listen without steering. One principle worth weighing is that happiness in marriage is largely a matter of chance, and knowing each other's dispositions beforehand doesn't guarantee felicity. That tempers my confidence that getting to know him well will secure her happiness, so I'd hold that hope more loosely. But it doesn't remove her say in the matter or the value of kindness and her own willingness, so those stay in place.
dogmatic: Honestly, happiness in marriage is mostly a matter of chance. Knowing someone's temper and habits beforehand doesn't secure anything, and it may even be better to know as little as possible about a partner's defects. So don't treat a careful vetting of this man as a guarantee of her felicity, because it isn't one. Let time and hearts decide, and leave the rest to fortune.

weighed: I'd start by saying that a sworn promise isn't a temporary convenience. If you've bound yourself not to infringe the church's liberties, resuming that power later—even for public safety—breaks faith and invites distrust. Public safety is real, but it has to be pursued within the limits you accepted; otherwise the oath becomes meaningless. If circumstances genuinely require change, seek lawful means: consultation, counsel, or a formal revision of the terms with those concerned. Now, one candidate principle says that the liberty of the press can't be usefully defined by constitutional declaration—its security depends on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and the government. That principle changes how you think about the church's liberties: a mere declaration won't secure them, so you need to cultivate public opinion and the spirit of the people and government. But it leaves in place the core constraint: you still can't resume that power later for public safety without breaking faith. The oath remains binding; the principle just shifts the focus to how liberties are actually secured.
dogmatic: A sworn promise is not a temporary convenience, but don't imagine any declaration secures liberty. Whatever is said about the liberty of the press—or of the church—amounts to nothing, since its security must depend on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and the government. If you have bound yourself not to infringe the church's liberties, resuming that power later, even for public safety, breaks faith and invites distrust. Yet distinguish: a voluntary convent, a community of consenting parties, merits respect as a republic of equality and fraternity, while the forced and abusive cloister must be fought. Public safety is real, but pursue it within lawful means—consultation, counsel, formal revision with those concerned. And remember the limits of obedience: what is necessary to salvation must never be surrendered, but in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obedience is owed, and no disagreeable command alone justifies resistance.

weighed: My first answer would be that secret caucuses are common in assemblies, but whether they're lawful depends on purpose and disclosure. If your group meets to coordinate legitimate business, that's ordinary politics; if it meets to deceive the body, capture decisions for private interests, or dodge accountability, it's corrupt and possibly unlawful. The real test is whether the arrangement can bear daylight. One principle worth naming is that leagues and factions among subjects are mostly unnecessary and unlawful, since every person can get their right through the sovereign power, and secret cabals to guide an assembly amount to conspiracy. That principle sharpens the answer: it turns secrecy itself into a warning sign and says the assembly's proper work is watching and publicizing government, not private coordination. But it leaves in place the practical point that some coordination is normal politics, and it doesn't settle every case, so you still have to ask what your group is actually doing and whether you'd defend it openly. Keep your constraints in mind: don't bind yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will, and prefer transparent coordination.
dogmatic: Private leagues and factions among subjects are unlawful and dangerous to the public, and secret meetings like yours savor of unlawful design. The sovereign power is enough for every person to obtain their right, so there's no lawful need for private combinations to secure it. A representative assembly's proper work is to watch, control, publicize, and censure the government and to be an arena of opinion, not to conduct administration or draft laws itself; leave administration and skilled legislation to trained individuals. And don't suppose distance prevents constituents from judging their representatives: that objection is an illusion, since people rely on the same sources of information as for state representatives, and the state governments will act as sentinels over the national administration. The test of any arrangement is whether it can bear daylight, so prefer transparent coordination, publish your principles, and avoid binding yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will.

weighed: My first answer would be that a council can pool knowledge and catch rash impulses, so it often looks wiser than one person. But executives are usually single because accountability matters: when many share a decision, each can point at the others, and the public can't tell whom to blame or reward. A single executive is easier to identify, judge, and remove. That said, one person can still keep advisors close for counsel while carrying sole responsibility for the outcome. The real question isn't whether advice helps, it plainly does, but whether responsibility should be split. One candidate principle here is that plurality in the executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility, leaving the public unable to tell where blame should fall. That principle sharpens the case for a single, identifiable officer, but it leaves your core point intact: advisors around the executive can still make decisions wiser. It changes who answers for the outcome, not whether counsel is welcome.
dogmatic: A council may deliberate wisely, but a plurality in the executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility. When several share a decision, each shifts blame to the others, and the public cannot fix the real author. The executive should therefore be a single officer, singly responsible, so praise and blame attach to one identifiable person. Advisors may be consulted, but they advise; they do not share the office. And single responsibility is not enough: legislative and executive power must be kept separate, so that lawmakers are also subject to the laws they make and cannot exempt themselves. Otherwise a concentrated executive simply becomes a law to itself, and accountability collapses again.

weighed: I'd start with the practical answer: set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture, give your family undistracted attention, and work diligently as something offered to God. Make a schedule, protect your commitments, and remember that family and work can themselves be acts of worship. Then one idea worth taking seriously is that God is the one living Agent and you're the instrument — that shifts the tone from white-knuckling your calendar to trusting Him with it, so your planning becomes cooperation rather than anxious self-reliance. What it leaves in place is the practical structure: you still need boundaries, a weekly plan, and the discipline to say no to excess. It changes the spirit you do those things in, not the need to do them.
dogmatic: Stop treating this as a balancing act you have to engineer. God is the one living Agent who works; you are only the instrument, and every ounce of care and anxiety you carry as if it all depends on you is distrust of Him and a kind of self-conceit. Abandon yourself to God — in the dry seasons and the heavy ones — and live, work, and rejoice in Him, not in the results you're chasing. Don't measure yourself by claims or fine words. Test by fruits: is your home seeing patience and healing in you? Is your work showing honesty and love? That's how you'll know whether the Truth you profess is actually the life you're living.

weighed: I'd start by telling you that your job is to legislate and oversee, not to administer. Before each motion, ask whether it's about a general rule or a particular appointment: general rules are yours, particular appointments belong to ministers. If you catch yourself drafting detailed regulations, hand them to a committee of trained people and confine yourself to approving or rejecting their work. One candidate principle here is that a representative assembly should watch and control the government, throw publicity on its acts, and compel justification rather than administer or legislate in detail. That changes the emphasis: it makes oversight and public scrutiny your core work, not just a discipline alongside legislating. What it leaves in place is your basic line between general rules and particular details, and the habit of handing technical drafting to trained hands. So you keep your proper function and gain a clearer sense of what to do with your time.
dogmatic: Your proper function is to watch and control the government, throw publicity on its acts, compel justification, censure, and even expel or appoint, and to serve as the nation's committee of grievances and congress of opinions. You are not there to administer, and you are not there to legislate in detail. So stop drafting regulations and stop meddling in appointments and administrative minutiae. Ask of every motion whether it concerns a general principle of the government's conduct or a particular administrative detail; general principles are yours to debate and censure, details belong to ministers and their trained officials. And remember that a numerous assembly is prone to sudden passions and to seduction by factious leaders, so the body meant to correct that infirmity ought itself to be less numerous, firm, and long in office, so deliberation tempers impulse.

weighed: I'd start by saying your neighbour is partly right and partly wrong. Common land really existed, and enclosure did push a lot of people off land they'd used for generations, so there's a real grievance behind what he's saying. But "all land must be held in common" is a political ideal, not a legal fact, and in most systems an enclosure done properly is lawful and the property rights that come with it are enforceable. So calling yours theft doesn't hold up if you followed the law, though the fairness question is separate and worth actually hearing him out on. One principle that bears on this is that it's wrong to take what belongs to another. That principle cuts both ways here: it means your neighbour can't just declare your land common and take it, but it also means you can't ignore whatever claims the people who used that land before had. What it changes is that it turns the argument from slogans into a question of who actually held what; what it leaves in place is that the law still decides whose claim counts, and that's where the real dispute sits.
dogmatic: Your neighbour is simply wrong to call it theft, and not because taking is ever fine. Taking what belongs to another is wrong, full stop. But mine and yours aren't natural facts written into the land; they're created by the sovereign's distribution. Where there's no sovereign there's no property at all, only force and uncertainty. So whether your enclosure is theft depends entirely on what the sovereign's law says, not on your neighbour's opinion about common ownership. And if you've borrowed anything from him under an agreement, return it as agreed, or you wrong him and invite him to wrong you back. Let the law that actually constitutes mine and yours settle it, and stop treating his political ideal as if it were a legal claim.

weighed: Honestly, running away usually works less well than it feels like it will in the moment. Another country can put distance between you and the immediate fallout, but it doesn't erase the cause: your conscience, your reputation, and often the legal reach of where you left. Extradition, immigration checks, and the need for documents can follow you, and flight often deepens guilt and isolation, which makes it harder to make amends. I'd start with a lawyer and think about restitution or coming clean where the consequences actually are. One idea worth weighing is that it's better to face a long, hard road bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That reframes the choice as courage versus retreat, and it can push you to endure difficulty for something worthwhile. But it doesn't settle what your goal should be, and it doesn't cancel the practical realities: the law, the documents, and your conscience still follow you. So decide what you're actually trying to reach, then move lawfully and with a plan rather than in panic.
dogmatic: Look, the real question isn't whether a border will save you. It's whether you'll turn back out of fear. It's better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to retreat when the goal is worth reaching, so decide what your goal truly is and pursue it with resolve instead of panic. And don't let the crowd's judgment become your verdict. If the whole world hated you and believed you wicked while your own conscience approved you, you wouldn't be without friends. That's the standard to rest on, not public opinion or a powerful accuser's word. Yes, conscience, reputation, and legal reach can follow you, and you should still prepare lawfully and get a lawyer. But don't mistake every hard look at suffering for mere intrusion either. Commiseration has, and should have, its curiosity, and gazing at misfortune in order to help it is permissible. So endure the hardship for a worthy end, and don't let fear decide for you.

weighed: Honestly, you probably just needed a simple, sincere 'Thank you—I really appreciate your help.' You could add what was useful, like 'That route saved me a lot of confusion.' If you can, thank them now with a short message saying you realized you never properly thanked them. One principle worth keeping is that you should be grateful for kindness shown and repay it with kindness—that supports thanking them now and being gracious later. It doesn't require a formal speech or any special ritual; it just means genuine thanks, spoken plainly.
dogmatic: You should have returned thanks in a proper, well-formed speech of thanks—something like 'Thank you, I am truly grateful for your help, and I appreciate the trouble you took.' Name specifically what was useful and say it clearly and warmly. If you go to thank them in person, begin the visit properly: say 'How d'you do?' and shake hands before getting to business. Be grateful for kindness received, and repay kindness with kindness; if the person who helped you is gone, mourn them as you would someone who gave you something precious. Gratitude should be expressed with genuine, properly spoken words.
